I am a sucker for stylized, artistic, games.  Its no surprise then that Aaru's Awakening caught my attention.  The cel-shaded environments combined with the beautifully painted backgrounds make this a truly gorgeous game.  However, it takes more then really good art to make a really good game.  Thats not to say this is a bad game but it certainly carries with it some baggage that weighs down the overall experience.  This test of reflexes and patience may not be for everyone.
The story of Aaru's Awaking is a tale of four gods.  The gods decided long ago to split the day into four equal parts Dawn, Day, Dust, and Night.  You play as Aaru.  A buff looking creature that lies to serve Dawn.  You're warned by you're master of an evil presence invading Night and must traveling through all four kingdoms to face this threat.  As Aaru travels through the realms the other gods sow seeds of doubt into his mind and he begins to question if he is on the right path.  This makes for a pretty interesting story which is narrated though story book cut-scenes between each realm.
After seeing someone play it on Youtube, Aaru's Awaking quickly caught my attention.  I proceeded to download a demo and was instantly impressed.  Not only was the game fun to look at but the mechanics were very clever.  Aaru was fairly maneuverable but the key mechanic of the game is teleportation.  This is accomplished by pressing the left mouse button to project out a ball of light then press the right mouse button to appear at the balls current location.  This makes for some unique platforming especially when combined with Aaru's dash ability.
For a simple concept the developers certainly push it to its absolute limits.  The later levels become extremely technical requiring immense speed and precision.  Although the first couple stages help get the player into a rhythm it still seems like the difficulty ramps up a bit too quickly.  I don't mind a challenge but I definitely didn't realize what I was getting into.  Towards the end of the Night chapter, especially the boss stage, it became so hard I just wanted to pull my hair out.  This was the point where I stopped having fun and I decided to stop playing soon after.  (About 90% through the game)
I'm glad I tried this game.  It had a really unique mechanic at its core and some pretty clever level design.  My favorite part is still the wonderful art and original soundtrack.  That being said, I was so focused on trying to stay alive I didn't get to enjoy the music that much.  (Not to mention in the end I got so sick of hearing Aaru die I took off my headset.)  Whether or not you'll like this game really comes to down to how much you like a challenge.  I don't quiet have the reflexes to really enjoy this game to the end but I'm sure there are gamers out there who do.

Aaru's Awakening is a hand-drawn, fast-paced 2D action platformer.
The player is put in charge of Aaru, a mythical creature with two unique abilities that are used throughout the game. The abilities are to teleport and charge which are used to traverse through the dangerous levels of Lumenox. They are at the heart of every level to make for a challenging and fluid experience and require split-second decisions to complete fast-paced puzzles.
The game is not too difficult but can vary greatly from level to level and especially if you want to hunt down all the achievements from obtaining gold medals.
The enchanting hand drawings as well as the stunning soundtrack are hugely appealing and really add another dimension to this platformer to make it a satisfying experience, but for the price it's a little too much and I would recommend waiting for it to appear in a bundle or for it to go on sale...

Disclaimer: I never played previous HOI games so I have no idea how different are the games when compared. Also I bought the Field Marshall Edition so my opinion on DLC pricing is not relevant to others.
Summary:
Hearts of Iron 4 is a strategy game that is set in WW2 that lets you take control on entire nations. This game is historic but there are plenty of choices for your in-game history to differ from our real-life history of WW2. This game is complex but its one of the most accessable Paradox game to newcomers (With stellaris being the most accessable due to its excellent tutorial)
This game is very fun, managing your nation from its industry and resources, to its armies and everything needed to keep those army functioning. Now one of the main feature of HOI4 is its National Focus which effect the nations you're playing or other nations when 'Focuses' are completed. these focuses can lead you to the more historically accurate patch like real life WW2 did or completly different and can change the entire outcome of the war (Or even if the World War 2 even starts)
The appeal I have for this game is a 'What If' scenario. What if America stayed Isolationist, what if German Reich didnt invade Russia, What if Britain colonies started to break away for independance? Theres a lot of scenarios that you can create in-game and its fun to see how it turns out.
Now the game is no where perfect and wont be for atleast a while, but the devs are constantly improving this game and overall, my experience with the game from launch till now is getting more and more better. I recomend this game if you dont mind a slightly high learning curve and investing a couple of hours to get the basics of the game.
How does it run:
Now for the most part, Hearts of Iron 4 isnt that graphically demanding but since its a simulation of every country during WW2, when war breaks out or late-game expect your game to start slowing down.

Skyborn is a turn-based RPG in the vein of old-school RPGs like Final Fantasy. You control a band of characters that are trying to save the world from the tyrannical yadda yadda yadda, you know the drill. It was all made with RPG Maker, but don't let that turn you off -- I'd say it's worth a look.
I found this game rather charming. While the plot, music, and graphics aren't the newest and shiniest things ever, everything is good quality and holds together well enough for me to enjoy playing through it -- I even want to run through it again later. There are moments between characters to establish them more beyond "insert hero person here", and the world combines steampunk with a more standard fantasy setting in a way that's enjoyable, with more going on than is apparent at first. While there might not be a whole lot more to do than just the main story, there are some sidequests for players who poke around looking for extra treasure, and there's a crafting/augment system for people who want to micromanage their equipment a bit more.
The battle system is pretty fun to work with -- each character has a threat level that rises as they do damage, and whoever has the highest threat will be soaking up most of the attacks. The key is to make sure the tankiest character in your group keeps their threat level the highest (easier said than done, at times!), and I feel it works fairly well. Most fights are fairly simple, though there are some trickier fights later in the game -- the final boss and bonus boss in particular are pretty darn hard to deal with.
All in all, I'd say give this game a try if a charming little steampunk/fantasy turn-based RPG with fun characters and a neat battle system sounds interesting to you.

Outstanding game.
Roughly 10-20 hours worth of content depending on how you play the game. The game encourages stealth, but if you want to run and gun you can also do so (but I wouldn't necessarily recommend it).
It's definitely not unlike Assassins Creed, but with more story and plot choices to make arguably.
The lovely thing about this game, not unlike other stealth games, is that you are given many, many different ways to solve the same problem, rewarding the creative player instead of the CoD MLG headshot player.
The game was fairly well optimized back in the day and it obviously holds more than a few years later.
The parkour/platforming was my favorite aspect of the game, though it must be said that the levels are open, but entirely linear; the game is divided into missions with  scores at the end that influence plot development (like an arcade game with a story).
If there is anything negative that must be said, it's that on the highest difficulty, the stealth becomes difficult, while the melee/ranged remains trivial: you will still be able to plough through enemies with ease, making it tempting to still choose the easy solution of mass slaughter instead of surgical stealth, but the game will later punish you severely for doing so.
Another negative would be the lack of puzzles (other than arguably the few parkour/jumping puzzles there were).
The positives outweigh the negatives though in my opinion and it would hard to not recommend the game, even so many years later and for the years to come.

For the purposes of this review, I'll be ignoring the things about this that make it a bad "game" and will instead focus on why it is a bad simulator.
I'll preface by saying that I'm currently a cadet at a maritime academy, and from our own simulators and my experience with ship handling, this "simulator" is anything but. There is almost zero representation of hydrodynamic effects such as bank suction, squat, bow cushion, and everything else that makes steering a ship a lot more complicated than just "make it go straight." If these are in the game, I could not, for the life of me, reproduce them. I even went as far as to bring a VLCC within 20 feet of a bank going 16 kts, and still, absolutely no bank suction or squat to be found.
In this "simulator," you can steam your ship into Rotterdam harbor at 8 kts or 18 and it makes no difference. Why does it make no difference? Because it still just as simple as "put the wheel in the middle if you want to go straight."
This lack of fundamental hydrodynamic effects not only takes the immersion out of it, but it also makes Ship Simulator Extremes absolutely worthless for those who are trying to actually use it as a simulator to refine our skills.
I wish I could say that it would be a fun game otherwise, but its lack of a decent soundtrack, graphics, or fun missions makes it pretty abyssmal at that too. I would be more lenient if it didn't have "simulator" in its title, but as it stands, it does, and it is a terrible simulator of what actual ship handling is like.

I'll give the short summary first.
In case anyone isn't familiar, this isn't a title made by the usual HDN folks, but rather a project farmed out to Tamsoft. So, if you're looking for a quick summary of what the game is, expect it to play like a less polished Senran Kagura game that's gone through a HDN reskin, yet doesn't have any of HDN's writing and humor chops.
Now, if you are a HDN fan and are looking for a button mash-y hack-n-slash game that you can pick up once in a while for half an hour to an hour and put right back down, presuming you can get this game on a sale and can put up with the awful camera controls, this will be a great fit.
--
Now, for a more thorough examination.
Pros:
-The combat is simple and straightforward. Mashing light attack and occasionally popping off a special move will get you through basically the whole game, which is great, if all you want to do is unwind and turn off your brain.
-On most missions, you are free to play as your favorite combination of CPU and/or CPU Candidate. Nepgear and Rom? Vert and Uni? Neptune and Blanc? Go nuts!
-The title runs perfectly fine and supports full 1080p. It also seems to control just fine with either keyboard or controller (note: I've only used my 360 pad. I presume it has solid DirectInput support since the games hail from Sony consoles, but I'm not 100% sure).
-All quests list their level requirements, so you'll know if you're about to get some much needed stress relief out of colorful monsters or be pounded into mulch.
Cons:
-The writing and humor. I don't know if it's just bad writing or a localization issue from the game being caught in the petticoats of the western nanny-states, but... Based on my experience with the HDN series, this was a big beacon that this was handled by someone else. If you've ever played a Senran Kagura game, it's about on par with that. If you haven't, just pretend that there is no story.
-I know that character balance isn't very big in hack-n-slash titles, but... There are certain characters that you'll bring out for certain quests and otherwise never touch again.
-Maybe, I'm just spoiled by the PC ports made by IF and Compile Heart, but... Somehow, the options menu is inferior to what you usually see on Vita or 3DS titles. Yes, you get windowed, fullscreen, and borderless windowed support up to 1080p, but... There's nothing above that, there's no graphical options what's-so-ever, and there isn't even an option to toggle how quickly you want the text to be displayed on the screen and are locked to the slowest pace in existence.
-My biggest gripe of all, though, is the camera. First of all, it drunkenly swings around, with the options making it far too rigid or much too loose. Also, unlike the other HDN titles I've played, there's no way to zoom the camera out, so I hope that you like having your camera be close enough to your character's head that you may as well be able to reach in and pick bits of dandruff out of their hair.

More of a test in psychological mettle than a fun pastime, Hell Yeah! is just one of those games that I vastly dislike, but just need to finish; Not for a sense of accomplishment, but just so I can say that I have the will power and pain threshold to survive this train wreck. The groan-worthy self-referential humor, poor 360 controls (playing with the keyboard and mouse is inherently better, so why even make using a controller an option?), nearly infuriating bosses/mini-games, a camera that is panned much too close (if the enemies are off screen, they can't be shot), constant need for backtracking, and incredibly horrific platforming are just a few chapters in Hell Yeah!'s grimoire of wretched gaming.
The worst part about it all is that I enjoy the basic concept. It's completely lost on this unfocused ludicrousness. If the art direction were more palatable and refined a bit (right now I'd describe the level appearances as borderline 5 year old, sugar rush, fever nightmare. Especially the "Cute" and "Club" levels), some of the mini-games a bit more clear and not detrimental to your health bar upon failure, and just one writer at Sega or Arkedo had a likable sense of humor, this game would be a sleeper hit.
It would have been a gem if they could have blended Metroid-vania level design with fun Warioware style mini-games to break the flow.
But no. This game bombards your brain with idiotic dialogue, collectibles that are a chore to collect, and brings you so very close to liking it before it curb stomps your hopes and enthusiams for it to be at least a mediocre game. It's almost a crime to put out something that could have just used 2 or 3 more months of development and clean ups.
Maybe if Sega/Arkedo gave a rabbit's♥♥♥♥♥about it, they'd patch it occasionally. But will they? Hell No!

I normally do not write reviews but this game is awesome for a medieval game! The combat is very fluent and challenging, a lot different than other medival games. It does not simply use the swing and parry mechanic, there are around 9 different stances according to how you hold your sword with your mouse and you attack/block with each stance. The conquest mode with 150+ players is very epic, it feels great running into a hoard of enemies and slaughtering them all.
I really like how this game is being developed. Instead of working on other core things like Open World or their "Epic" mode first, they focused on the combat and introduced a few modes to battle in combat aka duel and conquest. Combat is very important to me so I feel that by doing that first it will make everything else fun as well. They do plan on putting in open world later on and that's going to be awesome with this great combat and 150+ player battles. Also there is minimum lag for me in the large-scale battles.
Anyways if you are looking for pure medival mayham then get this game. If you are waiting for open world then you will need to wait a little bit longer. Either way I think $25 is well worth to support this guys for doing an amazing job.
Overall, best early access game I have played to date.

- the devs have made quite a few changes to the combat system that are a very good improvement: more fluid change between blocks, shields don't become ghosts while attacking and shields require directional blocking to be effective, although they offer an extra layer of passive protection (shields function as physical objects that stop swings when they are hit). A lot of these changes have a very positive improvement on the gameplay. Shieldwalls for example aren't static anymore (shielders can actually swing without exposing themselves fully), but teams will form very tight formations in the form of frontlines where the two opposing teams change out blows.
- Unlike Reign of Kings, Life is Feudal... the devs focussed on combat first and will build an open world around that. This means we'll have the guarantee that the core part of the game is actually fun and engaging
CONS:
- the game is unfinished, so don't expect a full game without bugs. There is a LOT that's not in the game yet and the lack of these things might make the current state less enjoyable. Just remember that a lot will change and new things will be added.
- although you can speak the devs personally on discord, they give a bit too little information through the forums
- because the combat is so different (although directional blocking skills carry over pretty much directly), a lot of people misunderstand the mechanics or don't want to put in the time to learn the controls and mechanics. It's them you'll find on the forums complaining about how every other class except theirs is OP. READ MY GUIDE BEFORE YOU START PLAYING, it will help a lot.

Overall, this a very good game. Although it's got a few problems, these can easily be overlooked.
The Good
________
Story: The plot is engaging, with a lot of neat moments where you feel emotionally compelled to keep playing. If you're playing an RPG, you NEED a good story to compel play. At the beginning you're forced to betray/trick someone to save your family. Who isn't willing to do everything they can for their family?
BGM: The music is very atmospheric, usually fitting situation well and sound very much like music from games on the PS2 or XBOX. The music is in stereo as well, but this is less useful than stereo sound effects.
Graphics: The visuals are reminiscent of the 16-bit era of console gaming in terms of color and the sprite drawing methods common on the NES/SNES, Genisis, and PSX. More than anything else I'm reminded of the original Dragon Warrior (Dragon Quest) 1-3 and Breath of Fire 1 and 2 games in regards to gameplay, with a Town overmap, a menu overmap, dungeon overmap, and world overmap, along with the turn based combat system. Also, when going full screen on my monitor the game doesn't look bad, but doesn't have 1080p support running at 640x480, so probably won't work well with or look good on TVs.
The Bad
_______
Sound: The sound effects are very subpar by todays standards, but equal to if not better than those of the 16-bit and 32-bit console era. The sound effects do not seem to be in stereo.
Sound/Visual Timing: Often sound effects, i.e. attacks in combat, will occur just before the visual identifier does. This tends to throw the combat immersion right out the window for me, but it's not overly horrible, and certainly doesn't break the game.
The Ugly
_______
Controls: X-input controllers, that is to say anything resembling the Xbox 360 controller, have wonky button command registers, with Menu/Cancel being assigned to B and Interact/Accept being assinged to X, and Previous Page/Next Page being assigned to Back/Start respectively. Worse, still, there is no way to reassign them in game.
The controls for D-input controllers, resembling Playstation 2 or 3 controllers, is much better with Menu/Cancel being assigned to X and Interact/Accept being assigned to O, and Previous Page/Next Page assigned to L2/R2 respectively. The Logitech F series controllers 310, 510, and 710, are able to switch between these input types, so I recommend using D-input with them. I've tested PS3, Wireless Xbox 360 for Windows, and Logitech F510 controllers with this game.
Mouse and keyboard are simple enough with the avatar attempting to take the shortest route to where you click on the overmaps or moving in the cardinals with the arrow keys, and clicking on commands and enemies in combat or selecting them with left/right arrow keys and pressing enter.

No Heroes Here is a TRUE co-operative experience that's rarely seen. Like another great example, "Overcooked", this game has perfectly captured the essence of co-operative play, and player co-ordination to achieve victory. Unlike most co-op games, trying to "be the best guy" doesn't fly here. You'll work together, running around the castle interior, creating cannonballs, powder, honey traps, and shooting enemy troops with cannons. It's a LOT of fun, and I would say a must buy for anyone who enjoys local and online co-op.
Pros:
+ Designed around co-operative play
+ The "lone wolf" mentality is rightly the worst choice, as should be the case in a good co-op experience (see Overcooked as another great example of this)
+ Quick to learn
+ Encourages participation from gamers of a variety of skill levels
+ Encourages strong communication between players
+ The screen is tidy, and everything sized just right to lend to visual clarity
+ Up to 4 players can play at once
+ The game respond really well to your inputs. Great controller support
Cons:
- No voice chat for online co-op (hopefully it will be added in a future update)
- No possibility for 2 or 3 local players play online (to have a 4 player party)

NOTE: Knowing precisely what you're getting into with this game especially if you've just finished "To the Moon" can drastically impact your opinion of the game.
For what it was, I enjoyed "A Bird Story". It isn't a sequel to "To the Moon" yet it is somewhat related. Much like Freebird Games' previous title, the "A Bird Story" is a very artistc approach that differs in its offering in comparison to many within the industry. The interactive portion of the game is quite minimal, though this title was attempting to tell a small and emotionally evoking story without exposition. In many ways I feel as though it succeeded.
+ Fantastic soundtrack
+ Charming premise
+ Innovative storytelling
- Minimal interactivity
Fact of the matter is, if you've come here for an experience on par with "To the Moon", look elsewhere. However, if you'd like to take a short ride and experience a charming tale of a boy, his bird, and dreams then I think it's worth the price of admission.

Modular Combat is an interesting game that has/had the potential to be so much more. Have just completed it after about 8h. Most people don't seem to need as much time but I played with a bad controller making everything extra hard. The game is a ridiculously challenging platformer with unique mechanics  (you spend most of the time air-dashing and teleporting at break-neck speeds) and visuals that are adorable in a rarely seen way. Can't stress enough how original and gorgeous the art is. Reminds me a little of The Secret of Kells, visually. On the down side, the controls are waaay too stiff for a game that revolves almost exclusively around impossible jumps and complicated mid-air manoeuvres. Once you jump, you lose all control of your direction... which is seriously punishing. The story is utter nonsense as well, but hey, a platformer can do just fine without one. All in all, it's a refreshing and fun game for platformer fans. I bought it at a heavy discount and am rather pleased with the purchase, but would not, honestly, buy it at full price.

3.7 hours it shows on my record as I write this. That's how long it took me to go from the beginning of the game to the end on my first playthrough. And I must say I really enjoyed my time on this one. With one caveat:
The final boss is like hitting a brick wall. Of my 3.7 hours, over an hour of that was JUST on the final boss. I knew precisely what needed to be done, but it required such pinpoint accuracy, and makes you needlessly repeat very finicky parts whenever you die. I would have had a better experience had the boss been better at maintaining my momentum, and if I'd been able to defeat it quicker. That is not a bad thing. As it is, I left the game feeling really quite agitated, rather than delighted at the other 95% of the game, which was GORGEOUS.
The controls appear at first to be very intricate, but they play out very well with an XBos controller - it's very natural.
Music and sounds are wonderful, atmospheric and totally add to the game experience.
Graphics - as mentioned - are stunning. I particularly adored the hand-drawn smoke effects in the latter stages of the game.
Story - really works well, it's simple, and effective. It doesn't ry to crowbar in tons of exposition, though the narrator's voice is grating at times, as she slurs and mispronounces words, which felt a touch sloppy. Her intonation was perfect other than that, however.
I'd highly recommend this game to anyone who's a fan of platformers, or puzzle games generally. Even though it has its quirks, I still have an overwhelming feeling of satisfaction having played this game.

This is one of those cases where I wish steam had a "meh" option because for a game like this, it's sorely needed. Okay. I don't usually do this but I'm just going to break down everything separately.
First off: I will quite frequently bring up this game's contemporary Environmental Station Alpha multiple times, since a comparison to this game is how I found ESA originally, and then what brought me back to this game was a comparison of this game to ESA, and since the games came out in the same month both heavily aping Metroid, the comparisons are almost begging to happen.
Story: It's pretty good, actually. I wouldn't say it's a huge factor in the game, but the story and the collectible lore are pretty intriguing, leaving just enough ambiguous to keep you guessing. I wouldn't say the story is the main draw of the game, but I definitely can't hold it against the game.
Graphics: Hmm. This is tricky to rate. On one hand, the pixel art is gorgeous to look at. On the other hand... it's a bit of a sensory overload sometimes, since there are so many bright colors all the time. It doesn't help that the only really noticeable graphically difference in most areas is the color. The game doesn't have very well defined "enivironments" like ESA, and though this technically has better "art" than that game, I dunno, I feel ESA just has a better aesthetic than this game. I wouldn't say the graphics are bad by any means but it's amazing how bland I find them for how well they're done.
Music: It's alright at first, it's very game-y music, but by the end of the game I was utterly sick of it. I dunno, it's way too blaring and in-your-face most of the time. Metroid had more atmospheric music, ESA has more atmospheric music, it added to the mood instead of overpowering it. I wouldn't say it's bad music, you'll probably enjoy it your first time through the game, but not for much longer.
And now... here's where things are really gonna fall apart.
Gameplay: Uuugh. I should love this so much more than I do. But. Okay, here's the key problem: This game is stubbornly rooted in Super Metroid, in almost every aspect. A lot of its mechanics are quite similar, for one, just "modernized", and for what it's worth, a lot of the "modernized" mechanics are good. The grappling hook is an utter travesty though, worse than any in Metroid and an absolute trainwreck compared to the fantastic grappling of ESA. It's just... thank god this thing barely sees any use because it's utter trash.
But that aside... the game design itself apes Super Metroid far too heavily, especially when it comes to collectibles. I did not enjoy hunting for secrets in Super Metroid and never bothered to get 100%, but I wanted to here because achievements etc. I did not get past like 75% without consulting a guide because there are just so many obnoxiously hidden secrets in the game... Some of the passwords in particular are total "how would you ever figure that out on your own" moments, and. Okay, maybe this just annoys me in particular, but sometimes... secret locations are shown to you on the map via the wall of the room not being finished. But other secrets aren't. There's no consistency for stuff otherwise hidden in the exact same way, it's just really strange. You have a fair share of pure fake walls that you can't find until you're touching them, and there's a ton of things you need to drill, a few strange glitched enemies you need to take advantage of, and absolute no item-finding tool to assist you, unlike Super Metroid. There is, amazingly, both indication of 100% map completion and 100% item completion for each specific area, but you'd never know until it showed up for you the first time, and even then you probably wouldn't know what it means.
I will be the first to admit that, yes, ESA did have a lot of the same stuff to it. But here's the thing. The way that game's map is designed turned an annoyance into sheer brilliance, because the map was 100% tightly packed. You could figure out where secret rooms are 9 times out of 10, because the entire map is solid as a rock. There was also a hidden map item that mapped out most of the main secret areas, too. And even with the secrets on the outside of the station, you did have a fairly limited scope of things to search. Stuff was hidden, but it made sense. In Axiom Verge, it just doesn't make sense. Add to that the fact that there's no "secrets" necessary to just complete the game, no fake walls, no maps lying to you, and you'd never know there were supposed to be secrets like that until you accidentally stumbled upon one, or noticed how low your item % was at the end of the game.
I've rambled on about this one element enough but this is legitimately the biggest deal I could ever have with a metroidvania:
Exploring isn't fun.
Any metroidvania that fails this is fundamentally doing something wrong, no exceptions.
I loved exploring in games like ESA, Guacamelee, La-Mulana, Knytt Underground, heck, even games like Dust and Ori where exploration is stupidly easy. Here though, it just ain't fun.
Onto the rest. Sigh.
The platforming is generally alright. I actually dig most of the movement mechanics in this game. The coats constantly upgrade your ability to move through walls, and by the third one you have this cool dash attack that speeds up movement considerably, and it's just really fun to use. The drone is far, far superior to the Metroid morph ball, being much more flexible and once you have the drone swap allowing for a lot of cool movement options. I'm legitimately excited to watch the run of this game at AGDQ as soon as I finish watching this review, because while movement in this game is a bit stiff at first, as it tends to be in most metroidvanias, it gets really fun later on. There's no real tough platforming challenges in the game, though, a few instances of grappling hook shenanigans but they're rare, and everything else isn't any harder than completing the first world of Super Meat Boy. Heck, probably even easier than that.
I have mixed feelings on the combat, though. For one, there are too freaking many weapons, and so few of them saw much use. Especially once you get one of the god-tier weapons that basically invalidates all the other weapons before it. The lightning gun feels like cheating, almost. Basic enemies start out pretty manageable, but by the end of the game they are waaaayyy too strong and waaayyy too durable, and possibly even waaayyy too prevalent. I guess, the game wouldn't have any challenge at all with the higher-tier weapons unless the enemies are this way, but it reeks of fake difficulty. The bosses fare a little better, though they're also fairly unmemorable. There aren't very many of them, they're all very standard in design, no clever tricks, just shooting and dodging stuff. Snore. The final boss is atrocious, by the way, being basically an RNG boss unless you're a god at dodging tons of projectiles and three huge hitboxes while also trying to hit one specific section of the ceiling. Seriously, who the hell thought that was a decent idea for a boss. It doesn't even feel rewarding to win, it just feels like "Oh, I got lucky with the health drops this time so I won. Okay." And it's just really anticlimactic. Though honestly the entire game feels really anticlimactic. The story itself is fine but never seems to go anywhere. I didn't realize I was approaching the end until the game was like "Oh hey by the way you're approaching the end". Ehh. Some of the guns are fun to use though. For a primarily combat-driven game though I really feel like this could've been better. Granted, I've never really liked combat in Metroid games either, and the bosses in Metroid games are even worse than the ones here in my humble opinion, but whatever.

After playing "To The Moon", I decided to continue the experience of "Freebird Games" by playing "A Bird Story".
The first part of the game it's more like a movie where you just have to stay comfortable on your seat and watch what is happening (I suppose that might be the prologue of the game). After that, it continues with the description of a child's life that’s on primary school. When he goes home through the woods after he has been punished by his teacher, he finds and saves a bird which was attacked by a skunk. He sees that the bird is injured so he decides to take care of it. This represents the beginning of a great friendship. He will give the bird a shelter, he will feed it, he will play with it and they will have a good time one with the other.
The game brings up amusement every minute and is so relaxing to play. The game also have some interesting parts like sky dives or moving trees into the woods which tend to reveal the fantastic layer of the story. This is very appropriate for the game because being a child you can imagine a lot of things which are possible only in your imagination. In fact, the reality and the fantasy merge together and alongside with the fantastic soundtrack giving the player an incredible experience he will never forget.
I can't wait to play the next game of "Freebird Games" which will come out "one day", as it is shown in the teaser at the end of this game.
As short as it is, "A Bird Story" it's a worth buying game.
9/10.

Evolve Stage 2 is one of the most polished, intuitive, and challenging Free To Play titles available on Steam.
Have you ever wondered what it would be like to hunt (or play as) massive alien monsters on extra terrestrial planets? Do you ever yearn for a challenging team-shooter experience? Maybe an Explosive game of hide and seek? If you answered yes to any of those questions then Evolve may be a good fit for you.
The classes in Evolve (Assault, Support, Medic, and Trapper) all feature exclusive abilities along side the great (yet noticably balanced) movement system. All of the classes play differently, with focuses on DPS, Buffs, Healing, and Tracking the Monster your team is hunting. The movement itself comes in your standard run with the additional aid of jetpacks for quick bursts, dodges, and virtical movement.
Characters come in five flavors, the usual hunters and their opponents the monsters. Each character has a few different abilities, and grants for some variation in playstyle. Here is where we meet our first issue. The in game monetary system rewards those that play often, rather than those that play better. Daily log in bonuses net you more cash to unlock characters than an hour to two hours of play. You can however purchase in game money, but there's a reason people come to free to play, and spending money isn't something most players would be aiming to do.
Now, when it comes to the monster. The monsters play like an entirely different game, as you are placed in a third person camera mode, trying your best to avoid the hunters for at least the first half of the match. The monster takes patience to play well and rewards those who know the hunters well. Making these beasts a deep challenge as well as a power trip.
For these reasons, along with wildlife, map size, and full controller support; Evolve Stage 2 deserves a spot in your library.

I don't really get all the hate for this game. If you like the idea of moving ships around fairly realistically, get this one, especially if it is on sale.
The graphics are pretty much par for a simulator released in 2010.. not really pretty, but they get the job done. The ship and water physics are very well done. Nothing could stop the ship from slamming into the seawall. The water physics are equally as good. I was taking a speed boat for a whirl, when I came up next to an ocean liner at full clip.. THE WAKE ACTUALLY PULLS YOU IN TOWARDS THE BIGGER SHIP.. as I approached the bow, the bow wake flipped my little boat over without mercy... 10/10, would drown again..
The missions are fairly varied, and can take 1-2 hours each. It is too bad that this game can't be modded, but there is enough content to keep you busy for awhile. If you are looking for realism, you will find it here.. it is FAR more realistic than the prettier, and moddable, Vehicle Simulator (a good title in its own right, just not realistic at all.)

For the first boss, I had no idea what I was dying from because there was so little time to react or observe the situation. Eventually, I got used to it and how gimmicky each territory was, but a lot of the challenge comes from just inputting the right controls after dying a few times to see what lies ahead. Literally, all you're doing is dying for the most part because you have no idea what to expect and things just pop up, similar to Eryi's Action (except that game is all about springing traps on people).
The game isn't long, perhaps that's why they padded on a lot of silly "difficulty enhancers"

In the end, most of the difficulty lies in finicky controls and blind jumps. The view is heavily zoomed, allowing for a lot of visible detail, but also denying the ability to plan ahead. So, you can't plan your route, but instead go in blind, and probably die because of it, but your death allowing you to scope the route ahead, so next life you can go in with foreknowledge.Of course, there's another blind jump immediately after, so you'll then die there and have to repeat the first section in order to get to your retry of the next jump.

Aaru's Awakening is a hardcore platformer, with a unique, hand-drawn graphic style.
I first saw this game featured in GameJolt, and assumed that it was a result of a game jam.
When I saw it come to Steam, I was pretty excited to try it out.
Unfortunately, this is a game that seems to be constantly in an internal conflict regarding exactly what it's trying to achieve.
I've completed the game in about 3 hours, and then played a bit more to get some better times, and look around a bit more. If you go for the leaderboards, you'll certainly take fairly longer. There's also an hardcore mode that seems infuriating.
The game is beautiful. I just played Child of Light, from a much larger company, and this game still looks pretty damn good!
Everything is highly detailed, the creatures look alien (in a good way) and the Bosses have a really nice design to them.
The menus and loading screens are also highly stylized, and give the game a very unique vibe right of the bat.
Even the animation is very nice! The main character follows the mouse-point/analog stick, with different walking animations depending on where you're pointing.
It's a pretty rare thing, especially with indie games. It's very well done!
However, despite being a beautiful game, it completely misses its target in regards to its genre :
.
I'll go over some crucial aspects of the genre (regarding its visuals):
Conveying information
, making it very clear what will kill you and what will not;
Good differentiation between foreground and background elements;
Keeping distractions to a minimum;
Clear hitboxes;
The second and third are, of course, to aid the first, the most important.
Of all of these, this game only manages the last. Its hitboxes are well limited.
All of the rest, unfortunately, has been largely ignored, it seems.
Of course, it's an aesthetic choice. And the game looks good. BUT, when everything has very similar colors, you simply cannot convey information quickly. Many, many deaths have happened because I couldn't see the obstacles.
In a game that requires fast reflexes, obstacles are usually identified by peripheral vision. This game has none of that, resulting in a very
experience.
There's also the fact that some foreground elements seem obstacles, and you can never be sure until you run into them.
It's a fast paced game, with leaderboards. Your objective is to cross the levels as fast as you can. So... where exactly, does the player take the time to look around and be amazed by the game's amazing style? ... There's no time for it. Even the bosses. I've looked at them, but not for long at all -- otherwise, I'd be killed.
And it's really unfortunate. The game is beautiful, but it's mostly wasted potential.
The visuals are in complete conflict with the gameplay, instead of taking advantage of each of their highlights.
Other than that, feedback could be stronger, but isn't too much of an issue, as you die in mostly 1 hit. The "death screen" is also kind of annoying, but hey...
The
is also pretty good! It's very passive, though, with mostly eastern sounding melodies, with some
textures. I enjoyed it, and it loops well enough. It also doesn't restart when you die (that I noticed, as least), and usually keeps playing, even when you go to the level select screen. I would have liked it to be a bit more active, but it's mostly personal preference. It works well in the game.
I'll give the
a paragraph, this time around. I think it was cool, to give the game some context, but I also have 2 issues with it.
The story is "original" (i.e. not taken from somewhere else), but it was pretty cliché. What it did, however, was give a bit of flavour about the mythological nature of the game, which is cool! And it has a nice cyclical theme to it.
One of the problems is that it was very barebones -- which is understanding in an hardcore platformer. However, I would have expected some more to go along the visuals.
The other one is that it's told
outside the game. It's just a narrated piece of text between each world...
The game has 3 tutorial level, and then 4 "worlds", with 4 levels each, plus a Boss-fight in the end.
Your character can walk around and jump, with a couple of abilities. The first is a
, while in the air. This dash can break some types of walls, and otherwise works as a double jump, essentially.
The other is
. You shoot a little ball of light, and then teleport to it. This ball richochets some surfaces, sticks to others, and can also be destroyed by some (and enemies). You can also kill some enemies by teleporting directly inside them.
With that, it's mostly a game of avoiding enemies, spikes, and pools (and other hazards).
It's also
physics driven. I say sort of, because the physics are extremely artificial, and often cause more problems than it solves.
Enemies kill you with one touch. I think the problem is self evident. If you do as much as miss the enemy by a pixel, you'll touch them after the teleport and simply die. This happens quite a lot. There's also the problem of "enemies that can not be teleported into" not showing any sign of that. So, you can also repeatedly try to kill them until you realize why you can't.
Enemies also shoot projectiles that will kill you and the teleportation ball. It's often a mess, with several enemies on screen.
Back to trial and error. There are enemies that come from off-screen. There are other that walk into you immediately, when you reach a new screen (usually Boss fights that rely on teleporting into another screen).
Then, there are huge spiked balls that fall when you enter a new area...
The game is full of these deaths. You're focusing on one particularly challenging section, and when you're almost reaching the end, the game "surprises" you with more death. It can be annoying, since it's just about memorization.

The game has some ramps to accelerate you, and throw you into a fast paced section. However, these don't actually function according to physics. When you touch them, your speed simply goes from 2 to 50. Even if you touch the extremity of it, you gain exactly the same speed. If you want to slow down and do the section in another way... tough luck.
Then, there's falling acceleration. Of course, your speed gets higher as you fall. Unfortunately, the teleportation conserves that acceleration, which means that successfuly pulling a second one in the air is virtually impossible. I could have seen some interesting sections, if you could teleport and reset your speed... Yet another limitation.
Level design-wise, the challenges seem to long. Usually (and I've mentioned this in the Yury game), platformers have platforms that make you safe. This game seems to think that's too easy, and almost every platform falls. This stretches the challenges a lot, at times, and makes the game quite frustrating.
There's one chance for everything. You can't recover from your mistakes. If you miss a jump, too bad... Everything falls and everything is designed to kill you. It's simply not fun. And it's not a fair challenge either. (Super Meat Boy is one of my favourite games)
It's an ambitious effort! But, for the reasons above, the negatives far outweigh the positives.
Ultimately, it's made of pieces that don't fit together... Still, the talent it clearly there, and I'll look forwward to their future games.

You have to understand that I rarely see a game all the way to the end, even a ~6-hour game like Skyborn.  My attention span runs out... but not this time.  I cared about the characters and really wanted to find out what happened to their story.
PROS
Extremely likeable characters -- nearly every time a new character joined the party, I was immediately drawn to his or her unique personality.
Interesting (though short) story.
Nice graphics... RPGMaker style, of course, but a really nice example of what that platform can do.
No time wasted on tedious, pointless questing.
No grinding.
CONS
Combat was... a little one-note.  There wasn't a lot of depth to it.
Short game. (Maybe a pro for some folks...)
No support for Steam Overlay features in Windows.
Er... that's mostly it.  I didn't have a lot of complaints about the game. :P

My biggest gripe is that progression can be slow. Somewhat on par with the earlier Tropico games. You spend all that time building a base, feel the highs of acheiving all those things, only to have it completely brought back to zero in the next level. That being said, unlike the earlier Tropico games, there's a storyline to support why.
The AI assistant is great, script writing is unique and interesting and the games storyline makes sense and carries though.
The graphics are a bit dated, no added scaling for higher resolutions and the camera angles can take some getting used to. It is however, a great example of the 'better' era of this style of creative game design. Well worth looking at, even at full price.

It's a beautiful, heart-touching, intelligent, fantastic and short pixel art visual novel of a cute little story about an imaginative young boy and his bird. It's kind of visual language to tell a wonderful, heartfelt story about friendship and loneliness which we do experience in our life. This is a quirky little almost-Metroidvania-like platformer that doesn't require too much skill to get through. You spend most of the game riding around in a spinning blade wheel (that doubles as a jetpack for limited flight) and fire various weapons to take down 100 bosses and all the little minions that get in your way. But there are segments where you pilot other ships with their own special weapons and even run around on foot without any weapons. The real selling point is the WarioWare style "microgames" you play once you've depleted a boss's health. They're all pretty easy and the end result is usually the same, but they're a fun little reward for your work.
With so much variation in the gameplay, it's a shock and a shame that it all ends up feeling so repetitive. Despite the large amount of boss microgames, a lot of them play similarly (stop something that is moving in a specific spot, press/mash specific keys/buttons, etc.). Add on the fact that there's far less than 100 of them and you'll start to get tired of them near the end. The special vehicles are a little bit of a letdown too with a couple of them playing exactly the same. Finally, outside of a few special cases, most of the weapons act essentially the same. To make matters worse, the shotgun is so overpowered and can blast through walls you normally have to drill... it's hard to justify using anything else once you buy it.
That being said, I'd still recommend this game. Overall, it's pretty fun, not too long, and has a silly sense of humor.

Oh dear, where do I start.
Okay. This game was unreal. I thought I'd get a couple hours of goofing off with a bunch of pigeons and that it would be all fun and games and laughs and then I'd leave and play something more serious.
Yeah...this game isn't just for sh**s and giggles. But there are many giggles.
This game is as cute as it gets. You've got all these birds and they're all so different. At first glance you might think they're stereotypes come to life, but as it is with most people, there's more than meets the eye. Everybirdie has something special about them.
I didn't even think I'd want to complete every single path, but sure enough I did. The BBL ending definitely gives you the most intriguing ending with lots of mystery and lots of Sakuya (eeeeee excuse me while I fangirl). I must admit my favourite endings were the more lighthearted ones though, the ones that were sweet and fluffy. And carve it into your soul, kid! There were many great endings. It's hard to pick a favourite.
Also I thought Ryouta's path would be a bit more boring because he's the typical childhood-friend-turned-true-love kind of story everyone seems to love, but I think it was the most rewarding end.
I really appreciate how the writer(s) approached topics like disability, status and even teacher crushes. There was never a point where I thought "Hmm, this seems inappropriate and harmful". Especially in a "dating sim" I even expected problematic moments, but there weren't any. I was overjoyed by that.
WARNING: If you plan to do all the endings, this game does have its share of the violent and the gruesome. While you're not going to see blood and guts, trust me, some of the content in this game is very disturbing. There's murder (which I thought would give me nightmares nearly), suicide (which is dealt with quite respectfully) and probably other stuff I can't think of right now.
For a so-called dating sim, this game isn't overly romantic. It feels more like a friendship sim than dating, to be perfectly honest. I loved that about this game. It surpassed every expectation.
One complaint is the typos, specifically in the BBL ending. Way too many, and it made otherwise hard-hitting lines come off a little...underwhelming. But seriously, don't let that deter you. Just know that it's there, but that's one of my only real complaints.
Lastly, I just want to mention the characters, who are all extremely rich and satisfying to learn about. I had a soft spot for Nageki, Ryouya, Sakuya and Yuuya. But surprisingly, the playable character is also super interesting as well! As you go through the endings, you learn about the bird of the hour but also quite a bit on who you're playing as too.

Once again I find myself in the land of difficult platformers with Lumenox Games' Aaru's Awakening (that's a mouthful). I'm not the best at the so-called “hard-core” platformers. Luckily for me, Aaru's Awakening only appears to be in the category, but mostly just skirts the line.
Most of the puzzles I've come across have been difficult, but not frustrating. It's an odd difference that separates this game, but in other games where I've died and died and died yet again, I haven't wanted to come back too often if at all. Aaru's Awakening had some boss fights and levels that straight killed me so many times it was rather embarrassing. I remember being stuck on one level (the levels are rather short) for more than thirty minutes. The very first boss fight took me about two days. I woke up early this last Tuesday to spend my last thirty minutes to finally tackled it.
The main pull is that the game is fun and with the tools given (not just jumping, but teleporting and charging) in Aaru's Awakening, when you fail, the successful attempt feels close at hand. If you've played any games in this genre you may know the difference between thinking a jump is impossible and being able to see how you can solve the “puzzle”. Lumenox Games accomplishes this well.
I'd love to say something about the story, but I feel it's a little lost in the action. Nothing is given to you while you are dying in the levels themselves. That's the main reason I know that (in the game) Dawn, Dusk, Day, and Night were at war and eventually decided to split the day in four parts and share the twenty-four hour period. (Sharing is caring right?) However, you (Aaru) are sent by Dawn into the others domain for... some reason, but like I said, I can't remember.
The game is narrated by a girl/woman who does a great job telling the story. The problem lies in that just after she's done giving you the setting for the level, you go into a meat grinder. In the game you come across stuff that will stump you and keep the end of the level just out of reach. Since the difficulty is tied to timing and the platforming itself, I can't turn down the difficulty to enjoy the story by itself. So the meat grinder just beats it out of my memory. When I get back to more narration I have no clue on why Aaru is confused with his actions or why he was sent into the domains of the other three parts of the day in the first place. Am I a bad guy? I just don't know.
Score: Gewd.
In the end, while I may not know what exactly is going on, Aaru's Awakening is fun. It's got genuinely hard parts for sure, but it never seems out of reach of being able to accomplish. When compared to other games in the platforming genre recently, this one feels friendly and approachable. This is very welcome because I've been bombarded lately by “hardcore” frustration-filled platformers. I'm kind of tired of them... completely tired. It's not that I'm terrible at them, but I'd rather be filling my gaming time with enjoyment. Aaru's Awakening delivers.

I put in around 25 hours into a game that apparently takes around 10 hours to complete and still haven't finished collecting everything. Yes Axiom Verge is a huge game full of sharp shooting, platforming and discovery much in the spirit of games like Metroid and Castlevania. It also reminded me of a little known classic called Wolf Child.
At times Axiom Verge feels almost imposible to uncover as it is so vast and choc-full of secrets to uncover some of which require a sharp eye, others a sharp mind. Unfortunatley not all the time I put into the game was pleasent however. This was due mostly to some momentary design flaws. For example there is a particular section of the game that took me hours to figure out and it was due to a puzzle that had no particular set up. The next moment came with the seventh boss who in a sharp turn from other bosses felt like more of grind than a battle of skill. These moments set me back hours grinding what is otherwise a smooth experience to a halt.
The dificulty level also takes a sharp spike towards the end of the game which isn't especially surprising (duh) but I felt the game doesn't balance your newly acquired abilities as well as earlier in the game resulting again in battles of health grinding or even worse dreaded retreads as you replay one area over and over and OVER... sorry.
Moving on. With much of the bad stuff out the way the game truly shines in pretty much all of it Metroidvania inspired glory. For the vast majority of the game exploration is incredibly fun, there are tons of fantastic enemies to face along the way and it all revolves around a intruiging story that is reminicent of sci-fi films like the Matrix. For the most part the controls are very tight however I did run into problems playing with my 360 pad (mostly cuz the D-Pad sucks). Also I really didn't like the implementation of the dash and double jump.
I absolutley loved the breadth of power ups, weapons and abilities. This for me was the most rewarding aspect of the game I squeeled like a school girl upon finally getting the infamous flame thrower! Also the drone is amazing and in conjunction with the field disruptor lead to some awesome puzzle solving. After stumbling awarkardly through the games jagged world for hours you will eventually move through it like a 16bit God!
Over all Axiom Verge is an incrediably fun if slightly flawed platformer. It's one of the best games I have played for some time and certainly the best platformer since Shovel Knight. To think this is the work of one man blows my mind. Hats off sir, hats off.

For the free price tag, it's certainly worth trying out. The variance in the abilities of each of the hunters makes every character unique in their own sense, and they all bring something different to the table. This game also has the capability to reward players that learn to play a class very well, unlocking new perks for game matches, finding new emblems/badges to display your status to other players, and earning currency to unlock more characters. Basic perks for the hunters range from health regeneration, faster weapon swap speed, and higher jump height, with more valuable perks going all the way to faster jetpack recharge, shorter ability cooldowns, and bullets inflicting damage-over-time: each perk of the allotted three per match brings a little extra bonus to each of the characters. Evolve has several different game modes to play, including: 4v1 hunters vs player monster; 4v1 hunters vs AI monster; a "training mode" where a player is paired with 3 AI hunters, an AI monster, and access to all fully-ranked perks and characters to test out different hunters and perk combinations; and an arcade style of play which has different modifiers for the matches, including map/weather selection, wildlife spawn, damage modifiers, et cetera.
I've found, in my experiences, that games are TYPICALLY balanced in the sense of finding, hunting, and killing the monster. I have had very few experiences where one team dominates the other. Some players that choose to play as the monster have more experience and have an edge in knowing their character, just as hunters do in knowing their own character very well. Key elements to victory as hunters are group coordination, taking advantage of your class' strengths, anticipating the monster's movements, and reacting accordingly.
Overall, this can be a very enjoyable and rewarding game, if you don't allow one game loss to make you quit altogether. Hard work and dedication is rewarded, and personally, many friends have been made in playing this game. Again: IT'S FREE. Give it a chance, play some matches with a few different characters, and if you hate it, don't gripe about it.

I loved this. Probably because I have a rescue bird myself, and my life from early childhood has been devoted to rescuing and recuperating animals. The story is simple, touching, and beautifully illustrated. The music complements the two wonderfully, especially the night the kid fell asleep at his desk and woke up tired the next morning :D Very cute.
I would definitely suggest this to any fan of interactive stories, or even just good short stories in general.
As for the ratings, like so many interactive stories on Steam, it receives many unjust thumb down votes for "lack of game" when things of this nature were never really intended to be a "game" to begin with. If you are looking for a game with choices and loot, and other things full fledged games have, this is not the story for you.

Beautiful little game, takes around 5 hours to play through depending on your difficulty setting.
The idea of multiple races not getting along and a group of protagonists attempting to fix society is definitely cliche, but the game does a great job of progressing the storyline in a way that tries to deviate from it.
The artwork and gameplay itself reminded me of a Zelda/Pokemon-esque setting, and the environments you travel through are very well made. The game devs did a great job with the worldbuilding and you can feel yourself in the protagonists' shoes. The characters are also developed very well, and you can see their progressions as you complete the game.
I wasn't a big fan of the combat system, it was turn by turn and was a bit boring for me, but it's not a big complaint. I also did not like the fact that there was no map or quest guidance system, but for the most part I was able to find my way after a minute or two of looking around the map.
Overall, the pros heavily outweigh the cons. This game is simply fantastic

I can't recommend this game enough. It draws heavy inspiration from Metroid, but it goes in its own direction with unique upgrades and weapons that give the game its own personality. The story is interesting and unpredictable, but it was a tad hard to follow for me. The thing I loved is that the guns are all different and you use them all in different ways, but a gun is still a gun and there's no "this is the only gun to kill this specific boss" restriction.
I could go on and on, but the bottom line is if you enjoy Metroidvania games AT ALL, buy this immediately. This game is a solid 9.5/10. I couldn't stop playing and I was genuinely sad when it was over.

There are many games that are throwbacks to earlier eras in gaming. They have become so commonplace as to be unremarkable, and it's not difficult to see why. Even setting aside the obvious power of nostalgia and the (relative) ease of production of such titles, there remains the matter of how often and how severely the gaming industry has changed. What graphics are considered acceptable by the general public, what practices are tolerated regarding downloadable content, what genres see growth, decline, and resurgence, and what platforms games are developed for... All of those things have changed over the years.
So what separates Axiom Verge from any other genre throwback? What makes it unique?
These things do:
Those are the game's highlights. What, then, are it's weaknesses?
All in all, do I recommend Axiom Verge? Absolutely. It's not by any means perfect, and its weaknesseses and presentation can understandably be divisive. Despite that, the game's strengths make it well worth a purchase for fans of its genre. Even so, watching at least one gameplay video beforehand is recommended. If it's not your thing, it won't be difficult to find out.

This sort of "game" is the exact reason I wish steam had a thumbside neutral option for reviews.
First, let me make it clear that this isn't a game. I actually feel "visual novel" is the most accurate title - and it is literally VISUAL. There is no dialogue, which is actually a plus. The story is told through interaction, dream-like sequences, and visual metaphor. There are no choices for the player to make, absolutely nothing you can do to alter the story in any way. It is completely linear.
During the paper aeroplane sequence, some very important instruction was missing and I ended up flying around for a full twenty minutes before lucking into what I was supposed to do. Those twenty minutes felt a lot longer.
The music is pleasant, the story is a little cliché but charming nontheless, and the art is pretty. Yet I struggle to recommend this. The description is up-front about it only lasting an hour, and I emphasise that it is completely linear. If you think the screenshots look good and just want to enjoy being shown a short story in which you occasionally have to press a button, A Bird Story might be for you.
Just...buy it on sale.

Wow, this game floored me--I spent over half of it fighting back tears. A Bird Story, just like Kan Gao's previous game, To the Moon, is fantastic visual novel that uses its terrific musical score to create genuine emotion. This is an adorable story presented in a fresh way. Highly recommend.

The Game has a nice concept but I just can't recommend if for various reasons. Its not bad, in fact, i'd give it a medium rating if i could. Its just not good enough to recommend. (The game runs fine on windows 10 for me)
What do i mean by that?
Well, graphics sure are not a reason why you'd buy this. The game is quite old so thats understandable.
Then theres the gameplay
Well the gameplay is the main problem here. It starts in the tutorial. The tutorial explains features like combat against other factions(which I sure can't find if they exist) but not the core gameplay elements. it took me a while playing the game until i realized that the currency "E" actually is energy and stored in the energy collectors. Thats quite a weird concept and i would have expected the tutorial to tell me that.
The tutorial doesn't really tell you anything about most buildings. so you end up just purchasing them, placing them, and checking after you already placed them what they actually do.
And as i already said, they tease some sort of combat mechanics against other factions(which would make the game more interesting) but there are just none in the main game. theres criminals and spies sometimes, but those are taken out by security bots and don't need you to hunt them with an army. Also, the combat mechanics are very clunky.
Well if we now look at things we do. one thing we don't do is losing. because the game is hillariously easy. I never had a problem where i was concerned about losing, i don't even know if you can.
So you buy buildings and build them. You fill up peoples needs kinda like some of those themepark management games. Also you can hire people that walk into your themepark to work for you. Its a one time payment and they can leave at any point(which is quite a weird mechanic). Different races work in different rooms, not all rooms need workers.
You can also trade with different ships. trading works pretty alright. theres also a biodeck which lets you create a little biotope with different climates and so on. kinda neat but the biodeck is way too small and serves no purpose at all(other than having people standing around).
But the thing this game is really missing is content. you'll notice that most people that rate this game haven't played more than 15 hours. thats because the game is out of content after 5-10 hours. you have just build every building and just build more of them. and since there are no paths or anything to organize your park you end up just putting the rooms down anywhere since the placement doesn't matter whatsoever. there's no sort of progress. you just build more of everything without and sort of visitor number or gain in currency(since there is a limit you can increase only by a small bit with huge buildings). it doesn't have any replayability to it since you just can't do anything special with your station
Its even missing content that is mentioned in tooltips and the tutorial(this one i've explained before). when i press f1 on the dock it tells me i can expand it so passenger ships can dock there. Aaaand nope. Looked it up, its not actually in the game. would've been a lot more interesting if you could expand certain buildings and have actual progress.
this game is something like a 5/10. fun for a couple of hours, but thats it. if you can get it for below 1$ its a pretty decent deal. but not nearly worth the 6$ they want here. But don't expect it to be fun for a long time if you buy it.

combat is not a strong point unfortunately and just basically boils down to amassing as many people as you can into the area of conflict. however, you periodically will get a bomb planted on your station by terrorists. and can beam it up and hold it and drop it on a bunch of enemies entering your territory for the lulz.
saddest part of this game is finishing the very awesome single player campaign and being left with the message "see you in startopia 2"....... sadly that will never be. buy the game, give it a go, its easy as♥♥♥♥♥♥and yet very enjoyable. great sense of humour, graphics that were stylised and have held up very well given there are kids out there driving cars younger than this game.

Let's get the easiest stuff out of the way and have me admit that the pervy fanservice aspect of this game is one of the reasons why I bought it, along with some battle arena goodness. It gets old real fast, though, seeing their clothes get ripped up, so you can equip your characters with unbreakable versions of their costumes. I did that for a while because I just wanted to kill cute things as cute girls, but then I was missing out on getting the boosts afforded from costume breaks, so I put the breakable ones back on.
I don't know what to say about this game. It's short, it's goofy, and just like the original Hyperdimension Neptunia Rebirth 1, I ♥♥♥♥ing can't stand the "story" and pointless dialogue. The story isn't remotely compelling and that's obviously not the point, but nothing about it makes you curious about what will happen next. Thankfully the dialogue is kept shorter than usual, and for Hyperdimension standards, that's all I can ever ask for because in the other game, they just took waaaaaaaay too long to finish talking about...I can't remember. That's how bad the dialogue is.
I can see how others might find the 4th wall breaking funny and the cuteness exchange, but it's not for me.
The first half of the game you're given an over abundance of quests to complete and you go at them at your own leisure. Which ones to do first and which characters to do them with. The only reason why I played for 10 hours is because I do like the hack n slash battle system, and I was worried at first about it being too easy of a mash fest, but there are times where you do get challenged. Not so much that you sweat bullets, but enough to grab your attention back from basically mentally checking out to start paying attention to your spacing amongst the hordes of enemies.
Yeah, that's what this game is good for. If you want mindless fun, play it. Turn your brain off and mash buttons and occassionally use the dodge button to get out of "tough" spots.
The sound bothers me, by the way. The music is fine and the voice acting is okay, but god the monster voices are annoying, and thankfully you can turn them off. But then all you're left with his hollow sound effects that don't make your attacks feel impactful despite of the physical force they cause in pushing enemies away. Then there's one real time cutscene that isn't in visual novel form and the mech monster was just silent. I had to close the game and turn it back on with allowing monster voices just to hear pointless stereotypical bad guy monologue.
I DON'T KNOW! I don't know why I ever bother with the Neptunia games. They're like one night stands that feel like a good idea at the time, but you regret it afterward. Great action, but nothing fulfilling to the mind or heart. I got this game for $20 because I did enjoy the visuals and the gameplay, but it left a lot to be desired. This game is good for $5, I would say, not at all worth the full price.
I would only gladly, without regret, pay full price for the next Action Release game IF the developers do the following:
- Have some more structure in tackling quests. Maybe one quest unlocks another rather than having a long list of them to do.
- Quest variety. How sad is it that I felt relief in a fetch quest of picking up treasure chests that didn't really give me any real items?
- The FIRST quest felt good in that you had to beat one part of the map to advance to the next, so why didn't the rest of the quests have that?! It was bland, but way better than being confined to ONE battle arena per quest with only a tiny option to move to another part of it.
- Rebirth 1 was fun for the customization of your characters and dungeons from item collection and crafting. That would be nice to put into this hack n slash spin off.
- Also, it wouldn't hurt to have more SP skills so it felt meaningful to go to the set up options and equip your characters with the moves you want instead of simply just having 3 per character.
- Combos should have more customization. Throughout the whole game you have the exact same combos from when you start. I think it'd be better if you earned more moves as you leveled up or even had the option, like in Rebirth 1, to customize different moves you want to have in each link of a combo chain.
- New monsters. PLEASE! Keep the ones they already have that's fine, but have some monsters that are the same size as the characters and more intimidating than a blob with a happy face. Killing those don't feel satisfying.
In conclusion, I don't play Hyperdimesion Neptunia games for what they are, I play them for what they could be: solid JRPG's with enough depth that you'd really need a long rope to get out of the deep chasm of customization. But that's not what these games are. They are a shallow waste of time and I have voluntarily wasted my time this week playing a game that has the potential to be so much more.

So this game is quite interesting. I'm quite happy with this game for a few reasons and I will explain them below.
This game was ported from the PS Vita and was developed by the same guys who brought us the Senran Kagura series. I LOVE the Senran Kagura series for the simplistic gameplay and the very well written story (Oh alright it's about the B00bs too) so how does this game hold up?
The story is simple. Two characters by the name of Dengekiko (Based on Dengeki magazines) and Famitsu (Based on Weekly Famitsu magazines) are having a battle for best reporter and best articles on the Gamindustri CPUs and CPU candidates. Soon something fishy happens and it's up to the total of Ten characters to find out what's wrong and save Gamindustri... again.
With writing this simplistic, it has to have a lot of charm, right? Yes. The charm of the characters shines as usual. The humor is well done as you hear lots of funny lines from the characters. Often making video game references and jokes. If you're firmiliar with the humor in Nep Nep games, you'll enjoy it even here.
Now onto the gameplay. Is it good? Well yeah. It's pretty good but it definitely still has that Portable Game feel with short, easy to do quests and repetitive actions. Not that it's a bad thing. This simplicity makes the game PERFECT for quick play without struggle. Not overly hard and satisfying when you get a long combo string going.  Each character handling pretty well despite a couple handling the exact same way.
Each quest can be taken on with a solo character or a two person team. Taking on quests with two characters is better for leveling up more characters faster. Each character also has an "HDD" form or Super mode to put it simply. This enhances the character by making them faster, stronger and gives them a different move set to play around with.
In the gameplay, there's enough here to keep you entertained.
The visuals are nothing too special but they get the job done with the bright and colorful look the Nep Nep games are known for. The characters look nice with the bright colors and all of them are adorable. Not too much to talk about here so we can just move on.
The sound is pretty okay with the voice acting and music being the best parts. The characters are fun to listen to and the soundtrack is well done even if quite a lot of the music is from the past Nep Nep games. This game also supports English and Japanese dubbing so there's a lot to love.
Oh yeah. There's a costume break system in this game! If you take enough damage, the character's clothes will rip and it's pretty revealing. Not a bad feature if you're into that sort of thing and yes, there is an option to give them clothes that don't break but it needs to be unlocked.
Overall, this is a good game and there's enough content to play for quite a while. If you're into the gameplay style of Senran Kagura and like the humor of the other Nep Nep games, This game is something you'll enjoy.

I've played hundreds of RPGs over the last 25 years.  There's nothing unique or revolutionary about this game, but it's definitely a step above most games developed using RPGMaker.  Despite the short length, I feel I got my money's worth.
Pros:
- All primary characters are engaging, relatable, and offer unique contributions to group combat.
- Combat includes a "Threat" mechanic, based on how much damage or healing is done by each group member. Monsters focus single-target attacks on the character with the most threat.  This lets you build a team with the traditional tank, healer and damage dealers, rather than just a bunch of toons with high stats that bang on mobs until they're all dead.
- Enjoyable storyline.  I also liked how the backstory was introduced.  There's more groups involved in the conflict than just humans and Skyborn.
- No bugs, glitches or typos.
- There's no grinding.  There's only a fixed number of monsters in the game, which are visible on the map and avoidable if you choose.  Instead, the game offers an alternative: "exploration nodes".  These grant experience (as though you won a combat), rewarding those who focus more on exploring.
- Several secondary conquests, including a gladiator arena and a deep dungeon with additional challenges.
- Forge mechanic.  You can collect some materials (iron, coal, platina) throughout the game and use it to craft some weapons and armor.
Cons:
- Preferred more character development for the antagonists, villains, and that one mysterious girl who talks about being hungry.  You'll know who I mean. :)
- Length of gameplay: only about 15-20 hours.  This is on par with old school 90s RPGs like Final Fantasy IV, Chrono Trigger, and Secret of Mana... although those 3 games felt like they have far deeper, more drawn out stories compared to this game.
- Lack of difficulty.  I played the game on Hard (max) difficulty and there wasn't much challenge, other than a little bad luck with RNG on a few midgame bosses.
- Lack of challenging puzzles.  It's mainly just finding the right buttons to open passages.
- Lack of side quests.  I found only one actual side quest (the rest were part of the main storyline).
- Not much actual exploration involved.  Lack of open world feel.  Game is fairly linear.
Final Rating: 8 / 10
