Space Station Management game.
It's a fun game, funny dialogue (Hitchhickers guide to the galaxy style humor), well put together core mechanic building, hiring staff, and resource management, Energy is the main focus while food, medical supplies, etc are more modifiers to buildings rather then a typical resource in resource management game. The learning curve isn't too hard to get used to, it controls a bit different then other games but it's easy to get past that learning curve.
-Cons
Combat is lacking, For spys and enemies in your territory of the space station setting priority to targets is effective and your forces can be rallied to a single point, but you can not rally your forces on enemy territory and taking over a section by force becomes a war of attrition and the side with the most security scuzzers wins.
The Game's story feels short, the core game mechanic is well put together but the campaign is short, and like the combat mechanic feels it was an after thought.
Even with the Cons, it's a fun game and I've enjoyed hours and hours of play (I owed a physical copy of Startopia before Steam existed) so if you like resource management games I'd reccomend getting it, on sale or not it's worth more then $6.99 (as of the time I posted this reveiw during the Autumn Sale it's 75% off at $1.74)

Skyborn is a game that was made with love by a handful of people with a Steampunk feel that's made with the RPG Maker suite of tools.  It's one of the best games ever made with that suit (to my mind) and I finished it in roughly 12 hours of play.  It's not that long.  I've played around 10 or 11 RPG Maker games, and I've always found it to be one of the better gaming experiences.
Skyborn has a lot of things going for it.  The game works pretty smoothly, the plot and setting are very interesting and different from a lot of boring "Dragon Warrior" or "Final Fantasy" clones.  The game has levels of difficulty I didn't expect, and the game is pretty standard fare for the engine.
The major character is a tinker and engineer lady who's had it pretty okay under the thumbs of the ruling class Skyborn that look like draconians from Dragonlance.  As she is set on her explorations, she finds a lot of people who have it worse than she did.  And she'll rally some folks to the cause, and set out to bring down the big bad and some of the Skyborn race.
If you just want a diverting throwback to the mechanics of old, but with modern settings, story-telling and concepts, then Skyborn is a pretty satisfying way to spend some time.  I enjoyed the time that I invested into the game.

A friend got this for me as a holiday gift after it spent a long time on my wishlist. I'm really happy I own it, but wow should I have nabbed it sooner! The aesthetic is very Giger, lovingly depicted with some truly amazing art. The sound design in each area is haunting, yet also uplifting. It makes you want to see what's around the next corner, what next powerup you will get.
The map lets you mark two places of interest per "zone", so you can know to come back once you get powerups. As for the powerups...
They're AMAZING. You have a few standard ones, and your first gun is pretty standard, but there are over 10 guns, all of them giving you more options instead of simply being raw power. While Super Metroid's beam modes were neat and all, this enables smarter, more personalized, creative play. Like playing close ranged? That's there. Like standing back, using obstacles, etc? Adapt to the situation with more and more tools to deal with each situation!
The lore is also very interesting, showing you glimpses of an amazing culture, a ruined world, and hints of who and what you are. I don't want to spoil anything except to say that I was as curious to find more lore as I was to get more powerups and kick more booty.
If you like metroidvanias, especially if you enjoy the brand that is less rpg elements and more item based (and not for stat ups, though those exist!), this is for you.
A pretty decent Metroid game that still manages to be different. Certainly worth what I paid for it. I still think I missed a lot on my first run though. Maybe I'll play it again soon.
As good as, if not better than, Super Metroid. I can give no higher praise.

TL;DR - Probably the best MetroidVania game to come out in the last decade. I'll leave detailled descriptions of what the genre entails to other, wordier reviews, and will instead focus on what makes this game stand out among the crowd.
The artwork, music and atmosphere are sinister and fitting. This is a metroidvania that feels like HR Giger was on the design team, but all the more sexual elements of his designs were removed. Biomechanical structures, grating noises, reality becoming undone at the seams.
The story thus far has been enjoyable. The game mechanics are tight and slick, with an enjoyable "glitching reality" theme. This is not to say the game itself is glitchy - your abilities have the appearance of glitches but are carefully controlled in what can effect what. Under the hood, you are still obtaining an increasing arsenal of weapons and abilities to move around a map in pursuit of plot-nuggets and story-critical thingammijigs.
I don't see much point in numerical scores, but this was very good.

This game is fantastic. Plays great, controls great and sounds beautifuly. I'd like to be able to zoom in on the map more, and have the map automatically mark spaces which are currently inaccessible (once I reach them), but other than that I can't find any things to complain. Marvelous.

Took you TWENTY years to leave Japan, Umihara! Was it a trip by sea, only for those mutated fish to continuously delay your departure by biting holes in your boat or what? This game is super difficult and fun. It's a puzzle platformer where you use a rubber fishing line as a hookshot to get around places, while avoiding puzzle-traps and rad enemies. The fishing line's length can be adjusted during use, and it can be used to pull enemies to their deaths. If you pull an enemy off a ledge and you're still holding on as he falls, he'll also pull you to your death. It's pretty funny. Most levels have multiple exits that will progress you one stage further, or let you skip stages if the exit is either harder to get to or a secret. Anything else I can tell you is obvious information you can learn from watching the store video.
Anyway, if you like Mario Bros. 3 for the challenge, this game is for you. It's a classic.

The best SNES game is now available on Steam and it's the definitive version too. It's more than just a port. It's fully-trnaslated, lagless and has an option to practice stages like in Shun and Sayonara. Practicing stages records your IL times too, with a leaderboard that is implemented seamlessly. I've put so many hours into this game on emulators that I just had to buy it legit. You should too.

First, Sayonara Umihara Kawase (3rd game) was ported to steam. Now the first game in the Umihara Kawase series is finally on steam and Umihara Kawase Shun (2nd game) is on it's way before the end of 2015. What a time to be alive.
Umihara Kawase originally came out on the Super Famicom in December 1994 but never got a proper English release until 2015 when it was included as a bonus game with the PS Vita version of Sayonara (and now the PC version as a stand alone release).
The objective of this game is to go from the beginning of a stage and get to a door (sometimes there's 2 doors that you can choose from, the harder to reach one being a shortcut to later fields) via your trusty fishing rod and by that I mean you gotta grapple, swing and fling yourself across wacky platfoming levels all the while avoiding enemies (fish with legs and a boss or two) and using your crazy rubberband physics skills to get to the exit fast (if you want to speedrun or impress your friends). The game ends either when you run out of lives or you reach one of the final exit doors.
Before some levels, the game shows you a thing you can do to get through that level, either how to get across some gap or dealing with an enemy or just stuff to help you win at the game.
I don't recommend playing this on keyboard as it has controller support and it feels much better imo playing any of the games in the series with a controller/handheld system. But if you can master keyboard controls then you're a pretty cool person.
Music is nice, pretty simple but catchy I guess.
One thing this game had going for it back when it first came out was the ability to save replays. That feature is still around but you also have leaderboards too so if you like leaderboard stuff then you're good to go.
It's easy to learn for most, a lifetime to master for some. It's Umihara Kawase.

Being shot at by cannons? Your crew will visit the roof. Raining that causes morale to drop? Roof visits for everybody! I just wish I could tell them to sit down a little easier.

And all that fish... useless, everyone just dies of scurvy and refuses to eat the fruit you have so you just go out for excess fruit and never bother fishing.
There are some things that people can use to increase stats/XP gain but they kept leaving to go do other things, I just want them to stay where I told them.
I had 15 chickens constantly leaving fecal matter, I had their cages and I kept them until they leveled enough to lay eggs. I still have the two eggs that they laid (and I had them for several hours). After those two they refused to do anything.
As far as teaching them skills, you almost always need cleaning because there is so much filth everywhere, swimming because insta-death sucks and before you know it almost everyone is practically a clone with skills that aren't so much choices but needs.
I even spent 15 minutes not knowing why a ship of mine wasn't considered sea worthy just because I had a piece of backdrop in a place that they couldn't reach. The backdrop doesn't actually do anything besides look pretty, imagine your pirate ship not being allowed out because of a colour you chose. And the 'problem indicator' just showed the highest right-most block rather than showing me the problem.
The weapons are either great or useless with little in-between. Through use or stones you can level them, either level 10, 25 or 50. But for so, so many weapons it's a useless waste of time or if it is useful a grind. Many have effects that aren't really useful because the weapon sucks. Weapons from stores also seem to display incorrect info? (Stores also sometimes don't display the in depth item info such as damage/DPS/stats/etc on certain items).
The fights are just your guys rushing them, healing is a bit of a pain.
And to travel from one place to the other you have to wait for your characters to get there, you can increase their speed with items but it is so tedious especially the first hour or so since you can't go too far from town or else risk running out of provisions.
All in all the start to mid game was nice with none of these problems being that bad but as the game went on it stopped being fun to play.
It's a lot of fun, can seem repettitive after a while but it's a blast to play and has a surprising amount of depth.

Now that they've had what I will deem a flop, they have no excuses, barring acts of god, to drop the ball again. This and three other games were all bought from my local gameshop for the usual reasons: someone recommended it and it was dirt cheap. I must say I was inordinately happy to find not just something to amuse for a weekend, but a "proper" game. By "proper" I mean that despite the long tutorials and even longer playtime of the levels (which still feel a bit tutorial-esque), I was gripped for a good 2 weeks or so. Just a couple of hours every night before getting online and getting my daily MMO injection, but it kept me coming back for more.
The slight predictability of the level structure after a while didn't deter me either, I wanted that next type of alien so I wanted to get to the next level just so I could get to play with them; see what they could do; work them into my now tried and tested Starbase designs.
I must admit however, that at first I didn't have much patience with it. After lengthy tutorials I was getting peeved at the smarmy John Cleese-esque narrator. I wanted to weld his cybermouth shut.
But, given time and a little bit of ingenuity with a Recycling Plant I was soon making efficient, profitable, teeming-with-life starbases that lit up the barren, war-torn cosmos ready for a new era of economic prosperity and peace.
Sometimes the control can be a little clumsy, and the camera controls take a while to get used to (much smoother now higher res is support). But the semi-intuitive control system and the nice clean HUD/interface more than made up for it. The graphics were good for its time of release and the sound wasn't annoying, on the 2 lower decks it was a background rather than a stimulus or a feature, but my favourite place to take a break from the credit earning worlds of the industrial/pleasure decks was up on the biodeck, with its bizarre yet soothing cosmic harmonies and whale-song-like chirps and blips.
As far as value goes you can't fault it; I first bought it in a Sold Out Software box and therefore paid very very little for it (especially as they were doing 3 for 2 and it was the cheapest of the three). This isn't a great game, but it is a good game - and that is a good thing. It couldn't have been much better and remain the same game, but it really only is a good game. But we all need a good game from time to time. Beautiful, epic masterpieces are all fine and dandy, but you'd be worn out if all graphics made your retinas melt and every story was an epic saga.
If you see it on sale and have a spare tenner then hell, buy it. It'll be worth the 2 weeks you get out of it.

A Bird Story is a short silent story about a boy who finds and befriend a bird. I said that it's a story because it can't be called a game at all; you mostly sit on your chair watching the screen. Sometimes, the game prompts you to move, but that's only a few times which looks like forced in order to have a sort of interaction in the "game". Although the interaction part makes me stay focused (i snoozed a few times at the start because it's so boring and plain), the long useless walk in the first few part makes it better to be automated.
For a "game" which focuses on story-telling, i have to say that the story is quite bland. And i haven't even mentioning the nonsensical part in the end which makes me feel disappointed. At first, i thought that this will be a daily life story with a reality setting. Well, actually, I love with how the boy can make a plane out of notebook (although i feel somewhat weird with it), and the scene when they fly together. However, the last part about the boy running from 2 adults, which doesn't even explained the reason why (if it's because they want the bird to be caged, that's even make it worse), by flying with the plane, and then crashed to the ground and survives without any scratches, doesn't make any sense at all.
Although i somehow get the feelings that the story tries to bring out, it doesn't conveyed very well at all. The story meant to be touching, but i don't really feel it.
Apart from the story, the graphics are awesome. The sprites are very detailed, such as when the boy taking out the bird from the bag, and how the boy interacts with the bird. All of them have their own sprites and you can see them clearly, unlike most RPG Maker games where you have to visualize whatever the characters are doing yourself.
The backgrounds when the boy flies are also awesome. I even have to stop for a while to look at the awesomeness.
Most of the sounds are played well with the story. I said most because there are some bgms which doesn't, such as the bustling sounds. Most of the bgms are using piano as the instrument which makes it a very soft and a great choice for a story which is supposed to be touching.

text:
If you're looking for a proper sequel to To the Moon, this isn't it. This is a side project to tide us over until the sequel; there's no dialogue, no frame story, and even less gameplay, not to mention that the whole thing can be completed in something like an hour.
However, if you're looking for a game that successfully walks the same emotional tightrope as To the Moon without feeling like a retread, or if you haven't played To the Moon and just want an interesting narrative experience, this is the game for you.
A Bird Story is billed as a prequel/midquel to Finding Paradise, which is To the Moon's upcoming sequel. (Got that straight?) While it certainly holds up on a standalone narrative, at this point, comparisons to To the Moon are pretty much inevitable. In that respect, while it may not quite have the magic of To the Moon, it does a pretty good job of capturing the best elements of its precursor: the complex and intellectually engaging themes, the visually interesting, slightly surreal (well, more than slightly in this case), and altogether pleasing aesthetic, and perhaps most importantly, the subtly integrated pathos that pervades both the game's expressed narrative and its underlying tone and theming, or, in language the internet will understand, "the feels". This is a very emotional game, and a lot of that comes down to excellent pacing, visuals, and music, the latter of which is, as always with Kan Gao, gorgeous.
But there is more to this story than "the feels". As I mentioned earlier, A Bird Story is very surreal, not just in the blatantly abstract elements, like a giant paper plane that is somehow able to support the weight of a child and still fly, but also in the subtler things, like how scenes come and go with little, if any, transition, often seeping into each other and, on a few occassions, blending together entirely. It gives the entire experience a very dreamlike quality, which depending on your interpretation of the story, could signify a number of different things, or nothing at all. And that's the thing about this game: the absence of dialogue leaves it very much open to interpretation. It can be a game about love, friendship, and acceptance, or about grief, loneliness, and depression, depending solely on where you're coming from and what you think is important. Personally, I see it as a story about accepting responsibility and coming to terms with reality, but you very well might see something different. This ambiguity is, I think, the game's strongest element, and what distinguishes it most from To the Moon. It may be dispelled once Finding Paradise comes out, but until then, I heartily recommend this game, especially if you're an INFP like me who likes analyzing and reading into things.
As for problems, there aren't really any major ones. The short length doesn't bother me, since it allows for a tightly paced story that I can finish in less time than it takes me to watch a movie, for less than half of what a movie typically costs. The surrealism can be a bit distracting at times, but never enough to completely take me out of the experience. A handful of story moments are a little bit too drawn out, but then again, I'm not the most patient of people. All in all, I really can't find many issues with this game, unless I start comparing it to To the Moon, at which point I could find a million things that To the Moon does just a little bit better, but I'm not going to do that, because that's kind of unfair to this one, which was never meant to be the same kind of experience as To the Moon.
Final Verdict: Excellent game, totally worth $4. To the Moon's still better, though.

I loved every part of Axiom Verge, but left unchanged and unsatisfied. The graphics are amazing, the music is great (along with the near death sound integration), the gameplay is good for what it is, and the story is surprisingly unique despite me thinking I knew exactly how it was going to play out. However, throughout playing I just felt this sense of generic-ness, this feeling I had done it all before. Yes, obviously this is a metroid spin off, but even above that, I just felt like there was nothing new for me to discover. Sure there are secret weapons, hidden worlds, life and damage powerups for you to find in every nook and cranny- but I am talking about the life behind the game's eyes, it just felt like there was no originality or drive there for me to continue playing. Furthermore, I found the enemy design annoying at best, most of the weapons useless but novel (I think I only used 3 for more than 5 seconds despite collecting 8 or 9), the backtracking tedious, and the price too high for what I got. In short, I had fun while playing but left disappointed and just overall very static on how I felt while playing the game.
Maybe I am looking for the wrong game out of this? To compare with another metroid clone released recently, I loved Environmental Station Alpha. But ESA is even more of a carbon copy clone of metroid, with much less interesting weapon and powerup progression. But the secrets were more engaging, the bosses harder, and overall it just felt like more of an immersive experience. Axiom Verge is constructed ten times better than ESA in almost every department however it just feels lifeless in comparison to me. I was not nearly as hooked or addicted, although I did beat the game in 2 sittings (but mostly because the game was pretty short and I'm a binge gamer).
I'm sure if you're looking for a new metroid game and have been waiting for a good spiritual successor for a long time, you will be satisfied and enjoy Axiom Verge. I'm also sure that if you just love any metroid/vania that is out there as long as it has a decent production value, you'll also enjoy Axiom Verge. I guess I just went into it expecting to be blown away, and left with a mostly forgettable experience besides the art and music. Based on personal experience alone, I do not recommend this game at it's asking price.
EDIT: Reading other's reviews, I immediately realized what I was trying to say but couldn't put it into words: The exploration was just not fun. I felt like I was going through the motions despite the game going "Look, you can explore all this stuff over here!" and never felt "smart" or "engaged" whenever I found a secret. The one secret world I found was drilling randomly into a wall, and the multiple pickups I found were just mainly backtracking to previous areas that had a non-hidden powerup behind a progress locked (literal key or powerup you get later in the game) gate to get a 1/6 heart piece that requires you to get 5 other pieces to get your health up a pip. The weapons you get are worthless usually as previously stated, so other than cool animations or some ridiculously niche usage, there is really no point to explore past some lore you might be interested in.

Neptunia U, the spin off of classic Neptunia titles. Closest comparison of this game is probably Dynasty Warriors - but simplier. You are put into the arena, you fight hundreds of mobs, and occassional (mini) boss. Let's break it down into points:
Satisfying.
Even through you don't have that many combos, and abillities are just 2 buttons + animation, it looks very satisfying (who doesn't love 20+ numbers on screen wih 5 and more digits, while everything explodes and your character flies around?).
It is easy to master too! I got handle of it in 2 battles. 10 characters also give you some variety in gameplay.
Hyping up
Just entering the title screen made me love soundtrack of this game. It hypes you up a lot, and fits gameplay.
My personal favorites are surely: [One, two, three] and the title screen one.
Great port
So, I play on my crappy laptop with i3 and an old Nvidia 520m, and I am hanging around 60FPS most of the time. Drops only happen when I get my camera behind a barrier, or if I stream the game via Steam streaming to my friends (drops to 30fps - game speed slows down, instead of skipping frames).
Well, some pictures are kinda blurry, which might be port's fault, but aside of that, game is very colorful.
I did already touch this in gameplay, but I gotta say, this game is totaly fine with a keyboard. Only problem I often have is a camera (I just don't touch it outside of reset camera button). Button mapping can be a pain at first, but after you learn keys,  it's easy. It is surely better with controler, but as someone who doesn't have one, I am glad I can play with my keyboard.
- Storyline is same as you would expect from other Neptunia titles - Not really super serious, funny dialogue, likable characters.
- Game also has a lots of Fan Service, which might be a pro or a con, depends on you. Anyway, cloth tearing can be disabled when your characters hits.. lvl 20 i think? You just need a "hard" outfit. Althrough it will remove a boost from teared clothes.
- Also, game is full of reused assets (ASSets har har) you might know from Re;birth 1 or 2... but hey, they made a spin off out of it, and it is fun to play, so I have no problem with that.
- Quests... well there could use some variety. Most of the time its just "Kill X monsters" or "Kill a boss" (which means you have to kill X monsters to spawn him). "Collect an item" is another "Kill a boss", but without "Kill X monsters".
Overall its a very fun game and a great port with nice to look at combat. I would totaly recommend to at least try it (You can refund games in 2 hours anyway!)

Okay, so I want it to be known, that I've never played the original Wii U release before... This game... THIS GAME! Is almost exactly what I wanted in a FPS zombie surivival game. Single player, challenging, dark with flashlight management, inventory management, and well, pretty all around balanced. The framerate is... questionable at times (but it's loads better than games Ubisoft has created in the past like Far Cry 3), you get absolutely no health from small healing items (although, there's probably a reason for it I have yet to figure out), and I personally thought that the SONAR system was a bit over powered for a game like this (press 'T' and you can see the location of all nearby enemies, whether behind walls, behind you, or even below you), but I say they balanced it well in a way, making it have to go all the way to the end of your map in order to allow you to update the map with enemy locations.
You can board and block doors (although, take this from someone that's played it for a bit testing things out, these things only buy you enough time to get set up across the room or run for a few seconds), scavenge areas for stuff, and usually find things that are useful, but on the other hand, I didn't really care for the fact that I was walked through the first 30 minutes of the game (how much I've played)...
The guns (especially the handgun) seem a bit low on ammo. I mean, 4 bullets until a reload for the handgun is a LITTLE ridiculous in my opinion. I mean, what am I firing out of it, 50 caliber assault rifle shells? Actually, that'd be cool, please make an update for that...
Let's talk about good things again though, if you save the game, you are healed fully. This is a mistake I made at the end of my first play session, I used a medium first aid kit to bring my health to the green before saving, and after having done that, my health was full, so I wasted a first aid kit... Another good thing about the game is that, instead of restarting you a few steps behind at a checkpoint with nothing wrong, the game makes you start as a new character. I didn't die to find this out, but I know from footage I've seen before of the game. But the best thing about that is, you can pick up your items from the dead survivor you left, and pick up your journey from where you left off. Another good thing is, you can opt out of this experience, and go with, what I'm guessing is this game's "hard" difficulty... You basically play the same game with the same enemy difficulty, but when you die, you have to restart from the VERY beginning. I chose this difficulty, but I don't know just how far I'm going to get since on the first horde fight-off to protect the Safe House, I almost died. Then again, I did it entirely with a bat in the dark, so I kinda made it hard on myself...
Either way, as short as this review was, I know hardly anyone will read it, so if you did, thank you, and take my first just over half hour into consideration, but don't base your decision solely on my thoughts...

First of all, don't trust the 'average' review score - the topic of this particular game (pigeon dating) has attracted droves of people trying to be funny with one line review quips.
Simply speaking, the positive rating has me very very very confused because this is a terrible VN for the price.
Story aside, there are some major issues with the game itself:
1) "Maximum text speed" actually means "scrolls a bit faster" so you need to click twice to clear every message if you are a decent reader. Extremely annoying.
2) No setting to skip only scenes you haven't watched. You either skip or you don't, and if you miss new content too bad. This is made worse by how some of the endings are very similar (ie, basically the same ending except for an epilogue) but you need to replay the entire game, not knowing if there are new nuggets in the game.
3) Loading glitches, many times when I loaded it would not work and just show an empty text box. Needed to exit to title and load that way.
Main problems with the plot/art:
1) If you are like me, part of the allure of VNs is looking at some cool anime characters. This game has virtually none of that. The teaser shots you see at the top of the store page are basically all there is, the rest of the "art" you can find by going to google and searching for "pigeon." Maybe spend some effort drawing characters in different poses? Nope, just the same cropped pigeon picture from google. In certain parts you may be lucky and get uncropped pigeon pictures when the game devs were lazy.
2) There is a severe lack of development for all birds. It is not that uncommon, but "the bachelor syndrome" of going on 2 dates and falling in love forever for no apparent reason is alive and well. As such, the birds are super one-dimensional, from the mentally challenged pudding bird to the psycho daydreaming bird - they just rehash the same joke over and over, not changing or developing other sides to the birds at all.
3) To build on #2, the game is generally not funny. A couple jokes initially could elicit a chuckle, but the joke rehash gets very tiring. As this game is a quasi-parody of dating sims, I don't think that's a good thing.
4) The relationship scoring system is at best hidden, at worst useless. This is one of those games where the relationship stat is hidden and you need to guess where you stand with everyone. One of the major systems, where you pick your classes, is 100% useless in over half the endings.
5) True ending - without using spoilers, this game tries to tie everything together in a grand true ending that answers all questions. You want to know why pigeons talk? Why there is a school for pigeons? The ending tells you! However, because the premise is so preposterous, the game just throws twist after twist at you, all of which are not coherent. From daddy issues to orphanages to secret agents, the game throws all the stereotypical tropes you could possibly dream up in one jumbled mess. To be fair, the ending does actually flesh out the characters somewhat and probably takes a solid couple hours to get through. Of course the content in the true ending is probably more than the content in the rest of the game combined, see #2.
Long review for me as I rarely disagree so much with popular opinion. Bottom line is that I would NOT recommend this game unless it was 90% off or something, it is simply a poor example of a VN. Of course if you want to write a one line quip of a pigeon dating sim then you have no choice?

Startopia. Do I have a single friend who knows this game at all? My younger brother would probably be the only one. This is an obscure game that for some reason was forgotten, even by the publishers who (I think) refused to keep the game up to date and thus the Devs themselves kept working on it, making unofficial updates to the small amount of fans it still had. Sad, really. I got it for free a megaton of years ago, and I ended up getting a copy of it on Steam, so I might as well give it a review. As usual, I’m gonna start with what the game does wrong, then move up from there.
First and foremost, the community of the game is long dead. And it’s a shame because the game was quite fun on the multiplayer department when it came out (well, “came out”. I got a retail version of the game months after it was released, but it still had players back then).
Something that also kinda sucks is that the aliens that can actually fight don’t seem to have any real differences between them when fighting. They just shoot lasers out of nowhere. Fights just go down to which side has more aliens, security robots and security towers.
Random events can also wreck complete f#cking havoc on any base, as while some of those events are quite helpful, others are CATASTROPHIC. Think of an alien going into your base, looking like any other of the nearly thousand aliens on your base. Now think that he has an alien parasite inside that, if not treated IMMEDIATELY will kill the host from inside and suddenly have a 5 METER TALL BLACK GIANT SPIDER DESTROYING BUILDINGS AND EATING PEOPLE ALIVE. IT’S LITERALLY THE FIRST ALIEN MOVIE BUT WITH SPIDERS AND MORE DEAD PEOPLE.
Lastly, the game can come off as childish in some regards and f#cking creepy and disturbing on others. I’ve already mentioned the damn 5 meter tall spiders, but on the other side you have child-friendly prostitution, as angels give “love” to people who need it. Are you f#cking kidding me, the retail version had a +3 PEGI sticker and 5 hours into the game I’m running a jail filled with serial murderers and having people EXPLODE INSIDE OUT AND HAVING MUTANT ALIENS KILL EVERYTHING. AND NOT EVEN MENTIONING THAT YOU CAN HIRE PEOPLE TO MAKE ACTS OF TERRORISM ON YOUR RIVAL’S BASES. WHO RATED THIS GAME, AND WHO THOUGH THESE THINGS OUT!?
Leaving the 5 meter tall spiders out of the way, what do we have left? An interesting take on Sim-like Strategy games. However instead of ruling and making sure a town becomes big and important, you create a space facility to do pretty much anything you feel like.
And that should be the biggest point of the game, the freedom on normal games to just rule your side of the station however you feel like. And there’s plenty of useful buildings and things to do, from researching technologies and offering them to other people in trades for more than they’re worth to transform your station into a gigantic space-tourist trap.
The game also offers enough feedback about what’s happening, something a lot of Sim games seem to miss entirely. At any moment you can click on an alien and get informed by him what needs your station seems to lack, or maybe you can open the visitors window and check that instead.
The amount of races is kinda low, but they’re well done, all of them expanding to their own set of works. Some of them are able to make recyclers and factories work, others can work hospitals, you get the idea. There’s a few that are completely optional to hire like the religious guys who’ll turn your upper deck into some sort of biblical heaven, while the purple medusa hippies will fill that same upper deck with tons of trees that will produce resources.
Something I also enjoyed back when I played this game are some of the player interaction stuff. You don’t like how others are attracting more people than you? Hire a spy, send it to some of them and watch on live feed as he places a bomb somewhere, then runs away. Or maybe hold auctions between players with buildings or resources you don’t need. Not many other Sim games offer a multiplayer aspect, and in that regard this game filled that, even though nowadays you will most likely only play against bots.
I also really like the laboratories and how the tech tree works. Sure, you can always buy those buildings whenever you get the chance (but for a higher price), but with a lab you can just pick ANYTHING and send it to the lab, where it will be researched and your scientists will discover something from it (for example, sending trash will discover recyclers and trash-cans). I also find it great fun that you can even send CORPSES OF ALIENS WHO DIED ON YOUR FACILITY, and thus quickly learn why they died, being either natural cause or not.
Do I recommend this game? Yeah. It’s a fun strategy-simulator game with a fun premise. Sure it won’t win any damn awards and it’s community is as dead as progress with Half-Life 3, but for it’s price, you get your money’s worth on value. Specially on a sale.
TL;DR Edition: A Sim-like Strategy game where you rule your space station and turn it into whatever you feel like, while 5 meter tall spiders try to eat your tourists. Fun game on a sale, and it’s price is already quite low.

A game that incorporates a strange mix of gameplay elements that have divided professional gaming reviewers. According to Metacritic, the game's average score is a 69; while it's range has varied from a 4 to an 8 out of 10. More on the later:
In the game, you're tasked with killing over 100 unique enemies, think of them as 'mini-bosses'. They're scattered throughout the world, in order to proceed in a map you have to kill a set amount. Along the way you gain weapon upgrades and progress through a loose story that might as well not be there. The maps are big, and while they have branching paths, you're always gently led to where you have to go next. So it's kind of like Metroid, but MUCH easier. You're NOT gonna get lost.
The stuff that contributed to its bad score: 1.the controls. They work, but don't expect to platform, aim, and shoot simultaneously and have an easy time at it. 2.The mini-games. Each time you get a unique enemie's health to 0, you're presented with a mini-game you must complete to finish them off (think 'Warioware'). Each game brings a unique death animation. It's cool, until you realize there are 100 enemies, around 20 games, and each death is 10-17 seconds long. It can get repetetive; but I found the games to be varied enough so that it never got tiresome.
Overall, I'd say its a game that OBVIOUSLY had a lot of love put into it and it oozes a unique style. While it's a little on the easy side, there are very few side missions, and the mini-game novelty (and death animations) wear off a fifth of the way through, its still worth a purchase if you want a decent platformer; 7/10.

Hell Yeah! Wrath of the Dead Rabbit is a modern day take, and parody, of classid 2D platform games.  I found it very entertaining, with fun gameplay, impressive visuals (seriously, the aesthetic of this game is incredible, it looks really good), and lots of beautiful, gorey, gratuitous violence.
Hell Yeah! sports great controller support, a nice soundtrack, and really reminded me of Jazz Jackrabbit in a way - it's the closest game I've ever played to it, and it really took me back.  If you've ever played Jazz Jackrabbit (if you haven't go play it now) you'll immediately see the resemblence, and you'll be reminded of a game Epic would have made had they had the resources modern day game creators do.  It has snappy load times, great optimization, a *huge* amount of customizable hats and skins for your character to unlock and find, and lots of weapons at your disposal to destroy your enemies with.
That said, it isn't a perfect game - the controls aren't very tight, they're actually pretty "floaty" (in a bad way), and dying can make you feel at times that it wasn't your fault, but rather the controller or keyboard.  It's not like Super Meat Boy where you know it was you and not the interface.  This, coupled with the fact that the respawn locations can get pretty far away from each other towards the later part of the game, can cause for some aggravating gameplay mechanics, where you're backtracking through stuff you've done 10 times before and keep dying at the same spot because you couldn't stop on a dime like you wanted to.  The game also doesn't have many options (graphical or otherwise) to set, it's really plug and play, and you can tell it was designed for consoles as well as the PC.  I couldn't even remap my buttons properly.
Besides those negatives, Hell Yeah! is a riot.  There are fun little minigames every time you kill a "boss" monster, but they do repeat themselves (there's 99 monsters, so this isn't too bad, as there is a large variety of the mini-games and they're all grapically pleasing and end with a huge explosion of blood).  There's also a section of the game called "The Island", and it's where all the "boss" monsters you've killed go to hang out - it's a neat little feature as you can micromanage them to earn you extra money, life, and special rewards like new hats and skins for your character.  I did find it a little weird you had to actually quit out of the game and go back to the main menu to access this area, but, as stated before, the game is optimized well so it wasn't a huge issue.
In conclusion, Hell Yeah! is a funny, fresh, current, and hip platformer that has a great aesthetic style.  I enjoyed it, although found it tedious at times.  Had it had better controls and a few more tweaks here and there this would be a must-play, but unfortunately as it stands it sits at the middle of the pack.  B

A Bird Story is a textless interactive adventure story that's about an hour long. The amount of user-input required throughout A Bird Story hits the fine line between immersion and control; it felt like I was in a movie and experiencing the story rather than watching the story unfold before my eyes.
In conclusion, I'd definitely recommend A Bird Story if you enjoyed To the Moon, or if you want a short story that leaves a warm and fuzzy feeling in your heart.

The Neptunia series isn't exactly well known for its "exciting" gameplay and this one's no different. The idea of going from RPG to beat-em-up/hack-and-slash thing was there but the way it's done I don't believe makes it anymore exciting especially when repetition is a trait this series comes with.
The default keybindings are abysmal, but rebindable. It doesn't help that the tutorial is meant for controllers and  that all the mouse can do when it's used at all is move the camera around but only while holding the LMB. The game was meant for a controller and not much work was put into the thought of keyboard (& mouse) play.
One piece of trouble with the actual game is that you're practically going through the same dungeon each and every time with a goalset barely different from the last. "Clear condition" for a "quest" may be to kill 300some enemies or find the exit but it all just comes down to "go here and kill what you see" with barely any form of thought into actually doing so, and that's the entire game up to the final boss and its "end-game" content.
There are a teeny few bit of combos from the melee characters (which having a minute number itself isn't helpful for this kind of game) but the three ranged ones have far less and when they transform it doesn't take much effort to obliterate everything and win harmless since you can keep floating around and shooting while keeping the loads of enemies stunned. The transformations are supposed to be temporary but all the ranged characters can go by transformed for the duration of an entire run because of how much of a mob they can keep hitting.
With the look of how practically all of the recycled enemies have always been throughout the series most of 'em don't exactly give off that threatening look so I didn't get a whole lot of fun out of wailing on loads of plush toy look-a-likes. They eventually hit pretty hard but the repetition still kicks in when doing the same task over and over again.
You're free to choose which dungeon you go to. Entering and completing "NEW" dungeons eventually progresses the story, which itself I found was very underwhelming & short, at least in comparison to its RPG counterparts.
Hitting the level cap doesn't take much work especially if going through the "end-game" content. Lily rank returns in this game and obviously increases for the partners you choose to go in a dungeon together and as usual the higher the rank with said characters the more benefits they get when paired up. Trying to maximize Lily ranks however proves to be more work though than leveling.
Supposedly with different Lily ranks per character you can press whatever button or key in the Lily rank menu and the selected pair will engage in small dialogue. If you've got the English dubbing off and can't understand Japanese, there aren't any subtitles to help for that since the dialogue itself is on-the-spot unlike the cutscenes that at least give you an idea of what they're saying if not something completely different because of the localization.
Apparently you can't pause during those VN cutscenes and can't rewatch them if you accidentally skipped 'em unless you've got a previous save in hand for the occassion.
So it's a badly localized, bare-bones action Nep game without a whole actual lot of Neps at least to give me a proper time with the addition of the usual repetition but with relatively more poor gameplay that more-or-less entices with characters being stripped when hit a lot, which in itself eventually becomes a bore. You can apparently be rewarded with clothing that doesn't break when equipped in case you get tired of the stripping and/or if you're a prude.

This could have been a good game. I could have enjoyed it. Scratch that; I did enjoy it. To a limited extent.
In theory this is one of the better games I have played of its kind. Simple, somewhat repetitive and grindy, and full of numbers, just the way I like it. In practice however... It's an unpolished, crude, and messy game.
Controls are weird and take a bit to get used to. I eventually got the hang of it and managed to play the game rather fluidly, but I can see that not being the case for a lot of people. There's a limit to how much you learn from the tutorials, and I would never judge anyone for failing to figure out the game and giving up. (Moreso than in other games, that is).
The menus are tedious and  break, items are grouped together weirdly and I've had cases where I've had to spend several minutes burning skill books on pirates to access completely unrelated items as there is no scrolling feature in the gven subset of items. Weaponry is weirdly nondescriptive, and I have refrained from buying a lot of weapons as the listed Damage Per Second for weapons in the store is greatly misleading.
The game also suffers from, as most other reviewers mention, late game performance issues. Once my ship's size reached some fifteen by thirty blocks in size, the game froze for well over half a second every time I placed a tile. Adding twentyfive crewmembers made the entire game experience run in a rather nasty way. I've had several crashes, and loading screens become waiting games at the point in the game I reached. In short, progress is punished by performance loss.
Had this game been shown a bit more love and attention, It could have become one of my more liked games. I like it as is, but it's in the way you love a dog who tries its best and is very soft, but poops on the carpet, rolls in any available mud, and conveniently has to go outside whenever you are asleep. It's debatable whether or not it's worth the effort in the end.
In short; it's a sweet little game that could have been much more enjoyable were it not seemingly a rushed and unpolished project, coding and content wise. Do not under any circumstances buy it at full price, though if you have the game sense necessary to figure out the control system and enjoy casual looting and leveling up it might be worth its price when it gets a solid cut off during some sort of sale.

Reasonably high quality take on the Metroidvania genre. Not the best example of it, though. If you need a fix, you can't go wrong, but maybe you could go back and play Super Metroid too?
Tight gameplay, feels very natural with a controller in hand, though teleport-dash input is a glaring issue. It -really- needs to be bound to a button and not directional double-tap.
The corruption/glitch aesthetic is a nice twist and spices up the regular gameplay, changing enemies with your glitch ray and whatnot, but outside from that application it is dreadfully underutilized and never explored in any meaningful way other than to provide roadblocks and ability requirements.
Large but inconsistent weapon variety (some obviously strong, some nearly useless, many in between that are outshined by the more useful ones), visually impressive but weakly designed boss encounters, somewhat forgettable music. Graphics seem to be hit or miss on people, I found them a little lacking; aside from color there's few strong, consistent, eye-catching features of a given zone and everything is a bit bland and lacking flavor. But the outdoor environments were a little more pleasing.
Plot is, without question, completely overrated by the majority of reviews I've seen. It's adequate, but there is little build-up and almost no sense of drama or weight to the events. The ending -- even the true ending -- is a little disappointing, and feels like there was supposed to be more gameplay to follow it up and conclude things better.
I'm harshing on the game a bit here when the truth is that I enjoyed the time I put into it. It doesn't hold your hand or tell you where to go, letting you get immersed into exploring each zone at your leisure. The exploration and puzzles are done well and hit all the right buttons, though it has a habit of throwing a lot of branching paths at you that result in dead ends, forcing you to backtrack because you don't have a given ability. But that's an issue about the genre itself, isn't it?
I would like to give this game a negative rating, just to balance out the average a little and make it more representitive of the quality of the game, but... I get the feeling that's like yelling into a windstorm so nuts to it.
(I personally think the teleport dash is kickin' rad, more games need teleport dashes)

This game is quite the throwback to every metroidvania you can think of and delivers on a lot of the same vibes while subverting your expectations at the same time. The story is interesting, and just the overall feel of the controls are tight as heck. In general If you're having that metroidvania itch this will satisfy it on literally all possible fronts but one
and that's with enemy design.
The vast majority of the game is thoroughly enjoyable, but at the same time the vast majority of enemies end up being bullet sponges, surprise punches in the face, or tiny ultra mobile whisps that chunk your health away. Regardless of the guns or upgrades you end up having they end up being a frustrating and demoralizing thing to be constantly fighting as you backtrack (or progress) through the world.
The saddest culmination of the bad enemy design is definitely the bosses, most of which either end up being "stand in one spot and shoot" or "find this very specific way to cheese it out". Neither of which would be a problem if there was something inbetween those two difficulty extremes.
In general I'd still say it's a great game with some cool inventive weapons, the sole issue is with enemy design, and it pains me to pick fault with it because of how incredible the game is otherwise. I would still say it's a game that you should experience if you can despite all of that

This is a great game; there are definitely pros and cons though;
PROS -
Great pixelated graphics, its very nostalgic, but its pixelated in a more HD type of way.
You can customize your ship fully, making it as big or as small as you'd like.
It keeps in the theme; not straying from it. It sticks to its name; pixel piracy, its pixelated and its pirate-y. What more do you need?
Its very fun and you'll generally have a good time playing it.
You don't need that good of a computer to run it, I have a 4GB RAM Integrated Intel HD Graphics on a Mac Laptop, and it runs just fine. The only problem is people say it has a memory leak; but I haven't experienced that.
CONS -
The whole game is repetitive in every aspect, lets start by saying the repetitive things;
--- start of repetitive ---
Every crew member says the same stale thing, even your character; "BLOW THE MAN DOWN" loudly and annoyingly, "AHOY SCALLYWAGS!!!!" every 4 seconds. It never changes and is very stale.
The buildings, islands, people, and everything in-between is extremely repetitive. Sometimes theres a banana bush in an island; thats about as extreme as it gets. You might think, "but they have different stores in different islands," yes they do, but ALL of the stores are the same. Its just annoying to have to go to different islands to get what you need.
The enemies are extremely repetitive; no spoilers but; the main story goal is to take down 4 Legendary Pirates. Could be cool, right? They're the same thing, but they're LVL 10. Thats it. LVL 5 pirates are easy enough, but JUST LVL 10? I was expecting more like LVL 100; but nope. Once you take down the 1st Legendary Pirate you just stand there thinking; "wow, that was it? talk about anti-climatic" and you go about your day. All the enemies have the same AI and don't have much variety. Sure, there are bombers, maybe even people who clean decks, but in all of those people, they're the same, act the same, and when you're fighting it doesn't really feel like your fighting.
--- end of repetitive ---
It is extremely annoying how when you're creating your character, you cannot go back.
Example, "I find a hairstyle I really like, and I want to see if theres another. If I do that I cannot go back to my hairstyle because you can only go forward, and if you DO go forward, you'll have to (even though I like the customization) scroll through another 50 hairstyles.
CONCLUSION -
Its a very fun game, and I would recommend it to other people!
I'm not saying its the best game out there, but I would suggest you buy it; but not for the full 9.99, get it on a sale.
I personally enjoyed it, and I think you will too.
It definitely has some flaws that can and SHOULD be fixed, but its alright other than that.
Considering this is made by 2 people, I think its a pretty fun game!
I recommend this game.
It's fun for few hours, but it gets repetitive pretty quickly, worth buying during sale.

Highly recommended for anyone who has ever played or watched Lacrosse, and young athletes who may not have been exposed yet to help learn the game. The AI engine and controls are top notch, with the light controller prompts on screen you will soon pick up how to play this very robust sports game. This is an amazing sports game release by any measure, especially as an independent studio release.

Simply put, this game is not worth $50. It is basically a reskin of the games for Xbox they released several years ago with added career modes. I played Lacrosse at the DIII level and while this game does do some things well, it gets bogged down by an unexplained control scheme, poor AI, and wonky physics. Half-field offense is extremely difficult as is 1v1 dodging because you can never accurately judge when the D can take the ball away from you. A story of rebellion against an unjust dictator(s), of human integrity, and of magic vs technology. There's also a random chick who threatens, emptily, to eat you but never tries. Unless you let her!
You play as Claret, a mechanic in the upper level of human society who repairs airships and makes the occasional automaton who can beep. She somehow understands perfectly because reasons. In her life are her brother and some random dude. Her brother ends up being an awful guy (for reasons you'll learn five minutes in), but only for the first 10 minutes. Afterwards, he changes into a damsel in distress and then we forget he exists. If you don't have character art/portraits, then no one cares about you. Welcome to video games.
The game play is typical old school RPG affair: you go to various lands; a desert, a volcano (that has surprising soothing music), a forest, ruins, and a multi-layered, caste style city. You meet various people from all background, five of which are usable in combat, and then save the world.
Combat is a bit different than many games. For the first half it's, arguably, optional. You can find shining dots across the map and use that to level-up which give more exp than the actual monsters (only early on). They're pretty easy to see to don't worry about missing any, besides, there's always the actual combat system to level up on. Once you get all five characters, the dots effectiveness diminishes and killing monsters starts to be rewarding. Fortunately, the battles can be fun.
Each character has a set of skills they learn, and that depends on their role in your party and the class you choose from. At several points in the game, you have the option (meaning it's also optional) to upgrade character classes and learn new skills and passively upgrade stats.
Here's the kicker, though. All of the skills are useful throughout all of the game. We've all played games where the early skills become obsolete about 10 minutes after learning it but Skyborn isn't one of those games. That level 1 skill is still useful throughout the entire game or, at the very least, becomes a bridge to the more powerful, expensive, skills learned later in the game. This is especially true for the non-magical characters who use energy (EN) to attack. These characters gain EN when using basic attacks, or 0 EN skills, and release the EN when using the more powerful skills. Buff/debuffs are one or two of a kind and are useful at all portions. There is also a threat system that works similar to MMORPGS where, whoever has the most threat, gets punched in the face. There is a bar that says who has what and is only relevant to enemy parties. You can still attack whoever.
You also have the option to play each character in a variety of ways. Do you want your mage to do damage with in-hands or with their spells? Do you one character to be the buff/debuff character or the straight DPS? Which character do you want to the tank? Even the gear add to this. Late game, there are multiple options for equipment for each character. Some raise INT to do more damage with skills, some raise STR to do more with in-hands. There are some limitations but there are freedoms not seen often in Skyborn. *Keep in mind, I was playing on easy mode. Apparently, hard has more set restrictions.
Characters are not on-screen in combat but the enemy sprites are. Sadly, there is no animation but animation is hard and expensive for a small 2-3 people company. Spell effects do exist and most are 32-bit pretty so there's something to look at while you shoot a “totally not a manticore” in the face. There are no random battles and each enemy cluster is visible on the screen and only enters combat when it touches you.
The characters all have a definite personality and the developers did a good job of trying to get you to emphasize with them. There's the strong, independent female lead, the rich guy who actually just wants to be the hero, the good natured girl-beast who has been treated like an outcast, the sick of being pushed around mage, and the always questioning “superior race”. When one character can no longer do a certain “thing” at the end of the game, you feel bad. When you find about the final fate of those captives, you're shocked and disgusted. I was torn during the middle of the game when faced with the moral dilemma. Alas, this is a linear game so the moral dilemma didn't fall into my hands but was played out as it did.
The game boasts an original soundtrack that is pretty good. Nothing spectacular but nothing ruins the mood. It's all very relaxing and worth listening to once or twice. I'd get into specifics but I'm a bad musician and everyone has their own tastes so here's some streamable links so you can decide on your own:
Art Work is pretty. I'm not familiar with RPGMaker so I can't say how much of it has been over saturated in the games. Typical retro style; look at the screenshots.
Overall, Skyborn was a fun experience and, since the game is often on sale, is worth the money spent and time “wasted”. I got 16 hours out of it and I've seen the game sell for a few bucks USD and it's worth it on sale.

Yep.  It's an otome parody, in which you play a human high school student dating sapient birds.  That's Japan for you.
is full of glitter, hearts, and silly, mindless entertainment... on the surface.  As you repeatedly play through to reach the various endings, the game will keep dropping hints - some big, some small - about a larger, more sinister plot.  Should you persevere and reach most or all of the normal endings, you'll unlock the option to play through the BBL route, which reveals exactly what's been going on behind the scenes.  That route is, if you ask me, the real reason to play the game.  It is its own special brand of crazy, going above and beyond the strangeness of the rest of the game, and taking it to a much darker place.  Moreover, it's considerably longer than any of the normal routes, and not marred, as they are, by having a shallow plot delivered in bite-sized episodes.  Unlocking it may become tedious, but at least the game provides a skip button.
Even if you're not interested in playing, I highly recommed reading
, which is clearly the single greatest review of any video game ever published.

This is a so-so stealth with combat game. Enemies have the usual limited vision, hearing, and intelligence that are hallmarks of the genre. The abilities and gadgets you have are decent. The setting and story are ok. If not for the hamhanded way morality works, this would be a solid middle of the pack game.
The game's intent is that your actions throughout the game shape the reactions of others and thus the story. Translation: the more you kill, the less you can do anything else. For example, if you killed a bunch of thugs in a previous mission, their gang leader in the next mission might not help you. Not a bad idea, right?
The first problem is the huge lack of non-lethal ways to neutralize people. You can have a total of 107 lethal items (bullets, grenades, etc), but only 10 sleep darts. None of your special abilities are non-lethal. The only unlimited method for non-lethal takedowns is a sleeper hold on an unsuspecting target, which leads to...
The second problem is that if you kill to defend yourself, it is no different than killing indiscriminately. So if accidentally alert some thugs while trying to avoid them, your options are to try to run away, kill them all, or reload your last save. Alerted enemies
use lethal force and you cannot negotiate with them.
The third problem is there's no way to turn the tide once violence has started. Your morality is cumulative over the entire game. If you killed several people in the previous mission because they accidentally saw you, the next mission has more people because there was a recent rise in violence. If you got seen and had to kill fewer people, what chance do you have with more people?
All together, these problems cause a perpetual escalation of violence. It's just not fun to constantly reload your last save to avoid killing the NPC that detected you. In the end, I gave up and resigned myself to not caring about who I killed -- the exact opposite of what the game intended to do.

I've played a lot of city building type strategy games, SimCity, Rome Total War, WarCraft, StarCraft, their sequels, and more. This one is unique in a number of ways. It has charm, amazing attention to detail, and an awesome set of missions that really introduce you to the game. I played this when I was younger and it had just come out and fell in love. I kept coming back to it even when I lost the disc and my graphics card couldn't handle the textures. I'm not gonna lie, I pirated this game so many times just so I could keep playing. And I bought it, despite the fact that I didn't necessarily have to, because it's just that good and these developers deserve the money. I don't know if you're still in business Mucky Foot, or who owns the rights to this game, but I would KILL for a sequel!
The economy is incredibly diverse and you can inhabit any sector of it that you wish or fits the mission. Grow or manufacture basic goods to sell, buy basic goods and research more advanced buildings, or be a straight trader and buy low from certain alien races and sell high to others. You can focus on tourism, religious pilgrimages, security and war, farming, or manufacturing and selling. Certain aliens will do certain jobs that are vital to basic functions and making money. There is fine detail control on what buildings charge for services, Roller Coaster Tycoon style. (P.S. SimCoaster is better!) And VAL, your AI helper, is hilarious.
If you like city building games with an awesome economy system ....in SPACE!, then get this. It stands the test of time. Graphics are a bit old, but they still look damn good. In fact, I've made myself want to play it again right now!

If you like the aspect of the half life series but want a multi-player theme this is it.

Like most others on here, I've played To the Moon first and was happy to see the next release by K Gao and FreeBird (ha ha). A Bird Story tells the tale of a boy who rescues an injured bird. It's a lot less gameplay-intensive than To the Moon, making it almost factually incorrect to call it a game; it's more like an extended cutscene with the occasional forced key pressing so that it can still pass as one.
That doesn't take away from the experience though. Its predecessor wasn't particularly hardcore either; they're basically both point-and-click stories and A Bird Story is unashamedly so.
As with TTM, ABS features a bittersweet story coupled with an incredibly moving soundtrack. Neither live up to the standards of TTM, but this shouldn't really be a comparison. It's good in its own right, albeit slightly pompous at times, reeling in on the player's emotional attachment when there is none.
Still, some scenes were a punch in the gut. Good experience if you're looking to relieve a mildly masochistic impulse. Worth picking up if it's ever on sale or you've got some leftover balance in your account.

It's a story of a lonely child who finds a friend in an unexpected place. This is a real highpoint in the art game/walking sim/narrative adventure/whatever genre - well worth the entry fee.

Finally, after years and three lazy ports they at least managed to fix Neptune's broken 3D mesh and idle animation.
Of course, with any other franchise you'd expect the devs and publisher to fix and improve a lot more than that, but that's not how Idea Factory roll. So,.... Yay!!!^^
The game itself feels quite polished for a Neptunia game, but it's also shorter and less "complex" than the previous titles.
Visuals are ok, most 3D assets were recycled from Rebirth1/2/3 anyway (the "HD"-textures, models and animations are "of course" even older), a quite convenient "running gag" with the Neptunia series.
Somehow the effects during fights look a bit nicer than in Victory.
Maybe they sacrificed a couple more minutes of their precious time to tweak the shaders, or maybe the game simply runs really well with the current Nvidia drivers. Who knows, and who cares.
The game goes really easy on my hardware, my primary GTX970 doesn't even bother to power up beyond P2 state and gives me constant 60 fps at 20-30% load, while my second 970 sleeps through all the action that is unleashed. CPU load is even less noteworthy. So, while the first "rebirth" tried to hog more resources than it deserved, this port seems to be far better optimised and will probably run smoothly on many laptops and older desktop rigs.
I use a XBoneOne controller, which is imo the best input device for games of this series, but mouse support seems to be further improved as well. ( by which I mean precision and input lag, you still have to manually edit the config file and add your desired key bindings, so a gamepad is still the way to go )
The rest is simply what you'd expect from a Neptunia game. Nerdy japanese humor, parodies and game references, lots of fanservice and yuri subtext,.. and of course the characters don't just occasionally break the fourth wall, they once more tear it down right from the start.
So, yeah... it's a Neptunia game, which means it's as charming as it is flawed.
A bit simpler and faster paced than the other games of the series, but basicly   moar  Nep Nep .
And like any Neptunia/ Idea Factory game this title is also rediculously overpriced.
I picked it up for 17€ (-40% promotion offer), which imo should be the regular price.
Maybe even a bit less.
Neptunia games are fun and entertaining with well written cute waifus, that's why we still buy them.
But even if you can create halfway decent sequels by simply writing new dialogue and recycling 99% of the 3D assets,
neither does it mean that you should, nor that such a garage kit game build is worth half the price of a AAA title.
So yes, buy it, it's a fun game like the other Neptunia titles, but buy it when it's on sale for half or less.
Even if it's not about the money because you're super rich or whatever, be patient and do it for the statement^^.

This game is basically XCOM put into an FPS game, and so it feels. Controls are pretty clunky for an FPS, and the weapons don't feel very powerful, even if they deal much damage. The only fun, but weak weapon I found to be the shotgun, which knocks the enemies back like you would expect.
The weapon variety is lacking, there are a few categories (Shotgun - SMG - Rifle - Sniper - "Heavy Stuff"), but each of them gets their "Projectile" - "Laser" - "Plasma" variants, which all essentially feel the same.
The story is subjectively better than what we got in XCOM 2, which is particularily hard, but still nice. Mission-Wise it's very linear, and many aspects seem tacked-on to resemble XCOM, even though it doesn't make sense for this setting (e.g. the global map).
The biggest issue are the controls and the team-management though. Your teammates will run straight into crossfire, roll into grenades or run straight in your line of fire. You can make them move and focus a target, but that's practically unusable since they will then lose all their brain and shoot into walls instead of the enemy right to their side.
I basically just used the Overview to make them use their abilities, which they wouldn't use by themselves. They have unlimited ammo, but no grenades, and deal way less damage than the player, which makes it unfeasible to send them anywhere on their own, because if they "die" (get knocked out), you have 10s to run to them and "stabilize" them, which stops them from dying, but removes them from the fight. Basically, I finished many big fights alone, because the teammates would just lie down and do nothing for 10mins straight (c'mon, I know XCOM was like this as well, but there were teams of 6 and not 3).
Controls then: Since it's a standard 3rd-person cover shooter, the magnetic-gluey covers can't be missing. I died multiple times to a cover not letting me go or not letting me get into cover. With a keyboard, "Get into cover" is bound to Shift, which also is sprint, so I would end up getting sucked into covers where I didn't want to go. Because the overview selects the agent based on your mouse position, I repeatedly selected the wrong agent, because the mouse position is not clearly displayed.
Also: Checkpoints are sometimes seriously ♥♥♥♥ed up. Hard fight coming up? Yeah let's put the checkpoint 3 rooms before and make you listen to 3 dialogs and 1 cutscene everytime you have to redo the fight.
All in all: It's XCOM. It's buggy and most of the difficulty just comes from either not having enough ammo because some freak just spawns a lot of imps or because the controls mess up. If you're a fan, you'll have a lot of fun with it, even though I'd rather play a more modern version of XCOM and not the beginnings. There are a lot of references and the universe fits.
Don't get me wrong, the game was fun. But if it wasn't for the XCOM-setting, it would be yet another generic and mediocre shooter that nobody asked for. I recommend this game for fans of XCOM. Shooterfans should be more careful.

Near the end of the first mission I decided to turn the difficulty of this game down to rookie.  Not because this game is hard.  If you use strategy and go very slow it's ridiculously easy though slow.  No I turned it down so I can get through this game faster.  12 hours later, I'm done, but I wish there was a faster mode.
The Bureau isn't a bad game.  It has all the modern convenience of games in the ps3 era of gaming, it has achievements, great menus, and an interesting hub.  Well not exactly interesting, but at least it's a good looking hub.
Problem is nothing else really is worthy of praise.  The combat is slow and plodding but relatively easy as long as you don't run out of ammo, and you tend to run out of ammo often enough to be annoying.  Again, not hard, just annoying.   The AI is tactical until it's done and then it gets stupid.  It'll run away form places you pin them too, or stay pinned to places at times when you need them to move.  Basically they'll do the opposite of what you want them to do.   And the levels... dear god the levels.
It's not that the levels are bad either.  They're just bland.  Most of the main mission levels are unique, but they get revisited in the six side missions, and they aren't exactly interesting.  Not horrible, but not good.  The levels also take about 90 minutes a piece which is very long in my opinion.  If you die the auto save is relatively forgiving, usually only losing you about 10-20 minutes of progress depending on how long you take on the current battle, but 10-20 minutes is still quite a bit if you die or reset often.  And the thing is 90 minutes starts to feel like a death march when you don't really do anything other than shoot enemies the whole time.  There's minimal talking, minimal collectibles (and they don't unlock an achievement, thank god) but it's still very plodding for the pace of the game.
The real reason I dropped the difficulty is I wanted to avoid risking losing even 10-20 minutes of progress, which still happened when I let someone die, but overall.  I want to spend a lot of time playing this game, in fact I wanted to finish playing it as fast as I can, and while it wasn't bad enough to quit right away as my rule is to try to "finish games" I wanted to make it as fast it through as fast as I could, and that was in the first mission, the first 90 minutes of the game.
I've played some REAL bad games.  Hack_me is an awful game and doesn't deserve to be played by anyone.  Ryse I'd argue is too awful to really be a full fledged game.  The Bureau isn't that.  It's not "bad" it's not "awful."  But it's not good.  It's the most average of average games, and I'll honestly say the game reviewers pegged this one right, it's about a 66 on meta critic.  That's about as average as it gets, and that's not a game I'd recommend.   This also isn't a borderline game where I'd like to push.  No this is a firm "not recommended", yet it's not a game I hate.  It's not worthless, and it was surprisingly not painful, just a game I wish was over because it wasn't that fun.
It's an odd feeling to really talk about it, but don't play this.  Want a Sci fi game exactly like this?  Mass Effect's original trilogy is far superior, go play that and you will have a great time, even the third one.   Want a strategy game? Xcom Enemy Within and Xcom 2 are absolutely excellent, go play those, they're not only better, not only good games, but they're excellent games.   But The Bureau?  I got it in a humble bundle that I bought for other games, and like I said I'm not angry about playing it, just disappointed more in myself and my waste of time.
