Reasonably high quality take on the Metroidvania genre. Not the best example of it, though. If you need a fix, you can't go wrong, but maybe you could go back and play Super Metroid too?
Tight gameplay, feels very natural with a controller in hand, though teleport-dash input is a glaring issue. It -really- needs to be bound to a button and not directional double-tap.
The corruption/glitch aesthetic is a nice twist and spices up the regular gameplay, changing enemies with your glitch ray and whatnot, but outside from that application it is dreadfully underutilized and never explored in any meaningful way other than to provide roadblocks and ability requirements.
Large but inconsistent weapon variety (some obviously strong, some nearly useless, many in between that are outshined by the more useful ones), visually impressive but weakly designed boss encounters, somewhat forgettable music. Graphics seem to be hit or miss on people, I found them a little lacking; aside from color there's few strong, consistent, eye-catching features of a given zone and everything is a bit bland and lacking flavor. But the outdoor environments were a little more pleasing.
Plot is, without question, completely overrated by the majority of reviews I've seen. It's adequate, but there is little build-up and almost no sense of drama or weight to the events. The ending -- even the true ending -- is a little disappointing, and feels like there was supposed to be more gameplay to follow it up and conclude things better.
I'm harshing on the game a bit here when the truth is that I enjoyed the time I put into it. It doesn't hold your hand or tell you where to go, letting you get immersed into exploring each zone at your leisure. The exploration and puzzles are done well and hit all the right buttons, though it has a habit of throwing a lot of branching paths at you that result in dead ends, forcing you to backtrack because you don't have a given ability. But that's an issue about the genre itself, isn't it?
I would like to give this game a negative rating, just to balance out the average a little and make it more representitive of the quality of the game, but... I get the feeling that's like yelling into a windstorm so nuts to it.
(I personally think the teleport dash is kickin' rad, more games need teleport dashes)

This game is quite the throwback to every metroidvania you can think of and delivers on a lot of the same vibes while subverting your expectations at the same time. The story is interesting, and just the overall feel of the controls are tight as heck. In general If you're having that metroidvania itch this will satisfy it on literally all possible fronts but one
and that's with enemy design.
The vast majority of the game is thoroughly enjoyable, but at the same time the vast majority of enemies end up being bullet sponges, surprise punches in the face, or tiny ultra mobile whisps that chunk your health away. Regardless of the guns or upgrades you end up having they end up being a frustrating and demoralizing thing to be constantly fighting as you backtrack (or progress) through the world.
The saddest culmination of the bad enemy design is definitely the bosses, most of which either end up being "stand in one spot and shoot" or "find this very specific way to cheese it out". Neither of which would be a problem if there was something inbetween those two difficulty extremes.
In general I'd still say it's a great game with some cool inventive weapons, the sole issue is with enemy design, and it pains me to pick fault with it because of how incredible the game is otherwise. I would still say it's a game that you should experience if you can despite all of that

One of the best games I played in 2015, this is a solid Metroidvania whose only real problem is that there isn't a sequel.
Great soundtrack, interesting weapon mechanics, a story if you're looking for it, and all of the map features a trace-your-steps simulator could ask for.

Now I loved Metroid Fusion and Zero Mission on the GBA. I've never had the chance to play Super Metroid (though I loved the Prime series (1st one is in my top 5 games of all time)) but I still have a grasp of why the Metroidvania games are so engrossing.
This is basically more GBA Metroid but with a new character, setting and super pretty magical HD effects to go with it.
Axiom Verge uses a fragmented narrative. You're not going to get much explained to you and even less if you don't find a way to actually decode the bits you do find. There is a real depth to it and the atmosphere is suitably creepy as it should be.
Now this game kicked my♥♥♥♥♥♥pretty hard. I got ruined by some of the later bosses and it wasn't until the ending screen told me why: I had missed over 60% of the weapons and powerups available to me by the end of the game. There is so much to explore and there are a ton of different weapon types that aren't even close to necessary but are still tons of fun to use because of the super solid feel of the game. If this game wasn't as tight as it is mechanically, I'd have likely given up about 3/4 of the way through because it would have stopped being fun.
This game was made by one dude which is what makes it all the more impressive. I'm definitely coming back to this at some point.

To me, metroidvanias present no nostalgic value, as in my childhood i played much more straightforward platformers. In fact, i've never actually played Metroid or Castlevania back then, so i've been introduced to the concept much later. I guess that proves that you don't have to be a hardcore Metroid fan to enjoy Axiom Verge.
There are three things that i loved about this game. Initially i've been lured in by its visual style, and it did not disappoint me. The colossal Giger-esque Rusalki are simply gorgeous, and overall, Axiom Verge looks just right for a dark sci-fi adventure.
The second thing is level design - you can really feel all the effort put into it. Every labirynth on Sudra is polished to the limit, which makes for a relly satisfying exprerience.
Finally, there's challenge. On Hard difficulty setting it's just enough to keep you going on and on, trying to find a perfect strategy to defeat another boss, or to finally gain access to that secret area you've encountered earlier.
My only minor complaint is that some of the weapons in the game are practically useless, since there's a lot of alternatives that are simply better. Other than that, it' really great. Go play it now.

For a game that's as old as it is, this is a surprisingly good management simulator. Essentially a 'space station tycoon' game.
The game does a good job of easing you into the interface, which at first glance seems a bit hard to comprehend. And once you get to grips with it, there are a number of 'missions' you can unlock. These are unlocked linearly, although personally I find that these are more different game modes than anything. I.e. you optimise for healthcare or profit etc. in different missions.
The gameplay goes much beyond a generic tycoon game though, because it delves into a full simulator, where you can manage right down to the level of individual aliens, of various types.
There's a loose story attached to it, but it's nothing big. But the character who is helping you along is quite funny, and the entire thing is quite light-hearted. It's not a causal game, but it's definitely not something super-serious.
There's some good music. The art is of a high quality, if very low resolution.
A pretty good management simulator.

It was the little details about this game that I liked. In pretty much all games where you collect resources they dissapear and the only reminder of their existence is a number on your hud. In Startopia your items and resources are all stored in these big storage racks and you can actually see each individual box and even pull it into your item grid or inventory by clicking on them. The teleporter is one of the things I like a lot about this game. At one point there was a terrorist dropping bombs around my spacestation and right before the bomb was going to explode I placed it into my item grid. I was then able to place it in an unpopulated corner of my station so it could detonate safely. When you purchase things from a merchant ship it doesn't just pop into your inventory. The ship has to first ask permission to dock with your station, then after the ship docks with your station you can purchase things from them and the boxes are dropped off outside of their ship, finally the droids that take care of your station come over and pick the boxes up and put them in storage. Or, if your impatient or the droids are busy then you can pick them up with your teleporter and place them in the storage racks yourself. It's things like this that make this game so amazing. I would really like to see more of this in modern games.
A great game today, an amazing game in 2001.  Deeper than many 2016 simultaion/tycoon games are.  Excellent mechanics, real humor and stellar interactions.

What an amazing game! Right after finishing it I felt I had watched a movie, read a novel and played a game all at the same time. It's such a well set science fiction piece of art. And the 5 years old the game has are not noticeable at all; it has aged so well.
I've been postponing this game for years thinking a game about science fiction mixed with black magic couldn't be that good, but I was wrong. Everything feels so in place, the stealth system is marvelous; I'm not a stealth games person, but this one got me playing most missions with the Ghost achievement (never detected by enemies, which is not easy to get) and using almost always non-lethal ways. And that's another thing to praise this game for: it really lets you choose your path, be it stealthy, guns blazing, deadly or not. Haven't played a stealth experience like this since Hitman: Blood Money.
But there's more, anyone who appreciates environment details will like this game a lot. There are storys everywhere from people talking to each other to manuscripts found in all kinds of buildings explaining life in that fascinating parallel world where this game takes place.
And the level desing, all levels got me amazed on their complexity and flexibility to let the player move around almost everywhere. Do you want to stay high up and see everything from above? You can. Do you want to stay on the sewers and wait for your moment to take action from below? Well, you can do so too.
I'm writing this because I can't recommend the game enough. And if anyone who reads this thinks he or she might not like the game for being about stealth, well don't think about it because it has available all the mechanics needed for an amazing first person action game. Ever thought about sword fights with teleportation, time and wind control? Well, you can have it in Dishonored. Do you want to possess animals or humans? Well, you can do so. When looking at reviews for this game, a lot of cons you'll find, just like with any title, are redundant and quite unnecessary or irrelevant to a review for a video game. Let me point out to those who find a point in putting it as a "con" to an online game - a toxic community, trolls, and smurfs are not a feature of the game and are not exactly removable by the developers. It's really quite pointless to bother complaining about it as though it were an actual feature, it's pointless with this game and any other game. The community, no matter how difficult they make the game experience for you, is not a feature of the game and is not enjoyably controllable by the developers of the game.
That being said, let me get into my review for Toribash.
I discovered this game in 2012. It was an interesting concept and still very much is to this day - in fact, I can say this is one of the best action game concepts I have ever personally seen in my honest opinion. The combat is fluid if you can learn to get movement down correctly, it's incredibly in-depth as well, which is I believe this game's biggest and only downfall aside from the bugs surrounding changing between fullscreen/windowed mode, changing resolutions, and tabbing out of the game (it displaces your registered mouse position and your visual cursor position horribly and makes it difficult to play, it's an issue that's been there since I started playing this game and it's not been changed which leads me to believe it might be an engine issue, but it can be surpassed if you go into the settings and set the game to fullscreen at your native resolution again, which can be a pain in the bottom). Now considering I started playing this game in 2012, please understand I have probably around 1,000 hours in this game past what Steam says I have and by no means am I good at it. In fact, claiming you are particularly good at Toribash is synonymous to eating three platters of your own flesh every two hours for three years straight - you're quite full of yourself if you honestly think that. This game is so incredibly in depth with its combat and movement system that the learning curve is insanely high. However, for people like myself who are willing to sit down and have fun learning to do your own thing to make your own fighting style and counter that of other people on the internet, this game is honestly a great experience. There are many "mods" from your traditional judo and aikido hand-to-hand combat, to bow combat, to parkour where you don't have to fight each other but race over obstacles using what you know about physics and muscle movement, and it turns this game easily from clicking around until you figure out what's going to smack your opponent the hardest and getting frustrated by people who hit you harder to a wonderful physically based player-vs-player sandbox, full of almost infinite possibility. If you can get over the learning curve and enjoy working with physics and turn-based player-vs-player mechanics, Toribash might be a game for you. There's so much I haven't even talked about here in this review, but if you're willing to find out what, then sit down, install Toribash, and give it a good go. It can provide laughs, tears, anger, and happiness, and it's a great way to make friends evidently. Even though it's the equivalent of starting a fight and becoming friends afterward, but over the internet. And a lot more sportsmanlike because you give each other advice for the future.
Long story short, this game is amazing. I've been in love with it for five years, and no matter how many times I stop playing I always come back for more. Give it a try if you're willing to put effort into learning a game's ins and outs on your own through experimentation - and even if you're not, give it a try anyway. It's really fun.

Graphically it reminds me of an RPG Maker game, with original assets, and some very nice backgrounds.
The game has no dialogues and they aren't really needed, which is okay, the interactions are mostly interpretable only in one way. However, due to the lack of dialogues, you do find yourself taking a backseat more often than not.

Apparently there is a pause... F12... I don't know if that means you can't take screenshots or not.... but there you go. Thanks, Top Deer.
Design overall is alright - There are issues with how the blocking of solid objects interacts with your walking space: i.e. it looks like you should be able to walk there, but there are 2 pixels of bookshelf on the right of that square and so you can't. My biggest complaint about the game, is the excessive panning. It's like the developer learned how to move the focus off the main character and decided it was needed _ALL_ the time. Instead of adding to the experience or helping me to focus on what the story teller was trying to point me at, I was rather annoyed instead. Pans to show things are great, but when they happen 4 times in the space of 20 secs and NOTHING has happened really... it's excessive. If you're not showing me something I can't already see, then no real reason to do it. You can just turn the characters head and make him look and guess what, I'll look too.

Finally, a quality lacrosse game. Easily worth the $50. There are some kinks but overall it is an excellent adaptation of a severely underrated sport.
Pros:
* Graphics
* Infinite customization options
* Realistic shooting, passing and checking
* Games can be low scoring and dominated by defense, or they can be high scoring shootouts decided by the offense.
* Sprinting is realistic - Most games have a sprint button that you press for the entire game. This game only allows sprinting in short bursts, after which you need to wait for that player to recharge. Saving your sprint until right after a dodge can decide whether the possesion ends in a goal or a turnover
Cons:
* The game isn't lacrosse "smart". Instead of being careful near the crease the you will run straight through it
* The wing middies are slow to react to the loose ball on a faceoff
* It's a shame the gamemakers couldn't get the rights to use the MLL teams and players, and instead used knockoffs. The customization is a decent work around but the MLL should have agreed for free just to get some publicity.
Some of the issues are a bit much to expect from the first decent lacrosse game available, but hopefully this is the first of many.

Somehow we made it through the 90s and 00s without a truly classic space station simulator. You would think Deep Space 9 fans or Babylon 5 loyalists would have pulled something together, but really all we have is Startopia. Despite the novel premise I never really got into this one as a kid, it being more Dungeon Keeper than I had hoped. Revisiting it now I see where it deserves a lot more attention than it got, and also why it was so overlooked.
Startopia sets you up as the administrator of a classic donut-shaped space station. The first thing that may throw you off about your position is that you're not actually building the station, just filling the interior. Each station is sliced into a dozen sections with three decks each, a service deck, a leisure deck, and a bio deck. You construct buildings within these cavernous spaces that provide all sorts of services to your visitors and residents. These are anything from space motels and bathrooms to research labs and penitentiaries. Most structures can only be built on a specific deck, and in fact you can't build anything on the bio deck, just adjust the landscape for growing different plants.
The result is a game that plays much more like Dungeon Keeper in space than a proper space station builder. Each visitor to your station is simulated, and you can watch them walk around, spend money, and see what they like and dislike about your digs. They also have stats that apply to their job if you hire them, as many of the buildings you build must be staffed. Hiring can be pricey if you go for talented employees, and in fact the economical side of the game can be quite difficult to keep balanced. You need a healthy mix of basic services, entertainment, industrial production, and trading to keep flush with cash, which is actually energy that keeps your station humming as well. There's enough going on to find yourself overwhelmed just keeping up with the basic operation of your station, to say nothing of garbage piling up or spies planting bombs around the place.
There's a five-part tutorial that'll teach you the basics of the interface, and then a ten-mission campaign that drills down on the different aspects of stations. You might have to run a medical station, or a trade hub, or take over a derelict station from squatters. The first five are almost like an extended tutorial, but the latter half can be intensely challenging. A mission will generally take you about an hour but the more difficult ones might need several restarts, their striking difficulty almost requiring foreknowledge of the mission's quirks. If none of that sounds appealing there is an incredibly customizable sandbox mode where you can set victory conditions and individual difficulties to your whims.
The basic 3D graphics have held up surprisingly well over the years, from picturesque views up the curves of your station to the little details on each of the aliens. Sound design also remains up to the task, with plenty of understated sci-fi effects and an inviting soundtrack. The big thing that might throw people off is how incredibly British the presentation is, with a dry AI assistant and plenty of off-color humor in facilities like love nests and space discos. Honestly it feels like a sim set in the Hitchhiker's Guide universe, and if that sounds like a good time then you'll get plenty of mileage out of Startopia. And even if it doesn't, there's a clever, if not perfect, management game to be had.

Zombi does white knuckle tension right. I use tension very deliberately here, because unlike Outlast, Amnesia, or Alien, I wouldn't call this game particularly scary. There are definitely some scary moments where I was quite sure I was going to die, but it never really caused the sheer terror those previous titles evoked in me.
That's not a bad thing. Something that Zombi does fantastically well is, essentially, telling an early Resident Evil story in first person.  They are very similar; a few jumpscares tossed in here or there, but otherwise you're mostly fighting a gnawing sense of tension. You're counting every last bullet down to the bottom of your clip, wondering if you should be beating that zombie to death with your bat instead of wasting a precious couple headshots. It does resource management very well, and for the average player, Standard mode will be very difficult. For Survival Horror veterans, I highly recommend playing it on Survival... where, note, you have to start the game from scratch if you die, which could get frustrating. I played on standard, and had only about 3 moments where I thought I was actually going to die. But that's irrelevant; this game does tension to a T.
Graphics are just fine for a game that came out originally on the WIIU and were ported to PC. My rig ran at a buttery smooth 60fps on the highest settings. Controls are responsive, and definitely suited for a slow and methodical style of play. If you're patient, take your time, and play tactically, you will find yourself always on edge, but always prepared for the next encounter.
Story takes a back seat and really only serves as window dressing for the setting; you never really get attached to anyone, except, if you're like me, your survivor. They have no lines, but after my first 10 hours into the game and surviving some horde events practically designed to off him, he just kept on trucking.
Any negatives I could mention are relative nitpicks; Zombi is rough around the edges, but not so much it's not enjoyable. Only real criticism I have is for the design choice where you are unable to drop your starting gun and melee weapon. Because of that, it made carrying around the silenced pistol and a better melee weapon more of a chore than it was worth, most of the time. Also, the finale of the game is rather unsatisfying; you think you're done, but one more level gets thrown at you, with simple instructions: Run, don't look back.
Doing so is the stupidest thing you could possibly do, as you'll get swarmed and die. There is no time limit, no horde of zombies closing in from the rear, nothing to stop you from very slowly and methodically mowing down that swarm coming from in front of you. I think a much stronger ending would have been one like the very intro, where you really did have to run at top speed to escape, stopping only long enough to reload or slap on a bandage. But still, a nitpick.
Verdict: Worth a buy... maybe not at $25.99, but I spent nearly 25 hours with Zombi, so really, at that rate you're paying a little over a dollar an hour of fun. And Zombi is definitely fun, if you like games that eat breath and live white knuckle tension.

Overall it was a good game. However it was painfully average.
It never really felt like the game knew what it was doing itself and was just throwing in new elements for the sake of it. I applaud it for trying to do something different as a zombie game, but all these things combined made the game just feel... messy. And that would be the perfect word to describe it, messy. It's clunky, yet sometimes smooth; it's interesting and then often boring; it tries to be different, but it's still another zombie game. And it's a perfect example of why there are too many zombie games on the market, it tries it's best to be different, but in the end, it just seems 'messy'. You see, Zombi does a lot of different things, a lot of which don't work, however it does these things very well... let me explain...
It has a system in which when the protaganist dies, a new one is introduced and has to find the old one's supplies, this here works very well as it means having to confront whatever killed you, plus you. It's ammo is scarce, which feels good as it introduces these heart-sinking moments where you find yourself surrounded by zombies with just your cricket bat. It tries to be scary a lot of the time, and it really does scare the player well. Without relying on jumpscares, it uses the placement of the zombies round the next corner with their silhouettes contrasting against the strong light to scare you along with their deeply disturbing, yet not ear-piercing noises to spook the player. Gunplay is good, the level design feels reletively well made and AI is actually rather good most of the time.
The game isn't any masterpiece, nor is it great, in fact it just barely reaches 'good'. I often hated the game for what it was trying to do, whenever it introduced a new idea I instantly discarded it and went off to play some other game. But the more I played, the more I realised it's new elements weren't entirely trash, and actually worked well a lot of the time. It's length is more than enough, and I would have settled for it to be a bit shorter, but overall it works.
In conclusion, it's 'messy', it does all the wrong things, and if you're stuck between deciding wether you want to buy this or Far Cry 3, you should go with Far Cry 3. But Zombi was made by developers who know how to make things well.  Ubisoft don't ALWAYS create with care and like to throw whatever at the player, but it doesn't seem to suffer from 'Ubisoft-itous', where they have a load of stuff to do with little depth to it at all.
From this review, you should be able to decide wether Zombi is the game for you or not.

I found this game to be both fun and unique.

The large battles are fun and this game definitely gave me a new experience in that regard. The battles were especially fun as a noob because everything was incredibly chaotic and brutal. Sometimes it was hard to decide what to do. Should I rush into the thick of battle or fight along the edges? The chaos could be intoxicating at times, but also frustrating if I was too reckless with my decisions.
Each character on the battlefield is controlled by a human in this game so it can be easy to suddenly find yourself out numbered and easy prey to 4-5 experienced fighters. You quickly learn to pay attention to where your friends are and fight along side them.
Even if the developers stopped making changes right now I'd say it was well worth the $20 I paid.

This was objectively a fantastic game.
Story: Dishonored has a complex story that weaves many characters lives together in unexpected ways. Without giving a synopsis, you simply have to trust that the story is well-written. The main story is interesting, but can only be fully realized by reading books and notes scattered throughout the game. I've heard some people say the story is confusing, and it can be, but reading and analysis really helps.
Graphics: The art style is unique. Everything looks dingy and decprepit, which gives a fitting atmosphere considering the city has a huge rat infestation and at least half of it's citizens contracted the plague. This isn't the most beautiful game, which I suspect is because there aren't any higher graphics options for textures. It really feels like console graphics to me.  The art design of the world is very creative. There's a very ornate, Victorian look to to the interiors, which I like.
Gameplay: It's fun and challenging. I chose to play on the hardest difficulty as I do with all games I play. I also didn't kill anyone in my first playthrough. In my second playthrough, I allowed myself to kill. I have to say that not killing was the much harder route, but it was so much more rewarding. The AI are smart and can detect you fairly easily. You really have to plan many moves a head in order to not be detected. The only issue I have with the pacifist playstyle is that you end up missing out on a lot of interesting game mechanics like combat, traps, and about half of the uses of your powers. I ended up basically skipping half the routes just because it made no sense to collect runes or bone charms for abilities I didn't indend on using. The combat is fun, but it isn't really a viable approach since basically every time you're detected, 12 guards dive on you. I think where the gameplay shines the most is through it's level design. Every chapter has so many paths you can take to reach your goal. The game rewards perceptiveness and creativity. Finally, I loved that there was always an optional pacifist route you can take that is usually harder than just assassinating your targets. Those routes tended to be more involved and they taught you more about the story.
Overall, the story is very interesting, but has so many moving parts and subleties that it can be confusing. The graphics aren't impressive, but the art is. The gameplay is challenging and advanced, but often techniques were never fully realized because of how much the game actually discourages them. The level design was the best part of this game and almost makes up for the gameplay quirks.

I've never been opposed to JRPG-stylized games, wherein you play with a top-down perspective on pixelated sprites, but it severely limits the amount of range and emotion many other 3D games can achieve- like Brothers, a game I fondly remember (primarily because I beat it a few hours ago).
A Bird Story is a story. About a child. And there's a bird in it. If you grew up watching kid's movies with an animal theme in them, I'm sure you can piece together the plot of A Bird Story.
Kid finds animal- adults try to take animal- kid loses animal- kid finds animal again.
It's as formulaic as it gets. And I wouldn't mind it as much, if there were some actual characters in this story. I don't mind characters without a voice (like the Naia and Naiee in Brothers), but all we know about the child is that he's a dreamer and likes birds. We know his mom loves him, but we never see her. We know little about his teacher and vet, except that they want to bird. To take care of it. Because it was injured.
Seriously, why would anyone sympathize with the kid, if he's preventing the bird from appropriate medical care? I don't often sympathize with children for this exact reason. They let their near-sightedness get in the way of something far more important going on.
And the way the child's imagination is handled is really strange and lazy. At first, it seems more like how he perceives the world, and how he dreams. But then he gets away from the vet by... dreaming up a giant paper airplane... and flying away...
Did I miss something?
A Bird Story can be enjoyed by somebody out there. Somebody who hasn't been exposed to the cliches of most animal movies for kids, and who doesn't mind bland characters, with some odd plot development. I'm giving this game a 3/10.

Old-school metroidvania, in essence. It's got an intrigueing story, although a lot of it is left to interpretation. Besides the main story line, there's plenty of notes hidden around the world that give additional insight to what is actually going on. The graphics are based on old NES style games and vary quite a lot in quality, with the Rusalki taking the prize. Concidering the self-imposed limitations they're absolutely stunning. The music has some really high quality tunes, though some are just plain annoying to listen to, and since it's a metroidvania game you'll be hearing each region's music quite a lot.
The mechanics are fairly straight-forward for the most part of the game. You run, jump and shoot. It gets old fast, but once you've gotten a fair chunk in to the game it starts to losen up with additional move sets, and nearing the end the flexibility in movement is quite fun. It never gets to Super Metroid levels of variety, but they've got some fun ideas that work well. As far as the weapons go (there's a lot of them), most of them range anywhere from highly situational to useless. The first few are more or less glorified keys to open locked doors.
The world is large, but it's deceptively linear. You can go to a lot of places, roaming around looking for secrets and whatnot, but the actual progression though the game is more or less straight. There are plenty of optional weapons and upgrades you can pick up whenever, but each essential item is required to get the next at every point.
It's a good game and I had fun roaming the world of Sudra. Wether it's a game for you depends mostly on if you like the old metroidvania games, since it's just that. There's some new ideas and angles, some of which work. Others not so much. Still worth a try if it's your cup of tea.

I have no idea why this game was so disliked among consumers and critics alike. It's a good game. It's not phenomenal, it's not bad, but it's competent, got relatively interesting characters and a not too shabby story. It's not terribly long, but there's only so much you can do with a 3rd person cover shooter.
Basic gameplay has you acting as the squad leader shooting at stuff and giving orders to your 2 companions in the field. Depending on who you take with you you get different abilities to level up, but your main character always has the same progression path up to level 10, though there are some mutually exclusive choices. However, you can take I believe 2 out of 4 different classes with you: support, engineer, commando, recon. Each of those have different abilities and can be levelled up to level 5, so, technically you can level up 1 of each class easily till the end, even without sending them on missions of their own.
The squad command menu is simple and intuitive though placing objects in the terrain is not. The camera would benefit from zooming out and movement gets obstructed by terrain too easily. Your fellow agents are also extremely stupid and easily incapacitated at early levels. They don't do that much damage either, compared to you, but I guess that's "ok". They're more a distraction and useful for the skills they provide you, like automated turrets, combat stims, or armor weakening effects. You yourself have access to ever more outlandish technology and abilities. Using the enemy strength against themselves so to speak. From gaining powerful new abilities by levelling up to finding new weapons in the field, that's all on you.
There's not a whole lot more to say. The levels are rather linear and there are a couple of side missions, which are still entertaining and have their own littly stories tied into the grand scheme of things. The story presents an interesting aspect and has some twists and turns as well.
If you could really hold anything against the game it's that it possibly doesn't really tie into XCOM: Enemy Unknown, which was released a year prior, in terms of story or enemy variation. You'll be fighting "Outsiders" mainly, which are not part of that particular XCOM universe afaik, but rather humanoid looking aliens. It wouldn't have hurt to throw in the more outlandish enemies from "Unknown", but there's still plenty of variation and challenge. It definitely doesn't deserve the bad rep it gets.

-%%% This review is coming from someone who previously knew absolutely nothing about this series %%%-
I bought this game just kinda hoping for a game to hack n' slash away and random shet because why not, and I ended up being pleasantly surprised.
I'd always see the games in this series pop up on steam but never bothered (personally not a turn-based kinda person), but a few days ago I saw this as a new release and just clicked on it, and found it was an action-y spin off of that one series I keep seeing everywhere. Look up some things on the game and thought it looked really fun, so I bought it.
From my understanding, this series is an RPG series set to kinda make fun of the gaming industry, and contains many subtle-and not so subtle-nods to things (i.e characters named Famitsu and Dengekiko) and such, and, well..
wao
So, what I really liked about this game is the fluent combat and the extremely colorful visuals, as well as the pretty cool characters (my fav character is probably Neptune, but my fav character to play as is Famitsu). The voice acting is pretty good, the dialogue and such is entertaining, the music is pretty cool and I like the change of tone when you transform into your HDD mode, and overall the game is quite fun to play. There's some pretty good character customization for each character and all characters except for Famitsu and Dengekiko start with 2-3 different outfit colors & hair colors for their normal and HDD forms, but you gain more weapons and such over time of playing.
But there are quite a few things that I absolutely hated about this game or just really didn't like; I feel like the sound design is absolutely terrible sometimes, most characters don't feel like they do much to enemies - like you're wacking things with nerf swords (with the exception of Dengekiko, Famitsu, and Blanc), some special attacks don't have sound effects or sound bland and boring even though they look flashy and cool af, and sometimes the enemies are a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ There've been multiple occasions where I'd get trapped in a circle of enemies that relentlessly obliterate both my characters in seconds without any hope of escaping. Also, sometimes it feels like the characters are really unbalanced, like how ranged characters transformed into their HDD mode are pretty much untouchable in most occasions. There isn't much of a story, but from what I've gathered, the main series has a much more involved story than this spin-off. One more thing, the combos feel a little strict and you won't find yourself straying from the same combos sometimes. Oh yeah, and there's a weird slow down when your framerate drops under 60FPS (don't worry, the game is reltatively easy to run, just run on lower resolution and/or windowed mode)
IN CONCLUSION:
Pros:
-Fun combat
-Pretty visuals & flashy attacks and skills
-Cool and relatively interesting characters
-Pretty good music
-Alright character customization
-Interesting dialogue
-Easy to run on lower-end computers (for me at least and I can barely run Tera and Skyrim)
-( ͡° ͜ʖ ͡°)
Cons:
-Awful sound design
-Weird speed drop with framerate drop sometimes
-Sometimes frustrating enemies
-Meh story
-Kinda unbalanced
Overall, I feel this was one of the best games on steam that I've bought in quite a while.

Casey Powell 16 is an excellent game that captures the speed, physicality, look and sound of field lacrosse, plus it strikes a good balance between being a fun sports title and a realistic sports sim.
On the field, the controls are tight and responsive ensuring fluid offensive and defensive play, while the AI keeps a realistic flow to play and player movements. It really does look and feel like lacrosse. And speaking of looks, this game looks fabulous. The players, field, and stadium are all decked out in lush current gen graphical goodness. Note: More on graphics below.) For an indie game, it has the visual look and feel of a big studio product and in my opinion this makes CP16 a milestone achievement for a crowd funded game. And there’s plenty of ways to get to the field - there’s single games, a decent (but not overly deep) career mode, and tournament modes.
And special mention for the excellent Lacrosse Academy in-game editor that gives you the ability to fully manage tactics, rosters, and starting lineups, plus create custom teams, players, coaches, and even referees. While this game doesn’t carry official licenses from either the NCAA or Major League Lacrosse, the developers have invented a fabulous trick the very first time you start the game. The first time you turn on the game you have the option to update all the rosters to the highest rated teams available from the community through the Lacrosse Academy. That means you can instantly update your rosters from the generic teams that come with the game to 67 real NCAA teams or the nine MLL pro teams. Granted, there’s not official logos for any of the college or pro teams, but it’s a great feature and one that I hope other studios picks up on with their titles.
With all that said, here’s the downer. As noted above, this game is beautiful but be forewarned that you’re going to need a powerful PC to play with decent graphics. This is an all out current gen game and to get the max out of the graphics (PS4 or Xbox One equivalent) you’re going to need a rocket ship of a PC.
All in all, as a representation of the game of field lacrosse, this game is very well done and compares to any sports game offered by 2K, EA, or other big outfits. Even if you’re not a lax guy, this is a great sports title.

This game -can- be a very fun game. It's easy to spend countless hours on this. You can build your own ship and gather your own crew to explore the very vast world while gaining numerous loots from defeating various enemies, both in land and by the sea (enemy ships).
The ship-building aspect is the most fun to me; different design gives you different advantages and challenges. Bigger ship doesn't always mean better. You gain parts to build your ship either from stores or from raiding other ships.
HOWEVER there are three glaring issues the devs need to fix.
- Very poor documentation. For the most part, you have to figure things by your own. Like cleaning your ship from poos (yes, your crew will poo from time to time). Not cleaning your ship affects your crew quality of life. I had to google for this simple information.
- Poor user interface. You won't feel it during early hours, but near the late game where you find yourself amassed with numerous loots, it will start becoming tedious to manage those hundreds of items.
- Lack of varieties. This one you will also feel near the late game. After you've traveled 50% of the world map, you'll know you've discovered most of the world. You've seen all varieties of enemy ships, islands, and towns.
Despite those three glaring issues, I still recommend this game. It's still a decent game if you like open world game.

Lots of fun but its a maddening game. Here's a couple of examples. Each alien has about five things that need to be satisfied like hunger, cleanliness, fun, etc. In most games you'd just click on the alien and you'd be able to see which category is the problem but in Startopia you have to click on each category and then wait for the delayed physical reaction of the alien. It can take a long time for one creature and there are a lot of creatures. It makes me nuts. Sometimes, yes, they do get a floating balloon which I think means they need fun. I'm never really sure. You also have to hover your mouse each category and wait for the tool tip to pop up. This is bad in a game where the doors to the next sector can open up and a swarm of enemies can disable your equipment and kill your guys in a hurry.
Then there's another aggravating thing that is just needlessly odd. You have a management screen. I didn't know this until I played for about 30 hours but you can promote people from this management screen. They sort of paste a promotion star to your cursor if the alien feels like it needs a promotion if its not going to quit it's job. Elsewhere you click on something to promote the alien so this different way of doing things on the management screen threw me off as I was trying to click on things and promote aliens whether they felt like they deserved it or not. The second failure in both these things is that they aren't mentioned in the tutorial and they make the game play quite a bit better. They're sort of essential.
Its too bad because Startopia is really neat game. Its fun, creative, unique and its deep. There are many hours of gameplay but there are things you have to put up with that other games like Tropico, Rollercoaster Tycoon and Railroad  Tycoon did better. Definitely a good buy.

So this title is in early access and it works really hard to make sure you know it. If you're looking for a complete and well implemented this isn't it. Yet. It may be down the road but if you're likely to get♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off by bugs or badly implemented modes don't bother.
I see a big dichotomy in the game modes here, we currently have duel mode and conquest mode. Duel mode does a really good job of showcasing exactly how good this game is at what it does right, specifically melee combat. Duels are beautiful to watch and have an incredible skill ceiling, the block, parry riposte and swing mechanics are great. The problem is that 1v1 dueling gets old fast and unless you grind really hard the XP is mediocre.
Conquest mode does an incredible job of obfuscating what makes this game great while simultaneously showing off some of it's biggest potential. I've seen people spontaneously form shield walls, I've had that great moment where I stand off three or four enemies and cut them down or send them running. It felt great, but the mode itself is 99%♥♥♥♥♥♥ There are too many people on the map, it's nearly impossible to fight without indescriminately hurting allies or being hacked down from behind by kill happy muppets who care not for friend or foe. It's extremely hard to tell ally from enemy sometimes because everyone's picking from the same armor visuals and there's no obvious built in indicator that someone is an enemy. The games are too long by about half an hour, each game drags accross 4-6 maps and you don't get any extra bonus XP for longer matches and you don't get any at all if you leave early. This means that players who are auto-assigned onto ♥♥♥♥♥♥ teams have to spend 45 minutes getting♥♥♥♥♥♥on or drop out of the game and get nothing, there's no grouping mechanic so there's no way to mitigate this.
Bottom line: This game has great mechanics, huge potential, and I want to see more, but they need a shorter more cassual play mode, because what it has doesn't cut it.

Axiom Verge is another game for which I wish Steam had a neutral ranking.  I'd call the game "tentatively recommended...with many caveats".  Lacking such a rating category, I'll have to lean on the side of not recommending it.
My number one complaint about the game is that the secrets, of which there are many, are handled in far, far too archaic a manner.  Basically there are tons of blocks which appear solid but can be passed in one way or another; some are telegraphed visually, but many are not.  This makes upgrade/secret hunting an excruciatingly tedious process of trying your several wall bypassing abilities on nearly every wall in the game.  This isn't fun.  Upgrade hunting in Metroidvanias is rewarding when there's some hint or indication that you can come back and get something later - and you remember it and do so.  Stumbling into a hidden room because you exhaustively tried every ability on every wall in the adjoining area doesn't make you feel clever, it makes you feel like your time is being wasted by a developer who has no concept of fairness.
I finished the game with barely half of its available weapon arsenal, which I only realized upon consulting a guide after the fact.  Some were hidden so fiendishly that I'm surprised a developer would go so far out of their way to discourage the average player from getting to experience some of the more entertaining weapons that said developer surely put good effort into creating.  Even if you do find some of them, most can only be obtained so late in the game that you never really have much time to play with them anyway, which is a shame because they are all pretty interesting and fun to use.
Many details of game's story are similarly buried in hard to find journal entries, and from what I gather it seems like the developer is a bit too enamored with his grand designs there as well.  It's overly complex and too obfuscated for the passive manner in which its delivered and I once again can't understand the logic of putting all that effort into it, only to then hide it except from the most obsessive of players.
Now that being said -  you can ignore the secrets, ignore the story, play the game in a straightforward manner - and it manages to be a decent Metroidvania, although even then not without foibles. Primary among them is a type of dash ability obtained roughly half-way through the game.  This is activated by double tapping a movement direction which, when playing with an analog stick (an absolutely fine input method before that point) is often accidentally activated when you don't want it to, and annoying to pull off with appropriate timing when you do want to use it.  A button dedicated to the dash would have been preferable.
The tile based graphics are also a little too slavishly retro for my taste, to the extent that I'd even call the game ugly in parts, and on several occasions I had trouble distinguishing between foreground and background tiles.  In my defense, this is because there are places the sames tiles are actually used for both - which is another of the misleading methods by which paths to items are hidden.
The difficulty can range from infuriating to a breeze, completely dependent on what weapons you've found.  While the ease with which some bosses can be dispatched with optional weapons would be a good reason to encourage exploration - as a new player experiencing the game for the first time, you have no idea that these weapons are out there to be found.
Ultimately, I had some fun with the core game, but took no joy in the exploration and backtracking because of how things were hidden and that's pretty damning for a Metroidvania.  There are far better examples of the genre in recent memory.

Great game! Gets a lot of influence from the Metroid series without actually being Metroid. This is not a clone. You run, jump, shoot, backtrack, find upgrades, but apart from that, it is very different. The upgrades and guns you'll find are very interesting and creative. It sort of recreates that Metroidish feeling of “I can’t get to that area yet, but I bet there’s an item that’ll help me,” but it is not an item that you’d think it’d be. There’s no morph ball, no space jump, no missiles. You instead get a creative tool or ability you wouldn’t expect and because of that, it really captures that first sense of wonder when playing Metroid for the first time.
The story is average. The premise is the common, “There is a bad guy, and you are the only one who can help us” with a plot twist or two. The setting is very interesting and unique, but being a unique and complex world, it can be confusing without finding and collecting the in-game notes about it.
Axiom Verge was made by one person, and I gotta say I am very well damned impressed this guy created all this. Kudos to you Thomas Happ! This game satisfied my Metroid fix. I wouldn’t say it is better, less than, or equal to Super Metroid, because it is a different, but enjoyable experience. I had lots of fun playing it.

What a waste of time this was.
If you like my went into this thinking "Hey, an otome game where you date birds? That's gonna be interesting." Don't. It is not. Under thin layer of novelity lays a rather dull game with a lot of problems. It's not bad enough for me to drop it outright, but it just gives you expectections and never delivers.
At the start game takes a pity on you by giving you an option to show you a human version of a bird when you're first introduced to them. It's like developers new people wouldn't be able to relate to expressionless birds so they gave you a glimpse at what anime cliché they were going for. And yes, birds have no expressions. It's always one picture of a bird unchanging. Everything is expressed through a dialogue.
Story feels flat. Sure at a first some events may seem interesting but then you realize that all of them are based on cheap tricks to induce emotional response. All of these events are not properly explored. After a while I just felt indifferent. It doesn't help that to get to the true-true ending you have to play it like 13 times? Half of those endings differ only by the fact that there is a few additional scenes. It's like reading a book with last page missing. You're like "that's it?", and then someone gives you that last page and you're just left disappointed.
You can't even save to see branched paths because they don't branch. Most of those "missing page" endings are based on your stats. In order to see them you have to play the whole thing again, choose the same options but rise different stat durring classes.
True-true ending has a terrible pacing. Story drags on and on breaking suspension of disbelief every time it speeds up a little. And even if you unlock everything to get the epilog you're left with a huge gaping plot hole and ending that's basically a cliffhanger which explains nothing.
Music is just bad. It's just a handful of generic elevator music tracks. After my 10th playthrough it was just driving me mad. It made me actually glad for these few moments where there was no music.
As for technical aspect, it's terrible. A lot of features you'd expect from a visual novel are missing. There is no history log and there is no skipping of read text, you can only skip on scene by scene basis. This combined with a fact that a lot of things happen in a common path makes it really easy to miss text. There is no way to tell at the beginning of a scene if you've seen it already or is it a variant of the scene with some events added to it. It's also far from bug free. More often than not, clicking on choices not register properly and you have to wiggle mouse pointer around for it to start working. Saving in some cases can also produce a save point that freezes a game when loaded from main menu (you have to load from a working save as a workaround and even then it sometimes doesn't work). Sometimes I wasn't even able to exit from save menu. And on top of that text not always fits on a screen.
Overall do I recommend this? No. After novelty wears off all you're left with is a very short, hollow, buggy VN with a lot of grinding. I almost want to spoil it to you (which wouldn't be hard as there is not much to spoil) so you wouldn't have to play it.

Fun romp but with a few kudos and gripes:
Kudos:
1) Interesting story.  The idea that your next character has to find, kill, and take the goods from the previous character you died as is pretty unique (I've never seen it before anyway).
2) Character and environment graphics are decent- not great but good.
3) The idea that "organizing your inventory" continues gameplay is interesting but the UX is poorly implemented so it seem unfair- particularly under duress (see gripe #1).
Gripes:
1) Inventory for ammo is stupidly implemented.  I have all my slots taken with empty weapons/health and I can't pick up any ammo?   Wouldn't the character be smart enough to load the ammo into the empty weapon?  As it is, you have to drop something from inventory, pick up the ammo, load it into the weapon, then re-pick up the item you dropped.   And of course when being attacked that means death.
2) False audio-cues.  There are a few places where the audio cues indicate danger or "scare" but there's nothing there.
3) Short game for the money.  The credits seemed longer than the game.
4) The pre-recorded cut-scenes are really low res.  I get the game is old but wow it really looks awful on a modern-day rig.
In the end, if it is on sale for under $10 go for it.  Fun game for that money.  It's no Dying Light but a fun variation of a zombie game.

The game is a revival of an older Wi game. thus the graphics may seem a bit dated to some. Like Silent Service II or DOOM!, the game is a classic of its genre, has excellent gameplay (except for an occasional crash) and a simple yet elegant story. You must survive the Zombie apocalyse. The pace is serene, except for moments of terror, including nasty surprises for all but the most experienced or jaded. Gameplay is fair. If you follow the Prepper's suggested techniques, you can survive and gather a box full of weapons and ammo. Some situations require close range blasting power, some a medium range balance of aiming and stopping force, some a long range precision shot, and others an area weapon. Like any "realistic" Zomie scenario, you exist in a world of fear and scarcity. But you can accumulate items that are needed and eventually prevail.
This is a game invented before the advent of "Open World" games, so it can be a bit linear. On the other hand, once a level has been completed, it is beneficial to return to each screen in order to gain resources. The play is a bit like an open world game after a while at the controls. It is evenly paced, and both challenging and soothing. There are safe houses at each level. A strategy of caution can pay off, but a furious fighter and runner can also make it through. Hesitation can be fatal, and the player's character dies forever. The games auto save feature is not defeatable on this point. Disclosure: I got this game for free from the MacHeist Indie Games Extravaganza promotion.
Let me start by saying that, even though I will be calling 'A Bird Story' a game, I do not consider it to be one; therefore, I will not be criticising it as a game. The fact that I do not consider this piece of fiction to be a game has nothing to do with why I won't recomend it.
Without going into much detail, 'A Bird Story' tells the story of an imaginative kid that has troubles when it comes to socialise with his classmates and that saves an injured bird. This bird becomes his best friend until it has to leave. I am inclined to think the kid is autistic but that is just speculation and it could be that I am reading too much into it.
When it comes to how the story is told, this 'game' is quite competent at it. The introduction is a bit weak but it gets better as you go through the game. There is no text and no voice acting and everything is told through the environement or the movements and expressions of the characters. The game has notes of humour and can be quite cute at times but it also made me cringe other times, although that may just be me. However, there is little to no interaction and almost no exploration outside the main path. The whole piece is like a set of cutscenes and you just have to walk from one to the next one or, at best, you have to interact with a couple items before advancing and, even then, those items are marked with big green arrows or green sparkles. Any interaction feels superfluous and sometimes it seems like it would have done better without them. The game is also very short, I fully completed the game in 71 minutes according to Steam. It is so short that I did not even earn all the Trading Cards and I will have to leave it open for a while to get the last one.
The artstyle, while a bit bland looks good and represents very well what it is going on and the feelings of the different characters. The music is good, mainly piano pieces. There is one song I did not quite like but it's part of a joke and saying which one it is might ruin it if you are interested in playing the game.
Something that is unacceptable is that there is no options menu to my knowledge. I was unable to lower the game's sound and music and set the game to windowed.
My biggest problem with this game and the reason why I do not recomend it (besidesthe ones mentioned above) is how boring the story is. Why is it that most games of this genre pick stories that are so uninteresting? It is as if it was a mediocre story for a children's book but I am uncertain as if a child would enjoy or understand this game without the help of an adult. There is good talent behind this game and it pains me to not recommend it but, overall, I did not enjoy it.

but anyways- this game is mediocre, it's passes standards, yes; it makes your heart churn at make you laugh at the same time, yes- I recommend this game to anyone who wants to experience playing otome games, but I wouldn't say this to be -the- best otome game there ever is
pros:
-Birds with personality! They also have their own unique backgrounds and you can adore them easily (with the exception of the doctor- I had the unfortunate luck to play Yuuya's before Shuu's and god frick I couldn't -stomach- Shuu's route at all, Yuuya was my second conquest after all :( )
-The options are pretty blunt. The protagonist would always say which characters goes with what option, although it might be pretty hard for you first time to actually organize your options for one exact route
-The routes are very short (in my opinion, I -am- accustomed to games like hakuouki, whose routes are v e r y long) so this game can easily become a past time if you find yourself doing nothing during a lazy day
-The endings are realistic- or as realistic an otome game can get, there's a dash of cliche tucked in there but the ending's can at least satisfy the player (or if not- the calming end credits music always helps, man I love that ost)
cons:
-The routes are too short for my liking. (Weird, this is -both- a pro and a con? huh) Short routes don't usually immerse the player too much into the story, and I sometimes just find myself playing this game for the achievements alone
-There's no compatibility/likeability/love gauge (or whatever you call that) for the characters you're aiming for. You're only going to realize that you've done the right thing if his dialogue is different from the other options, and sometimes not at all. Love gauges are v e r y important in otome games, especially if it's just at the start of the game, so you can know if you're going through the right path, so the player can easily be killed by the hawk's party if without a guide at their first try
-It kind of gets repetitive over time until you finally get near the end, when both of you and your conquest are really bonded. I found myself skipping dialogue a lot, making this already short game even shorter
-The stats system is very vague, like sure, you'll find yourself passing if you go to math class a lot and meet your conquests a lot more if you take classes associated with them, but suddenly you're faced with a turn based battle with your damage and hp depending on your stats and you wouldn't even realize how important that one class was to this route until you're hit with it with a loud smack, heck, even some endings require attending only one specific class for the whole year, and if you stray even one time from that class, in hopes of balancing your stats, you can say bye to your true ending
that's all I can say for now, but this is a fun game nonetheless, this game is worth the money, although I still recommend waiting for sales if you're tight on the money (this game was just on sale a week ago, and I was so angry because right after I bought it for its full price does steam decide to put it on a 75% sale, I was raging over twt so much)

So, i bought this game as kind of a joke game, much like you'd buy a game like Bad Rats or Slaughtering Grounds.
But boy, was i surprised. As it turns out, this game is actually pretty well-written! There are some corny jokes and puns here and there, but most of the jokes are pretty good! Even when the game is getting more serious, it still manages to be pretty good. There are moments in this game that will actually make you cry, at which point you will notice that you are crying at a pigeon dating sim, and will probably start to question your life choices up until now. This game is THAT good.
There are six main love interests (three of which have secret complete endings that can only be achieved after clearing their routes at least once), two extra secret love interests, and a final secret route: BBL.
"Bad Boys' Love", also known as "Hateful Boyfriend" or "Hurtful Boyfriend", is pretty much the "endgame" of this game. You can enter this route before getting all other endings, but i would not recommend doing so. If you clear all other endings beforehand, you get an extra post-credits scene.
Now, about BBL's plot itself. I can't tell you much, because of spoilers, but i can say this: it's a murder mystery.
Now, you might be thinking "oh, okay, it's a murder mystery parody, right?"
To which i will reply: "NO."
For, you see, this is actually taken completely serious. And you might think that this is when the game gets sucky, but no, this is THE BEST PART OF THE ENTIRE GAME. It's full of expertly done plot twists, that will make you play through the game again and go "oh my god, the devs of this pigeon dating sim had planned it all out, ALL ALONG!".
By all means, you MUST get this game if you like VNs. It's much more than you'd expect from looking at its Steam page.

You have these typical class systems (assault, medic, engineer etc) which have a somewhat different but not entirely original spin to most games that use the same system have.  What I did like was how they implement a sub-class weight system, but wish they took better advantage of it.
I like the the weight class system, basically they restricted weapons to certain weight classes and provided base perks to those classes.  Light weight, are the most mobile but have access to the least amount of weapons;  Heavy, are slow but tough and have access to all weapons in the game (namely the most devastating); and Average build lies somewhere between those two.  It allows you to play a tank-like medic or a nimble one, or a rapid assault character or a heavy assault character.  It's somethin to play with.
There's also a perk system for each class, and general perks.  I believe there's a limitation to how many perks you can upgrade so it adds an interesting dynamic to how you build a character to fit your playstyle.
I remember people hating on the gunplay in this game, honestly I had no trouble with it.  It's not as accurate as other games of it's time but I believe that was te point.  Speaking as someone who has actully shot guns before I thought it added a degree of realism or challange to shooting that has been lost since the red-dot, point and shoot accuracy made popular by most COD games I played.  I think the real problem is that sometimes enemies feel "spongey" (they soak a lot of bullets).  Attachments are pretty average, red-dot sight, different clip sizes...etc.  Not nearly enough options compared to COD games, and definitely not compared to the ridiculous combinations in Ghost Recon Future Soldier.
Character cusomization is pretty neat, The options are somewhat limited but still provide a breadth of diversity.  Don't expect sliders like in Bethesda games, From Software or Korean RPGs.
I liked the look of the characters and the levels tell a neat story in and of themselves.  The game's narrative can change somewhat based on your success and failures.  I realy wish there was more of an online presence still but I guess that's what I get for buying it so late after it initially released.
TL;DR
If you see this game on sale I think it's worth a pickup, at the time I'm writting this however you're probably too busy playing Overwatch, or some other MP shooter.

This was objectively a fantastic game.
Story: Dishonored has a complex story that weaves many characters lives together in unexpected ways. Without giving a synopsis, you simply have to trust that the story is well-written. The main story is interesting, but can only be fully realized by reading books and notes scattered throughout the game. I've heard some people say the story is confusing, and it can be, but reading and analysis really helps.
Graphics: The art style is unique. Everything looks dingy and decprepit, which gives a fitting atmosphere considering the city has a huge rat infestation and at least half of it's citizens contracted the plague. This isn't the most beautiful game, which I suspect is because there aren't any higher graphics options for textures. It really feels like console graphics to me.  The art design of the world is very creative. There's a very ornate, Victorian look to to the interiors, which I like.
Gameplay: It's fun and challenging. I chose to play on the hardest difficulty as I do with all games I play. I also didn't kill anyone in my first playthrough. In my second playthrough, I allowed myself to kill. I have to say that not killing was the much harder route, but it was so much more rewarding. The AI are smart and can detect you fairly easily. You really have to plan many moves a head in order to not be detected. The only issue I have with the pacifist playstyle is that you end up missing out on a lot of interesting game mechanics like combat, traps, and about half of the uses of your powers. I ended up basically skipping half the routes just because it made no sense to collect runes or bone charms for abilities I didn't indend on using. The combat is fun, but it isn't really a viable approach since basically every time you're detected, 12 guards dive on you. I think where the gameplay shines the most is through it's level design. Every chapter has so many paths you can take to reach your goal. The game rewards perceptiveness and creativity. Finally, I loved that there was always an optional pacifist route you can take that is usually harder than just assassinating your targets. Those routes tended to be more involved and they taught you more about the story.
Overall, the story is very interesting, but has so many moving parts and subleties that it can be confusing. The graphics aren't impressive, but the art is. The gameplay is challenging and advanced, but often techniques were never fully realized because of how much the game actually discourages them. The level design was the best part of this game and almost makes up for the gameplay quirks.

I REALLY want to recommend this game because my first few hours were so wonderful. They really were: building up a crew, leveling up all those skills, attacking and plundering other pirate ships, and discovering all of the game's features one after another. Here's the thing: this game IS roguelike. Like any good roguelike, a huge chunk of the fun comes from trial-and-error. It comes from building up this wonderful crew only to make one stupid mistake, have everyone die, cry for ten minutes straight, and then start again. And this WILL happen a few times.
Then, it'll never happen again. It only takes a few hours to basically know everything you need to know to beat this game.
From that point on, it feels like manual labor. Like you're just going through the motions to get finished. And that feels TERRIBLE. What makes it worse is how the design defeats itself: wanna go back to town and stock up? TOO BAD, FOUR UNECESSARY LOADING SCREENS TO "SIMULATE" SAILING AND MAKE UP FOR THE GAME'S LACK OF A STREAMING ENGINE. Wanna go treasure hunting? I HOPE YOU LIKE USING THE MENUS IN THIS GAME BECAUSE THAT'S THE ONLY WAY TO SWITCH BETWEEN SHOVEL AND SWORD.
Some other design flaws:
1. It's possible to become attached to your crew members. Awesome. You can specify their skills on a very technical level, and you have complete control over how their stats are distributed. BUT you're also expected to have fairly large crews, 20+ people there. At this point in time, personal attachment just isn't an option, and there's no way to automatically distribute points. No way to automatically assign weapons. No way to automatically ANYTHING. It feels like manual labor.
2. This game features randomly generated worlds. Randomly generated islands, ships, characters, etc. Sweet! The best thing about randomly generated content is that it takes SO long to get old. Except in this game, it doesn't. All the islands look the same. All the characters look the same. Some of the ships were interesting and when you see a new class of island it's interesting, for the first time.Too bad there's only ever one first time.
3. One of my favorite things about games like this is this sense of personal narrative that builds on itself. Like, thanks to the circumstances of this world and the traits of this character, I might make different early-game decisions that dramatically impact the entire playing experience. Every game is its own, unique story. This game is so close to achieving this, but so far. Everything it does to make each experience unique goes out the window with how boring the game gets later on. That's a shame, because there's so much potential here with the randomly generated crew and custom-built ship that it just hurts.
4.You WILL turn pirate voices off in this game. They're so irritating and stupid that it's more embarrassing than playing HuniePop.
5. The ships are my favorite part of the game. I love the sense of progress that's there when you watch your ship grow from this tiny little plank of wood to an epic pirate ship with flags, rooms, cannons, etc. It's really fun and really rewarding. In fact, it's one of the things that kept me motivated through the manual-labor portions of the game. Probalem is, as my ship got more grand, my crew more numbered, and my opponents more fierce, --my framerate got lower, and lower, and lower.  I by no means have a powerful computer, and I understand indie developers don't have the resources to deeply optimize their games, but if I'm struggling to play a fairly basic 2D game on a modern i5 laptop, that's a problem.
6. Lastly, this game is riddled with little stuff that just makes no sense to me.
Why can't I zoom in to better enjoy this game's gorgeous visuals?
Why the HELL are the controls so counter-intuitive?
Why does the game tell me it costs TP to learn skills, but it doesn't?
Why does the game need to fade and load between islands and encounters?
Why does the game offer little "sailing" sections, but never let them last more than 4 seconds?
I mean, honestly, this is a really fun game, especially the first few hours, and if you can get it for $5 or less, it's worth it.
It is so deeply flawed, though, that, honestly, it feels incomplete. Like the first half of the game is finished, but we're still playing the alpha version of the second half.
