So i just beat this game, and here's my checklist for whether or not you will want this game.
You will like this game if:
-You were/are a fan of the hyperdimension neptunia series
-You like Dynasty warriors/ Hyrule warriors eseque gameplay
-You aren't looking for a particularly in depth story
-You want to turn your brain off, bash some trash mobs and listen to the BGM
-Idk, maybe your just here for the fanservice, which is literally just canned stripping animations and less clothing
You will not like this game if:
-You are looking for a game that has any sort of replayability or multiple endings(only has one ending)
-You are looking for a game that is long-lasting or has varied gameplay (game lasts about 14hours if you do all of the side missions, around 8 if you just bum rush the main story)
-You are looking for a good hack-n-slash game. Its an average hack-n-slash game with a plethora of colors and like a hundred enemies on the screen at any given time
-You are looking for a challenging video game. You could probably beat this game whilst playing tetris.
Alright, now on to the actual reveiw, which  will include more specifics on what the game does, how it is similar and differnt to the main game series, writing style, and other random gripes and praises. Warning: Word soup ahead
Review
First off, the main allure of every hyperdimension neptunia game is the characters, as they are fairly quirky and funny takes on various sterotypes and are generally quite funny. This game... it seems to have forgotten part of that, as eveything that makes the characters who they are is dulled out a little bit presumably because there is less dialouge to work with, meaning the character's individual personalities are shown 75% less and instead is replaced by inter-character interactions... Which would be great if only there was, i don't know, an actual REASON for the characters to interact? like a conflict of interest? or literally anything other than a random string of jokes, compliments and backhanded insults? A huge part of what made following the character development in the main games was the fact that they were faced by a tangible conflict in the form of other characters and subsequently overcame that and became friends/ tentative allies. This game has none of that and instead mostly replaces it with proof of character relation, which basically means the games spends a lot of time talking about how the characters interact with each other, but in a very one-directional way. so yeah thats my veiw on the overall writing style and no, i'm not going to comment on the fact that some of the lines are literally just super-cringeworthy memes. Moving on, the next thing i found intruiging is how they modifyed all of the assets from the main game( everything from game mechanics to maps) and how some of it was good, some of it just weird. The good part is that they made all of the various stats streamlined AF so you dont really have to think to hard about your strategy for hitting things, as well as the way the various meters(SP and EXE) are made easy to manage in a 3d fast-paced game enviroment. I also really like how they did the menus: if i needed to check something, it took like 3 clicks tops. Now the weird parts  are the map implementation and the enemy aggro mechanic. The maps are pretty much copy-paste from the main games, except they added barriers that basicly just railroad you down a single path, which would be fine if these maps served as awesome arenas, but they dont(in fact in some cases you wonder how in the world your supposed to fight in such cramped spaces). However, this problem is partially alleviated due to the inclusion of a few actual arena levels with lots of space, which i thought were the most enjoyable levels. Second flaw is kinda minor in that the enemy aggro ranges dont work right half the time, they suffer from the same problem the enemies in the main series did in that if you do anything but walk in a straight line they lose sight of you and just sit there for like a whole 5 seconds before noticing you again. Again, minor problem that only really presents itself if you try and kite a group for a mass wipeout. Next up, character imbalance, which i realize has existed in the past games and directly corellated with the characters confidence/skillset(which was awesome by the way) but it just doesn't mesh well in the genre because you cant have the party protect the weak character anymore, they are at the mercy of stun-locks and crazy high dps and there isn't♥♥♥♥♥♥you can do about it. For example, Rom and Ram are made as glass cannons in terms of stats... except that every other character is a ♥♥♥♥ing railgun in comparison, complete with reinforced metal plating. This differentiation leads to an unavoidable gap in how fun it is to play one character(the OP one) vs the other(the weaksause character), and thats a problem beacuse the game requires you to use every character every now and then. Next on the chopping block: the story. The ♥♥♥♥ing "story". want me to sum it up for you?
. If you didn't read that spoiler, then just take my word for it: It is more threadbare then the characters after the "outfit break" which is a problem because, as I pose at the begining of this giant ♥♥♥♥ing text wall, this game is about character, but also what the characters do and how they do it. Also, there are points in the writing were it uses taletale signs of leadup, like characters worrying about something hyper-specific or various off-handed would-be foreshadowing, and then does nothing with it and just sort of moves on. Anyways, my next point is the items and equipment system, aka kill stuff and get stuff. Yeah, it does away with the JRPG shop system in the main game and instead uses a medal system where you kill monsters and unlock gear in unlimited supply for all characters. The pro to this is, as mentioned before, stats become easy to manage. The bad part is that customization is narrowed down to which cosmetic outfit your character wears beacause the stat items uprade super linear-like, "A is better than B in every way" style. Overall, i feel like the system could  have been a lot more fleshed out, but at least it works(i guess). Finally, the moment you probably would be waiting for if you haven't left already: The combat and challenge. So, as you probably read on the store page, your clothes are not that of Geralt of Rivia whose silken cloth can witstand dragonfire. No, instead they will eventually rip and tear, resulting in fanservice, and(if your me) increased crit rate, EXE drive increase and increased damage recieved. Know how many characters fighting style this fits like a glove? All but 2, those being Rom and Ram, because they have low health and high base crit rate to begin with. This means that the game is mechanicly encouraging you to lose your clothes as it were, and gives you bigger numbers when you follow along, which i guess is to be expected of a mechanic of this variety. BUT this mechanic actually create a weird problem in that it locks the player into an aggressive playstyle because it is so disproportiontly rewarded. As a direct result, the already repetitive gameplay that is dynasty warriors punchy punchy is made even more one-dimensional due to the fact that you pretty much have to play it out in the same style everytime. Maybe this isn't a problem for you because your attack plan is always aggro, but many people like to play hack and slash cautiously, setting up for big efficent mass wipes by kiting and getting out of the way and turning into a damage sponge. Ok, now that that word pudding is done, time for me to talk about the challenge of the game. Basiclly, unless you equip that one item that makes you weak as paper  or go into a quest that is a much higher level, the game hands you victory for free.
That concludes this reveiw. Final verdict: its ok

So..The Bureau:XCOM Declassified.
The Bureau: XCOM Declassified is a science fiction video game in the X-COM series, developed by 2K Marin and was released by 2K Games. It is a third-person tactical shooter with strategy video game elements.
In Bureau we are stepping into a boots of William Carter,a CIA special agent who is tasked with delivering an important package at the Bureau's research labs at Groom Range. But in that moment something goes wrong,and by that i want to say a freacking aliens,or "Outsiders" if you want to call them like that,attack the Earth. Sorry,they attack the USA and no other country even knows about this or they are not even trying. Don't ask me how or why.
So our protagonist has to join a secret organization called "The Bureau" and stop the invasion.Simple right?
So,about the game itself.
Original setting,which is the 60's of a XX century is one of my favoruite that is why i love it. From music and clothing to cars and buildings it gives you very good feeling of those times..of course not so beautiful when there are aliens around you but still,you can enjoy it when not being shot.
Graphic is good,not impressive but you won't cry about it either. Since i prefer gameplay over that i am not really talking about it.
Sound is also decent,with a whole 60's music,a gun sounds and aliens. What i don't like is voiceacting,kinda stiff if you ask me,and Carter himself sounds angry most of the time.
Gameplay.
We got aliens, and different versions of them,from simple Sectoids through Mutons and Sectopods to Commanders that can make drones,control your soldiers and more. Most of the time bullets will work tho but it won't be easy.
On the field,we can also control our 2 squadmates,each one of them can have different abilities to use and perks that can help us or make things worse on some stages,so be careful how you pick them on higher difficulties.
If you played other XCOM games you know how it works. Squad teammates can get 5th rank level,but Carter can get a 10th. And we have 4 classes of teammates to choose from,each has it's good and bad things,and only you can decide which one you will use(in the meaning of class,not bad/good thing!).
Fighting itself is good and you have to use a lot of abilities,tactics and aim to beat enemies. Until you get Heavy Plasma Pistol which is OP as heck,then you beat everyone solo. Still AI is smart,uses a lot of cover,flanks and abilities to kill you.
Game is like Crossover between Mass Effect 2 with whole combat system,a XCOM universe and a 60's magic.
Game is very good,and very highly recommended if you enjoy those types of games. Voiceacting could be better and the whole "talking system" ripped from ME is not needed but still...very good game.
Strong 8/10

Hell Yeah is a game that is pure style over substance. Its most redeeming aspect is the sheer quality and quantity packed into its art style.
The game itself is spent hunting down and destroying 100 "unique" monsters scattered across several large labyrinthine maps, evoking an almost Metroid II feeling.  The nature of this large fetch quest becomes tiresome after a while, and the liberal sprinkling of mediocre power ups do little to keep one engaged.
Technically, the controls are a little spotty and downright uncomfortable with aiming of projectile weapons being handled with the right analog stick, and the playfield never feels properly presented, with enemies almost always being offscreen and too much of the screen's real estate being taken up by gobs and gobs of art.
It's stylish and wacky, but everything underneath its unique coat of paint just isn't enough to carry this game.
Do you like the humor of Ren and Stimpy? Do you long for a comedic platformer like Earthworm Jim? Buy this game. Humorous boss fights, collectibles, and tons of minigames make this game a fun ride,

Axiom Verge is an incredible game.  It's heavily inspired by Metroid, so if you are a fan of the Metroid series, get the game now.  Although the influence of Metroid is heavy, the game is completely unique:  the story, characters, art, and music are all excellent.  I think the biggest surprise for me was the story.  The story in this game is strong and compelling, whereas the early Metroid games featured little to no story.
Aside from a few rough spots, I feel the difficulty of the game was fair.  You can expect to get 10 - 15 hours of playtime out of your first run.  Enemies in the later areas are more annoying than I would like:  they are hard to hit and drain your health quickly.  Do expect to get stuck on bosses until you learn their patterns (or watch the helpful boss guide on Steam).  There were parts where I got quite lost, and I feel that was more of a problem here than it was in any Metroid game, but it's a fairly minor complaint.
Overall, I'd give Axiom Verge a 9.5/10.  There are some frustrating bits, but it's easily the best game I've played in ages.

The game also has additional side content that I didnt complete in my 8 hour playthrough. My only complaint is that the weapon/armor crafting system in this game seems tacked on and forgettable. As the stories progress and you accomplish different endings, you'll learn a bit more about different characters. Their stories, their backgrounds, their aspirations and their wounds... They'll look just like real people and you'll start to love them. Bit by bit, the details of each bird story will form the background scenario for the true ending that's completely thrilling, gorgeous and unexpected. Get ready to shed a lot of tears.

This is a very fun and well-designed management game. You get the freedom to set your space station up how you want; you pick your buildings and place/design them, hire your people, trade your goods, research technologies and design your own bio-deck. The game achieves a good balance, often times keeping you very busy and struggling to keep your station running. The game is not too hard, but there's definitely legitmate threat of losing everything you've worked to build. Sometimes you might feel like you're absolutely crushing a mission or opponent, other times you're getting breached and don't have enough employees to repel the breach, and you just know you're kissing a part of your station goodbye.
I'd say just in missions alone you can get 30-40 hours of play time, depending on how fast you complete them. And the sandbox mode will add some time on top of that for you. This game has some replayability, too. You could come back to it in a few months or a year and be sucked in all over again.
If I had complaints, one would be the combat in the game. You can take sections of the station from other administrators, but the combat is pretty hands off for the most part. You initiate the breach and your people take care of the rest. I also found myself wanting a little more interaction with the employees I hired. When you first look at a potential candidate for hire there's a whole interface, but I was slightly let down when I realized all you can really do is hire, fire and promote. But that's just a very small "I wish I could do more!" thing. This is an older game, and the graphics are pretty much on par with games of it's age. Overall, I'd say great game. If only there were a sequel, or something similar that's on-par.

First Free Bird took us To the Moon and now they take us a little closer to home with a Bird Story.
A Bird Story takes its place in the Sigmund corp. timeline as a prelude to the sequel to To The Moon. It follows a young boy in an unidentified urban setting who clearly feels alone and estranged from other kids. He eventually rescues a bird from a predator and places it in his backpack, carrying the bird home to nurse it back to health on his back porch. From there the story follows the emotional journey of this Young Boy as he tries to find the bird’s place in and world and struggles with what could happen. Despite the lack of more then archetypal characters the story has, it’s extremely endearing.  The young boy, as the only dynamic character, cycles through emotions of depression and joy as well as love and pain. The story is sympathetic to his emotions. The reactions of nature will change with his joys and his pain. In short we have a character driven story with a young boy we can greatly relate to and other static character built to draw out his reactions. In the end it’s a tearjerker of a story and certainly worth experiencing. The presentation of A Bird Story is very similar to its predecessor in that it keeps the 16 bit art style. Once again this is used excellently to connect the two stories together in the same universe and the art style itself is very quaint. It’s not the most realistic or the most dynamic but there is something about it that’s endearing all the same. The weird hand drawn cut scenes are also gone which leads me to believe that the developer has realized their limitations within A Bird Story which goes a long way to strengthening the piece as a whole. As far as game play goes….well there isn’t any. The game acts more as an interactive short story then as a game. The few challenges that are present are “jump here” or “move here”. These do enhance the story by making the player step into the shoes of the character, but they are gimmicks which don’t really affect the overall game. In the end we simply have to realize that A Bird Story is something more akin to an interactive book than a video game. Sound design is where this game thrives. The OST is extremely memorable because each track connects to a certain instance in the story where the emotions are elevated. Not to mention the instrumentalists put together just beautiful music. The sound effects and cues are well timed and have a level of depth to them. When your skipping through puddles or flying over the city skyline the sound effects help ensure you believe it. Everything feels homey and inviting until the main character feels fear or foreboding. During these moments the OST is haunting. Honestly buy the soundtrack edition of this game, it’s amazing. So then does A Bird Story succeed? Let’s look at the summary.
Pros:
-Memorable OST
-Engaging use of SFX
-Emotional and relatable story
-Extremely well developed main character
-Visuals are quaint
-No more weird cut scenes
-Emotional replay value
Cons:
-Little to no game play
For you completionists out there, this game is not much of a challenge. By that I mean there is no challenge at all. A Bird Story is completed simply by playing the very short game. Upon finishing the story you will receive the only achievement. So of course, there is no completion bonus.  With that in mind I give this game a rating of 8.5/10 and a completionist rating of Finicomplete it!

This is a game, that, unlike a lot of greenlight games, doesn't deserve punishment for low effort.  Why, then, is Brink a bad product?  Because it's the perfect product to show off everything that's BAD about the new era of online gaming.   A huge amount of effort went into look, feel, quality, construction.   But they did just enough to achieve that, and ignored all gameplay, but they hit you hard and fast with demands for DLC purchases.   It could have been a contender.  But it's everything that's bad about the microtransaction era and nothing that's good about it.   We have a lot to learn from this failure.
Technical:  No support for 4K earns an immediate thumbs down when your strategy is to release a high graphics cutting edge game.   It's smooth and fluid enough, but optimisation could be better.
Graphics:  They hired artists and put in a huge amount of effort refining the look and feel of the game, as well as hiring great voice actors, so you would think this is thumbs up territory.   This is why we have so much to learn from this game.
Gameplay: Now here's where it gets controversial.   It's a mediocre arena shooter (like there aren't hundreds of these) with a fairly well done art style and even a plotty single player campaign.   But the single player is just the mediocre arena shooter with mediocre bots.   But balanced around PvP, badly.   No effort was put into gameplay balance.  No effort was put into refining this after the massive amount of effort put into polishing the game.  There's actually a single player storyline that might be quite interesting if it wasn't for the horrendous miscarriage that is the gameplay.
All the effort in this game went into polish and DLC options, and none of it into the heart and soul of gameplay.  They give you no doubts when it comes to making sure you know they want your money.  But for what?  There's far better free arena FPS games.
Final note:  At this stage it's 4 years after launch, and the online servers are abandoned.  Even if you wanted to pay money to have a worse experience than the free arena shooters, you can't because there's not enough players.   They still want $10 for the full package though.   Go buy $10 worth of donuts and play TF2, you'll have a much better time.

Another game that's a great example of an interesting idea that was poorly executed. The general gameplay and story would have made this an okay-ish experience but combined with the MANY flaws this game has, trying to enjoy it felt like an exercise in futility.
To start off, damage with melee weapons is frustratingly inconsistent. You can smack a zombie in the head a dozen times and it'll pop back up at you like one of those inflatable bounce-back targets or smack it just once and it's head pops like a melon. Add to that the horrible ragdoll physics that either send the zombies flying into the air like a shotgun blast or somehow get ragdolled behind you and already nibbling at you before you even realize it.
Then there's issues with inventory. You start off with a pretty small amount of space and later get the ability to get a (barely) bigger backpack, but in the meantime you quickly run out of space as the slots fill up with random food and healing items, weapons and ammo, and things like flares and other traps. This honestly wouldn't be so bad if the items actually stacked though, but of course they don't so you have to make constant trips back to your safehouse to deposit them in a storage box in the hopes you'll have space (and a use) for them later. Which you won't. One of those reasons being that as soon as you find a new melee weapon and gun, you realize that you can't even remove your old crappy ones from your inventory. In a way this makes sense. The game forces you to keep a melee weapon and a ranged weapon so that you're never unarmed. The problem here is that you're forced to keep your OLD stuff throughout the entire game, never even able to put them in storage.
The looting system itself isn't much better. Any time you want to  check your items or loot a body, your character has to stop and drop his backpack to the ground first, leaving you all too vulnerable to attacks. While this may sound realistic in a sense, what's not realistic is the looting UI covering your screen as you do and blocking you from actually seeing what's going on around you, so it feels like a pretty moot point. Lastly getting actual loot from enemies and containers is pretty unlikely, so you'll spend a lot of time clicking corspes and opening things up trying to find loot that just isn't there. You can scan them instead with your fancy PDA and get a reading on whether they have loot (the science of this is beyond me), but regardless you're going to see the screen prompt to loot the empty stuff anyway and scanning around is pretty time consuming (especially since you can't move while you do).
To me the game says that it wants to be unique and it wants it's ideas to be relevant, but the fact is the way they're implemented in the game creates an impractical and overall a frustrating experience instead of an enjoyable one. The lack of polish and those issues in mind, I really can't recommend this game. If you find it on sale and you know what you're in for beforehand, I can only wish you luck and hope you enjoy it more than I did.

I want to start out this review by saying I love XCOM. Even when I quit the old ones due to frustration with the difficulty (XCOM: Terror from the Deep deserves a mention here), I still loved the premise. Some of the recent XCOM titles have been very rewarding and polished - if XCOM were cuisine, the originals would be a home-made Thanksgiving Day meal (difficult but rewarding),and something like XCOM: Enemy Unknown would be like a sit down dinner at Bonefish Grill. Delicious, slick and addictive.
Following this analogy, The Bureau is like Jack in the Box or a box of Chex Mix: a jumble of cheap food with no discernable thematic connection. Unlike Chex Mix, you can't even pick out the little bits you like either.
I wanted to like the Bureau: a tactical third-person shooter based in the XCOM universe with a slick 50's style, slathered with a dressing of RPG elements and cool weapons. It could have been Rainbow Six with ayy lmaos.
Instead, most annoyingly, it's a cover-based shooter with lots of chest-high walls put into set-piece battles - and it gets old. It suffers from consolitis, the controls are definitely geared towards gamepads (I'm a mouse and keyboard guy).
Your attention is constantly pulled between navigating sticky walls while trying to manage two other (and only two) soldiers. Yes, you 'pause' the game to give orders (sort of like a tactical VATS from Fallout), but frequently you'll need to shoot and move at the same time you should be managing your soldiers. You can either give orders, or move. This wouldn't be an issue, except Bureau is unforgiving - death is frequent even at lower difficulty levels, and squaddies suffer from permadeath easily. Don't get to them in time? Well, they're pretty much goners. This isn't an issue for a fully turn-based game like Enemy Unknown, but when you're being suppressed or dealing with a gaggle of grenades thrown at your feet, it's teeth-grindingly annoying. You usually don't have enough team members to suppress enemies at the same time you try to revive. If ONE of your guys go down, you have to send yourself or the other teammate to revive him and with a team of only three people, this means that a single downed trooper can essentially reduce your strength by 2/3rds.
Grenades are particularly annoying: you'll need to scoot if you see the icon, but the sticky controls make it difficult to get out of the way - frequently I found myself . Grenades aren't even a two-way street! It's annoying slow to throw them (can't toss them during the pause), and the AI has no issues with moving out of the way quickly enough to negate their usefulness.
The RPG elements are lackluster: there's little choice because the are immediately obvious and won't ever want to use anything else. Weapons and abilities are pretty interesting, but ultimately unsatisfying because they won't change your playstyle very much.
Storywise, it has its moments, but the character development is lackluster. The main character is the standard cliche badass with a bad past that is played out and even borders on parody: times when I wanted him to react with interest or surprise were spoiled by his awful demeanor and lack of conveyance of any emotion. He acts more like a janitor having to clean up some kid's puke for the third time this week at school instead of a man thrown into an underground resistance against an alien foe.
Just like I understand that some people love Jack in the Box, and some people are going to like The Bureau, but why? You can get better tacos (Fuzzy's) and burgers (Carl's Jr or Red Robin) elsewhere. Likewise, you can get better cover based shooters (Gears of War and Mass Effect), tactical games (just about anything else in the XCOM universe), or retro-themed RPGs (Fallout: New Vegas).
I don't even know where it falls into the XCOM universe, it's just so odd. If it's free, it's worth a few hours, otherwise avoid.
Full disclosure: I was hungry while I wrote this review.

A Bird Story is told in a surreal blend of dream and life sequences. There's no text; the graphics tell the story, while music and color evoke the mood of each scenario. One dream sequence, for example, manages to convey a threat to the boy and the bird solely through imagery. It's a powerful example of both the child's imagination and his perception of threats. It speaks to the emotional strength of the tale.
There's more story than game in A Bird Story, but it effortlessly conveys volumes in short cinematic sequences. The experience is tightly controlled, and the player interacts at key points such as rescuing the bird, giving it food, and playing with it. The sweeping sequence where they go on a paper airplane flight to help the bird find its family is magical and literally a flight of fancy. The experience may be incredibly short, but it's powerful, and players will marvel at the sense of imagination and storytelling without a single word being said.

A classic, charming space station builder. (Can it be 'classic' if it was released in 2001? Well, in my mind it is.) You oversee a space station which aliens visit in the hopes of enjoying classy resorts, getting medical care or just grabbing a bite to eat and a nap before their next flight.
Building is usually done by creating a room, then placing objects in the room (much like Theme Hospital). You build on the inside of a torus, and you can move the camera around with great freedom; it's fascinating to look through your torus and see rooms curving upward into the distance. In addition, there's a 'biodeck', where you can shape hills, valleys and lakes with great detail, as well as define different 'climate zones'; alien plants will grow there, which you can harvest for goods...Or you can transplant the plants around your station as decoration.
As for gameplay, there are about a dozen missions that introduce aspects of the game in sequence; they're fun, although they can be challenging! You can also rule over a station in your own time in the 'sandbox' mode. Most missions have to do with building a certain structure and making sure all the other basic facilities are in place; a hospital mission, a prison mission, etc.. There's also a mission where you have to trade goods with passing ships; buy low, sell high!
One last thing I absolutely must mention is the light-hearted atmosphere of the game. It has a very British sense of humor. Your 'assistant', VAL, sounds like a cross between the Dungeon Keeper narrator and HAL 9000. It's clear the designers were at least influenced by The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy. The British slang might occasionally be a bit obscure for Americans ("boffins", "butcher's hook") but the game has a great deal of charm.

Axiom Verge is an indie pixel art Metroid-vania. That means you'll be slowly amassing an aresenal of power-ups and weapons to beef up your player character, and using lateral thinking and exploration to unlock and discover new parts of it's mysterious and seemingly massive map. In Axiom Verge, by the end of the game, you'll likely have a massive weapon wheel, all with their own little quirks and benefits. You'll think about areas in a totally different way by the end of the game, as your movement options will increase exponentially. You'll chip away at the Map screen until all those squares are filled in. It's a classic, satisfying formula, and it works here. The level design matches the mechanics quite well, and the exploration feels very natural.
I adore Metroid. I remember I went on a total binge of purchasing Metroid-vanias when it became moderately clear to me that Nintendo is currently kind of neglecting the franchise. ANYWAY. Axiom Verge is a love song to Super Metroid. It's the Interstellar to 2001, in a way. It's a hard game to live up to; most consider Super Metroid to be a masterpiece. And you can tell it's likely that Thomas Happ, the creator of Axiom Verge, probably does too.
And therein lies one of the issues with the game. While there are many Metroid-vanias coming out nowadays which innovate the genre, Axiom Verge itterates does very little to distinguish itself in any truly meaningful way. Looking back, I can remember very little memorable or particularly excellent. Nothing truly bad, but nothing that had me enraptured. I thought the "Rusalka" were really cool, I remember some really neat puzzles, and the soundtrack having quite a few killer tracks, those stick out, I'll admit. But I don't really remember any unique level design. I don't really remember the name or feel of any areas (other than an area that takes place above ground). I don't really remember developing any engagement or attachment while running through its glitchpunk corridors.
But I DO remember the clearly Geiger-inspired visuals not being my cup of tea (this is ENTIRELY SUBJECTIVE, however (obviously)). I remember boss battles which were so poorly designed they seemed like jokes. I remember combat that often felt finnicky and imprecise. I remember monotonous crawls through combat areas. I remember maybe a dozen weapons I never touched after acquiring them. I remember a plot so convoluted, silly, and engrossed in itself it just came across as pretentious. But most importantly, I remember a moment in the game where a necessary item was hidden in a giant mass of breakable blocks, inside a soulless random tile. At that point, I thought to myself, "Something about this game isn't working."
Hey. Axiom Verge is by NO means a bad game. It's actually pretty good. Mechanically, the game is solid, with a few neat inventions here and there. If you're looking for a fix of Metroid like I was, this is a fine way to go. However, I would never introduce someone to the genre this way, and I find myself having trouble remembering anything I found truly notable or excellent about the game. Which I suppose isn't a bad thing. But it's not a good thing, either.
So, I guess Axiom Verge is a thing, that isn't necessarily bad, but isn't necessarily good either. Axiom Verge is a game. It's definitely a game.

Some people have complained about the dungeons, but to be honest I liked them and didn't feel like being slight variations of the same dungeons I'd already explored. I did, however, miss a full map that I could check so I could locate my position in the dungeon or track any possible hidden areas with chests.
Speaking of treasure chests, I couldn't help it but feel a bit down when I finally got to some particularly pesky chests only to find that they only had a potion or another healing item that I wasn't gonna use anyway. Some of the treasure chests' contents could have been better.
And lastly, one of the things that bothered me the most about skyborn is that the game doesn't give you any information about stats and you can easily play through chunks of the game the wrong, or at least not in the most optimal, way.
Other than this, there are only minor issues that could have been improved to make the game better. For instance, moving through the menus can sometimes get chaotic, I really missed the FF battle option of remembering your last action, in Skyborn you always start on the "attack" command and the forge system is one of those things you think is important and you're going to be using in the future but you end up not using, or at least not as much as you think you would. Also, the Colosseum could have been improved, the augmentation system should have been explained in depth and Skyborn would've benefited greatly from Steam achievements. But none of this flaws break the game.
In short, those are all the issues that I found in the game, but don't let that distract you from the truth. Despite everything, Skyborn is a really good game, very enjoyable with a nice difficulty curve (provided you play on Hard mode) which presents several innovations, such as a new battle system and an engaging story, that could have made of skyborn another "Chrono Trigger"-like quality game but doesn't quite reach the top as it stands.
Overall: 8.75/10

Starting this review, I want to emphasize that this game is mostly for Hyperdimension Neptunia fans. If you're fan of hack n slash genre but don't know Neptunia, there are most likely better options out there. That's not to say that this one is bad though. If you don't know Hyperdimension Neptunia this is bad game to start the series - the story somewhat assumes you know the characters already. It's much better to play Re;birth 1 instead.
The later part is aimed mostly to HDN fans.
On positives - In this game the good neptunia humor is still out there. The hack n slash mechanics are relaxing, albeit not too demanding, and the characters are distinct enough with their playstyles. I really enjoyed new additions to the roster - Dengekiko and Famitsu. Both are really cute and entertaining. I also love attention to small details in this game - like secondary characters comments during combat, lily rank dialogues, or even small coments the characters make when they are chosen or withdrawn for quests. I'm not really fan of fanservicey stuff, but I love the embarassed faces some characters make then, like Famitsu. It's adorable in it's own way.
On negatives - while jokes are there, there aren't too much of them, because story is really sparse. Re;birth counterparts are much more rich in plot (THAT plot as well). In addition Fanservicey stuff went a little too far with Rom and Ram. It's not that much of the problem though, as there are unbreakable clothes to equip. Still cringed for a moment. I'm not CFW Trick :( The balance is also not really there - some characters have much stronger combos and control than other ones. But all characters work well, so it's similar to RB games where basically any party worked. Game also lags at times, especially in snow stage for me or at beginning of the quest. Which is weird given my rather high-end PC. There is also an issue of sound - "Boss of DOS" track plays to often, and monster sounds gets annoying after short while. Hopefully they can be turned off while keeping godess' (and journalists) voices. And last but not least.... LILY RANKS. Thanks satan for reminding me times of korean grinder MMOs where leveling pace of 0,7% per hour was normal.
To sum up...
Positives:
+Good old Neptunia wit
+Dengekiko and Famitsu
+Fun hack n slash mechanics
+Diverse cast
+Funny enjoyable small dialogues thrown here and there (lily ranks, secondary character comments, character select comments)
+/- Quite heavy on fanservice (but it can be "turned off" by wearing ubreakable clothes so it's not the big issue for those who don't like it)
Negatives:
-Lackluster, sparse story
-Rom and Ram cloth breaking.... come on IF we're not CFW Trick in disguise :<
-Characters aren't really balanced
-Some technical issues - rare lagging
-Annoying monsters' sound effects and repetitive "Boss of DOS" track
-Lily rank grind
To me as HDN fan it's solid 7,5/10 game. It's not as good as RB counterparts, but the fun is still there, and if you like Hyperdimension Neptunia games, you'll most likely like this one as well. If you don't know HDN, you should definitely check out Re;birth 1!
TL;DR
Decent Neptunia entry, not as good as Re;birth counterparts but enjoyable enough.

TL;DR: It's a third-person X-Com game in real-time. It's not bad, but I'm sure there's better in the series and in the genre.
I've played the original X-Come games in dos when they came out - except everything after apocalypse. This feels like the new X-Com: Enemy Unknown but in real-time, and commanding a small squad from the ground.
I enjoyed the 1960's atmosphere, and found some scenerios creepy and had a lot of fun with it. It feels like a breeze to get through so far, and too linear to come back and replay - unlike the original X-Coms and the newer ones. Action sequences are also too infrequent for what I like, and there's rarely any aliens outside of staged shoot-outs. I was never expecting one to jump out, or be caught in a room with a couple of them.
I haven't played enough third-person shooters, but I found this one lacking - especially around commands and weapons. Ie. I can't tell my squad to take cover and protect themselves, and the weapons are the same series of pistole, rifle, shotgun, sniper rifle, rocket launcher but with different technologies.
My only other complaint is that I felt that running to and out of cover felt sticky (I take cover everywhere), not sticky enough (I need cover but can't get down), and delayed interactions with cover - like rolling or running out. I'm using a keyboard and mouse and heard that gamepads feel better to use.
I think those complaints are too minor to pass up this. It really feels like you're taking a small squad from Enemy Unknown and playing out their combat during the 1960's. Your fights depend on your skill, creativity, how well your command your squad, and your attention to the battlefield. The storyline is interesting, and I'm glad there's options in your interactions - although I don't know how it affects gameplay or the story.

I haven't played this for a while, but I do love ships, and this sim lets me play around with ships large and small.  It isn't a game as such, there are scenarios which give a variety of tasks to complete - not all of them terribly easy.  Some of the physics can go awry - towing the bulk gas tanker is one where having tugged too hard to get the big devil moving, I couldn't find the brakes (!), and it ended up pulling my tug backwards.  There is a lot in here to enjoy, though, if you have that kind of interest in things to do with ships - they don't behave like cars, or aeroplanes - everything goes quite slowly until that crucial monent when a turn or change of rudder or throttle has to be timed to the split second or there will be a bit of a disaster!  I find the level of immersion to be deep and most enjoyable - but I think it requires some research and quite a bit of understanding.  Parking the P and O cross channel ferry in Dover is an example - reverse parking is not everyone's forte.  It is possible. but even skippers with several years sea experience can find it unnerving.  If you don't want to have to persevere and reach an understanding of the physics and hydro dynamics maybe you won't enjoy this sim - but for me, it is by far the best out there at the moment.  I'd love to see a warship game with graphics and physics as good as this has.

Axiom Verge is basically a Metroid clone and a great one at that. Thomas Happ did an excellent job in creating not just a metroidvania game, but the classic 2D Metroid game.
Just one look at Axiom Verge and you'll immediately get that Metroid feel. From the overall look & feel and level design to enemy types, weapons and play mechanics, Axiom Verge draws heavily from Nintendo's cult classic. And that is certainly a good thing in my book. This game is basically the original Metroid on steroids, made with modern tech and little to none of the annoying old limitations.
Yet, despite drawing so much from Metroid, one shouldn't dismiss just how original Axiom Verge actually is — Thomas Happ has created a unique world with interesting characters and story. Nor should anyone doubt the high quality of this game: the graphics and overall visual design are gorgeous, music and sound effects are atmospheric and fit the game perfectly, controls are spot on and everything is pretty much just right.
Just as any Metroid game should, Axiom Verge features an extensive map, which is made up from different zones, all of which feature their own design and style. As you play you will slowly uncover more and more parts of the map, with some of them becoming available to you only after you'll get new upgrades and abilities. As you would expect, there is quite a lot of platforming in this game, with some of it being rather challenging, but none of it's really unfair — if some of it may seem that way, then you probably don't have the necessary equipment yet. Unlike most metroidvania games, which almost exclusively take place in rather small enclosed areas, Axiom Verge features some broad open areas, which nicely break up the the regular flow and add some additional variety to the game.
The boss fights in Axiom Verge are exciting, with bosses being interesting and huge, in fact some of them are so huge that the screen zooms out to be able to show them completely. As with most things in this game, some bosses are better fought with particular weapons that you may not have when first encountering them, so it may be a better option to keep exploring than fighting at the first possibility. As with the bosses, enemies in this game are very interesting both in design and behaviour/attack types and patterns.
Among the more unique game mechanics in Axiom Verge is the glitch gun, which serves many different purposes (like opening up passages, traversing the map, etc), but also can modify the enemy units. Glitching the enemies causes them to change in one way or another, gaining new properties, which you can utilise for your own purposes.
All in all Axiom Verge is a great game which you definitely should play, even if you aren't a fan of the genre. It's a darn shame that almost nobody did — at the time of the review, SteamSpy estimates the sales at ~29K copies.

This game is really damn good. With my only prior meteroidvania experience being Castlevania Symphony of the Night, I didn't know if I'd like a sci-fi one. The visuals in the game ALMOST look like they would belong on an NES, but just barely make it to the 16 bit look due to multiple layers of scrolling, and amounts of color on screen (would probably be on a turbografix 16/pc engine). I got this game through Indiebox, and I'm glad I did, because I got a bunch of stuff, including a map of the game, which helped out a lot. I only really have 3 issues with this game. The first one, is backtracking. This metroidvania doesn't really have a teleportation system, exept for the INDI area, which is a glorified version of a teleporter that takes longer than one. I didn't mind the backtracking too much, but it's something to keep in mind when buying this game. Second is the PC port. I think the PC port is fine for the most part, but I'm experiencing an issue where when I'm simply playing the game, my computer doesn't recognise my controller's input as an input to the computer, so it goes into sleep mode. This is really annoying, but it can be circumvented by using big picture mode (even though it's inconvinient). My third issue is the end. I'm not going to spoil anything here, but this isn't one of those game where you feel acomplished at the end for overcoming what you faced, at least not to the extent of a lot of other games.
Other than those issues, I can reccomend this game. I'd personally wait untill it's on sale to get it, but if you like super metroid/metroid/metroidvania games, then you'll like this one.

Received free from Humble Bundle, and for a free game it's okay, but if I had spent money on it I'd be really disappointed.
At the core it's a nice game, but there are just too many flaws that in the end ruin the whole experience. Would not recommend unless you can get it for free (or really cheap).
PROS:
- excellent voice acting
- good graphics
- nice story
- relatable, believable characters
- 1960 era setup is a nice idea
CONS:
- story feels rushed at times and sometimes it feels like they cut things out, also decisions made during side quests have no impact whatsoever
- friendly AI is garbage, teammates are almost useless and you have to babysit them
- unbalanced weapons, some are useless due to an ammunition limit that's way too low
- enemies are bullet sponges, which is made worse by the aforementioned limited ammo
- obvious console port, keyboard&mouse controls feel clunky and checkpoint system is annoying (checkpoints too far apart, no manual save)
Bottom line: Game tries to be both a tactical shooter and an FPS, and fails at both. It's also only barely an XCOM game because the core concepts of XCOM games (base building, researching of aliens and their technology, resource management) are completely missing.

Ship Simulator Extremes is a Simulator which allows you to helm various types of vessels, in a variety of different modes. Free roam the seas, or play various campaigns, single player missions, or through multiplayer mode, Ship Simulator Extremes has a lot to offer the Ship Simulator enthusiest; However, there are also a few serious drawbacks. There is no playable tutorial, which teaches you how to operate the various ships, so you are thrown into campaigns, missions, and even free roam, completely blind. This makes the learning curve difficult for people who are casual players even if you have prior experience with other simulators. The piloting controls are based on realistic controls for each ship and you will need to figure it out as you go, which does give the game an interesting challenge, but could be seen as a turn off by those who do not want to spend hours doing what a playable tutorial would teach in minutes.
Another problem this particular game is notorious for is difficulty running on high end machines. I only experienced one crash in the little over an hour I played, so this is something to keep in mind if you have a decent gaming rig. The scenery looks great and the boats are very detailed, but it takes a while to get from point to point, so you need to have a lot of patience to play this game. All in all, I thought it was great as a simulator, though I have to knock it for the lack of a playable tutorial. The missions you can do are interesting, such as stopping cargo ships from dumping in the ocean, and so on. There is a lot to do in this game and the DLC's offer even more ships and missions to experience. Just make sure if you spend the money on this game, you are prepared for a steeper than normal learning curve and have a boatload of patience. (Pardon the pun).

I feel like I've put enough time and effort into this game combined with enough knowledge to be able to accurately describe Hearts of Irons positives and negatives.
Positive
As someone who personally loves the topic of History, Hearts of Iron 4 executes the progression of World War II very nicely and it can be used to accurately display many events that occurred during this time period. I loved looking through all of the nation's focus trees and looking at what each country had to deal with during this time and how they dealt with opposing forces such as German invasions or outside influences by other countries. The game requires heavy level of knowledge and multitasking ability, although demanding at the beginning, this game gets extremely fun once you've played it a few times and gotten the hang of how things work. The achievements provide a sense of challenge and progression to show how you have harnessed your abilities to create unique scenarios. The modding community for this game is also especially large, I've created a mod myself and it's actually fairly fun to create a mod for this game; there are tons of mods available on the workshop to increase your game time and overall player experience. Millennium Dawn, Road to 56, and Kaiserreich make the game so much more enjoyable and provide so many new ways to play the game.
Negative
Although stated in almost every single negative review, the DLC released for Hearts of Iron 4 does make the game significantly better than the base version, however, as stated earlier, this can be fixed easily using several mods that I would consider as must needs especially if you don't want to spend that much money. The learning curve is quite steep in this game as well, if you're playing as a bigger country there's a lot of multitasking that needs to be done and micromanaging as well; I could not recommend this game to people who can't keep track of all the little things.

This game starts out really slow.  I had some trouble with it at first, figuring out the economy.
But after playing for a little while, it quickly becomes very engaging and hard to stop playing!  This is an under-appreciated gem - very cute graphics and endearing characters, and the game flow is captivating.  There's always something to deal with.
It's a city-building game - but you're building a city on a space-station which is a spinning ring to generate artificial gravity.  There are 3 layers (levels) to build on and associated costs for unlocking more space to build in.  There's also space management (not very fun) for cargo holds.  There's also occasional sabotage, which can bring your whole economy down if you aren't careful and run out of funds after a bomb goes off.  The driving force behind the game is 1) the character personalities and 2) the economics.

Even before buying it again on steam, I had this game years ago and must have played it for over a hundred hours. I can't explain why, but it doesn't seem to get old. There are very few gems like that around these days.

Since its release, this is a game that I have gone back to in my mind, even if I haven't been able to play it. While the gameplay is a slightly challenging resource management with a dash of The Sims, the atmosphere and universe the game takes place in is what has always sold me on it. A Douglas Adams/Red Dwarf sci-fi universe in which two-headed scientists need love from sultry sirens, four-armed farmers grow crops alongside alien monks. Your assistant is a sarcastic AI who is a bit more Marvin the Paranoid Android than GLaDOS.
The missions are challenging, combat isn't super intuitive, and it has glitched out on me a few times. Why do I keep going back? I want to see what happenes when you research the alien artifacts, or what kinds of plants give me what kinds of cargo. There is always something to do in this game, some way to expand, some way to grow and become the best Station Administrator in the 'verse.

Pretty damn good for a game made in 2001, in fact one of the best theme park/tycoon type games ever made.
It's most unique and fun feature is the biodeck, the third and innermost floor of the station which allows you to raise and lower terrain, change the soil wetness and tempurature. You can also place pools of water in order to make puddles, swamps, lakes and oceans. It's not just for looks though. Conditions on the biodeck effects what plants you grow, which ties into the game's economics, crafting and research systems.
The game does have a few annoying design flaws. You have to do some tedious micromanagement once and a while in order to avert disasters and the game doesn't really give you any tools to automate things. For example, employees need promotions once and a while or they'll quit, and the only way to know that the need them is to check the employee list and look for flashing stars, then click each one individually. You can get free energy due to a random event, but you need to notice the event notification and click it as soon as possible.
There's also combat, but like in other similar games such as dungeon keeper, it tends to heavily reward getting a huge bunch of guys together while heavily penalizing not having overwelming force. There's really no need to charge the players an energy penalty when one of their units dies in battle. They already paid energy to recruit the unit and it just means losing a battle loses you the game. Unlike dungeon keeper, battles tend to be fairly dry - rather than different units having different kinds of attacks, everyone just uses a sci fi blaster. It's really the weakest part of the game.

Played this game when it originally came out over a decade ago and it's still one of my favorite simulation games.  The scope of things to do in this game is awesome, especially with the sandbox mode.  I believe this was made by some members of the team that developed Dungeon Keeper and this game was originally billed as a Dungeon Keeper in space.
You are in charge of a space station containing 3 different levels (Industrial, Commercial, Bio) and expandable sections of a Torus (Wheel) style space station.  Either completing set-objective missions or in a sandbox environment either alone or vs an AI/Multiplayer.  The bio deck was touted as revolutionary at the time and still is quite the novel gameplay feature.  Essential you terraform the landscape of the deck in terms of altitude, moisture and temperature in order to grow different alien flora to harvest as different resources either for trade or manufacturing.
Resource Farming (Biodeck), Combat, Staff Management, Building Management, Sanitation (Beam up that trash or you'll get space rats that mutate in huge monsters!), Trade, Spies, Religion just to name a couple of the myriad of things to keep track of as station administrator... it really does make this station feel alive.
Pros:
So much to do on 3 different decks of your space station
Great voice acting (Guy who was the voice of the Hitchhikers Guide to the Galaxy Tertiary phase is the main actor in this)
Biodeck was/still is a great feature.
Cute graphics and humor
Cons:
No first person mode like in Dungeon Keeper
Being over a decade old, expect no updates or fixes.

I don't throw around Super Metroid lightly, that game is still one of the all time greats, not only in its genre, but amongst all games and I consider Axiom Verge to be in the same rank.
I have yet to complete the game, but my experience so far, exploring, collecting weapons and upgrades, trying out new powers in previously seen areas has been a joy. The story so far has me asking myself "WTF!?" and exclaiming "oooooh sheeeeeet!" and I expect there are more twists and turns to come. The graphics are lovely, a really nicely crafted pixel art style with some modern effects and I really like the glitch motif. The soundtrack has a nice moody sci-fi electro vibe (I bought the soundtrack and actually have to stop myself listening to it all the way through as to not spoil the aural aspect of the game). The weapons and upgrades are mostly unique and interesting, some are your standard fare (rapid fire, spread shot, high jump, etc.) others are rarely if ever seen in a game (I don't want to spoil anything). There are however a couple that don't seem to have anything much special over another already equipped weapon (out of the 8/9 weapons I have found, maybe 3 of them seem a little redundant).
All in all, I am really satisfied with Axiom Verge. If something goes horribly wrong between now and when I complete it, I will update this review, but I can't even imagine how big of a ♥♥♥♥ up would be necessary to diminish the enjoyment I've had so far. If you're looking for a game that is not "just another Metroidvania" but actually a game that can stand next to Super Metroid, this is it.

Neptunia U is a Hack N' Slash, and is a spinoff of the Hyperdimension Neptunia franchise. It was originally released for the PS Vita.
The story is that Gamindustri is in a very peaceful state, so two journalists called Dengekiko and Famitsu (Based off real magazines in Japan) ask the CPUs and CPU candidates to do some quests that they planned to get a good story going. Afterwards, the gang just completes more and more quests for the journalists, but there's been a rapid increase in quests, and everything is not what it seems.
The story obviously isn't as rich or deep as the main series, but it still has a plentiful amount of cutscenes and the writing is still solid. However, it isn't a huge chunk of the game like the mainstream titles. Fans of the series will be pleased with it, even if it is a little shallow. Due to the game's simple plot and gameplay, you won't find anything too interesting to write home about. At least the character interactions are still as good as ever.
Plus, the English dub is 100% voiced acted; there are no missing voices in any cutscenes, unlike the Re;birth series. (If that's your preference.)
You can choose from 10 characters: The CPUs, the Candidates, Dengekiko and Famitsu. Each of them play a bit differently, and all have their own stats. For example, Uni has a rifle so she's most effective at mid-range and building her special ability, while Neptune does quick but weak melee attacks. It's mostly melee oriented, excluding Uni, Rom, and Ram. The character's melee attacks are different though; some of them hit hard but can't string combos very well, and some can do the opposite. Everyone has the same run speed. There's also equipment that the characters can equip, adding or taking away certain stats like defense and SP. You earn these by killing a certain number of a certain enemy.
Related to all that stuff, there's a feature called "Costume Break" (Yes, this is where the fanservice comes in). If you take enough damage, your character's clothes will almost completely rip apart. What that does is that you're prone to taking more damage. However, you do more damage, so it's actually a risk vs. reward kinda thing. If you like or hate Costume Break, you can get variations of clothes that will affect this by leveling your characters up. There's unbreakable clothes that never trigger the break, easy to rip clothes that'll trigger break very easily, and pre-torn clothes to where you're immediately in Costume Break.
Gameplay is pretty different as you might of guessed. It's something like Dynasty Warriors if you wanna make a comparison. You can bring along 2 characters or go solo, and they fight one at a time. You're able to switch your character at any time unless they're KO'd, and the character in the back will regenerate HP. You have light attacks, heavy attacks, and special moves, and of course you can string together light and heavy attacks. Everybody has special attacks, and they take up either 1, 2, or 3 SP bars. You build up SP by simply attacking enemies. So because it's a Neptunia game, everyone can transform into their HDD counterparts, which upgrades all your stats and gives you superior attacks. (You'll also get all your clothes back if you were previously in Costume Break) You have an "EXE Drive" meter which builds as you attack enemies; this is how you go HDD. The character currently not being used will build EXE much faster than the one fighting. This is really all I can say about the gameplay, it is rather shallow sadly. Luckily, it's a lot of fun to slash down dozens of enemies at once, and if you're a fan of hack n' slash or want some dumb but frantic action, this is definitely for you.
The quests are where you'll choose which missions to do. They all carry a "recommended level" that your character should be, and some of them require 2 specific characters to use. The actual objectives are usually very simple. You either kill the boss enemy, kill a certain number of enemies, find a specific item, or locate an exit. There really isn't much variety to the missions, and they're all fairly simple. There are certain quests that don't have an objective, called an Irregular Quest. You simply hop into the mission and figure out what to do. (The description provides a hint)
After you beat the story, you unlock various things, including cheats, extra quests to complete, what's called "The Gamindustri Gauntlet" where it's a tournament style type of game mode where all the characters face off against one another in a 1v1 battle. You can pick whoever you want to play as and put the characters in whateve order you like. (You can even have HDD counterparts as separate characters.) If you win, you will win some new cheats and accessories that the characters can wear.
So anyway, Neptunia U is a pretty fun Hack N' Slash that just provides stupid fun in killing tons of enemies with a story that'll satisfy Neptunia fans enough. I recommend picking it up on a sale.

Next there are 1001 apples, loaves of bread, coins, books, notes, hidden throughout another 101 cabinets, chests, shelves and dumpsters in each level. This attention to detail is kinda cool at first but becomes just a mind numbing and boring way to spend most of your game time sifting though.

Its all quantity over quality.
NPC character development was poor, but the fact that the game assumes you would actually care about these characters is the insulting part.
You talk to these people a few times between missions where they usually just dribble at you. Then you move out to your mission and spend the next few hours saving and reloading while you eat apples and search for coins between the cushions on abandonded sofas.
Come back to base, they dribble at you a bit more. Rise repeat. Curiosity for some of these NPC's lives might be piqued once or twice, then story starts to wrap up. It turns into a giant trope and before you know it you are at the end of the game. Then along comes the ending and I am meant to feel something when I see their faces in some stupid cutscene???!
At the start of the game one of the tool tips mentions that if you kill people you will see more rats and have a darker ending, while if you don't kill people there will be a happier ending.
So at this point I decided to give myself a challenge and go for the low death count method.
Now the 'choices matter' element the game is going for becomes completely transparent.
Also I now have zero use for half the skills and items of the game since they are lethal.
Looking back would I have enjoyed it if I went for the bloodbath route instead? Probably not since then the game would be even less challenging.
So yeah, a game that is 90% great but was ruined by encouraging players down a very boring path.

For those unfamiliar with the origins of this game, this was originally a Wii U title. What does that mean for you on the PC? Well, a few things.
Graphics:
-Coming from the Wii U, graphically this game does not look very good on the PC. This can be a plus if you have a low to mid tier PC, as im sure it will run well on most systems. I dont find the graphics TOO horrible really, but dont expect much in the visuals department.
Gameplay:
The Wii U version of this game used the gamepad for many features such as the inventory screen, the scanner, and the map.  I feel like the PC version incorporated most of these fairly well. The map is shown on the screen and is straight forward. The scanner on the other hand, feels awkward to use. You will have to use it for certain objectives, and it can find items and containers to loot, as well as zombies and other things, but it is not very reliable and i found myself being slightly frustrated by it on a few occasions. You have to stand still to use it, and i feel like if you could walk while it is up, even slowly, it would have made it less of a hassle.
On the plus side, combat is GREATLY improved by using the mouse and keyboard.  Anyone who has ever played a shooter on a console can attest to the fact that aiming can sometimes be difficult, and most of the time console shooters mask this by having an auto-aim feature.  That is not a problem for this game. Combat feels leagues better than the Wii U version, and aiming firearms could not be easier.
OVERALL:
This is a very fun game.  If i had to compare this to another title i would say DayZ, but a very, VERY lite version of DayZ taking place in one city, with no other players.  The atmosphere is very tense and little things like showing your character as he has to stop to open up his bag while exposing himself is a nice touch.  You have to survive, and if you die, you start off as a completely different character who has the chance to kill the old zombified you to retrieve your items.  There is also a survival mode where if you die once, its game over.
I highly recommend this game if you are interested in zombie survival games.  The price tag is a bit much in my opinion, but if its on sale DEFINITELY grab this, you wont regret it.

"An alpha game with potential", would be the appropriate thing to say here, even then I must give credit to the developers for managing to create a clusterf*ck medieval battle-game where hundreds of players are smashed into eachother with no real lag or delay to speak of. I cannot however recommend this to the "usual customer" of this series as the game is currently plagued by a number of pretty serious issues.
For you people that want a solid medieval combat game right NOW and are looking at this title, read this list of current in-game problems to keep yourself informed before buying:
---------------------------------------------
1. EVERYTHING is bound to M1 & The mouse. Aiming, swinging, turning the camera, blocking and aiming your blocks/parries. Needless to say, It's an incredibly clumsy standard control scheme for this specific genre that has already been throughly explored by other titles such as Mount & Blade and War of the Roses which makes me question the developer's ability to learn from both the lessons and mistakes of others.
2. The hitboxes simply don't work / are grossly inaccurate. People hitting through shields and blocks is the most common complaint of this but after playing extensively as an archer, painting every visible inch of the human body with precise arrow shots, I can also confirm that during motion hitboxes can be EXTREMELY random with arms, shoulders and hands being the biggest offenders of the in-game dubbed "sudden ghost" syndrome.. Even if you've got a ping as low as 20-40.
3. The graphical options don't seem to work at all right now, failing to both properly apply themselves and having the lower settings give no noticable FPS boost while some of the maps are abyssmal, both visually and from a balance point of view. There is also no matchmaking to speak of whatsoever which may cause incredibly long, drawn-out onesided battles which happened to me during my 1 hour of play where the winners will just endlessly slaughter the other team to grind XP rather than finishing the game by doing objectives.
4. The game is very imbalanced. Two-handed weapons can be spam-flung to repeatedly one-shot people from far away in melee with insane speeds whilst shields often fail to even protect against arrows, much less 2handed weaponry. Bows are also INCREDIBLY hard to use and do pathetic amounts of damage (5-15%) when you hit someone square in the chest. To land headshots on someone, you need to tickle the 3 top most pixels of someone's helmet, everything else (face, actual head, neck) currently does not register & count as a headshot.
5. Community for this game is incredibly toxic with the chat being frequently flamed while griefing is becoming a more common sight everyday as people teamkilling/spam kicking eachother left and right for sh*t and giggles, especially after the round ends.
Their worst sin however, is running around on the Steam storepage, religiously spam-voting down anyone who gives this game criticism with "Not helpful" votes on reviews. Proof of this can be seen right here on this review that has been hammered without a single comment being left to point out just how It fails to be helpful. :)
---------------------------------------------
May be worth a try for WotS & M&B fans but I'd still recommend a healthy dose of "Buyer Beware" right now by keeping tabs on your 2 hour Steam refund time limit in check.

I've been following this game since it was first announced, and I've been playing cRPG (mod for Warband and predecessor to OKaM) since mid 2010.  I honestly had no desire to back the game in its early stages, and originally planned to wait on purchasing the game but my friend had a spare key and was kind enough to give it to me.  I'd agree that my opinion on this game is probably pretty biased, but here's my best objective review:
PROS:
The music is pretty great, they did fantastic work on the main menu song.
The combat system is interesting and neat in theory, I like the different historical stances they animated for the game.
The UI is simple and only kind of confusing.
The bows have no crosshair, so you aim with the arrow / bow.
CONS:
The sounds in the game are all over the place.  Ambient birds are way too loud, the shouting and yelling pretty much sounds like it came straight out of Mount & Blade.  I don't think you can turn down the volume on the menu music, either.  I imagine these problems can be chalked up to early access, and will be resolved in the future.
The combat system feels very unintuitive to me.  LMB does virtually everything, and even with stance locking on it can be very frustrating, and most of the weapon animations are weird and I personally have a hard time telling which swing I actually have prepared.  Honestly, you could probably bind the move forward key to your right mouse button and play the game only with your mouse, unless you're an archer of course.
I don't believe you can bind anything to any mouse button that isn't LMB / MMB / RMB, but that may also be fixed in the future.
The combat in general is very clunky. Everybody moves incredibly slowly, seemingly nobody can turn as fast as they'd like to, and the animations are awkward and slow.  This makes for a pretty hilarious scene when you have a♥♥♥♥♥♥load of people on the field slowly running in circles trying to hit eachother in the back.
Ultimately, I think the Donkey Crew is quite dedicated to the game, and I believe they'll do their best to make the game as smooth and enjoyable as possible.  However, unless you're a fan of taking the early access risk, I don't recommend purchasing this game quite yet.  Maybe once they've worked out of the bugs and smooth the combat out a bit, and once they release the Epic gamemode, it'll be worth buying.
EDIT:  for those of you looking for comparisons:
Mount & Blade - this game most resembles M&B, and I feel like the combat system would be better if they had stuck with RMB for blocking.  Character control is vastly superior in Warband, however.
Chivalry - I don't really know, they aren't the most comparable games, but I'd say Chivalry's combat is probably less clunky.
War of the Roses - Without a doubt OKaM is vastly superior to this game.  Clunkiness levels are comparable at times, but considering it's early access, it still blows WoR out of the water.

At first glance, Axiom Verge looks to be a direct copy of Metroid. You start on a strange alien planet with nothing more than your wits. Progression comes by acquiring new abilities that give you access to new areas. The world eventually opens up, and there are lots of places to explore and secrets to uncover.
Very quickly, however, Axiom Verge subverts your expectations of a game of this sort, especially if you've played Metroid before. You'll see blocks and places and think "Oh, I'll use bombs here" or "I'll get a morph ball later". By the second ability you get, the game gives you a completely different way to progress past them. The methods of travel and manipulation tools you get crazier as you go on, and like any good entry in the genre, by the end you can zoom around and steamroll enemies with ease.
Getting there will be a long road, as the game puts up a decent challenge at its regular difficulty. The regular enemies start off simple enough, but later ones have attacks and abilities that will catch you off guard the first time you encounter them. While you can brute force your way through them, knowing your abilities and weapons will give you an easier time when dealing with them. The bosses don't evolve quite as much, but they mostly manage to be intense, fun encounters. If you love exploration and puzzles, this game has you covered as well, as some of the most difficult secrets will require you to know the game's mechanics and require you to pay careful attention to your surroundings to claim your rewards.
The exploration and fights are a pleasant experience since the presentation is excellent. The world of Axiom Verge looks very nice and retro, with a style that gives an appropriately otherworldly feel, and even manages to make graphical glitches significant. The music has an old-school feel, and like the graphics manages to evoke the feel of a wondrous,  unfamiliar place.
The high points Axiom Verge hits makes the low points all the more glaring. The coolness of the best items makes the ones that aren't as subversive or useful that much more disappointing. While each map looks great on its own, they don't connect together well, with one example being an area with a night sky connected to an area with a daytime sky. The story has potential, and looks like it might go in some interesting directions, but it drops plot points and world elements as quickly as it introduces them. In the end, most of the consequences of the game's events are waved away, although the ones that aren't leave things open for interpretation.
Even then, the flaws don't detract enough from the game's best moments. Axiom Verge is a great experience that looks like a straight tribute to Metroid, but eventually forges its own path, and largely succeeds at it. If you enjoy big exploration-based sci-fi adventures, this comes highly recommended.
Ive been waiting for a good 2D side scrolling Metroidvania game for years and Tom Happ delivered.  Axiom Verge is a fantastic game that oozes creativity.

Hatoful Boyfriend is a game which lures you in with its ridiculous premise and the promise of comedy. Indeed, the game does have some very funny moments (and a handful of
puns).
And then, when you dig just a little bit deeper, Hatoful Boyfriend rips your heart out. It rips it out, throws it on the ground like it's an insignificant piece of litter, stomps on it, and pecks furiously at it like a pigeon pecks at a half-eaten sandwich clumsily dropped on the sidewalk.
Underneath the jokes and the otome/romance game parodies is a genuinely emotional, heart-rending experience that just wouldn't work without the premise of humans and intelligent birds living together. I have to admire the obvious care and work that went into worldbuilding; it would have been so easy to just say "There's a school of talking birds and a token human!" and leave it at that. Without giving too much away, Hatoful Boyfriend managed to make me invested in this universe where humans and sapient birds coexist and a human girl falls in love with a bird because why the hell not.
That said, there are more than a few typos, some formatting errors, and a couple bits of stray code lying around. Not enough to diminish my enjoyment, but still noticeable. There's also an annoying bug where attempting to load a game saved in certain particular spots doesn't work, making that save useless. But besides that, there's not a lot I can complain about in Hatoful Boyfriend, easily one of the most pleasantly surprising experiences I've ever had with a game.
