Evolve was the game that could have and should have gone so far. I admittedly got into them game when it went F2P like most people, but when I started playing I regretted not giving it a fair shot before. The game had so much bad publicity but when I look back on old gameplay, it seemed to still be a solid game. This is less of a review and more of a love letter to a long lost friend. A lot of bad reviews come from founders who had pre-ordered the game before it went F2P and I get that there is probably a bit of resentment, but in the end they also have fair points.
The issue with going F2P is that you get a lot of attention but not all of it is a of a good variety. People came in and wanted the game to be easy, its not. They didn't understand how to play and they didn't want to learn. They wanted to be the solo carry badass of the game that went off as bucket and gunned down the monster 1v1. They wanted to be the Stage 1 Kraken that left limbs and blood in their wake. And thats not how it works.
The game has a strong sense of Hunter vs. Hunted and changes throughout a match. At the start, the monster is at genuine risk of being put down before the fun starts, and if you don't know how to be mobile and make yourself scarce, then you will die. Mechanics like crouching to hide footprints was rarely seen in regular matches and there weren't any dark maps anymore, so you couldn't really hide in plain sight. People wanted to be able to run around and 1v5 immediately without eating for buffs or ever evolving. If you haven't played, this is the fastest way to lose, and I could understand how this would be frustrating, especially when a veteran tells you it was your fault.
This left the devs in a tricky place. They needed players and so they tried to pander to the new ones who struggled to understand a game that needed practice and communication and they left dedicated fans feeling dejected, wondering what happened to the game they paid for. They also knew they couldn't change too much for the would really lose those fans, and it left new players with a confusing experience. The game floated around in this place where the devs listened and tried but the writing was on the wall for ages. The game was going to die whether the devs liked it or not.
While people bash the developers I gained a bit of respect for them. They at least tried. They didn't want all that work to go to waste and they didn't want to give up on its, while small, dedicated player base. They tried Evolve Stage 2 in hopes that F2P could fix the issues but it wasn't going to happen. Turtlerock studios actually said they wanted to keep going, but as they don't own their own IP, 2K, the publisher, had all the power to pull the plug and claim the game was completed.
Should you play Evolve : Stage 2?
If the game seems likes something you would enjoy, I emplore you to at least give it a chance, but I hear that since the devs have fully abondened the game, it has some matchmaking issues I am yet to test for myself. I will edit this apon new experience with this game. Be warned that the player base may have waned and you may struggle from lack of experience against people who have been here from the start. I want to badlly say yes, but the game is certainly dead. It's still twiching, but make no mistake, its quite dead.

[Note: I played the game for about 30mins, this is just my initial impression]
+ Visually the game looks fantastic, with great lighting, detail, and great water wave physics which seems very realistic.
+ The Coast Guard ship you drive is very detailed. Amazingly you can actually walk around the ship, and even go inside the lower cabin which is built to scale with a bunch of rooms you would thing would be on a Coast Guard vessel like a kitchen, bathroom, interrogation room, a cell for prisoners, and so fourth. There is awesome water cannons that you can shoot to put out fires, and a smaller boat in the back which you can undock and drive around.
+ Epic soundtrack at certain points in the game
+ There's a story! Really glad they chose to add story elements as most simulators are rather dull in that department.
+ As a simulator, I felt like this game really "tries" to be somewhat realistic.  You play as a Coast Guardman (or basically a police officer at sea), and must go around investigating and interrogating various criminals while also rescuing others from sinking ships and so fourth. You even have to ask for license and registration, and find out if everything matches up in the database when you track someone down which is pretty neat.
+ For the most part the controls are easy to learn, and there's lots of camera angles
- The UI is pretty poor at times, especially when trying to drag inventory items around on the screen to activate various things.
- This game does a really bad job at guiding the player to the next objective. Most of the time (if you are not reading the journal) you will have no idea what to do next. For example, one of the first missions involves pumping out water from a sinking ship, when you attach the cable it just says "This will take some time", and does not tell you anything else. Little do you know, you actually have to go around talking to people and find out other things to progress.

Feels like the budget or timeframe for release was severely curtailed.  Spend half your time going to what sounds like a cool  mission... but that mission doesn't actually exist, just a waypoint that is in reality a delaying tactic to occupuy your time while the narrative catches up.  The time-frame jumps around distractedly, to confuse the player to build a so-so mystery-plot.  Too little coast-guard gaming, too much jumping around.
Could have been great.  Should have been great.  But fails any expectations.
Buy ONLY on extreme sale, and only if there isn't another game you want.

consider my playtime with this game triple what it is stated on steam.
in one sentence:  still better than 80% of the "early access" games available in it's loosely defined genre, and usually 1/3 or less the price.
the player takes on the role of a space station manager in a "hitchhiker's guide" inspired universe.
the main areas that require player management are: trade, expansion, visitor needs, hiring staff, collection of resources, combat, budgeting, research, and balancing resource needs.
there's plenty there to keep the management style "hectic" and serene at different points... a player can find themselves at times hectically searching for hard to find planted terrorist bombs, negotiating 2 trade offers and fighting off a breach attempt; and at other times, finding nothing to do but to watch your hippies sowing plants in the bio deck.
a classic and well aged "management" game.  i played this game from 3 different data sources over the years, and steam's is quite good.  nothing much bad to say about this game, other than at higher levels of resolution the text can be hard to read, so should be played at something more native to what it was made to be played at.
buy it if you management games, specifically theme hospital or evil genius.  buy it if you like dry stupid British space humor.

I played Mount and Blade for a some time and I was a decent player who easily fought other human players without needing to use a shield. I bought this game because after seeing it has a combat that is similar to what M&B offers.
Controls of this game may take a few hours of dueling to get used to. But once you get used to it, you will see its superior to M&B. The reasons why I find this game's combat better:
1) You have to block directionally even with a shield. So shield users are now at an absolute disadvantage versus 2-handers, but their shields protect them from archers. In mass combat, I believe sides will need a healhy mix of all three classes.
2)You both block and attack using LMB. At first it will be confusing but after a few hours of dueling, you will see you are figting much more smoothly this way.
3)There's bash in the game in addition to kick, which allows you to deal with face-huggers like never before.
Dueling servers have no lag or fps problems for me but Capture The Flag servers where 100+ players fight in the same map at the same time need a little bit of improvement, but even CTF is playable and enjoyable.
You can only play duel or CTF at this time, but i think even the current content justifies a buy.

Damn now Im left with one less con of having 2 nice things.
I must say I found Uplay to be not annoying at all with this game.  Either my expectations from Uplay are similar to the 7 levels of hell or maybe its gotten less intrusive.  It would seem that if you have one ubisoft game on Uplay it can actually realize that and streamline you into playing the game.  What a novelty, must be a reaction to the Cthulhu  tendrils of Viviendi.
Things took a turn when the PC graphic options were either baffling or non existant.  Im not exactly sure what 10% FOV means but Im assuming it means wider than 5%.  The game starting in a bizarre resolution was also a bit disapointing.  With what little options could be tweaked I moved into the game and....
I have to say its a shame Ubisoft brought this to the Wii U as an exclusive unless Nintendo wrote a golden check.  Its not like the game has the highest production values, but its a shame that in 2012 when zombie survival was very popular they didnt make this and add a little more to the budget.
While the gameplay and game mechanics have been de-gimicked (Sorry Nintendo cultist please dont try to kill me I just got a new spring axe for my front door at the home depot) its still kind of funny to see what clearly was origionally added only for the gamepad.
Graphically this game isnt very impressive but makes good use of fog similar to Silent Hill 2.  If this is graphically upgraded they are either exaggerating or it looked really bad in 2012.
The story so far has me interested and I do find myself actively looking for clues.  The gameplay is great in terms of atmosphere and the zombies, but average in terms of its mechanics.  I wanted to turn the crosshair in the game off, but with no ironsights and only an akward zoom your putting yourself at a silly disadvantage.  Im not saying the game needs ironsights but its one of those why is this an option things.  The zombies are missleading in that they can seem like cake one moment and the next moment you've gone and made your last mistake.  At least for that character.  The rogue element is interesting but the games narration seems to not recognize it.  The sound is solid.  Weather effects, your character huffing and yelling lowder the more you blugeon a zombie is great.  As is the sound work for the zombies.
This is definately one of the better zombie survival games I have played recently which is sad considering how many there are.  Not that this game is bad or anything, but it is still a port from 2012.  It does the one thing it needs to do and that is make every encounter feel like it can be easily handled or horribly failed.  The way health seems to work in this game isnt so much getting killed by 1000 cuts, but simply getting devoured in one instant.  Many times you die entering a situation with full health but you cant get away and cant heal.
I love this game and recomend it for anyone who enjoys zombie games

Mao Zedong or Mao Tse-tung  December 26, 1893 – September 9, 1976 also known as Chairman Mao, was a Chinese communist revolutionary and founding father of the People's Republic of China, which he ruled as an autocrat styled the Chairman of the Communist Party of China from its establishment in 1949, until his death in 1976. His Marxist–Leninist theories, military strategies, and political policies are collectively known as Maoism or Marxism-Leninism-Maoism.
Born the son of a wealthy farmer in Shaoshan, Hunan, Mao adopted a Chinese nationalist and anti-imperialist outlook in early life, particularly influenced by the events of the Xinhai Revolution of 1911 and May Fourth Movement of 1919. Mao adopted Marxism–Leninism while working at Peking University and became a founding member of the Communist Party of China (CPC), leading the Autumn Harvest Uprising in 1927. During the Chinese Civil War between the Guomindang (GMD) and the CPC, Mao helped to found the Red Army, led the Jiangxi Soviet's radical land policies and ultimately became head of the CPC during the Long March. Although the CPC temporarily allied with the GMD under the United Front during the Second Sino-Japanese War (1937–45), after Japan's defeat China's civil war resumed and in 1949 Mao's forces defeated the Nationalists who withdrew to Taiwan.
On October 1, 1949, Mao proclaimed the foundation of the People's Republic of China (PRC), a one-party state controlled by the CPC. In the following years Mao solidified his control through land reform campaigns against landlords, and perceived enemies of the state he termed as "counter-revolutionaries". In 1957, he launched the Great Leap Forward campaign that aimed to rapidly transform China's economy from an agrarian economy to an industrial one. The campaign contributed to a widespread famine, whose death toll is estimated at between 15 and 45 million. In 1966, he initiated the Great Proletarian Cultural Revolution, a program to remove "counter-revolutionary" elements of Chinese society that lasted 10 years and which was marked by violent class struggle, widespread destruction of cultural artifacts and unprecedented elevation of Mao's personality cult. In 1972, Mao welcomed American President Richard Nixon in Beijing, signalling a policy of opening China, which was furthered under the rule of Deng Xiaoping (1978–1992). Mao suffered a series of heart attacks in 1976, dying in that September, aged 82. He was succeeded as Paramount leader by Hua Guofeng (1976–1978), who was quickly sidelined and replaced by Deng.
A controversial figure, Mao is regarded as one of the most important individuals in modern world history, and is also known as a theorist, military strategist, poet and visionary. Supporters credit him with driving imperialism out of China,modernising China and building it into a world power, promoting the status of women, improving education and health care, and increasing life expectancy as China's population grew from around 550 million to over 900 million during the period of his leadership.In contrast, critics consider him a dictator comparable to Adolf Hitler and Joseph Stalin who severely damaged traditional Chinese culture, as well as a perpetrator of systematic human rights abuses who was responsible for an estimated 40 to 70 million deaths through starvation, forced labour and executions, ranking his tenure as the top incidence of democide in human history.

I had a lot of fun playing this game. This is review might be a bit like a guide if you read later on about stats.   As I recall, I managed to get this game from one of the bundles so I got my money well invested here.   In this game, you start with the first character as a captain of your measly ship with no cannons.   Early on, you will have no money to hire pirates to work or fight for you.   There are many different skills that can be learned from books which can be purchased from stores or uncommon drops from pirates and loots.   The funny thing is that you need Cleaning skill to sweep your ship clean of poop, literally.   So naturally at start, you will be having bundles of poop on your ship before you come across a Cleaning skillbook.   I'm going to make a list of Pros and Cons:
Pros
1- Design and build your ship (check out screenshots submitted by players, one looked like Star Wars' destroyer ship)
2- Can hire up to 20 pirates making you feel like you have a real army going.  Especially if you had 15 of them as boarders...or even gunners...shreding ships apart before 30 seconds timer to expire allowing boarding
3- Different game every time (But as I noted under Cons, the ship/island scenarios are repetitive)
4- Variety of melee and ranged weapons
Cons
1- This game is not exactly finished as there are few things I can tell that need to be fixed or implemented (you may encounter some bugs.  I once encountered a game-breaking bug when I was stuck on a corner of a block on enemy ship, they would not target me, I could not fire my pistol at them...making it seem like I no longer exist there, had to reload but all was fine that point on)
2-  Now, I said that you play this game different every time as this is a good thing.  But the scenarios is probably 1 major patch away from being just about right.  The ship and island scenarios is all you will encounter in the game.  Once you see both of them,  it is pretty much 90% the same.  The only difference is levels of difficulty, which increases as you move farther away from your starting point.  So naturally this hampers replayability.
4- Interface need some optimization or something.  In-game scroll is a bit of pain as I can't use my mouse scroll button. This is enchanced when you got a long list of items to navigate. (and that is another thing, no subcategories of items)
5- While this was fun at first, but after recongizing the optimal way to develop your war-oriented priates and yourself,  the fun start to fade out quickly as you and your pirates become overwhelming powerful.  Case in point,  getting your dodge chance (via increasing points in AGI) to 500% (if you are a lone wolf attacker; and 500% because the more enemies on you, the higher penalty on your dodge chance)  No one can really hit you.  Up against 8-10 pirates on the ship, they get to hit you maybe 2 or 3 times.   As I said about ship/island scenarios being all virtually identical other than levels of difficulty (Edge of map is 8 to 10), it gets dull after while seeing you single-handedly shred them apart repeatedly in the virtually same way over and over.
6-  As some reviews may have noted, the stats are vague,  what they directly tell you is what it is but there seem to be additional things that impact them.
The stats are (and you start with 1 in each):
STR:  +5% bonus damage
VIT:  +1 hp regen / +1 armor per 10 VIT points / +6 health per VIT point (You also gain healthpool via leveling)
INT:  +2 passive XP
DEX: +5% ranged damage / +2% hit chance (Base is 90% hit chance so you start at 92% because 1 point already)
AGI:  +5% dodge chance
LUCK:  +1 critical chance
I finished my first full game as of this review so my comments and experience with stats are:
STR's 5% bonus melee damage per point is very straightforward.
Next game I am going to try maximizing VIT to determine the effect of +1 armor per 10 VIT points.  As of now, I assume it reduce damage taken by 1.  From my experience from taking damages,  it looks like I take up to 30 damage or little so.  This exclude  bombers as they hurt quite a bit (Gunners that happened to have cannon ammo on their hands when I boarded)  So in theory, if I manage to get VIT to 100 (can be more)   I probably would be immune to about 30-40% of enemies in the game.  I will try this in my next game.
INT's passive XP is what it is, you actually gain XP periodically.  Increasing INT allow you to gain more passive XP over time.  But this alone is junk.  At level 120, I need about 30k exp to level which I can level once per high-difficult level pirate ship scenario.   What it does not mention, is that increasing points in INT seem to increase % learn from skillbooks.   I noticed that myself had just 1 point in INT (as I never bother with it) while my ship crew  have all points in INT to help them level faster.  When I read skillbooks to increase my already-learned skill levels, I didn't gain very much which meant I needed multiple skillbooks per level.   Now when I gave certain books to my shipcrews with high INT, they only needed 1 skillbook per level.   So increasing INT allow you to benefit more from skillbooks however in the long-run this is not worth it for pirates including yourself that board and attack pirate ships.  INT is for pirates that stay on the ship and do duties.
DEX's 5% bonus ranged damage is straightforward,  now about hit chance%.   The higher difficulty pirates have more points in AGI which higher their dodge chance.  So naturally you will want to increase DEX a bit to compensate for that.
AGI's 5% dodge chance.  This is what that is going to break the game for you.   If you invest (and you pretty much always should)  AGI all the way to 100 (500% dodge chance)   you, as a lone wolf, can single-handedly deal with Legendary Pirate's ship alone.  The more enemies on you, the higher penalty on your dodge chance, so naturally at 500% dodge chance already, you still will have near-100% dodge chance.  You might take 2-5 hits in the entire battle.
Luck increases your chance to critical hit by 1%.  Naturally this might not seem worthy to you at all.  But to be frank, after AGI, this is the best stat ever.  STR is pointless as if you invest all 100 in Luck.  You will be critically damage enemies every time.  5x critical damage.   Naturally you will want fast attacking weapons to take advantage of critical.  Technically STR's 100 points = 500% damage which match critical but this does not include ranged weapon.  So Luck is definitely better.  After 100 points in Luck,  every point you invest in STR or DEX for ranged,  the 5% bonus damage is actually 25% because of critical.
The game is already seemingly trivial with 100 in AGI,  with addition of 100 in Luck,  everything became comical...and dull after while.  I quickly went straight to the corners of map to deal with 4 legendary pirates and get it over with. (but you can actually keep playing after this,  the game goes on forever, pretty much which is nice for players who adore this game.
Anyway, my rating of this game is 7.5 / 10. Probably would be 8.5 or 9 if they release just 1 more major patch for this game but they already moved on to making next project with 10 people.
Edit: with my test game focusing on nothing but VIT stat, at level 20 with 40 points in VIT.  I felt no  real improvements with +4 armor.  Either armor stat is a placebo or too small % reduction. I compared during combat against a single person. Was #9 VIT then added 1 VIT point to make it #0, gaining +1 armor, yet to see any reduction in damage. Abandoned test game, +10 armor (100 VIT) isn't going to be worth it.  So I am now considering these stats of  STR, VIT, and INT to be useless. The gain to get from these aren't worth it compare to other 3 stats.  Invest only in DEX (up to max 40 for optimal hit chance against high difficult pirates), AGI (up to 100) and Luck (100).  Anything beyond, just invest whatever.

This is probably the greatest homage to Metroid Ive ever seen. Its just beautiful. Its a standard 2d Metroidvania with mazelike maps, areas you cant get to until you get certain powerups, backtracking, savepoints, many different interesting weapons and items. That all is pretty vanilla for the genre. The story is minimal (so far) but is interesting enough to make me want to keepo uncovering more of the plot. You are a scientist who was performing some kind of high-energy beam experiment when *dun dun dun* something went horribly wrong and the building you were in collapsed on your head. But instead of dying you got sucked into a world that looks like one of Geiger's fever dreams. You have no idea why you're here and you hear a voice in your head...
What makes it beyond awesome is the atmosphere and music. Creepy biomech monsters and pulsing slimy organic-looking masses in the background seem like something right out of Aliens or Metroid, and a driving electronic musical score that perfectly matches the creepy bio-alien feel. Its Metroid if Metroid was done by an indie studio in 2015. Its pixel art, but very very well made pixel art with modern depth and DPI. The controls are fluid and very well executed which is always an absolute requirement in a game like this, and the controller mapping is fully customizable. If you f'd a jump or got hit,  its your fault, not the fault of the controls. That is a breath of fresh air in and of itself.
Theres a whole other aspect of the game I haven't even experienced yet, something about "glitches". You encounter areas where the graphics are glitched out, and eventually you aquire a power that allows you to inteact with them. I cant wait to see what thats about!
This is hands down one of the best Metroidvanias (emphasis on the Metroid) I've ever seen. Screw all those FPS Wii Metroids, *this* is the true sequel.

As someone who's grown up with the original Contra, Metroid, and Megaman I understand your tastes toward fleshy alien atmospheres. A lot of the environments in the game are quite visually striking too, albeit a bit self-indulgent. Lately that's the only thing that kept me going through the game.
But even so, the design of these maps are painfully outdated. The original metroid could get away with endless vertical climbs and recycled enemies with boosted health because of hardware limitations. I hate to use this cliche', but it's 2015, level design must have meaning (I'm talking to the thoughless amount of dead ends through corridors in Axiom Verge) many of the places I jump to, have no meaning, no puzzle, it wastes the player's time.
What made metroidvania games so good in the past, was their incredibly fast pacing and constant gratification of finding secrets throughout the map. Some of those "metroidvania" traits exist here, but they are too far apart, or you're busy jumping to a place that leads to a dead end. It's a horrible paradox to make such bad mistakes in level design, then forcing the player to explore it.
This review is critical on purpose, because your style enticed me- "Megaman, Metroid and Contra all packed into one, this game was created by someone who appreciates videogames" or so I thought.
This game has the clunky shooting of the original Megaman (you can't run while shooting down, you must stand still everytime you want to shoot) and the painstaking backtracking of the original Metroid.
You obviously have a talent for creating spawling alien atmospheres, you're an artist, I appreciate your tastes. I see you made this thing all my yourself too but you must have input from other people, especially for map design.
Don't recommend.

A lot of people seem to call this game a love letter to "metroidvania", and I can't fault them for that. This is one person's attempt to create a truly modern 2D Metroid-like game, using all the lessons learned from the best of the best in genre and adding new elements, that weren't tried in the genre before. This game has exciting exploration, varied locales, fantastic soundtrack, unique visuals that mix old-school 8bit and 16bit era art with subtle modern effects, surprisingly good challenge for the most part and a very interesting atmosphere that can probably be summarised as "sci-fi adventure as if Another World/Out of This World was designed by H.R. Giger".
It's not without flaws or questionable decisions. Challenge in the opening parts, before some upgrades, feels higher than you'd expect from a Metroid-like game, with action not being tight enough to justify that. Boss battles look great, but only 2 actually feel fun to play, with most others just being "shoot shoot shoot die already it's getting annoying shoot shoot" deals. Game features some random elements in the way of "Secret Worlds", which, in concept, are cool, but make the "exploration" part of the genre most loved for it, a bit less rewarding, because the areas are random and you have no chance of getting everything in one run. Some of the navigation moves just feel clunky to pull off, especially the very important one, that requires directional double-tap - most of the run-and-shoot actually plays better with an analogue stick, but these are very hard to pull off and are frustrating even on a d-pad, no matter what gamepad you use. And finally, the story and dialogue feel rather averagly written, which is sad simply because the setup and situations they show are actually very interesting. So, story, while often predictable, is exciting to experience and the world lore is out there to be found, but both are just told in a very mediocre way.
That said, the game is still fantastic, especially due to its innovation in treating death more like a... well, Souls game, I guess will be the most understandable comparison. That is - death does bring you back to the last save room you used, but you keep all the unlocked map squares, items and everything that is permanently done (like killing a boss or triggering a cutscene) stays done. This, along with the idea that enemies do not respawn immidiatelly after leaving the room and instead after you move two rooms away, makes exploration so much more fun, while not simplifying the rules to the point, where it gets boring.
One of the best recent games in genre which, while probably isn't as full of awesomeness as La-Mulana or Aquaria, still feels like a solid "proper full game" that you'd get full priced 15 years ago and love it. A real treat for anyone who wants to explore some amazing worlds in Metroid style.

I wanna preface this review by saying I love To the Moon (developed by Freebird games) and I think that game is a masterpiece and that everyone should play through it at least once. A Bird Story is kind of a spiritual successor to that game, in that it was made by the same team, has the same artist and I believe was stated to be a story in the same world, albeit with no reccuring characters. The difference between To the Moon and A Bird Story though, is that the latter has no dialogue, no actual characters or tangible story to relate to. It has very few interactive elements and that makes it just feel like an unemotional, less deep version of To the Moon. I'm not one of those people who says games have to have deep mechanics or even a lot of interaction to be considered games, but to me A Bird Story just feels like 1/10th of the game To the Moon is. To the Moon's dialogue and story and characters and storytelling elements are all so beautifully done and made an emotional and touching experience that I adored. I just can't say the same for A Bird Story. It was by no means a bad experience, but it just left me kinda disappointed and unimpressed. Maybe my expectations were too high. I usually love minimalist storytelling, but to me there has to actually be a story hidden under the surface. A Bird Story is not that kind of game.

Everyone just wants to find love in this wild, crazy world of ours. Everyone just needs a shoulder to lean on, or an open ear to whisper their darkest secrets to. That's all anyone really wants. Even the ones that don't seem like they want love, they're the ones that need it the most.
Some people find love in family, or camaraderie. Some people find it in romance, or art. Some might find it at the bottom of a family-size bag of Cheetos while they jack off to pictures of girls with tails. Hey, everyone has their thing. Everyone is entitled to their own form of love. Unless they're humping their dog or their child, in which case it's illegal and they can find love in a prison shower.
People can find love everywhere and anywhere. Life finds a way. Even if you must go beyond your comfort zone. Beyond your race, your culture, and your people. Love knows no limits. Not even the sky. Because who wouldn't ♥♥♥♥ a bird?
I know I sure would. And if you don't think you're up to it, you haven't played this masterpiece yet. This isn't just a game. It's a journey. A life-changing experience. Prepare to have your eyes opened to the truth.
Hatoful Boyfriend actually falls under the category of visual novel, as it's a Japanese otome game. Otome is Japanese for sausage fest. You're playing a girl getting aggressively humped by every guy in the immediate vicinity. Which, in this case, are all birds. And you get to make the exciting choices that will determine not only who's eggs you'll be laying, but the fate of the world as we know it.
Hatoful Boyfriend was originally developed for the PC in 2011, later seeing multiple rereleases and upgrades before getting an HD remaster that released on Steam, PS4, and PS Vita.
Hatoful Boyfriend is, simply by existing, worth checking out. No where else can you experience the excitement of being the only human girl at an all-birds high school. It's the only of its kind, and simply the premise itself should warrant at least a single playthrough.
Not only is it relevant simply because of its premise, but it also works rather well simply on its premise alone. If you're picking it up simply because "LOOK, BIRDS" you'll get exactly what you're looking for. It's wacky, zany, kooky bird fun. Good stuff.
But underneath that simple premise, a surprising amount of depth is layered. Spoiler alert, dating birds at an all-birds school is not something people usually do. Usually. It's not quite a mainstream way of life yet, but we're rallying for our lifestyle to be recognized by the masses. Someday, human-bird relationships might be accepted. Birds don't even have access to public schooling yet, so we have a ways to go.
Shockingly, Hatoful Boyfriend is a parody dating sim. A joke game of sorts, satirizing the otome genre. All of the cliches, all of the character stereotypes, they're all here. You can expect all of basics to be here. Maid costumes and all. It's tasteful satire, not in an overbearing "LOOK GUYS WE'RE MAKING JOKES HERE" kind of way. The writing is hilarious, and carries a sort of ironic whimsy to it. It's fully aware of its nature, but runs with it regardless. It is a visual novel, which means reading, which means no this is not an action game or anything vigorous like that. Unless you wanna dip your little parakeet perch in honey and bird seed so you can stick it through the bars of grandma's lovebird cage while you play. Those HD character portraits are pretty feathery.
It's not only poking fun at otome visual novels, it's in fact written well enough to be a competent example of the genre that it's making a mockery of. The characters are interesting and compelling in their own right, even if they are just caricatures of otome stereotypes given bird form. They're fleshed out with a surprising amount of detail, given that the nature of the game didn't require much to begin with. Just "look, they're birds that you can date, this one is the jock bird and this one is the nerd bird" would have sold just as well.
If you happen to fall in love with the excellently written birds and words, a lot is in store for you. They've done a beyond fantastic job of rewarding the player for dedication. As a dating sim should, there are multiple endings. At least one for each character, and sometimes two. One "true ending" should you flawlessly woo them, and the just okay ending. Where you confess your love and they say "thanks". Going the extra mile for more endings will reward you by unlocking even more endings. Better endings.
And should you stick around long enough for every single ending, you will be generously rewarded with the best part of the game. There's a lot of tough choices to make, but if you make them all it will be so worth it.
Fantastic writing, characters, atmosphere, and a stunning amount of depth and meaning really make Hatoful stand out among other visual novel games. But it's not without issues, though they're more to blame of the genre itself than anything else.
After you've played through the game for the first time, regardless of which bird you hope to woo, much of the game remains the same. You'll be going to the same classes, seeing a lot of similar dialogue, and riding the fast-forward text button a ton. That's the biggest flaw with the game.
The other being, as I mentioned, the game rewarding people that stick through the game until the very end. Because it's a really big reward. Like, possibly the size of the rest of the game itself in its entirety. I can totally understand why they did it, because the reward itself doesn't carry quite the same impact and meaning until you've played through every ending. It's a steep hill to climb, with a pay-off to match.
To go any further would spoil just how perfect the ending is, but it stays true to its absurdity all the way to the end. It honestly blew me away how much depth they put into it. It's really not a one-trick pigeon, as it might lead you to believe.
People might dismiss it as "that weird bird game" or "creepy Japanese♥♥♥♥♥♥quot; or "memes". They might play it purely for the "look at me lol I'm so random" factor, or the jack off to those luscious, feathery bodies. But you realize you're dismissing, stereotyping, and fetishizing a way of life. There's more to it than that. There's depth here. We're more than a stereotype, and I'm tired of needing to hide who I am.
Educate yourself, open your mind, and accept that some people have a different lifestyle than you. Some people want to have a nice family with kids in a suburban house. They want that white picket fence life. And some people, they really like birds. Not that there's anything wrong with that. And if you think there is, I think you need to check your privilege. ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.

An interesting and compelling game from start to finish. Skyborn is an RPG-Maker made game with it's unique style, the environments throught the game are very well detailed which just goes to show how much work and time the developers put on it.
The game is very story-driven so if you're not so much into story and more into constant action this isn't the game for you. The characters are well designed, each one having it's unique objective and background explained in the game through constant flashbacks, which in turn translates into a nice storytelling. Skyborn features a crafting system which allows you to craft armors and weapons from ores you pick along the way and an augment system which allows you to enchant them, the system itself is really simple but at the same time really addicting and you'll find yourself more often than not looking at every wall in search of ores (I know I did!).
Not all is good about the game however. Some changes to the battle system for example (which still features some RPG-Maker standard sprites and grid system) could have been explored way better. The mouse feature, here strangely introduced, also doesn't make much sense for this kind of game, you'll find out that using the mouse will only make things more complicated and unnatural, luckily the developers added an option in the menu to toggle on/off the mouse feature. Achievements for Steam also not supported which is actually a real bummer since you have so much to achieve in this game! Oh well :)
Overall a great game with over 12+ hours of content to explore, be it sidequesting, following the main story line or crafting in your free time. Congratulations to the developers. 8/10

For the life of me, I cannot remember ever buying this game, and yet as soon as I saw the screenshots of the game I remembered the gameplay. Since I had been pining over a space-station sim (since the other game like this one that was on Early Access recently flopped, releasing early without the full range of planned features) I decided to revisit this game. It was well worth the price of admission.
You can read up on the history of Startopia on Wikipedia (there's a full article there) which talks about its lighthearted humour and cartoonish aliens and how the game was developed by ex-Bullfrog employees (after Bullfrog was absorbed by Electronic Arts.)
While the game was not fantastic for its era (and while no game improves with age), it did sell 110k copies at the time and it has stood the test of time remarkably better than one might have anticipated. The torus floorplan (rounded floors, tiered levels, unlockable sections around the radius of the space station) holds a certain charm. The Targ race of aliens is reminiscent of Grunts from Halo: Combat Evolved (which makes it an interesting bit of trivia that Startopia and Halo were released the same year.) The varied races with their unique professions, the wide variety of mission objectives keeps the game very engaging: mining rest station, medical station, trading station, and even prison station are examples of the first four map objectives.
Startopia even supported multiplayer (although I do not expect to be able to actually test that).
The game lacks primarily in that it was designed for desktop machines of 13 years ago (as of the time this review was written). The graphics tear periodically as the graphics engine tries to render and hits a snag in translating from the old style graphics code to the newer hardware requirements. The alien avatars are fairly simplistic (although there is lots of emote activity going on and even some dynamic interaction AI that adds a sense of believable life to your aliens.) But the game doesn't take itself too seriously and plays up its cartoonish nature with narration that sounds like it came from Douglas Adams (of Hitcherhiker's Guide to the Galaxy fame.)
In conclusion, while the game may not have been worth the full price tag (whatever it was in 2001) it is most definitely worth the lower price tag of today.

I've heard a lot of bad press about The Bureau. Never thought I would play it myself as a result, but Humble Bundle saw to that.
What I discovered was a surprisingly interesting experience. Let's be brutally honest though: The Bureau is technically not good... Game has a lot of bugs, and I'm not just talking about some small discreet ones, I'm talking about characters models actually ending up climbing on the geometry and each other when getting too close of said geometry or characters, for exemple. I'm talking about characters teleporting to follow you too. Things which are so glaringly obvious that anyone with an ounce of common sense should have never shipped the game in that state. It's extended with the game being crash heavy when PhysX is on(despite the game itself proudly displaying supporting it). A bug which exists since at least 2016.
The gameplay itself is... Well, it's bland. It's a third person shooter with some amount of tactical aspect with you giving order to your two teamates in real time. Problem being the system is unwieldly, handling difference of height poorly, teamates are honestly underperforming quite a lot, and only their skills are really what help you. The arenas you fight in are uninspired and overall give very little use to tactical acumen. Managing flanking manoeuvers is pretty rare, and honestly not that efficient. By the time you get a guy to move to a flanking position, you've already killed everyone yourself if you are a proper shot. The weapons are limited in selection, with only a few of them really good.
So what actually makes The Bureau interesting. Well, in my opinion, the first thing is the ambiance. It has that 60s retro feel, with the whole looming threat of the Cold War pretty well done. The environnements are pretty representative, with those big and bulky calculating computers, people smoking cigaret afer cigaret, attrocious sweaters(which probably influenced Bradford's trademark one), suits, fedoras and ties. While in the field, sometimes I felt like I was in an episode of Stargate. Where puny humans use retrofitted technology and ballistic weapons to try to fend off technologically superior aliens. Game also has a bit of a Mass Efffect feel to it. Characters also ask some pretty interesting questions, like how do you deal with aliens refugees, and how could aliens be potentially integrated in society, and the prejudices they could meet. The scenario also manages to pull an interesting twist I would love to talk more in depth, but can't due to spoilers. It takes risks, to not say it does some things actually quite right. The writing isn't always stellar, but it definitively bears interest.
Game also has some threads linking to others X-com games. For exemple, it kinda link to the mysterious anonymous Councilman, and I was amused that the plot of X-com 2 was actually a copy of a very important plot point of The Bureau. Except X-com 2 actually does it poorly, while the Bureau does it far better. The reason for that is The Bureau put emphasis on the story, while X-com 2 pushed its story in the background to focus more on the gameplay.
There is definitively a lot of potential in that game. With more funding, quality control, fixing, and better gameplay, it could have been really good. As it stands, it's pretty mediocre, but make no mistake, this game deserves to be seen and played as it definitively has the little something, a spark of greatness that didn't fully come to life.
If you didn't get it for free, well, try to get it under 10 euros, I would say 5.
For all its flaws, I actually enjoyed playing it from beginning to end, despite how short it is.

The Bureau is not a bad game, It could of been a great game but a lack of clear vision and execution make it hard to love.

My biggest issue I had with the game is the lack of manual saving. there were only a few bugs I ran into, only one required me to restart from a check point.
It is not a great game, but I think its a game worth checking out.

There's an excellent concept here, the mechanics aren't too horrifically unbalanced, and the play (once you get used to it) is pretty fun for a while.
On the other hand, extremely poor documentation (There are 6 wikis I found in my googling for answers, each of which was incorrect about the game in multiple, significant ways), exceedingly poor performance with big ships (My 720 block ship with 18 crew members caused the game to grind to a halt on a computer with 4x the system requirements whenever I entered combat, or the ship editor), lacking control over the crew (Want to have your crew repair the ship more than clean? Too bad. If they know both skills, then in the middle of combat, they'll run around cleaning. Want to have all the pirates on the island return without disrupting the pirates on the ship? Too bad, there's no way to do that.) and a general feeling that this game is not merely incomplete, but fundamentally flawed in multiple game ruining ways makes this an experience to avoid.
There's very little in the way of a tutorial, which makes the initial experience Googling laden, and more than a bit frustrating.
There's bugs. A pirate hit by a cannon blast can be knocked into a wall, and unable to escape it. If that pirate poops before you can get to a dock to remove the wall, the poop will prevent you from removing that block, leaving the only option to take another ship, or entirely rebuild yours.
There's incorrect documentation, everywhere, on every site, regardless of whether it says official.
I expected better from Re-Logic, and I'm unclear on why this is out of Early Access.
Some things that make this game feel incomplete:
When you are on the map screen, pressing wasd doesn't move your view of the map screen around. Even worse, pressing up/down switches you over to the character screen, for some reason. For that matter, pressing up/down on the ship builder also drops you unceremoniously into the character screens.
There's no way to manually aim cannons, or continue the cannon fire when ships are in boarding range.
Ships don't move closer to each other as they approach boarding range.
Cannons don't become more accurate as ships come into boarding range.
There's no way to prevent your cannons from firing, if you wish to capture the enemy ship.
You have to click a button to open treasure chests. Seriously, in what circumstances would a pirate not want to open a treasure chest?
Crew that you have trained up in levels don't become more valuable if you go to sell them back. The same applies when they learn skills, which costs you for the books.
There is no option for networked play, non-randomly generated worlds, or multiple humans on a single system controlling different pirates.
You cannot place food on your ship if you aren't at a town/island. While we're at it, you can't have a pirate whose job it is to keep food stocked on deck.
There's no options to change the frequency of pirate dialog, add or remove some lines, or include custom audio snippets.
There's no option to import a pirate flag from an image, or export one to share around.
There's no option to capture a picture of your ship to share.
There're no options to automatically spend TP.
Your gunning crew doesn't move closer to the cannons when you're heading towards battle. Your boarding crew doesn't move closer to the front of the ship when battle begins, or when you're heading towards battle. If you order the boarding crew to the front of the ship, they will disperse after a short time.
If your captain is in the midst of battle, there seems to be no way to make him retreat, even when he's fast enough, and dodging enough of the blows that he could easily get away. Sometimes clicking furiously where I wanted him to go seemed to work.

The lacking interface is one of my main complaints about the game: there's no backlog, inconvenient skipping (skips over unread dialogue), no ability to save on choice points. Still, this VN is still worth reading for the true ending alone, which develops the plot in unexpected ways, not unlike Ever17 or the transition between Muv-Luv Extra/Unlimited and Muv-Luv Alternative if you're familiar with these works. Hatoful Boyfriend is a parody of dating simulators, in which you play as a high school girl entering an academy populated entirely by intelligent birds.
Even by the standards of dating simulators, there is relatively little in the way of mechanics.  The basic mechanic is you choosing which bird you wish to grow attached to, and thus picking the options that allow you to spend time with and grow closer to them.  To the games credit, each bird is both amusing and, in their own ways, charming; each bird has their own backstory and personality, which go a long way to making play feel rewarding.
Behind the scenes, the game will adjust the story and the options you face.  The end result is that past a certain point, the game understands who you are aiming for and will direct the story based on your decision, making the end of a playthrough decidedly more linear than the beginning.
One of the defining choices in the design of Hatoful Boyfriend was to include more than a dozen different endings, and compensating by making each playthrough completeable within an hour.  Unfortunately, this approach simply does not work.
The joke is over by the end of a half hour, and even with the mechanics described above, there is a lot of repetition between multiple playthroughs.  At this point, the game needs something weightier to drive the player forward, but nothing in playtime managed to pull me in.  While the characters are fun, there is neither much actual romance nor character development; storylines end almost immediately after the big reveal of the birds' backstory, and so the game does not give any closure, even when dealing with more serious topics.
There are clues of a deeper mystery, and the implicit promise that completing all of the endings will reveal the justification for the premise.  Unfortunately I must admit that I never discovered this reveal and do not care enough to; ultimately the characters are too 2-dimensional and our time with them too brief for me to care about what happened.
If, despite this review, you play Hatoful Boyfriend, take this piece of advice; create a separate save as soon as you hear talk about joining a school club.  This is the first choice you get, and saving here will prevent you having to go through the intro multiple times.
In conclusion, Hatoful Boyfriends' laughs and heart are equally shallow and short-lived. Given that I expect many people on the fence of buying to abandon the game part-way through as I did, I cannot recommend the game for any price above 2 to 3 $

Ten years after it first came out, I finally got around to playing this, and it's as good as people made it out to be. I love the dark, witty dialog and aesthetic - throughout the game, you're increasingly made aware that something is wrong, and the overall tone can become deeply unsettling at times, while retaining its sense of humor. I won't go too much into the plot; you should play it for yourself to experience it, and there are wikis if you really don't want to. But seriously, play it.
The mechanics are simple in theory. You have a portal gun that lets you create an entry and exit hole on select surfaces, so you can warp to locations that you couldn't otherwise reach. In practice, this is more complex, as you also retain your momentum while running/falling through a portal, which allows all manner of crazy stunts and lets you fly over hazards or catapault up to impossible ledges. Thank goodness there's no falling damage, or this game would be absolutely maddening. Sometimes, it can be a little bit annoying to reorient yourself while zooming through the air, but after a while of playing, you mostly get used to it.
The level design works well, too - once it's done hand holding, it pushes you into the deep end, subtly (and sometimes not so subtly) giving hints at what you're supposed to do, but still requiring you to think your way through the levels. You end up spending a decent amount of the game examining the level layout for every last nook and cranny that you can plant a portal onto. It's good at making you feel smart once you figure it out.
Apart from the dizzying weirdness of the maneuvers you have to pull off (which again, you generally get used to), my only complaint with Portal is that it's a bit short. Then again, as a first entry in the series, I don't know that it
be longer. Portal 2 and its heaps of community content should fix that itch, anyway.

Cats are Liquid is an indie platformer based on the idea of, well, playing a cat with no bones that can slide through small holes and at incredible speeds. Unfortunately, it's bogged down by more gimmicks than your standard indie platformer, most of which are useless outside of when you specifically and clearly need it to proceed, and one of which breaks the game wide open for as long as you have it, as well as hilariously janky physics.
For basic controls, your blobcat can jump by pressing up, or turn into a liquid by holding down, in addition to moving left and right. Turning into liquid allows it to move through narrow spaces, but it also gives a speed boost, which can be used to reach incredible speeds for long-distance jumps. Oddly enough, jumping - the staple of almost every platformer - is the messed-up core mechanic here, since you can jump any time you are in contact with a surface, or sometimes just in midair for no clear reason. Jumping increases your upward speed, even if you are already moving upward at the maximum speed from a previous jump, allowing you to scale walls incredibly rapidly, or fly through the air by jumping from under a physics object, pushing it up with you and guaranteeing you have something to continue jumping against.
Later on in the course of the 90 levels of the main game, you get the ability to turn into steam, which makes you move much slower but you slowly float upward instead of falling downward, summon a weighted companion square which can't do anything but move left and right, but which can't be harmed by a lot of hazards and can press switches only designed for it, and drop bombs that destroy small diamond-shaped walls. On top of the liquid form, this is a relatively large amount of gimmicks for an indie platformer, most of which only have one major player gimmick. While that's not bad by itself, the weighted companion cube and bombs are never useful except in the situations where they're specifically called for (walls of fire you can't walk through with switches on the other end, and small diamond-shaped walls, respectively) and the bombs are basically never used in any interesting fashion. Flying with steam, meanwhile, lets you ignore basically every hazard or difficulty for the entire time you have that power, making it far too useful. The only reason I didn't use it more is that it's fairly slow, and I wanted to be done with the game faster even if it meant running my cat into hazards a few times.
The collision detection is also pretty bad - as I mentioned, there were a few times where it seemed like I could jump despite not touching anything. This also unfortunately applies to hit detection sometimes, and while you have to take three hits from most things in order for your cat to respawn at the start of level or a checkpoint, some hazards will send you back to the start instantly. It wasn't all that frustrating, especially due to how quickly most levels could be solved if you knew where the hazards were ahead of time, but it still didn't leave me with a positive impression of the coding.
The 30-level Companion Square campaign, on the other hand, was more typical of indie platformers, given that in each 10-level section, your companion square has one special ability: boosting its speed in the first ten, jumping vertically in the second ten, and stopping in place and becoming unaffected by physics and objects for as long as you want in the final ten. The companion square's indestructibility in the core game carries over, so instead these levels are timed, with new purple hazards either draining your time or sending you back to a checkpoint or the start. While these levels were refreshingly different, I found the first twenty kind of limited in what they offered, and only the last set were interesting. Also, the time limits were not well-implemented - your time continued ticking down if you were sent back to the start, until you ran out of time (which also sent you back to the start, even if you'd hit a checkpoint) or manually restarted the level. This meant that I had to manually restart Companion Square levels fairly frequently, because being sent back to the start with only half of the time remaining was pointless.
Finally, while it's not a major part of the game, I was a bit bothered by the story in Cats are Liquid. It starts off cute, but ends on a note somewhere between depressing and horror, which wasn't exactly what I expected going into this. It didn't really make coherent enough sense to me to register as anything other than a sad creepypasta or something, but... eh!
In the end, I went into this expecting a silly $1 cat game. Cats are Liquid delivered on that, but not in a way where I feel I can really recommend it to anyone.

The game itself can not seem to decide if it wants to be realistic or arcadey and is trying to compromise between the two in the worst way possible. First of all you have 8 stances from which you can attack from. That's a pretty realistic mechanic and in theory is good, but in practice even just getting to a stance requires a level of technical mouse finesse that is beyond irritating.
If the game is trying to be realistic it needs to really do some hard reworking. I was getting 360ed by a glaive.
Additionally the block mechanic is good in theory, but because it is so irritating to get to the proper stance half of the blocks feel like random chance. The parries are even worse and I've yet to even see one be pulled off, much less do I know how to perform after reading "Left click then right click" a million times.
If the game really went in, polished, and made the realism stand out it could be a good game. At the moment I can not recommend it and I'm deciding whether or not to get a refund.

I would give this a little bit of time. At the moment im personally dealing with a game which has a lot of problems, a lack of content, and a high price tag for those things.
My first issues are performance and bugs. The menus are awful, extremely strange to navigate, there isn't feedback for clicking things either in the menu OR when you score a hit in combat. The latter being a huge issue, especially when the hitboxes are so iffy at the moment you can die from someone swinging 10 feet away from you, but not register a hit when you watch your sword pass directly through their body. I had a lot of fun the other night getting the learn the combat system in the duel mode they have, but currently the conquest mode isn't very much fun, generally being a chaotic zergfest in which friendly fire and teamkilling is rampant because of the clunky movement and hitboxes, and that confusion during combat does NOT mix well with the confusion of a hundred people fighting eachother with swords. It needs to be precise and clear whats happening, and thats just not the case right now. The lack of any feedback, whether its blood spurts, flinching animations, or even a sound most of the time really hinders the experience. Archery isn't really viable right now solely for the fact that the arrows do an obscenely low amount of damage, i suppose to balance out people being constantly one shotted by arrows, but they really need to increase the damage per hit and work on their system of aiming and firing.
Balance and the leveling system is also kind of strange to me, and feels not very satisfying at the moment. I think others have gone into it in more depth, but its ok. I suppose its too early to really know where that will end up, seeing the release of Epic mode shortly.
The thing is, the game has a lot of potential. If they release the Epic mode and work on the issues mentioned above, it will surely be an enjoyable medieval warfare experience to have. My concerns hopefully will ultimately be unfounded in the end if the devs follow a path of open communication with the community and work on core gameplay issues, tightening up the melee combat being number one on my list.
Ill be looking to see what they do with this, but for now ill be waiting anxiously for Bannerlord to come/

A lot of people seem to call this game a love letter to "metroidvania", and I can't fault them for that. This is one person's attempt to create a truly modern 2D Metroid-like game, using all the lessons learned from the best of the best in genre and adding new elements, that weren't tried in the genre before. This game has exciting exploration, varied locales, fantastic soundtrack, unique visuals that mix old-school 8bit and 16bit era art with subtle modern effects, surprisingly good challenge for the most part and a very interesting atmosphere that can probably be summarised as "sci-fi adventure as if Another World/Out of This World was designed by H.R. Giger".
It's not without flaws or questionable decisions. Challenge in the opening parts, before some upgrades, feels higher than you'd expect from a Metroid-like game, with action not being tight enough to justify that. Boss battles look great, but only 2 actually feel fun to play, with most others just being "shoot shoot shoot die already it's getting annoying shoot shoot" deals. Game features some random elements in the way of "Secret Worlds", which, in concept, are cool, but make the "exploration" part of the genre most loved for it, a bit less rewarding, because the areas are random and you have no chance of getting everything in one run. Some of the navigation moves just feel clunky to pull off, especially the very important one, that requires directional double-tap - most of the run-and-shoot actually plays better with an analogue stick, but these are very hard to pull off and are frustrating even on a d-pad, no matter what gamepad you use. And finally, the story and dialogue feel rather averagly written, which is sad simply because the setup and situations they show are actually very interesting. So, story, while often predictable, is exciting to experience and the world lore is out there to be found, but both are just told in a very mediocre way.
That said, the game is still fantastic, especially due to its innovation in treating death more like a... well, Souls game, I guess will be the most understandable comparison. That is - death does bring you back to the last save room you used, but you keep all the unlocked map squares, items and everything that is permanently done (like killing a boss or triggering a cutscene) stays done. This, along with the idea that enemies do not respawn immidiatelly after leaving the room and instead after you move two rooms away, makes exploration so much more fun, while not simplifying the rules to the point, where it gets boring.
One of the best recent games in genre which, while probably isn't as full of awesomeness as La-Mulana or Aquaria, still feels like a solid "proper full game" that you'd get full priced 15 years ago and love it. A real treat for anyone who wants to explore some amazing worlds in Metroid style.

When it comes to “Axiom Verge” there are two certainties, one it’s a complex and challenging experience, and two it’s down right addicting. Axiom Verge is game that pays homage to the Metroidvania genre, made famous in the 90’s by games like Super Metroid and Castlevania. If still unfamiliar with either of the titles the primary objective of the game is to explore an environment slowly acquiring new equipment in order to traverse other parts of the map. Axiom Verge excels at recreating what made those games so special.
the 2D side scrolling gameplay is a wonderful compliment to the vibrant colors in each of the different areas. As the player traverses the game’s many different environments a massive sense of nostalgia is bound to kick in as every sound and pixel is reminiscent of the past games. There is a real feeling of retro gaming, but like most modern games there is a wonderful twist.
Axiom Verge is a game that pays excellent homage to games of the past like Metroid and Castlevania while still doing it’s own thing. The map may be confusing at times, but Axiom Verge is still an amazingly addicting experience.

Okay, so... To be perfectly clear, I'm thumbing up the game BARELY because the price is out of control. I got it on sale for $14 and that's a lot closer to what it's worth.
This is a metroidvania (clearly) and is more similar to the original metroid in aesthetic and exploration than most recent entries. Unfortunately some of the upgrades are very nice but others fall very flat. Specifically, the primary weapon is a bit ridiculous. There are serveral types of "beam" that you can pick up, but you can only have two equipped at once and toggle between them without going to the menu. Further, they're all really very boring weapons. I found myself relying mainly on the first gun until I got the other one that shoots straight for long distances, then my alt weapon was the one that could penetrate walls a little. Not very exciting. Another annoying design quirk is the "lock" button. In Metroid games you can lock your firing angle in various ways depending on which entry in the series you're playing, but in Axiom Verge you hold a button to lock your position instead, so the d-pad controls firing angle instead of movement. Look, the Metroid systems aren't perfect, but they allow for highly mobile combat and they feel natural. The position lock in this game is immersion breaking, even after having been used to it for a couple hours.
Some of the other items are quite nice though. Instead of a morph ball you get a remote drone that you can fire and then control. It can go just about anywhere so long as it's not blocked by high jumps or otherwise un-navigable terrain. You can even leave the area you left your body in and continue exploring. When the drone dies or self-destructs you return to your body. That's pretty neat, really.
The other main items are a disruptor and a laser drill. The laser drill is kind of a more convenient version of Metroid's bomb weapon - mainly intended to break holes in certain walls. The disruptor works to corrupt the reality of certain blocks or enemies and can make some interesting things happen when used in the right place. For example, there's one enemy that looks like a big coral and shoots out annoying projectiles that fly around in random directions. If you get the leve 2 disruptor you can corrupt it and it shoots out health instead.
The length of the game isn't too bad. I've been playing for a few hours and I'm at less than 20%. I'm smart enough to not use a guide/FAQ until after I've beat the game though, so YMMV if you spoil yourself.
Anyway, it's
not worth $20. At this point I'd say that the $14 I paid for it is about right for a metroidvania fan.

"ZOMBI is an excellent port of the original Wii-U title, even with the servere lack of graphics options. Controls are tight, atmosphere is tense, and it's still one of the scariest zombie games on the market. However, the terrible AI and the extreme shortness of the game make it hard to recommend at full price."
Ah, ZOMBI. I remember playing ZOMBI-U on the Wii-U when the console launched, and I remembered it being one the scariest console games I've ever played. The great sound design, tense atmosphere, and dark areas really immersed me into the world of a plague-ravanged London.
Basic Plot: London has been torn by an unknown virus, turning the people it infected into mindless zombies who hunger for human flesh. As a survivor, your job is to escape, with the help of the mysterious "Prepper", and other characters you meet along the way.
Pros:
-Perma Death: This bears special mention to me. While others might not like it, I think it adds another level of horror to the game. When you die, the character you played as stays dead, and even when you begin as a new character, your previous wanders the map as an infected, depending on how they die. There's also a mode where you can play until you die- then it's game over.
-Great Music: The OST for this game really sets the tone and really sells the horror vibe.
-Good Level Design: Areas in the game are modeled realistically after their real life counterparts.
-Excellent Combat: From using firearms, to bashing an infected's skull in with a shovel, the combat feels right and is very satisfying.
-Challenging: Even if you play on the easiest difficulty, be prepared for a challenge.
- The Horror: While there are some jump scares, this game largely relys on the atmosphere and the number of infected on the map. The more infected, the scarier it will be to run by them or fight them, as the threat of death looms over you.
Cons:
- Crap AI: This goes without saying. I've seen my fair share of infected walking into walls or in place.
- Graphics: The game looks like a Source Engine mod. While that's not BAD, the lack of graphic options to choose from really hurts the game.
- Clunky Controls: Might not be the case for others, but for me, I played with a keyboard and mouse and found myself struggling at times because the movement controls would stick. It could just be me, though.
- The Price: It's worth like $10.
- Uplay.

Overall: 8/10

I absolutely loved this game from start to finish.  You play a young boy who appears to be somewhat of a loner, he doesn't have very many, if any, friends in school, and tends to stick to his books and writing in his journal.  One day while coming home, he happens upon an injured bird.  The injured bird has lost track of his flock, and is all alone.  So the two are essentially kindered spirits, and this tells the story of how the two become the unlikeliest of best friends. and how their friendship changes and alters the life of each.
It's a story that will make you laugh at times, you'll smile over the moving relationship between the bird and the boy.  At times, it will make you feel so sad that you'll wonder if someone just sucker punched you in the gut.  The story hits a myriad of notes, and that's truly the mark of a good story, when you feel all sorts of emotions, and this game does that, clocking in at just over an hour.   Interesting enough, there is no dialogue in this game, the story is conveyed through sound effects, and pictures.  You wouldn't think you would find yourself getting attached to characters, but you certainly will.  The soundtrack is stunning, and conveys the atmosphere and story of the game perfectly connecting with the scenes transpiring before you.  Big kudos to the developer and artist behind the soundtrack, splendid job.
There isn't much to say about the gameplay, I'd even say that telltale games have more actual "gameplay" as far as that's concerned.  You essentially get to the play as the boy and guide him down pre-deteremined routes, there isn't any skill required, no quick time sequences, you simply keep moving in the direction the story takes you.  Which is fine, because the story more than makes up for it!  I purchased this game for a buck and some change during the winter sale, but i would have paid 5 for it having played it, I think it's worth it.

8/10 Gameplay – Dishonored does a lot of things right for a stealth action game. Huge levels, literally dozens of ways to complete an objective, but several of the mechanics needed more work. Specifically, the fact that your skills are geared much more for killing than being nonlethal and in a game, that chastises you a lot if you’re just a little too kill happy, it just didn’t sit right with me.
9/10 World – Dishonored is set in a steampunk Victorian-esque seaside town. It is full of NPCs, hostile, neutral, and friendly. As you make your way through the game, you can stop and listen in to various NPC conversations, and they talk about a variety of things ranging from their families to their hatred of their job.  The city feels very alive (till you murder everyone), ironic since there is a plague going on and NPCs constantly talk about how the city has gone to♥♥♥♥♥♥
7/10 Story – Fairly standard revenge rampage plot. You are framed for the murder of your empress and after breaking out, you murder (or not) everyone who is in the way of you and the heir to the throne. There is a bit more to it than that and there are one or two obvious twists along the way. The story probably won’t keep you on the edge of your seat, but it’s not terrible either.
8/10 Overall – Give it a try if you like stealth games or if you have a fondness for creatively killing people.

The game has real potential, and the different elements mixed together do work very well - sure, the first person sequences are rough and require work, and there's bugs galore, but there's the essence of a great game in here.
Unfortunately the simple lack of a basic save system meaning you pretty much lose everything once you stop playing unless you're lucky enough that you passed a (unidentifiable) checkpoint means the game is basically alpha and not fit for public release.
Doors which don't actually work properly, to interface elements which simple haven't been playtested properly, this is a game in early development which has evidently been released in borderline alpha state.
Shame really, it really is a good game underneath the hood, but unfortunately it's rather broken and stops you enjoying it as much as you'd want to.
Polish it more and this is a definite yes, but as it stands it's just too rough to justify the cost - if it had been early access I'd have been infinitely more forgiving.
Come back when you've done more work on the game, fellas.

One of the best zombie games I've ever played.
Combat is up-close and brutal. Gunplay is limited to scavenged ammunition and your acquired skills with ranged weaponry. Headshots are not a guaranteed solution; monsters will often resume their attacks with half their cranium gone, or crawl after you when incapacitated. Some are wearing helmets, leading to prolonged showdowns and tense crowd-control situations as you are forced to decide on the fly the best choice of tactics.
Semi-open world; unlock new areas as you progress, with many sections permanently off-limits until you upgrade your kit. Story is simple, but well told.
Most notable is the save system. Death is permanent; if you die, you continue on as a new character, and have to fight your former self-- now undead-- to retrieve your lost items. It's creepy. This is an intriguing setup that invites the player to form a superficial bond with their character.
Unfortunately, there are a handful of "traps" scattered throughout the game that result in cheap deaths unless the player is psychic; zombies will occasionally spawn in large groups as part of a scripted sequence, and there are these acetaline tank SOBs who pop up out of nowhere and explode, killing the player instantly. I made it through the majority of the game with only a couple deaths; when I got to the church, I died 10 times within the span of an hour. Beware.
The confined inventory system works well, except that I found med packs mostly useless since failed encounters almost always resulted in a quick death; candy bars and energy drinks were far more effective in the long run. Initiating a loot results in an animation that sucks if there are other zombies in the room. I did not appreciate that the cricket bat and pistol were permanently bound to my backpack, so that I couldn't swap them out at home base for better items.
It's also worth pointing out that ZOMBI is a port of the WiiU title of the same name, designed for a wide-screen television, meaning that if you have a 1280 x 1024 native monitor (like me) you'll be playing with letterboxing the whole way through, which is distracting, but not a deal-breaker.
Lastly, the whole thing feels a little short. Considering it took me 16 hours on my first playthrough, exploring everything I could, this is a compliment, not a detraction.  I simply wanted MORE.
Don't let these criticisms dissuade you from a quality single-player experience. At the end of the day this is a solid, genuinely terrifying horror-themed shooter with great production value. It's been a while since a game drew me in and filled my skull with dread as much as ZOMBI.
