This game is, simply put...NOT good.  I tried to like it.  I love zombie horror games.  But this one...  One of the many problems with it is that you expect it to tell you the truth.  What do I mean by that?  You melee a zombie until it hits the ground.  Up comes the prompt telling you to left click your mouse to finish it off.  Well, that is a lie.  If you think there is a finishing move you are wrong.  You have to hold the right mouse button down and THEN left click...then left click again...and again...until you beat the zombie to death.  Ammo is a rarity in the game.  And don't expect to have that ammo for long.  Unlike in the real world where police riot outfits are NOT bulletproof...in the game they are.  Trying to shoot a zombie riot police to death is a total waste of ammo.  So you have to melee them...but to kill them you have to first knock off their helmets, then beat them until they fall on the ground and then keep on hitting them until they are finished.  It isn't difficult unless there are 2+ of them...but extremely dull, repetitive and annoying.  Here is a fun fact.  When you die you start off with a completely new character with none of the good weapons and items you previously had.  Think about that for a second.  You are playing through a long level where there are NO SAVE POINTS.  Then you meet your very first exploding zombie, you get zero warning of it and die.  Basically, the game makers wanted you to die just so you  could get used to starting with a new character...fighting your way back to where your previous character died and picking up everything you previously had.  Normally this wouldn't be so bad.  But when "safe house" save points are few and far between you will be spending a lot of time running from the original safe house along the winding path that eventualy leads you to your items.  THAT is both FRUSTRATING and ANGER INDUCING!  Another way the game makers purposely kill you is by the general gameplay.  You are playing the game, you encounter a normal amount of zombies but then, all of a sudden, ZOMBIE HOARD!  Let me remind you, ammo is scarice...  Health is scarice...  So you will be low on health a lot and using melee weapons.  So you versus the hoard.  You melee until you hit an exploding zombie and you die.  You run back and with low ammo encounter a spitting zombie that blinds you so melee and guns are worthless.  You wait until you can see enough to kill it and you either have zero ammo and medium health or some ammo and low health.  No big deal right?  Did I mention there are zombies that use electricity?  With these you get zero heads up so you can formulate a plan.  Playing this game your HUD is extremely limited.  Have a nice new sniper rifle?  Well guess what?  There is no precise aiming with it.  Right clicking the mouse moves the gun a bit forward and the cross hairs (if you can call them that) slightly shrink to show you where your shots will generally hit.  Want to press the space bar to jump or climb things?  That DOES NOT EXIST IN THIS GAME.  In order to jump, climb things, go under things, etc...you press "E".  Climb a ladder in the opening sequence and not used to this game?  Then you will die in the opening sequence.  Why?  Because if you immediately press "E" when the game prompts you to press "E"...well, nothing will happen.  You have to be closer to the ladder and directly in front of it.  Know this, you can be to either side of the ladder, on the side facing it from either direction or the wrong distance from it and you will STILL get the promt to press "E" to climb it.  But NOTHING WILL HAPPEN.  Press "E" to go through a door, turn around and have the prompt to press "E" to close the door.  But if you press it the door will not close.  Silly you, you are not in the exact position for that to work.  Add that into the crashes.  You exit the game and it freezes your computer.  You enter a new area in the game and it crashes to desktop.  You sleep in the game in order to save and when your character wakes up it crashes to desktop.  You change the resolution in the game and it freezes your computer.  This game is NOT WORTH IT.  If you are young and haven't had decades of gameplay experience...well, your threshold for what constitues a good game might include this.  But for someone like me who has been gaming since the 80's...this game shows NO respect for PC gamers.  If you are a console fan...well you are used to this type of steaming pile that game developers constantly shovel onto the various consoles.  But, if you expect a game to deliever, at a bare minimum, what it advertises...then this game will feel insulting to you.

First of all, its innovative gameplay blends the apparently incompatible genres of Crew Management and Roguelike-RPG, and does so surprisingly well. The freedom given us from the very start of the game is total, and the possibility of building and customizing every part of your ship and any aspect of your crew gives a real forward boost in the overall freedom experience given to the player.
Even if it has colorful palettes, a minimalistic (but indeed functional) HUD and rather simple base mechanics, you will be surprised at the complexity of the overall system as you proceed in the adventure: from a small group of pirates, you will be in charge of managing a large crew, composed even of tens of individuals, each one with its up and down sides, needs, skills and behavior. Soon you will take the role of a true captain, assigning each member of your crew to the job which suits them best, ration the food supplies, teach the right skills at the right guys, and be careful to do that, because in Pixel Piracy every mistake costs lives, and coins!
If the management part seems deep enough, then you will be lost in the exploration one. The game features procedurally generated worlds, this means every game will be different, every island a new discovery, every encounter a different fight. Repetitivity is a stranger to this game, because with the combination of hundreds of randomly generated items, tools, ships and enemies, it is successful in mantaining itself fresh and new every time you play.
The combat system is also full of fun and depth itself. Battles will be always different in relation of where they take place. A battle on an island can see your fellow footsoldiers roam through the sandy beaches, staining them with red blood, aided by the ship's artillery team raining death upon their foes, while a battle in the open sea is a true confrontation of two captains and their own vessels: cannons blazing, bullets flying, pirates drowning, hulls breaking and men boarding each other's ship with fierce brutality and desire for loot. Only the best skills, tactics and yeah, also luck, will determine whi wins and who sinks.
Well, that's all folks, there are other features in the game but i decide to leave them upon you to discover. There is a big world in these little pixels, and it is full of wonders.

This game had it's issues in early access, but the devs are really dedicated to making it better, and as it is now I would have to reccommend it to anyome. If you love RPGs, and you love customization this is the game for you.

After falling in love with To the Moon, I immediately looked up A Bird Story as it's from the same creator. However, I didn't buy it until recently due to the game's underwhelming length. I waited until the time and price was right. That being said, I still highly recommend buying A Bird Story full-price if you enjoyed To the Moon--I regret waiting for a price cut myself. We need to support the creator (I forget his name) in his love for story telling because he is insanely great at it. The game on its own isn't really worth the full price, I'm sad to say.
It only lasts an hour, which doesn't give the player enough time with the characters and story.  I appreciate that this is just a set up for the next game, but I can't help longing for more time with this adorable story of a boy and a wild bird he befriends. If the next instalment follows up on A Bird Story, then I will be delighted. It's still a great story even if we don't get enough time to appreciate it. Just like To the Moon, it made me smile, chuckle and a little sad. It most of all made me  feel sentimental. Thinking back to my childhood I easily related with the boy we play as. That's probably why I wish for more. A Bird Story feels almost entirely cinematic--even more so than To the Moon, which isn't a bad thing at all. Considering my only complaint is that I wish there was more of it and that I had spent more of my money to play it, I can't help but recommend A Bird Story. If you appreciate the storytelling, soundtrack and sentimentality of To the Moon, then you will most certainly appreciate what this game accomplishes. Now I just have to wait for another instalment.

I have a love-hate relationship with dating sims. I love almost everything about their writing, the nature of the narrative slowly unfolding non-linearly with each replay, and the exploration of character and testing the player's understanding of character.
I love also how it critically looks at various staples of love-interests in romance in a way that romance novels rarely do. We have more than just the standard alpha-male.
What I don't like about dating sims is that I have yet to find one which lets me just skip (not fast-forward - SKIP) scenes I've seen before and the sheer amount of grinding involved in stat building. Sometimes I want to do-away with stat-building completely and take a page out of Moacube's book where you have other types of decisions which advance plot define your character's character and "stats".
Hatoful tries to make stat building more connected to plot by actually providing you with a unique scene along with each stat building time point. However, I still found the stat building unecessary. I also found the needing to romance a character in two different ways in order to unlock the epilogue really...arduously boring.
That said, Hatoful Boyfriend improves on a lot of other dating sim mechanics and really invests in taking the player's preconceptions of whimsy and istead offers a genuinely good science fiction story. There is a lot of depth in this game should you commit to seeking it and a lot of heart.
I still await the day where we work towards dating sims that remove grinding, whether that's re-doing vast stretches of story to get to new scenes or improve (or do away with) the stat building. Sadly, Hatoful Boyfriend still suffers from both, though to a lesser extent than the average dating sim. This detracted from my experience. I still heartily recommend this game as amongst one of the top games you can play in its genre. (Seriously.)

Once again the cast of the Neptunia series returns for another title! But wait! This time it's a Hack'n'Slash ARPG instead of the traditional RPGs that Neptunia players are so accustomed to. So... How is Hyperdimension Neptunia U: Action Unleashed?
First things first, the gameplay is rather smooth with natural combos - this is coming from a player who is absolutely trash at action games and prefers to stick to turn-based RPGs, so little issue there. The game runs rather well, even without a high-end setup, though some may find the graphics lacking as compared to other Neptunia titles.
The aim of the game is to select up to two characters from the roster (CPUs, Candidates as well as 2 new characters) and slash your way through hordes of familiar Neptunia foes. By performing combos, the EXE gauge fills up, eventually enabling the use of HDD, which transforms the character and boosts their stats and granting new combos. That said, this system is simple but rather robust. Another "unique" aspect of HDU is the addition of "Costume Break", which is basically  a system that reduces characters' clothing as they get hit. Less clothing results in a loss of defense but offensive stats increase. Seems somewhat unnecessary, but hey. It is what it is -.^*
Customization is similar to the older titles, bringing back some of the costumes from previous Neptunia games. More of a just-for-fun aspect that enables you to make your Neptunia Goddesses look the way you like them. Weapons and Accessories can be swapped out, so theoretically it's possible to challenge yourself considering the games' difficulty isn't all that high (especially compared to the grind factor in previous turn-based RPG titles). But this is a Neptunia game, these games aren't all that hard anyway.
Still the same old RPG x Visual Novel we all know and love however, with a storyline that seems much quirkier than the traditional games, but still filled with fourth wall breaking and Nepnep style humor nontheless. Always fun to read through (plus, as usual, Japanese voices are included if you so desire).
Only issues so far are some minor gameplay elements including difficulty. Overall a fun title for Neptunia fans, so long as you don't hate ARPGs or dislike the Costume Break mechanic.

8/10 Gameplay – Dishonored does a lot of things right for a stealth action game. Huge levels, literally dozens of ways to complete an objective, but several of the mechanics needed more work. Specifically, the fact that your skills are geared much more for killing than being nonlethal and in a game, that chastises you a lot if you’re just a little too kill happy, it just didn’t sit right with me.
9/10 World – Dishonored is set in a steampunk Victorian-esque seaside town. It is full of NPCs, hostile, neutral, and friendly. As you make your way through the game, you can stop and listen in to various NPC conversations, and they talk about a variety of things ranging from their families to their hatred of their job.  The city feels very alive (till you murder everyone), ironic since there is a plague going on and NPCs constantly talk about how the city has gone to♥♥♥♥♥♥
7/10 Story – Fairly standard revenge rampage plot. You are framed for the murder of your empress and after breaking out, you murder (or not) everyone who is in the way of you and the heir to the throne. There is a bit more to it than that and there are one or two obvious twists along the way. The story probably won’t keep you on the edge of your seat, but it’s not terrible either.
8/10 Overall – Give it a try if you like stealth games or if you have a fondness for creatively killing people.

In my opinion, this is a very engaging game. The story is mysterious, very creatively told via lines of text set in the environment
.

The protagonist herself is comprised of a collection of malleable orbs which stick together in a sort of cloud; movement consists of an assortment of different methods, including rolling, sliding, wall-jumping, and another ability that you can discover early on. To date, I have purchased just over 15 games on Steam. Some of them have been complete wastenados of my money - one in particular I shelled out a lot for and only got a couple of hours of semi-enjoyment out of it. Startopia is the exact opposite of that game - I paid very little for it and, so far, I've gotten more hours of fun out of it than any other game I've purchased on here.
You're managing a space station which is being visited by nine different alien types, each with their own preferences and skills. You have to build facilities to ensure these aliens are healthy, well-rested, well-fed, entertained and other things like that, make sure any aliens who cause trouble get rehabilitated, keep the station clean, and make sure you have enough energy to keep it all running. You're aided by this artificially intelligent being called VAL who often peppers his advice with a degree of snark and you get occasional visits from a trader named Arona who I swear is a cross between a Vogon and Moneybags from Spyro 2.
Speaking of Vogons, if you pay attention to VAL's messages and the descriptions of each individual alien, you might notice qutie a few sci-fi references in this game, particularly Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy ones.
The graphics aren't brilliant and a lot of the animations do look kinda like the aliens are miming their actions rather than actually performing them, but they're good enough for what this game needs. The music isn't particularly great either but it does help to provide a great atmosphere. You're given a few tutorial missions to help you get to grips with the mechanics and then there's ten proper missions for you to do, each one focusing on a particular aspect of gameplay, like healing sick aliens, putting criminals in the slammer and cultivating resources on the bio deck. And then there's sandbox mode, where you can set things up how you like. Personally, I like just using it to see what I can actually do.
Not that this game is perfect though. The combat system feels kinda loose. Like, I know that by clicking on the enemy I'm telling some of my guys to attack, but how many? And placing and managing muster points is just awkward. There is also this bug where if a gem slug sits at a table in a cocktail bar or gets in one of them slug baths, it will never ever leave the table or bath and it will die. I don't think this is too bad because, by the time you're building those things, you should already have plenty of energy in reserve in case of bad things happening. Plus, you could always handwaive it as the slugs dying in their own excesses or something. Finally, after completing all ten missions, unless you're willing to use sandbox mode to make your own, the replay value of the game diminishes.
Really, though, those are the only bad things I can think about with this game, and I'd say it's easily worth at least double the price it's being sold for. I'd be willing to pay triple.

Plus, microtransactions hadn't been invented yet so you can actually just enjoy the sim rather than grinding to get "coins" or "gems" or whatever.

You will laugh your head off when you zoom in and look at what your inhabitants are actually doing. In short, you'll love it!

TL;DR: Waited for a year until this game was released and instantly picked it up...... the week after it got released had that urge of exploration that i lost ever since i finished Metroid Prime 2
Axiom Verge, made by only 1 guy: Tom Happ and holy crap Tom, some serious kudos to you for this amazing piece of art,
before i go into the game itself here is a little backstory about myself: i LOVE the orignal 2D and 3D metroid and prime games, heck i even played a bucketload of Metroid Prime Hunters and i enjoyed playing Other M as well(sure it wasnt as good as Metroid Prime or Super Metroid but it its fair share of fun as well) my favorite being of course Super Metroid for its sense of exploration as well as Metroid Fusion for its amazing story and tension. i finished fusion so many times that i litterally broke the game, it wont save anymore. and the exploration is incredible as well as the amazing level design. but enough about Metroid, we are looking at Axiom Verge, while being similar is very different and takes a more original approach to its gameplay mechanics
you play as Trace, a scientist who during an explosion ended up in an unkown world in an egg-like incubator without any recollection of what happend after the explosion, you have to explore the caves and ruins of the planet Sudra,
the gameplay is simple yet incredibly engaging: it starts out like your standard metroid game, you need to explore the enviroment for new pieces of equipment to progress to other places, the first weapon you find is the Axiom Disruptor, the main mechanic that is mainly used in the game is the so called "Glitch Gun" a scan-like weapon were you can change  bits and parts of your enviroment so that you can glitch through walls, change enemies and sometimes even change the very fabric of reality.
the level design is one of the weaker points of the game, like the original metroid for the NES you travel to various locations where each of its levels has its own design, but as you move deeper in one area you notice that the assets for the levels feel copy-pasted together and it can become a bit of a bore to look at at times(i had that once when i was stuck in the second area of the game)
The Weapons are one of its strongest points together with the story, there is a HUGE amount of weapons that can be found and utilized in Sudra, and later in the game you see small corridors where trace is to big to walk to, so you think(when you played metroid a lot before) that there would be something like a morph ball, NOPE! instead you get a drone with its one health, damage and attack for small corridors or to scout ahead of areas which is not only very clever to make a safe route to your destination but is also pretty fun to attack with at times, but that is just an extra function for the Axiom Disruptor, the most broken weapon is the Flamethrower pretty much incinerating every-living-thing in your path.
the sound design is also well made, the songs fits the enviroments and gives you the feeling of isolation yet, determined to push ahead to the dangers to come.
but the most challening part of the games are the bosses, in metroid all the bosses are somewhat bigger to fit the levels they are made in, but they arent that huge, BUT in Axiom Verge the bosses are HUGE, and instead of just shooting what moves you actually have to plan carefully what you do agains them and where their weakpoints are and how you approach them.
if you need another reason why you need to play the game, check out plenty of other reviews.
have fun and game on!

Axiom Verge's biggest inspiration was clearly Super Metroid, one could even call it a cheap copy of it and I wouldn't object, The level structure, the world design, the enemy design, the pacing, everything really feels like Super Metroid and I can say that as someone who didn't even play Super Metroid for that long. However everything also is a bit worse than in Super Metroid to be honest. That doesn't mean it's a bad game, it's still very good actually, but in this review I will mainly talk about the things I didn't like,  because I think those are always more important factors for someone who is thinking about buying the game.
There are a surprising amount of weapons in the game, some of them are also a bit harder to find, and that's cool, but the difference between the weapons is so minor or some weapons are so extremely situational that you will maybe use it just 3 or 4 times or so. I think the developer could easily "merge" the functionality of some weapons together who kinda fullfil the same role. For example you get a spreadshot which shoots 3 projectiles in a cone with very low range, but then you get a weapon which shoots electricity in a cone but this one can also shoot through walls and does more damage too.
Or you have like 4 different weapons which just shoot projectiles forward with just really small differences, and then you have a weapon which covers the whole screen but does little damage. The sound design of the weapons is also not great.
Then there are the enemies. A lot of enemies just have their movement pattern and technically "ignore" you, you just have to watch out that you don't touch them or their attacks. The game had too many enemies like that for my taste. I find these enemies annoying most of the time, because they prevent you from traversing the enviroment, because they crawl along the paths you have to go most of the time. And that is a problem since this a metroidvania and you will backtrack A LOT in this game. There are also more aggressive enemies, some really cool ones, but also a lot of really annoying enemies. Some have attacks which are undodgable, well, in theory you could dodge some attacks I guess, but in practice it's just annoying. Much later in the game there are enemies you can only dodge using the teleport ability, but using the teleport ability is really fiddley so sometimes weird things happen.
Because the weapons aren't well designed overall and there are more annoying enemies than fun to fight, the combat isn't the strongest suite of this game.
What was really dissapointing, like REALLY dissapointing, were the bossfights. Visually they are really really well designed, but they have extremely weird attack patterns, weird weak spots and the fights mostly consist of standing in the right spot and spamming the shoot button. It also doesn't help that the bossfight music is the same for every boss.
All of these annoyances get even worse at the last quarter of the game where the game sends you from one end of the world to the other just to get an item, then back to the other end of the world and then somewhere else. On your way the game throws one room full of enemies at you after the other with the thoughest enemies of the game. But because this gets so tedious and annoying I just wanted to rush through past all enemies or was too lazy to go to a save room or something which even led to more frustrating moments.
Anyway, that was a lot of criticism, I still really like this game. First of all I think the game does a good job with the metroidvania aspect (good, not great). There are a lot of different pick ups you can find, not only weapons and items you need to progress, but also stat upgrades and stuff like that. I also like how all the areas are connected with each other and how the game guides you a bit through it`s world. However you can easily forget where you can go and where you know you need an item for. This could easily be solved if the game just let you put notes on the map, an infinite number of notes with custom text, currently you can just mark 2 spots per area which doesn't help at all. A good example of what I mean is Legend of Grimrock 2. The difference between your character at the start of the game and at the end is so extremely huge, you really feel the progress you made.
The story of the game starts really simple and boring actually, and after reading the first lines of dialouges I thought this will be a throwaway story, but over the course of your journey the story gets more and more interesting. The game also has some really neat surprises for you. The presentation and atmossphere are also really strong, the pixel art is really really good except for a few enemies, but sometimes you come across some really huge and incredible looking things. The music also fits the game really well, I especially like the subtle sounds when you are in the room before the bossfight.
So. The game has functional combat, good exploration, interesting story and nice atmossphere and music. It is also over 8 hours long which is nice, however as I said the last quarter of the game is really tedious. If you are a fan or metroidvanias the purchase is a no brainer for you, you probably already purchased it. For everyone else I recommend waiting for a small sale.

I have a love-hate relationship with dating sims. I love almost everything about their writing, the nature of the narrative slowly unfolding non-linearly with each replay, and the exploration of character and testing the player's understanding of character.
I love also how it critically looks at various staples of love-interests in romance in a way that romance novels rarely do. We have more than just the standard alpha-male.
What I don't like about dating sims is that I have yet to find one which lets me just skip (not fast-forward - SKIP) scenes I've seen before and the sheer amount of grinding involved in stat building. Sometimes I want to do-away with stat-building completely and take a page out of Moacube's book where you have other types of decisions which advance plot define your character's character and "stats".
Hatoful tries to make stat building more connected to plot by actually providing you with a unique scene along with each stat building time point. However, I still found the stat building unecessary. I also found the needing to romance a character in two different ways in order to unlock the epilogue really...arduously boring.
That said, Hatoful Boyfriend improves on a lot of other dating sim mechanics and really invests in taking the player's preconceptions of whimsy and istead offers a genuinely good science fiction story. There is a lot of depth in this game should you commit to seeking it and a lot of heart.
I still await the day where we work towards dating sims that remove grinding, whether that's re-doing vast stretches of story to get to new scenes or improve (or do away with) the stat building. Sadly, Hatoful Boyfriend still suffers from both, though to a lesser extent than the average dating sim. This detracted from my experience. I still heartily recommend this game as amongst one of the top games you can play in its genre. (Seriously.)

Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing

Basically this went from the JRPG turn system to a hack and slash system kind of like Dynasty Warriors or the RWBY game, and you basically play as one tag team of which you can switch between two selected characters during a battle.
Character customization is great as always but finding and getting new equipment is a bit less simplistic to do so than in the other games.
Why am I talking about the gameplay mechanics, the highlight of this game is a new feature called "Costume Break", the entire focus on this new mechanic is definitely fanservice, basically your character's clothing functions like a seperate health bar but you don't lose if it gets torn up, the weaker your clothes are, the weaker your character's defense but it increases critical hit rate and EXE gauge fill. (It's basically charge for a special attack if you don't know what it is.)
If you are a fan of the series and don't mind hack and slash gameplay then I reccomend this game, controls are different from the other games but like the other games, the controls grow on you and are easy to remember.
Being a new release, expect it to have several glitches and errors, I had to re-download the game because the first time I set the resolution to 1920x1080 and full screen and it deleted the .exe file, but apart from that I've not seen any other game breaking issues.
Of course this review is not finished and will be seeing updates but so far it is a pretty good change from the JRPG style and still maintains the Hyperdimension atmosphere and blahblahblah Nep-Nep everyone!

REVIEW:
While very skeptical when first acquiring the game, I decided to give it a go and was not let down. Very similar to the RPGs of old, those seeking to re-enter that kind of world won't be let down either!
Story - While perhaps not the most deep story ever written for an RPG, it certainly wasn't bad. It had, to me, plenty of depth for the length of the game as a whole. It also had a good amount of all the story elements one would look for. While it wasn't necessarily evoking particular emotions for me, it might for you. I give the story a solid 8/10.
Audio - The sound track for the game was particularly good, which caught me by surprise. I never found myself thinking "Man, this track is annoying..." and muting the sound. Do you remember how Chrono Trigger's amazing sound track really set the atmosphere for the different areas in the game? Skyborn does the same. I give the audio a well-deserved 10/10.
Visual - Again, this game takes me back. There's nostalgia everywhere. With that in mind, the graphics, sprites, artwork, etc. don't let down. Very pleasing to the eye, in every area of the game. I can't think of an area or situation in which I thought something looked like it could have been done better. The different artwork and visual effects all fit in their respective areas, and paired with the music really brought everything together. Visuals get a 10/10 from me as well.
Gameplay - Here's where I get really nitpicky. There are a few things here that could be done better, so I'll list them in no particular order:
1. Mouse controls - During battles (which were handled great! no random battles!), I found myself accidentally clicking on an option I didn't intend to. For example, a few times I misclicked and ended up "Guarding" on a turn that I needed to do something else... because the curser was "stuck" on the icon beside it. It's kind of hard to describe, but if you're careful it isn't too much of an issue.
2. DEBUFFS - This one is a major gripe for me. You can track buffs/debuffs on your party with a visual alert in the upper-right corner of their portraits. Enemy debuffs, however, you have to deliberately watch for "-DebuffName" to appear in text near the bottom of their image when it wears off. This can be very, very debilitating to your plans if a necessary debuff (Majesty, for example) falls off without you noticing it... which is very possible if the enemy uses some form of buff that either removes it, or grants them all kinds of buffs and your debuffs just happen to fall on off that turn anyway.
For future games, I would most definitely recommend some kind of visual aid for enemy debuffs, if possible. Granted, there was really only a few situaions where it was of dire importance that I had to keep track of enemy debuffs, but it meant a party wipe (no joke) if one fell off and I didn't notice.
3. Difficulty - Not necessarily a gripe, but also not necessarily something I can comment on entirely. The game has 3 different combat difficulties: Easy, Medium (Normal?), and Hard. I played through the game on Normal, and found it to be far too easy in parts. I haven't played through it again on Hard, so I can't comment on Hard mode; however, given the resources available to you, "Normal" difficulty becomes a little too easy. (Except for a few parts, but I'm not going to spoil anything here.)
4. Game Length - I put in 15 hours to this game before completion. This is with about a 99% completion rate. While 15 hours is a far cry from the 50 to 60 hours a game like Chrono Trigger or Final Fantasy 3 (6) had with a similar completion rate, it was pretty generous for this game. Also note that about 4 of those hours are me back-tracking in the damned forest.
With those small issues in mind, I'm going with an 8/10 on the gameplay. It had everything I liked, a little more, but also a few issues I feel could have been handled better.
VERDICT:
Over all, I give Skyborn a 9/10, and a high recommendation to anyone who grew up with the great RPGs from the SNES era, who are looking for a piece of nostalgic greatness. A true diamond in the rough, I really hope to see more like this from the developers. (Even a sequel would be great!)

Skyborn review:
Skyborn is a small rpg game (took me 8 hours to complete, there are some undone side missions, I think)
Basically you are a mechanic girl who's life gets turned upside down and a whole lot of♥♥♥♥♥♥happens... There is another race called the Skyborn who are opressing humans and half skyborn half humans. You eventually... <spoiler!!>
Well, just play the damn game, its well worth it if you are in to this genre.
Pros:
Saturated content, like all good RPGs should have.
This game is amazing, so many things to do, so many secrets and areas to go to.
Good characters and story (the jungle mission was freaking amazing, learning the past of another character and some other things. I was like holy♥♥♥♥♥♥I just had fun).
Amazing soundtrack. Everything just flows.
AMAZING character customization, it beats many other full scale free rpg's (mmorpg's too for that matter) that I've played. You can improve, augment, create and do many more things with your items. And too many extra things to name.
A lot of side missions that the npc's give (they give hints on secrets too!)
And not to mention the npc's all have their little attitudes and get you into the lore of the game. I reccomend for having more immersion, take your time and read all the dialogue (thats what these older top down games are about guys!!!)
Cons:
Nothing in particular, it's an rpgmaker game, so expect dated graphics, but this game isn't for gamers that care about that sort of thing.
Also, this game is not for people new to the genre (it is, but some whole game quests like looking for the playing cards will get messed up if you dont literally walk on every inch of the world in every mission, or you need to go back later).
End result: 9/10, not for everyone but it nails the content in every way possible for this genre.

The Bureau: XCOM Declassified is a game developed by 2K Marin and published by 2K Games and tries it's hardest to be the next new XCOM game which it fails horribly
The Bureau: XCOM Declassified could have been something great but seeing it was developed by numerous other 2K Games' development studios, I think it became beaten around whilst in transit
The nest part of the game is the exposition, the great setting and the good premise, bit is plagued with a terrible script, terrible dialoge and atrocious gameplay. The game had so many bad design decisions and the game primarily focuses on a real-time FPS tactical combat shooter which is just bad and the cover/damage modifier hybrid RPG nonsense is absolute rubbish
The AI for your teamates is also terrible and braindead, simply to use this insane cover system, they often get killed while behind full cover because they peek out to shoot at the air. Also it's very obviously designed to be played on console and the UI reflects this and while I must admit it's less obnoxious than other games it still is what it is, absolute rubbish
If you want to play an XCOM themed tactical shooter for about six to seven hours then get it, but in my opinion you aren't making a good purchase decision, there are many more themed tactical shooters out there that are better then The Bureau: XCOM Declassified. Whether it's worth the full price or not is a different question entirely and one that's up to you, however, in my honest opinion, it's isn't...
To point out what's bad with it - pretty much everything. The movement is slow and clunky, combat is fairly simplistic and not very intuitive, enemy types are not very varied at all, your squad members are not really all the useful, the story is average at best and it's basically a poor man's Mass Effect in a XCOM skin. More or less like Mass Effect: Andromeda with the XCOM name slapped on it
The Bureau: XCOM Declassified is a huge mixed bag but in my honest opinion, it's not a very good game... no wonder Humble Bundle gave it away for free

While I am not a huge fan of stealth games I decided to play this one, albeit years after its initial release. I have to say that I had a blast playing it.  It is a story rich game that is fabulously designed.  The graphics are nice even today and played well on my mediocre laptop, although the game is far more than its graphics. To begin with, I loved the degree of freedom it allowed for - giving you the opportunity to play the game as you see fit - be that as a super stealthy predator - or a full on carnage oriented maniac, although I have to admit that it was for sure created with the stealth approach in mind and it is obvious in how the game is far more rewarding to those who take the stealthy road.
My first run was a mix of straight out killing most of the enemies I encountered (except those I deemed not worthy of dying) and I finished the game without any issues, except perhaps the way my actions affected the outcome. It was the effect of my actions during that first play-through that compelled me to immediately play it a second time (a rare thing for me), taking up the super stealthy approach, and I have to say I am glad I did, as I enjoyed the game (again) in a completely different way.
Overall its not a difficult game - with the exception of a few circumstances. If you go the stealthy road, its more an issue of discovering the way to a goal, figuring out how you should move in order to take out your enemies without killing them or being noticed.
The story is interesting, with some cool characters (if not overly cliché) that complement the game style very nicely, urging you forward towards your end goal. The areas you go through are very well designed, offering a plethora of ways you can approach each situation, giving you a sense of freedom that is not often present in such games.
There is a nice character development system (with abilities) that also allows you to further customize your play style. Its not very deep, but its just right for this type of game. Additionally each stage/area offers certain discovery challenges, offering the perfectionists an additional fun aspect.
Even if you are not a big fan of stealth games (like me) I would still highly recommend this game, its simply great.

This game was tons of fun. There is no base building or tech research, instead tech improves by finding it in missions. I rather liked that there were some "missions" you could send recruits that were not in your squad to work on and bring rewards (including new recruits) and that sending them in those missions would also level up the recruits. All in all a very fun game. If I have to pick a negative point, I will mention that sometimes the AI decides to send some member of your squad running towards some crazy place in combat, which sometimes can be annoying and require more micromanagement than I care for, but I quickly learned how to place them and command them to avoid that most of the time and the crazy movements ended up happening seldom enough that they didn't bother me much.
This is an OKAY game... not great... not terrible, just okay.

Made by the very same hands of the author who gave birth to "To the Moon", here is another simple, yet sublime story based RPG, which you can roughly complete in 1 hour of gameplay.
Be therefore ready to enjoy this experience, and fasten your seatbelt before being projected in a parallel world which rejects the child you're playing: struggling to find your way and a new friend you will be accompanied with emotional music and the force of the images of the enviroment which surrounds you, since as you can easily see by yourself in the very first minutes of "A bird story" the game does not contain dialogues, but rather drawings in a chat form which well suit the format, leaving a free interpretation to you, and making therefore YOU decide and speculate upon the plot and events that occur.

A lonely kid, that has no brothers or sisters, and apparently no other family because his (her?) house is always empty, finds a bird and they become friends and then go fly and stuff.
It's always an incredible feeling when I reach the end of a game and feel very emotionally attached to it. This is a tale about friendship most of all, and about helping one another: the kid, emotionally, the bird, physically.
Story is basically all that matters here, as there are no action-packed scenes, scores, enemies or anything like that. It's just you and the world and bird. It's well written enough to keep you playing for the short time it lasts (I wished it lasted more, but it's just about 2.5 hours long).
There's not much to it, actually. You move in a 2D world (with that impossible perspective) and interact with some objects but mainly what drives the action is the moving around and finding things. I don't remember if you actually control the bird, but that's not really important.
Very simple 2D (low bit rate) stuff, but enough to keep you interested. Again, it's about the story (look at the title) not about the graphics.
Sound design is awesome and the music is dreamy and top notch. Since there are (if I remember correctly) no words in the story, after the general feeling and visuals, the music and sound have to be the most important factor for you to be pleased. And they are!
I would, in a few months, just to have enough time to almost forget it but not that much time to forget how good it was.

Brink has a lot of potential, but has not even come close to matching it yet. I'll list a few points that you should really consider before buying it.
The Bad:
-ATI Support, you WILL not experience good framerates with an ATI card unless you have very old drivers.
-There is a known glitch that sound cuts out, thats right, you will have NO sound.
-Graphics, they look muddled, not great
-Movement is sluggish and even glitchy at times
-Heavy guns are underpowered, I don't see heavy classes played very often due to this.
-Engineer/Medic are going to be far more played than Soldier, and WAY more than the Op (which really sucks imo)
-Virtually no in-game stats, at the end of a match you don't even know how well you technically did beyond points and "awards"
The Good:
-Plenty of guns, plenty of different attachments for most guns
-Lots of different combinations for customization, so your guy can look relatively different
-Teamplay focused game
It has lots of potential, but honestly the bugs are literally so bad that I get annoyed after playing for a few hours...

While I am not a huge fan of stealth games I decided to play this one, albeit years after its initial release. I have to say that I had a blast playing it.  It is a story rich game that is fabulously designed.  The graphics are nice even today and played well on my mediocre laptop, although the game is far more than its graphics. To begin with, I loved the degree of freedom it allowed for - giving you the opportunity to play the game as you see fit - be that as a super stealthy predator - or a full on carnage oriented maniac, although I have to admit that it was for sure created with the stealth approach in mind and it is obvious in how the game is far more rewarding to those who take the stealthy road.
My first run was a mix of straight out killing most of the enemies I encountered (except those I deemed not worthy of dying) and I finished the game without any issues, except perhaps the way my actions affected the outcome. It was the effect of my actions during that first play-through that compelled me to immediately play it a second time (a rare thing for me), taking up the super stealthy approach, and I have to say I am glad I did, as I enjoyed the game (again) in a completely different way.
Overall its not a difficult game - with the exception of a few circumstances. If you go the stealthy road, its more an issue of discovering the way to a goal, figuring out how you should move in order to take out your enemies without killing them or being noticed.
The story is interesting, with some cool characters (if not overly cliché) that complement the game style very nicely, urging you forward towards your end goal. The areas you go through are very well designed, offering a plethora of ways you can approach each situation, giving you a sense of freedom that is not often present in such games.
There is a nice character development system (with abilities) that also allows you to further customize your play style. Its not very deep, but its just right for this type of game. Additionally each stage/area offers certain discovery challenges, offering the perfectionists an additional fun aspect.
Even if you are not a big fan of stealth games (like me) I would still highly recommend this game, its simply great.

SInce its release back in 2012, I have been wondering why it was taking so long for this game to get ported to PC. Now we know, it's because a great WiiU zombie-survival game, makes a mediocre PC zombie-survival game. Make no mistake, this is a REALLY great zombie game; however, having core mechanics designed around the WiiU's bizarre controls/interface makes it impossible to port very well to other platforms.
On the positive side, it has a somewhat fresh take on zombie survial gameplay. The London setting manages to be both fun and dreary in equal measure. Also, the stakes are raised by giving players only one life. When you die in the game, that character dies and you resume from the perspective of a different character.
Unfortunately, this PC port is not the way to experience it. A lot of the gameplay was conceptualized around the WiiU's controller, which features a second screen and touch interface for that screen. When playing this PC port there are a lot of arbitrary game concepts left over that are either infuriating or downright broken.
If you're looking for a good, PC + FPS + single-player + zombie-survival game then checkout Dying Light. If you are some kind of Zombie game aficionado, then try to find a WiiU to borrow to play this game.

Dishonored is an amazing game for experimentation. It gives you a bunch of different tools, abilities, paths and options and then lets you loose in relatively open environments to play around with them as you will. Through upgrades you can focus on the playstyle you find the most fun. There's even an achievment for essentially finishing the game without using any tools and abilities, which I actually found really fun after I'd already finished it a couple of times.
The story itself is interesting enough, though a little predictable, but the setting where it truly shines. Dunwall is uniquely realised city. Think late 1800s London where the primary power source is whale oil instead of coal, with a dash of totalitarian martial law mixed in. It allows for certain areas with respelendent and beautiful buildings of highly refined culture just down the road from a rat-infested slum without feeling any sort of dissonance. The Outsider is also chillingly interesting, a being of apparently immense power who sits just on the boundary of reality essentially watching the world, occassionally intervening apparently just to see how things might turn out.
The one area where it falls over is that most of the really cool abilities and tools are lethal, when the game itself really wants you to play non-lethally. This means your non-lethal playthrough always seems a little more boring than the lethal playthrough, as you have much less to work with. Interestingly though the Non-Lethal playthrough is not really the "kind" playthrough. It feels like sometimes the more merciful option is simply to kill your target, but considering your whole quest is about revenge you are encouraged not to feel too bad.
All in all an amazing game to sink yourself into, highly recommended.

This game is a definite improvement over the first Chainsaw Warrior. While I liked the first Chainsaw Warrior, it had some problems which were addressed in this game:
- The inventory screen was clunky, only displaying two cards/items at a time. The user interface for this game is a significant improvement and much more streamlined, letting you see everything you have in one screen.
- Similarly, whenever you attacked, you had to always pick your weapon, which could be a pain because it required you to keep telling the game "Yes, I want to use this weapon". Picking a weapon to attack with in this game is just one click on the bottom of the screen, plus you have the option to not use a weapon, which isn't in the first game.
- Rerolling in the first game was TEDIOUS, since there was no way to do it except to constantly restart a new game and roll every individual stat. In this game, all your stats are rolled at once and there's an option to reroll right in the character creation screen. You don't know how much less of a hassle the game became because of this alone.
- Ranged weapons were harder to use in the first game. First you had to roll for reflexes just to get a chance to hit, then you rolled for your chance to hit, and each weapon had its individual numbers to roll for each enemy type, which was affected by your marksmanship. In this game, it's less complex: marksmanship is the ranged version of your hand-to-hand score and is rolled against the enemy's reflexes or power (depending on if they're ranged or not), with some weapons offering a bonus to marksmanship. It makes ranged weapons less of a pain to use.
As for the new/reworked elements, I rather liked them. There's a little more replayability with unlockable items now, especially with different chainsaws (also, you start with a chainsaw automatically now). Using ranged weapons is a little easier now (no more botched reflex rolls), plus having weapons that can take out multiple enemies is very nice. Some of the more oddball items from the first game are gone, and nearly every item in this game has its uses and doesn't feel as situationally-useful as in the first game.
Also, you can punch Darkness. That's cool.
Overall, a much improved sequel to Chainsaw Warrior. If you liked the first one, this is definitely worth getting.

Never usually write reviews but felt i had to because of all the hate this game gets. Originally bought it for Xbox 360 and LOVED it so bought it again for PC.
Pros:
Some of the best character design I’ve seen in my life, the games art direction is impeccable and so it looks stunning. The character customization is probably the best in an fps game I’ve ever seen with so many awesome different helmets, tattoos etc. (You can even decide your characters voice!) Overall the visuals and aesthetics of this game are near perfect. Intriguing story sets up game nicely and gives it a unique feel although they could have gone more in depth. There are two campaigns from both sides of the conflict and also what if scenario missions so a decent amount of single player content. Shooting mechanics are basic but there is a nice variation in classes and absolutely awesome parkour mechanics.
Cons:
No one online so the multiplayer is pretty dead, sometimes the AI in single player can be a little dumb but only occasionally. Apart from the story missions there isn't much else to do apart from some challenges (however they do have leader boards).
Conclusion:
One of my favourite games of all time, I can’t understand why it gates so many bad reviews, with some tweaks to the AI more content and a living multiplayer base this game would be PERFECT.

text:
This game, man. This bloody game.
Never before had I thought a game where the main objective is to date a bird would be so engrossing.
The characters are a likeable blend of personalities, from flamboyant to caring, to silly and dramatic, and everything in between. The story, which at first seemed simple, became very interesting, and even pretty dark in some places, with a great mix of absurdity and humour mixed in, as if Boris Johnson on every drug imaginable decided to contribute to the game after playing too much Final Fantasy and ate too much pudding. The music was nice and charming, and the multiple endings definately added quite a bit of replay value. The game WAS rather short, but, in all honesty, I feel like it was the right amount of short. It didn't drag on, and something usually interesting was going on in St. Pigeonations.
And the final storyline, oh god, the final storyline... It was something else, let me tell ya.
In short, if you have the cash, buy this game. that's all I can say, really. This game is one of those examples where you shouldn't judge a book by it's cover.

This game is quite good. It tries very hard to be Super Metroid, and
succeeds, and that's pretty good.
Actually, it has this weird identity crisis where it can't decide whether it wants to be Super Metroid or not. Despite having a nearly identical atmosphere and basic gameplay structure, not one of the upgrades you get works the same way as any upgrade in any Metroid game, except for extreme basics like your first gun and health upgrades. Trace starts out controlling much the same as Samus does at the start of Super Metroid, but then the two diverge wildly in play style as they progress through their respective games. In that sense, it is refreshing, and that makes it feel less like a simple retread of Super Metroid.
The game has many guns, but very few of them are useful. The handful of guns you are required to get by the plot are sufficient for most of the game, as ALL of your guns get more powerful when you find weapon upgrades. There is one secret gun that is absurdly overpowered and shreds the game's otherwise nearly-impossible final boss.
The plot is entirely incomprehensible. If you just focus on Trace's character, and the way he copes with the bizarre situation he's in and matures, the story is all right. There's a very good scene in one area where Trace begins hallucinating, and the area becomes more nightmarish as you progress through it. But if you try to actually make sense of the game's backstory from the various scraps of documents you find, good ****ing luck. The game has two endings; neither is substantially different from the other, or makes any sense.

Sadly, I waited this long to play it because I love To The Moon (TTM) and I was swayed by the fact that this had negative reviews when it came out. I thought "Was TTM just a fluke? There is no way something could be that good again." I put off buying and playing A Bird Story for fear of being let down. I couldn't have been more wrong. This game defys what people think a game needs to have and be to make an impact. No fluff, no wasted time, no silly or useless mechanics.

I guess I'd put it somewhere between the two To the Moon holiday mini-episodes, one of which is very good, the other of which is only ok (while the original game is excellent). It's not that I don't like it as much because it's different, which it is, but because it's not as good. It's fine for what it is, and I'm all in favor of people trying something new if that's what they feel inspired to do, but it's a lot more simplistic than To the Moon was, and the use of interactivity didn't really work for me.
The story is 100% linear (and without words), and the actions you take are too, to the degree that most of the time you're walking along a narrow path/to a highlighted location or activating something highlighted on the screen. With how frequently it switches back and forth between having you do things yourself and taking control away for mini-cutscenes you keep constantly almost-but-not-quite having a chance to take your hands off the controls to just watch what's going on, which started to get a little frustrating after a while. With how little I was participating in it to begin with, couldn't I just sit back and watch what was going on during some of the more tedious running around sections?
That said, it's alright otherwise if you're into that sort of thing.

In theme, Chainsaw Warrior resembles an ultra-violent 1890s-era action film - in the few comic-style cutscenes that make up the story, I cannot help but hear the one-liners in Arnold Schwarzenegger's voice. Gameplay-wise, it seems to be a pretty direct adaptation of the original Games Workshop card and dice game. So, one must bloodily shoot and saw your way through three areas (a.k.a. drawing from three decks of cards), battling an assortment of monsters and avoiding traps (a.k.a. rolling dice), in order to defeat the forces of evil evilness.
The combat itself is fairly simple - choose a weapon and combat range, roll your dice, and hope. The challenge is mostly one of ensuring you have a combination of the numerous weapons and items (such as armour, radiation pills, metal detectors, etc) that will give you at least a chance to retain enough health and firepower to make your stand against the final boss, with the occasional choice to risk a battle with unique mini-bosses for a reward.
And a challenge it is - one will very likely lose repeatedly. I have had a thief snatch away my titular chainsaw, leaving me to struggle with just my bare fists. I have been delayed by dicing crocodiles long enough that the round timer ran out. I have had the only weapon that can kill the final boss miss with each of its limited shots. The randomness of the dice is punishing for sure, though as some consolation, the randomisation of the deck, along with the chance to try a different selection of gadgetry, keeps each playthrough fresh.

Dishonored is an amazing game for experimentation. It gives you a bunch of different tools, abilities, paths and options and then lets you loose in relatively open environments to play around with them as you will. Through upgrades you can focus on the playstyle you find the most fun. There's even an achievment for essentially finishing the game without using any tools and abilities, which I actually found really fun after I'd already finished it a couple of times.
The story itself is interesting enough, though a little predictable, but the setting where it truly shines. Dunwall is uniquely realised city. Think late 1800s London where the primary power source is whale oil instead of coal, with a dash of totalitarian martial law mixed in. It allows for certain areas with respelendent and beautiful buildings of highly refined culture just down the road from a rat-infested slum without feeling any sort of dissonance. The Outsider is also chillingly interesting, a being of apparently immense power who sits just on the boundary of reality essentially watching the world, occassionally intervening apparently just to see how things might turn out.
The one area where it falls over is that most of the really cool abilities and tools are lethal, when the game itself really wants you to play non-lethally. This means your non-lethal playthrough always seems a little more boring than the lethal playthrough, as you have much less to work with. Interestingly though the Non-Lethal playthrough is not really the "kind" playthrough. It feels like sometimes the more merciful option is simply to kill your target, but considering your whole quest is about revenge you are encouraged not to feel too bad.
All in all an amazing game to sink yourself into, highly recommended.

My hours played in this game are a bit inflated simply because I leave it on between play sessions, just paused, because every time you start it...you have to sit through the developer's advertisement scenes. I got this game for $2.49 on sale. And It's easily the best money I've spent on a game, ever.
This is the best stealth game I've played since Tenchu (old school Playstation 1 game).
I love the fact that you can finish each level in literally any way you can think of. They basically just put a map together, and if you can see it, you can get there. If you can think of it, you can do it. Want to literally jump on top of a guy's head to throw him off balance, and then shoot him in the face while he stumbles? Totes McGotes bro. Do it. Want to snipe a dude from across the map with a sleepdart just to watch other guys come running confused? Do it. Want to not touch a single other soul and just slip past like you were never even there? This is the most "fun" way to play through, for me, after quicksaving of course.
I haven't cared about a game world or the characters in it as much as this game has made me care in a long long time. The story works and is revealed with great pacing. The twist at the end, while possibly "predictable" if you're a super jaded player, still provides an emotional reaction that makes you want to see it through to completion. One thing I hate is when a game doesn't give me any good reason to keep playing it. Dishonored absolutely does. I really like the voice acting and the stark contrast created between each character.
Some people don't like that Corvo never speaks. But I prefer it this way. It lets me project whatever personality onto him that I want to play as - be it mass murdering assassin hellbent on revenge, or unlikely hero doing what he has to do to clear his name.
Buy the game. Then buy the DLC. That's my next step.

The game is a 2D, pixelated side scroller where you control a crew of pirates hopping from island to island in your customised ship, making landfall and either killing anything you come across or buying new skills, equipment, hiring more crew and accepting and handing in quests. As the individual battles only last a minute or so its an ideal game to pick up when you have 10-15 minutes spare. This game made me chuckle a lot. It's a lot of fun and I'd definitely recommend it.
When you start the game you first get a configuration window where you can select the screen resolution, full screen or windowed, graphics quality & monitor as well as mapping any input controls.
On the main game screen you can start a new game, load an existing game (there are four slots available for saved games), set the options, view the credits or quit the game.
When you start a new game you select the data slot to be used to save the game, pick from the the three available modes, Sailor (easy), Captain (Normal) & Legendary (Hard). You can enter name for your captain & the world and select whether the tutorial is enabled or not.
The tutorial mode, which is switched on my default, takes you through the basics and although short (around 10 minutes) is definitely worth doing and paying attention to! (Yes you guessed it I didn't pay attention and my crew died of starvation) The tutorial gave me enough information to understand the basics. Hitting F1 brings up a help screen which is a useful reference.
Before starting you have to answer three multiple choice questions from three answers each. How you answer them has a bearing on the gameplay.
You are able to choose from some preselected options how your captain looks.
Once all this has been done you are informed your mission is to defeat four legendary pirates so you can call yourself the most fearsome pirate in the world and you are ready to start the game.
The gameplay is fairly simple. You control a crew of individual pirates and move from island to island using a world map and if you encounter any pirates en route or when you reach your destination you then switch to 2D side scrolling gameplay where you can click to move groups of pirates to the point you clicked. Combat occurs automatically when you get close to enemies and you have no direct control on the combat in real time. Defeated foes drop items and gold that you can pick up and use throughout your crew. You also have the choice of leaving your own ship and taking over a ship of a defeated pirate.
Each member of your crew  has their own stats, skills & inventory that can be increased as you progress.
Some islands have shops, where you can buy and sell items, taverns, where you can hire new crew members and where you can get quests.
The crew have hit points, food & morale scores and all must be kept positive.

I loved To the Moon, and expected at least a tiny bit of what made To the Moon great exist in A Bird story. I didn't expect this.
A Bird Story's no dialogues design approach, and I do mean absolutely 0 dialogue, is what I found the most problematic. Even in AAA titles with full facial motion capture cannot convey all details into a game with just that alone . They require speeches to help. That just goes without saying that 2D sprites/ RPG maker is even less up to par with that job. No matter how much effort were put into drawing each sprites for different animations, the full intent simply does not convey well and at times it becomes tideous to guess what the characters are actually feeling with no dialogues or any text at all to understand what they are really thinking. It's like reading a Sims chat in the Sims, yes the general feeling is understandable, but I have really no idea what the character is thinking/ saying exactly, and it hurts a narrative heavy focus expierence like A Bird Story deeply.
The game continues on worse than a silent movie- (a silent movie do have at least some text to help audiences know what the actor is reacting to or thinking), with things that aren't making any sense keep on happening (moving trees, environment kept changing etc.)  makes following the story incrediably dull and hard to endure. All my interactions- as rarely as they are available, are most often meaningless and did not really make me feel any bonding with the bird, which is supposedly the character I should care about.
A Bird Story is the first game I ever requested a refund, and I truly hope Finding Paradise would turn out better.

Axiom Verge is a 2D, retro-styled metroidvania game, with a heavy emphasis on the Metroid part. Like most metroidvania games, you explore a large and connected world doing things like platforming, shooting enemies, getting powerups, and getting new abilities that will help you solve puzzles, beat bosses, and generally progress in the game. There are also a good amount of secrets and some interesting story bits thrown in. The overall story is confusing and mysterious, which helps add to the alienated vibe of the game as well as making the plot more interesting. Without spoiling anything, the basic plot is that you play as Trace, a brilliant scientist that gets caught in a lab explosion, loses consciousness, and winds up in an unknown place. It's up to you to figure where you are, what happened, and how to get home.
As mentioned, the gameplay is mainly platforming, shooting, exploring, and some mild puzzle solving. You can find a good variety of items if you look hard enough. You can get powerups to increase the damage, size, and range of your weapons, as well as expansions to your health. There are some passive powerups mixed in with tools that will give you new abilities, helping you progress through the game. There are some interesting notes you can find scattered throughout the world that will give you more bits and pieces to the mysterious story as well. However, the coolest part is that you can find a lot of cool weapons. A few are required to get through the game, but many of them are found by exploring. These weapons all have their own unique qualities. It's nice because they are well balanced and do not require extra ammo. They all have inifinite ammo, meaning you can play around with them all you like. So you can use certain weapons to effectively fight certain enemies, cycle through all your weapons to vary your gameplay, or just pick your weapon of choice and have a ball! It adds a layer of fun to the discovery of new weapons. Plus, the controls are tight and the control scheme is fairly comfortable.
The art is very colorful yet fitting to the world of unknown mystery and wonder. I also found myself really liking the soundtrack a lot. Sounds a bit John Carpenter-esque to me. It's crazy how Tom Happ has managed to do such a great job with the gameplay, the art, and the music basically all by himself. The package as a whole comes together beautifully. The dark, mysterious atmosphere and cool techno influences mixed with a bit of alien flair make for an engaging experience that sucks you into the game for hours.
As great as I think Axiom Verge is, there ARE some negative arguments to be had. It didn't run flawlessly on my computer, but my computer is a bit dated and worn out as well so I'm sure it was not a fault of the game... just thought I'd mention it slowed down in some of the larger, busier areas for me. Hardly worth complaining about. This game is clearly heavily inspired by the Metroid series, and while I love that... you could make the argument that it is borrowing from that inspiration a bit too heavily. I personally think it has enough differences and unique twists to make it work as an original game expanding on the genre, but I could understand some people not finding it distant enough from that source. It'd also be cool to have a bit more of a choice in some story elements, but ultimately it is a story that you have to follow and your character is Trace, not you, so I suppose it makes sense the way it is. My only real complaint with the game is that you get a dashing ability, but once you get it you cannot turn it off. This can be troublesome for precise movements because you dash by double tapping in a direction. So if you're trying to move forward and then stop to dodge something and move forward again too quickly... you'll dash instead of just moving. You can lock your position or turn all the way around on stopping to remedy it, but it is a touch adjustment and can still get you killed in some hectic situations while you move eradically. As far as replay value, it's probably not a game you'll start up again immediately after finishing it. There's hard mode, which seems to be about the same but harder, and speedrun mode for... well... speedrunning. So unless you want it to be more difficult, you want to speed through the game, or want to go hunting for achievements, then you probably will leave it alone after your playthrough. Though it DOES have good replay value in the sense that you'll definitely be coming back to it at some point to experience it all again, and the amount of playtime in your playthough is pretty good.
So there are a few bad points, but the good clearly outweighs the bad in this case. It's a decent length game with tons of things to find and a neat story. The music and art are very interesting as well. If you like Metroid, Super Metroid, or metroidvania games in general, then you'll definitely appreciate this game. Honestly, it's probably one of the best games I've played on Steam. So the question is... is it worth the price? And for this one, the answer is yes. 20 dollars for 15-20 hours of great gameplay is definitely worth your time and money. If you're on the fence about waiting for a sale or just getting it full price, get it. It's worth it and it's worth supporting with the purchase. I couldn't wait either and I certainly don't regret it one bit. Axiom Verge gets a 10 out of 10 for being one of the best metroidvania experiences I've ever had.

Full disclosure: Super Metroid is one of my all-time favorite games. If you're afflicted with a similar bias I can say with almost 100% certainty that you will love this game as much as I did.
This is a true 'metroid-vania' style action platformer and as such relies heavily on exploration and item-progression to advance the story. Warning: this isn't a game that will hold your hand and a lot of back tracking and trial and error will be necessary as you traverse the tunnels and corridors looking for a way forward. Thankfully, this isn't much of a chore as the gorgeous 16 bit world has been crafted with loving attention to detail and your entire journey plays out to one of the best video game soundtracks.. full-stop. The weapon system is a blast, combat is entertaining and the item-progression is rewarding and inventful. I love the ability to 'glitch' enemies and environments and found myself constantly experimenting as I progressed.
If I had to level a criticism it would be that the story falls absolutely flat, especially near the end as the intrigue and mystery so carefully cultvated in the beginning has all but dissapeared. But that's a small compaint to levie against what is otherwise such a superb game.
Bottom line: if you've been looking for a game that would re-kindle your love affair with this long neglected genre look no further. Axiom Verge is a beautifull and charming send up to a classic and stands on it's own one hell of a good time.

I recieved this game for my birthday, being a major fan of the metroidvania style.  This game leads much more to the Metroid side of that equation; in fact, one of the biggest criticisms I've seen of this game is that it feels like a Metroid clone.  To me, that's more a matter of personal taste - if you enjoy exploring alien worlds, finding powerups and secrets, but don't mind missing out on the Castlevania staples of leveling up and finding new equipment (with some exceptions), then you'll probably like this game.
On the aesthetic side, the game duplicates the retro NES style fairly well.  I don't think it sticks 100% to the NES' 4-color palette, but the illusion is there.  Something that bears mentioning is the glitch effects seen in game - as someone who owned and operated a NES for several years, I'm quite familiar with what happened if a cartridge was inserted crooked, or if the contacts were dirty.  Axiom Verge duplicates these with startling accuracy.  On the style side, this game isn't for the squeamish - if Metroid's environments were biomechanical, Axiom Verge is BIOmechanical.  Tentacles, fungal growths, pulsating organs, and some very Giger-esque imagery gives me the impression of walking around inside some huge creature, rather than an alien planet.  This is alleviated when you get to the surface areas, but I never liked the Monstro scenes in Pinnochio as a child, so this combined with the music (a pulsating, semi-atonal electronica selection) makes me feel uncomfortable.  I believe this is intentional, as someone suddenly ripped from their homeworld and plunged into a dying alien world would probably have a bit of culture shock.
Storywise, the game does very well.  I'll not spoil anything, but it kept me guessing, and it's very hard to figure out who to trust as the game goes on.  It's delivered through in-engine cutscenes and dialogue boxes, without voice acting - this is probably due to a combination of budget concerns and adhering to the NES style, but I do hope for a larger budget for Axiom Verge 2 (or whatever the studio's next project is).
On the technical side, the game is superb.  The controls are very tight (more like the original Metroid or Mega Man than the slightly floaty Super Metroid) - my only two complaints are the double-tap teleport command (would be better if it was assigned to a button) and the weapon quick-swap (it takes a bit to figure out how to assign weapons to the quick swap, and on my controller one of the quick buttons is R3, with the right stick being the normal weapon swap, which occasionally leads to accidentally opening the weapon ring).  Still, use a controller with this game, and you shan't be disappointed.  Additionally, the game has a built-in speedrun mode.  Speedrunning is a staple of metroidvania games, though I've always been bad at it.  Speedrun mode removes all cutscenes and adds an on-screen timer that automatically splits at every boss kill, which is wonderful if you're into that.
The achievements show that the developer knows the metroidvania audience; aside from the standard achievements (beat the game, beat it on hard, beat it without dying, and beat every boss), they included achievements for both 100% and low% collection, 100% map completion, and finding some very well hidden secrets.
Overall, if you played and enjoyed any modern Metroid game, you'll probably enjoy Axiom Verge.  If you like modern Castlevania games and aren't adverse to sci-fi, you'll probably also get a kick out of it.
