What's Good:
+ Fairly well done combat and mood setting, interesting mechanics.
+ Good deal of variety in weapons, all of them feel purposeful in some way
+ Environment is interesting, game feels "tense" and zombies are actually formidible
+ "Lose all loot" mechanic is engaging, albeit kinda tedious.
+ Enjoyable experience when it worked.
+ Great port considering it's from WiiU.
What's Bad:
- Massive issues with random crashes, and game does NOT save your place unless it's inconvenient (NOT EVEN IF YOU CRASH NEAR THE ENDING). And yes, I've tried all of the fixes, which fix some of the crashes, but not all.
- NO AUTO SAVE. Prepare to lose a LOT of progress.
- Inventory management is BONKERS.  Dedicated bank is too small for the massive amount of loot. Cannot remove ammunition from guns (or if you can, I STILL have yet to find a way). Cannot remove your starting pistol and bat from inventory. Cannot move around currently equipped item.
- Some of the UI is useless. The map especially.
- Exploration is minimal despite what it might seem like. Places feel very recycled in areas. I can describe this game as "extremely overwhelmingly dark for no reason hallway simulator". You'll get tired of dark storage rooms within minutes.
- Story is barebones and uninteresting, no characters to latch on to. Quests feel pointless.
- Suicide zombies are TERRIBLE in a game about survival. Two of my deaths in the game came from a suicide zombie that appears on my shoulder at the wrong time. Also, LITERALLY: Ghost zombies. Not even kidding. Like why the ♥♥♥♥ is that a thing??
- No control over how your character looks in a game where it looks like there are several different ways they can look. I can accept no customization after the first death, but can I at LEAST customize my first guy so it hurts even harder when I lose him?
- Missed opportunity in having a nursery level without children zombies. I know why they didn't do it, but it was still a let down how manufactured that whole area was.
- Audio/Graphics options are minimal.
Overall:
I enjoyed it but it was a giant missed opportunity. It plays exactly like a game that would be decent on the WiiU, but terrible when compared to how great it could have been. It's also very fustrating how broken so much of it is. Despite that, I'd recommend it when it's on sale for a fun 9-10 hours... otherwise, I give it a no.

I bought this on Steam release despite owning and never playing it on the WiiU... mostly just because I was shocked that they didn't try to charge more than $20 and because they confirmed a FOV slider. Of course I promptly left it on the pile just like I did with the original release until now. I definitely feel bad for doing that since the game is just as cool as it's fans say it is. The developers did a really smart job of borrowing some Souls game design and wrapping it into a slow-paced zombie survival horror game. While the run back to regain your weapons and supplies isn't quite as punishing as the Souls games, a death does feel more fittingly punishing than just a checkpoint restart. The level design is surprisingly clever and does a really nice job of feeling just layered enough to make revisits to areas interesting (being able to mark locked doors on the map is really handy). The combat feels just the right level of clunky. The melee weapons are pretty poor for mobs, while the guns feel slow and weak unless you nail headshots consistently. The balance works well and keeps each engagement interesting as you weigh your options. I loved the mood of the game too. It's aggressively British and the fog and grime help out the weaker aspects of the visuals.
Verdict: Give it a shot.

The Bureau: XCOM Declassified is another take on the "alien invasion" trope with the XCOM name. It's a squad based, tactical combat shooter. The missions being incredibly long to compensate on the limited amount of missions. Unlike normal XCOM, you won't have inumerable amount of stuff to do until the next story mission. This game is all about those missions and combat.
I will state that the combat reminds me in-a-way of Mass Effect. You need to enter cover to survive. Your squaddies have different abilities to use to give you an edge in the gunplay. A multitude of weaponry for the player to use and influence their game styles. There are aspects drawn from the XCOM strategy games, like "percentage chance of hit" for the AI or bonuses to flanks. Full cover and half cover. While these aspects highly effect the AI and their personality, it really doesn't effect the player that much. Enemy in half cover? Snipe them out when a piece of their body is poking out. Full cover? Just wait for them to peak. However, their is strategy to the game. You have to make sure you squaddies are in cover for the majority of the time. You need to rotate and bring your squaddies along when dealing with a bigger enemy.
Admittidely, there isn't much that the game can do in a third-person shooter in response to the player.
The story missions are all entirely based on combat. This is what the game is about, combat. But the story missions progress and unlock new things for the player to use. Different backpack bonuses that you can find and equip. Sci-fi weaponry compared to the Cold War ones. The problem lies with the only thing that you really can do are missions. You can communicate with people at the home base, and find out the lore for this version of XCOM. But the fact remains, the game is all about the missions.
Surprisingly, you can talk to other people in the game. Whilst the conversation partners, and choices, are limited. You are able to find out the lore of the game. Or find out what's going on in the daily life of the people in the base.
However, if you were to look at the DLCs, you would discover that you really shouldn't buy them. Probably only when they're on sale. The only one of worth is the Hangar 6 R&D, as it gives a new character to play as for that DLC, and more gameplay.
I would recommend this game just for the experience. However, I would recommend you purchase the game during a sale. Like most shooter games, it has limited replayability value. The only replayability would be to find out what the other choices that you could've make do.

If you are a sci-fi fan, like star trek, red dwarf and hitch hikers guide to the galaxy you will love this game. The game itself works in a similar way to other management sims where you will need to keep visitors happy by ensuring there are enough facilities. The game has a simple tutorial that eases you into things and the missions are structured in a way as to not make things to taxing at the beginning. The game can be saved at any point and even if you finish a mission you can still continue on if you want to expand things a little more.
I highly recommend this to anyone who likes the genre and setting. I can't recall playing anything else similar to this and the sandbox mode ensures you will come back to it time and time again.

So I got way more invested in this game than I expected to. Mechanically, it is a minimalistic platformer, you navigate a strange world as a cat who can turn into liquid and gas. You even get your own companion cube, or in this case square.
It's not particularly difficult, though there were a couple of levels in the last world that took me a while and even made me ragequit once. But all in all, this is a pretty easy game.
The bit I got strangely invested in was the story, which is told through bits of narration on screen as you navigate the levels. The story stays pretty vague and a bit cryptic, though the companion level pack clears a bit of it up. It's mostly the inner monologue of the cat and it is weirdly bleak and borderline existential. This is what sells the game for me. Without the story it would have been a fun but forgettable platformer, but with the story it'll stay with me a while.
I think it's worth more than the asking price, and it's definitely a dollar well spent.

I'm one of the many coming to OKAM from the Mount and Blade: Warband mod cRPG. Although the mod is totally dead now, I'm still one of the 15 or so NA admins for those servers and have been since roughly 2012. It was a decently sized community of loyal and active players dating all the way back to its release. I'm very fond of cRPG, Mount and Blade, and the combat system developed by them. Most all of us are, and I state that confidently.
OKAM is a deviation from tried and true. While their combat mechanics are interesting, they're clunky. Both attacking and blocking are controlled by the same left mouse button. Movement feels like a mixture between MS and a 1990's Dodge Caravan in wet cement. The main menu music is wonderful, but the in-game sound effects are currently atrocious.
The developers, Donkey Crew, did a wonderful job in respect to graphical detail, and for an alpha game, I haven't run into many major hiccups. This has surprised me; it does seem quite stable. But, if it's meant to be a game, it needs to be fluid. While they very well may work this out in Alpha and Beta, OKAM currently appears to be in pre-pre-pre alpha, or so I hope.
If you're interested in picking this game up, consider waiting awhile. Remember that many of the new reviews being posted are likely coming from behind the rose-tinted glasses of former cRPG players. I do have hope for OKAM, but I strongly advise those of you interested in the game to hold off a bit and check back later. Please do keep an eye on their website and stay up to date with the game's progress!
Edit: Keybind support was added.

Despite this game being released 4 years ago, I picked it up and wanted to give it a shot. Lots of people were furious over this game and how disappointing it was. Lots of awesome trailers and mechanics to show off such as Brink's S.M.A.R.T. mechanic (Smooth Movement Around Rough Terrain) and dynamic objectives.
Even as it is right now, I'm loving and hating this game.
There are less than 20 players global. Unless you are lucky and get some friends to play with you, you won't get much fun out of this deserted game" (That is if the game doesn't give you connectivity issues).
Well...there isn't exactly a story. The "Singleplayer mode" is just multiplayer maps with bots. However, I liked the setup for Brink.
Humanity has fled to a manmade island called "The Ark". This island was able to renew resources and allow a safe last place for people to live in. "Was". The Ark is running low on resources and has lost communication from the outside world. Two factions: The Resistance (made up of refugees) and the Ark Security (basically the cops), are at a war. The resistance wants to escape the Ark while Security is trying to save it.
Besides a short one minute cutscene at the beginning of every mission with some interaction between characters, that's as much as you will get storywise.
I'm guessing the developers made the AI "dumb" so that in multiplayer, the AI would not be able to "play the game for you" (similar to the bots in Titanfall that don't alter the gameplay much).
However, the singleplayer mode is going to torture you. The AI will constantly go for the secondary objectives such as taking command posts (you will hear them chatting about this A LOT) and build turrets near your spawn. Medics will still revive you, but that's even if they don't get swarmed by three enemies. It doesn't help that the enemy AI seems to be much smarter than your team AI. Also, the difficulty of the AI scales to your level so playing a hard mission at Level 1 is just as challenging as playing an easy mission at Level 10.
Gunplay...well, it plays like your typical modern shooter. You have 4 classes: Assault, Medic, Engineer, and Operative (Like the spy from Team Fortress 2). There are 3 body types: Light (moves the fastest), Medium, and Heavy (Terrible because you gain only an additional 40 health and you can barely move as fast).
Level design isn't helping Brink much either. Levels will either end with stalemates or they are extremely one sided. Take the mission "Early Launch" for example. On the security side, it might be a bit hard to repair the crane controls at first, but eventually, when you have to hack the missile controls, its ridiculous. Why? Because the Resistance spawn point is RIGHT IN FRONT of the objectives and the security spawn is all the way at the other end of the map. It also doesn't help when you have the AI as I described above.
Alright, I can at least give some props to the design team. I really liked the customization options for styling your character, even if you rarely look at characters in game. You could get tattoos, change color of your clothes...and that's probably it.
Weapon customization is a bit nice. You can customize sights, barrel attachments such as grenade launchers and bayonets, and different sizes of magazines.
A smooth art style with "unique" character design. Backgrounds would look nice if they weren't so low res. Otherwise, the art style is similar to games like Team Fortress 2 and RAGE.
The only reason I wanted to give Brink a shot was because I found a Youtube playlist with game soundtracks and Brink's main theme was playing. While many FPS games have fast adrenaline pumping music, Brink's OST is calm and ambient. Weapon sounds aren't much, they are self explanatory.
Unless you are like me and you want to experience what a game that was supposed to compete with TF2 should have been, then buy it. The Agents of Change DLC may give you an extra hour or two of funtime. Otherwise, I would not recommend buying Brink. Not even during a sale.

A short, whimsical, bittersweet interactive story with surreal elements, lovingly detailed and narrated without any dialogues.
_____
A bird story is one of those games where much of your enjoyment will depend in your pre-existing expectations of games, and in what you will read into the themes and the story. It is only mildly interactive and quite linear, and much of the time you are simply watching scenes unfold, yet I personally found some of the interactive moments all the more impactful because of that. It is simultaneously visually impressive for what it manages to create out of its tools, and pretty simplistic. The sometimes funny, sometimes sad visual story will be very evocative for some and almost saccharine for others, and I can easily understand both points of view. And yet I could vividly remember every detail of the 1 hour experience, a week after first playing the game. Emotionally, it hit all the marks for me. The way it manages to utilize the pixels, the colour palette, the music, the sound, the subtlest of animations to create its unspoken narrative is masterful. A second playthrough made me smile when I realised how much it uses little gaming conventions (taken out of their usual contexts) to help tell the story. There are just so many clever design details jam-packed into this tiny story, that a second playthrough actually felt worth the time, despite the fact that there is no new content to experience.
Similarly, its narrative can be as complex or simple as you are willing to let it be: It's a simple story about a boy and a bird, but it could also be about how memories are altered by time, about childhood, imagination and dreams, about loneliness and companionship, about belonging, about breaking and healing. You could just enjoy it as a lovingly animated collection of small moments and dreams in the life of a lonely kid, whimsical or heartbreaking but always delivered with an inimitable attention to detail. But it is also a story within the "To The Moon" universe, with characters and details foreshadowing the next game of the series "Finding Paradise". Of course you don't need to have played "To the Moon"  to enjoy this standalone game (though why haven't you already?). Nonetheless, according to the developer, Kan Gao, they are all related, in ways he occasionally likes to hint about in social media. If you're curious about this aspect of the story, the Freebird Games forums are worth a visit: you can find theories and conversations like
about what it may or may not all mean.
Or if you're like me and have ever enjoyed the pleasure of a feathered friend, you could just sit, smile and awe at the beautiful attention to detail that brings the minimalistic bird animations to life. Clearly I'm reading my own experiences into this, and those are some very rose tinted glasses, but a lot of love and understanding for birds and their behaviour seems to have been poured into the game, and some may just fly above the head of anyone who hasn't spent time with a pet bird up close. (Btw, if you're hesitating to play this because you're worried the birdie will die for dramatic effect
.)
There's just so much about this game that genuinely moved me, made me think, smile, laugh and be sad, and it's all contained within such a tiny, lovingly wrapped package, that I am obliged to wholeheartedly recommend it. I realise that it will mean different things to different people and that not everyone will love it as much as I do, but maybe this is exactly what makes it great.
______

A fun old school-style platform game with great artwork, soundtrack, and intriguing story. Definitely would recommend this to fans of games like Metroid or Castlevania: Symphony of the Night.
Probably the feature that makes Axiom Verge sand out the most is the sheer number of weapons to collect (nearly 30), and just how creativily hidden some of the secrets are. Most of these are optional and you can complete the game finding only a fraction of its' secrets, but it definitely adds replay value.
Axiom Verge isn't without flaws however - probably its biggest flaw is the combat itself. Many types of enemies and bosses are cheaply placed or have attacks which are almost impossible to avoid . Enemies will sometimes also block the doors to rooms, causing you to hit them as soon as you re-enter said room. Forcing the player to take damage is poor design and hopefully the combat will be ironed out in subsequent patches or the sequel. The bosses are also a slight letdown, as for the most part they don't react to the player's presense at all, and simply cycle through scripted attack patterns. The final boss is probably the worst example of this poor enemy design, as its attacks are more or less impossible to avoid, and the battle boils down to simply mashing the attack button while hoping your health bar holds out, rather than requiring any actual skill.
The other major flaw is that the game makes little effort in telling you where to go next. Other than occasional "hints" in dialogue you're left to figure it out on your own. For example, after defeating a certain boss, your only hint is to take an elevator up. But it turns out that to continue onward you actually have to find a special item (which was never even mentioned) and then go underground to access a completely unrelated area. I admire games which don't just spell it out for the player, but there's no way a player is going to be able to figure this out without using a guide other than through pure trial and error, which isn't fun.
In spite of these annoying issues the core game is good, the world is intriquing and ominous, and trying out all of the weapons is fun in of itself. So I can easily overlook them and give this game a recommend. Fixing the poor enemy behavior should be top priority as it's the single biggest flaw in an otherwise great game.

Cats are Liquid states the obvious.  I know that no matter how much fencing I put up, or how careful I think I am when I open the door, sooner or later I will find my cat in the neighbors yard.  The fact that cats are liquid is really the only rational explanation for this.
Here though, we finally have proof that this is true.  As you guide your cat through the levels of the game, you can clearly see the ability to become liquid, or even gaseous, is the primary way cats navigate through narrow areas or over wide gulfs.  This educational documentary presents these facts in an entertaining format that is simple enough for children to understand, yet amusing enough for adults.
The idea is made very plain.  Navigate your cat to the exit of the level, while not touching anything orange.  Wise use of the ability to transform into different states of matter allows travel in any direction, and skillful play is rewarded with, well, a cat that is still alive.  That should be enough though, since we must watch over our cats, and not let them perish in a pit of lava.  That's what we call bad cat parenting.
At least it isn't terribly difficult to keep this cat safe.  While the simple geometric graphics may remind you of some of the more brutal platformers out there, Cats are Liquid, at least as far as I've played, is a much calmer experience than games like LOVE, or VVVVVV.  Think Thomas Was Alone, but with a cat, who really is alone.  I mean, Thomas wasn't really alone all that long was he?
Anyway, I find Cats are Liquid a casual platformer, something that you could easily play with your kids.  If they get to cocky, give em Electronic Super Joy, that'll learn em.

I would highly recommend this game to any fans of Dungeon Keeper, Evil Genius, The Movies, and even games like Dwarf Fortress and The Sims.

The main thing you need to know: this game is ridiculously buggy. It's like it received just enough testing to not crash (and to be fair - it never crashed for me, unlike the first Chainsaw Warrior) but the intricacies of equipment, mechanics, unique enemies and all their possible interactions were left to their own devices. I spotted easily upwards of 20 bugs, from purely cosmetic ones like HUD indicators not updating to reflect various gear-induced bonuses and maluses, through irritating ones like items having broken mechanics or achievements being shoddily implemented, to downright progression blockers that force you to start a new game (if you don't know the workaround).
With that out of the way, let me now say I still enjoyed the game a lot. It's a significant improvement over the first Chainsaw Warrior in terms of graphics and content and audio as well. All the ingame interaction buttons are now clumped together in the bottom-left corner of the screen, which lends itself to less swinging of the mouse back and forth across half the screen for every card, which was my main gripe with the previous CW. There's more items, weapons, enemies, achievements, everything. It's good, old-fashioned fun.

You're probably well-familiar with the Hyperdimension franchise by now. Alongside Compile Heart's most popular RPG series, Idea Factory has commissioned the assistance of various developers, in order to produce spin-offs. It seems like every year, two or more Neptunia games are being released. Are we heading towards complete global saturation? It's too soon to tell. For now, let's look at the first spin-off to hit Steam:
. In the interest of sanity, I'm shortening the title to
for the remainder of the review.
is by Tamsoft, the same developer responsible for the
and
franchises. Those games are known for their fast-paced hack & slash action... among other things, but let's not get side-tracked just yet. Anyway, the plot of this game follows Famitsu and Dengikiko, two rival gaming-magazine writers looking for the next big story. Since Gamindustri revolves around the actions of the CPUs as well as the CPU Candidates, you can guess where this is going. Neptunia and company team up to complete quests and slash hundreds upon thousands of monsters.
Fans of
-styled games will feel right at home upon starting this one. Each quest consists of a small arena where monsters constantly spawn. By pressing the X and Y buttons, Nep & the gang perform a dizzying array of moves to decimate these hordes. There are also special attacks as well as HDD transformations for that touch of variety. For most quests, it's best to form a tag-team. Each of the 10 playable characters can team up, so if nothing else, you have Nepgear for backup in case Neptune takes a dirtnap. Your mission is usually some variation of "kill everything", but sometimes there can be hidden objectives or mid-boss battles. The heroines also level-up and earn monster-medals, which can boost stats and unlock equipment.
Since this is a Neptunia game and it is by Tamsoft, a little somethin' somethin' is provided for the fans. You know what I'm talking about right? Fan-service. Unlike most videogames, clothes are not immune to damage. Depending on the severity of the attack, the ladies can get stripped to their skivvies. This affects HDD forms as well. The loss of clothes can result in more damage, for you as well as the enemy. Visually, getting stripped affects some characters more than others. For Vert's HDD form, her attire changes from "leaves little to the imagination" to "Who needs imagination?" In case all of this makes you uncomfortable, damage-immune clothing can be easily acquired.
Overall I think that the combat is fun, but also not very deep. This can be attributed to the lack of difficulty. While the monsters can hit pretty hard, in most circumstances, they'll never get the chance to attack. The ladies of Gamindustri are usually too powerful to be threatened by these pitiful creatures. Their moves have a lot of range, and monsters are easily stunned. When the ladies are transformed, whatever semblance of a sliver of threat that the monsters had slips away. If a quest is giving you trouble, it's probably because you're attempting something that is too high a level. Unfortunately, the level of difficulty never really achieves the right balance. As with the Neptunia RPGs, the challenge of the post-game is in dealing with monsters that have mountains of HP, and are capable of killing level 99 heroines in a couple hits. It might be best to approach this portion of the game with a "don't get hit" mindset. There are a couple accessories that trade survivalability for increased damage output. Dodging projectiles and other attacks is pretty satisfying, but for the most part, you'll be too busy crushing everything to notice.
Alongside the lack of challenge is the absence of conflict. Unlike the Console Industry, everyone in Gamindustri gets along like chocolate and pretzels. Didn't the first Neptunia RPG start off with the CPUs fighting to the death? I know they're all friends now, but shouldn't some attempts have been made to introduce a rivalry in NepU that goes beyond mild teasing? In the
and
games, you might cut through a lot of mindless zombies and kunoichi, but you also have to contend with rivals. These opponents have abilities that are on par with your own. Aside from an optional and underutilized bonus mode, there aren't any instances where the CPUs and Candidates fight each other.
This to me is the perfect example of a missed opportunity. I've played and enjoyed the three Re;Birth RPGs, and while they're all pretty easy, their storylines feel "earned". The characters in these games might have wacky personalities and form-fitting attire, but they also run into problems, argue, and even fight each other. Eventually they rise up to the challenge and defeat the villains that have troubled them throughout their adventure.
doesn't have any real adversaries, and the big bad boss is only fought twice, in two very lop-sided battles. There isn't even a lame excuse for the heroines to fight each other. Even if it was something petty like Noire accusing Blanc for stealing her quests, it would make for a more interesting story. Naturally, this would translate into a more dynamic game, especially if you had to adopt a second style of fighting, in order to deal with rivals. Perhaps these opponents could have monsters under their control, and... well you get the idea.
The PC port is fantastic. Support for a plethora of resolutions and 60 fps? This game's got them. If you're looking for crashes or major bugs, you'll have to look elsewhere. The load-times are also far better than in the Vita version. I suppose that's to be expected, but it's welcome all the same. While not specifically related to the port, I really appreciate that all of the skits are voiced in English. This wasn't the case for the Re;Birth games, and I found myself defaulting to the Japanese voices, because the silence was irritating.
In conclusion,
succeeds if you're looking for something different from the Neptunia universe. There are some hilarious moments, and the process of gaining levels and slaughtering monsters is dumb fun. However, this game just isn't designed to remain compelling for a long period of time. Other hack & slash titles, including those by Tamsoft, offer far more depth and content. While this game is just a spin-off, I sincerely believe that more could have been done with it. Even die-hard followers of the Nep-Nep faith should take caution before plunging into this amusing but shallow diversion.

When I began to play Dishonored I asked myself why I overlooked this game back in 2012. How could I have waited four years to add this game to my Steam library? I can describe Dishonored in one word: immersive. This game absorbed me into its gameplay from its prologue to the very end. Many games have a strict, linear path that you must follow to complete your objectives. Dishonored is totally nonlinear, as it allows you to play the way you want to play by choosing your playstyle. It is much like the Deus Ex and Bioshock series.
Dishonored is a game in which an Empress’ bodyguard is framed for her murder. You play Corvo Attano, the first bodyguard of the Empress born in a foreign country. The game is set in Dunwall, the capital of the island of Gristol. Dunwall is a port city that has profited from the sale of whale oil, but has been under siege by a rat plague. It feels like London, England in the late 19th or early 20th century during the industrial revolution. There is political corruption, gangs making power grabbing moves, and Corvo trying to vindicate himself and avenge the Empress’ death.
You can choose to play the game in High Chaos, meaning that you can kill all enemy guards like a mass murderer. You can also choose to play in Low Chaos, which means that you can stealthily move your way toward completing your objectives without killing anyone or being detected. Killing your way to the end of the game has consequences on how the game will progress and how the game will end. More kills mean more rats on the streets and more alert guards. It even affects how the Empress’ daughter draws on her pad in the pub designated as the home base for Corvo and his conspirators.
Each of the nine missions is unique and never boring. Some of the locales include a prison, a palace, a high-class brothel, and a flooded district filled with slums. There are many hidden alleys and secret areas that can be useful to avoid enemy guard detection or to find items like bone charms, coins, and runes. You can also hide to listen to conversations about what is going on and what plans are being made by some characters. Runes are the currency used to purchase supernatural powers, both active and passive.
Corvo’s arsenal includes traditional weapons and supernatural powers. Traditional weapons include a sword and a variety of ammo that you can use according to your playstyle. You can shoot bolts with your crossbow to kill if you decide to play in High Chaos. You can shoot sleep darts to render enemies unconscious if you want to go through the game without killing anyone. Supernatural powers are magical powers powered by your mana and can be upgraded to level 2 and include Blink, Dark Vision, Bend Time, etc. Blink is the most basic power that allows you to move in the blink of an eye to reach otherwise inaccessible areas that are above or below you. One very interesting power is Possession, a power that allows you to take possession of a rat and move through tunnels humans cannot move through. When upgraded to level 2 you can take possession of humans for a short period of time. I remember taking possession of a guard so that I can move to another room without being detected. Bone charms are perks scattered in each mission that enhances your abilities, including the ability to choke someone faster, the ability swing your sword faster, and the ability to increase your max health.
As you progress through the game, there are new factions introduced to the story. The new factions introduced can lead to numerous side quests. Like the main quests, you can choose to neutralize a target by lethal or nonlethal means. The more time I spent playing the game, the more I enjoyed it because the game truly encourages exploration and experimentation. The save system allows you to save anywhere, so you can create multiple save files to see which gameplay you prefer in certain scenarios.
The artistic design is awesome and contributes to the immersive nature of the game. The locales feel very real and aesthetically look like an oil painting in motion, whether you are on urban streets, industrial warehouses, fortresses or regal palaces.  The character models are excellent also.
The AI of the enemies is very good, as enemies will enter search mode when they see a dead or unconscious body. It is fun to use Corvo’s pickpocketing ability to steal pouches from unsuspecting guards while crouching behind them. Stealth can be enhanced by finding a blueprint that makes Corvo’s boots very silent while moving in stealth mode.
I played and completed Dishonored three times and I played like a mass murderer the first time. My second playthrough was pure stealth and managed not to kill one person and was not detected once. My third playthrough was Low Chaos, like my second playthrough, but I killed a few people. The purpose of my third playthrough was to play without using any supernatural powers except Blink. I think this game encourages players to experience the game multiple times to find alternative paths or to take on challenges they did not take on in a previous playthrough. The mouse/keyboard control scheme worked great for me as I climbed ledges, blinked from the ground to nearby rooftops or balconies, and neutralized unsuspecting targets from behind.
My only criticism of this game is Corvo Attano’s lack of personality. Much like Gordon Freeman of Half-Life, Corvo never says anything throughout the game. I wish Corvo could say something in the game to inject some personality into himself. Of course, it does not ruin the overall experience by any means.
My experience with Dishonored is one of the best I have ever had in my life. It is a genuine classic game that I strongly recommend to anyone, regardless of the video game genre they prefer. The vast number of ways to play each mission makes for high replay value. If you have not played this game, you are missing out on a classic.
My Score: 9.5/10

The Bureau: XCOM Declassified is a strange beast when placed alongside other entries in the XCOM series. Lurking somewhere in the shadow of 3rd person action shooters like Mass Effect, it forgoes most of the role play aspects and conversational choices for a combat oriented approach that, while it isn't bad, lies somewhere in the middle of the road.
Sliding into the suit, and later tactical sweater, of Agent Willian Carter you're well, for lack of a better word an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. Carter is a man that's driven by the ghosts of his past, he enters nearly every conversation with his chin down and his chest out ready to bark and bicker. Though early on it can be a bit grating the writers did an admirable job of following it through to the very end and while it can be seen coming it pays off fairly well. You're presented with a rather static and sadly shallow cast of side characters that the setting would have better served with a bit more fleshing out. Something akin to the loyalty missions of Mass Effect, or simply squadmates with any real personality of their own, would have greatly helped in pushing this above a by the numbers corridor to arena fighting affair.
Now, for the player sitting beyond the screen you'll need to maintain a strangle hold on your squadmates if you're playing beyond the squaddie difficulty as they'll make some of the dumbest tactical decisions you've ever seen. Leaning out from cover to fire on a Muton that's an arm's length away. Moving and firing after you've ordered them into a position for no clear reason, though in their defense they don't do this very often if you stay on them.
When it's all said and done the early game can be rough due to the units that are thrown at you but it isn't impossible, just frustrating. If you enjoy the world of XCOM, though make no mistake this is NOT your Dad's XCOM or the Fireaxis games you might be used to, there's enough here to keep you entertained for a breezy twelve to sixteen hours or so.
If you've caught this game on a deep, deep sale or managed to snag it for free then I would say you'll get your money's worth but only if you really enjoy XCOM as there are better third person action shooters out there in the current market.

A fun old school-style platform game with great artwork, soundtrack, and intriguing story. Definitely would recommend this to fans of games like Metroid or Castlevania: Symphony of the Night.
Probably the feature that makes Axiom Verge sand out the most is the sheer number of weapons to collect (nearly 30), and just how creativily hidden some of the secrets are. Most of these are optional and you can complete the game finding only a fraction of its' secrets, but it definitely adds replay value.
Axiom Verge isn't without flaws however - probably its biggest flaw is the combat itself. Many types of enemies and bosses are cheaply placed or have attacks which are almost impossible to avoid . Enemies will sometimes also block the doors to rooms, causing you to hit them as soon as you re-enter said room. Forcing the player to take damage is poor design and hopefully the combat will be ironed out in subsequent patches or the sequel. The bosses are also a slight letdown, as for the most part they don't react to the player's presense at all, and simply cycle through scripted attack patterns. The final boss is probably the worst example of this poor enemy design, as its attacks are more or less impossible to avoid, and the battle boils down to simply mashing the attack button while hoping your health bar holds out, rather than requiring any actual skill.
The other major flaw is that the game makes little effort in telling you where to go next. Other than occasional "hints" in dialogue you're left to figure it out on your own. For example, after defeating a certain boss, your only hint is to take an elevator up. But it turns out that to continue onward you actually have to find a special item (which was never even mentioned) and then go underground to access a completely unrelated area. I admire games which don't just spell it out for the player, but there's no way a player is going to be able to figure this out without using a guide other than through pure trial and error, which isn't fun.
In spite of these annoying issues the core game is good, the world is intriquing and ominous, and trying out all of the weapons is fun in of itself. So I can easily overlook them and give this game a recommend. Fixing the poor enemy behavior should be top priority as it's the single biggest flaw in an otherwise great game.

Boy, do I love this game.  What drew me in initially was the H.R. Giger style of the "cover art."  I adore dark alien imagery, and Axiom Verge is full of it.  The world the game takes place in just feels...wrong (in a good way); like a place that shouldn't ever exist in any part of the universe (a bit like the Far Realm in D&D).  This feeling is helped by the cyberpunk-style soundtrack constantly pulsing in the background as you explore the tendril-like labyrinthine environment.  I just have to say, the game nails atmosphere perfectly, and that's not even getting to gameplay and story.
The action feels tight here, and it's always satisfying to blast hostile aliens into pulpy goo.  There are also a ton of weapons to find and play with -- and believe me, there are *a lot* of them, each one with a different feel.  Some of them I'd say are objectively better than others, making the "lesser" weapons you find pretty much useless.  But that's a minor complaint.  There are also a ton of other optional items to find: everything from health powerups, damage powerups, range powerups , projectile size powerups and so-on.  That leads into one of coolest aspects of this game: just how much there is to explore.  I spent about 20 hours on my first playthrough and only managed to find like 70% of them total items in the game.  And believe me, I spent a long time exploring.  Although, to be fair, I'm pretty bad at metroidvania games.  I think the average time for a playthrough is 12-13 hours.  Still, for an indie game, that's pretty huge.  There are also some really fun mechanics introduced into the game, like being able to "glitch" enemies (which changes their appearance and how they behave).  It's always fun to figure out which enemies' "glitched" versions do what.  You also get the ability to teleport through walls with your badass sciency labcoat, which is just awesome in of itself.
The story is pretty darn great, too.  I won't spoil anything about it, but I was pretty impressed with how well-written it was.  My only issue with it was how it ended -- not necessarily what happened, but how it was executed.  The pacing sort of felt a little rushed in the final encounter, but that's a pretty small complaint and doesn't take away from the experience, in my opinion.
Overall, this is easily one of the best games I've played in the last few years and deserves your attention.  The asking price is a little steep for your average indie game, but this game is *well* above average.  :)
I'd give it a 9/10 overall.

Normally I'm not a fan of love stories. I often find them boring and in most cases predictable.
Still I tried some Otome games out, because I was curious. In the end I just got confirmed what I thought beforehand: Dating Sims, wether they're for girls or boys, are pubertal immature sex/romantical fantasies which feature stupid stories and stereotypical/sexist/sexualised characters.
I despise this genre of video games.
But then I heard of Hatoful Boyfriend and that it would be a parody on this genre. That got me interested and I bought it.
And I absolutely don't regret it!
You're going to a school, can choose a route with a specific character you like and fall in love with him. Due to that you can get different endings. If you want to see all endings you have to play it several times. The basics are absolutely the same as in other Dating Sims.
But the differences are awesome!
Let's begin with the protagonist: She's not a weak, whining little girl like in most other games, but actually likeable and funny- due to the game having a satirical undertone.
I just couldn't stand the protagonists which I've met in other games, they were extremely annoying.
I think it's definitely doing justice to it's reputation of being a parody.
It's poking fun at rpg games, at PETA, at generic anime situations and also at stupid gender roles.
Dialogues are on the one hand very funny and hilarious, but on the other much less stiff than in other games, but in certain occasions even very serious or sad.
While in other games characters are often superficially done, here the characters are lovely and have a well-thought-out background.
The story or rather stories (because of all the different characters) are well done!
What I like about them is, that they make much more sense than in other games and are even logically. In other Dating Sims they're just stupidly predictable. But the endings here surprised me.
Then there's also this special route, which you can unlock if you have a specific number of endings. This special story answers the questions, that many had already in their head when they heard of this game the first time: Why birds?
I loved this route and how every other piece of story the player gathered while doing the other routes came together to one and explained everything that's going on there.
By the way: If you want to have every ending then you have to play the game several times. There's this nice fast forward button with which you can skip everything that you already know. Otherwise it would've been a bit frustrating, but fortunately that's not the case.
Hatoful Boyfriend also showed that game developers shouldn't be afraid to do something with the fate of the protagonist...
To put it in a nutshell: I love this game. The characters, the story and the dialogues are awesome. And while it has a lot of funny moments, it has also some very serious, sad and deep moments.
Don't be fooled by their appearance, those pigeons are much more human than you think.
When one of my friends told me about this game, I just thought it sounded silly.  Now I have a Yuuya Sakazaki poster in my room.  Birds, though.

I bought it as a joke, but I got emotionally attached.
You've been warned!
Hatoful Boyfriend is the modern Shakespearean piece. Revel in its glory.

Fun, but get it on sale.
+ Deep customization: from designing your ship from choosing your crew to deciding on your skills and ability points.
+Wide selection of in-game items: Weapon and ship items/upgrades are not lacking.
+ It's a pirate game.
+/- Micromanagement makes an appearance. Example: it's not enough to buy fruit to keep your crew from getting scurvy, you also have to place the food out for your crew to eat, and you have to do this frequently. Then, you have to ensure the resulting bowel movements your crew takes all over the ship get cleaned up, else your morale will plummet.
- It lacks replayability/gets tedious. Encounters quickly start feeling samey once you become strong enough to fight top-tier ships, and islands are nothing more than small platforms that hold stores, or a group of hostile creatures. Your crew and your ship are deeply customizable, but the world around you feels very limited. A shame.
- It feels unfinished. You can take animals as pets, only some of which can actually level up. If your ship becomes unfit to sail (say, because ONE BLOCK cannot be reached by your crew) you are kept from sailing, and are not told what part of your ship is the problem.
-The AI is kinda bad. Example: you better hope the crewman you've assigned to fish knows how to swim, because he'll sit at the front edge of your ship and get blasted into the water while you engage an enemy vessel.
All in all a fun game to play for a few days, assuming you like pirate games (who doesn't?) and games with roguelike elements.

Despite how the graphics will look they are just fine.You will end up spending most of your time at a view that the ol school graphics will not be a bother.A great deal of simulation mechanics involved that all work well with one another making for a fun and challenging game. The A.I. has a various range of difficulty and can become your best friend or worst enemy.Loads of content in the game you will not feel short handed.The game has both singe player and mp hosted via peer to peer.Skirmish mode gives you a  variation of options,from playing solo no A.I. opponents,to having A.I. opponents,to having win conditions.
There is a tutorial but you can skip it and just start the campaign because it progresses as a tutorial.Each mission you work for a different race and learn about how that race acts.The campaign is a lot of fun and I suggest playing it.There websites that provide custom campaign missions.If you like sim games,city building,strategy,trading,warring, check this game out.
This game has quite a lot going for it.You have 10 different races in the game that serve as customers,clients, and employees. They come with their own likes and dislikes and even have abilities separate from one another.Each race works a specific job in the game so remember this will be crucial if you want to have a fully functioning station. There are also worker droids which serve as maintenance and security patrol and are always needed. Outside of the 10 races and two types of droids there will be events that pop up in which can effect the outcome of how well or not you are doing.Solar flares,meteor strikes,plagues,etc a good host of  events can occur. The events come in flavors that are helpful and harmful and add spice to the challenge of the game.
There are three floors for every section of the space station. Floor 1 is the lowest and acts as the industrial section.Here you build your port.These allow passengers to board your controlled area of the station.Other items such as factories,sickbay,cargo holds,labs,recycle center,prison,security control center,etc are built here.
is the commercial services section.Motels,Hotels,Inns,stores,bars,etc get built here and will be where the build of your money unless you decide to focus on trade.
is the bio dome which acts as you would expect.You can grow vegetation here which once mature enough can be harvested and the products traded for energy or used to create items  or supply your commercial shops and services.
The Currency in the game is energy.You produce energy by building energy collectors(like a power plant),power boosters,medic bays,sleeping champers,stores,hotels,etc. When patrons go to shops,hotels and such they pay you in energy while at the same time the facilities use energy in order to run so be aware of any facility that is costing you more power to run than it is making. Luckily thanks to the detail in the game, you can power down the facilites if you desire or even deconstruct the whole thing and sell or store the building units used to build it.
Expanding your control of different sections of the station can work in two ways,you buy the sections with energy or you hack the enemy control neighboring section.Combat occurs of someone (you or the A.I.) is under/starting attack.Once you have your security staff and just about anyone else that can help to defend/attack they will head immediately to the way point you set.If an enemy is in your ranks and attacks someone in range of a employee capable of attacking,that employee will attack.Outside of the security staff & drones you can build turrents which are quite useful but require energy to fire and function so be careful using them.
Mechanic wise is where I love the game the most.Everything has needs in order for you to gain access to them or use them properly.To get trade you need a com and a port otherwise no ship can dock in.In order to have some commercial services running you need the races that work in them.To get those races to come after time has passed you need to make sure their most wanted items are on your station or that the conditions they prefer exist. These are just examples but its how the whole game works.Everything gets used,has a need,serves a purpose.If you choose to specialize in  different economic areas they come with their own negative/positive aspect keeping everything balanced and challenging.
There is a campaign in the game that plays with you being hired by each race that is in the game to build the type of station they like to visit.In total there are 10 campaign missions 1 for each race.Their difficulty increases sometime throwing you tol the wolves.From my experience each mission was harder than the last.This serves to teach you how different portions of the game work as well as teach you about the race you are working for and what they like/dislike.Since you will need to know this about the races each mission gives you more of an edge as you carry over what you learned but still throws new things at you.

The poster-boy for failure to launch. The trailers and previews were dotted with lies, talking about a "seamless experience" and how you would want to fight with your faction to "control" parts of the ARK. Consistently, they implied it would be an MMOFPS-style game, where you'd move between zones, then be pulled into multiplayer encounters.
What we got was a bog-standard, class-based, objective-focused FPS with a half-baked parkour system, decent character customization, janky controls and extremely spotty hit detection/lag compensation. Regularly you will die without knowing why, or pound a clip into an opponent only to be killed by a single shot in reprisal.
As others have said, this game is garbage. Ignoring the fact that the servers are likely dead as hell by now, it should be a stern reminder (and is to me,) to never preorder without all the facts. I wish that the store rating system had existed back when Brink came out--I could've helped save a lot of people 60$.
I still wear the TF2 hat they gave me for preordering as a reminder to be vigiliant.

Let's consider a couple of the very best zombie/b-movies ever made. Army of Darkness (hell, the whole evil dead trilogy) and Braindead. Besides being awesome, what do they have in common? A badass mowing through zombies with a powertool, be it a chainsaw or a lawnmower. Chainsaw Warrior distills this to its core experience, throw in a bunch more 80s cliche and lets rip. You want a chainsaw to match your mood? Feel magnificent with the master-crafted 'saw or guts'n'gore manly with the diesel noise machine. Maybe you want to get your 'Murica on with a shotgun or go full "I watched a video on how to build this on the Youtubes" crazy with a flamethrower? This game's got you covered. Just maybe you want to go old school knife a zombie. Can't be bothered to walk over there? Throw it at that stumbling fool.
Now just in case you're thinking the game will leave you feeling like a over-powered, zombie slaying, 80's thowback, macho, deity, think again. Lords of the Night is difficult enough to actually feel rewarding when you eventually finish a run through and unlock some of those sweet new items. If you're really looking for a challenge, there's the classic board game mode which lumps you with random stats, random items and the faint impression of a dev laughing at you as you go forth into the jungle with every chainsaw in the game and a hand-to-hand rating of -2 (slight exaggeration of the desperation you will inevitably feel). Want a quick restart button so you can keep trying to get good stats and items? Too bad, you asked for this. Now go try and punch some zombie to death and hope the air drops are kind.
While Chainsaw Warrior gets a hour to save the world, you'll only need 15 minutes or so to blast out a play through. Just quick enough for a sneaky game on the crapper at a reasonably relaxed work place.

I had a few extra dollars in my steam wallet and decided to pick this game up because I've always enjoyed card games, and this one looked interesting enough. I was satisfied with my gameplay experience.
If you like dice-based (D6) card games and the Aztec theme, then you will enjoy this game.
The aesthetics are nice and simple - the detail in each card is well done. There are visual effects whenever you do an attack/use an item, but most of the time you will just be looking at and reading the cards on a static background. The music and sounds are decent, however, I quickly muted the music in favor of my own. The story involves you racing against time (nightfall) to stop The Darkness from destroying the world.
Controls are entirely mouse-based and simple. There is an optional tutorial that very quickly shows you everything you need to know, however, improving your playthroughs will require you to die a lot and learn through trial-and-error. The learning curve is mostly minimal depending on your knowledge of D6-style gameplay, and the most difficult element of the game is probably understanding how to best optimize your loadouts for each run (for example, if you roll a character that is weaker in hand-to-hand (hth) combat, how do you compensate for this?).
Gameplay consists of you drawing cards until you encounter the area boss (this can occur before all the cards in the deck have been revealed). Defeating the boss will allow you to progress to the next area, until you reach the last boss in the third area. After each action you take, a "round" occurs, decreasing the time on the clock. Once darkness falls, your character will take a hit to his hth stat. If you reach 0 on the clock, The Darkness will automatically win. As you draw cards, you will most likely encounter an array of enemies, however, you can also run into different types of traps, airdrops (allow you to restock/change equipment), temples (protected by a powerful guardian and will give you a blessing buff if you defeat it), or events.
Before you begin, you will randomly generate (roll) a chainsaw warrior to play as. This makes each playthrough a bit different, as you will have different values in your Wounds (hit points), Venom Resistance, Radiation Resistance, Range, Reflex (ability to dodge), and Hth stats. Enemies do different types of damage, and falling to 0 in wounds, venom, or radiation will result in your death. Your character will roll a special perk, which may be something like decreasing each area deck by 5 cards, increased reflexes, etc. You may also select your starting equipment, and you will usually start with 3 to 8 equipment points (this seems to be offset by high or low starting stats). You can choose from different melee, ranged, and heavy weapons to help you survive the Aztec jungle. There are also a number of devices (ex: medpack, extra ammo clip, etc) you can take with you. Finally, different armors can help you fend off enemy attacks. If you select the "Classic" difficulty, all equipment will be replaced with a ?, only to be revealed once you start your run (truly making everything random-based).
Your starting equipment selection is a critical part to your playthrough because you can end up making your run easier or much more difficult depending on your choices. For example, if I roll a character that is a bit weaker in the hth stat, I may decide to grab a Stun Nux, which adds 4 to my hth stat whenever I am fighting a living opponent (ex: cultists). Taking advantage of a higher range stat is highly recommended because many of the enemies you will fight will prefer hth combat.
When you draw an enemy card, they may have a special effect (ex: deal x type of damage immediately or ambush: go immediately into close-ranged combat) and/or do an extra type of damage (venom) on top of normal wound damage. Different enemies will prefer either hth or ranged combat, and using the opposite tactic on them will give them a debuff of some kind. For example, many of the initial zombies you will encounter are hth fighters, so using a ranged weapon will almost always hit them without the need for a dice roll (unless they have a really high reflex stat). Some zombies will counter this tactic by having an ambush ability, which will allow them to immediately put you into close-range (there is a device that will negate the ambush ability). In close-range, you can use melee weapons or try to evade your opponent. Every action in combat involves dice rolls, and succeeding in an evasion will result in no damage taken (failing will still cause you to evade, but you will take some damage) and put you back in ranged-weapon distance.
During combat, your enemy (multi-enemy battles are still fought one-at-a-time) will roll two die (D6), adding this value to their hth or range stat depending on the level of engagement (ex: you are using a melee weapon against a melee opponent). Next, you will roll two die, adding this value to the appropriate stat (in this case, your melee stat). If you have a higher value than your opponent, you will instantly kill them unless they have armor, in which case you will do 1 damage to armor (until it goes down to 0 or 1 - at 1 armor weapons like chainsaws can pierce through). There are weapons that allow you to ignore x armor. If your opponent's attack value is higher than yours, then you will take damage depending on the type of your opponent (either wounds, or both wounds and venom). Armor will allow you to negate some types of damage if you roll a 5 or 6 during an armor check. You also have the option to try to escape, however, you have to roll a 6, otherwise you will take 1 wound damage.
In a situation where you are using a ranged weapon against a melee opponent, the enemy will add their roll value to their reflex stat instead of their attack stat (since they cannot attack you at range). If they beat your roll, you will miss and they will close the distance. Against enemies with significantly lower reflex stats, you will automatically hit with your ranged attack because they are too slow.
Some of the tougher opponents can only die to special weapons, so conserving your laser ammo is critical to survival and progression. Your equipment can become stolen or even broken, which can be fatal most of the time. Multiple playthroughs will help you refine your preferred playstyle.
Overall, the game is very nice and simple - a good filler game if you want to spend a short amount of time playing something. I always try not to mention price in my reviews if I think it is unnecessary, however, I will say that I purchased this game on sale for $3.24 CAD, and I think that is a much fairer value than it's original price of $6.49. I suggest you wait until it is on sale, unless you are dying to play it.
For people that enjoy D6 card games, you should definitely give Chainsaw Warrior a try.
Recommend!

In 1987 the world nearly ended. Nearly. In the 11th hour one man, one hero rose to face Darkness and banished it from this world, saving us all.
But evil will always find ways into the hearts of men. Now, eighteen years later, deep in the Mexican jungle, the followers of a forgotten God have found a new ally, and an old enemy we had thought defeated returns to finish what they had started eighteen years ago.
Darkness has returned and only one man can stop it from destroying the world.
It had been a suicide mission then. Noone thought he could succeed, much less survive. Then, against all odds he prevailed. Can a million to once chance come true... twice?
In a  desperate race against time, cutting his way through the jungle, hordes of zombies and a crazed apocalyptic cult, the Chainsaw Warrior has only 1 Hour to reach and banish Darkness or all will be lost.
New dangers lurk among the trees and in the swamps. The ancient guardians of the aztec ruins have awakened. But with great challenges come great rewards and the Chainsaw Warrior will need all the help he can get if he is to save us... again.
Prepared to make the ultimate sacrifice. Armed with his trusty chainsaw. He is ready to once more be the hero the world needs.
Are you?
Game Facts:
Like the original Chainsaw Warrior, Chainsaw Warrior: Lords of the Night is a game of turning cards and rolling dice. Each card you turn, each action you take will thake 30 seconds and you only have 1 Hour before the world ends.
You move through the jungle by turning cards and encountering enemies or traps and just sometimes finding something to help you on your mission. What equipment will you take with you? What risks will you take? And yes, how lucky will you get? These all will determine your success or defeat.
Pros:
+The Chainsaw Warrior games manage, with simple mechanics, to capture the pressure of time, the sence of emergency, that mad, desperate dash. You frantically turn cards willing that clock to stop ticking, the doom counter to stop its count.
+ Three difficulty settings affecting stats, equipment points and whether you get to see the equipment you pick or are forced to select blindly
+ Equipment allows for various tactics to reach the end. Even though in the end it comes down to one thing: Destroy Darkness or die trying.
+ Classic mode truly is challenging
Cons:
- Like any game based on dice, luck is very important.
Changes from old game:
* Ranged combat has been completly rebuild, making ranged weapons far more useful. You can now manouvre from melee to ranged distance and put that assault rifle to good use.
* Instead of two decks there now are three: Jungle - Ruined City - Temple
* Old Aztec temples can be found and explored to recieve special blessings - but beware, they are guarded.
* The Meat Machine and Slime have company: more unique enemies have been added and act as mini bosses at the end of the first two decks.
* Darkness is spreading as Shades. These offshoots of Darkness may be encountered sepparately and defeating them will weaken Darkness, making that final battle easier.
* New equipment to match the new setting, including new versions for your trusty chainsaw. Some of this equipment has to be unlocked through playing the game.
Verdict:
The clock is ticking. While you were reading, Darkness has come this much closer to killing us all. Go, Save the world.

Rating - 57/100
This "game" is nothing if not unique. Made by the same team that did To the Moon (TTM), A Bird Story is more of a mildly-interactive experimental pixel art piece than an actual game. There's very little input needed from the player, absolutely no dialog at all, and not much explanation for what's really going on.
It's worth seeing it for yourself, as it is an endearing little adventure about a kid and a bird, but it's extremely short (about 1 hour), it moves rather slowly, and it feels pretty arbitrary when the game wants your input and when it doesn't. Many times, you'll be watching a little scene play out, then you'll hit a few buttons, and it's back to the scene. It felt somewhat like a little bar popping up, saying "are you still paying attention?"
I'm not sure if TTM is the same way or not (I haven't played it YET), but on the surface this game felt cutesy, while lurking beneath was a deep, strong current of melancholy. There's charming music throughout the various scenes, but something felt unsettling. Maybe it's because other than the bird, the kid feels as if he's barely attached to the world at all. Other characters and animals appear as specters that he can walk right through, a few impossible things transpire that are straight out of a bedtime story book, and various parts of the world start to blend in with each other. It almost feels as if there's a deeper meaning, like the whole thing is a metaphor for illness, or the kid is really an old man reliving beloved memories as his loved ones watch him slip away, or something.
It's not overtly a sad story, though, and there are some smile-worthy moments (even if the Yakety Sax section is a little painful), but the whole thing is over just a little too quickly, and with a bit too little weight on some of the emotional moments. I wish I could go into more detail without giving major spoilers, but there were a few sections that seemed to say something big was happening, and then they simply end, and it's on to the next thing.
I enjoyed my time here, but only just. It's extremely short, the game seems to not really need you to play it, and it feels like there's more to the story that simply went over my head. On the plus side, it's a charming story at surface-level, the music is fantastic (and written by the writer/director!), and the pixel art is well-enough-done.
I don't remember how much I paid for this game, but it couldn't have been more than a couple dollars. If it'd been $10 or something, I'd be a little upset, but I enjoyed my time here, and if you're able to immerse yourself in a charming, somewhat-shallow little adventure story, you might too.
One final thing, and it disgusts me that I even need to say it: If you buy this and end up liking it, please don't get a Steam refund after finishing. It's short enough that you can, but please don't.

To be clear I bought this game many many years ago and I've played it a LOT longer than my listed time. Just happens I lost my original disk registration key and had to rebuy. So I -do- know what I'm talking about on this.
This is kind of a mix of a "The Sims" title and a potluck of many other game genres. There's combat, there's construction, there's 'farming' of a sort, trading, healthcare, and well.. You run a space station 'ring', or waystation as the game calls them. All in all it's often head and shoulders above anything that recent science fiction, future space life sims have given us in the recent year or two. And I'm not just talking about blowing Moonbase Alpha outta the water, that could be done by a wet dish towel and a piece of cheese. (Don't try to imagine how that'd work, any method you think of would be inestimably better than Moonbase Alpha)
At seven dollars, currently this game is a bloody steal, and can provide hundreds of hours of engaging, even if a tiny bit repetitive once you figure out what you think are the 'best' arrangements of rooms and facilities on the various station decks. It has a curious sense of humor, kind of charming really, and never misses an opportunity to poke fun at various sci-fi references. If you want to know what I mean, look up "Startopia Intro" to find the original game introductory video, and that'll show you exactly what sort of strange humor you might be dipping into. Personally I love this game to bits, and I really think everybody in my friends list who has even a glancing interest in science fiction or simulation games should pick it up. Heck, everybody who ISN'T in my friends list should pick it up too, Mucky Foot was an excellent development studio, and should never have flatlined like it did. Just the times they were in, I guess?
TL;DR - Buy this game now or I'll have a skrasher feast on your lower abdominal organs. Seriously, don't mess with the 20 foot tall murder-beetle. BUY IT.

This is a hugely enjoyable game despite its age. Anyone who's ever played Bullfrog games will be familiar with the design influences the Dev's carried over from their previous titles blending elements of Theme Hospital and Dungeon Keeper while evolving it into its own retro-future setting.
The game has a sandbox mode, multiplayer via ipx or tcp/ip (with AI settings allowing pvp or compstomp co-op or ffa.) SP campaign mode which is more a series of individual missions.
Single player is well thought out with each mission requiring a different style of play and focus in order to complete and while not difficult they are engaging and challanging. Unlike many games of this ilk the different scenarios keep the player from grinding out the optimal stratagy without feeling either too handicapped or still on training wheels.
There is a mission editor and although the MuckyFoot may have fallen by the wayside there are still plenty of missions still to be downloaded without to much effort with a little searching on the internet.
The game setting is kept small in scope, space management being a resource unto itself and there are many novel and characterful ideas intermingled with the tried and tested;  blue print room, object placement, research, resources and peeps each with their own preferences and specific role, style of strategic managament.
The player needs to keep an eye on three different tiers or decks developing them all simultaneously which while initially daunting is actually fairly intuitive after a game or two.
Graphics while dated hold up well enough, nice animations and fully 3d objects and sprites and full camera control with extra sounds and animations when zoomed in close or using the follow camera.
I use AMD HD7850, win 7 64bit, 8gb ram, i7-3770k with corsair mouse and razor keyboard. On my rig the game runs smooth and i've yet to experience any game stopping bugs. Full admin rights but no compatability specific settings for the game itself. My friend uses nvidia 560ti, vista 32bit, 4gb ram, quad core intel, logitech mouse, again full admin rights and our multiplayer has been solid.
The black flicker refresh experienced can be solved by selecting the graphic card by model in options rather than using auto, this has to be done every game start-up but only takes a moment before several hours of gaming.
The issue with space-slugs dieing in their chambers isn't apparent (they enter and leave without any issues in all the games i've played)
Summary - engaging, characterfull, fun!

Dishonored was one of those games that you've heard about but never get around to. I've heard great things about it, and when it went on sale recently, I decided that I should at least try it out. I'm glad to say that it was well worth it.
As a basic summary, this game revolves around Corvo, the bodyguard of the Empress who was set up to make it look like he killed her. Set in an industrialized city called Dunwall, a couple of militant characters make his arrest, sending Corvo to jail after some time. A group called the Loyalists help you escape, and ask you to help them save Emily, daughter to the Empress. The story evolves from there, depending on how you execute each mission, giving you a either a grade of high or low chaos. This will affect the story and what happens to the players within it.
As soon as you boot up the game, you can tell the game is a little dated, but still great. I should probably preface that my computer is rather old and can't take much, but the game runs smooth enough with no screen tearing or graphical difficulties. First impressions is that this game was well made, and accomidates the power well. There are also plenty of options for the player, like if they want to play with a minimal hud for a more immersive experience, and most of which can be adjusted on the fly. Speaking of adjusted, I must praise the musical score for this game; absolutely fits the setting, mood, and tone of the story as it plays out.
My first go around was the classic stealth and full murder-spree on every area. I found the plot to be simple yet effective, and though it may not be the most complex, it did it's job well. The character arks feel very fleshed out, and the small sidequests never really deter from the main story. What this game really hits a homerun on is the setting; it feels like there's history to the world, history that I would actually read more on, and I could with the in game books they provide, scattered across the plague ridden world. They certainly hold the niche for best first person steampunk stealth game.
The acting is rather well done as well; characters like Emily and Grandma Rags, with the few lines they had, really showcase their innocence and craziness (respectively). Overall, the characters are believable and well done; however my favorite part about them is the perfect ragdoll effect and throwing bodies. I'd consider buying a body throwing simulator if you could throw them like you could in Dishonored.
Really my only complaints against this game is the mana using abilities are deceptively costly, and how short the game is. However, Dishonored is so good replaying it is, for a casual player like me, is just as enjoyable as the first go around. I guess a complaint could be made that the combat is rather sophisticated for a stealth game; I never once fired my pistol or dueled someone after the first mission during my first playthrough. How that could be a complaint bewilders me, as it feels almost second nature for the bodyguard of the Empress of the kingdom. I recommended this game to all my friends, and I recommend this game to you.

I was pleasantly suprised as they had polished and added to the first game quite nicley. Now the clock although a factor is not so harsh. You also get to fight two randomised mini bosses between the three stages, The inventory and skills are also more intuitive.
The only gripe that I still have is that 'The Darkness' can only be destroyed with two items The Laser Lance and an Implosion (suicide) vest. Sometimes you will end up reaching him without the a good enough marskman skill to hit him or sometimes without the Laser Lance itself. Most of the time I can only kill him with a lucky shot, which doesn't have great odds either. There are a few security measures to help with this, like the teleporter. Also this time around you can destroy a few of his minions to make him slighlty weaker. However, I still think this can be a very irritating game mechanic in an otherwise fun game. It would have been nice if they'd have thrown in a few more weaknesses this time around.

I presume you've played the original digital edition of Chainsaw Warrior. If you did not, let's say it's faitful digital recreation of very interesting postapocalyptic single player game which lets you pretend you're a mixture between Duke Nukem, Ash Williams and Snake Plissken.
Chainsaw Warrior: Lords of The Night came as a surprise. The original (digital) game is a great one, but it was done by indie studio Auroch Digital and you know how things go... sometimes you don't really get enough dough to work on a sequel.
Well, fortunately for all of us, not in case of Auroch Digital and Chainsaw Warrior. LoTN sequel is capitalizing on the first one and it's doing it in such a style, it's unbeliveable.
From the trashy, John Carpenterish ruins we've moved south to Mexican Jungle, where the blades of our chainsaw will meet up with the flesh of Aztec zombies aaaaand... Slime (♥♥♥♥ YOU! ♥♥♥♥ YOU!!!), crocodiles, zombie crocodiles, zombie monkeys, moon cultists, armored cultists and so on. Enemies are many and different and you better read what those cards say or you're gonna get yourself in trouble.
Apart from that we now have to work our way through three decks. I've realized it's usually taking me around 20 minutes to get through the game... if I'm lucky.
There's a ton of new items which really makes this sequel a perfect gagball for all those people who've complained about game being way too random. Of course, the rule design of this new title stayed as close as possible to the original one (read: bad dice rolling, you're going underground), but new items and ways you can use them will bring extra strategy and options in your games.
Apart from this, now you'll have an ability to visit temples, kill monstrous enemies along the way and receive godly blessings which will help you on your way to destroy The Darkness. And yeah... punch crocodiles. Kill 'em using only your fists.
To sum it up, Chainsaw Warrior: Lords of The Night is all-better, all-improved, all-more-fun version of the original. If you didn't pick the original, pick this one up. If you did, pick this one up. In any case, you can't really miss. And don't wait for no discounts - this indie dev deserves ALL OF YOUR MONEY. Go, through money at the screen NOW!
