I must admit, I was both surprised and just a teeny, weeny bit excited to hear that they were sequelizing the Chainsaw Warrior board game adaptation from not-so-long-ago.  In all fairness, I'm writing this review with very little play-time up my sleeve, but on the whole I have to confess that the aforementioned excitement has dulled ever-so-slightly into mild disappointment.  Let's see now...
My first hesitation is the setting.  While I completely applaud the decision to not just set this in a post-apocalyptic New York - AGAIN - choosing to situate the continued adventures of our titular hero in an Aztec-ian jungle suggests, to me at least, that we're slowly moving towards more Serious Sam-styled territory (though all of these characters ultimately owe their lineage to Ash of "Evil Dead" fame, suffice it to say).  Now, whether this is a good or bad thing is up to the individual, but personally I miss the urban decay / Escape From New York aesthetics...but that's just me.  If you harbour a particular hard-on for the Aztecs, you'll obviously be right at home here.
Oh, and the music has changed accordingly, and while there's basically nothing wrong with the more jungle-y flavours on offer here - well, except perhaps for the fact that it's all a tad too laid-back and "muzak"-y to generate much tension or momentum - on the whole, I must say that I miss the super-synthy goodness of the earlier game's soundtrack.  (Oh, and there's also a completely needless and irritating "punch" noise every time you enter melee combat, even if you choose to use the chainsaw or what-have-you; other than this, though, the sound effects are perfectly dandy.)  Now onto the mechanics...
My earliest impressions of the game are that it is SLOWER than the first Chainsaw Warrior; and with that, arguably a tiny bit more cumbersome.  The 2013 game was VERY fast-paced, with cards turning over at lightning speed and enemies defeated just as quickly.  This time 'round we have ARMOURED enemies, who effectively take "damage" and gradually weaken rather than simply being defeated outright.  There are also some more "tactical" combat situations, such as a giant statue guardian who you can either attack directly, or firstly choose to target the stone hands of to reduce its ability to defend itself.  The overall effect of all of this is that combats seem to take longer, and therein so does the game.  Again...personal preference.  But for better or for worse, that "jump-in-jump-out" / "I'll just play one more quick round" quality of the original game seems to have been lost somewhere in the shuffle.
Things are also arguably slowed down (read: overcomplicated) by the fact that the devs have opted to make this a tad more of a full-blown "video game" this time around; and thereby less of a "board game adaptation".  Simply put, there are less cards to look at (equipment is just a list this time 'round), and the cards which ARE portrayed are visually less varied in content (one type of zombie crops up repeatedly, as opposed to the original, in which we had a healthy rogue's gallery of the nasties in question).  On a purely personal note, I also simply don't "like" the artwork as much (a very important factor in ALL games, be they video / board / card / whatever).
There are also BOSS FIGHTS - some optional and some unavoidable in nature - which again, slow the pace for a moment whilst you♥♥♥♥♥♥yourself wondering whether or not to waste precious Laser Lance ammunition on something other than Darkness himself.  And I'm also pretty sure that all the new-'n'-improved "card-decimation" animations (chainsaws cutting through enemies, cards exploding, etc) take longer to resolve than the more modest equivalents from the first game...though this may just be a figment of my imagination (but even then, still contributes to my overall argument of things generally "seeming" more sluggish).
So the overall feeling of hurtling-towards-the-inevitable-final-confrontation has been hampered somewhat in favour of more conventional video game dynamics, and that oh-so-modern notion of the "side-quest" (in the form of temples and the aforementioned optional boss fights); again, and I can't stress this enough, PERSONAL ♥♥♥♥ING PREFERENCE.
I don't know...perhaps I'll warm to this one more in time, but I think I found the charm of the 2013 game to lie predominantly in the speedy "casual"-ness of its nature, and that can't quite be said this time around.  And I'm sorry, but I really just don't dig the jungle as much (hell, I'm a bit of a John Carpenter fan, as you may have guessed from my non de plume).  Having said all this, it's still a good game, especially at that price, and anyone who appreciates board / card game adaptations is liable to get at least SOME jollies out of it.  I dunno, maybe they should have set it in post-apocalyptic London, and had zombies in bobby hats?  Full points for trying something truly different, I suppose...
Verdict: 7/10.
(PS There is one genuine improvement over the original game:  Thanks to "air drops", you no longer have to back-track all the way to the START to replace a lost or broken Laser Lance...without a doubt, the single most annoying feature of the earlier game.  So full kudos for THAT one!)

Although I did enjoy the original
, I did find myself burning out quite quickly on its randomness - there were some choices to be made, but you more or less were at the mercy of the dice.
I'm glad to say Lords Of The Night improves a lot on this. Don't fear, you'll still die multiple deaths because of crappy dice rolls, but you do have a lot more tactical choices to make, both in weapons and equipment. Airdrops of new equipment during the game, also help give back a sense of agency.
Then there is the addition of 'blessings', basically an active or passive power that can help you during your gruelling trek through the jungle (think along the lines of "heal 3 points", or "immunity from radiation damage"). New blessings can be acquired by entering a temple and killing a high powered monster (the game's equivalent of a very basic side quest).
The pulpy setup of the original game is still in full effect, and I would say that the new setting adds a lot of flavour to the overall John Carpenterness of it all.
Personally, I'd recommend this game over the original
(although at these prices, why force yourself to choose).

Chainsaw Warrior: Lords of the Night is a lot like the origional Chainsaw Warrior game made by the same Developer. Lords of the Night gives you a bunch of new things to fight from jungle critters to Armor wearing Moon Cultist. They also added a lot of new weapons and items, some of which you need to unlock to use.  The UI has been imporved and the over all game feels much faster than the origional.
You start the game on one of three difficulty levels. Normal and Hard which both give you a good chance of starting off with some decent stats, and you get to choose what items you take with you at the start. Then there is Classic Mode which plays like the origional board game and puts you at the mercy of the RNG gods with no boost to your stats and random starting items.
As you progress through the game you will get Air Drops that will contain a collection of weapons and items for you to choose from, you have 3 item points for each drop and get to spend them how you want.  You can also replace your lost Laser Lance from the Air Drops, so there is no need to backtrack to the start of the game to replace it.
My only complaint of the game so far is the lack of a save system, but that is a feature they will be adding soon.
If you enjoyed the origional Chainsaw Warrior game then you likley will find enough new content in Chainsaw Warrior: Lords of the Night to make it worth your time.

Did you enjoy Metroid games as a kid? I definitely did, and I LOVE Axiom Verge. Hell, even if you've never experienced a Metroid game (which, personally, I'd remedy some time in the near future), this game may yet be up your alley. This game contains colorful 16-bit visuals with the occasional stylish twist, catchy techno beats that I listen to even when I'm not playing the game, over a hundred collectibles hidden throughout nine worlds, over twenty unique weapons with special properties, a very interesting mechanic where you can "glitch" enemies to completely change how they behave (sometimes even turning them into your allies!), a drill to pierce the heavens with, the ability to warp through walls, a grappling hook (à la Super Metroid), and a cute little remote controlled drone that looks like a headcrab!
For $20, this game is a steal; at the time of this review's creation, I spent 19.2 hours in Axiom Verge, and I JUST NOW completed it for the first time. Also, there's a speedrun mode for those who are interested in feeling rewarded for knowing the game like the backs of their hands. If you wish to experience, or relive, gaming's glory days - when everything was shrouded in mystery and you felt like you discovered something awesome each time you unearthed a new upgrade or weapon - then PLAY this damn game! For an optimal experience, I suggest that you do not refer to a walkthrough unless absolutely necessary. And no, there is no fast travel, there are no objective arrows, and you won't be submitted to torturous tutorial dialogue.

The metroidvania genre is mostly a sea of mediocre games trying to emulate a handful of legendary classics.  Axiom Verge is not a new genre touchstone the way, say, La Mulana was.  But it's certainly miles ahead of the rest of the pretenders.
Axiom Verge has unusual items in its library of powerups that do well to reintroduce an element of surprise for people who've played too many of these and know what to look for.  The game also rewards exploration with inventive, purely optional weapons, which is a great improvement over a hundred missile expansions.  Unfortunately all weapons do roughly the same amount of damage, even ones that are awkward to aim, so many are not as good as the default gun.
Metroid was inspired by Alien, and Alien was inspired by H.R. Giger.  Axiom Verge looks back to Giger's works and often feels even more Metroidy than Metroid itself.  It's a great decision, and the game looks gorgeous.
The game doesn't do anything exciting to enable sequence breaking - some breaks are possible, but it doesn't do anything as bold as Super Metroid's walljump or Bunny Must Die's parrying.  This, and fairly stiff, accelerationless movement controls, probably curtail any hope of it becoming a great game for speedrunning.

Recommendation - Pick up on a sale if you're into lightweight interactive stories
Rating - 57/100
This "game" is nothing if not unique. Made by the same team that did To the Moon (TTM), A Bird Story is more of a mildly-interactive experimental pixel art piece than an actual game. There's very little input needed from the player, absolutely no dialog at all, and not much explanation for what's really going on.
It's worth seeing it for yourself, as it is an endearing little adventure about a kid and a bird, but it's extremely short (about 1 hour), it moves rather slowly, and it feels pretty arbitrary when the game wants your input and when it doesn't. Many times, you'll be watching a little scene play out, then you'll hit a few buttons, and it's back to the scene. It felt somewhat like a little bar popping up, saying "are you still paying attention?"
I'm not sure if TTM is the same way or not (I haven't played it YET), but on the surface this game felt cutesy, while lurking beneath was a deep, strong current of melancholy. There's charming music throughout the various scenes, but something felt unsettling. Maybe it's because other than the bird, the kid feels as if he's barely attached to the world at all. Other characters and animals appear as specters that he can walk right through, a few impossible things transpire that are straight out of a bedtime story book, and various parts of the world start to blend in with each other. It almost feels as if there's a deeper meaning, like the whole thing is a metaphor for illness, or the kid is really an old man reliving beloved memories as his loved ones watch him slip away, or something.
It's not overtly a sad story, though, and there are some smile-worthy moments (even if the Yakety Sax section is a little painful), but the whole thing is over just a little too quickly, and with a bit too little weight on some of the emotional moments. I wish I could go into more detail without giving major spoilers, but there were a few sections that seemed to say something big was happening, and then they simply end, and it's on to the next thing.
I enjoyed my time here, but only just. It's extremely short, the game seems to not really need you to play it, and it feels like there's more to the story that simply went over my head. On the plus side, it's a charming story at surface-level, the music is fantastic (and written by the writer/director!), and the pixel art is well-enough-done.
I don't remember how much I paid for this game, but it couldn't have been more than a couple dollars. If it'd been $10 or something, I'd be a little upset, but I enjoyed my time here, and if you're able to immerse yourself in a charming, somewhat-shallow little adventure story, you might too.
One final thing, and it disgusts me that I even need to say it: If you buy this and end up liking it, please don't get a Steam refund after finishing. It's short enough that you can, but please don't.

I admit that this game is entertaining for a time, but as your playtime adds up, the games flaws become ever apparent. In summary, this game feels very unfinished and its developer has labeled it as complete feature wise. The novelty of building your own ship and the comedy of the little crewmembers wears out quickly because of the frustratingness of the gameplay. Yes, I know this is a roguelike, but your ability to progress through this game is not so much a matter of skill as a mater of mind numbing patience and frustration. As you venture farther from the start you realize that encounters scale so sharply that you need to spend countless hours playing boring simple battles over and over, exactly replicating the same actions of attacking, moving your pirates into the enemy ship and back out, then when the time comes going back to port for necessary items so that your crew (which I must add is your worst and most annoying foe) can operate. There are so many small mistakes in the game design that ruins any type of a streamlined gameplay. The menu system is clunky and is far to often necessarily accessed. The upgrading of crew (which you must do a ton of to go anywhere) is extremely tedious just to add skill points into the only two categories that matter, strength and vitality. The skill system is another tedious menu process that is costly, slow and generally unrewarding. Don't get me wrong, I love blasting enemy ships and plundering other vessals. At least, I really do want to, but the game will make you so frustrated you will abandon it before you wish you would.

Cats are Liquid is likely supposed to be a charming game, and for less than a dollar, it seems like a smart purchase.
You play as some sort of liquid cat as the name would have you assume, and explore blocky, minimalistic environments until you find the door to the next blocky, minimalistic environment. Everything, it seems, is all one or two colors. Pretty early on, a third color is introduced, orange, which hurts you. It's pretty simple. Boringly simple.
It's insane the amount of speed you can get in this game. Holding down turns the cat blue into some sort of extra watery form and you can speed by horizontal sections simply by hugging the ground with your watery cat body, and you can fall quickly by repeatedly tapping it. The cat can also slowly climb up verticle surfaces, but I discovered pretty early that you can exponetially speed this up by tapping jump.
This led to me speeding through the boring levels as fast as I could avoiding anything orange, which amused me for some time, but eventually wore down into monotony. After about a dozen levels, the cat gets a new power up which allows it to sloooowly float upwards as a gas cloud. Also boring when hopping up walls is three times as fast.
It doesn't help that this game's idea of ramping up difficulty seems to be adding things that just kill you in one hit. When the game introduced lava, it made sense, but later on you get jumping blocks that kill you at a touch, even if it hasn't crushed you.  Around the same time as that, it also added springy blocks that often push you into orange objects or the one hit kill hazards. A proper platformer would likely have them as trampolines but with such a boringly versatile moveset that the liquid cat has, the only thing the bouncy blocks can be is annoying. It was around there that I just said '♥♥♥♥ it' and left the game.
Most levels also have a copius amount of writing on the walls, most of which is uninteresting or stating the blatantly obvious. Growing up, the first RPG I ever played was Dragon Warrior on the NES, then it was Zelda, then between the NES and SNES I played the Final Fantasies, etc.  JRPGs were a genre I loved, even if I didn't really know the genre name back then.  I haven't played a JRPG-ish type of game since Albert Odyssey on the Sega Saturn back in the mid 90's honestly, so when I saw Skyborn pop up, I was intrigued.
I was hopeful that Skyborn would capture that spirit and feel that made me fall in love with the genre (but not rely on nostalgia).  My expectations were met and exceeded.  This is a fantastic JRPG game that has all the elements that make the genre great.  The story is fantastic, the battle system is tight, the graphics are clear and crisp and the musical score is extremely well done.
Another thing I enjoy here are that there are elements of random turn-based battles, but it's not random at all.  Enemies walk on paths that you can somewhat predict.  If you engage an enemy, you battle.  If you avoid the enemy, you don't.  There are certain narrow walkways where it would be hard to avoid an enemy, but honestly, you could probably play the entire game with only accidentally engaging a few enemies.  Or, you can choose to engage all enemies.  I love this option, because you still get plenty of fighting time, but you have a say in exactly when you'll be battling.
The end result is a 8 hour (if you play just to win) to probably 15 hour (if you do all the quests and explore everywhere) JRPG that anyone will love who is a fan of the genre.

Preface:
It appears, Dancing Dragon Games, developed Deadly Sin as their first commercial release.  Deadly Sin II came shortly after. Their latest, steam available title, is Skyborn. If you play all three games, you will noticed that the underlying battle mechanic and misc. scripts have changed very little between the three. The largest change being the simplification of skill advancement, and the 'GUI' in the battle scene. But the crafting (augments), threat system, etc... All pretty much identical.
TL,DR version:
Skyborn isn't all that different from its predecessors Deadly Sin I & II, but it is different EXACTLY where it matters the most. I am referring to the story of course... If you've played the other two games and fought a single battle, you've played Skyborn's as well. While it  may look different, battles really aren't in any measurable sense.
However, Skyborn has a far superior story line.
While it has a few pacing issues that DS1 didn’t suffer (IMO), it is FAR better packaged, along with accompanying graphics and music. This game plays like an interactive movie... A 'B' movie with almost no budget, but respectable movie none the less. This strength outweighs its flaws to where I will recommend it, even to non RPG Maker enthusiasts.
Pro:
- The Intro is GREAT. (First hour or so)
The main character is well spoken, and has very HUMAN reactions (as opposed to typical JRPG tropes) to the nature of her circumstance. The camera movement, NPC introductions, and 'framing' of the events, that sweep you off into an adventure, are spot on. This is without a doubt the best written intro to ANY RPG Maker game to date. (IMO) It is a BIG reason why I recommend it.
- Unlike Deadly Sin, the maps are pretty & reasonably designed.
One of my biggest gripes with RPGMaker games is the haphazard nature of their maps... And while this developers previous games have been above average (in presentation) they were quite 'typical' in floor plan. Until Skyborn. Yes, it is still very linear, but there aren't nearly as many pointlessly long hallway dead ends, nor inexplicable road blocks.

Con:
- Difficulty Spikes.
Ugh... UGH!! ARGHAHH!!!!!
Why is this so difficult for RPG Maker developers to get even SLIGHLY balanced?!?
(Read my Deadly Sin review if you want to read my small rant)
- One collection side quest - time sink.
A flower collecting side quest... /sigh
The reward wasn't even worth it... Not in the slightest.
- This is Deadly Sin, re-skinned with a new story...
If it wasn't such an improvement over the previous titles, this would have counted for more, and likely caused me to not recommend the game... It screams laziness.  It wouldn't be so bad if the game was LONGER and BETTER BALANCED for its complete repeat of the guts of the DS titles. But it's NOT. It actually feels shorter... though that may simply be my bias.
(Yes I realize that they made the transition to a newer RPG Maker tool set... It's still no excuse.)
Wrap Up:
If you liked the Deadly Sin series. Buy this one without hesitation. Even at the MSRP. It was that enjoyable for me.
However, if you are NOT a fan of RPG Maker games... This is worth the discounted price IMO. As long as you understand you are not buying a balanced game with satisfying combat. You are buying an interactive novel with a reasonably well done story.
That also happens to have JRPG levels of grind.

Skyborn is a short RPGMaker-made game that's very good looking (in the japanese anime classical style) and has great music.  It exposes interracial and social classes conflicts in a steampunk-fantasy sort of environment. The story is good but the arcs of the characters' stories are not very complicated and there are no important choices to make or crossroads where several endings can develop.
Fights are not at every corner of an alley because you can visually choose (most of the times) if you fight enemies or you just ignore them. The story/fighting ratio is well balanced, but while some generic enemies are a piece of cake some bosses are a pain in the mouse's left button. By the way, while some enemies' design goes according to the world presented, some others seem to have been taken out of other very different projects.
Gameplay is easy either with a keyboard or with the mouse, but the UI both in the character menus and in battle is a little bit of a mess and if you pause the game for a long time you will have to re-learn almost everything. Fights are repetitive and turn-based and the special effects are not outstanding but acceptable. You can upgrade your characters' classes and abbilities but even then some of they are left behind while others grow.
I recommend Skyborn if you like classical J-turn-based-RPGs and you are not too exigent.

Startopia is a gem, the kind that is usually hidden.
If you ever played god games years ago you probably heard of a company called Bullfrog, and you probably liked the games they made because they were the sort of games where the innovative design and tight characterzation of every game element?
Startopia is half of them continuing to do that with (Muckyfoot) while the other half goes to work with EA(Lionhead studios, formerly led by Peter Molyneux).
You are in charge of a part of a circualar space station and your job is to take care of the aliens tourists, hire employees kill intruders and do whatever it is you have to do in each mission (same as multiplayer).
The game is full of sci fi references but that's not a bad thing because unlike today's game, the jokes are incorporated into the gameplay, instead of having them blatantly put in your face (well, at least for the most part). There's the narrator and advisor AI VAL, who sounds like he is voiced by Stephen Fry which is awesome. There is the queue of items you can teleport around with sound effects that wouldn't look out of place in a star trek episode. and there's aron daal, a shady trader that might have been a reference to star wars i guess.
Besides all that, the presentation is near flawless. If black and white blew my mind by how much you can have your world open and explorable in a god game while still having tight gameplay, StarTopia excells by giving you amazing possibilites with limited space and set pieces.
If I have to give criticsm, I'd say that there's maybe a bit too little things to actually do, which might date the game a bit compared to the average run time of a modern game. This is a nitpick though, the game is fun as balls and you should really get it and see for yourself.

A surprisingly underrated tactical shooter - judging by my friends who have played it long ago complaining about extremely bad AI and some egregious bugs, and me experiencing way less significant bugs and quirks, I would assume that was either patched out before I got it or something.
Anyways, this is an X-com game. Except it's a third-person tactical shooter, which surprisingly works. You have a character who gained some strange powers after an unusual encounter, you can take up to two more squaddies with you anytime, and you get a slow-mo order giving mode where you can tell them where to cover or what abilities to use. Also it's a set in the 60ies, so you have people smoking cigars and wearing fedoras and using bolt acton rifles against alien forces. Which is actually pretty cool too, seeing those American dream homes with white picket fences being wrecked by ailiean menace spawning their strange construct everywhere. Aliens themselves are more close to a modern interpretation than some campy half-a-century old flick martian - not sure if that's good or bad, would nontheless make a game way more campier but could be fun. Though can't say the atmosphere stays for long. Later in the game you will have abandoned every single conventional weapon there is for laser or plasma, your soldiers will have more alien toys to use than an average alien, and you'll spend more time in metallic alien bases that on the street or inside human buildings. You'll spend a lot of time in the X-com building, though, and it's very lovely with lots of detail, NPC conversations, and some side quest investigations.
Combat is pretty decent, there's lots of staying in cover and using abilities - any despite the setting and genre those feel very X-com, it's stuff like mind control, friendly construct summoning, luring enemies from the cover. Pretty cool, though the way how quickly your teammates will earn it makes me think that clashes with the story where similar technologies get adopted way later. In any case the abilities are crucial, you are msot often outnumbered, and where most basic enemies are easy to take on, the heavy elites can wreck your crap on their own. By the way, this thing has good ol' mutons. Have fun!

Nothing inspiring, just your average PC.
I laughed here and there, but a lot of the things I laughed at were merely things that could've been done better or faults in logical human behaviour on behalf of the game designers.
An example:
Personally I found nothing about the story fascinating other than

Most of the conversations you have with NPCs have no impact on the plot of the game other than unlocking a side-mission for loot. So if you want to look through all the dialogue it's all for interest rather than consequence. I personally found myself skipping most of it - even the essential story parts couldn't hold my attention, but that might just be me.
The lip-syncing in this game isn't too high of quality either, but the animations for everything else are decent.
Gameplay is clunky at times.
I found myself attempting to fly over terrain when using a squadmate's abilities, only to find myself have to physically walk the ability around obstacles and over the land to finally put it where I want to, as if I was moving the guy himself.
And about moving your men - a lot of the time they seem to wander off on their own and sit in areas where they can be easily shot. I had one encounter where my Commando ran straight up through the enemy forces and around to their backline, without my input, where he promptly got downed and killed.
They're usually pretty obedient however, though you should make it your job to keep a constant eye on them. They like to yell for more orders and tell you they're pinned down or need assitance when the one enemy left is on the other side of the map with 25% HP.
Overall it's a pretty decent game. I loved the fights despite their problems.
The action and pacing of the battles is great, I've found. Tactical positioning of your troops is a must unless you want them to get downed in three bullets thanks to an enemy flanking even on Normal difficulty.
It became very easy as you get higher ranked squadmates however. There really is no insentive to play with lower-ranked classes to get them higher levels unless you're just running your agents in to die in the first place, or want to try out a different class of agent.
Even then, there are side fetch-quest like missions you can only send agents on in order for the ones you can't take into the field (maximum of two with your character being the leader and third) to get some experience and level up without you needing to do anything. You could just level up the agent you want to use next while you continue to advance the story missions and bring him in when he's max rank.
I found it strange that you couldn't participate in those missions no matter what, they were only every for your teammates to do. They're not timed either, none of the missions are. You can take as much time as you like doing whatever you want.
The abilities are easily spammed by all classes, and considering they can deploy turrets, drones, heal each other, give each other combat buffs, pull enemies out of cover for almost no cost to themselves, and mind control enemies into fighting for you, it gets pretty broken.
It became more of a grind than anything towards the end of the game, though it was still fairly enjoyable. I found myself worrying less about the health of my squad, and worrying more about the cooldown timer dictating when I could deploy my drones and sentry guns again.
It's nothing special, but it's good if you want a little bit of tactical turn-based-like combat in your real-time action game.

After beating Axiom Verge in just under 12 hours for the first time, I must say this title just blew me away.
I have always enjoyed the Action Platformer type genre since I can remember. Many offerings in the past have come close to emulating the perfection achieved by the benchmark Metroid games. Axiom Verge I am pleased to say goes above and beyond. The story is intriguing and the setting completely engaging. As you progress the reality of the situation slowly pieces together and even though I've completed it, I still haven't 100% collected everything. So the finite details of the story are still out there to be found and pieced together.
Soundtrack was deliciously retro and completely unique, I've never heard anything like it.
The levels are superbly designed and there is plenty of exploration and back-tracking as you collect more and more gear and become capable of navigating the terrain. It is dark, organic, and mechanical all at the same time. A unique flavor all its own.
Highly Recommended

Since Super Metroid, only two 2D Metroid games have come out: Zero Mission and Fusion.
Fusion was a really spectacular and different take on the Metroid 'verse, but some thought it was too linear, and had too much dialogue.
Zero Mission improved on Fusion's mechanics and is a better aging version of Metroid 1, but the rehashing of areas, while certainly nostalgic, did not bring much new to the series.
Super Metroid itself, while not my favorite Metroid game, is the best 2D game ever and had a lot that was completely original as well as all those little nostalgic areas while still managing to keep things fresh every step of the way.
Axiom Verge is a worthy successor.
You start off extremely confused in a giant mechanical egg. All you remember is there being an explosion in the laser lab you were working in. A mysterious voice tells you that there is a gun in the next room. The way to the right is blocked by Norfair bubbles, so you go left. You grab the gun,  then everything lights up like Super Metroid and you're blasting your way through bubbles and zoomers all over again. You could mistake this game for the next Metroid if your  wasn't wearing a t-shirt.
So you blast your way along and eventually find yourself in a room with a flying Mother Brain that calls YOU a demon.
Later, you see what appear to be texture glitches.
Everything begins to make sense eventually, don't get me wrong, but I won't spoil any more.
Overall this game is spectacular. A new and innovative Metroidvania that has unusual solutions to problems, a new and sometimes surreal world, good combat, tight controls, and a decent plot.
I am honestly giving this game a 10/10 because there is nothing wrong with it.
It is a perfect and fresh Metroidvania.
Now stop reading this and go buy it.

Old-body-text:
"Pixel Piracy" is a waiting-game done outrageously wrong.
Let get into some details:
The winning combination for combat-gameplay itself consist of mainly just getting 20-30-swabbies and equip them with long-range-guns as soon as possible, making sure all of these squabblers learn "Swimming" to avoid cheap-drowning.
Lastly of course is to make sure everyone attacks in a single group.
Congratulations, you have already (almost) half-beaten the game!
After the initial chore-levelling (until about raising all the stats to ~30 or so, alongside feeding the crew with all the various combat and chore-books), now you should have already reached the biggest obstacle in the game which tests everyone: "The Waiting-Game".
Not only sailing between each square on the map takes ~40-60-seconds in top-speed-ship, you will also be encountering the "unresponsive-loading-screen-of-blackness" twice during the traversing-phases; once before the sailing-sequence (or as I'd like to call "Babysitting-phase in which you'll have to constantly sure that already happy-enough-crew aren't hogging the playing-cards all for themselves), and once before landing/encounter. Each of these loading screen lasts ~60-seconds again; granted, maybe not at the start of the game, but majority at least as soon as you get the "winning-crew" which already is over 1/4 of the game beaten.
Oh and, of course make sure to only purchase "Watermelons" for food; anything else is just both waste of gold and money.
Also morale is just more simple to upkeep with Playing-Cards and paying salary; you will be getting that +100K gold in quite short time as long as you don't do the mistake of ever capturing the ship(s); Always plunder them so you don't lose your own equipments (especially the Playing-Cards!); it's simply better off building your semi-small two-deck-ship.
By the way, the map of size of 31x31-squares, and every single square is populated at the start of a "run" (/New Game). So if you're one of those people who'd want to try searching everything (mainly for the two achievement), here's a small calculation you'll ending up just to use for waiting, in which you mostly have no control over anything:
- 31 x 31 = 961-squares
- 961 x 1 x 2 = 1922-minutes just waiting during "loading-screens"
- 961 + 1922 = 2883-minutes in total if you'd have the full-speed-ship right from the beginning, but you don't, so we'll make it 2900-minutes.
But wait! There is even more waiting out there: If either of the ships during encounter has cannon(s)!
There is a "cannon-fire-phase" before boarding is allowed, which is from 30-seconds up 60--seconds, And, considering how horrendously this game runs (which itself already is an achievement for a pixel-based, full-on-2D-plane-plane with very, very simplistic mechanics), the cannon-phases are actually doubled most the times!
Of course, the amount of encounters alongside the map is randomized, and also when both (yours and theirs) ship don't have cannon(s), you simply instantly board the ship.
In the end though, we'll be generous to say that (in the current state of the game) every player wanting to explore the whole map will be spending ~3000-minutes for just waiting the game "Load"; that's "50-hours" right there.
As of writing this, Steam as Registered that I've run this game for ~27-hours, which also includes two captain-creation sessions alongside all the menu and various other micro-management-hassle. I wouldn't be too much off if I'd say that I was actually playing (as in, actually in controls and such) only the 1/4th of the time (mainly combat, looting, shopping, etc. actually controlling-wise), which could probably barely reach to 7-hours; rest of the +20-hours I was doing anything but sitting next to my computer "playing" this game (I literally went do some cooking at my kitchen, watched Youtube-videos via my PDA, etc. things, because multitasking on computer while this game run halts the sailing-phases always around at 94% of the trips).
Most of the video-games have those moment where you simply have to wait; "Pixel Piracy" was able pull off the stunt of making the waiting happen in almost all of the wrong spots, if not downright making the game unfinishable due the style of increasing the wait times further and further...
Fun for a half hour or so. Gets repetetive really soon. Buy something else with your money.

I got this game for two reasons:
1. I like pirates
2. Re-Logic had their hands in this game, and I love what they did with Terraria.
Turns out, despite Re-Logic's best efforts to make this game good, they failed.  You can polish a turd all you want, but it's still a turd.  Speaking of turds, way too much of the player's effort in this game is, no joke, literally removing turds from your ship.  It may seem humorous at first, and perhaps it would be if it were just a minor easter egg thrown into the game.  But no, it's pretty much a major activity that you spend a significant amount of resources on.  I didn't realize I purchased Poo Scrubber Simulator.
And it's not just about cleaning up your crew member's defecation.  You also have to keep their morale high, their bellies full, and their immune system free from scurvy.  Again, I wouldn't mind this bit of realism if it required an appropriately small amount of the player's effort.  But no.   Your crewmembers are pretty much constantly contracting scurvy, losing morale, getting hungry, and pooping on your ship.  Seriously 95% of the game is mitigating this tedious stuff.
The other 5%?  Sending your crew into a disorganized foray of indistinguishable health bars.  There's really no way to tell what's really going on during the battles.  You just send your crew in and hope the random number generator is kind to you.  Then you get♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off because of the permadeath of your crew members that you finally potty trained.

I did not encounter any bugs with the game during my play through, the music is nice and graphics are nice and run fine on my laptop. I've been wanting to get into speed running for a while and have been trying out multiple games, and this seems like it's going to be the first one I put serious time into for the reasons I said in the TL:DR.

What immediately struck me about this game was the perfect control mechanisms. Most platformers I play have their individual quirks that you have to get used to at the start of the game such as a slightly delayed jump or unusual movements. As soon as I climbed up a wall (with controller) it just felt right and natural, the jumping and floating had exactly the right amount of speed and responsiveness, it was a joy to play in that respect.
You are a 'cat' navigating a maze of physics obstacles. Your movement is like that of a water-filled balloon, hence the 'liquid' in the title. You can ooze through tiny gaps, hop up high vertical walls and float up/along as a gas cloud. Later in the game you can use bombs to break walls or release and control a square on a time limit to move ahead and unlock a passage for the cat. You play as only the square in the Companion levels, under time constraints.
A couple of hours after playing it I can't even remember what the background music was like, it was so unobtrusive, which is a good thing. Likewise the graphics are minimalistic and functional, nothing wrong with that. There's a loose story written in the background based on the cat being trapped and complaining about the prolonged journey (she has a point!)
The "90+30 levels" claim is a bit cheeky, it's actually 9+3 levels each with 9 waypoints where your 3 lives are topped up (or time reset).
From the levels menu the escape key doesn't work so you have to start a level and exit from there in order to close the game. Took a while to work that one out.
On completion of both Standard and Companion the screen fades to black and everything becomes unresponsive so the only way you can get out is by forcefully crashing the game. Perhaps this is intentionally consistent with the storyline, who knows!
I've definitely completed Companion because I reached the end credits but 22/30 of the levels remain locked. I've repeated many levels (by starting at the last unlocked level) to double-check but no, still locked.
I'm on Linux if that makes a difference. Maybe if the developer reads this review the bugs will be fixed by the time you read it. None of it affects the actual gameplay anyway.
Experienced platform players should be able to complete the game in their sleep with very few retries - for much of Standard you can effortlessly float past most obstacles. The Companion levels have time constraints but are also easy.
The consistency of the game mechanics unfortunately extends to the predictable, monotonous gameplay and many of the levels are identical but played with different abilities. There is no innovation here, just the usual elements you've seen in countless other platformers.
I completed Standard in 4 hours and Companion in 1 at medium pace. I may attempt the 2 clean-run achievements later to 100% it but probably not. I'd say the quantity of gameplay is very good value for the price.
These entail completing each level and then playing the whole thing again in a perfect uninterrupted run. Pretty unimaginative, but then again there are no remarkable gameplay features to warrant an interesting achievement. I still don't have the 'Always There' achievement so I don't know what it is. I'm happy it has achievements at all anyway, and the developer has just said he's considering trading cards in future.
Most of this review may seem negative but that's not the case at all. I did enjoy this, it's just that lately I've been playing very challenging and unique physics games like Portal, Nihilumbra and Metamorphic, so this seemed pedestrian by comparison. If it's a casual experience you're after then I highly recommend this, especially at the rock-bottom price. It's like a mass-produced japanese car: well-built, familiar and comfortable but rather bland.

In a strange sort of way, this game reminded me of Calvin and Hobbes. Social misfit kid disconnected from parents finds happiness in his imaginative interactions with an animal. Bad comparisons aside, as long as you don't play the game with the expectation that it will replicate To the Moon's format, you'll be in for a pleasant hour. It does replicate many of the things that made TTM great (great soundtrack, throwback 16 bit graphics, quirky sense of humor), but eschews the more complex story of TTM for a stripped down narrative that focuses more on emotion than complex narrative development.
I've seen a lot of backlash against the lack of dialogue in the game, with the general impression that, as RPS put it, it just adds a "bonus sense of pomposity" to it. This strikes me as an overly cynical view of the game. As I experienced it, the lack of dialogue forced me to search elsewhere to fill in the narrative gaps, a search that A Bird Story rewards by layering the game with a series of subtle, effective cues. A blanket placed around a sleeping child's shoulders. A pile of briefly read notes scattered on a table. Taken in isolation, none of this means much, but I found that the sum total of these snapshots was enough to make the experience sufficiently immersive.
A Bird Story didn't move me to tears, and it didn't have me laughing so hard that I couldn't catch my breath. But it did make me smile, and its whimsy and simplicity carried me back to my childhood, if only for an hour, and that's where I think this game succeeds. It's a brief ode to the boundless imagination of childhood, to the inherent mutability of what we perceive, and to the small joys and miniature heartbreaks that we encounter in our daily lives. The game never aspires to be more than a brief snapshot of a lonely kid, but within those confines are small moments of levity, loneliness, and genuine warmth, and that was enough for me.

A Bird Story is a rather short story about a neglected child's encounter with an injured bird, and their imagination-fueled adventures together thereafter.

ABS has the same beautiful pixel graphics and soundtrack in TtM. Also, it has just one achievement that is rewarded when you complete the story. An easy 100% game. As for its flaws, it really isn't as interactive and gaining control of the character felt cringey. I feel that participation was forced, and Kan Gao should consider releasing these shorter-than-TtM titles as a steam movie.
Also, the game takes 1-hr to complete, and steam doesn't even reward you with the trading cards by this time. So now I'm forced to let it run and stare at the title screen. Running it in the background doesn't seem to increase the gametime.

First and foremost, A Bird Story has wonderful music, narrative (even without words) and overall story and was enjoyable in those aspects.

The controls are clunky and meaningless. Having to 'navigate' a linear path with absolutely no gameplay (no, jumping on puddles does not count as gameplay) is uninteresting and this piece would be much better without it.
I avoid calling A Bird Story a game because it's not. Even interactive story is misleading because there is very little to interact with. There are no choices, no exploration, no paths, just a story. And there's nothing wrong with that and I wish the devloper would stick to their strengths, the story, the music, and the way the story is told. Using pixel art to tell a story in the form of a movie is perfectly fine, it does not have to be forced into a peg it does not fit.
The gameplay elements of both To the Moon and A Bird Story exist only to hinder the game, drop the expectation that a 'game' is needed when the focus is the story and this is still a pretty enjoyable sit through.

Don't buy this game. Yet.
It's basically Chivalry with a better combat system but slightly worse graphics (graphics are reminiscent of MnB: Warband). However, the only modes available are a zerg-y CTF and what's basically a 1v1 mode. They're fun, and I'm sort of enjoying myself, but I can't help but think I'm only having fun because I just spent $20 on this title.
I think this game has a TON of potential. It has a great dev team with many great ideas, and in a year I think it might be a must-buy off of Steam (Crowfall will be out by then, though, and it seems to have a more polished but similar game design). Right now, though, the game is buggy, combat is a bit wonky, and the advertised game modes have not been released.
The only reason for you to click buy right now is if you're a huge fan of MnB: Warband multiplayer, which, I think, few people are. That or you don't care about spending $20. Definitely tuck this one away for later, though.
All that said, I really enjoy the game myself. Combat is getting a bit better day by day, and while sometimes blocks/hits just don't register, I suspect it will be a really incredible combat system come release. I really enjoyed MnB battles, and was hoping for a similar effect but with other players. Right now, that feature is pretty far off into the future, and when it comes I'm not completely sure it will play out as fun as MnB was.
If the game can evolve beyond the crazy zerg-fest that is the CTF mode, it will be something to behold (tactical formations, strategy, cavalry charges; these all sound ♥♥♥♥ing dope) but we'll  have to wait and see. Again, if you think that's all something you're super interested in, drop the $20. If you're just bored, don't bother for right now.

Got my hands on Dishonored during 2012, or early 2013, played through it a bunch of times, and now finally picked up the complete collection with the dlc´s on steam.
Dishonored is a great one, its a game that gives you an objective and allows you to complete it however you choose, many RPG games obviously do this, but non rpg games usually fail with the consept. Dishonored, in my opinnion, doesnt. There are a lot of ways you can go about with this game, weather its no alerts no kills stealth, full high chaos, or something in between, theres always multiple ways to dispose of your targets, many times its more then two options. You also are given a wide array of powers to invest your runes (upgrade points) in, some of them excell with high chaos, some with stealth gameplay, or you can go with no powers at all if you want to.  So you will be looking at an exceptionally good stealth experience, or straight up really fun killing simulator in one backage.
The maps are filled with different paths to take, lore to read, stuff to steal, puzzles and some side objectives, i mean i found pathways and secrets during my third playthrough which i didnt discover during the earlier two runs.
Whats nice about that freedom is that the game has a pretty well done chaos system, which means that the more aggressive you play the game, more people you kill and so on will have effects on the world, dialogue, endings and conversations, and how other caracters perceive you.
The game looks pretty good, im okay with the art direction, but i know it probably wont please everybody.
One thing to note is that the game is farily short, if you are thinking about playing it through only once, you are looking at around 8-12 ish hours of gameplay from the main story.
I mean i have 45 hours clocked in at the moment, a few of those hours are idle hours too.
And i´v done the main story three times (high chaos, low chaos no alarm no detection run and not using any powers besides the mandatory one run)
DLC 1 two times (high chaos and ghost run)
same with DLC 2
So to get everything the game has to offer, i would absolutelly recommend doing a few playthroughs. The lenght of the game is not a problem for me, it doesnt feel like the game was cut short, or that something was left out, and if you are okay with playing it through few times, then the relatively short length is not a negative thing.
So the entirety of the main game can easily be played through in one weekend, both story DLC´s are great, but they last about 3 - 5 hours each, so they can be done in one sitting.
TLDR:
PROS:
- Freedom to complete objectives however you want to.
- Open maps with many pathways to support this.
- Solid main plot.
- Combat is TONS of fun, just check out some of those youtube compilations, some amazing things can be done!
- Stealth works great too.
- I encountered absolutely no bugs.
- Game runs great.
- Lot of lore can be found about the world and characters.
- Two great DLC´s (Knife of dunwall / Brightmore witches)
- some of the non lethal ways of disposing your targets are absolutely the best poetic justice.
- Okay replayability, its not hugely different on each run, but playing through with different styles kept me entertained enough to do that three times.
CONS:
- Voice acting is pretty meh, there are exceptions and some really well done characters.
- There could be a bit more life in the city, more NPC´s and so on, theres some of them, but in my opinnion, could be more,
that way you would see the effects of chaos level more too.
- A short game if you only play it through once.
- One weak DLC (city trials)
- Main character is not voice acted. (Improved on as the DLC main character is voice acted)
- Music is pretty weak.
Overall, you can get the complete edition really cheap, and it is definitelly worth the money.

For a one man team game, this looks amazing.
Heavily inspired by Metroid and from an esthetics PoV, HR Gieger's work. If you haven't played metoird, it's an exploration/adventure game where by collecting power ups you can expand your areas of exploration. Discovering new power ups along the way.
Music is very nicely composed, providing a sense of the unknown, uncertain of what's to unfold or what is up ahead.
Story is told through diaolg(text boxes) and lore about the location and what happened is unconvered via logs, which are scattered around the world.
But the best part about this is the address disruptor, I may have gotten the name wrong so pardon me if I did, but this weapon allows you to bend reality. Enemies will change their properties, speed and attack strategies if they are exposed to the ray long enough. This opens up new areas and its crucial to use if you want to get 100% in this game.
Bringing the old exploration/adventure game back in a good way, providing good music and excellent gameplay. Axiom Verge is well worht the 15$ asking price.

It's probably one of the most fluid Metroidvanias you'll ever play. Not to mention this game has original weapons and abilities, which is crazy for a genre that has been quite saturated the past couple of years. Also the main character has a lab coat which is always a plus. Definitely buy this if you enjoy hard exploration and platformer games. The soundtrack is also a beautiful asset.
First playthrough is not all that long, probably six or seven hours if you're known with the genre, but again there's lots of things to get 100% of after you're done.

Tom Happ does what Nintendon't: make a new 2D Metroid. Axiom Verge is a brilliant game made by one man and it easily rivals Super Metroid in its quality. Don't bother waiting for Nintendo to revive 2D Metroid, they won't do it. Instead, give your money to Tom and play Axiom Verge, which brings back everything you love about Metroid and adds its own unique style to the mix.
Metroid might be dead, but this game keeps the dream alive.

One dude made this. Graphics, music, gameplay - everything. And it felt like playing Super Metroid for the first time again. That's amazing to me. And Super Metroid took a team of 15 to make. Granted, the tools are better today and the retro inspirations are obvious. But, there's enough originality here to make it a love letter to Metroid, rather than a boring clone. TL;DR: Totally worth your time & money.

............OK, good and bad.
Good: It's like Metroid
Bad: It's like Metroid.
To explain, this game seems to have all the sins and virtues of the Metroidvania genre in one convenient package. The game, unlike some others of its ilk (Shovel Knight, for instance) focuses a lot more heavily on the METROID aspect, involving the level design, futuristic world, etc.
Problem is, it's a little too similar for its own good. Those long vertical shafts where everything looks the same? Yep.
Enemies that are very similar to their Metroid counterparts? We got Rinkas, we got Sidehoppers, we got Shriekbats...yeah, this base is covered.
The corruption gun is sorta a unique mechanic...
I recommend this game, but just know when I say it's like Metroid in every way, that includes the sins of the genre as well.

What I've found here is Mass Effect meets The X-Files, thrown in with Cold War era paranoia and the Space Race in this alternate history third-person shooter. If only for theme alone, this is an instant favorite.

(I haven't played To The Moon so I didn't have any expectations of this.)
I don't mind that it's a long cutscene with no gameplay
I don't mind that there's no dialogue. In fact I think it's great how all sorts of subtle stuff (like a bird saying "thank you") was communicated with just motion.
I don't mind the slow meandering pace... well okay, it can get tedious, but it's no big deal
I don't mind the pixel art, I think it looks great and so do the more painterly backgrounds
The music is excellent, and I'm buying the soundtrack DLC right after I finish this review
Why am I giving this a thumbs down then? Because it's hollow sentimentality. It's trying to tug at your heartstrings without substance. There's few things I dislike more than sensationalism and emotional manipulation.
From the Steam reviews I can tell it worked on most people. "Moving", they call it. I'm  really not seeing that. Yes I got the metaphors, the music is really lovely, and yes an isolated kid and an injured bird are sad things. But that doesn't make an engaging story.

I can only recommend this for a select type of person. That person must have a wistful personality, a personality where imagination is not dead.
This is another example of a visual novel with barebones interactivity.  It has the same feel as "To The Moon" (which this reviewer believes to be a far superior story), but it has a cute story, with pretty darn good music.  The graphical style is 16-bit sprite/pixel art.  Basically it's like watching a cute story on Super Nintendo with a nice soundtrack playing in the background.
Playtime (or runtime, really...) is basically right at an hour.  It's good for a quick storytime break.
All in all, I would not call this a game.  The bits of interactivity are actually rather pointless unless the point is to keep an uninterested person from falling asleep.
The TL;DR version:
Good music, 16-bit graphics, visual novel, short runtime.  Wouldn't pay more than 99 cents for it, but I didn't consider its purchase to be a mistake.

For a multiplayer game, which is basically all it has, it feels like i said, lacking. If it wasn't multiplayer, it could have had much more. It's an FPS that is much more of what you feel, and the only explanation for its errors is Bethesda's intervention and the game being based on multiplayer instead of anything else. Not enough variety with guns or attachments either, which does make me quite sad. Without a proper explanation or feelings, or a proper single player campaign, picking a side is more of which one looks coolest or something, and the resistance looks like a bunch of idiots, instead of being a group fighting for a cause. We barely got a explanation of what happened in the world for the ARC to be so important, but all we know is that we need to fight. The team-work is well designed, though the aspect of not dying normally feels really bad as you spend most of your time waiting to respawn, making the fast paced gameplay feel much less "fast paced" than it really is. Speaking of fast paced, it doesn't feel fast paced. Not at all. I wish this was a successful game and that it had more time to be made; It'd be a benefit for Prey 2, and a benefit for how this game would turn out. Sadly, what remains is a fun FPS game that can really hold itself together as being overall memorable, but you know that it could have been much more, and that it isn't quite enough either. However, this is a game that recieved a very small cult following; And that being of me, too. Oh and the art style for this game isn't good. Art direction is meh.

A true Dystopian metaphor representing the aftermath of our demise as humans and the inevitable swarm of Bird Overlords.
You live in a cave. Your world is centered on cherishing the only thing you have left: education.
Perhaps one day they will eventually find a way to merge human and bird DNA but until then, you are second to a superior, majestic species.
What do you eat and drink? How truly cold is the stone bed you sleep upon at night, when you dream restlessly of the Utopia our Earth had once been - a damaged, often brutal Utopia, but a world in which humans bowed to no one but themselves. You toss and turn and wake with a sore neck, wondering why you can't simply end it all.
However, you cannot possibly do that to your only pigeon friend. Truly, as an outcast amongst many, you gravitate towards one another. Rules be damned! You need to talk to someone when you feel alone.
The game unfolds, adhering to a strict timetable of work or conversation with your plumed peers. At home, as you scavenge fruitlessly in a barren cave, you start to miss the time spent with others, if only to avoid the gut-wrenching hunger that is merely temporarily assuaged with nuts, berries and seeds.
The ending surprises you but you've given up now. It might as well be, laws of Nature aside. You have no idea how you'll survive, and you're sure that you are unlikely to procreate. At this point, life has worn you down to a shadow of the person you once were. Sometimes you entertain the idea of gluing feathers yourself in order to fit in....

tl;dnr: Solid gameplay and Story, though not amazing. Worth your time and money.
Dishonored is a Stealth game set in a steampunk society modeled after Victorian London. You play as Corvo Attono, former Bodyguard to the Empress. At the beginning of the game, you are framed for the Empress's Assassination, and you must fight to restore the rightful heir to the throne and regain your own honor, with the help of a supernatural entity known as the Outsider and a group of rebels known as the Loyalists.
First, the Gameplay. Dishonored fuses tried and true stealth mechanics with non-linear level design and unique supernatural powers that enhance your mobility, ability to gain information, and to fight. You have options not only in how you complete objectives but even what your objectives are. You can choose non-lethal objectives for your targets, going unseen and unheard, or cut a bloody path and kill all who stand in your way. The game can be easy at some times, so it's best to strive to complete challenges like going undetected or play on the harder difficulties. Your character is often spoken of in mystical terms for his legendary skill in combat, and the game gives you this feeling not through gimmicky mechanics or squishy foes but through how the mechanics feel; your every movement seems smooth and methodical no matter how much you as a player have screwed things up. Overall, the gameplay is fairly solid, even if it doesn't knock you out of the park.
Second, the Story. Dishonored tells interesting narratives through unique characters and plot twists, and excels at world building by avoiding focusing on meaningless details and instead showing how the people within the world live and feel. The game handles Morality in an interesting way that isn't necessarily bad; the world gradually becomes a worse place the more people you kill and more wrongs you commit. This is actually enhanced by you being a silent protagonist; without the ability  to interact with other people, you are forced to let your thoughts of Murder and Revenge stew in your mind, until finally you get fed up with the crap you are dragged through and decide you really need to off the people who wronged you. Dishonored abandons the "press A for Good, B for bad" formula, and instead makes the moral choices the mechanically harder of the two to pull off, even if what's right is clearly cut out: Sure, it would be right to leave the person alive and drag their corpse 300 yards while fighting off guards, but it would be easier if you just stabbed him now.
Aside from Revenge, Dishonored, to no surprise, explores what it means to have honor. While this theme is not fully explored (and I'm not even sure if it's intentional), Dishonored shows us that Honor is only a facade that people use to put themselves above other people, and is abandoned when convenient. This theme could be more fully fleshed out, but it is there.
Third, the Art and Sound. The game is old, no doubt about that, and the graphics reflect its age. But I’m willing to gloss over graphics if the art is good. For art to be good I have to be able to tell what something is, and the art has to fit in with the style of the game. The Style of Dishonored is dark and gritty, though certainly not drab or boring. Nothing seems out of place, and I’m never left puzzling about what something is. Even if the visuals aren’t stunning, it all works well enough and has no flaws worth noting. The voice acting is OK, and maybe a little below mediocre. The soundtrack does its job; never so good enough or bad enough for me to notice it.
Rather than reduce games to a simple numerical score, I judge a game by two criteria: Is it worth your time to experience it, and is it worth your money to purchase it?
Dishonored is worth your time, and is certainly above average and it is good, though not amazing. As you can see, I've played the game for quite some time, and I enjoy it. Not the best, but definitely good.
But is it worth your money? Most certainly. Dishonored is a short game, and lacks replayability even if it does have multiple endings, since your choices don't mean much until the end (which won’t mention most of your choices anyway). You can squeeze more time out of the game by trying different tactics to get through the levels, but this can be done once or twice at maximum. In spite of all this, $10 is small for a game like this.

For anyone who wants a great Metroidvania type of game, this is a great choice.  Borrowing from past 8-bit and 16-bit conceptualizations is only half of the formula.  The graphic design inspirations borrow heavily from HR Giger, and the music has a wordly enough variation to allow the overall attitude of the game to be within the definitions of modern-day video games.
The only weakness that is obvious is the fact that there is not a Boss Rush mode or a Survival Mode.  However, there is a Speed Run component, and the game has a Passcode function allowing for costume variations, among other ideas and concepts.
Seeing that this title has only been out for about 3 months, it may seem premature to claim that Axiom Verge will become a classic.  But, anyone who has a chance to experience its many beauties will discover retroactive reminiscences of a game worthy to be in any old school gamer's library.

This game is a great Metroidvania with interesting game mechanics. It's a solid title even if you don't know it was made by one guy. There haven't really been many pure Metroid style games recently- most similar try to blend the Metroidvania genre with other gameplay types. That's well and good, but this goes closer to the roots, and, in my opinion, is stronger for it.
However, there are a few minor issues.
First off, sometimes your progress is completely halted because of a detail you couldn't realistically find out on your own without a guide, unless you either get lucky or experiment more than should be necessary. (1 specific room and 1 specific boss.)
Second, the aiming controls could use some work- although they're usually fine, sometimes they force you to move in a specific direction to shoot the way you want to. There is a button that's supposed to help with aiming, but it locks MOVEMENT rather than aiming, which I found strange, because being stationary is usually a bad idea. Simply changing the movement lock to aim lock would be very helpful in this regard.
Third, the "glitches" don't ever really feel like you're actually messing with the game.
Here are the things they do, based on my memory:
Make enemies bigger/smaller
Make enemies shoot slower
Make enemies shoot with less spread
Turn enemies into a different type of enemy
Make enemies, or their attacks, destroy some specific walls
Make enemies, or their attacks, create
Kill enemies prematurely
Make enemies slower
Make enemies stop moving
Make things solid/disappear/turn into blocks you can destroy
Go through walls
These are used to good effect for unique gameplay that revolves around finding out how to best use these changes, but the "glitches" never really feel like glitches, other than the aesthetics. Going through walls is the closest it ever gets. For someone who's actually glitch-hunted in games (notably Super Metroid) this isn't like HUNTING for glitches, because you're given a gun and told "Use this to make things work differently." It's more like solving a combat puzzle in Megaman, or switching between worlds in Guacamelee. The glitch aesthetic is really just that, an aesthetic. It typically works well, but I was a bit disappointed it wasn't a bit more like actually finding glitches for yourself. There are also secret worlds that appear at random, but these felt more like random secrets than glitches to me from my limited experience with one.
Finally, an issue that was more of an annoyance than any of the other things on the list. The enemies all tend to be damage tanks. This is meant to be a catalyst for players that use strategy over simply running and gunning. However, what it tends to do is make fights drag even after you've found out the best strategy to use against an enemy.
One more thing: I think the game is actually TOO well-designed- the creator knew all the limits of the player at any given time, and prevented sequence breaking. I like sequence breaking, so this makes me sad.
Overall the game is very enjoyable (I finished the game, which I only ever do when I think it's worth playing all the way through.) However, go into it with the knowledge that the game is more about combat puzzles than realistic glitches.

TL:DR at bottom-
I love Super Metroid. I love Super Metroid so much that I searched out fan made ROMhacks of the game. One of the best I have found is Super Metroid: Redesign by Drewseph. He changes everything: the physics, the weapons, and game mechanics. It is completely different, but it is still fundamentally Super Metroid.
Axiom Verge is very similar in the regard. The gameplay is different, the physics are different, the weapons are different, the story is different...but it is still fundamentally Super Metroid. Rather, it takes what I love about Super Metroid and distills it into the amazing experience that is Axiom Verge. I cannot recommend this game enough.
If you like the classic 2D Metroid games, Castlevania games, or even run and gun games like Contra, this game is for you. If you like classic 2D platformers like Mario or Sonic, this game is also for you. If you don't like either of these game types, then this game might not be for you, but I would recommend getting it anyway for one simple reason: Steam offers refunds on games now.
You have literally nothing to lose if you get the game and immediately dislike it. You can use the refund option. However, I have a feeling that if you get Axiom Verge, you will want to keep it.
The music is very well written, and one of my favorite things about it is the prevalence of a heavy bass kick in most of the tunes. To me, this is Trace's heartbeat. It increases during boss battles, it decreases during calm areas. Another cool thing is the low health beep. Anyone who has played Zelda of Metroid is familiar with this; it is an annoying, jarring way of telling you that you might die if you don't get health soon. Axiom Verge uses this mechanic, but instead of overriding the music, the low health beep is implemented into whatever song you are listening to. It slows down or speeds up depending on the BPM of the song. The first time I heard it, I was amazed that I hadn't seen that used in any other game I have played as it is such a good way to let you know that you have low health.
The environments have some areas where the backgrounds have pulsating objects that move to the beat of the music. I am a huge fan of how this is added. It helps to suck me into the game, and make me feel more connected since the music is an integral part of the experience.
The jumping physics are top notch, and able to offer precise movement control. Some of the upgrades you get are very cool, but I won't go into them since finding them and figuring out what they do is a fun part of the game. There is only one part of the map I am less than impressed with, but that is just because there are a lot of small, white creatures that sort of blend in with the background and can disrupt your jumping if they hit you.
The difficulty of this game comes in normal mode and hard mode. I finished normal mode in about 10 hours, with something like 80% of the map revealed and 75% of the items found. There is a lot to find, and doing it is fun. There are an amazing amount of weapons that do various things, making some boss fights easier with certain weapons.
Overall, this is an amazingly well made game, which is made even more incredible by the fact that it was made completely by just one man: Thomas Happ. He designed the game, composed the music, and created the story. This game is a huge win for independant developers, as it shows that good things can come to those who work for them.
Get this game. Just...get it. As much as I love Super Metroid - the lonely atmosphere, taking down large boss enemies because Samus is awesomely powerful, the music, the exploration and cycle breaking...I am conflicted to say that this game may even be better than Super Metroid. They are very similar in game type, and this game does so many thing right. Super Metroid and Axiom Verge may have to live in my mind as co-favorite games.
TL:DR Get this game. If you hate it, Steam will refund you. Trust me, you won't hate it.

I'll tackle this first with a basic breakdown.
On the grahics
It's a pixelated game. Many gamers avoid these types due to them looking either dated or well there are just so many out there badly done. Bird story however, is well done. Some of that is the use of gray scale mostly which even in pixelated graphics adds wonderful shading. The game looks good simply.
On the audio
Firstly there is zero voice acting. No one ever talks. In fact the game uses thought bubbles which are either filled with (.....) or an image for the "need this" use.
Then you have the music. Considered soothing by quite a few out there. Personally I find it sad and depressing with no cathardic release. Think elevator music without a beat. It may be played well but you still don't really want to listen to too much of it.
On the gameplay
All you ever use is the arrow keys, the enter key, and the space bar. Walk this way, jump here, and pick that up.
And here is where I explain why I don't care for this game.
Sure it's visually apealing, but that just isn't enough for me. The protagonist is never apealing partlly because he's never really fleshed out. Bored in school and abandoned by parents is a flat and nearly facetless presentation. Walking around in a world where everyone else is a voiceless shadow requires a dynamic protagonist and they just don't give you one. The game tries really is supposed to be trying to get a deep emotional responce from the player. But you can't do that if there is just so little for a game to connect with.
Pros
Well made.
Kinda pretty to look at.
Has one accievement, if you manage to play through the whole game.
Has cards.
Cons
The music.
No one talks. Ever.
You never get to make any choices, it's all predetermined.
Linear one way plot.
Can a game be too short and yet entirely too long...
Honestly I understand a lot of players love this game. But I've played visialy graphic novels with vaster character depth than Bird Story delivers. There has been a lot of discussion on the age of players in regards to this game. Perhaps younger users get more out of this. I may be too worldly or mature for what it presents.
