ZombiU is arguably one of the best launch titles for the Wii U. A gritty survival game that managed to make great use out of the extra screen in the form of the Wii U gamepad. Unfortunately, the game sales was considered a flop to Ubisoft, and as such, I don’t think we will see a sequel anytime soon- if at all. ZombiU was one of the few games that made me actually wish that I had a Wii U, and I’m glad that this port was made so that I can play it without purchasing a brand new console.
Now titled Zombi on PC, Xbox One and Ps4- players will find themselves deep inside the heart of London after a zombie outbreak. With your base set up in the London Underground, you must traverse the maze of tunnels to reach other locations for supplies and other mission based challenges. You are able to find a variety of weapons and ammo, such as; Shotguns, Assault Rifles, SMG’s and so on- this is all fine and dandy, but you will end up using your trusty cricket bat more often than not, Shaun of the Dead style. The cricket bat combat can become repetitive for some players.
Combat is not fast paced, if you are going into Zombi expecting a run and gun Left 4 Dead esque game, then Zombi may not be for you. The game has instead gone for a slow style combat- before you can swing your cricket bat, you must first raise the bat using right click to which you can then swing at your foe. Weapons also take a while to reload, so you can definitely feel the tension as a small group of zombies start getting too close as you scramble to find a weapon that is loaded. As mentioned previously, people may find the cricket bat combat a little repetitive, and it is- you do the same swing and when you make contact with a zombie the same animations will appear- at first the skull will crack open and you continue hitting it until it stops moving. There doesn’t really seem to be much of a variety in the zombie combat, sometimes you can take one down with just one strike of your bat, sometimes it takes a few more strikes. I do not find the combat repetitive,  yes I am doing the same thing again and again, but the tense and adrenaline filled moments that I get really do mask up the repetitive motions- and the combat is definitely one of the main things about this game that makes it as tense as it is.
If you find yourself surrounded by zombies, there are a few things you can do. First, throw some flares to distract the zombies, and then throw a grenade to kill the zombies. Secondly, run-  run away as fast as you can to a safer location. If all these fail you then I’m afraid you may be dead, and this is where an interesting game mechanic comes into play.  If at any point you die in the game, that’s it for you, but that doesn’t mean that the game is over and you need to restart from a checkpoint- instead, that character is dead and you get to respawn as a new character. Any items that your previous character had on their person is now gone, unless you get them back. The character you previously were is now a zombie in the world, you can either find and kill them to get your items back, or just leave them. I found this game mechanic to be very interesting, and it definitely made me ponder on whether it not my previous character had enough items of value on them that it was worth tracking them down and killing them.
One of the concerns I had going into Zombi, and concerns that many people had, was how well does the game hold up without the use of the Wii U gamepad. Surprisingly, it holds up pretty darn well. On the gamepad you open barricades by tapping on the screen, on the PC version you just need to mash the Use key. Inventory management is very similar- On the Wii U they showed how all inventory management is done on the gamepads screen as the main game still plays around you. This is the same on the PC version, press Tab to open up your inventory, but be careful as a zombie may get you while you are busy searching through your bag. The Wii U gamepad was also used as the games scanner, a device where you can scan objects to see if there are any items in them, or to other tasks such as hacking.  On the Wii U, you had to hold up the  gamepad to and pretend it was a scanner – so at least on the PC version I feel like less of a fool when I have to use the scanner.
A problem that some of you may have, is that the PC version does use Uplay. I have no problem with this, I would much rather it was just Steam, but it caused me no problems. However, I do understand that many people do have problems with Uplay, so I am just pointing out now that Zombi does use Uplay. Most of the problems will come when you are trying to verify your game code so that Ubisoft knows you have legally purchased it, but if Uplays services are down, you are not going to get very far.
How is the port? Not bad. It maintains a solid framerate throughout the game, but I wouldn’t have expected any better from this game, because there is’t much on show to really lower the framerate. The texture quality isn’t great and everything looks a little rough around the edges- you can easily tell that this was originally a Wii U game, no doubt about it. There seems to be a bug that occurs when you have a controller plugged in but are using a mouse and keyboard, the button prompts will always display as if you were playing on a controller -so if you are not using a controller, make sure you unplug it from your computer.
Zombi is a well done horror game. It has made me jump on a number of occasions from scripted jump sequences and from the atmosphere the game provides.  If you have a Wii U, it may be better to purchase ZombiU instead, but if you do not own that console then you are not missing out on much when you play this version. Despite the game being a little rough around the edges, it is still an experience that I thoroughly enjoyed and I would recommend that everyone gives it a try.

You've probably already heard all the "Metroid-clone" comments in regards to this game, but to be honest I really didn't feel like I was playing a Metroid game. It honestly felt a bit more like what Half Life would be as a side-scroll adventure. There's a LOT to discover in this game, and quite a bit of it can be tricky without using Google (at least, it was for me). The story, environments, and creatures are all very bizarre, but in a way I found interesting. A lot of it is told through notes that are hidden around the game's world, and some of it could possibly be a bit of a challenge to grasp. There was more than once I would read a note I had found, and then say "So... science and♥♥♥♥♥♥"
Pros:
Good, tight controls (mostly, see cons)
Music is fantastic
Gorgeous pixel art, if you're into that sort of thing (which I am)
Interesting, thought-provoking story (mostly, see cons)
Lots of neat weapons and tools
Lots of hidden things to find
Boss fights were fun (mostly, see cons)
Cons:
One particular tool obtained later in the game tends to activate by accident very easily
Some of the guns lost their usefulness later in the game. Others never seemed to have any.
Story is inconclusive and barely explains itself
Final boss was a bit disappointing compared to the others
Personally the cons do little to keep me from loving this game. If you like what you see and hear in the videos, then you'll probably like it.

It's familiar, and yet it's not - and this works incredibly well to its advantage.
Taking the basics of the formula established by the Metroid series, it goes and builds upon it in a variety of ways. From the large assortment of weapons and equipment, to the glitches and how they allow for advanced traversal in the world.
Then there's the art style, ranging from simple 8-bit, to introducing more and more colour as you explore the world.
Plus, the soundtrack - ranging between unnerving, dischordant, and pulsing, which works incredibly well with the tone, and nature of the world.
All up, it feels, provides an good challenge - between the exploration, the bosses, and the exploration which you need to put in to be able to get to the end. Though, it has to be said, there are a few design choices I'm not the biggest of fans of - primarily the requirement to teleport by double tapping the thumbstick or d-pad - I felt it far too fiddly, and really only used it to get through environmental hazards as a result.
It's not a game you'll be putting down in a hurry though, and if you're in the mood for a platformer like this, then you'll absolutely love it.

It's so much like Metroid that I was convinced the entirety of my play through that I was playing a genuine NES/SNES Metroid. I'd go as far as say it's even better than Metroid. It has a clever way of copying stuff from Metroid while keeping the dynamics new and fresh. For example, instead of morph balling through narrow cracks, you drive a remote drone and later on in the game you get an ability to teleport where your drone is. This allows you to navigate to places that the drone couldnt reach, inside areas where you could not get in without the drone in the first place.. If you ♥♥♥♥ers know how Metroids play like at all, you know what I'm talking about. Just play it damnit and enjoy the eerie music.

An enjoyable metroidvania, what I really love about this game is the world it immerses you in. The aesthetic is a glorious effulgence of transhumanism, biopunk and simulationism. While I am hooked on the story, and I did feel compeled to suck every piece of information I could out of the text logs, it's been left rather open to interpretation by the time the credits roll. Questions remain unanswered. It's always very hard to know with these things, whether the answers the series will eventually provide in its sequels(And there better be sequels!) are going to be satisfying.

As a big fan of the Metroid series, I had a good amount of hype going into this game. I'm happy to say it lived up to it and more. The gameplay is a lot of fun and the difficulty curve was just right for me.

It seems a little expensive for a retro metroidvania platformer, but once you see just how good it looks, sounds and plays in person you'll understand how incredibly worth it this game is.

The original DUNGEON MANAGER ZV was very.... unpolished. It had a lot of spreadsheets and numbers, and very little visual information. This is much more of a game than that was, but in a way it suffers for that. The original was all about manipulating movement and building a very deep dungeon, with lots of strange mechanics; this is more of a tower defense. You still can build a dungeon, which is neat, but rather than the complicated free-play mode there's a campaign in which the starting dungeons are set up to challenge you. So it's more of a puzzle game or a tower defense than the strange dungeon MANAGER sim of the original, and I'm not sure I approve of that change... Still, it's a neat game, it's just different from the original. But if you're into dungeon keeper and stuff like that, then you'll probably dig it!

Okay, I'm recommending this game with a few caveats.
1. In about five days the main portion of this game, The Epic, will be released. Once that happens, you can expect a dramatic decrease in players on the other game modes. For Conquest, this is going to be catastrophic since it relies on many players to join a match. Therefore, do not buy this game for the gamemode you have seen streamers and YouTubers play.
2. There is a bit of a learning curve at the beginning. It's just a matter of learning the basic attacks (where to move your mouse for a certain attack) and developing tactics to better capture and defend the flag.
3. If you've ever played War of the Roses and read the cancerous messages in chat, you can expect that here and then some. Teamwork is a distant notion, it's like a giant public TF 2 match.
4. Servers have been acting up. Devs have fixed the issue as it occurs, so expect downtimes but not for long.
Other than that, it's a fairly solid game. No game breaking bugs.

This game isn't even big on the dating aspect. Compared to other visual novels/dating sims, Hatoful Boyfriend is a lot more straight to the point and fun to read, no endless rambling from the mc here. She is actually quite transparent but not in a dull way that you expect from most otome games.
Most routes can be completed within an hour, but rather than actually seducing the pigeons it's more like you get to know them better. All in preparation for the BBL route which you get once you've unlocked every boy's ending.
Hatoful Boyfriend seems just like a random silly game you'd play so you can comment 'Pigeons lulz!!" and make crappy bird puns on the internet, but the story turns out to be dark enough to keep you coming back for more. The way every character is woven into the big scheme of things here was really well done. Also there are no ero-scenes, which doesn't impact the game in the slightest. Nevertheless the endings (There are 16 in total) are very rewarding.
I thought it would just be a silly game, but I found myself really enjoying the narrative and trying to piece things together. Also I got a few laughs out of this and have a crush on a few characters. The soundtrack isn't bad either and the dialogue is quite funny.
Overall, a lot better than anyone would expect.

The Obligatory Disclaimer
Before I start this review, I feel I should mention two things...
1. Being the oldest of 7 children, I shared a room with two of my siblings. As a result, I spent a portion of my early years dreaming of what it might be like to be an only child, and to have a room all to myself.
2. I can't remember if this game came in a bundle, or if I impulsively bought it during a Steam sale, but upon rediscovering it in my library, I thought.. Oooo a very short game, with only one achievement!?  Should make for an easy 'complete game' to display in my Achievement Showcase.
And so, that is how I approached A Bird Story.
The Review
A Bird Story is a sweet, visually pleasing, children's story... Not that it's, necessarily, for children, but its goal, I believe, is to touch the mythical child within us all.
And, I suppose on that level, I would have to say that this game was quite successful.
Unfortunately, though, the child that awakened within me was this restless little brat who got bored after 35 minutes and began whining about wanting play Rocket League, instead.
Maybe it was the soft and subtle silence, of this game, that made mini-me want to seek out the big noise of Rocket League?  Or, perhaps, my inner little one's dream bubble burst, when it realized that, it actually might sometimes get lonely, being an only child?
Still, whatever the reason, in the end, it was the "grown up," achievement driven me, that finally completed A Bird Story.
A Bird Story is a fantastic and short pixel art visual novel that you need to experience.
I shared my ice cream with my bird like the boy in the game did. But my poor bird died. A bird story is based on lies!

A quaint stop-gap between To The Moon and Freebird's next major project. A Bird Story is more of a visual novel than a game. If you want a relaxing hour of entertainment without much thinking, this game may well be for you. The plot is as flismy as a paper plane, but it's worth playing for the soundtrack alone.

However the game is buggy - and these bugs are most pronounced when you die for something that you didn't deserve (say, clipping through the floor of an elevator and falling to your death, or clipping off a ladder and falling to your death - lots of falling to your death) and you lose a character that you may have put alot of time into. The game is just about good enough to keep you wanting more in the face of these really frustrating problems... until you factor in uplay.
Uplay is a pile of filth, not only because the very idea of it being forced on you is abusive but because it is a grossly incompetent service. The game failed to launch at least half of the time and would occaisionally crash back to desktop, but the real cherry on top, the real reason I am even writing this review, is when uplay stops everything to say you need to re-enter your activation code to bring the game up but then says the code you enter is already in use (because you entered it when you initially started the game) and then just leaves you stranded with a game you can no longer open. The initial levels introduced you to the concept of portals, game mechanics, play style and controls. The physics of the movement feel like a standard FPS, but add two portals and you have a whole bunch of new tricks up your sleeve! Ironically once you get your portal gun, the game stops feeling like another FPS. It looks like a shooter to on observer, yet it plays like a puzzler but with the new portal physics. I was recommended this game a long time ago, but I had never played it until now, I found it to be extremely fun and everything it had been hyped up to be.
You feel like a lab rat running a deadly maze, armed with your trusty portal gun and the promise of cake. You eventually find out all is not all as it seems, with secret rooms and crazed messages from other test subjects, making you thirst for more information about what is going on, who you are, and why you are here.
The first few levels really show you how the new portal physics can be worked to your advantage, how to grab things like crates to throw switches that open doors (familiar to the original Zelda puzzles), then new skills where timing your shots is thrown in the mix. A new switch is then introduced in the form of a deadly floating ball of plasma that you need to put back in its home. The gradual build-up of skills is in the Goldilocks zone, it’s not too hard, not too easy, it's just right. Whenever you feel stuck you just need to stop and look for the signs, because there is always a path to follow to get to the end of the level. There are signs in the form of visual cues (like lighting effects highlight a point of interest) to show you the order of the maze and its puzzle pieces. I found these subtle cues a great part of the game, as it helps the player navigate each step. The players can always see the WHERE, the challenge is figuring out HOW to get to the next bit. It usually involves improving upon already developed skills built on the previous levels. This gives the game a steady, natural flow.
So, I felt the game had a good flow, it starts with easy levels that progressively get harder as they balance your skill set accordingly. With each level being long enough to entertain, but also short enough to quickly jump on and just finish a single level. I spent many hours playing in one sitting which felt to me like minutes.

This is a very good example of what Indie games can be, besides Slender of FNAF. This game is a basic RPG that did a lot of things right, with only a few little fall offs. The story was good, not an intricate multi-level story, but enough to drive you to want to continue the game. Meanwhile the combat is the basic RPG maker system, which is not THAT bad, but could feel more engaging.
The art work for the game is actually pretty good, it melds the color pallete nicely, it gives the game a rust-like brown that shows its metallic and manmade (Which I think fits the story nicely).

Awe, that's the end? Okay. Well, that was a good game. I just beat it on normal and I am wondering if there is a game plus or an alternate ending. It holds true to the classic metroid feel with some additions that I really love. The awesome array of weapons is fun and offers a lot of solutions to "problems". The enemies vary greatly and have the kind of AI I would expect in a game like this. The glitch mechanics are a blast to play with and the exploration was rewarding. The music fit well and only bugged me in one area. The art direction was VERY nice. It fit well with the games feel, well crafted, really felt like a turbo graphix 16 game, but with some occasional warpy effects.
A couple of things to watch out for, the sound has a weird glitch on my system where everything becomes louder when the music is not playing. That is annoying, but not a game breaker. Unfortunately the biggest hurdle in this game is controls.
I had to remap my controls several times as I got new abilities that crowded up my controller. Some items become kinda worthless as well, but still demand a button. I wish I could disable items in my inventory. The best thing I did was learn to use the D-pad again, because THAT thing is ONLY for direction and does not double as a button. The "double-tap" on the analogue stick is janky as hell and you'll  be dodging all over the place when your just trying to move about normally or are aiming and running. Same with the bombs! I had to put bombs on R3 and quick select on L3, learn that D-pad, and it's all good.
All in all, solid game with some really nice surprises.
Looking forward to the rest of the game, aka, resolution of the cliffhanger with sooooooo much unresolved. Make more games T-Happ! I will buy them!

Skyborn is a short but well executed RPG. It is an RPGMaker game, but the creativity present in this game allows it to shine despite the limitations of the engine.
Unlike many RPGs, Skyborn has zero random encounters. You encounter enemies by running into an enemy sprite on the map. The downside of this system is that enemies do not respawn, limiting resources somewhat. The lack of spawning enemies might be a limitation of RPGMaker, but Skyborn is so well polished that I can't even call this a limitation.
As a result of the enemy encounter system, there is effectively no gringind. Though this did shorten the game considerably, it kept it very much to the point. Leveling does very little to make things easier. Rather, what you do with your items, skills and equipment will ultimately determine the outcome of every encounter.
During battle, the order in which each character may act (both allies and enemies) is displayed, allowing for deeper levels of strategy. The display wasn't immediately self-explanatory, but I couldn't help but get excited once I realized what it was. A character's speed reflects the number of times they can act before another character. Speed is a critical factor in Skyborn. It can be increased with some careful planning, but will fall drastically if a character is loaded up with equipment that is heavier than they can handle.
The graphics are pleasant to look at, and are of a very high quality for a retro 2D RPG. If you don't believe me, check out the screenshots for this game. There's no background graphics for battles (the map graphics are darkened considerably), but this ironically kept me more immersed in the battle itself. The environments are varied and gameplay elements encourage exploring. Even when it's detrimental, I never go straight for the boss. I can't help myself.
The story is decent, well executed, and draws you in. On the down side, it is a bit short, and nothing surprising happens. Optional quests are also somewhat lacking due to the game's length, but most are quite fun and challenging.
There is an optional super-boss very near the end of the game. If you have any plans on beating it, you'll probably want to keep a save file before the point of no return, so you can experiment with equipment and other such things.
Skyborn is a much more casual RPG experience than I'm used to. But there are plenty of other casual RPGs that are phenomenal (Chrono Trigger and Earthbound to name a few). Skyborn isn't among the best RPGs I've played, but it is a clean, well polished game with its own unique charm.

I came into Axiom Verge ready to love it and while I did enjoy it I can't categorically recommend it. If you are into old school platformers and challenging combat scenarios, then you'll probably get a lot out of this game. Personally I really enjoyed the exploration aspects, but I found the controls and the combat too clunky. Normally I would be able to look past this, but I found the game frustratingly difficult, especially some of the boss battles, on the Normal difficulty. Unless you are really looking for a challenge, I would recommend going for an easier setting and then hopefully you might get a more enjoyable experience out of the exploration.
On the plus side, the art is great and nails the retro style of the Super Metroid era. The music and sound design is also pretty good and meshes well with the visuals.
Overall I enjoyed the game, but after beating the end, I was happy to be done with it and had no real drive to 100% the game.

Hearts of Iron has always been a favourite of mine.  I have played each game since its release and each new morph has always presented positive new challenges.  I like many of the aspects related to the game and endorse what they are trying to achieve.  However, HOI4 has the same frustrating aspects associated with HOI3.  When you start from 1936 as Germany you follow the progressive development of the nation and build up the overall forces of the nation.  You can conquer Poland, netherlands, Belgium, Luxembourg, france with a decent challenge,  Then it comes to Russia.  before even declaring war your forces are without supplies (just like HOI3).  Suddenly the game stalls because you can no longer offer anyhing of an attacking force.  It seems the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s who created HOI3 did not learn from all the negative press regarding the supply issue of HOI3 and have systematically included the same defects in HOI4.   Russia becomes an unconquerable domain because you do not have enough supplies to manouvre your forces into any real invasion force.  This was similar to HOI3 when all things were doable until you fought Russia and suddenly your supplies drained without any reasonable explanation.  Do not buy this game  - (I use the term game loosely because any enjoyment received at the early stages becomes quickly diminished once you reach Russia). They have completely failed to take on board customer feedback identifying that they care not for the overall enjoyment of their customers but are too engrossed in the accumilation of funds to listen.  I can say, with an element of disappointment because I genuinely think the game has many enjoyable features, that I will be discouraging all from purchasing future games of HOI, a game I fully endorsed until HOI3,  due to their inability to recognise their own failings, even when they are presented to them by genuine fans of the game

Longer review version:
The good
-Generally fun.
-Easier to play compared to previous installment (Hearts of Iron 3).
-New battle orders are supposed to help ease the tedious work of micromanagement in Hearts of Iron 3. They are useful to help automatically cover your flanks as your main spearhead advance.
-Less micromanagement needed for controlling navy and air force. Instead of fighting from province to province like the land force, they now operate in regions of multiple pre-designated provinces.
-With experience gained on the battlefield, you can now create variance of your equipment, and name them however you like. For example, Tiger 1A has increased armor; Tiger 1B has less armor but better engine, hence faster moving speed.
The bad
-No air supply available, a very important aspect of warfare omitted by the developer DELIBERATELY.
-You have no control over creating convoy route, the AI will do it, in a very careless manner. They will create route where it will pass through enemy controlled sea area and you can't do anything but to helplessly watch your convoys getting raided from time to time until you don't have any ship left.
-No longer have Support Attack option, which allows divisions from adjacent provinces to support the attack of your main attacking force without moving themselves away from the currently situated province.
-Battle plan executed by AI is very dumb, it relies on sheer number and strength of your army to win. The AI will keep throwing your troops to fight even when there is no battle advantage on your side. Which leads to the fact that it keeps draining out your manpower and equipment reserves. This is okay if you play with a nation that has huge resource reserves, but as Germany or some small countries, this is suicide.
-AI don't know how to protect themselves, if you don't take a look at them for a while, they will get themselves surrounded and you can't do anything but to watch them being circled and annihilated.
-AI keeps moving divisions around for no reason when you give them battle plan order. Even worse is that they may move your troops on sea even when there is just like 2 provinces away on land, which makes your divisions extremely vulnerable to naval attack. I personally almost lost 3 divisions because of this, luckily I had a fleet nearby to intercept (thanks to the extremely fast moving speed of navy in this game somehow) but then as they were getting back on land, the enemies already moved their troops into that province which leads to the situation that I now have to fight an amphibious landing and received all the penalties to go with it.
-Frontline orders are supposed to help move your divisions forward together as your force punching through. But they always waste time surrounding empty province with like 4 or 5 divisions, which leads to huge deficit of troops to fight on the ACTUAL frontline.
-Naval invasion progress of many small islands is now extremely slow because you have to create a naval battle plan order for every single island and it requires preparation time before execution.
-Transport ship no longer available in games and their role is replaced by convoy, which means sometimes their reserves are used up for trading instead of moving troops.
-Extremely clunky user interface, which makes it difficult to switch between the Army, Navy and Air Force view, and since you always have to switch between them...
Other technical issues:
-Slow loading screen.
-Minor bugs when creating battle plan at times like you can't choose the destination for a naval invasion, and have to turn it off and on again in order for it to work correctly.

Or perhaps you're the temp file in someone's porn directory, who knows. You're thrown into the game without much context of anything, and unless you read the About This Game section on Steam, you won't even know that the secondary weapons don't do damage until you're left staring the enemy you just launched a missile into straight in the face.
For the most part, the game was a straight learning experience. I was drawn to this game because of its pseudo-80s banner art and the bright colors in the trailer. Also, because Steam recommended me it. Since I've been playing all these garbage games, Steam must think they should be able to sell me all the bad games at this point, but I digress. The game plays
; if okay is a seizure inducing buggy shoot-em-up. You're able to clip through walls by applying your back to any wall, and shooting whatever weapon you have. The recoil puts you into a wall. . Other than that, you can't do damage to yourself, but you can throw yourselves off of buildings and try to test your sensitivity to epilepsy. I actually believe this game may actually begin to be used to diagnose epilepsy by all the top hosptitals in the country.

Originally made for the Wii U as "Zombi U" but then ported onto PC. This game is...alright at best.
I have to mention that Zombi is prone to crashing....combine that with the fact you can only save by going to the safe house and this can be very anoying. When I first started the game I lost about 40+ mins of playtime and then the next day I lost 4 hours of progression. Just take every single chance you can to save your game. Also quite scary sometimes.
Now to the gameplay...its very fun overall even though it doesnt really do much special throughout the game. The majority of the time you will be using the cricket bat (or one of the other 2 better weapons later on). Killing zombies with these is very repetitive which mostly consists of hitting them over and over and over and over using the exact same head-hitting animation for every zombie in the whole game. Default weapons/items still take up your limted inventory space as you cannot remove them to put them in storage for some reason, despite having a better version weapon of the default cricket bat you have to carry this useless thing around because survivours love cricket apparently. Ammo is very scarce but in my opinion its like candy because it makes the game feel fun compared to everything else. I found around 12 guns in the game, half of which are better variants of the same weapon however weapon upgrades are everywhere.
Though you can see the game has some empty content as in the weapon upgade menu you can see supressors and scopes are an blanked-out option  so you are only limited to slight stat-increases. In addition some guns are basicly useless due to finding them near the end of the game and having almost no ammunition in the game aside from the very rare chance a ZOMBI drops 1 bullet (I'm looking at you magnum).
The story of the game is what you expect from a zombie survival game (almost no-existant, exculding a select few) and the game feels sort of short if you dont try to look for the extra weapons or upgrades (the letters are required for the story though).
Overall the game is alright. play it long enough and you can see it was made to be bigger and more polished but never reached the point. I recommend it if its on sale but remeber it may crash and anoy you.

Overall I felt this was a good game, good story behind it and plenty of jumpscares which kept it interesting. I had only 4 issues with this game, two of them small and the other two intertwined.
Problem 1: Melee Combat, this can get very repetetive even with the new melee weapons you find throughout the game.
Problem 2: You can't use the scopes on scope weapons or aim down the sights, I find this to be a big issue as with some weapons you could be hitting your target at a range easily with aiming using the sights is not possible in this game, especially with scopes. Sure this problem is remedied slightly having upgrades to your weapons to reduce spread, but it only remedies it to an extent.
Problem 3: Saving the game, i'm used to going through doors and the game saving for me or "fast travelling" or going into the menu and pressing save game, in ZOMBI this is not possible as you have to sleep in a designated save bed/sleeping bag.
Problem 4: Crashing, so far I have only crashed once in ZOMBI and this was a hug pain in the♥♥♥♥♥because I was just about to complete a mission, getting the anti-biotics from the nursery and as those of you who completed that mission know how easy it is to♥♥♥♥♥♥your pants in the process. So it had to load me back before I even started the mission, this issue ties in with saving as the save system is spot specific.
Well thats what I think about this game so far and I thouroughly enjoy the game aside from these problems and I reccomend this game to those who like games in the horror/zombie genre.

In short, this game is fantastic and well worth playing.
It's impressive enough that Axiom Verge was designed and created by a single person. What's even more impressive is just how professionally crafted it is. The level design is superb, the items are unique and well thought out, and the massive array of weapons are varied and useful in their own particular ways.
Even more importantly, the controls are spot-on (I played on a PS2 controller run through a USB converter). This is especially apparent when using the Tethered Charge weapon. With the full collection of items, there's some crazy acrobatics you can accomplish.
The story is told primarily through text boxes and SNES-esque cutscenes, and never felt overdone or particularly obnoxious. It's also pretty compelling, and I was curious to see how it'd play out. Furthermore, playing on Speedrun mode removes all the story elements completely, for a pure run-through.
My only real complaint was the lack of difficulty on most of the bosses. With the exception of the later few, bosses were complete pushovers (even on Hard difficulty). Considering how impressive and intimidating they are, it was odd how most enemies posed more of a threat.
That aside, Axiom Verge was an absolute blast to play, and having just finished my first play-through, I'm already starting on a second!

This game is an absolute dream for those interested in both history, and alternate history alike, specifically that of the Second World War. What is truly compelling and easily engrossing is that the game is engineered to give you the option to play in accordance to the true historical timeline (I.e. Soviet Union invades Finland, Japan expands throughout Asia/bombs Pearl Harbor, German Reich pursues Anschluss with Austria, etc.), or you can turn off the historical timeline and instead exerpience a Europe where it's nations pursue their own agendas, many different from what they were in reality. For instance, with the historical timeline turned off, you could very well have Poland form the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, have France turn to Fascism and ally with the Reich, or watch as the British Empire engages in a colonial war with Portugal then annexing its African imperial possessions. The possibilities are endless. From the main menu, you are given the option to pick out of a selection of the more prominent powers within this time period and play as that nation. Wish to try things a little unorthodox and choose not to take the helm of an international superpower? Fine. The game gives you the option to play as literally every country on the planet which existed at that time. Want to take the reins of rule from Ghengis Khan and aggressively pursue the expansion and eventual restoration of the Mongolian Empire? You can do that in HoI4. Play as Switzerland and pursue an aggressive policy of expansionism and militarism, expanding the Swiss armed forces drastically through conscription and arming them with the latest weaponry designed by the Germans. Expand Switzerlands borders southwards, easily exterminating Italy's incompetent garbage soldiers and annexing vast swaths of Italian land, giving the Swiss a coastline for the first time in their history and thus pursuing the formation of a Navy. All of this is possible in ahistorical mode. Regarding the games mechanics, I can happily say, as one who indulged 100's of hours playing HoI3, that this game is far more intuitive and easier to get into than its predecessor. Albeit you will certainly need to play the tutorial first, as well as looking up advice from experienced players on YouTube (as I did), but once you get the jist of it then it becomes easy to catch on. Commanding military forces this time around is way more intuitive than before. You create an army group, fill it with divisions up to a certain limit (unless the army is led by a field marshal, than there's no limit), assign a front line on the border of the nation you wish to invade, draw an offensive line over the city/general area in which you want your forces to conquer, give your army time to prepare (info is available on army icon at bottom of screen), than click the arrow that corresponds to the army in question and the invasion begins! That easy! Of course there are other elements of warfare that play a vital role, such as fighter planes, close air support, and strategic bombers, all which should NOT be neglected. Then of course you have your navy, depending on the nation you choose and if it has a coastline of course. The naval warfare element in this game is arguably the easiest to learn. In your production menu, you can choose from a large variety of ships and submarines to build and use at sea. Some take far more time to finish building than others which can be a burden to some. I usually amass a fleet of coastal and attack submarines to protect my shores from enemy invasion as well as to intercept precious cargo inbound to an enemy nation, which doing such in time will continually weaken the nation as it lacks the needed resources to expand their military. Beyond this relatively easy part of the game to learn, you are also a nations leader and have to make decisions, this is where the focus tree comes into play. You are given a vast selection of choices to make on matters ranging from econonony reform and industrial expansion, to forging alliances with other nations. While this certainly adds more depth and interest to the game, it does have its flaws. The main issue is that all focuses require a certain amount of time to pass until they take effect. Usually 70 days on average, but sometimes 180. For certain decisions that are vital at times when you need them quickly, like when the enemy is at your gates and your nation's fate relies on the outcome of that particular focus tree yet you unfortunately have to wait 120 days for it to activate, which by then your capitol has already been seized and your nation overrun by enemy armies. And I absolutely cannot end this review without mentioning the MODS!!!! HoI4 is directly integrated into the Steam Workshop, allowing you to browse the vast selection of mods available and simply click what you like and it automatically installs. No fuss or complicated installation procedures. The mods available for this game are nothing short of incredible. I personally cannot play this game without the mods, they are that amazing. The array of content you get from them is significant. Certain mods give you an alternate history setting where essentially everything in the normal game has been entirely changed when the mod is activated. One of these for example is the highly acclaimed mod 'Kaiserreich', which takes place in a timeline where the German Empire was triumphant in the Great War and is the leading power in Europe where you start at the usual 1936 date, but the entire world is vastly different compared to our historical timeline.
Overall, I think Hearts of Iron IV is a fantastic game that can suck you in for hours upon hours at a time. To me, that is a good thing. The flawed format of the focus trees are an issue but nothing that takes too much away from the game. The ability to play ahistorical and witness how Europe pans out if different decisions were made is simply incredible, and it keeps drawing me in for more. My main gripe with this game is it's downloadable content. Their prices are far too high while the content they offer is incredibly minimal. They usually price at $15 while realistically they should cost only $5 for what they offer. Perhaps down the road they will produce an expansion that really overhauls the game and adds rich content to it, therefor it be deserving of the $15 price tag.
While this game is not for everyone, it is certainly one of the best of its genre and I highly recommend it to those who enjoy challenging strategy and are properly versed in history.

A Bird Story is a simple but sweet game that I really enjoyed. A Bird Story was the prequel to the next game (Finding Paradise) in the To The Moon series. As an avid follower of this series, this game did not dissapoint and let down the To The Moon Standard. This game has no text in it, and some people may be turned off by this. However, I beg to differ as this game brings all its key messages through its emoticons and expressions. This is a high quality RPG Maker XP game and it is really made with excellence with me being a RMXP programmer before.
The story really gives a sweet start and conclusion all in an hour and at the end of the hour I was tearing slightly at the end. I really look forward to how the protaganist changed from this experience in his adulthood in the next game Finding Paradise. The Original Sountrack was well crafted and appropriate and is a great job done by Kan Gao and team.
Not much to be said about this game except that: A Bird Story is a short but fully enjoyable high quality game offering a fufilling one hour of gameplay that will touch your heart through a simple story. I strongly recommend this game to be played and if you haven't picked this one up! Please do yourself a favor and enjoy the story. If you haven't picked up To The Moon as well, the game before this one. Do pick it up from either steam or its standalone version. It's a great game alike.

Skyborn took me by surprise, not just because of the setting and the lush steampunk visuals, but the fun gameplay. The combat has a threat system that's not groundbreaking, but it adds a certain amount of strategy other than button mashing.
For reviewers who complained about Skyborn not being an open world, it is not that kind of a game. This is a narrative-driven title where the player takes on the role of a surprisingly endearing female main character. I say surprising because JRPG females usually bore me to tears. Here, Claret is spunky, smart and has dialogue that actually made me smile.
+The other party members are equally memorable, and their portraits really communicate their expressions well.
+The story is also decent, predictable yet enjoyable, with a twist I did not see coming!
+The game was short enough that it didn't outwear its welcome.
+Exploration and gather resources is fun, if not indepth
+I have to applaud the developers for NOT piling info dump on us, and letting the world and the dialogue describe the setting.
Not So Good is what feels like an unexciting crafting system, and the story's tendency to remind the player of Skyborn prejudices again and again.
: This is definitely a worthy buy! I actually found myself wishing I could explore the game more at the end. 8/10

So I want to start by saying I have not finished this game, nor do I plan to. Overall, it's not a bad game, really. It has a few hiccups here than there you come to expect from indie games such as collision detection issues. For a game created in RPG maker, its really nice.
I also noticed when I was dual wielding pistols, and one was very weak the other very strong, but they both hit for the same damage. I don't know if they just calculate the formula then split it that way, or if its really only taking into account one; this was an annoyance when testing weapons.
The game itself was pretty fun, I enjoyed the crafting and augmenting system a good deal, the story was pretty nice, and the characters were all solid. It had one major factor that ruined it for me: the difficulty.
As i said I havent finished this game, so maybe it gets harder; but I am currently 2 hours into it, and have yet to have any party member die nor have I felt the need to use an item. After two hours I feel I should have something to think about, but instead I have a character with 3 AoEs that an pretty much wipe the map (and this is with pretty bad weapons) and a tank that can always hold aggro and never dies. The bosses are laughably easy, I dont think any of them have brought any of my characters below 80% health.
Aside from the mobs being horrendously easy, there is also never a point where you are in danger. All the mobs you can simply ignore and walk past, no line of sight or anything to really worry about, so anytime you are low on health you can just go to one of the various healing points (which are free) and heal up. Their is usually one somewhere in a dungeon, so if you wanted you could go in between every mob you fight. The mobs also don't respawn (not a big deal, since you will never find yourself needing to grind) which is just a personal annoyance of mine.
I even gimped myself a bit, i began to not augment things and not really buy any upgrades; hell, two of my characters didn't even use all their gear slots, and I still had no worry at all.
If you want a casual game to walk through with a decent story, by all means pick up this game. Just expect to kill all the mobs using the same tactic and never having a real challenge out of it.

The initial levels introduced you to the concept of portals, game mechanics, play style and controls. The physics of the movement feel like a standard FPS, but add two portals and you have a whole bunch of new tricks up your sleeve! Ironically once you get your portal gun, the game stops feeling like another FPS. It looks like a shooter to on observer, yet it plays like a puzzler but with the new portal physics. I was recommended this game a long time ago, but I had never played it until now, I found it to be extremely fun and everything it had been hyped up to be.
You feel like a lab rat running a deadly maze, armed with your trusty portal gun and the promise of cake. You eventually find out all is not all as it seems, with secret rooms and crazed messages from other test subjects, making you thirst for more information about what is going on, who you are, and why you are here.
The first few levels really show you how the new portal physics can be worked to your advantage, how to grab things like crates to throw switches that open doors (familiar to the original Zelda puzzles), then new skills where timing your shots is thrown in the mix. A new switch is then introduced in the form of a deadly floating ball of plasma that you need to put back in its home. The gradual build-up of skills is in the Goldilocks zone, it’s not too hard, not too easy, it's just right. Whenever you feel stuck you just need to stop and look for the signs, because there is always a path to follow to get to the end of the level. There are signs in the form of visual cues (like lighting effects highlight a point of interest) to show you the order of the maze and its puzzle pieces. I found these subtle cues a great part of the game, as it helps the player navigate each step. The players can always see the WHERE, the challenge is figuring out HOW to get to the next bit. It usually involves improving upon already developed skills built on the previous levels. This gives the game a steady, natural flow.
So, I felt the game had a good flow, it starts with easy levels that progressively get harder as they balance your skill set accordingly. With each level being long enough to entertain, but also short enough to quickly jump on and just finish a single level. I spent many hours playing in one sitting which felt to me like minutes.

The Bureau: XCOM Declassified is the first XCOM game I played, and the only one I have played through completely (on 360 hence the low gameplay time here.) Owning it again now, the game (and its DLC) are still enjoyable, despite showing their age in graphics and occassionally falling flat via the over the top cheesy "gee, shucks!" portrayal of the era.
The Bureau is more or less a third person shooter mixed with some tactical elements, including a time slow which you can then order the other 2 (of your 3 person squad) around to flank enemies to increase the damage they are doing, deploy shields for other team members to hide behind, throw a mine behind them, as well as a variety of other actions determined by the classes you set for each one of them. While you are issuing these commands you can also browse the battlefield for nearby ammo or an assortment of guns including shotguns, sniper rifles, pistols, and a variety of alien technology.
Each member of your squad will focus on a particular ability set and weapon. For example, the engineer style class will have a shield to deploy and be limited to using SMG pistol type weapons, while the recon class will be able to cloak and deliver high-damage singular shots to targets but be limited to sniper rifles. As you and your squadmates level up, you unlock more abilities, however you have to choose which of two available at times, such as choosing between a turret that fires exclusively machine gun rounds -or- exclusively rockets, each with their own benefits. Beyond that there isn't much character customization. You can change the color of their outfits or equip them with a backpack which will add a buff such as increased headshot damage. You do find quite a few of these backpacks throughout the course of the game if you browse the environment enough.
The game has a good variety of levels and you see many different locations from an abandoned, desolate high school during the first of the invasion, to the interiors of complex alien spacecraft, to bombed out farms scattered amongst hillsides. While these all look pretty good and alternate often to avoid tedium, you also don't spend too much time exploring them aside from what's ahead of you, and the game can feel a bit linear.
The cutscenes between these are mostly over the top action shlock, and the game has a certain Independence Day meets Mars Attacks! level of sincerity in what it's delivering, balancing between fun retro sci fi  to seeming shtick early on in the story, the game concludes on a really high note and I felt immersed in the story and characters as I tried to keep my entire squad alive during the playthrough. I wasn't expecting to be as invested in the characters and story by the game's conclusion, as the early depiction of them can be a bit one-dimensional.
I enjoyed most of the game quite a bit and have been enjoying this 2nd playthrough on PC as well, however the game is beginning to look a wee bit "old" graphically... Still, its lighting effects, enemy design, level variety, and particle effects (smoke billowing from fires, lasers cutting through the air, etc...) still look pretty sweet. If I recall, I had to disable a certain video setting (NVIDIA PHYSX possibly?) to avoid the game crashing while playing on Windows 10, and looking at the forums for similar issues before determining to buy the game wouldn't hurt.
All-in-all a fun game with a setting that fans of retro sci fi / horror / "military opposing alien force" storylines may enjoy. Its blend of third person shooter and strategy elements may not appeal to everyone, but I found its time pause mechanic, issuing orders to teammates, and wanting to keep them alive to be a cool experience with an in-depth, evolving storyline.

A true sidescroller in the vain of Metroid and Castlevainia. It should be remembered that this is NOT an rpg or a multiplayer game - if youve played a metroid game for the GBA then you get the picture...
Depending on your prefferences a complete campaig lasts 6 - 20 hours, including exploring and collecting the decent number of upgrades and powerups. The upgrades themselves are interesting and intuitive, most being fairly usefull while not being crazy - a remote drone, a grapplehook and so on.
Aside from this their are also a BUNCH of weapons, some of which you almost have to pick up, but a lot of which are hidden and require some attention to find. These are mostly varied and unique, tho there are several which are barely useful.
The the campaign is story driven, and although you are mostly left to play the game yourself when a cutscene appears it does not break the flow and proves to be both interesting from a story point of view and effective in terms of creating atmosphere (which this game has in buckets and more) and directing your attention in game to the next objective. On top of this, you can collect notes and notices to pad out the world and all its glory.
Long story short, a game well worth playing for anyone who enjoyed the early sidescroller/exploration games, or for those looking for an engaging scifi experience.

Oh boy where do I begin?
Well I guess I start of by introducing the man who gifted us his love letter to the metroidvania genre.
Thomas Happ, or Tom Happ as he’s called, might be a name you could be familiar with if you played games like
or
.
Axiom Verge is his
part-time hobby which started in March 2010.
After 5 years he went ahead and released the game on March 31st, 2015 for the PS4 and for the PC on May 14th.
Now here comes the thing that amazes me the most. He worked
on the project.
So Tom Happ is responsible for the amazing pixel art, the fitting soundtrack, coding and of course game design.
So after I’ve introduced the man himself to you let’s dive into
You slip into the role of Trace, a scientist in the near future. After your labor blowed up you awake on an alien planet and you hear a strange voice , which you can barely understand …
Now before I get into the Story let me talk about something else first.
Boy I really fell in love with the game. Despite my lack of hours I’ve put in, thanks to that thing they call
(sigh), I’ve seriously fallen for the game.
Nostalgia … NOSTALGIA!
Excuse me. Now let me explain. It’s nearly impossible to talk about
without talking about
, one of Nintendo’s finest.
Basically this game looks, feels and plays like a love letter to
. And this isn’t even a bad thing! Au contraire!
Well you see for the
, or let’s be a bit nicer and say for us
it’s something we longed for. We wished for. We needed.
While there are numerous good games on the market, be it 2D, 2.5D or 3D there’s nothing quite like a Metroid or a Metroidvania for that matter.
And boy this game is one of the best if not THE BEST Metroidvania which was released in the last years.
As you might have noticed, I do have quite an affection for Metroid and the Metroidvania genre.
But let that not blind you! While I get critically hit by the games Nostalgia strike, I have to say it’s damn near perfect. Especially if you consider that one sole human being was responsible for it.
I don’t want to spoil too much so I try to keep it rather short, since exploration is key for any
.
As I mentioned earlier you slip into the role of Trace, a scientist, which awakes on an alien and high-tech planet after suffering a fatal injury. Confused as to where he is and whether he’s still alive or not and what this is all about he tries to makes sense of his situation.
After hearing a strange voice which seems to try to help him he ventures into the next room and finds a Weapon …
Thus begins your Story in
.
With a weapon in your hand, it’s now up to you to explore your new environment and try to make sense of your situation. Death? Illusion? Afterlife? Reality? Dream?
It’s now up to you to figure out what exactly happened to you.
After you’ve explored a bit you might notice the game has several glitches. Those are intended. Those glitches can be anything. Power Ups for your character or even Secret Rooms. It’s up to you to find them to gain new powers so you can explore every bit of this weird place you’ve found yourself in.
You’ll find numerous Power Ups which will help you out in one way or another.

The Drill for example allows you to, while dealing damage to enemies, destroy certain rocks which will occasional block your path.

This is an amazing game!  It plays like a sequel to Super Metroid from a universe where 3D games never happened, except that it manages to set up an almost completely distinct set of power-ups that work in subtly different ways from the standard Metroid loadout.  The game has the same great sense of exploration and discovery as the best games in the Metroid series, but is a bit more modern and forgiving in some ways (for example, you keep your power-ups and explored map tiles if you die).
One interesting divergence is that it provides a ton of optional weapons.  These mostly don't unlock new progress through the game, but many prove very useful in certain situations.  Clever weapon selection can completely change the difficulty of some of the boss fights, for example.  There are almost *too* many; in my time with the game I've barely touched at least three or four.
This game is one of my best recent buys, and easily one of the best PC "Metroidvania"-type games out there.  Worth every penny!

Pros:
+ Interesting style and concept.
Cons:
- The serverlist doesn't work, or there are just 0 people playing this game. In other words, you're not going to play this multiplayer.
- There are no bots when you host and you have no host options. In other words, you're not going to play this singleplayer.
- The FPS is capped at 42 for some reason, or it's just so horribly jammed full of the visual effects that it rests at 42 FPS on a rig that can run CS:GO at 200. In a time when 60 FPS is standard and 144 FPS is competitive, making an arena shooter capped at 42 is ridiculous.
- The physics and collision are tissue-thin, letting you walk through walls with next to no effort. Player physics is supposed to be one of the heavily QC'd elements of an arena shooter, as mobility directly relates to strategy in fast-paced games like this.
- None of the options in the options menu do anything. But there's not even options for the things that there should be in arena shooters, i.e. heavily adapatable graphics options to let you strip away all the flashy nonsense. But the main selling point of this game is all of the ridiculous visual effects that occur when you shoot people, so that's out.
I understand that this was a Jam game and was probably made in a weekend or something, but I expected some kind of actual gameplay. Selling something that you can't play for $3 on Steam is an insult and a scam. Valve should remove this "product".
If you want a novel arena shooter, play Robot Roller-Derby Disco Dodgeball, as it's infinitely better than this.

Ahh the ’80s, what a time to be alive! Mullets, tacky clothes, seizure-inducing neon colors, cheesy movies, synthpop, the golden age of gaming, AIDS and so much more. What a crazy time, the ’80s are truly the pinnacle of the 20th century. Everybody loves this decade because it was too damn fun. Alas, RAM is not.
RAM is an arena shooter set in an epileptic’s worst nightmare, hope you like neon and flashing lights, because boy you’re in for a treat. See, I like the game’s theme – the sounds, the atmosphere, they’re spot on, they make you feel as if you’re playing the intro sequence to Transformers G1. The gameplay, on the other hand, will make you want to phone home.
Health bar, guns, arena. Where can you go wrong? Ahahaha, what can go wrong, will go wrong. To start with, you can only deal damage with one weapon, an SMG that does so little damage, it’s as if your enemies are all T-800s . The other weapons (not that there are a lot of ’em) glitch out your opponent’s screen with flashy pop-up ads and blue screens. Funnily enough, these effects physically assault your eyes and will give you a headache, so if you want to harm your friends, RAM is a good choice. Your “Rambot” is no Rambo, since shooting will push you back, better hope your back isn’t against a wall, because guess what, YOU CAN NOCLIP THROUGH WALLS. Maybe RAM is a social commentary on the Berlin Wall, it’s eluding to the fact that it was a monument to mankind’s ignorance and that it was a wall just because we let it be a wall. That or, the devs slept through the first classes of Game Development 101.
The maps are bland and poorly thought out – just a bunch of platforms with so many pitfalls, this game would have been a hit on the Atari 2600. There is no scoreboard, no way to rebind controls, there is an abundance of glitches, you can either play it in full screen or beat it, the music loops over and over and over and over and over and the real kicker: nobody plays it. The game is a ghost town (and it just released this week!), you’d have better luck finding another player in No Man’s Sky than in this game. At least you can play with bots, I mean it is an arena shoo — no, there are no bots in this game.
Performance wise, the game at least runs well. The FPS hits numbers so high it might even go back to the future (hey, they don’t need walls where they’re going). The game is also pretty small (~200 mb), so you can install the game, play it and then uninstall in just under 15 minutes! (rest assured, I put much more time in this game for the review)
The game isn’t unplayable, no no no, I mean you can walk forwards, you can jump, you can even look around with the mouse! But if you can’t even nail simple FPS gameplay, why even bother in the first place? Perhaps I’m being too hard on the game, the devs promised character progression, patches and much more in the future, they may or may not deliver and hey, the game does have an interesting premise and the ’80s feeling it conveys is cute … but in its current state, the game is definitely:
/ A Try During Sale / A Must-Have
Hmm the game does have a neat name though. A nice play on words, reminds me a tad bit of that Daft Punk album (Random Access Memories). It’s also cheesy enough that it would have made for a great action movie title, 30 or so years ago.

Now, first of all, since this is not mentioned anywhere on the store page, the actual name (from the game credits) is The Girl and the Robot - Act 1. Game ends on a "To be continued" and the developer says on the forums that the Act 2 will be most likely a separate game. This seemingly intentional "shyness" to say what the game is, however, is not why I cannot recommend it.
I cannot recommend it because it doesn't feel like a proper made for release game to be sold for actual money.
The Girl and the Robot feels like a suprisingly long (3 hours) game jam game, made by inexperienced but talanted people as a "hey, a cool game can be made out of this" demo. Except no cool game was made out of this, this IS the game. And it's a frustrating experience from start to non-existent finish.
Controls and animations never feel right. Combat is either easy (because it's dumb and seemingly made to be exploited) or stupid annoying and based on luck (because the encounter is designed to remove player-favorable exploits but leave in enemy-favorable ones). Occasional jumping moments feel random with it being as easy to overshoot the target as undershoot, depending on if you try using the rather badly done running before or not. "Puzzles" are more tedious, then challenging, with one requiring you to constantly switch between characters to see where to go, watching slow transitional animations every time. And The Girl simply dies if any enemy touches her once. Now way to escape, no way to save her even if when standing one step away as The Robot. She's touched - Game Over. Restart from a usually stupidly far away checkpoint.
The roughness of the game is obvious even in how every single transition in every single cutscene is a sudden gray screen for few seconds and how several locations lag horribly due to optimization issues. And in how so many things are just "there", how many things make no sound at all. How the world, despite the pretty art style, simply feels like a fast made map you'd find in a mod or a old multiplayer map, not in a puzzle and exploratory singleplayer game that really wants to look good.
The Girl and the Robot is not fun to play. It's not finished. It doesn't even feel like a game, rather than a concept, something to show the investors to get money for the actual game. It doesn't achieve what it promises, doesn't come even close. And it's a damn shame.

Before the WiiU launched, Zombiu was hotly tipped to be its first killer app, and whether you agree with that or not, it made a big impact upon its release. Critics and players alike were divided though, with many calling it “ugly”, “slow” and “repetitive”. Much noise was made around its novel use of the gamepad as a map and inventory screen, drawing your eyes away from any lurking zombies approaching on the TV. Yet, even the game’s harshest critics conceded that there was something special lurking beneath ZombiU’s rotting facade. But what is ZombiU without Nintendo’s unconventional controller? Zombi, as it is now known, plays the same as before but it is, arguably, all the better for having dropped the “U” from its name.
For all intents and purposes Zombi is the same game you can pick up for a fiver on WiiU, with the exception of a few changes. Combat is still clunky and dull, but a few new melee weapons thrown into the mix, and a slight attack speed increase. Graphically, the game is as dated as ever, with big ugly textures and asset repetition being commonplace. Multiplayer features have been ripped right out as well, leaving you with just the single player campaign to fight through. So, why then, is Zombi still so appealing, even with its many imperfections and cutbacks?
Playing as a lone survivor you’ll sneak around the derelict streets of London, while they are teaming with infected. Guided by “The Prepper” – a cynical ex-military survivor – you’ll work your way across the city from the underground to Buckingham Palace, all in a bid to stay alive, and escape to safety.
Survival is your focus in Zombi, and you’ll find plenty of equipment scattered across London. You can carry a limited number of items around with you in your bug out bag (B.O.B); a bag that holds your food, first aid kits and weapons. And here’s where things get interesting. If you get overwhelmed by the undead you’ll re-spawn in the underground as a new survivor – and you’ll need to get all of your old equipment back. To do so you’ll have to track down your previous character, cave their head in and make off with your loot. Lovely.
Once you’ve got your stuff back you’re free to pick up where you left off, before your previous survivor had their brains scooped out. You could argue that Zombi does little to endear you to your character, perhaps subtracting from, what is otherwise, an immersive game. You never really learn much about them, except for some intro text every time you re-spawn, so there’s no real personal connection tying you to the game.
As previously mentioned, Zombi is a little rough around the edges in the graphics department, but it still manages to succeed in creating a foreboding atmosphere. Expert use of lighting, shade and audio serves as proof that graphical fidelity comes second to well-designed environments and sound. This is a game where you’ll tentatively turn corners, flash your torch every few steps, and stop to listen for nearby undead. Paranoia becomes an asset rather than a burden, leading you to decapitate already dead enemies, look behind yourself every few seconds, and take the long way around to avoid encounters.
Zombi’s combat is never the focal point, and neither it should be because it’s rubbish. The game’s main appeal lays in its ability to mess with your head, make you preempt things and expect the unexpected. Outright scares are sparsely dotted throughout the game, evoking panic and disorientation at the worst possible times. Zombi doesn’t want you to win, and that’s why it’s so great.
The majority of horror games I’ve played simply try too hard to evoke a reaction from the player, but Zombi is different. It’s all too happy to let you become comfortable with your surroundings. It lets you become sloppy and the pounces on you with expert precision.
Although it’s far from perfect, as an original IP Zombi is among some of the better games and deserves a second chance to live.
Temper your expectations,  close the curtains and lose your head in its undead fantasy.

Longer review version:
The good
-Generally fun.
-Easier to play compared to previous installment (Hearts of Iron 3).
-New battle orders are supposed to help ease the tedious work of micromanagement in Hearts of Iron 3. They are useful to help automatically cover your flanks as your main spearhead advance.
-Less micromanagement needed for controlling navy and air force. Instead of fighting from province to province like the land force, they now operate in regions of multiple pre-designated provinces.
-With experience gained on the battlefield, you can now create variance of your equipment, and name them however you like. For example, Tiger 1A has increased armor; Tiger 1B has less armor but better engine, hence faster moving speed.
The bad
-No air supply available, a very important aspect of warfare omitted by the developer DELIBERATELY.
-You have no control over creating convoy route, the AI will do it, in a very careless manner. They will create route where it will pass through enemy controlled sea area and you can't do anything but to helplessly watch your convoys getting raided from time to time until you don't have any ship left.
-No longer have Support Attack option, which allows divisions from adjacent provinces to support the attack of your main attacking force without moving themselves away from the currently situated province.
-Battle plan executed by AI is very dumb, it relies on sheer number and strength of your army to win. The AI will keep throwing your troops to fight even when there is no battle advantage on your side. Which leads to the fact that it keeps draining out your manpower and equipment reserves. This is okay if you play with a nation that has huge resource reserves, but as Germany or some small countries, this is suicide.
-AI don't know how to protect themselves, if you don't take a look at them for a while, they will get themselves surrounded and you can't do anything but to watch them being circled and annihilated.
-AI keeps moving divisions around for no reason when you give them battle plan order. Even worse is that they may move your troops on sea even when there is just like 2 provinces away on land, which makes your divisions extremely vulnerable to naval attack. I personally almost lost 3 divisions because of this, luckily I had a fleet nearby to intercept (thanks to the extremely fast moving speed of navy in this game somehow) but then as they were getting back on land, the enemies already moved their troops into that province which leads to the situation that I now have to fight an amphibious landing and received all the penalties to go with it.
-Frontline orders are supposed to help move your divisions forward together as your force punching through. But they always waste time surrounding empty province with like 4 or 5 divisions, which leads to huge deficit of troops to fight on the ACTUAL frontline.
-Naval invasion progress of many small islands is now extremely slow because you have to create a naval battle plan order for every single island and it requires preparation time before execution.
-Transport ship no longer available in games and their role is replaced by convoy, which means sometimes their reserves are used up for trading instead of moving troops.
-Extremely clunky user interface, which makes it difficult to switch between the Army, Navy and Air Force view, and since you always have to switch between them...
Other technical issues:
-Slow loading screen.
-Minor bugs when creating battle plan at times like you can't choose the destination for a naval invasion, and have to turn it off and on again in order for it to work correctly.
Pretty bad optimization i have to say.

this game isn't what it appears. of course, i'm not going to give anything away in this review, but i think the reputation hatoful boyfriend has gained as some kind of goofy novelty game does it a disservice - it's telling that only 7% of players have actually fully completed it. the game's concept is silly, yes, but it's fully aware of its own absurdity and uses that against you. this was unexpectedly one of the most bizarre games i've ever played, and not even for the reasons you might be thinking. i don't think many people play hatoful boyfriend beyond their initial "haha bird dating sim" amusement, and thus miss out on the full intended experience.
on its surface level, yes, it's a bird dating sim. the birds each have their own quirks and personalities, and if you like any of them in particular you can find ways to gain their favor and romance them. the writing is humorous, the characters are memorable, and each ending is surpising and entertaining. after a certain number of endings, the game will unlock the "Bad Boys Love" route, which is practically an entire game on its own and where hatoful boyfriend really, really shines. it's in the BBL route that you finally get to learn the full history of the game's world and its inhabitants; characters become more thoroughly fleshed out and interesting, beyond their original simplistic dating game personalities, and the plot takes off in a far more complex direction than anyone would expect. in my opinion, the BBL route
hatoful boyfriend - it's by far the most satisfyingly thorough and well-rounded storytelling in the game. unfortunately, not many people seem to make it this far, and it's difficult to explain what makes it so great without spoiling everything.
if you don't mind visual novel gameplay, and you like surreal, sometimes twisted humor, get hatoful boyfriend. it's definitely the most unique and enjoyable visual novel i've ever played, and it might be entertaining even for those who don't typically enjoy this type of game. be patient, go into it with an open mind, and give it a chance to take flight.

Pixel Piracy is a fun strategy game / simulator that follows the lives of pirates. Randomyl generated, it provides a very large world to explore and conquer.
The gameplay itself is fairly diverse, allowing you to choose different styles of attack. You fight with a cannon-only approach, or go all-in ninja equiping everyone with shurikens for throwing.
The AI is fairly good, with different ships taking different tactics on how they attack you in return. Some have boarders that come to your ship, others stay at a distance and use cannons.
This, along with the massive amount of choice you have in how your ship looks and how your crew is set up makes for a great game.
The management aspect of the game is also very good. You can micro-manage pretty much anything you want, by levelling up particular skill sets for each memeber of your crew. Something important to note though: Pretty early on you want to equip one of your crew with the cleaning ability, or things will get hectic.
The style of the game [the graphics, and the music] are very nice. I felt that the bloom they had added was a bit over the top, but luckily the devs made that a disable-able option. I did find issues with the text not rendering very well at lower resolutions, but at anything above 720p you should be fine.
The major problem in the game only appears after you've been playing for a while. Due to the way the game saves data, you end up with a massive file that gets re-written to the disk every time you save your game. This makes moving between regions very difficult unless you turn off auto-save.
Also, the longer you play the fewer frames you get. Something in the game's logic means that each "turn" of movement takes much longer if your game has been going for longer. This makes going for 100% completion extremely difficult, even on a high end machine.
To put this in perspective: At the start, mving from one island to another might give you 20 seconds of prep time on your ship. At the end of the game, I ended up waiting up to a minute or more to move the same distance, due to the game running so slowly. This also makes it difficult to keep tabs on your crew, if they are ina  battle they could suddenly lose a lot of health and die without you having time to act.
This is a bit of a killer for me, and I would suggest that you avoid this game until the devs fix it. Unfortunately they seem to have "finished" the game, and the chances of this happening are slim. Which is unfortunate, as when the game is actually playable it is a very nice game.
