This review was last edited after about 10 hours play in the first 36 hours after early access release. It's probably worth mentioning I'd not played Mount & Blade before OKAM and never heard of OKAM until a few days before the EA release.
A 3D third person real time multi player only medieval fighting game that gave me a real sense of what I thought taking part in a medieval battle would be like. Its surprisingly addictive and fun to play.
Yes, there currently are issues with the server loads but nothing that anyone with a realistic expectation of an early access game should be put off by.
The first time you play the game there is a short tutorial to take you through the various stances. Whilst it shows you the basics I feel it needs to be substantially expanded
The main screen has the options PLAY, THE EPIC (currently just displays a map), OPTIONS, CREDITS & QUIT. A news log is displayed in the bottom right with latest gme info. A rather excellent song also plays whilst you are on the main screen :)
The OPTIONS screen allows you to set graphics, sound, controls, game & key bindings. The graphics options were all fairly obtuse to me. To switch between full and windowed screen use ALT Enter. The sound options were fairly straight forward, just using sliding bars for loudness. controls were again pretty obtuse. The game option was my favourite and had a single slider for "corpses limit". The key bindings seem to cover all possibilities. Note that the text on the main screen actually displayed through onto the options window and so made it difficult to read.
The PLAY option takes you to the "Barracks" screen where you can view your character stats and gear and choose to fight. It's all pretty basic.
CHARACTER stats are current experience/level, Skills (Damage, Hp, Speed & Attack speed) & Points which are awarded each time you gain a new level and can be traded to increase your skill level.
GEAR is where you choose which clothing & head pieces to wear & which equipment to equip. Currently melee weapon choices are: Studded MAce, Pole Axe, Small Axe & Cleaver Falchion, and a shield can be selected with the latter two weapons. There is also an option to equip a short bow. Progression options are displayed and you need to gain a certain number of points before they are available. I assume the points are awarded for using the current weapon in the progression. Better armour appears to be come available as you gain levels
The FIGHT option displays a match making dialog with up to four options: Duel, Skirmish (currently disabled), Conquest & Epic Battle (selectable but it never finds a match for me).
allows you to fight against a single opponent at a time by challenging them on a battle field. Only you and your opponent can damage one another although they may well be other duels going on around you!
is where you play on a team for capture/attack/defend the flag scenarios. The conquests occur in randomly chosen locations varying from open plains to small villages.
Everyone on your team starts off at one spawn point and everyone on the other team starts off at an opposing one; both seem to be on pretty much opposite sides of the flag location. Initially there can be a lot of jostling as you set off as the players are packed in tight at the spawn point.
There is a small arrow above players from your own team. I have to say though that I found this initially pretty difficult to spot, especially in the heat of battle. And yes there is "friendly fire" and yes I have killed soldiers on my own side.
There is an on screen indicator showing you the direction of the flag and how far it is away from you in meters; who'd have known these medieval bods were working in metric ;)
You are able to re-spawn a number of times if (or in my case when) you are killed and there is short wait before you appear back at the original spawn point, usually along with a number of other unfortunates. Once you have used up your re-spawns you can either view the battle field as an invisible entity or choose to follow another player around. Your re-spawn count seems to be reset each time a phase of conquest is completed which varies but about 5 minutes is the longest I've had to wait. Your quiver is restocked with arrows when you respawn.
Note that if you move close to the edge of the map the screen turns monochrome and if you move off the edge of the map you die. I know this from experience.
At the end of the conquest a stats screen displays your number of kills and number of times you've been killed. You can also bring this screen up at any time by pressing tab.
Currently the controls are pretty limited. You can move forwards, backwards and sideways as well as run (no jumping nor crouching yet). You use the mouse to ready and use your weapon and so move your vision around.
There is a global chat displayed on the fight screen where you see comments from both teams. There is also a window that shows recent kills.
Hit and experience points are displayed as bars in the bottom left of the screen.
You gain experience for assisting in or actually landing the killing blow on an opponent as well as well as being "close to the action" and capturing the flag etc. Each blow landed on you reduces your hit points and be aware a couple of well landed blows can kill you. Obviously each blow you land on your opponent reduces their hit points. There is no indication of an opponents current hit points.
If you want lots of gore you'll be disappointed. There are no actual wounds displayed by landing blows, although arrows do stick in and I assume give you an indication of the direction of attack.
Note that there are no NPCs, except in the tutorial. Every other character is another real life player

If you have an itch to play an old-school 2D Metroid than Axiom Verge is the game for you.  The game follows the classic Metroid formula with some modern game improvements.
For example, the various weapons are tactical in nature.  As opposed to Metroid where the guns just get predictably more powerful, the various guns in Axiom Verge display radically different characteristics.  Picking the right gun for the right situation is the key to succeeding in combat.  Fortunately, switching between the surprisingly large arsenal is quick and easy with a controller (native PS4 controller support!).
Another surprising aspect is the story.  Though at first glance it appears to be a minimalist tale like so many other Metroidvania games, notes scattered around the world reveal a deeper and more convoluted plot than what is initially presented.  Combined with a cryptic ending, there is definitely a path paved for a sequel.
The only downside for me was that the game was rather easy.  I played it on Hard for my first run through and the game only started to get challenging towards the last third or so.  The main reason for this is that the enemy behavior is not very complex or varied.  Most enemies fit into one of two categories: moving in a set pattern, and dashing straight towards you.  The first type are always easy to kill, while the second require more thought but are usually easily defeated with proper tactics and the right weapon.  Boss behavior is similarly limited with most bosses only exhibiting one or two patterns.
Ultimately, I feel that $20 was a bit much for what I got.  While I enjoyed the game, the lack of enemy variety and challenge doesn't inspire me to do multiple play-throughs.  I would say it would be a must-buy at $10, but for $20 you need to be a fan of Metroidvania to really appreciate it.
In conclusion, great controls (played with a PS4 controller), great music, cool pixel art, and all designed by one man.  I'm definitely interested to see what he will do next.

To start: I used to add a much longer header to these reviews, but since it often made the reviews too long to submit, I've opted to leave it on my Backloggery page.
Gameplay: o boi guiz its another indie metroidvania gaem. Yes, as we all know, Metroidvanias are a dime a dozen in the realm of indie games, and it's easy to see why: It's a genre that is very easy to make, but takes a lot of talent and effort to do really well. For every Cave Story and La-Mulana there's a deluge of mediocre to straight up awful Metroidvanias a few meters behind them. Axiom Verge is a Metroidvania style game in which there's a lot of Metroid and not a lot of Vania, which I do quite like, as the Metroid side of things allows the designer to go really crazy with the atmosphere and world building as opposed to "get the thing to increase your numbers."
As mentioned above, Axiom Verge feels a lot like Metroid, even down to the very first area of the game feeling a lot like Brinstar, complete with long vertical shaft with a bunch of enemies that run along the walls. It does start to branch off from there, as rather than breaking walls with things like power bombs or missiles, you are instead equipped with a drill. This drill can be used for combat purposes, but it's not too recommended as it does bugger all for damage. Another way in which this game branches away from Metroid is that you get a LOT of weapons throughout your playthrough. I ended up with ten different weapons by the end of the game, and while they're all pretty fun to play with, odds are you'll fall into one weapon and just use that for the rest of the game. This was a little disappointing, as I would've liked to see more environmental puzzles that made use of the characteristics of the weapons.
Powerups in this game are pretty neat, and there are a fair few of them that are pretty cool, but there are a few that feel like completely arbitrary gating mechanisms, with the most egregious example being one of the later areas in which you have to mine through more blocks with your drill than the average Minecraft player, only to receive a key "powerup" that moves literally two blocks in the world and that's it. In fact, there were more than a few powerups that felt like completely arbitrary gates, something that I think could've been fixed with more of a focus on environmental puzzles that make use of the weapons you have.
One of the most important things that you need to do right if you're going for a Metroid feel in your game is to get the world itself correct. The world itself is big, very big, but it does have a tendency to feel somewhat sparse after a while. Another problem with such a big world is that if you ever need to backtrack, it gets annoying very quickly. There is no teleportation powerup (unless I just didn't find it; if there is, let me know and I'll change this review accordingly), which really doesn't make sense given that you teleport to the last save point when you die. Speaking of such, one thing that I was definitely happy that this game did is that you never game over, so even if you die, you don't lose progress.
Enemies are your typical Metroid fare, wall-crawlers, spiders, things that shoot at you, and they do more damage as you go along because reasons. Bosses are really disappointing, especially given how cool they look. In fact, there is one boss where you can spend most of the time crouching and be perfectly fine. I did play through this game first time on Normal, so maybe the AI was tweaked for the bosses on Hard mode to make them actually threatening; I dunno. There was only really one boss that I would call challenging, and that's just because it does a lot of damage. The final boss was just a mashfest, honestly; dash around everywhere and shoot the thing from time to time.
Overall, I had a pretty good time with Axiom Verge. The world was pretty good, despite all the backtracking; there were pretty well hidden secrets that were fun to find, and even though bosses could've been a lot more fun to fight than they actually were, this could be something that was fixed on Hard mode. If you've played something like Environmental Station Alpha, I'd definitely play this on Hard first time through. It manages to be pretty good, but not fantastic. 7/10.
Story: The story, or at least what all I got of it from this playthrough as you need powerups to translate some of the alien text, is actually pretty cool. It's written quite well, even though it gets a little bit up its own♥♥♥♥♥♥from time to time (a line from a page that goes, "As everyone knows from the Euclid Equation..." Yeah, as *everyone* knows...). The only "real" character in the game - and that's somewhat questionable from time to time - is the character you play as, called Trace. Trace is/was a scientist at a facility that blew up, science happened, and now you're in an alien world. Without going into too much detail, the game does a very good job at making you wonder whether your "benefactors" are really that, as well as making you wonder whether what you're doing really is for the best. Despite this, there doesn't seem to be any alternate endings, for better and for worse. While there isn't much in the way of character development in the game, the focus of the writing is not on the characters; it's on the world, and building of worlds this game does pretty well. 8/10.
Graphics: When I saw the art style of this game, I instantly knew why the person who recommended it to me did so: the art style in this game is pretty dang excellent. One shocker is that it was all done by one person. An even bigger shocker is that this entire game was made by one person, although I don't think witchcraft makes you one person still. All joking aside, this game does look really, really good. As mentioned above, the bosses look really, really cool, which makes it all the more disappointing how boring and easy almost all of them are. Funnily enough, the boss that looked the least interesting ended up being the hardest of the bunch (the bee thing for those who were wondering). Still though, the art style of this game is very, very good and it's all the more better considering that just one person worked on it. As for the technical side of things, the game fullscreened to 1080p and ran at a solid 60FPS throughout; just what you'd expect. It can be run windowed, but I never messed with that option as I like having things searing off my retinas at glorious full screen. I don't really need to say much more on this one than, "look at the screenshots." 5/5.
Sound: Another thing that became very surprising once I learned that this was a solo project is the music: the entire game, as well as the music, was still made by one person. This is surprising because the music is quite good. It's kinda chiptune-y in some areas and kinda not in others, which normally shows a bit of a confused direction with the audio, but since the whole game is "kinda 8-bit, kinda not," it never becomes too distracting. Plus, I don't know if these tracks would offer as much atmosphere as they do in a strictly 8-bit format. Speaking of sound direction, every enemy in the game makes the same exact noise when you hit them, which is a bit weird but again, one of those things that you notice if you're really nitpicking. I don't know if the OST is good enough to make me wanna buy it for myself, but it at the very least works really well in-game. 4/5.
Overall scores are: 7/8/5/4; cumulative score of 8.0/10. Quite a good showing, especially from one person, but it does some issues with level design and bosses that keeps the game from being as good as it could be. Still though, if you're looking for a Metroid-style game that you can blaze through in a couple of nights, this is a very good one to pick up. I got 60% item completion and 90% map completion in the ~7 hours that I played it, so I could see 100% being possible in under 15 hours.
You don't play as Samus in this Metroid, but it's pretty good.

Usually I don't write reviews on steam and I'm not even very far into the game yet, but Skyborn has surprised me with it's quality so far and that's why I'll write down my early impression of it now.
Okay, since I don't know much about the story yet, I'll just say that I enjoyed the events that happened around the main characters to start up the adventure so far. That's probably because the characters are really charmingly written and there weren't any cheesy lines that made me cringe like in most of the homemade RPG-Maker games. Even the character that I thought I would hate at the beginning, turned out to be very likeable and sort of funny very fast =)
Next would be the music, which is in my humble opinion very solid orchestral music that always fits the environment. The dungeon music is mysterious and calm, the battle music is kind of epic, majestic and uplifting and overall the music is just very nice to listen to. Stylewise the tracks feel always very gentle, atmospheric, diversified and not just right up in your face, which I like a lot.
Now to the battlesystem. Optically it has a typical RPG-Maker interface, without dynamicly fighting charactermodels, but that's fine for me, because all and all the drawn character models and the interface are very pretty.
The battles are turnbased and revolve around the classic HP / MP formular with the little change that is the Threat-Bar. Everytime your characters attack the enemies the Threat-Bar of those characters fill up depending on how much damage they deal and the character with the highest Threat get's attacked by the enemies, except of course when the enemies use multi-target attacks. So since you get a tank-like character very early on you want to use him exactly like that and let the others do damage/healing/status effects while keeping up the Threat-Level on the tank. Also i would recommend anyone to play this game on Hard, because that is when the battles actually get fun and strategic. So, uh... I like it =D
Last but not least, the graphics are very well meshed together and the mapping is always very detailed, pretty, and never feels unnatural. Also, getting around in the dungeons never felt tedious so far, since the maps feel very natural to get through and the monsters are optional obstacles to fight (don't know if that changes later).
Also I dig the Steampunk-Style =)
To round this review up:
It's a very fun classical RPG with charming characters, good dialogue, a (so far) promising story, a slightly changed turnbased battle-system, very nice music, nice mapping, good pacing and a nice steampunk environment.
I like it !!! =)

After going through the game twice I decided I'd review it. Let's start with the good:
Pros:
Probably the best overall of the RPG Maker games.
The protagonists are generally likeable and believable characters.
The antagonists do a good job of making you hate and want to beat them.
The game mechanics have a reasonable amount of depth and options that are introduced gradually throughout the course of the game which prevents information overload.
With one exception, the game plays fair and enemies generally have access to the same options and resources as the player.
Cons:
Very short, especially for an RPG.
Very easy, even on Hard difficulty. Even the optional superboss.
The final boss has an unavoidable death combo and the fight lasts long enough he usually gets at least one chance to use it on you at which point everyone dies. He is otherwise entirely trivial.
Mostly linear. There aren't many side quests overall and most of them are along the lines of complete an additional objective in the area you were going anyways instead of directing you somewhere else. It's also rare there is more than one place you could go and get something done at any given time.
Once you get past the first few levels you no longer gain skills by leveling up, only by reaching certain points in the game.
What I'd like to have seen:
At least twice as long.
Buff the difficulty considerably (leave Easy easy for those not looking for a hard game).
Buff all the final boss' attacks except for the unavoidable death combo, then either make sure you always have time to react or make it not always kill everyone instantly. That way he provides a hard but legitimate challenge.
More side quests and side areas.
Instead of class changing instantly granting all the skills, make it give one now and the rest with level requirements.
Massively buff the super boss. She's honestly a joke, her best attack does 2k or 3k on all at full power. Anyone complaining she's hard didn't go in prepared at all and is taking much more damage than that.

Skyborn is a simple RPG maker game, and to be fair that might already pull away most of the people interested in buying it, but for some reason, even through there are countless other RPG maker games like this one. I just can't call it bad. I love it. I love the taunt system even through it's  been reused in other games like Deadly Sin. I love the structure of the story and how you never really get overwhelmed by things to do but you still feel free enough for it to not be 100% linear. All and all the only critizism I have towards the game originates from it being made on RPG maker and possibly, like I said before, that the taunt system is a reused asset from other games the group has made, but even then, for this price, it's a really good first entry for JRPG styled games.
I won't follow a number rating system, so I'll just list a few major cons and pros :
- Good structured storyline
- Memorable and likable characters
- Strong female lead
- Tactical gameplay due to the energy and taunt system
- An interesting crafting and mining system
- Generic JRPG formula
- RPG Maker graphics
- Reused graphical assets
- Reused taunt mechanic
-
(Okay maybe that was too much to ask for)
Now that I look at all of these points, I realise that there is a specific kind of person who would enjoy a JRPG game. I grew up with the old Final Fantasy games so I never really cared for graphics, but I do know that there are people who require beautiful tree physics or else they'd rate a game bad despite what the game has to offer at the gameplay or story standpoint. There's also the fact that I do read quite a bit, so I find reading through the lore of a JRPG quite normal ; there will always be those people who are too impatient to read the text on the screen. So I do suggest people who are hesistant on buying this game to spend some time and anaylse if you're patient enough for the reading and don't mind the look of a game too much as in the end those two are the biggest factors in liking a game like this.

Before starting this review I have to say that most of the games I have ever played from RPG Maker can't stand a chance with this one. Now we can start.
In this game you take control of young lady in a world where humans are mistreated by a new race called Skyborn, from that comes the title. You discover that this new race acts like dictators over humans because they won a war against theme years before and that half-breed, which are a combination between humans and Skyborns, are treated worse that humans.
You join a rebel organization trying to defeat the Skyborns and free the half-breeds.
This is the main plot.
Now let's go with a more in depth classification:
The gameplay is really simple, taken from the classic RPG games. You have an exploration part where you can find lots of collectibles, and the fight parts where you have to slay enemies like in the good old days.
During the exploration you can find gems that will give you experience just by wandering around, stones that are used to craft objects, and other useful things. In this game you can find materials that will be used to craft items (weapons and armors) at the anvils in the world: the idea is good, really good, but the limited number of materials an the more limited number of items to be crafted will make you forgot of this feature really soon. The other great things are augmentation: you can add stones or other items to your equipment to increase some stats and make them stronger.
The battle system is really well done and the "Threat" mechanics add a bit of strategy to the game. In few words, attacking, killing and using skills generate threat, and the hero with the highest threat is the one that the enemies will always attack.
The game is set on a flying world but most places are totally different from how I would have imagined a flying world. In any case the places are well designed, with lots of details and the dungeos are very well done. The music are almost perfect: i said almost because in some places it can't express the feelings of the situation well.
The most orginal classic RPG Maker game I have ever played. If you have the possibility to play this game do it as soon as you can because you will not regret it.

The Bureau is a third-person shooter with an emphasis on squad-based tactics. The player controls the agent William Carter and commands two additional agents in each mission. Carter has several unique abilities, such as healing his entire squad, lifting enemies out of cover, and summoning combat drones. The other agents are divided into four classes: Commando, Engineer, Support, and Recon. Each class is proficient in a different set of powers and weapon types. For example, the Commando class is specialized in offensive abilities and rifles, while the Engineer class relies on land mines, automatic turrets, and the use of shotguns. As Carter and his squad gain more experience points during missions, more abilities become available.
By entering "Battle Focus Mode", which slows time significantly, the player can order their agents to move to tactical positions and activate class-specific abilities. Agents have customizable outfits, weapons, equipment, and abilities. As in XCOM: Enemy Unknown, if Carter is unable to revive agents who have taken too much damage, they will die (variable difficulty levels also determine whether or not it is possible for downed agents to become battle-ready when revived, or if replacement agents will appear during a mission). The agents who die will be dead for the rest of the game.
Throughout the course of the game, the player can collect backpack schematics and alien weapons, which then become available for the entire squad. Each backpack provides a unique bonus to the agent wearing it. For example, the Sharpshooter Pack provides bonus head-shot damage, and the Guardian Pack reduces damage taken from attacks. These equipments can be altered before a mission, or at Resupply Stations located in each mission.

I have to admit that I used to love zombies but the rather over saturation of media concerning the undead in recent years has somewhat slowly put me off more so when it comes to video games where we've seen loads of dull zombie related times crop up in recent past with only a few titles being good (left 4 dead 1+2, and Tale Tale's The walking Dead being the exceptions). So the revival of Ubisoft's long since dead (pun not intended, and yes Zombi was a game that Ubi pushed out in 1986/1990 not just on the Wii U) Zombi franchise has had me interested. Why? Because people have said that it's actually very well done, and actually favours traditional survival horror over undead skull bashing.
A few hours in and I do believe them here.
Essentually Zombi is a first person survial horror game, that pit's you as a random surviver trying to stay alive in a fairly corny "tourist trap" version of London. You're aided by a man calling himself "the Prepper" who comes over as one of those tin foil hat wearing survivalists (only in this case he was right about the end of the world).
However it hits all the right notes for fast paced survival horror. Ammo is far from plentiful, combat sluggish and inaccurate, and running, sneaking, and avoiding is sometimes and quite often better than a straight up fight. You can also barricade doors or have to remove barricades in order to escape.
One of the big features is death in this game, oh and you will die, you will die a lot in fact. Death in this game isn't a return to the last saved checkpoint but a "permadeath" of your last character. He or she is gone for good, but will leave their inventory in the game for your next character to collect. Sometimes your last character may even "reanimate" and will require you to kill them again before you can get your stuff back. Die BEFORE you get that bag back and it's gone for good! Even on the easiest setting of the game. Characters also can level up too as you go, but this is also reset on each death adding to the sting, and more so if you kept them alive for quite some time. This is a line of mechanics I normally expect to see in indie games, but here they are on a full release from a big brand company.
The only real pain with this feature is that while you do have a health bar, death in this game can be sudden and instant (more so when the annoying exploding guys start to show up). It's still fun but the slightly unforgiving nature might be a bit too much for some.
Some of the more novel features concerning the WiiU's controller have now been ported over as onscreen overlays. Nothing seems to have changed though or removed beyond the novelty. As far as I can tell the menus are still in real time to keep in sprit of the WiiU version.
However if I have to take a pot shot at the game then it's over the typical Ubi ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. Yes there is UPlay but given some of the advantages for multiformat gamers, that hardly bothers me. However if you are the strict PC gamer then the addition of having to use the service right next to steam feels like a pointless exercise. Just take it or leave it TBH.
I can't however say the same for the quality of the PC port which is grotty to say the least. There is a lack of detail options, and the visuals are somewhat low-fi and muddy to say the least. Worst is the current state of stability, this game crashes a lot, and I mean a lot. Crashes that can easily wipe 10 to 15 mins of game time away, can and will ruin your day.
Overall Zombi even with the grotty port issues on the PC is a good game, it's the sort of old school survival horror that we don't see much of now in 2015. In short it's worth a look in.

Ok I bought this knowing it is a PC port but I fancied a game set in London rather than Moscow, New York or Chernorus.

Gameplay - linear and managed. If you die (which I did a lot) you respawn back at base and can then work your way back to where you were quite quickly. There's a bit of problem solving but you're spoon fed by a voice in your ear, the Prepper. It's not in the league of Dinocrisis where you really did have to use your brains - but guess with walkthroughs out there on the www this is quite an old fashioned view for me to have anyway.
Combat - simple, unsatisfyingly simple. Dead Island set the standard for combat in my opinion. In Zombi - LMB = shove with weapon, RMB = raise weapon, then LMB again = strike with weapon, Not very effective and there are no other strikes etc to play with.
Reason for not recommending the game - none of the above issues would have put me off. What makes me say don't buy this game for PC is that the game is heavily bugged with crash to desk top when your character gets back to the area where they last died. This is frequent and problematic. There is no official fix coming that I know of, and many of the player developed work arounds seen on Steam relate more to wishful thinking than actual fact, and don't seem to work for each and every player.
Additionally, having asked for a refund on the basis that the game isn't fit for PC release, Steam have declined as I have played 8 hours. Seeing that I have only been affected by the bugs in the last hour of my gameplay this is not a very happy outcome. My advice is - if you're in doubt about whether it will work on your PC, don't buy it, as you may not be able to get a refund.
EDIT: it seems the game devs have now debugged the issues that led to constant crashes - which is good. However, I am still dissatisfied with the Steam response re the request for a refund. Having carried on playing, the game has got boring, mainly becasue of the game play and strategy which is very very linear and micromanaged, plus the introduction of sudden death explodng zombies. There's no real sense of fun or exploration - just follow the route map, swing the bat and occasionally get blown up.
Finally decided to quit and uninstall when I was kidnapped and you are then forced to play a minigame of sorts in an arena to move on and I just cannot be arsed. If you're a sugar fuelled teen with lightining reflexes you'd possibly not mind, but after a  long day at work I don't care for it.

On a surface level, this is like any other Japanese dating sim - except with pigeons. As Pigeonations High School's only human student, Hiyoko Tosaka, you have the option of romancing a number of birds, each with their own unique personality and backstory, and can even unlock secret birds. Most dating scenarios end with a surprisingly heavy twist, even if you achieve the "good ending". The atmosphere of the dating scenarios is very bright and pleasant for the most part. SPOILER WARNING AGAIN
But the dating scenarios are just a facade. The true game is unlocked by achieving the good ending for a few certain birds. Once you have unlocked it, you find yourself in a post-apocalyptic, dystopian world wherein the majority of the human race succumbed to the avian flu. As a result of experiments conducted on birds to combat the virus, birds have gained sentience and human-like characteristics and intelligence, and now rule the earth. Hiyoko, the human protagonist, is gruesomely murdered, and all Pigeonations students are under lockdown. Playing as Ryouta, your duty is to discover the disturbing circumstances of Hiyoko's death, and reveal the true nature of Operation Hatoful.
I don't know what I just played but I know I'm going back for more!

The newest addition to the Hearts of Iron series is the most user-friendly (almost as the Civilization 5) and war-mongering as always. Just like so many other Paradox global strategies, you take control of the one particular state (which can be as big as Soviet Union/USA or as small as Luxemburg). You're making calls with industry, technologies and infernal politics, preparing for the grand war, which is so close. And then you must fight. Even if you choose some state on the outskirts of the world, like New Zealand or Haiti - it doesn't mean you'll evade the global skirmish. You'll be bored all the way - but eventually, the war will come to you as well.
I have ambivalent opinion of HoI 4, and don't recommend it as an instant buy. Maybe Paradox will patch some questionable features sometimes... But maybe they'll just make the next, better game. Or they'll make the next HoI even worse, who knows? Yeah, surely, it developed alot in little details since the 1.0 up to 1.4 version, I can easily agree with that. But, some things, are not too right in the very basic concept.
The most noticeable pro point of the 4th volume (above the 3rd HoI) is an aeons more acceptable interface and tutorial. The game's mechanics are still very complicated, but, at least, you can learn it without your head boiling too hot. However, there is a catch: once you'll learn "the better way" for every country, it's really not fun to play it again. The limit of replayability is still quite high - but it's countable. It's good for game sellers, so they can sell the next almost-similar game faster (the Call-of-Duty syndrome). But it certainly lowers the overall score of the one particular game for me.
What is worse, while basically every country have ar least 3 different ways to go, Democratic, Socialistic or Fascist, it's obvious that for the most cases, the Fascist way benefits the player much more. "C'mon, game, make me a Fascist! Faster!" - that's a common phrase among Youtube letsplayers. Some may argue, like, would Paradox make it other way - the Axis would be loosing way too often. Maybe. But look at the achievements. There is one, "NewWorldOrder", make all the world brown, but why there isn't such trophies for Blue and Red sides? Well, it's not a secret that the dev's are favouring Hitler - maybe not as a person, but as a political figure... But, even in the 3rd Hearts of Iron, where Adolf get a cameo in so-called "tutorial", it wasn't so one-way oriented.
Turning fascist as a key strategy to win the war is only one minus point. The much more severe case is all diplomatics in general. First, there are political blocks. And if you're, say, choosing Allies, you can't then skip to the Comintern or Axis during the war. And even if both Allies and Comintern are fighting Axis together, like as in known history, they are still not counting as allies between each other. Next, even worse, is about running some of those blocks yourself. Example - an achievement for Mexico, to land onto Europe, either not allied with anybody, or having the alliance only with South America countries. For Mexico, it's crucial to make at least small alliance - without it, you can't open the 5th research slot, therefore, you'll be loosing the tech race. So I made a fine alliance with Colombia, conquered the USA (for another Mexico achievement) and started preparations for the invasion on Europe. All goes well, until Germany and Italy both lose. Then, all the small states, which were associated with Axis, suddenly landed into my faction, without even asking! Just because of some game rule, it can sometimes apply or disengage some countries in your alliance. And You - Don't. I understand it was made not to ruin some multiplayer games, but now it certainly ruins single-play.
Next, the wars. At first, they seem much clever than in the 2nd and 3rd HoI - you can issue your generals some master plan, and they will be persuing it by themselves - which especially cool, if you have multiple wars or fronts simultaneously. But then you notice than every war where you move troops yourself procedes much faster and better than leaving it to AI. So, no, the micromanagement is still a must, for almost every operation. You have to move your troops yourself, and you always need to observe all your territories, or enemies will make an invasion far in your safezone and conquer your capital city, while your main forces will be very far away, like in Africa or India... AI battleplan logic, even based on the stats unknown to player (like the size of fortifications, for the most obvious example) - still lose too many manpower in the every war, every single battle, with constant zerg rushes and zeroed organization stat. Remember human waves cliche? Well, it's the most obvious tactic for the AI, not for Russia or China, but for every country.
More to it! By some strange logic, if your forces are attacking from territory of another state, the game counts them as the forces of that state. Like if Soviets goes through neutral Poland straight to Berlin, the game greets brave Poles for Their success! And if you conquer some distant land like Australia, you can't be sure, that the game counts that victory to you. In my case, another (allied) nation landed in another part of that continent, haven't got at least one city - but was awarded as a whole winner when I took Canberra.
Or, another case, back to weird diplomacy. Civil war started in Norway, Sweden and Afganistan. One side marked as Axis, other as Comintern, the game merged all civil wars together with some other conflicts, basically, the World War has started. I, as Soviet Union, with help from Finland, took the northern parts of Norway and Sweden, and all was going well, I was so close to their capitals, when Soviet Afganistan have lost its domestic war. Right away, the game makes some automatic treaty, and counts all three civil wars as closed, and Axis forces as winners. All the northern parts of Sweden and Norway now belongs to Axis, and all the local forces that was on Soviet side, now are enemies. Just because the game says so. Yeah, very logical, very realistic.
I can proceed with examples, but they will take us too long. Aviation and artillery cases still far from perfect... Even the sound options menu is still far from perfect, as it counts some random and totally irrelevant background sounds like shooting and howling of planes on fly-by as "effect" and not not "ambient". And if you don't want to hear all those stupid "wruum, bah-bah" all the way, but want to hear sounds when clicking buttons - sorry! It's 1+1 type of deal! Take the good with the bad, or leave it be!
Just like that, there are too many sides of this really good and complex game, which aren't feel alright. Let's finish there, with quick summary. Is the game better than the 2nd or 3rd Hearts of Iron? With visuals and lower entry level, with the better aid of modders straight from the Steam Community - Yes, naturally.
You'll still need to learn many things there to operate successfully. But once you'll manage that learning curve (about 30-100 hours average) - you'll start to lose your interest, as it's all not that random, as with Civilization games, and not that logically and historically correct, as previous Paradox games. On the other hand, those questionable game decisions made multiplayer much more acceptable, in general gaming sense. As a solo player, I can't really agree with that turn of tide. With all disadvantages from diplomacy and other game mechanics, I can't value it higher than 7/10. Buy it on your own risk. There are no such limitations as with previous games, like you've might heard, "play it only if you're good enough with Europa Universalis" or so, but, if you're wasn't daydreaming on history and logic classes, the 4th HoI still leaving too much to wish for sweeten the taste.

A very solid "meh". I tend to enjoy story-centered and exploration-based games, but this one just never got my attention.
Most of the game drives itself, and you don't have to make any decisions. When you need to accomplish specific tasks, there are clear onscreen cues. I'm OK with all of this.
The game felt slow. It may have mostly been a problem of character movement speed, during both player-controlled and automated portions. There weren't any surprises to the plot. It's a predictable story and an unoriginal plot. Some graphic elements seemed well-done, but nothing struck me as exceptionally magical or impressive. (The "nest quest" sequence was the most interesting part graphics-wise, I'd say.) I wouldn't be surprised if (nearly) all of the sprites were from a generic sprite pack.
Nothing was exceptionally wrong about this game, it just failed to impress. When this genre was new, this game may have been worth a try. Now that we have plenty of exploration/story games to choose from, I think this one can very safely be skipped at any price.
Since it's so short, though, it won't ruin your day if you pick it up for less than a dollar.

Great game. Best one line description: "Mount and Blade but more fluid, more beautiful, better animation and better gameplay". Those massive battles are just breath-taking and it's all fluid. Never exeperienced that in M&B.
The combat system relies on a chambering / counter-chambering system. Holding left mouse button makes you "chamber" your attack. Moving the mouse while holding the button makes you change your stance. Releasing the button releases the blow. Chambering is also your parry stance. You have to observe your opponent and adjust your stance to parry his attack. Check some gaemplay videos if you can.
It looks great and it's pretty instinctive. It gives very fluid combat where skill, timing and footwork is important. SOmetimes, you exchange parries and riposts during 1 min without a single drop of blood ... and then suddenly, you hit that one mighty blow in the head because of a nimble feint and your opponent drops dead. Delightful.
Oh and btw, there is an "epic" gamemode. It consists in a strategic map in which clans fights for strongholds in organized battles, recruit players to fight for them, build stuff with resources. Looks cools, arrives in 6 days apparently.
Oh and did I mention this uber-cool gear system? All those weapons to unlock ... :D
10/10 would recommend. Support the devs ;)

"The Witches Return!"
Based around the original PC version, but with different artwork and easier to play controls, it is Trouble Witches Origin, which is yet, another re-release, besides the Neo version that used to be on the X360.
The gameplay is still the same as the previous versions, shoot stuff, earn coin, get cards, and survive, with the use of the Magic Barrier system. The game's story per charter varies by version, but more or less the same/different, where finding the pieces of the Drapunir ring would grant one's wish and taking down the Daughters of Amalgam which are causing trouble, and rendezvous with Amalgam herself (and the entity possessing her).
It is up to Pril and the other witches, which go on their own separate adventures to claim their said wish, but...will it be worth it in the end?
So the differences between this and the previous versions...
+Gameplay similarly structured based on AC/Neo's mechanics.
+Vocals and Artwork differ between versions as stated. (However, there are JP voices only, and none of the weirdly sounding En. dub that TWN! had.)
+All characters from the original presented (Pril, Yuki, Aqua, and the returning Sies, which was missing from Neo as playable, although she is/was in other versions), plus new original character to Origin...Kozakura! Plus, guest starring Cotton and the returning AC/Neo cast as DLC. (Louis, Symphony, Conan, Lyla. However, no Sakurako and Luca though.)
- Spell Card switching, unlike in the original, is still missing from all other versions, which could have helped in the dire situations on the stages.
-Co-op Play, which was in AC (Nesica-X-Live ver.) and Neo, is not in the original and in Origin, either Local or Online.
Either way, awesomely recommend, especially if on sale. Now if only Trouble Witches 2 would actually come out and not still be in development limbo, lol.

I just couldn't sit bywith this game having such a low review score as it does. I love the "Lost Planet" series, especially the second I just don't understand how they all have such crappy scores. For starters they are all flawed that's for sure. Gosh darn it though if you're decent enough to look past the flaws they are something else. If you ever look anything up about these games (typically excluding this one) people love them. All that aside lets get into this review.
So I literally just beat this game and I'm cracking my fingers and sipping on my juicy juice ready to jot down an opinion or two.
For starters I'm sure if you've looked up anything about this or read some other review this one is jsut deadspace 3 and weellllll for a good bit they're not wrong. They ditched the crazy style of the older ones and adopted a close over the shoulder more cinematic feel. Its even softcore horror in some places. That's all fine though just a little disappointing coming from the other two. The gameplay though is solid, you have guns you get through out the game that you can get upgrades for and make them a little better, you have a big machine you can upgrade through the game. Enemies aren't terribly varied, but they switch some things up for a little at the end which was nice. The world, setting wise I liked a lot, but they turned in into a sort of semi-open-world that you had to slowly walk through in your rig which was a little obnoxious. It worked well for how they told the story since you had to revist lots of places and was a contained story to a certain place, but man could it be tedious to slowly walk around sometimes. Graphically it was very nice no complaints at all there. Voice acting was very good. All the characters were good and so were their voice actors, even a bit of character development. Music is nothing to shake a stick at if I listened to the soundtrack I'd probably recognize like two songs from it and swear on the hairs of my left nipple that i've never heard the other songs. There were a few bosses that I had problems with. One boss I couldn't kill and another just made no sense how to kill it, but otherwise the boss fights were a little disappointing for the series. The series is built on massive bosses, but this one they were "massive" and not very varied and you'd often run into the same boss a few times.

Calm down kiddies, it's not as bad as you think.
Yes this game has more than its fair share of issues, but I think it has plenty of potential. The entirety of the game revolve around an open arena where you shoot at other players, causing them to glitch-out and die. You have you primary weapon which is the only one that deals actual damage, and scattered around the arena are four other secondary weapons (there might be one or two more but I only remember 4). They secondary weapons don't damage enemies, but they do privide "glitches" that temporarily stun or slow down the enemy to deal additional damage with the primary weapon. These "glitches" include pop-ups, returning to the desktop, pinging, and turning everything low-res.
The concept is original and sounds like a good idea, the execution however suffers a little bit. For example, one of the secondary weapons also causes the affected player's screen to flicker uncontrollably. Now personally, I don't suffer from photo-sensitive seisures, but these sequences are still murder on my eyes. So much, that I have to look away whenever I get hit from an enemy (hopefully an update might tone that down a little bit). Another issue is clipping. Depending on how you approach a wall you can easily phase through it. Players can use this to their advantage, as you "fall" through the map, can see through most walls, and can shoot everyone you see; however they can't shoot back at you. It's cheap but, I'll admit, I use it whenever I get a chance to rack up some easy kills. This clipping issue also happens at arena boundaries, causing you to accidentally fall to your death. It may be a glitch or a feature, either way, there has to be a better way to implement it (or remove it completely.)
Now, this game is far from perfect as it is, but for its 3 dollar asking price, I think it's more than fair. Some features I would love to see would be actual gameplay modes like team deathmatch, free-for-all, or king of the hill. The game as it is currently just throws you in an ongoing game where you shoot each other with no time limit, no kill/death ratio, and no stat progression. You basically derp around killing each other until you get bored and start leaving the game one by one. Some sort of level progression or stat tracking would be a more than welcome addition to this game, as well as some new game modes. But as the game is right now, yeah it's a little on the broken side, but it's still a stupid, fun time.
TL;DR: Humble Bundle adopters feel cheated for this game being lumped in with their latest bundle, won't give it a passing glance. I gave it a chance and I kinda enjoyed it.

Axiom Verge is styled after the original Metroid, both in art direction and gameplay style. You are almost completely unguided, which does have some problems in that the world is large and figuring out where to go can be frustrating. However, it also lets you be creative - you can often get places you aren't really meant to be at yet through the creative use of abilities.
The game's plot is not overly extensive or twisty, and ends in something of a cliffhanger, but there are notes and other things laying around for you to pick up which add a bit of depth to the world. At one point you get an item which allows you to quite literally hack reality, which really raises a lot of questions as to just what exactly is going on.
The controls take some getting used to but are responsive and work quite well for the type of game it is. There is a huge variety of weapons, and even if a few of them shine brighter than others all of them are useful in one situation or another, Getting hit is punishing, there aren't too many areas where it's truly difficult to do things, and most bosses are fairly easy once you have their patterns down.
Art wise, the game has a very "organic" feel to it, and the music goes along well with it. Even the low health beep, which is infuriating in most games, is timed to go along with the music and fades in and out, so you notice it, but isn't irritating.
I only have two real issues with this game. Backtracking can be quiet slow, even once you've unlocked the intermediate area that connects all others, and you will be doing quite a lot of backtracking. Beyond that, there are several hidden zones which are unique to each save file, but the only notification these are nearby is a slight visual change that's easy to miss. However, these hidden areas don't count towards your 100% completion or any achievements, but they are a fun throwback to the glitch zones of the original Metroid, and they can contain unique (and powerful) weapons.
The characters, such as they are, are typically interesting and the mish mash of English some of them do works very well to fit in with the game's alien feel. If you're looking for a retro exploration game, this is definitely right up your alley.

The difficulty level is probably a good bit less than the original Metroid, but it is still engaging. Player skill is still a big factor and the demands on your skills only continues to ramp up as you get some of the late-game items. It also rewards exploration and clever solutions with its "glitch" mechanic to some rather unclear puzzles to get some of the more rare items.
My only complaint is that it was a little too short. Even though a veteran of these types of games, I was taking my time on this game, and it still was only about 12 hours.

It's important to understand what is currently in the game. At the moment it's basically multiplayer battle with several game modes and persistent character progression but more will be added very soon, a basic version of epic will be released on September 1st. The developers want to make sure they get the combat system right first and then build other elements around it. It is a decision I completely agree with.
There have been plenty of open world sandbox games that are enjoyable while your building up your castle but seriously lacking when it comes to the actual fighting, at least for me it ruins the entire experience. This is definitely not the case here. The combat system is the best I have experienced in a medieval fighting game next to warband and considering it's still in early alpha it definitely has the potential to surpass it.
You should also understand it's not quite going to be a traditional open world sandbox game such as Life is Feudal, Reign Of Kings etc. Epic is something rather unique that has not really been done before. It would take a rather long review to adequately describe so I will instead refer you to OKAM wiki where you can find out more about it:
Having said that, there are of course still some issues that need to be worked on and some very basic features that are missing as the game is still in early alpha. If sandbox and building elements are what mostly appeal to you it makes sense to wait a while until they add more features. The developes are also very active in communicating with players and take feedback and suggestions daily both in discord and forums.

you're looking for a game review you've come to the wrong place. But if youre looking for a fantastic ravioli recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients
- To Make the Dough
375 grams (3 cups) plain flour
1/2 teaspoon salt
2 eggs
1/4 cup (50 ml / 3½ tablespoons) olive oil
1/2 cup (120 ml / 8 tablespoons) water
Extra flour for dusting
- To Make Cheese Filling
15 ounces (425 grams) container Ricotta cheese
5 ounces (142 g/about 1/2 cup plus 2 tablespoons) "3 Cheese Italian Blend" (Parmesan, Romano & Asiago)
Note: grate these cheeses yourself and create your own custom blend.
1/2 cup cheddar cheese
2 eggs, lightly beaten
1/2 teaspoon salt
1/2 teaspoon pepper
- Extras
Your favorite sauce for the ravioli (i.e. marinara/ marijuana)
Parmesan cheese
Basil
Fried vegetables
Shrimp
Fish slices
Chicken pieces
Make the Ravioli filling.
- In a small mixing bowl, add the ricotta and mash with a fork.
- Add in the 3-cheese blend, Cheddar cheese, eggs, salt, and pepper.
- Mix all ingredients thoroughly until you have a smooth, paste-like consistency.
- Cover the bowl with plastic wrap and place it in the refrigerator for about 30 minutes.
Make the Ravioli dough.
- Crack eggs into a large mixing bowl and beat them with a fork. Add water, oil, and salt. Mix.
- Add 1 cup flour to the bowl. Use a fork to mix the flour with the eggs, water, oil, and salt. Repeat with the rest of the flour. Mix until a smooth dough is formed.
- Clear and clean off a large work surface and dust it with flour. This is where you are going to roll out your dough.
- Take the dough out of the mixing bowl, shape it into a ball, and place it on your work surface. Knead for at least 10 minutes or until it becomes elastic.
- Dust a rolling pin with flour to prevent the dough from sticking. Roll out the dough until it is about 1/8 inch (1/3 cm) thick, or about the thickness of 2 stacked quarters.
- With a cookie cutter or upside-down water glass, cut out circles in the dough (will make about 15-20 dough circles).
- Ball up the unused dough and either roll it out and make a couple more raviolis, or wrap it and put in the freezer for another time. Dough can keep for weeks when frozen. Just make sure to wrap well so that it doesn’t suffer from freezer burn or absorb freezer odor.
Fill the Ravioli shells.
- Take the ravioli filling out of the refrigerator and place a tablespoon of it in middle of a dough.
- Fill a small bowl with water, dip your fingers in, and moisten around the outer edge of the dough circle.
- Fold the dough in half over the filling, making a half-moon shape. Be sure all the filling stays inside. Pinch the edges together and then seal the edges of the ravioli with a fork. Make sure to press firmly and go all the way around. This will add a “homemade” touch as well.
- Repeat this process for all your dough circles.
- Dust the finished ravioli with flour to keep them from sticking together.
Form the Shells and Fill Using a Ravioli maker.
- Roll the dough into two sheets
- Place one sheet on the ravioli maker, and form the filling cups.
- Fill with the ravioli mixture.
- Lay the second sheet of dough on top, and roll it out. This will seal in the filling.
- Remove and separate the finished raviolis.
Cook the Ravioli.
- Fill a large pot with water and bring to a boil.
- Place the ravioli in boiling water for 5-6 minutes, or until they float. You can also test for doneness by nibbling on the edges to test.
- If you don't want to make all the ravioli at one time, you can freeze the rest
- Take ravioli out of boiling water with large slotted spoon and place on warmed plates
Serve it up.
Top with your favorite sauce, grate some fresh cheese over it, and enjoy!

I just finished the game, and I must say it was more than I thought.  The game follows humans and half-breed who are trying to rebel against a tyranny, the Skyborn.  At the beginning, you don't really know who is who, but in the end you find out how all three factions relate to each other and what went wrong.
The game play is quite good.  Most of the time, you move the group around by manipulating one of the characters, the others automatically follow.  The combat system takes a few tries to figure out what to do, but then I learned to love how combat worked.  Each character has a default attack, plus skills to use during combat.  They also have access to a few items.  Just attacking will get your group killed.  You need to have the characters work together to defeat strong foes.  For example, one of the characters, Claret, does tech attacks.  Another character can lower an enemy's tech resistance.  So first you lower the resistence, and then you attack.  While that mean the character lowering the resistence doesn't do an attack, the resulting damage adds up to more in the end.
The storyline is well thought out, the characters are interesting, and the plot might leave you thinking.  Overall, I loved playing Skyborn and I recommend this game to anyone who likes playing RPGs.

I haven't played any other Lost Planet games, but this story worked fine as a stand-alone adventure.
All the criticisms I’ve read about the gameplay were on point, but I still enjoyed the overall experience. Lost Planet 3 spends more time on character and setting development than I’m used to seeing in action games, making a fair attempt at giving plausible motivations and backstory to the people and events. It turns into predictable action movie stuff by the end, but the early investment in the characters kept me interested.
The main character in particular is very likeable: relaxed, level-headed and practical. The setting was well-realised, detailed and spectacular. Puddles in the crew room, fog from characters’ breaths, overheard conversations, gave it a sense of being a real, lived-in place.
Unfortunately, the combat becomes very repetitive. There were upgrades and unlockable weapons but they didn’t change things much. This aspect of the game often felt like a chore, even if that was sort of in keeping with the scenario.
It was a stunningly bleak planet to wander across - if only there was more to do than combat. More side quests and secrets (there are a few) could have made revisiting areas more worthwhile. Some potentially interesting ingredients (like sentry guns) went under-utilised, appearing only a few times.
Despite this, I enjoyed the world and characters, and the game works well enough as a vehicle to tell its story. Even when the main character was just trudging across the icy tundra in a mech suit, his normal working days on the harsh planet were as interesting as the space opera plot.

Skyborn is . . . competent, I guess I'd say. Not amazing, but not bad.
Its strongest points are the setting, story, and characters. Admittedly, there are a lot of bog standard tropes across the board, but they're pretty well-executed. The world is interesting, and I found myself wanting to know more about it. The characters are well-written and more fun than I expected. The story could have benefited from more development and better pacing, but still, it was engaging enough to keep me playing to the end (seven hours or so).
That's more than I can say for the combat, however. My biggest issue with the game is how boring the combat became. I'm not an RPG veteran by any stretch, and I paid almost no attention to Skyborn's mechanics, yet I was still able to snooze through all but one fight. Sooner rather than later, Claret got some mega-OP skills that obliterated anything that tried to get in her way, which completely trivialized most of the enemies and turned encounters into tedious detours. Also, the combat screen uses default RPG Maker enemy sprites, which often look weirdly out of place amongst the otherwise consistent anime aesthetics.
Final verdict: yes, it's worth playing, but wait for a sale.

Skyborn is a Steampunk styled, RPG Maker game with quite the enthralling story. This game was a nostalgic piece for me due to my love for RPG video games and Steampunk in general.
The game takes roughly 7-8 hours to beat and is overall a really interesting game. I enjoyed many aspects of Skyborn, especially the combat machanics, the soundtrack, and the story. I won't spoil anything about the story, for I recommend that you should definitely play the game for the full experience. I must say, however, that the characters are very easy to get attached to. All of the characters have a personality of their own, and I found them quite charming and interesting. But, in regards to the soundtrack, each piece fit the mood whenever it was necessary. Of course, this is my own personal preference, and some may or may not feel satisfied with the soundtrack.
The combat mechanics were easy to understand and very enjoyable. I was overjoyed when I realized that combat was unavoidable for most enemies. I've always disliked random encounters to a degree, and I truly love the option of avoiding or jumping into combat. I would fight some enemies in order to gain experience and eventually continue on when I believed I was ready for the next stage. The combat itself is turn-based and very strategic based on your playstyle. I'm a sucker for strategy-based systems, so the combat mechanics were some of the best I had seen in a long time.
There are only a few cons I found within the game. I found the crafting somewhat cringeworthy due to the fact that I crafted  and bought some of the highest-level gear near the middle of the game. I soon found the crafting system to be somewhat miniscule due to the fact that I did not require it at all after I crafted 3rd tier armor and weapons. I understand that this could be because Skyborn is not a lengthy game, but this incident made this system, which was excellent in the beginning, seem almost useless near the end.
Another con I found was the lack of backtracking. Once again, this is probably because the game is not lengthy. I somewhat expected a larger world with backtracking requirements here and there. The game has enough content to complete the story and satisfy the player, but it almost felt like the world was somewhat empty. I enjoy engrossing myself in the world of the characters in the game, so, when I'm limitted as to where I can go and what I can do, I question the condition and lore of the world as a whole. This is simply a personal arguement between me and other games. Other players may or may not feel the same way.
In all, Skyborn is a wonderful game and I recommend it. I only wish that the game could be longer. If Skyborn was longer, perhaps the cons of the game would have vanish. However, I do highly recommend Skyborn because of its story, fascinating characters, and overall enjoyment. I guarantee that you will enjoy this game.

This game is a bit of a mixed bag, but if you're generally someone who wants to support RPG Maker game developers and try out a game that is pretty well put together, you might be interested in this title.
For a RPG Maker game, the game uses a lot of the default settings, but adds onto it and makes the new ideas work, class trees being a big one; however, I generally found myself just obliterating all opposition by using blood magic and buffs, so most of the time boss battles really didn't feel that epic.  Its nice that the option is there, but overall combat in the game was rather easy, possibly too easy.
The story of the game usually left me scratching my head.  For example, there's one point in the story where one of the bad guys does something bad, but the protagonist asks how the bad guy followed her and his reply is that he just tracked her good deeds.  But the player never sees her doing any good deeds like what he implies and you were really just running around in caves, so the excuse is just really bad and makes no sense.  It just threw me out of the story a bit, and there's a few moments like these where something odd breaks immersion.  It doesn't happen too often, and sometimes the game does a good job of telling a story where you do feel a bit invested, so it does try to make up for it.
The game itself is a bit short.  I'd say you could probably beat this game in about 7~10 hours.  Meeting the final boss and quickly dispatching him sort of surprised me, because then the game was over.  I could tell though that some ideas were there to try to extend the length (since he didn't die too quickly), so I will give the makers credit there, but the game's difficulty sort of countered that.
Overall, I'm not sure if I could fully recommend this game, a lot of the issues are pretty minor and not too destructive, but mainly the game's length and the difficulty of the game doesn't really warrant the current sale price (which is $14.99 as of this review) to me.  I would say get this game if you still want a simple story with good visuals, fairly varied combat, and a game made with RPG Maker that you want to support.  Mainly the last part, because for a RPG Maker game, this is pretty well done.

This is a recommendation with some caveats.
Buy and play this if you only bought and played (and liked) To The Moon before. Since its art style is not for everyone, and uniqueness of it is actually the weakest point of it.
What do I mean by that? This game is so unique that it is actually not a game. Its interaction level is actually below than most of the visual novels. Most things happen without your interaction, or happen with your "moderation". For example, the bird will fly no matter what, you can choose which part of the screen you want to be in with no gameplay results. You can choose how long you want to wander around the house, but at the end you dont have any choice which room you will go.
So the gameplay is actually a complete illusion. Ilusion of being a game. Like in Sid Meier's quote, "A game is collection of meaningful decisions." There is no decision here. So some disadvantages of the game are, not being able to kill the bird, to destroy the house during the absence of the parents of the child,to punch some highschool bully in the mouth, to not choose to help a bird to fly.
What are the advantages? Being dictated to help the bird fly, not destroying the house, not seeing any other characters during the story etc. Basically being dictated to story. Since the story is good. And as a different side to the Moon, the story is told without the help of words, and you can see this would fail as a visual novel with this approach. It would also fail as a usual game with decision trees etc, since a meaningful story is often build as a compact, uniform experience. So this story is A Bird Story, it features a bird, a child, and clouds. It is a good story, not a good game, not a semi finished visual novel etc.
Another thing which worths the mention is cute graphics and superb music. But again, this is also a shortcoming since game does not have fullscreen support, any sprite scaling whatsoever. Sprites are generally heavily modified RPG Maker assets afaik, so there is nothing to praise that much. It does its job, you dont think the bird is a dragon, or boy is actually a ruthless mercenary, so it is ok. But the music... The music is again (like in to the Moon) great. Laura Shigihara did a great job again. Not only it enhances the mood, but also it defines the experience to make it worthwhile to remember.
Any other thing. Yes. The "gameplay" time is fairly short. If you wander around too much, so delaying the inevitable in every stage, the longest gameplay time might be around 2 hours. But there is no any additional content or hidden clues etc to justify this silliness.
Calling this story as a game, and criticizing it about its not being a game by definition is a bit harsh. But being sold in steam is an acclamation of being a game I think, so I must warn fellow gamers: This is not a game.
This is a good story which uses your input as decoration, and visuals as scene. Music also enhances the mood, and maybe being able to move, minimally interact but not being able to change the outcome is also a good representation of being a lonely child.
But I still think that this would be better as a story. Like Jonathan Livingston etc.

Don't get me wrong. I love this in some ways, but I just can't in good faith recommend it.
To gush a little bit about it, it's bright, punchy and it has a very unique combat system. You always have a pistol, which dumps garbage data into your enemies' RAM and when their RAM overloads they "crash". The garbage pistol isn't super effective by itself but you can make it easier by picking up one of the special weapons lying around which don't do any damage but disrupt your enemies view in a number of ways. For example there's a sniper rifle that minimizes their interface to a Windows 98 desktop and they have to reopen their interface to move around again, a shotgun that puts pop-up ads onto your enemies' interface and a bazooka that turns it all into ASCII. All of these make it harder for your enemies to react as  you pump garbage data into them.
This is all great but the game does nothing to tell you of any of this. The game really doesn't tell you a lot at all. There's no reload indicator on your special weapon, there's no indication of cooldown on your pistol and with no labels or anything on any of the weapons or no in game explanation about how the combat works or what the weapons do.
Even though it's nice looking and has this fun combat system, there's no real -game- to play with it in. As it's only a multiplayer game, it's as strong as its serverbase, which it does not particularly have. And the game seems only deathmatch, but without a round timer or score limit, or even a scoreboard. There's no progression or ranking or any sort of goal to work towards. This makes it more of a toy than an actual game.
It's stylish and unique but it's all flash and no substance.

I'm not normally one to leave reviews, but I feel I should document my (albeit very brief) time with this game. I will say I recieved this game for free as part of the Humble Monthly Bundle for August, if that makes any difference.
Upon opening the game, I was brought to the main menu, which only showed buttons for find server, host, options, or exit. It also had my name at the top (I chuckled, as it was clearly not designed for a name as long as mine), and some colors underneath that I could click on with no explanation. Clicking on find server, it showed a few large buttons with seemingly random numbers on them. Clicking on one of those brought me into the game, and oh what a game it was.
I started in a dark arena like what you see in the trailer. Very reminiscent of TRON in its style. I had a pistol which as far as I could tell had unlimited ammo. I turned to my right to start going up a nearby ramp, and started walking through a wall. Thinking it was a secret area, I forged ahead, and fell to my death. Not a good sign. Respawning very quickly, the only indication I had died was a brief text in the top left. No scorecard or other tracking as far as I could find.
I made my way up the ramp successfully this time (Fool me twice, wall...), and found a large black glowing object. Touching it teleported me to a new arena, where I saw something moving. A foe! I start shooting at it with my pistol, but while I seem to be hitting it, as he was flashing when my bullets impacted, there was no real indication that I was doing damage, or how much. After a moment, my screen went into a fake blue screen of death, and crashed to a fake desktop. Reopening the fake game from the fake start bar, I found I had died. I still don't know if dying caused the crash, or if I was killed when I crashed. Again, very quick respawn with only text in the top left indicating I had died, or that someone was doing better than me.
Third life, starting to get the hang of things, I go back through the teleporter, and this time find a weapon. It looked to be a sniper rifle of some sort, but I couldn't find any way to zoom in or anything other than shooting as normal (I would later find that shift is ironsights, never tried it with the rifle). Shooting at enemies, I couldn't seem to hit them or cause any noticable effect, so I ran off and into another teleporter. This one took me to an endless expanse where I fell to my death.
That couldn't possibly be right. I immediately run back to the same teleporter, jump through it, and again am brought to an empty area. No platforms that I can jump or fall to, not even another teleporter to escape with. I again fall to my death.
From that point, I continued to explore for a moment, shooting at some more enemies with some kind of rocket launcher that seemed to do more to my own visual effects than it did to my enemies, before falling through a new, different wall, and to my final death.
I would not recommend this game, at all, in its current state. The most basic idea, which seems to be glitches caused by damage, is neat, but not enough to support it. If in the future it is updated, supported, and improved, it could be worth a second glance, and I honestly hope that ends up being the case, but at this time, it is not worth the download.

Mind-bending puzzles? Nary a one.
Super-whizzy realistic graphics? Definitely not.
But if you've got any child left in you, any fondness for simple, charming stories, you'll love it. I did.
For those that are old enough to remember (cough), it feels like a whimsical version of the old "Fighting Fantasy" books where you make a decision and then get told to turn to page 120 for the next bit of the story. Nothing nearly that forced here, it's all beautiful, smooth, stylish animation telling a seamless story which weaves in and out of almost invisible choices. And it means that the next time I play it, there will be a different story told.
And pay attention to the backgrounds... Poke a puffin, tickle a chicken, furtle with fish.
Beautiful, charming, childish, innocent. Not words you usually associate with video games, but this one deserves them all. It made me happy.

I did not play the original Wii version so I cannot compare it to the original.  The PC version, however, is generally disppointing.  The game does get some things right, namely the moody and atmospheric setting, the music, and the jump scares.  The graphics, however are just not up to the current standard.
The game world is quite small and you'll find yourself going over the same ground time and time again.  In many cases, there are areas that simply cannot be accessed until you aquire the right item or upgrade (and for which there is no clue or hint of where it might be found), which forces you to go back to areas you've already visited.
The weapons you can aquire in the game are terribly underpowered and ammunition is extremely rare, which limits their effectiveness even more.  You'll find yourself using your trusty cricket bat 90% of the time and simply bludgeoning zombies over and over again until they die.
Speaking of which, every time your character dies, you respawn at the original location without any of the items you have found.  Your only choice is to go back to where you died, kill your former self and recover your items, or forget it completely and start with no items.  After a while, I didn't bother picking up any of the advanced weapons (shotguns, assault rifles, etc), since you only get enough ammo to ensure that they run out in the middle of fight.
The game can only be saved from certain locations and only if you have discovered them
All in all, I really like the atmosphere and the "feel" of the gameworld, I just wish the actual gameplay wasn't so frustrating and repetitive.
