Hrm,  mixed feelings about this one.
The game itself is a solid,  although not exceptional survival experience.  You roam around the metro tunnels and abandoned streets of London in search of snickers bars and handgun ammo.  Ocassionally you run into zombies,  whose heads you must beat in with your trusty cricket bat.   The combat isn't particularly deep or even very satisfying,  but it provides some basic sense of tension and fun because of just how hard it is to keep a zombie down.  The gore / damage modeling is pretty basic with the head being the only 'destroyable' part of the zombie (that i've noticed thus far).
So that's the game, and on its own I'd say it's kind of a 7/10 type experience.  Not bad, even pretty good.  But not exceptional.  But then there's the whole 'Port' side of  things, where its clear that nobody gave a single ♥♥♥♥ about making this work correctly on the PC.
- Must restart game to change resolution
- Letter boxing, and no support for different aspect ratios.
- Xbox controller UI art,  even when you're not using a controller.
- Clumsy inventory system which is a nightmare to manage
- Unskippable intro cinematics
- Muddy looking graphics with non-optional post process effects.
- Requires Ubisofts lame 'UPlay' service to run
- etc. etc.
It just adds up to drag the game down to more of a 5 or 6  out of 10 type experience.    If you're REALLY hooked on zombies,  I guess it's worth a punt.  But I'm starting to think I should have just bought "Dying Light" instead.

Don't take the "Not Recommended" thing too hard, fans. This is actually a fairly solid title, the death mechanic is a nice twist on most Survival Horrors I've played, and resource management isn't easy if you're profligate with your ammo (the way things should be). But there are a few gripes I have with this games that I'd like to point out.
It's short. Really short. It took me, not including AFK time, around 6 hours to finish this game. Plus it has little to no replay value and I very highly doubt there'll be extra content, even then I don't know if I could handle how disappointingly short this game was.
The sound design is pretty sub par, and that's a huge caveat. The survivor's sounds are pretty well acted (from the few actors I heard) but things like gunfire sound wholly unconvincing and unexciting. They tell you that gunfire is a surefire way to attract zombies, but they sound like pop guns. I hate that.
The map design is fairly uninspiring, some areas (especially underground) look homogenous to the point of being identical, and there's very little to explore outside of where you're supposed to.
It's not the best looking game, either. Not terrible but hardly exciting, with no graphics options at all. Plus the torchlight in dark areas looks incredibly hazy, not really helpful.
Overall, it's got some solid ideas and for a few hours to kill you could do worse, but don't buy it at full price, there simply isn't enough content to justify it and no reason to replay when you're done.

A.I. isn't great, available powers don't do much interesting (I think the only one I used more than once is Blink), and overall it just feels dull to me. This game is one of the best & most original Metroidvania games I've ever played & it deserves much more recognition than it's currently getting.

-Great Artistic Style

You play as Trace, a scientist who experienced some sort of tragic accident & awakens to find himself in some strange new world with a voice in his head.  The voice tells you to go get a gun in the next room & then tells you she's unable to communicate anymore due to her injuries which she needs to you help her with.  As you go on you find out you're infected with some sort of pathogen that wiped out all intelligent life on the planet you're on.  It's slowly eating away at your nervous system & will eventually kill you.  So, you need to not only save these mysterious machine beings but yourself as well.  The story does get deeper than just that but saying any more would be spoiling so I'll just end it there.
The game starts out with you getting a gun & later getting various upgrades to help you on your journey.  These are mostly upgrades for your gun but they also give you some sweet looking attire like the Lab/Trench coats.  There's also health, damage & even projectile range & size upgrades hidden throughout the game. You eventually get more weapons that all have various uses like a big beam that takes up most of the screen, but deals very little damage to a laser that pierces through enemies.  There are so many weapon types in this game that it would take a small list to fill so I'll leave the rest to official guides or let you find them whilst you play.
The game has the main story mode with two difficulties.  Normal & Hard.  I suggest anyone new to this game play on Normal as I tried Hard (which I usually do play hard difficulties) but I found it much too difficult.  The game is fairly difficult even on Normal so I recommend playing it on that setting for your first run.  There are several boss fights in this game & each boss has its own weak point which you'll need to find & hit using one of the weapons in your arsenal.  Some weapons are better suited for each boss but it's your choice of which to use.
There's also a speed-run mode which I haven't tried yet so I won't comment on it.
This game doesn't hold your hand as you play it either.  The voice in your head gives you a task but it doesn't tell you where to go so you're free to explore at your leisure.  That's a good thing, too because there is a ton of exploration in this game.
The game looks very good & it's pixel art is fantastic.  There are some areas where you may need time to adjust because the foreground uses the same colors as the background so it can be hard at first to tell what's on screen.  Eventually you're eyes get used to it, mine did anyways.  Overall the graphics look very unique & the game does things I've never seen before in any classic pixel style art game.  You really need to see it to appreciate it.
The music in this game is god-like.  Try to imagine some really techno-metal sound effects, atmospheric music & trippy sunni style vocals mixed all together in one.  That's pretty much the only way I can describe it but the end result is fantastic.  I can't really compare this game's music to anything else I've heard before.  You really have to hear it for yourself.
The game utilizes every button on today's standard controllers.  You may not be able to use a retro controller for this one.  Everything feels solid from jumping & shooting to dashing & grappling.  You may need to get used to the dash & grapple at first but after you figure it out you'll be grappling off the ceiling & dashing through enemies like a pro.
This game is one of the better games I've played in recent memory.  It's on par with games like Shovel Knight, Freedom Planet & even Super Metroid for quality & originality.  It may even surpass those games as a whole due to how unique it really is.  If you like 2D Adventure games that have a lot of exploration definitely pick this one up.  It's worth every penny spent.
Lame jokes about Super Metroid aside once the game gets going you don't wanna stop.

A lot of people seem to have a problem with this game not being Super Metroid, leading to some negative reviews, but it is a genuinely impressive game in its gameplay and atmosphere.
Pros:
-Tight controls

-Mostly hidden/optional weapons

-Seriously the gameplay is ♥♥♥♥ing amazing it controls so well

-Glitch mechanics are unique and cool
-Enemy variety and visuals contribute to atmosphere of surrealism
-Justin Bailey :^)
Cons:
-Boss fights feel claustrophobic
-Areas don't make geographical sense with each other
-Unsatisfying story
-Some mechanics don't flow throughout the game
To speak to my criticisms, the reason I have such problems with these few things is because of how polished the rest of the game feels. The first boss fight teaches you that the faces of the enemies are the vulnerable spots, but this doesn't hold true for the rest of the bosses. Following fights have similar face areas on the bosses, but 2 of the 4 similarly designed bosses do not follow this same fight strategy. This would be perfectly acceptable if it weren't for the fact that it is established so early in the game that the particular spot is the weak point. In addition to this, multiple boss fights felt as though there was no space for dodging projectiles and attacks, and some of the attacks were too fast with too large of hitboxes. This left me feeling cheated at certain points of the game, having to fight a boss over and over, hoping I would make one mistake less than the last time (I'm sure I just suck at the game). The most memorable and well designed boss fight was the 3rd one, where the player could shoot different parts of the boss to disable those weapons. There was also an arena that punished reckless gameplay while rewarding thoughtful execution by providing cover to certain weapons at varying times. This fight also followed the first boss' damage design which made the other two fights with similar face designs feel more confusing. The arena was spacious and provided plenty of room to dodge the projectiles.
In regards to the overall world design, I liked the visuals and the different areas, but I found that they didn't make structural sense in the context of a world (and I hate to compare to Metroid) like Zebes from Super Metroid. Where in Super Metroid the levels changed gradually and made sense in their placement relative to each other (lava is deeper in the planet while the crashed space ship is at the surface, burrowed partly into the crust), Axiom Verge had a world which seemed to feel more like a variety show à la Metroid Fusion. In Fusion this made sense because Nintendo created a scientific environment testing vessel, but Axiom Verge is supposedly a continuous world.
The story of Axiom Verge is told through notes and written dialogue/cutscenes, and while I have no problem with this method of storytelling I found the story itself to be far less ambitious or consequential as I thought it would be. This is where I bring my first direct criticism of Tom Happ himself; he has stretched himself too thin in creating Axiom Verge as a one-man development team. Happ has a strong grasp of the metroidvania genre and he clearly understands implicit level design where the player can find the next area and item through exploration. Where he struggles is storytelling and designing a compelling narrative for players. This is fine of course because Happ is great at making a tight game that controls like none other, but with such an ambitious story for Axiom Verge, I would have preferred someone else's touch on the narrative and how the gameplay and world reflected this story.
All of these gripes are minor because I simply loved the overworld, the combat, and the sense of progression based on items and powerups. I look forward to seeing what Happ develops in the future, and I hope he can collaborate with others to create a masterpiece following this promising first major release.
TL;DR
THE GAME IS GOOD, NOT PERFECT. BUY IT AND PLAY THE♥♥♥♥♥♥OUT OF IT.

Remember the demonic imagery and disturbing backgrounds of Ninja Gaiden as you got closer and closer to fighting the demon? How about the sci-fi creepiness of Metroid? Or the creepy alien lair of Contra?
Axiom Verge takes these elements and cranks them up. The setting is creepy, the music unsettling, and the story increasingly disturbing. There's even some impressively melancholy chiptune music at one point.
The game first starts out as an utterly shameless ripoff of Metroid. I'm talking totally shameless - everything from the enemy types to the types of environments encountered early in the game, to the Super Metroid-esque map - it all screams Metroid, and it's painfully blatant, to the point where I rolled my eyes and thought "Does this game have *any* originality?".
Well, it does.  Not only does the game not continue in this direction, it even deliberately subverts expectations.
See that thin space that you just can't fit through? In Metroid, you'd get through it by turning into a ball. Axiom Verge never gives you an equivalent ability, but rather, a drone that can fit through spaces that you cannot. High up areas that you can't reach? Grappling hook - there is no Space Jump. Thin walls blocking your path? No, you don't speed through them and break them - you teleport through them with a special jacket. You don't freeze enemies to stand on them - you "glitch" some of them to stand on them, or you "glitch" the world on occasion.
What's this about "glitches"? Well, Axiom Verge has a little fun with the fourth wall. Remember how NES games looked when they weren't working right? When graphics glitches caused things to get garbled and strange looking? When in some cases, a graphics glitch would even transform an enemy or object in such a way that its behavior became totally different? (as just one example, Chip and Dale on the NES had a weird glitch in the sewers level at the point where you went up, where if you managed to get the water at the bottom of the screen to turn white, you can suddenly stand on it as if it were ground)
Well, this game does that for deliberate and sometimes unsettling effect. There are "fake graphics glitches" you encounter quite often, which perfectly simulate what actual NES games looked like when they malfunctioned. The glitches and how they are used almost make it seem as if the world is tearing itself apart - an impressive way to take an error from our childhoods and use it as both plot and gameplay device, not to mention to add atmosphere. There are even some creepy "outer world" areas that look like unholy glitched up messes with some filters that approach the fourth wall, such as filters to make the game suddenly look like it's being played on an old TV that's dealing with interference.
Your "glitch gun" weapon (it's called the Address Disruptor) can invoke this deliberately to a degree, as it transforms enemies into glitchy abominations and even changes their behavior. An enemy may slow down, change its attacks from ones that harm you to ones that break through walls, or even try to escape you. Some of these behavior changes are the sort of thing you'd expect to see from a messed-up Game Genie code used on the NES. Or, appropriately, what NES games do when the memory addresses of objects get disrupted. This game's sole designer, Tom Happ, really knows the NES.
The graphics, while retro-inspired, actually use certain design elements of the olden days to intentional effect. Areas tend to have their own color scheme. While NES games tended to do this out of necessity (without going into super technical detail, the NES had strict color limits due to how it handled its 8 palettes at any given time), this game does it deliberately. It starts out looking a lot more NES-esque, but gradually, more color is used. It works, and the areas, while generally not having more personality beyond "creepy and alien", "super creepy and alien", "disturbing and alien", and "kinda creepy but cool, and alien", still look distinctly different. They range from tunnels with pulsating organs hanging on threads to a very strange forest that looks like something that could not only never exist on Earth, but on any planet in this universe.
The music and sound design is... interesting. Sounds are often loud and piercing, similar to old games. I assume this was intentional. The music is entirely different, and is quite the genre mix. One song I found particularly memorable started out as a melancholy NES chiptune with echo effects, and started getting louder and with more electronic non-NES instruments added. Another song features alien lyrics and chanting.
The world is huge. You will get lost. You gain new abilities and new weapons constantly, giving a rather impressive feeling of progression that few games match. As you get new abilities that aid in travel, you'll naturally have to use them, and that's when it's time to look at the map and see which areas haven't been filled out. The hallway that seems to cut off on the map - is that because you got stopped by something and were unable to reach the end? Might want to check it out.
The problem is that backtracking takes longer the further you get in the game, and there just aren't enough connecting areas or fast means of travel to really speed it up that much. I didn't find it a dealbreaker, and some enjoy that aspect of the game, but just be aware that it's there.
My other complaint is that the end of the game ramps up the difficulty to such a degree that I had to use cheap tactics to fight the last few bosses and deal with annoying, tough new enemy types. I felt like I was fighting cheapness with my own cheapness. Not the best way to end the game.
Despite these complaints, Axiom Verge is an amazing game, especially for being made entirely by one person in his spare time over 5 years. It's more than just a nostalgic throwback to the creepier side of the NES with its Contra, Ninja Gaiden and Metroid inspirations along with its oddly unsettling use of "glitches". It's also an amazingly creative experience that plays with the expectations of the 30-somethings and late 20-somethings that it's aimed at. Even if you hold no such nostalgia for that era and that style of game, it's still a great game.

Burly Men at Sea,
This game can be summerized as an interactive story with gorgeous visuals and calming sounds.
In short, it'll be a game that you can play during your down time to take your mind off the events of the day and just relax a little.
The game works like this: you, the 3 brothers, are inside a circle, which is your view of the world, by dragging this imaginary circle left or right, you explore the world and find new adventures. The game isn't linear, it has a number of branches and stories that you can explore, each with their own tales.
The writing is amazing, although it's more or less a series of short stories, I really appriciate it. There are some funny jokes and some serious moments which all together set a beautiful tone to the world. Mix that with the wonderful sounds and music (and trust me you will enjoy this part a lot) and the wonderful, colorful minimalistic visuals and you end up with a true indie gem.
Now to my understanding this isn't a very long game as you can tell from the price but it isn't lacking. Considering the gorgeous artstyle, sounds and the charming writing I think it's worth the price point and it should give you around 2-3 hours of entertainment.
What you need to know is that this isn't a game for everyone, this is a series "of soft-choice based intractive short stories" so that's up to you to decide if that description is appealing to you or not.
When i say "A series of soft-choice based interactive short stories" I mean that you make choices that shape different adventures and branch a path for you, however in the end once one adventure is over, you end up looping around to start another.
This game isn't a "oh you died cause bad choices scenario", hence why i used "soft-choice based" as the description.
Your choices still matter and give you different and unique paths and different stories, but it's more like a series of short adventures rather than a really driven out novel with major choices that drag on and affect you later on.
So in short, some of the choices you might make are as simple as going left or going right and this'll give you a new adventure based on what you chose.
I hope this serves as a good description for someone looking to buy this game and that if you're interested in that type of game, ends up as a buying point for you.
Finally I'd just like to point out, there is a mobile version of this game as well, which you might find more suited to you. (since it'll be swiping left and right instead of dragging the screen with a mouse)
In any case, buckle up and enjoy this one :)

This game is youth itself. It's a beautiful and engaging story of friendship and love, happiness and fun, sadness and grief. It shows you ways of dealing with loss and tragedy and overcoming one's own fears and trauma in order to once again grasp the happiness that awaits beyond. A rollercoaster of emotions, created by Key, the masters of their craft, who have incorporated their experiences and new ideas, gained over a long process of writing stories that tightly grip the hearts of their readers time and time again.
The Little Busters have set out on an important mission: To make new friends and have as much fun as they possibly can while they're still young. Their leader Kyousuke never runs out of ideas as they transform their everyday lives in memories of happiness with their silly antics.
Beginning with an energetic narrative of youth and friendship, the story then becomes more serious as our protagonist, Naoe Riki, discovers love and is faced with harsh trials of life that may hit anyone, at any time. This is where the friendship of the Little Busters truly shines, as they come together to help their members endure the pain and deal with their problems and eventually become stronger.
Little Busters is my favorite game. It has become a part of me and taught me many things. Even among the masterpieces of Key, this game will always be special to me.

Video review (including score):
Ten years after its initial Japanese release, Little Busters! finally makes its way to English audiences. It is a game that I have been wanting to play for years now, as I am a big fan of Key’s previous works, having seen all of their respective anime adaptations. Clannad is my all-time favorite work of fiction across any medium, so I had very high expectations going into this game.
As with Key’s previous works, the game is built around its characters. The whole goal is to build up these characters so much so that the player becomes attached to them and really gets to know them. This is an aspect that Key has always been good at and Little Busters! is no exception. The character routes expand on each character in-depth, usually by exploring said character’s past, giving the player insight into why each character acts the way they do. During that process, these characters are really brought to life.
The Clannad Original Soundtrack is my all-time favorite soundtrack, so knowing that the Little Busters! soundtrack shares some of the same composers, I had similar expectations. These expectations were met for the most part. There are several standout tracks in the soundtrack, with only a few on the weaker side. “BOYS DON’T CRY” is a great example of one of the better tracks from the game and might be my favorite, although it is hard to choose.
It is not just the excellent background music that makes this soundtrack so good. The opening theme is just as good, with the English localization even including karaoke on-screen when it plays, just as one would find on a lot of today’s fansubbed anime. The different ending themes were of varying quality, but none of them were bad. The main insert song, titled “Faraway”, is easily the best vocal track in the game though. I would be lying if I said I did not shed a tear or two when that one started playing during the Refrain route. Overall though, the Little Busters! Original Soundtrack is just another great work to come out of Key Sounds Label.
I had a great time going through most of the character routes, but all of them pale in comparison to the game’s true ending, the Refrain route. Sure, the character routes are supposed to invoke some sort of emotional response, but I did not shed a single tear until I got to the Refrain route. This is coming from someone who rarely feels any emotion for fictional characters, let alone shed a tear for one. I can count the number of times this has happened on one hand, Little Busters! now included. It is just that good. The emotional payoff in the Refrain route is easily worth the 60 or so hours it took to get to that point. This all just further cements my opinion that Jun Maeda is the best writer in the industry.
The Busterpedia is a great addition for the English version, especially for those that may not know a lot about Japanese culture. It is basically an in-game dictionary, highlighting certain words, phrases, or names that the player may not know. Clicking on the highlighted word, phrase, or name brings up its definition. It can also can be accessed at anytime from the main menu or the in-game menu. I consider myself at least somewhat knowledgeable about Japanese culture, but there was still several terms and names that I was not familiar with, so the Busterpedia was rather helpful in that regard. The definitions range from simple words that are rather well-known, like Tatami, up to terms like Ogura Hyakunin Isshu, the name of a Japanese poetry anthology published in the 12th century.
Despite Little Busters! being a visual novel, there are plenty of mini-games included that span a variety of genres. First, there is the battle system. This aspect of the game basically has the player collecting items to increase his/her stats and up his/her position on the battle rankings leaderboard throughout the course of the game. There is also the batting practice mini-game, which is a bit more involved compared to the battle system. This one has the player moving left and right then pressing space when the perfect pitch is lined up. Playing this mini-game builds stats for each character participating in the practice, which helps in both the battle system and the actual baseball game played during the common route.
Even more involved than the baseball mini-game is the dungeon crawler present in Saya’s route, which can be accessed after clearing Refrain. It is a full-blown dungeon crawler implemented right into a visual novel, with trap rooms and a shooting gallery mini-game when enemies appear. There are a few others as well, but these three are the standout ones. These mini-games do not hinder the experience at all and can be disabled by the player if he/she does not want to bother with them. They just serve as some additional fun to have while playing through the main game. I personally had a lot of fun tracking down the different achievements that can be earned by participating in these mini-games.
Steam says I have logged over 150 hours in this game and, while some of that time may have been spent idling, I would not be surprised if my actual playtime came in at around 80 hours. It took over a month of on-and-off playing to finish the game. There is simply that much content present in Little Busters!. The common route is very long, with each character route taking a reasonable amount of time to clear as well. The true ending, the Refrain route, is also of decent length. Adding in all of the extra content, such as the bonus routes and mini-games, and you are left with quite the package.
I did mention previously that each character route takes considerable time to clear, but that does not mean each is well-paced. There were a few character routes that felt rushed towards the end. It was as if the one writing the route was suddenly out of time and had to crank out an ending as quickly as possible. This was very noticeable with Kud’s route, my least favorite in the game because of just how jarring the sudden shift in pacing was towards the end of the route. Without spoiling, I will just say that the last 15% or so of that route became quit the mess, a very different feeling compared to the rest of the route. This was not the case with all the routes though, just a few. It is quite the shame actually, as a couple of these rushed routes started off great, only to lose their appeal as the pacing increased.
The game is made up of over one million words, so I expected the occasional typo or two. They were not all that common, not enough to really bother me, but it should be noted regardless. I noticed that the majority of these typos appeared during the Ecstasy routes, the three routes unlocked after completing Refrain. Perhaps it is because the Ecstasy content was never translated prior to this release, whereas the translation of the base game has been out for years and served as the foundation for this English Edition, allowing for any typos to be ironed out.
With each release, Key continues to set the standard for what a good visual novel should strive to be. The game met my high expectations and it is the first visual novel to have impacted me on such an emotional level, enough so that I had to fight back tears. From its great characterization to its fun mini-games, Little Busters! does just about everything right, with only a few rushed character routes bringing down the experience. Highly recommended for visual novel fans and those that enjoy impactful stories.

TL;DR: if you're looking for an improved HoI 3 - with all the complexity of that game -, this isn't that game. If you're looking for a simplified, easier HoI 3 - without all the complexity, but with all the surface-level features -, this might be for you.
Now to the actual review:
I really wanted to like this game, bought it on launch, and kept playing it on-and-off until now, hoping some updates and mods and whatnot would make this into the game I wanted. After a year, its time to admit that this will never be a good Hearts of Iron game... it might eventually become a decent strategy game, but there are plenty of those. And most of those don't have such bloody annoying DLC-spam.
What is wrong with HoI4:
1. The UI:
Incredibly, Paradox managed to make a UI that is functionally as bad as HoI3's clunky, opaque, hard-to-use and ugly creation. This time it's at least pretty, but even just slapping a couple excel sheets on the screen would be more effective.
The production of equipment is a very neat idea, good mechanic, but the implementation on the UI is... bad. You have 6 lines of Inf. Equipment 1, then research the next level, and want to switch them to the new one? You better like clicking, 'cause you have to do them 1-by-1, and and ofcourse good luck even finding them between the other 50-odd production lines in the category. This just gets even more out-of-hand if you install mods that add more equipment types (Black Ice becomes boring as hell because of all the clicking you have to do just to producte a new division type). Why can't we have a searchable list of equipment types, and a numeric input field for how many factories you want? Oh... because Paradox UI designers don't seem to know the concept of a numeric input field... its bloody sliders and heaps of icons everywhere, even thought this is a PC-exclusive, with access to a perfectly good keyboard with 100+ keys on it.
Want to start production of new divisions that require 2 new eq. types? Sure, why not just start production, then in the same context add the new equipments to the production queue and set them up to get up to a total of 20 factories each. Oh... wait, you can't do that... you have to go back to the cluncky production menu, find the eq. (a search function is hard to make), add it, then adjust the qty of factories. Oh... you wanted to add two lines of that equipment for these new divisions. I hope you really like clicking....
The trade UI is... okay, actually. Only thing it's missing is an automate button, with some settings (use up to x factories in trade, for instance). It would be nice to be able to see the actual number of resource points lost and gained from bonuses/maluses. I'm pretty sure I'm not exporting 30% oil, I'm exporting an actual number of oil resources... so just tell me as a straight number, so that I can play the game without first having to figure out how your algorithm rounds up all the different percentage modifiers, then reach for a calculator to get a number. But that automate button from HoI3 is sorely needed, because interacting with the trade screen is boring (its yet another couple clicks you have to make, because god forbid for there to be a button that just balances your damn resource needs). I'll get into the stupidity of the linked game mechanics later....
The logistics screen... is... almost undescribably stupid. It shows a lot of information, some of which is irrelevant, and some of it is actually wrong. Naturally, it isn't sortable or searcheable in any way, because why would a table containing values would need to be sortable. Also, it doesn't share the categories with the production screen, it dumps everything into a single list, that is apparently haphazardly thrown together without an organisational element.
And we get to the part where it displays misleading information: if you're in 1944, and have been building inf. eq. all along, you'll have a sizeable stockpile of outdated and captured eq. sitting in storage. And this screen bundles it all up when showing you the amount you have, making it entirely useless in determining wheter or not you still need to produce stuff. Good job. Should you open the details for an eq. type, it will get to showing you actual numbers, and the different versions of the stuff you have. It is just the cherry on top that while all other screens display production per day when possbile, this display stubbornly display is per week, for no apparent reason. But that's nitpicking...
2. The World Map:
.... I dunno where to even start with this pretty but utterly badly designed mess... so I won't right now. I'll just go play some HoI3 and come back to finish this review some other day...

Random Access Murder is a Humble Monthly cash-in that should have been made to be a Humble Original rather than a featured game in the bundle it was included in. It's a very generic FPS that relies on a "tron" aesthetic, with very little features and not much to set it apart from other games in the same genre.
The one unique feature this game has is its use of "glitches" that occur when you're damaged by other players, which include blue screen errors, pop-ups, crashes to desktop, and other similar visual effects which are designed to mimic old Windows hardware errors or signs of a virus/malware infected machine. This is pretty much the only cool aspect about the game and it can be more of a frustration the longer you play the game as it tends to get in the way of the gameplay. These effects tend to hide how crappy the shooting mechanics are rather than help the aesthetics in the long term.
There's very little gun and level variety, and the guns tend to be very unreliable for the most part. The most efficient gun to me seems to be the Rocket Launcher, which has more of a direct impact than every other gun. There's also a grenade launcher (that has a flash effect) which is interesting at first, but quickly gets tiresome when you realize it doesn't have much of a damage effect. Other guns are a bit ambiguous as to what effects they have, which can be a fatal flaw for a shooting game. There are currently 4 levels included in the game which are uninspired. The game could benefit from workshop support, I doubt it'd be very complicated to design your own levels.
As far as the interface goes, there are barely any options you can customize, and there are basic features that seem to be missing like a scoreboard or the ability to edit control bindings. Someone please correct me if I'm wrong, because if there is a way to access the score list, I haven't seen any. There's no way to check for control bindings in game, you just have to assume what the default controls are. I'm also not sure if the server names are currently working, every server I see pop up has a generic number which is indistinguishable from the rest. I've had no issues connecting to games at least, so the game does have competent netcode working for it.
The dev claims that eventually character progression and customization will be added, but in the current state I can't recommend this game at ANY price. There are better shooters that you can play for free, and if you need something with a retro "tron" art style, then I suggest playing Robot Roller Derby Disco Dodgeball. It's not an FPS but it's leagues better than this game.

A Bird Story is a brief, surreal tale that has little in common with To The Moon, a game that is sort of a relative to this from the same developer, aside from aesthetics and a touching story. A daydreaming, and somewhat set apart boy finds a wounded bird and tries to nurse him back to health. The wordless adventure will leave some players feeling a bit lost or disconnected from the characters: none of the pantomiming seems to be confusing, but it certainly does have as many shades as language does. It is also a fairly simple story with no twist, and in that sense it is markedly different from To The Moon.  It is story that is told in a few hours, but it is simple and sweet in a way not often seen, especially in this medium.
The gameplay aspect is on the minimal side, so you are playing to watch a wordless story. The interjections of gameplay (mostly button prompts) is a slight experimentation on the developer's part that adds a bit more to the experience. The minimalism of the game, in story or gameplay, did not detract from the experience. It is a short buy enjoyable game.

Undecided review, marked as "thumbs down" so it's visible more easily to those who want to know what's perhaps not so good about it.
A very short tightly story-driven game about a boy bonding with a bird. There is no real gameplay to speak of other than walking and hitting a use button once in a while but that's good if it's just a story to be told one is looking for.
Nice about it: How the story is explained despite the utter lack of text and voice. You can select a text language when the game starts but fun thing is the "start" and "exit" buttons as well as the credits are the only texts you'll ever see. The story is told only through sparse sounds, basic reactive symbols or thought bubbles above people's heads and just as minimal but effective movement, gestures and facial expressions. It's supported by equally simple but fitting music.
So-so: The story. The game felt somewhat pretentious to me. The drama in it is highly artifical. The boy you control is lonely and seemingly a bit detached from reality. Maybe even mentally ill. But he acts silly regardless. Even it's cute and kinda adorable: I very much doubt you'd ever see anyone bond and fool around like this with an animal, least not see the same sentiments in return as you project them towards it. This is part of why the game sometimes feels detached from reality too and thus loses some of it's authenticity or "power" to me. It's hard to relate with a topic that should feel like an ordinary thing that could happen to anyone but that has as much strange or unrealistic elements and moments as "A Bird Story". I reckon the bond between human and animal could work just as much or better when it was grounded in more solid matters. I know a manga about a couple witnessing the slow death of their dog in a perfectly ordinary time, place and dimension and that one impressed me better. "Abusing" some lost child on the other side to do half the groundwork for it as in "A Bird Story" feels almost like a chliché in comparison.
Furthermore, the way the boy acts and how other characters and the world is shown (the boy is the only character with an actual face - all other people are simple shades/vague silhouettes, and most of the time when he stumbles into other people it's either him or them acting in hostile or evasive ways) could give already sufficiently misanthropic or animals-obsessed people the idea that their ways were perfectly fine. Or support the misconception of humanizing animals. Animals are not people. People are not animals. Whoever thinks otherwise probably sees the world only in black and white. And I'm afraid the small world in "A Bird Story" is just that even if obviously seen through the eyes of a naive and perhaps delusional child who couldn't be expected to see it with less shrouded eyes anyway.

is an attempt to create a realistic hunter/survival game in which your aim is to hunt bucks with guns and survive. There are currently 5 levels at the time of writing this review (8/7/2016). Each level has a different environment. In order to progress from a level to a higher level, one must hunt a buck or survive the initial half day, night and the following day. You must also explore the map to find provisions such as food and medicines which help you survive longer.
After playing the game for about 5 hrs (2 hrs offline) I made short notes about what I felt was positive and negative about the game. The following are the positives and negatives of my experience of the game.
I like the environment and the lighting specially how the environment is slightly brighter when the moon is out at night as opposed to when it is coming out or going down. I liked the graphics on the trees. The shooting mechanic is challenging and requires time getting used. I think generally the graphics are mediocre, but the bucks/game camoflauges really well in the environment and it is challenging to find them before they see you. I like how the provisons are scarce and you have to learn their locations and navigate to them when you need them. Survival in the night is challenging when you know that a coyote is after you.
The menu is really simple and there is little graphics/game customization in the settings. The game could not run correctly on my laptop`s native 1080p resolution even when I checked the box in the settings. The screen was cut from the right side which did not allow me to see the helath bar. So I played in a lower resolution.This could have been a bug or a one-off but was still annoying. There is no pause menu in the game. I learned it the hard way in my first serious attempt to complete the first level. Press the escape button and you simply go to the main menu and none of your progress is saved. The graphics are mediocre and the game simply does not look like a game from today but something that was built in some old 2005 engine. The sound the hunter makes while walking is very loud and annoying, it barely changes and hinders hearing buck movement. There is no running or fast walking option moving forward, you just walk really loudly. But what I found funny was that the hunter can move quicker when you press the forward and one of the side buttons at the same time. Though that could be a bug. The game feels like its in beta and not polished enough. The deer AI needs to be improved and there is no hardcore tracking mechanics like hoove prints etc. The deer do not have realistic running animations. Finally there is no tutorial.

This game has a good concept and some very challenging mechanics but mediocre graphics, bugs and minimal customization options make it more of a challenge playing it than actaully being challenging. There is no reward system or flow in the game and it does not currently satisfy it's aim or it`s pricetag. I would
recommend buying this game unless it is improved.

Short Version: This game is worth a buy and a playthrough or three.
Long Version: (Note, there will be spoilers below, so read at your own risk)
GRAPHICS: Beautiful, from the sprites to the art. The sprites themselves had excellent articulation (Claret's hammering and Dhacian's sword come to mind), and the various expressions of the characters were extremely well done. The Claret-in-Prometheus-Engine sprite seemed a teensy bit off (color-wise) in a couple of frames (and I was dissappointed that it didn't replace the standard walking sprite in the final dungeon), but not jarringly so. The artist really should get a round of applause.
WRITING: This game's writing is very well done. In terms of plot, the story is familiar without being boring, and unusual without needing a compendium's worth of beforehand knowledge. The dialogue is both written and presented well. I know you don't know me, but that is very high praise coming from me; I am unbelievably nitpicky when it comes to dialogue and dialogue presentation. Skyborn does both quite well. The characters are believable and well-written, and especially unusual is that I did not find even one single character annoying!
SOUND: Very good. The music always fit the mood of the scene and was never once annoying. The choice to not use the battle theme in tense moments keeps the player immersed in the feeling of the scene. I have no complaints about the music.
MECHANICS: Autodash is wonderful, as always. The battle system works well with all available features and functions. Sometimes I swear I just couldn't keep threat on Sullivan, but the threat system was rewarding and satisfying no less. Mechanically, the game is sound. I do have a few issues that I will outline below:
- The Platina Coin augment does not confer blind as is stated by its description, but silence instead.
- The status effects are not adequately described ingame; without having and using a skill that causes them, it's difficult to know what a status effect does when it's inflicted on you or an enemy.
- The overall effect of the +1-4 Metal Ingots could have been explained better. I had no idea that it affected more than just attack damage and weight.
- The Exploration Points (sp?) seemed oddly out of place. There was no counter keeping track of how many I'd found, and frankly, they seemed like a last minute addition to re-balance the game. They come off as a bit of a clumsy afterthought to me.
AESTHETICS: All in all, this game is pleasant to both look at and play. The maps are well made, being both intuitive and easy to figure out (and believe me, I've seen some downright OFFENSIVE mapping in some games). The art was fantastic (Saehral really outdid herself), the sound was great, and the dialogue was arranged well. In terms of battle animations, I'd have perhaps liked to see some more custom ones, rather than stock RPGMaker animations, but they still convey what is necessary. There were a few capitalization errors in a few item descriptions, in particular the Branch of Life, Ether, Medical Herb and Potion, but not everybody is a Grammar Nazi.
CONCLUSION: This is more than an above-average game; this is a very good game that's easily worth the full price. It'll keep you busy for 10 hours minimum - more if you take care of all the bonus content - and you'll have a good time while you're at it.

An incredibly fun, if short, RPG that has incredible potential.
Length - 2/5
The game lasts maybe 6-13 hours per run, assuming you explore the massively huge areas that you get.  Unfortunately, you only have a handful of areas to explore, and the game itself feels a little short.
Content (Dangerous zones) - 4/5
Although you only have a few areas to work with in the game, each zone is HUGE.  One zone takes maybe an hour or two to actually explore every nook and cranny of it.  Not only that, you are rewarded for exploring the huge areas (that you can also easily get lost in) with small consumables to ore for crafting to ultimate armor and weapons.  Each zone is beautifully and realistically made just for its terrain alone.  In addition to the beautiful zones, there are appropriate lighting effects to really add to their flavor.
Unfortunately, the variety of monsters, their formations, and skill splash feel painfull average.  Although you don't face the same three enemies over and over again, you also don't face very many different enemies in random battles.  Some of them, sadly, only have one or two skills to take note of.
Content (Safe zones) - 5/5
The towns and villages in this game are incredibly made with vibrant NPCs from start to finish.  The lighting effects, incredibly beautiful terrain, and heartwarming NPCs bring life to these massive towns.  There are also rewards for exploring towns through exploration nodes (grants exp) and some small items.
Balance (Early game + Mid game) - 4/5
Not too rough; not too easy.  Just the perfect blend.  Random battles don't take too long, but they aren't excruciatingly long either.
Balance (End game) - 2.5/5
Unfortunately, the balance is heavily skewed when nearing the end of the game.  2 or 3 characters start dealing insane amounts of damage while the others are unable to provide significant contribution to DPS.  In addition, random enemies and bosses start to hit you with insane AoE damage (and healing doesn't seem perfectly tuned with that).  It doesn't help that some characters can take out most end game boss's (not optional but mandatory) HP bars to 25% with one skill.  Overall, this part of the game, combat wise, seems to be a little rushed or trying its best to cope with its new conditions (no spoilers, but it should be obvious which party member I'm talking about).
Lore - 3.5/5
The lore of the game felt interesting, and it hinted at a bigger depth than what the game actually provided with us.  Unfortunately, the depth and significant parts of the lore felt slammed onto the player near the end of the game with little to no mention in the first parts of it.  Lore was great; execution was a little sloppy.
Plot - 5/5
In the short time in the game, I constantly felt excited to keep the plot rolling.  There was little time for resting, and I knew that every action my party did was significant to their cause.
The premises were amazing, if a bit cliche.  It can be summarized generally in a sentence: The Skyborn, conquerers of the world, are imprisoning all half-breeds (half Skyborn and half Human), and a small group of rebels want to stop this injustice.

This game has many unique plot interests and story points that truly feel planned and thought out rather than the scripted tropes many RPG Maker games force on players. Also, there is some room at the end for a possible sequel. The locations to explore, though somewhat easy to lose one's self in, remind me of old school RPGs that did not hold your hand with a map or perfectly linear routes (I honestly prefer this style, it makes you have to think or make notes). The music to this game was very fitting and truly gave me the full experience I'm sure the developers were intending. I appreciated how it flowed well with the art style and visual feel of the game. The one thing I wished to see was character pictures in chat for all talking NPCs that did not have character busts.. it's odd to me seeing a text box show up with no image. I also wish the game had cause to visit more locations, since the game could've easily extended to a total of 12 hours with how much backstory and develpment they could have entertained.
Overall, this has been one of the better RPG Maker derived games that I have played, and truly one that was worth the money. I hope you folks out there on Steam give this a chance, and I hope that you developers reading this are already working on a followup for this excellently crafted game. Thank you.

Remember the demonic imagery and disturbing backgrounds of Ninja Gaiden as you got closer and closer to fighting the demon? How about the sci-fi creepiness of Metroid? Or the creepy alien lair of Contra?
Axiom Verge takes these elements and cranks them up. The setting is creepy, the music unsettling, and the story increasingly disturbing. There's even some impressively melancholy chiptune music at one point.
The game first starts out as an utterly shameless ripoff of Metroid. I'm talking totally shameless - everything from the enemy types to the types of environments encountered early in the game, to the Super Metroid-esque map - it all screams Metroid, and it's painfully blatant, to the point where I rolled my eyes and thought "Does this game have *any* originality?".
Well, it does.  Not only does the game not continue in this direction, it even deliberately subverts expectations.
See that thin space that you just can't fit through? In Metroid, you'd get through it by turning into a ball. Axiom Verge never gives you an equivalent ability, but rather, a drone that can fit through spaces that you cannot. High up areas that you can't reach? Grappling hook - there is no Space Jump. Thin walls blocking your path? No, you don't speed through them and break them - you teleport through them with a special jacket. You don't freeze enemies to stand on them - you "glitch" some of them to stand on them, or you "glitch" the world on occasion.
What's this about "glitches"? Well, Axiom Verge has a little fun with the fourth wall. Remember how NES games looked when they weren't working right? When graphics glitches caused things to get garbled and strange looking? When in some cases, a graphics glitch would even transform an enemy or object in such a way that its behavior became totally different? (as just one example, Chip and Dale on the NES had a weird glitch in the sewers level at the point where you went up, where if you managed to get the water at the bottom of the screen to turn white, you can suddenly stand on it as if it were ground)
Well, this game does that for deliberate and sometimes unsettling effect. There are "fake graphics glitches" you encounter quite often, which perfectly simulate what actual NES games looked like when they malfunctioned. The glitches and how they are used almost make it seem as if the world is tearing itself apart - an impressive way to take an error from our childhoods and use it as both plot and gameplay device, not to mention to add atmosphere. There are even some creepy "outer world" areas that look like unholy glitched up messes with some filters that approach the fourth wall, such as filters to make the game suddenly look like it's being played on an old TV that's dealing with interference.
Your "glitch gun" weapon (it's called the Address Disruptor) can invoke this deliberately to a degree, as it transforms enemies into glitchy abominations and even changes their behavior. An enemy may slow down, change its attacks from ones that harm you to ones that break through walls, or even try to escape you. Some of these behavior changes are the sort of thing you'd expect to see from a messed-up Game Genie code used on the NES. Or, appropriately, what NES games do when the memory addresses of objects get disrupted. This game's sole designer, Tom Happ, really knows the NES.
The graphics, while retro-inspired, actually use certain design elements of the olden days to intentional effect. Areas tend to have their own color scheme. While NES games tended to do this out of necessity (without going into super technical detail, the NES had strict color limits due to how it handled its 8 palettes at any given time), this game does it deliberately. It starts out looking a lot more NES-esque, but gradually, more color is used. It works, and the areas, while generally not having more personality beyond "creepy and alien", "super creepy and alien", "disturbing and alien", and "kinda creepy but cool, and alien", still look distinctly different. They range from tunnels with pulsating organs hanging on threads to a very strange forest that looks like something that could not only never exist on Earth, but on any planet in this universe.
The music and sound design is... interesting. Sounds are often loud and piercing, similar to old games. I assume this was intentional. The music is entirely different, and is quite the genre mix. One song I found particularly memorable started out as a melancholy NES chiptune with echo effects, and started getting louder and with more electronic non-NES instruments added. Another song features alien lyrics and chanting.
The world is huge. You will get lost. You gain new abilities and new weapons constantly, giving a rather impressive feeling of progression that few games match. As you get new abilities that aid in travel, you'll naturally have to use them, and that's when it's time to look at the map and see which areas haven't been filled out. The hallway that seems to cut off on the map - is that because you got stopped by something and were unable to reach the end? Might want to check it out.
The problem is that backtracking takes longer the further you get in the game, and there just aren't enough connecting areas or fast means of travel to really speed it up that much. I didn't find it a dealbreaker, and some enjoy that aspect of the game, but just be aware that it's there.
My other complaint is that the end of the game ramps up the difficulty to such a degree that I had to use cheap tactics to fight the last few bosses and deal with annoying, tough new enemy types. I felt like I was fighting cheapness with my own cheapness. Not the best way to end the game.
Despite these complaints, Axiom Verge is an amazing game, especially for being made entirely by one person in his spare time over 5 years. It's more than just a nostalgic throwback to the creepier side of the NES with its Contra, Ninja Gaiden and Metroid inspirations along with its oddly unsettling use of "glitches". It's also an amazingly creative experience that plays with the expectations of the 30-somethings and late 20-somethings that it's aimed at. Even if you hold no such nostalgia for that era and that style of game, it's still a great game.

A Metroidvania in the purest sense, Axiom Verge combines Metroid and Contra.  In particular, the original Metroid and Super Contra, in both gameplay and aesthetics.  The controls are snappy and responsive, and you can lock your feet like in Super Contra.  The game applies modern graphics to old NES Metroid aesthetics.  Environments and music are spooky, and enemies are disturbing.  There are many items, and you will not find them all on your first run.  The map lets you lay down markers to investigate secrets earlier.
Also, like Metroid and Contra, the game is tough as hell.  I highly recommend this.

I want to like it. I really do. It feels like a good game is there, somewhere, but it's lost in all the fluff. The game's biggest feature is that you play as a new survivor and your old one is zombified with all your old gear, but I've only died once and it was to an environmental feature, not zombies (A doorway on fire looked fine on the other side, so I dashed through it and instantly died).
I wanted to play the game, but dropping the coin on a WiiU for a launch title was not appealing. At least I know the quality of the game now.
PRO:
Survivors becoming skilled with weaponry is a good incentive not to die
Zombies hiding around doorways and pretending to be dead does add a decent amount of tension
Scoring headshots feel satisfying
Certain weapons have enough ammo to carry you for a while (Special mention: Crossbow bolts are retrievable)
CON:
Touted as a survival horror game, the only legitimately scary part of the game is brief and never mentioned again
Very little is explained, and what is does not deserve mention
Too many different weapon categories relying on different ammo types - Do we need a pistol and a magnum? In a game about inventory management, there's a lot of useless noise. (Looking at you, planks)
Secret areas were a bit of a disappointment - Usually it's not about being clever, but finding the right item to come back and unlock them.
It's pretty hard to die. Most - If not all - Encounters can be completed just by kiting the zombies backwards in a large circle and clubbing the leader over the head.
Despite the game early on telling you to do it, there's little point in barricading doors.
Characters you play as are very disposable - We're told a name, job, age, and are shown their appearance, but they add nothing to the story. It'd be more interesting if there was at least a blurb of randomized backstory and some skills/deficencies already existing for survival skills.
Game is linear. You can wander around for supplies, but generally they're scraps you might use up during a scuffle while you're out anyway. There's no zones just for exploring.
Items in your secure safehouse disappear, and your storage has limited inventory. This might be a gameplay feature, but it's just a weird decision.
It's just so close to being good. It needs to offer a more open world experience - If you had to find food and water supplies for other survivors, or if there wasn't always just one route to every step in the story, it would have been a much richer experience. Instead, it's a straightforward shooter with an emphasis on melee. Get it on sale if you must, but there's no meat here and no replayability.

I love Little Busters. I love Key.

A wonderful visual novel about friendship, growing up, and muscles. Lots of muscles.
Little Busters is two tons of fun, and is arguably some of the best entertainment I've had reading a VN. It has minigames and choices sprinkled throughout, and plenty of shenanigans/jokes to keep you entertained. The pacing overall is pretty good, and there were very few times when I felt like things were dragging on. This is crucial because of LB's staggering length of nearly 1.5 million words (almost double the length of the Bible) and over 90 hours of content, making it one of the longest visual novels ever written.
LB isn't all fun and games though. Later on it will hit you with tragic stories and heavy character drama. While it's not as potent as Clannad (one of Key's most famous VNs) in that regard, don't be surprised if at the end of a character route you're in tears.
That brings me to Little Busters' other strength: investment in characters. The male supporting cast of Kyousuke, Masato and Kengo is outstanding, which is a rarity in non-otome visual novels. They all have depth and complexity in their character, even the silly comic relief Masato (one of my favorite comic relief characters ever). For me, the female characters ranged from very good to mediocre, but these three guys stole the show. I'll definitely remember them long after I've moved on to other stories.
The character routes are a bit of a mixed bag for me. Some of them I loved, others I only thought were ok. However, when Little Busters lands a hit, it really knocks it out of the park. And that's why you should play it.

The Steam release marks the 4th time that I'm reading Little Busters, and it's still making me laugh and cry.
Probably the visual novel that had the greatest impact on me, and definitely the one that I like best. The stories and the characters are great, has a very good mix of serious and dramatic parts and fun and relaxing ones, and it has quite a lot of very different completely optional minigames.

Have you ever wished for something? Something you wanted so badly, that you would move heaven and earth to have it, even if your wish could only give a fleeting moment of happiness?
There are times in life where despite still being not too old, I yearn anyway for those blissful days of bygone youth, where you felt nothing could stop you and your friends from taking on the world. Those innocent playful days felt endless... But time never stops, childhood innocence is never for granted, and the oftentimes crueler hardships that come with this reality are ready at a moments notice to overtake us all whether or not we're ready to deal with them.
This VN captures those youthful days as it follows the lives of a small group of friends who call themselves the Little Busters, a group made just to enjoy those days while they last. They spend their days playing baseball, causing a ruckus, and maybe even solving some problems along the way. Always cheerfully pushing forward with song and smile. Always looking to enjoy the moment and help others enjoy the moment too when they really need a helping hand.
It's a beautiful story about friends and how we mature and grow stronger to face those issues that life will just hurl at us. Each character develops and matures from where they start out to the point where you just feel proud for them when they do overcome their hardships. Some characters even surprise you in how they handle their lot life has drawn for them. Things get deeply emotional and heartrending at times with the plights of some characters, and the game can easily veer off into the melodramatic at times for some people's tastes. But I think the game has so much more stronger moments than these weaker moments.
In terms of the quality, this is a labor of love from the translators. The folks at Fruitbat Factory did the original fan translation and have now finally their hard work is officially approved. I can only imagine the elation they have over this, and I would think this would be the dream of any fan who is passionate enough to do something like a fan translation. They deserve it though, as the VN is as perfect as it can be. Absolutely no complaints about the system. It does its job.

Undecided review, marked as "thumbs down" so it's visible more easily to those who want to know what's perhaps not so good about it.
A very short tightly story-driven game about a boy bonding with a bird. There is no real gameplay to speak of other than walking and hitting a use button once in a while but that's good if it's just a story to be told one is looking for.
Nice about it: How the story is explained despite the utter lack of text and voice. You can select a text language when the game starts but fun thing is the "start" and "exit" buttons as well as the credits are the only texts you'll ever see. The story is told only through sparse sounds, basic reactive symbols or thought bubbles above people's heads and just as minimal but effective movement, gestures and facial expressions. It's supported by equally simple but fitting music.
So-so: The story. The game felt somewhat pretentious to me. The drama in it is highly artifical. The boy you control is lonely and seemingly a bit detached from reality. Maybe even mentally ill. But he acts silly regardless. Even it's cute and kinda adorable: I very much doubt you'd ever see anyone bond and fool around like this with an animal, least not see the same sentiments in return as you project them towards it. This is part of why the game sometimes feels detached from reality too and thus loses some of it's authenticity or "power" to me. It's hard to relate with a topic that should feel like an ordinary thing that could happen to anyone but that has as much strange or unrealistic elements and moments as "A Bird Story". I reckon the bond between human and animal could work just as much or better when it was grounded in more solid matters. I know a manga about a couple witnessing the slow death of their dog in a perfectly ordinary time, place and dimension and that one impressed me better. "Abusing" some lost child on the other side to do half the groundwork for it as in "A Bird Story" feels almost like a chliché in comparison.
Furthermore, the way the boy acts and how other characters and the world is shown (the boy is the only character with an actual face - all other people are simple shades/vague silhouettes, and most of the time when he stumbles into other people it's either him or them acting in hostile or evasive ways) could give already sufficiently misanthropic or animals-obsessed people the idea that their ways were perfectly fine. Or support the misconception of humanizing animals. Animals are not people. People are not animals. Whoever thinks otherwise probably sees the world only in black and white. And I'm afraid the small world in "A Bird Story" is just that even if obviously seen through the eyes of a naive and perhaps delusional child who couldn't be expected to see it with less shrouded eyes anyway.

You like boys and birds? Oh boy. But there's such a lot of boys and birds. In some countries like China there are even more boys.  And birds! They are all over the place: think of Angry Birds, Thunderbirds, McNuggets, and all -- the world is kind of filled with these animals. But what good does a seagull do to you?
And here is more boys and birds, although the bird may not be a seagull as the colour is not right.
"A Bird Story" could be muuch better. Put in a girl and a rat and call it "A Rat Story".  Sneak in a sizzling soundtrack sounding like old Slayer or at least Doom.  The girl could have a mohawk.  The game could have clever mazes and chases and wonderful gleeful moments of eating away the knees of the nasty teacher together. Revolution! But such stuff is not at all in "A Bird Story". It is all goody-good, a railroader. There is dull, lethargic boy, there is paper planes, there is sleeping at school, a big apartment dismissed, taken for granted with the piano plunking on. Nobody can speak. Have they lost language? Only symbol exclamations remain! Its a pity for the boy to have all this when more-deserving people live in cardboard boxes.
In "A Bird Story" it sometimes happens that it is time for action. You get to press the arrow keys, for the boy go where the boy must go, a blurry-eyed puppet of the great scripter in the pixel-tiled sky. Press the keys, make the boy go. The script now has another boy. Is it you?
If you like boys, perhaps you are a boy, can relate to boys, birds? Rescue poor birds, nurse back to health. Maybe in some strong sedation together, dreamy with paper planes, finger on arrow key, pressing like the script says. So nice. Lookies no further.

Take Deus-Ex in a victorian 'steam-punk' setting, add some dark mystery and some extremely gritty characters and voila! You've got yourself Dishonored!
A bit more detailed:
Problems include:
-dated graphics (still servicable, but... ehm... they say it's unreal engine 3, but it might as well be Source. Not exactly what you expect from a game released at that time).
-easy difficulty (well... easy-ish. If you want to reload A LOT, try to get the 'ghost' achievement. Good luck! But the regular game is rather easy, especially if you don't care about being spotted or killing someone. And after all, you are an assassin!)
-short campaign (again... short-ish. If you want to explore the very nice, detailed levels, find all sorts of little stories and rob every nobleman, you come across, you will definitely end up with a decent playtime. But I imagine speed runs of this game tend to be very, VERY short.)
Pros:
-Nice mechanics that allow for a good variety of play-throughs for each level and situation
-very detailed and 'open' level design. The level don't have the sheer size of Arkham maps, but the amount of details and alternative routes is impressive!
-Interesting story and characters. Not a game changer, but definitely enough to get invested!
-Very good use of the graphics. Sounds a bit schizophraniac... here is the deal: The graphic engine is dated, but what they do with it is rather impressive!
-Dense and fascinating setting! Wale-oil powered gadgets, that need a constant flow of the pale gold, dark and damp side-alleys, wrist crossbows, mystical wale-bone charms, witches and assassins.... hell, yeaaah!
Bottom line: If you like games like Thief, Deux Ex or even the Arkham games, you should definitely consider trying this one!

I gave the game a fair shot, and my experience was mixed.
First of all there is a lot of great custom art for this project.  Bravo to the artist for literally carrying this game.
Sadly they left in the default sounds effects.  For a small budget you can get loads of free on the right sites with enough leg work.  It doesn't seem like the developer knew to do this. I broke quite a few events and even managed to find multiple passability bugs.  It really seems like this was someone's first RPG maker game as it has a lot of quality errors.
*To the people who quality tested this game: Shame on you.  You missed a lot.  I won't go further into muck racking than that.  You failed at your job, and it blatantly shows.*
Good music was another positive quality.  The theme was used enough and remixed to the atmosphere of the areas that it wasn't tired, but invigorating hearing it.  I was enthralled enough to keep playing with the BGM going.
The story was patchworked at best, with things shoe horned in that left me confused at times without explinations. I enjoyed the ride, but the story didn't go anywhere.  The big reveal at the end came out of nowhere and literally stopped the story dead to justify the end boss.  Even then the ending showed that a support character was the most important and invested character in the game, not Claret.  Claret was the falling star of Skyborn, and is sadly on the cover.  She has no place on the title, because this is not her story.  It's Claska's story and rise to power.
The battle system is simply steam rolling enemies at any difficulty.  The side boss is not worth revisiting, nor does she make any sense in the explaination of this world.  She seems to be able to go to the Fae world, so I assume she is an Earthenfae too.  Not that we are given any reason to invest in her.
Items weren't worth investing into.  At a point in the game where major upgrades are bought you replace them with found treasure almost instantly.  It's a big time sink that didn't need to be there.  Had weapons been upgraded like Claska's claw it would have been a bit of a smoother transition and better use of the anvil and synth system which fell short of simply buying better gear.
Skyborn can't decide what the Prometheus Engine is.  It tells us it is an Airship Engine at first, then an anti magic shield, and finally it turns out to be a mecha robot.  It has all but 30 seconds of screen time and isn't used in the final encounter.  Big build up and grind for little pay off there.  Claret focus quickly dwindled.
Sully's focus happened at the wrong times with his father being shoe horned in, and then almost forgot about his sister nor does she appear in the Fae Realm with the other half breeds.  His part as the Red Spectre had little to do with anything other than baiting the player.
Corwin is the ultimate silent character.  I feel like he wasn't even there.  He didn't even so much as chew the scenery.
Alda's derpy blonde face with it's crossed eyes had me amused, but her character's motivation kept changing to the point I felt she wasn't a liability so much as a natural blonde.  She is the over kill character.  She is far too powerful to be in the group.  EMP blast and Missle Launch had nothing on her Mystic Blade and Lightfury.
In the end it was worth one playthrough.  Was it perfect?  No.  Was it good?  Yes.  But it felt hastily put together and poorly tested.  You really need to pick and choose your testers.  Their laziness and inability to grow with the project's need hurt all of your custom materials.
It wasn't the developers fault with this game, his staff didn't measure up to the challange.  Hopefully Phil finds better people.

Let's be truly honest here.
Sometimes, playing with real people tends to get on your nerves. Whether it be people who don't know how VOIP works or just idiots trying to ruin a game for everyone, sometimes you just don't want your mind to be muddled and just want to hunker down after a hard day's work.
In the following paragraphs, I'm going to tell you how BRINK can give you that and so much more.
BRINK has had a rather unsteady history. I was one of the few people who bought it at launch and actually experienced it's rather disastrous start.
It was a mess. Massive lag hampered the game as well as netcode issues plaguing even dedicated servers. It also didn't help that ATI card didn't even run the game properly, and it even had problems on the Nvidia side of things!
So BRINK's launch-that-was-not ruined its reputation with the community, and sadly, a lot of people abandoned it as a failure.
I, however, did not. Determined to get the bang for my buck, I and many other souls soldiered on with the game. And that's where it started to show its greatest strengths both as a competitive and casual shooter. Let me talk about a few of these.
For those like me, who are not interested in playing with real players due to the stress or those who just simply don't have good internet connection, BRINK still allows you to play the game the way it's meant to be played through a single player (or co-op) bot mode.
Now I do admit, the bots were way underdeveloped when the game first released, but Splash Damage, even with the mostly negative reviews, didn't abandon the game and continued to patch it, which I believe the company should be lauded for.
At the games current build, the bots are smart, strategic, and will keep you on your toes. Even on normal difficulty you see the bots employing new strategies to outsmart you. They will play the objective and they will play it well, and you can rely on the enemy team to keep up the tense firefights.
In my almost 100 hours of play, I've seen bots use every ability available to the average player, even the ones you unlock at the highest level! These bots have come a long way from simple peashooters, and now are a decisive enemy that can be the fuel for hours of entertainment.
Sadly, the servers have been long dead for this game for a while, so bots are the only option if you want to play this game. I find this to be a shame, since BRINK was an excellent competitive shooter to. I'll get to that in a moment
Now you might be asking "Why play a game with bots? Where's the drive to keep me playing?" Let me show you.
BRINK used a system called "Mingleplayer". What that basically means is that you can play the game however you want, without the game punishing you. Wanna just play with bots solo? You can and can still gain experience and levels! Wanna play the games as an ultra competitive shooter? You can do that to (at least, you could if the game still had servers. Though you could always copy the competitive format of the game into a custom bot game, a feature in itself that has given me hours of entertainment). BRINK rewards you, however you want to play the game, and that for me is it's biggest strength.
Aside from that, BRINK made for an excellent competitive game as well. Way back when my online experience was almost entirely 5v5 scrims. That's the beauty of BRINK, it can be played both as a casual shooter where you join a server and blast away and as a highly competitive team shooter, voice comms and all. Each class (Medic, Engineer, Soldier, and Operative) had their distinct roles in the battlefield. Every class had its own skill tree and abilities, allowing you to customize to your playstyle. At the highest levels of play, all sorts of gadgets could be used from healing fields to UAVs. This gave BRINK endless replayability both at the lowest levels of play and the highest levels of play.
So you might be asking, why buy a dead game? Well, you'll just have to trust me on this one. Splash Damage gave this game the support it deserved and it has grown beautifully into a hidden gem. I can guarantee you the bots will give you a run for your money and you will have a great time with this game. The game is a beautiful tragedy, as it didn't get to reach its full potential in its lifetime, but can still offer you countless hours of offline bot play. I heartedly recommend this game to anyone who has an itchy trigger finger, and wants something new in their fps library!
So after a hard day's work, BRINK's got you covered. No screaming children. No Trolls. No idiots.
Just you and the game.
BONUS: The only fundamental DLC is Agent of Change, as it adds two new missions and several abilities and attachments, as well as raises the level cap. The others are purely cosmetic.
Thanks for reading!

Brink made it's debut as a fast-paced parkour shooter, and to this end it has been successful. Wall-jumping, vaulting, and sliding into enemies to knock them off their feet are all movement-based features integrated into the game. Players can also heavily customize their characters features, such as weight, tattoos, scars, clothing, ect.
