The environments are varied, and some of them can be quite beautiful, but aren't more explorable, or impressed upon the player, which is a shame, because some maps really have a lot of potential. To be honest, the story mode is quick, generates more questions than answers, and doesn't have all that great of a story in and of itself. You can take the sides of either the Resistance or the Ark Security forces, fighting each other for the fate of Ark. Nonetheless, story notwithstanding, the action is fast, gunplay better, and for sure this game is worth a try at least. Overall Score: 9.5/10

Let me start off by saying that I didn't come into this expecting the whole offering. I understand this is an Early Access game, and I understand that a huge amount of the promised content isn't released yet.
Still, I'm disappointed in this game so far. I expected a polished multiplayer melee game, similar to M&B's own multiplayer mods, not a grand epic. I was definitely sold by the long-term promises of town and army building, and the whole "persistent world" aspect, but I came into it knowing it was just a multiplayer combat game for the time being.
The combat is clunky and unreliable, first of all. I move and release for strikes and - not exaggerating - about one or two in ten actually end up in attacks. A good 80% of the time, my character is moving his weapon around like a medieval raver, hugging it close and waving it back and forth when he should be swinging it to attack. And it's not that I'm dying and getting frustrated or that I just "don't know how to play". I was actually killing quite a few people and staying alive a surprising length of time. I'm not disappointed or crying about it, as I definitely don't get mad or frustrated when I die (it's part of the game), it's just honestly that annoying and buggy from my experiences so far. I've even seen enemy attacks get parried when I wasn't even guarding, so the bugs are definitely unbiased and not out to get me. The game is just buggy and combat is unreliable.
And the conquest/capture the flag game is just as glitchy. I've seen enemy teams lose a game they were obviously winning. My team wouldn't even have a man on the flag and we'd somehow get a capture while the enemy was capping. Despite the positive Steam reviews, in the games I've played, most people were mocking how clunky and buggy the matches were, so that was kind of a surprise for me.
While those are the only experiences I've had to far in Early Access, it hasn't been fun. Even the UI is ugly as hell and the main menu is clearly just a rip of M&B's own. The preview screens are shiny and gorgeous, to be honest, but even at max settings with a fairly geared PC, mine looks nothing like the screens, so those are a little misleading. I know previews and demos are meant to be as shiny as possible, but in the case of OKAM, the actual game as it stands is somewhat ugly. The text in graphics doesn't fit at all, some of the little summary boxes get bugged out by existing menu text, and the way most things are laid out either offer little info or use or just seem out of place or shoddily placed.
In short, this is just a $20 mod for Mount and Blade as it stands, but not as good. It has the potential to be a good game, but as of now, I'm left wondering why I spent $20 for something that's better - and free - on a game I already own.
If they want it to be what they promise it will, there's a LOT of work for them to do. It sounds like they have a lot planned for it, and I was honestly sold on the concepts more than the existing product, but even the existing product is worse than I thought it would be; so the finished project better be a massive overhaul or I'm counting this as $20 out the window.
EDIT: To clarify, since most of the replies seem to think I don't know what the LMB is, I'm aware of HOW it's supposed to work, guys. That's not the issue, I promise. And I'm aware that it's not a finished product. I'm not saying "don't ever buy this game", I'm saying "as it is, they have a ton of stuff to fix and polish" and "I didn't really find it fun". Hence the negative review. So, if you feel the need to get mad or dislike the review because I don't like a game you like, then by all means, it's your prerogative. I'm not insulting your honor by giving the game a bad review, I'm just giving my impression of the game and explaining why I didn't enjoy it and don't recommend it - as it is now. If you enjoy it, I'm more than happy for you, and I hope when they DO finish the game and fix all the bugs, it's nothing but medieval heaven for you.

A fantastic Metroidvania. Gorgeous pixel art, excellent music, interesting game mechanics, an intriguing story, and an art style I'm absolutely in love with. Honestly, I love nearly everything about this game. My only real nitpicks are: one important maneuver is executed by double-tapping a direction, which is inconvenient at times and there's no option to bind it to key or button; some flying enemies are straight-up annoying to fight rather than engaging; and the map doesn't display any markers that show where uncollected/collected items are, which makes it difficult to determine exactly when you no longer need to keep searching an area.
Putting all of that aside, this is a title that takes the weirder, creepier environments the Metroid series occasionally dips into and makes an entire game out of it. As someone that likes H.R. Gieger-esque art directions and has been a Metroid fan since the age of 6, Axiom Verge was an absolute joy to play.

Axiom Verge is the Metroid game that any fan has been waiting for. If Nintendo is unwilling to give the consumers what they want, then someone else will make it. Thus, Axiom Verge was created. It is full of beautiful music, sound, and gameplay that makes you question if it really is Metroid. But, it isn't, and that is the beauty of it. This is a must buy for anyone that has been dreaming of a game that pays homage to the 8-bit/16-bit eras and to Metroid.

Not just extra health and such, but many/most of the weapons can be skipped if you're in a hurry. But, if you're taking your time you get rewarded with extra power that works really well for certain enemy setups, including against the bosses.
Extra bonus points for running around in a lab coat and bailey.
The only thing I can fault it for so far is the gadget on the B button. It's a return from Super Metroid, but it actually feels a lot more like a different classic NES game. One that I didn't like. It's really clunky next to the precise controls you have for everything else.
It's great.

"Axiom Verge" is a one-man masterpiece. That it comes even close to the quality of its forebear, Super Metroid, is a genuinely huge accomplishment. It's been a long time since I felt this fascinated and this compelled to complete a game (Pixel's "Cave Story" comes to mind as well, speaking of similar genres), to see as much as I could, to come back as often as I could, never wanting to stop playing.  The soundtrack is gorgeous and memorable, the controls are -- with one or two quirks kept in mind -- as tight as can be, the items are truly clever and innovative, and even though the game is inspired by Nintendo's brilliant game-changer, it never feels like it's flat-out aping the game Tom Happ so clearly adores.  "Axiom Verge" is its own game, through and through.  And then there's all the hidden items and map sections and secrets galore.  You'll be so proud of yourself when you find some of these cartographic riddles.
If you have ever enjoyed a "Metroidvania"-style game, support this fella and buy this game.  $20 is a small price to pay for a game that would've been $50+ in 1994.  Oh, and the story?  Well, it's a lot deeper than you might be prepared for.  This has immediately gone into my All Time Best list.  No one was more surprised than I was, believe me.

TL;DR: if you're looking for an improved HoI 3 - with all the complexity of that game -, this isn't that game. If you're looking for a simplified, easier HoI 3 - without all the complexity, but with all the surface-level features -, this might be for you.
Now to the actual review:
I really wanted to like this game, bought it on launch, and kept playing it on-and-off until now, hoping some updates and mods and whatnot would make this into the game I wanted. After a year, its time to admit that this will never be a good Hearts of Iron game... it might eventually become a decent strategy game, but there are plenty of those. And most of those don't have such bloody annoying DLC-spam.
What is wrong with HoI4:
1. The UI:
Incredibly, Paradox managed to make a UI that is functionally as bad as HoI3's clunky, opaque, hard-to-use and ugly creation. This time it's at least pretty, but even just slapping a couple excel sheets on the screen would be more effective.
The production of equipment is a very neat idea, good mechanic, but the implementation on the UI is... bad. You have 6 lines of Inf. Equipment 1, then research the next level, and want to switch them to the new one? You better like clicking, 'cause you have to do them 1-by-1, and and ofcourse good luck even finding them between the other 50-odd production lines in the category. This just gets even more out-of-hand if you install mods that add more equipment types (Black Ice becomes boring as hell because of all the clicking you have to do just to producte a new division type). Why can't we have a searchable list of equipment types, and a numeric input field for how many factories you want? Oh... because Paradox UI designers don't seem to know the concept of a numeric input field... its bloody sliders and heaps of icons everywhere, even thought this is a PC-exclusive, with access to a perfectly good keyboard with 100+ keys on it.
Want to start production of new divisions that require 2 new eq. types? Sure, why not just start production, then in the same context add the new equipments to the production queue and set them up to get up to a total of 20 factories each. Oh... wait, you can't do that... you have to go back to the cluncky production menu, find the eq. (a search function is hard to make), add it, then adjust the qty of factories. Oh... you wanted to add two lines of that equipment for these new divisions. I hope you really like clicking....
The trade UI is... okay, actually. Only thing it's missing is an automate button, with some settings (use up to x factories in trade, for instance). It would be nice to be able to see the actual number of resource points lost and gained from bonuses/maluses. I'm pretty sure I'm not exporting 30% oil, I'm exporting an actual number of oil resources... so just tell me as a straight number, so that I can play the game without first having to figure out how your algorithm rounds up all the different percentage modifiers, then reach for a calculator to get a number. But that automate button from HoI3 is sorely needed, because interacting with the trade screen is boring (its yet another couple clicks you have to make, because god forbid for there to be a button that just balances your damn resource needs). I'll get into the stupidity of the linked game mechanics later....
The logistics screen... is... almost undescribably stupid. It shows a lot of information, some of which is irrelevant, and some of it is actually wrong. Naturally, it isn't sortable or searcheable in any way, because why would a table containing values would need to be sortable. Also, it doesn't share the categories with the production screen, it dumps everything into a single list, that is apparently haphazardly thrown together without an organisational element.
And we get to the part where it displays misleading information: if you're in 1944, and have been building inf. eq. all along, you'll have a sizeable stockpile of outdated and captured eq. sitting in storage. And this screen bundles it all up when showing you the amount you have, making it entirely useless in determining wheter or not you still need to produce stuff. Good job. Should you open the details for an eq. type, it will get to showing you actual numbers, and the different versions of the stuff you have. It is just the cherry on top that while all other screens display production per day when possbile, this display stubbornly display is per week, for no apparent reason. But that's nitpicking...
2. The World Map:
.... I dunno where to even start with this pretty but utterly badly designed mess... so I won't right now. I'll just go play some HoI3 and come back to finish this review some other day...

Little Busters is one of my favourite VN(Visual Novel). I probably completed it 3 or 4 times before it was released on steam and I completed it here again.
What's to say about LB?
-It's basically Little Busters Perfect Edition from Japan with English included, the latest version of it ever.
-Made by KEY(known for Kanon, Clannad, Air, Rewrite).
-One of the writers is Jun Maeda, who besides working on many KEY VNs, he's known for the anime Angel Beats and Charlotte.
-Good story, with plenty of friendship and drama.
-It's hilarious and fun. The kind of reading where you smile even when there aren't any jokes.
-9 routes and all of them worth reading.
-Memorable characters, I like even the male dormitory head who has I think about 6 lines of dialogue.
-Great art.
-Good music.
-A big cat.
-Friendship.
-Battles.
Now there are few things I'm not a fan of:
-Baseball minigame gets repetitive fast(all minigames can be skipped).
-Game was made originally in a 4:3 aspect ratio and this edition is 16:9. It doesn't affect much most of the time, but CG scenes will be cut and you need to press "space bar" and use the scroll wheel of your mouse to zoom out to see the whole picture. It should've been included an option to play in the original aspect ratio.
-Some CGs were changed slightly from the first released version of Little Busters. I don't know if they changed it in the Perfect Edition but even if they did I find it annoying.
Also, I don't care but it doesn't have any 18+ scenes and it's highly doubtful it will have a patch, the Perfect Edition of LB! from Japan doesn't have it, too.
To sum it up, I think Little Busters! is the best VN you can find on steam right now.

Simply put, A Bird story is a beautiful, short trip. Even playing the game briefly, brings you sights, sounds, and a charming story. The key factor that drives this particular title is lack of dialogue. Everything is explained through the pixel characters or its masterfully done score. The music itself in this game is done so that it actually feels like its own character, I could write an entire review about the music, but I won't. Now keep in mind just like Freebird's other game, To the Moon, A Bird Story is a light hearted tale. The game is very light on the actual gameplay elements, other then moving the character around from point A to point B, there isn't much more. Never been more surprised that a game had positive reviews after playing it. I guess it is the type of people that try to find sybolism in rain falling from the sky in movies. In reality  this is a game with a JRPG  look, without anything else. It tries to tell some sort of story, but in reality all it is is you walking around, looking at shadowy figures, while a bird flies up to you sometimes, and you ride a paper airplane. Its literally 1.5 hours of that. Most of the game you don't play, you just watch yourself repeatedly walk through 4 total environements: classroom/school, forest, bedroom, and city. There is no dialogue, which is supposed to be "artsy", but just makes the game more boring. It was literally the longest 1.5 hours of a game in my life. The few times you get control it is only just to walk around for a bit, and do nothing besides open a door or two or pick something up and put it back down/give it it someone. You do the exact same things, see the exact same repeated scenes, in the same environments, with the same 2 actual characters (everyone else are just shadows). I call this game the walking simulator. Furthermore, you can't acess sound/video settings from the pause menu, meaning you can't mute the game, unless you quit your current game?? Then there is no real save feature, just certain pictures of specific points that aren't clear that you can apparently start back up, but you don't know exactly where that is, so that's kind of worthless. I became so disinterested and uningaged that I started watching DBZ while I finished up the game, as most of the "game" (loose terminology) just plays itself. The story of DBZ was better, and it's free to watch online, instead of paying for this poopshoot. I couldn't have cared less how the "story" (could sum up 1.5 hours in about 10 seconds, that's how much actually happens) ended up, or what happened to the bird and the boy, because surprise surprise, I couldn't form a connection by neither of them saying or doing anything of interest. If the idea of watching nothing really happen and sporadically taking over to walk around interests you, then this is the game for you. But with anyone who has something better to do (sharpen a pencil, get a colonoscopy, etc.) look the other way. 3/10.

Lock’s Quest, a beloved game from the DS years, makes its way onto Steam.
When it comes to ports there are two ways to look at it. The first usually is, “Hey that game I loved is coming to a new platform I have access to, cool!” The second is, “Oh sweet dear lord what is this buggy mess!” I feel we have more of the former then the latter, but that isn’t to say I haven’t ran into bugs.
Lock’s Quest originally released on the Nintendo DS back in 2008. If you aren’t familiar with Lock’s Quest, it is a hybrid tower defense/action rpg. Mostly tower defense though. The action/rpg aspect takes the form of your main character being able to individually attack enemy units and even use spells. The new port features a streamlined version of the original campaign unlocking all sorts of new and different towers as you go along.
The story remains true to the original. Lord Agony has returned with his army of Clockworks and it’s up to young Lock to stop them using his Archineer powers. In all, the story and the some of the new art does a good job of making the game feel fresh again. The game looks fantastic and when it came to visuals there is really nothing I could find a fault in. The music has also undergone an overhaul and it shows. There is an orchestral score, and most of the tracks sound a bit sharper.
The problems began for me when I finally hit combat. Lock’s Quest has a wash-rinse-repeat type of gameplay. Nothing new if you are familiar with tower defense games. Everything you loved about the original is there and it plays rather well with the new built in controller support. You have a build phase where you lay down walls, towers, and traps, etc. Then the action sequence. Rinse, repeat. You gather resources from defeated enemies and usually just have to outlive the timer. There are of course the bosses, special abilities and plenty of different strategies to formulate. Experimentation is usually rewarded.
As far as bugs go, there are times that animations get stuck, your cursor gets stuck in the corner requiring a restart, and there are also ways to completely break the game, gaining unlimited source. While I personally enjoyed the game. There is a part of me that thinks this game was still best suited to the DS. Mainly because you begin to feel the repetition rather quickly. This is especially tiresome in later levels where you need to rework your entire defense as the level just ever so slightly shifts.
Better to have something then nothing.
Not all is bad though, as I mentioned before the streamlined progress. You also have “Antonia Defense Battles” and a new endless mode if you just can’t get enough of Clockwork killing action. This certainly adds quite a bit of replay value and length to the original campaign of Lock’s Quest.
Keep in mind the developer and publisher didn’t have to add or do anything to Lock’s Quest. I have seen ports that are just awful, lazy and slapdash. They took the time to go back over things and at least cared to enhance it for PC. I give them kudos for that. In this day and age we have plenty of games that have been lost. Lock’s Quest could’ve easily been one of them. So as they say, “Don’t look a gift horse in the mouth.”
I can recommend Lock’s Quest to fans of the original and new fans who are looking for something a little different then the usual TD style game. It has a good story, good art, and gameplay for those that enjoy tower defense games. While it isn’t quite so innovative anymore, Lock’s Quest was impressive for its time. I personally would love to see a Lock’s Quest 2 revived with far more RPG elements mashed in. Given its price and how much gameplay you are going to get, it’s more than a fair deal. Lock’s Quest is a classic and it would be a shame for it to be completely forgotten.

Lock’s Quest is a 2D real-time strategy action/RPG game that incorporates some tower defense elements into the mix. If you played the original on the DS, there are some key differences to note between it and this port as noted in the blurbs on this page:

- The new remapped controls for keyboard/mouse and gamepad
- New Antonia Defense Battles featuring a new Map
- Turrets unlock at certain points in the plot with the new progression system
- Endless Mode
- Pixels are enhanced in high resolution and optimized for PC
- Revamped UI and remastered music

Some of these are welcome changes and add to the game. While others take away from the experience. Most notably, the controls. The keyboard/mouse controls feel very sluggish or awkward. Playing with a controller feels much better and I recommend using a controller.

Some attacks were hit or miss or animations would not trigger. And as another reviewer noted, there were instances where commands would loop and I would be unable to progress or make selections. Closing the game down entirely and restarting works, but shouldn’t be necessary to play.

When it works, it’s a fantastic game. I almost beat the original DS version and was pretty stoked to find a PC port was in the works. The game features a great tower defense system where you buy, build, and place weapons along with walls to help defend your area.

The level begins in Build Mode which grants you the chance to reinforce your area as much as your wallet will allow. Once you’re done, you’re in Battle Mode and the enemies will begin to filter on screen. You can engage Clockworks directly, killing them or weakening them before your turrets finish them off. Killing Clockworks will drop parts you can salvage as well, so be sure to grab the drops when an enemy dies.

Walls and structures can be repaired by playing a minigame, when successful, repairs your structures and let’s you get back to battle. I found that these mini-games ported over well to PC. Unfortunately, the mini games don’t work that well with keyboard/mouse, but work just fine with a controller. There are various enemy types that will try to thwart your efforts, but if you plan and build accordingly, you should have no trouble in tackling each level.

The graphics are just as refreshing as they were on the DS and look great on the PC in high resolution. The music is also catchy and a welcome remastering. The new orchestrated intro and outros are also a nice touch.

Unfortunately, I can’t quite recommend Lock’s Quest. It pains me to have to thumb it down, but even though it's among one of my DS favorites, as a PC port, it just does not hold up well as I had hoped when I played it at Pax East this year. With it’s clunky controls and inconsistent glitches where turrets would misfire or structures would be rendered useless because I could no longer select or move them until I restarted the game, progressing can become very frustrating very quickly. The game looks and sounds great, however, but those don’t help the at times broken gameplay.

If you’re not at all deterred by the weird controls and bugs that linger in this port, then have at it as I didn’t find these problems particularly gamebreaking, but as someone who's impatient, it irritated me to have to close out the game numerous times just for something to work correctly. I find the pricing is fair considering the DS version came out in 2008. So, if you enjoy tower defense with some action/RPG in the mix and the occasional hiccup in gameplay, Lock’s Quest might just be your fix.

"Axiom Verge" is a one-man masterpiece. That it comes even close to the quality of its forebear, Super Metroid, is a genuinely huge accomplishment. It's been a long time since I felt this fascinated and this compelled to complete a game (Pixel's "Cave Story" comes to mind as well, speaking of similar genres), to see as much as I could, to come back as often as I could, never wanting to stop playing.  The soundtrack is gorgeous and memorable, the controls are -- with one or two quirks kept in mind -- as tight as can be, the items are truly clever and innovative, and even though the game is inspired by Nintendo's brilliant game-changer, it never feels like it's flat-out aping the game Tom Happ so clearly adores.  "Axiom Verge" is its own game, through and through.  And then there's all the hidden items and map sections and secrets galore.  You'll be so proud of yourself when you find some of these cartographic riddles.
If you have ever enjoyed a "Metroidvania"-style game, support this fella and buy this game.  $20 is a small price to pay for a game that would've been $50+ in 1994.  Oh, and the story?  Well, it's a lot deeper than you might be prepared for.  This has immediately gone into my All Time Best list.  No one was more surprised than I was, believe me.

Axiom Verge is a 2D side scrolling platformer that is the spiritual successor to old school Metroid games. Most people call this genre Metroidvania but it's really just Metroid.  This game captures the look and feel of the classics making it an amazing throw-back. It's full of secrets, promotes well paced combat and hosts a variety of weapons. I was especially impressed at how the game approached similar Metroid problems in different ways (ie. mini-bombs replaced with a giant drill)
The story is interesting and engaging but ultimately it's the exploration loop and combat that keeps you coming back. The boss fights are what you'd expect in an NES type game and most can be beat fairly easy (even on hard).
On hard you are looking at 11 or hours to get 75% completion and around 20 hours for 100%. Do yourself a favor and stay away from guides. I never had any particular problems difficulty wise. As long as you take your time you'll win. The last boss can be tricky if you don't have the correct weapons though.
I would recommend this game to anyone who enjoys Metroid style games.

This game is a love letter to the old school metroidvania fans. The environments are a blast to explore, the gameplay is challenging, and the music goes from moody and atmospheric to tense and energized. I could not put this game down until I finished it. The story isn't something you'll get at first glance, but the concepts are almost unsettling as you piece together the existential themes of the game. This is best played with a controller and some headphones with good bass. I love this game and can't wait to see the sequel.

If Contra and Metroid had a kid, they named it... um... Controid I guess.  Or Metra. If I was Contra and my kid was Axiom Verge, I'd suspect my spouse to have slept with someone else, maybe Dark Seed.
I observed Axiom Verge's development (by only Tom Happ) for quite some time and was looking forward to its release. I cried a little when I heard, it'd be a timed exclusive for PS4, however it's all okay again, since it was just one month. And what I got completely satisfied my thirst for a next "true" metroidvania.
While games like Guacamelee! or Strider (2014) are great and fun in their own regard, the metroidvania feel gets lost when they show you where you have to go on your map. In Axiom Verge, there's no such hand holding (at least not that I was aware of). You get put in a maze and have to figure out on your own how to get through it. I backtracked wrong a couple of times, but that's more fine by me, as this defines what metroidvanias should be about - to be beaten by your own urge of exploration. And when you didn't (and I didn't...) set the markers, the game generously give you, you'll be there for some time to explore.
It took me little more than 10 hours to complete the game, if don't explore every inch, like me, and sometimes pointlessly backtrack, you can finish it in about 8. For me, this is a perfect duration. In fact, I expected the game to last about three to five hours, like, say, Insanely Twisted Shadow Planet, so I was pleasantly surprised when I hadn't reached the ending at all after five.
The game feels even more amazing, when I think about that it was developed by just one person. Also, this ensures that the whole game experience is a lot rounder, however it doesn't come without at least SOME downsides. I thought, that some controls (I mean you, double tapping! And you, grappling hook.) felt a bit unintuitive. The music, while providing an excellent atmosphere to the game, was looped a bit cheap in the areas, that might have been better.
Otherwise Axiom Verge brings an amazing experience to every lover of the metroidvania subgenre or frightening, HR Giger like artstyle or, preferably, both.
Highly recommended!

In ZOMBI you'll be controlling one (or more, if your first one dies) random survivor in a zombie infested London as you try to survive and build up a supply stash in your safe house: as the story goes forward you'll start hearing rumours about a possible cure and you'll try to see if there's any truth to them.
While a lazy port of the original ZOMBIU and sporting a few technical hiccups the game does justice to the term "survival horror" while providing a tense and fun experience.
-infested London is a great setting
-good ambient sound and nice minimalistic soundtrack
-decent variety of zombie models
-the aforementioned zombies are very menacing and remain so for the whole length of the game thanks to the slow introduction of new and dangerous infected types (some of which can two shot you if you're not careful) and certain environments that put you at a disadvantage
-true "survival horror" feeling thanks to the dangerous enemies, somewhat scarce ammo, limited inventory space and single save slot (which is also forced on you if your survivor die, so there's no saving one even if it was your favourite)
-having to kill your own previous survivor, now turned zombie, is a nice mechanic: if you die before you get to him you'll also lose your whole bag inventory and risk gimping yourself until you can replenish your supplies
-lots of different models/ clothes for the random survivors you'll be controlling
-good amount of weapons, all upgradeable if you find enough kits for it
-while the levels aren't big the game rewards exploration with hidden items, secret codes that open rooms containing weapon kits/ save spots etc
-some truly tense and frantic moments when you explore desert locales or have to face an horde of zombies while waiting for a door to unlock
-nice ending sequence gives a good sense of urgency
-cliched story and hurried ending cutscene
-simple melee combat, firearms feel clunky
-unremarkable graphics, also basically no graphic options
-some reported crashes (happened to me only once) could lead to losing progress since the last save
-multiplayer modes are not present in this version
-some deaths can feel frustrating once you start over from the safe house and have to go through a long route with little to no supplies apart from what you start with and what might be stashed in the safe house
ZOMBI is indeed a lazy port, the graphics do show their age and we get no options to make them better, you can't switch controls (actually, having a controller plugged will remove keyboard prompts), there might be some crashes and all the multiplayer stuff is missing: issues from the main game are also still present like a very simple melee combat where you just swing over and over and firearms that feel clunky and somewhat imprecise even when using a mouse and movement that feels a bit lacking (can only jump over certain placesor use ducts with a prompt, there's no jump or crouch button).
But all this can be, at least in part, forgiven due to how well this game depicts a zombie infested city and how fun the resulting gameplay is. Since the beginning of your journey you'll quickly realize that being cornered, failing a melee hit or simply walking about without checking a corner'd easily spell your doom: while a single zombie can be easily dealt with if you aren't surprised two or three of them will have you flee as you look for a way to separate them or avoid them completely. While you'll find a good amount of weapons and a decent amount of ammo if you use them wisely they're not a "win button" at all, they're loud and might attract even more attention, the firing rate is a bit slow and the reload time is generally even worse making them risky in close quarters.
Last but not least while the survivors have no dialogue and differ only by appeareance and name you'll grow attached to them and find it hard to realize you've just lost one: I finished the game with my 4th one but still remember the falling deaths of my first two and how my third one was downed and turned into a zombie himself after fighting through a horde of them. The game truly provides memorable moments and keeps you on your toes for its whole length, it's fun, it's tense, sometimes scary and enjoyable from start to finish.

What can I say about Evolve. I loved it. Many games have tried assymetrical multiplayer before but I feel like Evolve was the first to get it right. The hunter side bored me. Who cares if I can team up with three people and kill one player? But the monster, that was where it was at, where you could best four opponents at once.
The feeling of pressure as they chase and track you across the map, near helplessness when they dome you at Stage 1, the narrow victories at Stage 3. Better yet were the Stage 2 wins, where balance was most even. Winning against a good hunter team at any stage provided me with some of the most exhilirating, heartpumping, adrenaline filled game moments I've ever experienced. In it's prime, when there were still a lot of players, there was nothing like it.
This is a sad goobye. As queue times grew to surpass actual game time I found myself opening it less and less. It's a shame, but a select few of us shared this amazing competitive experience that has no equal on the market right now.
Stage 2 opened the doors for new players, but also simplified the game and removed several of the pieces of magic that made the original so compelling. As long as they decide to keep it running, and you can find players, Stage 2 will give you a sense of possibility of what the game was and what it could be.
Play it. Try to find others that own it and convince them to jump in for a few games. It's worth experiencing.

I had great fun with Skyborn. It's an old-style RPG with a grand adventure, turn-based battles, and dungeons to explore.
Heard it all before? Well, Skyborn stands out from the crowd as one of the most focused and enjoyable games in its genre.
In particular:
- Good music. Uplifting, drives you forward, and doesn't get in the way. Absolutely as good as the big-budget RPGs.
- Great variety of locations and atmosphere. This game is only 8-9 hours long (exploring everything, on normaly difficulty) - but you'll see as much variety as you'd expect from a 40-hour game. It's not just palette swaps, either.
- No filler - see above. The length is short but the story's still all there.
- No grinding: it's not even possible. If you want to make the game easier (or harder), you can change the difficulty level.
- No random battles. The enemies are all visible on-screen. Most of them can be avoided, if you wish to; and once they're dead, they're gone. This means you can finish exploring the dungeons without a battle every 15 metres.
In short, this is an RPG that's very respectful of your time. I would have liked to see a few more sidequests, and a little more interaction with the environment (if I walk past a piano, I expect to be able to play it) - but mostly, I'd like to see a sequel.

Good RPGMaker Game that reminds you of the "Golden Days" of RPGs during the SNES Era.
The Battle System is what amazed me about this game. A Threat System, in a Turn-based RPG? Awesome! The Action List reminded me of games like Final Fantasy X and Final Fantasy Tactics, while the Threat System clearly takes ideas out of MMORPGs.
The Crafting system has its flaws; you can't see WHAT you're about to make until you've already made it, but thankfully you can save anywhere so you can save before you use your materials. A couple hours into the game and I'm already making "Tier 3" gear, so something tells me the game isn't hugely long. But then it doesn't have to be; I've played a lot of Sub-5 hour games and enjoyed them for what they were.
The story seems well-written thusfar, it is basically a Final Fantasy in a Steampunk setting. Pretty standard fare, though this isn't a bad thing for those looking for some nostalgia. The characters seem fairly well-done, each with their strengths and weaknesses (though the Claret seems a touch overpowered). The Magic and Energy Systems are well-implemented and make sense, and the Class Changes were an interesting addition as well.
Overall: 8.5
Short, enjoyable nostalgia trip for those of you who remember the SNES Era Final Fantasy/Lufia-type games fondly.

TLDR: PC keyboard mouse controls harder than the NDS version, 1st map unusually hard, other bugs, hard but playable, mixed recommendation but hopeful. Probably should wait to see new updates, caution advised.
I was about to write an angry rant for my favorite NDS game remaster, but took another crack at beating the first map before I posted. I have now finished the game and updated this review. The controls on PC keyboard and mouse for ratching and special attacks are indeed harder than the NDS version and changes absolutely must be made to make them easier. At the bottom are my ideas for keyboard changes, but here are other important differences between the PC version and the NDS version:
1) The first map is unusally hard.
On the NDS, the first map is a breeze, but you can and probably will lose structures on this map. The biggest part of that is the controls for ratching and special attacks, however, there are a few more problems that contribute to the overall difficulty.
2) Clockwork aggro is not exactly the same as the NDS version.
They will not target Lock as well as before, meaning your structures take more damage and the game becomes harder. This actually feels present mostly on the first map for some reason and less on the later maps.
3) Targeting lag and suspended fire from turrets
Assuming a straight wall going left to right, turrets sometimes do not attack clockworks if they are attacking a wall piece to the left or right of the turret. I know the archer clockwork is made to be partially out of range, but this happens with the melee clockworks. Furthermore, Lock can have some problems when chosing a target, but that was already in the NDS version so its not a big problem. Brutes do not counterattack if Lock attacks them mid charge, and they stand next to Lock perpetually charging while they are killed. Brutes don't stop their charges if they don't reach a structure, which wasn't in the NDS version, but it helps when they get stuck against terrain. Some targets for Lock to free or set explosives etc. have trouble being targeted when first right clicked from a distance. Many or nearly all physical barriers do not stop arrows, this can be a problem when archers are out of tower range, but that is their intended role.
4) Build mode selecting and rotation and support towers.
Selecting from a cluster of structures is harder on PC than the NDS version. At the stone fort on the second map the stone structures cannot be rotated. The NDS version allowed for this, so I am unsure if the developers intend for us to move them. I feel these stone structures should be allowed to be rotated because that was how the NDS played out. I am not sure that helpers, the support towers, do much. The tower for detecting phantom clockworks works properly, but the repair helper did not seem to repair anything no matter the orientation relative to the damaged structure. I cannot speak for the other helpers because even in the NDS version I never really used them.
5) General movement problems.
Movement problems were in the NDS version too, but on PC, clicking and draging to guide Lock in a timely NDS like manner is not possible. I use left clicking to get by, then right clicking while on the way to a target.
6) The later levels will become harder if you are not prepared.
Given the differences in controls and movement, strategies that I used to get by the first few levels with as little resources as possible do not work as well as before. I play an extremely agressive Lock that looks to engage in fisticuffs and tactical pick-offs, but I can definately say the game is harder with PC keyboard controls. I definately use more resources than before to passby all levels than the NDS version.
If you cannot bank resouces you may have trouble on some levels where you must defend two to three targets.
7) Seige Mode is replaced and there is no post game like the NDS version.
The cute seige minigame-like defense of Antonia is replaced with the new Antonia defense, the one with the Kingdom Force. It is a sad tradeoff. The far worse change is the disapearance of the post game. I wanted to go to the developers hall but no, the file resets to day 74 every time after completion.
8) Personal differences I noticed (the little things).
The brute charge cannot be stopped by using Lock as a meat shield and this makes me sad, but hey, at least they reduced the charge damage. Where are the scrap pieces too? They give the structures unlike the NDS version. Graphical errors are present too, I saw a knight in a cutscene freeze in a hurt position, but there are other cases throughout the game. Some images appear to be partially behind the background or flash in and out of view. Lock can also phase though a lot of terrain that used to be impassable in the NDS version. However, this phasing actually helps you to repair your structures. When a clockwork is being healed by a healer clockwork, its healthbar and maybe sound effects may stay around if it dies during healing. I don't like the new healing sound effect, its loud. Mute, the mage clockwork boss is much easier than before. The special abilities must be selected at the start of every battle round, unlike the NDS version where your preferences stuck.
9) Story and cutscene changes.
Kenan's recruit quiz is gone. I believe there are a few dialogue changes but none that I can say are game changing. There are fewer days so the story is easier to follow, but it's a shorter game now.
I have played all of the PC version as of now, and I can say that there are problems with this version, particularly the difficulty increase. If you are a veteran who has enjoyed Lock's Quest who is considering to play this version, the answer is yes if you want to revisit the story and gameplay. But, you may be better off not playing it if you own the NDS version. If you are not a veteran, you should consider if you want to see a unique tower defense rts with a nice story albeit difficult and buggy. Hopefully they will improve it; it is playable but harder than the NDS version. It is possible to finish the game.
After playing the game I decided to make a strategy guide for new players:
Don't sit in your base idle, you need to be an active player; you cannot wait for the clockworks reach your walls. If you run out at the start of the round you can kill or damage one clockwork. Prioritize types you hate the most. For most towers you should try to connect them to walls, they gain damage reduction bonuses based on how connected they are as seen through the shield and wrenches above them. Try to angle you towers so they face the clockworks directly in front, especially since of targeting issues (and always make sure your towers have their front sides forward because they have reduced range in the back). There is no hope for the first map. Try your best. For some reason its hard, probably because of the strange controls. Always try to reduce total costs for your runs, you need to save up for the end map at the Antonia gate to spam when the bosses come out. Use traps asap, they make the early maps easy until the fliers come out (poison freeze poison freeze...). I only use the basic and splash turrets, sometimes the last turret they give too. Not every level will have fliers, phantoms or burrowers, don't be afraid to reset your defenses to save money.
Personally, I hope special attacks will allow for keyboard controls. For the strong hit, 12345 will work. For the other abilities that I know appear later in the game, maybe Q,E, and R will work for different rotations on poison touch, maybe going up and down between arrow keys or Q and E will work for freeze touch, and maybe vampire touch can actually be the sliding bars with the mouse. The stylus on the NDS is simply far faster than the mouse on PC, so keyboard keys should be adopted for speed. The most important thing in my opinion, is ratching. It needs to use the scroll wheel up and down on the mouse.
Needs a bit of polish, but overall I had a good time

This is a balanced role & objective-based fps. Gear & abilities unlock as you level, and it unlocks quickly. There are also training levels that unlock gear as well. You also unlocks fashions at the same time. Each of the roles have a specific advantage that support each other and the objective through buff and abilities (which is tweakable each level). You can semi-switch your role on the fly - you go to consoles your team controls. You can alo switch your weapon loadout the same way. The only thing you can't change is your build type (you have to quit the match, tweak, and then join a new match), which is related to the size of weapons you can hold, how quickly you move, and how agile you - which is related to whether you can parkour and to what extent.
There is no jump or run button in the game, it's just a movement button of sorts. You hold it down and you'll run, and based on your movement inputs it allows you to go under or over objects, or to climb up things. It also has tactical value because you can use it to not only manuever, but to also knock over your opponents and avoid fire. It's a very slick mechanic. Melee attacks aren't designed to kill, they're designed to knock opponents down so that you can do other stuff to them. Everything has a specific design, even grenades - it's all very well balanced. You don't immediately kill people when their health is exhausted, you incapacitate them, which gives their allies a chance to revive them. You have to specifically go out of your way to finish them off with another melee or expend some of your limited ammo and hope your allies are the appropriate role and are buffing you with ammo. When you are incapacitated you can either wait for an ally to try and heal you, and it'll show you where the nearest ally capable of healing is and whether they have the supplies to do so, or you can die and wait for the spawn timer which you can also see - giving you more tactical choices.
Each player has limited supplies of their buffs/abilities, but they're slowly regained. Everything is designed so that you have to rely on each other. This game really didn't catch on, as much as I wish it did. It's clear that it was thought out very well. Unfortunately no one plays it anymore, and I have a feeling it was a nonstarter on PC. I had a lot of fun with Brink.
I purchased the game for the 360 when it released - I had an injury to where playing it with the keyboard/mouse was nigh impossible. I got a couple hundred hours on the xbox and when I could use my hand normally I picked it up on the PC. At the time they had a notice that they 'now' had controller support, so I thought why stress out my hand I'll just use the controller, besides the PC always has more people to play with right? Not so. Well the controller support didn't, and still doesn't work and if you try to get it to work expect to put about 10-15 hours of messing around with it before you decide to go back to keyboard and mouse and hope that all that registry editing didn't break anything permanently, because it will break the game - expect to reinstall a couple of time trying to get the controller to work. So a note about the keyboard and mouse controls - this game was optimized for the use for a controller with it's movement options being tied to one button, but it doesn't have built-in controller support. So the keyboard controls are very simplistic. There are also more players on the console than on PC.
Brink has time trials, single player/co-op, and multiplayer - though the SP/co-op and multiplayer are a matter of semantics, playing against bots or players. The story is interesting and there are two different factions to play through with their stories, points of view, and ideas. Accomplishing or not accomplishing objectives fulfills one side or the others story affecting the ending of the match and what team advances in their storyline. All-in-all I'd recommend this game, it's fun, fast, and interesting, even with it's flaws. You might like it just for the fashion mini-game - each character you create comes with a different version for each faction that needs body type, heritage, tatoos/scarring, clothes, and armor all with a mix of colors and styles - and each different based on their faction. If you decide to jump in you should probably get a copy for all your friends unless you're willing to stay up to weird hours in the hopes to play with people you met on the forums - which is unlikely since the multplayer is dead. I remeber matchmaking with trying to get friends all in the same match being an issue, but I haven't played in a while, so I'm not sure if that was fixed. Either way it's still fun solo for at least one run through of each faction, which will be about ten hours of playtime.

is approaching its tenth anniversary, but continues to hold up excellently.  Indeed, in some ways, it's even better now;
jokes and references are not nearly as ubiquitous as they where a few years ago, making it easier to go into this game without its best moments feeling tired.
At its heart,
is a puzzle game, and any such game faces a balancing act.  The puzzles must be hard enough that solving them is satisfying, but not so much that you quit in frustration.
threads that particular needle expertly.  Sure, the first couple of puzzles really are easy, but after that you get an expertly pitched difficulty curve.  New elements are added at just the right rate, building to a highly satisfying conclusion.
Of course, what made
as famous as it is is its brilliant humour.  If you're unfamiliar with all the jokes and memes that sprang from here, then welcome, youngster, you should immediately play this game.  But even if you've heard those quotes and quips, that shouldn't put you off.  For one thing, there's so much humour packed in here, you probably won't know it all.  For another, don't you want to know the context?
is ultimately just excellent.  Unless you have an aversion to the first-person perspective or otherwise are physically unable, you owe it to yourself to play this game.

After seeing the good graphics and atmosphere in trailers and screenshots I decided to buy this game and try it out. A good survival horror for 20 bucks? Hell yea!
The graphics and atmosphere are good, despite the fact there being little to no graphical options, I certainly had nothing to complain whilst in game. The atmostphere is awesome allover. I like the element where you are turned into a zombie when you die, and respawn as a new survivor with the possibility to get the gear back from the last survivor you played.
You can hack boxes so that the cameras connected to it in a certain area create an up-to date map for you. That together with the possibility of barracading doors and planting mines creates interesting options to master a certain area, which can be useful (and imo added to the gameplay) when forced to flee from a horde of brain-thirsty zombies.
After 2.5 hrs of play however the game started to be less and less entertaining for me. The reason for this started out with some minor frustrations within item interaction. Then I got the feeling that it was the same all the time. Just smashing or shooting zombies with a new weapon that looks almost the same as your previous, and has no new graphical effects. Again a quest where I have to retrieve this from that area. The storyline didn't bring enough for me to keep these quests interesting. And this "Prepper" guy... After 4 hrs of playing I got obsessed with finding him and shooting him through the head. There is no option to turn his voice down and for some reason he can't seem to shut up for atleast 3 mins. Most of the time babbling the same crap about how important it is to survive. And when he was used to develop progress in the storyline, he had already frustrated me to a point where I just put off my headphones.
Keep in mind I played this for only 4 hrs, but here is my conclusion:
For a 20 buck game pretty solid, but not the surival horror I expected it to be
+ Graphics
+ Atmosphere
- Promising elements not worked out sufficient (barracading and mining, upgrading weapons)
- Uninteresting story
- Most weapons have the same graphical effects, stronger zombies just have a glow
- Almost no options to adjust graphics/sound (most annoying being "the Prepper" who can't seem to shut up)
Unfortunatly not a 20 buck miracle, but stands decent for it's price.

I wanted to like this game. I waited a long time to play it. I was a fan of LP1. I played it on the 360 when it first came out. It was a good 3rd person action game with fun mech style multiplayer. I did not get a chance to play LP2; so I was seriously stoked when I saw the trailer for LP3. But no matter how stoked I am for a game, I do not preorder!
I never preorder anything; so I was glad I didn't purchase when I saw the inital reviews. The game had bad controls, it wasn't a great PC port, the game itself wasn't anything like the other 2. So I waited. I waited for the bugs to get squashed and the memory of LP1 to fade before I dove into LP3.
From a development standpoint a lot of LP3 has been borrowed for the LP series, but they missed some very fundamental aspects: Action Shooter would be one. This game introduces cover shooting which was a popular mechanic at one time, but by the time this game released, it was a tired trope. They also took the game in a darker tone. As well, they upped the production value of the game and focused more on telling a real story... however, part of that story production included quick time events. These were not needed to make the original game fun, nor were they welcomed by most players.
Another issue for the game was it's story. They put all this effort into scripted in-engine storytelling, but the moment you play the game the story that's happening around you gets drowned out by the action or your own focus on playing the game. The one special thing that they put a lot of extra effort into developing, and that would have improved the game experience, got washed out. Why? Because LP has always been an action shooter! Either put the story in only movie form, like Blizzard does in their action games, or don't worry so much about it like earlier LP titles.
On the positive side, the voice acting is good. I like that they had people with different accents in the game. They weren't corny accents either, they sounded geniune. The story was good for what I played. You could see where things were going. I never felt like I was being lead to a big reveal, but the writing and acting were done very well. The way they programed the NPC's to move about and interact with the player helped emerse you in the game. Enemy AI plays well enough.
Although I found myself multiple times seeing the AI pattern, but my own animations prevented me from taking the appropriate actions. Part of that may have to do with my own poor aim with a joystick. Despite owning a 360 and playing games on it for a while, I have always been a PC gammer. It's been 10 years since I used a joystick to aim with. Coming from mouse aim to a thumb stick was frustrating and felt unnecessary. I was told the game was terrible with PC controls; so I used a 360 remote. I am no good at aiming with a remote! I found myself in reload animations more times than I actually killed things. For me that was the biggest let down and the reason I do not recommend it.
Yes Lost Planet 3 is a flawed game. Yes it is a bad departure from what the series stood for. However, there is a good game here, but the poor control scheme left me frustrated and wishing this had been a proper PC port.

The game is a story about a boy who meets a bird; the bird gets injured and he takes it upon himself to care for this bird until he can recover. Even though he is still a school boy he does what he can to care for his new friend. They begin an adventure together and share many good moments.

I picked this up on a whim after playing "To the Moon" knowing it was from the same creator, and since I dearly loved "To the Moon" I figured it would be worth it.  I went into it not really knowing anything about it, just with the assumption that it would be wonderful.  I was completely correct.
This is short, meant to be played in one sitting taking about an hour to finish.  There is no dialogue and minimal "gameplay" in the traditional sense; it is more of an interactive story.  I'll leave off any information about the story itself other than "it's totally worth it" because I think it's better to go into any story-driven experience without pre-knowledge.
It is surprisingly emotional for a short story, with moments of hilarious and moments of heartbreak.  Without a single spoken word, you really get invested into this little boy's situation.
Music is, as I would also expect, STELLAR.  As in "To the Moon" the music is perfectly suited to the story.
All in all, I'm pleased I picked this up and anxiously await their next release.  10/10 would cry over birds again.

I owned the original NDS version and it was (and still is) my all time favorite handheld game. But this port is not the same game. Overall, yes, it is the same game. The story is there, the mechanics are there. But in the hour I've played it, here are some things I've noticed
+ The music is catchy, it's not the original soundtrack that I adore but it still fits.
+ Some of the graphics have been redone to be HD, (IE my profile image is a grayscale version of the original source texture), and although it's much higher quality than the rest of the game, it still is aesthetically pleasing and looks as though it fits.
+ The controller controls work very well. Other reviews have stated that the KB+M controls do not work well, I cannot vouch for them as I have not tried them, but I do recommend trying a controller if you can.
+ The combat bonus minigames have been adapted very well, but again I have only tried using a controller.
However, there are a few things that tell me not to recommend this game...
- On Day 7, I already saw a frozen texture, (one of the knights stuck halfway through an attack animation during the cutscene).
- There are audio cues which are supposed to inform you when a structure is close to destruction, which now seem to activate randomly when any structure is attacked.
- The turrets seem to have very poor tracking. They won't attack Clockworks that are clearly within their range, (I've played enough of the original to know when and when not Clockwork are within range). Sometimes they're barely within range, other times they're right next to the turret and can wail on it until I send Lock in to stop them.
- Sometimes after a wall is placed, I try to select it for destruction and instead it gets shifted one tile backwards and nothing else. I had to restart the game to fix it.
And, personally, the fact that they replaced the Antonia Defence with more waves disappoints me. That was the one thing I loved most from this game, it was a refreshing change from the normal gameplay and it's not something that I think would be impossible to port or replicate.
The problems aren't truly gamebreaking, and if you can get past them then it's still a really fun game. But, if you're looking at this game with the mentality of "Hey this looks nice, maybe I'll try it!", then there's a chance you'll get frustrated.
Again, I played the original, and personally this port is a bit of a letdown, but it can still be fun if you let it. In the future, if and when there are any updates I will try and update my review as well.

And with that it is finally on Steam. Before I say anything else, please note that this is more of a preliminary review in case you'e been wondering what the game is like.
I've played the game right after it came out all those years ago and jsut fell in love with it. THis is probably my favourite NDS game and one of my all-time-favourites in general.
That said, here is my (slightly nostalgia biased) list:
This is basically a story heavy tower defense game in which you have to hold off a constant stream of different enemies for a certain amount of time.
What is different from the old version (as I've seen so far):
The soundtrack has been updated and greatly improved (better quality and all that), although it does seem to lose some of the vibes the original gave off, mostly because the original was more limited sound wise and thus had a certain feel to it that's hard to describe. Don't get me wrong, the soundtrack so far seems top notch although I had the impression that sometimes they went overboard with it and caused the rythm/melody to not be felt as much.
The graphics themselves have kinda improved, but mostly the sprites displayed during dialogue, the rest seems the same (can't really tell a difference). EDIT: The graphics have been much improved and the environment looks way better now. The only things that seem the same are the character sprites during combat.
EDIT: Also: the segments where you had to defend Antonia's walls with a turret have been replaced by a normal combat section where you can deploy soldiers. Something that I'm not quite sure I like all that much since the wall defense was kind of refreshing once in a while.
Some other small things also disappeared (e.g. the quiz Kenan originally has for you, not sure about the hidden areas, though.)
The only thing that I have some problems with are the controls.
The original was meant for the DS and you can definitely feel that. While not particularly clunky, it jsut feels a bit off at first but you can easily get accustomed to it.
Now, I don't know what it's like when playing with a controller, but with a mouse, power attacks (like the first press the buttons in order thing) feel weird and unprecise, same with repairing. It would be better to be able to utilize the keyboard a bit more for the M&K controls at least. Like pressing the 1-5 buttons in the right order for the first combo attack.
However, I may have just overlooked some options, but I don't think so.
EDIT: There also seem to be a few bugs here and there. Characters stuck in an animation, enemies unable to complete their attacks and stuck in one place,small stuff like that. Also some poor gameplay choices like only being able to repair walls and stuff from behind.
EDIT: After some more testing, I can say that I find the M&K controls to be horrible. Everything's fine and fluid in bulding mode but in combat... You cannot properly dot he mini-games to get that bonus effect. It worked fine on the ds because you could be really precise with the stylus but it jsut doesn't properly work with a mouse, at least not with the speed needed to do combat properly.
Overall: If you like tower defense, action and awesome music wrapped with an great story, plase consider giving this game a try. It's not at all expensive for what it offers and, while still feeling a little rough around the edges, I am certain the game will be further optimized. Thank you for reading this review.

I've played this game quite a lot in the past before it was released to Steam. By no means was I good, especially since the game has a rather large learning curve. This learning curve comes from the fact that various joints must be manipulated to get results, but casual players (especially friends) will often find hilarity due to the manipulation of their characters sometimes in rather awkward positions. Multiplayer games are rather fast-paced compared to singleplayer sessions due to the timer which limits the time players can think before it runs out. Otherwise, various mods come with the game which adds plenty of PvP options (arena type, weapons, body sensitivity, etc.), or solo challenges (parkour, skateboarding, sports, etc.).
In terms of play by more seasoned/veteran players (not including myself), other players can find interest in the rather complicated techniques used to simulate real fights or complete parkour maps.
Overall, this game takes a long time to fully understand since the tutorial does not completely cover everything, but once players get past this, they'll find many challenges to overcome.

is approaching its tenth anniversary, but continues to hold up excellently.  Indeed, in some ways, it's even better now;
jokes and references are not nearly as ubiquitous as they where a few years ago, making it easier to go into this game without its best moments feeling tired.
At its heart,
is a puzzle game, and any such game faces a balancing act.  The puzzles must be hard enough that solving them is satisfying, but not so much that you quit in frustration.
threads that particular needle expertly.  Sure, the first couple of puzzles really are easy, but after that you get an expertly pitched difficulty curve.  New elements are added at just the right rate, building to a highly satisfying conclusion.
Of course, what made
as famous as it is is its brilliant humour.  If you're unfamiliar with all the jokes and memes that sprang from here, then welcome, youngster, you should immediately play this game.  But even if you've heard those quotes and quips, that shouldn't put you off.  For one thing, there's so much humour packed in here, you probably won't know it all.  For another, don't you want to know the context?
is ultimately just excellent.  Unless you have an aversion to the first-person perspective or otherwise are physically unable, you owe it to yourself to play this game.

A love letter to Metroidvania that still manages to stand on its own; it's well worth the play, even if it's a little rough around the edges. I beat the game on Normal difficulty with 100% completion in 16 hours.
It gets the feel mostly right, but dialog and cutscenes happen just often enough that the sense of pleasant loneliness that comes from exploring a hostile alien world is lost. In addition, the story, while generally fine, is told somewhat strangely--too much detail to hold much mystery, and yet not enough detail to appreciate its scope. I actually think it's fine that you can't really relate to most of the characters, being that they're supposed to be so alien, but the one that you are supposed to connect with is still fairly bland.
Controls are fine--the addition of a lock button to hold still while aiming is a nice touch, but there's a dash ability that requires double-tapping a direction that gets kind of old, and probably should have been its own button. Nonetheless, the game presents enough interesting ways of maneuvering around the environment that just traversing rooms feels pretty satisfying.
Item collection is probably the game's weakest aspect--there's a ton of backtracking, and the map doesn't have any indication of what items you have or haven't gotten--it only tells you if you got them all. This would be forgivable if there weren't a pretty sizable number of items that are almost impossible to find without a cheat sheet or a lot of obsessive checking of every single wall, and some require even more unorthodox solutions--I'm all about out-of-the-box problem-solving, but the game gives little indication of even where to start in some parts (helpful hint: try 'scrambling' every enemy at least once to see what it does.) When you don't feel like you can trust the information provided by the game--when you aren't even given indication that you *should* be curious about a room--it makes for a pretty tedious exploration experience. This is further exacerbated by the lack of a final powerup that essentially trivializes navigation in the early areas of the game--an important element that helps mitigate the fact that the threats of the areas you're backtracking through are no longer challenging to someone with all the weapons and power-ups the endgame affords.
Visually, the game knocks it out of the park--environments and enemies are beautifully bizarre, and come in almost endless variety. Nothing more to really say about it--it's a visual treat you'll be happy to pore over.
The sound design is similarly excellent: the music has good variety while keeping a certain pulsing feel that makes every area feel alive and alien; your weapons sound appropriately powerful, and your enemies sound appropriately monstrous. The only two knocks I have here are the low-health alert, while cleverly timed to the beat of the music, is rather piercing, and the "clang" you get when you hit an invulnerable part of an enemy becomes overpowering when you start fighting large bosses with rapid-fire weapons (since they tend to be almost entirely invulnerable save for a small weak point.)
Overall, this is a great game, and my complaints are really mostly nit-picking--I enjoyed it thoroughly, and I can't wait to see the next game from Mr. Happ.

"God save our gracious Queen, long live our noble Queen, god save the Queen."
In ZOMBI, the shambling dead have taken over the streets of London. Few survivors are left in the city, but those who are still alive are doing their best to survive. You play as a random survivor of 'The second blight', a plague that would kill everything it touches and cleanse England to begin again. That random survivor that you are assigned with is saved by a man who calls himself 'The Prepper', he will give you certain tasks that you must carry out through the game, while searching for supplies and weapons. The game has some interesting characters with great motives, like a scientist stuck in Buckingham Palace searching for a cure, or 'The Prepper', a man who is convinced that there is no cure and the only thing possible is to survive.
The game can be finished in between 8 to 10 hours, depends on how much time you'll take searching for supplies. Melee is the main combat in the game, that can get pretty dull after you smack a few zombies with a cricket-bat. There is also a large amount of firearms in the game, which are mostly used for an emergency. You'll get a couple of quests that you must carry out in the whole game, all mostly fetch quests, but enjoyable to play since most of them will send you too new locations. And a new location means: New weapons, new supplies and a new way to die. Most locations are also very grim and full of atmosphere. This game is one of those examples where atmosphere is done right.
ZOMBIU (ZOMBI for the WiiU, the original title) was famous for the interesting death mechanic. Once your randomized character dies, he's dead, no going back to that guy. You'll spawn in your safe house with a new randomized character, stripped for all supplies next to the things you decided to leave at your safe house. The now dead survivor will be a part of the undead horde with all your supplies still safely in his nice little backpack. So the first task at hand is to get back your supplies. Once you reach the area where your survivor died, you must put him out of his misery and regain your supplies, and so the cycle continues.
The zombie survival genre is bloated with the same 'Online zombie survival crafting sim' game. It's refreshing to see a linear open world zombie game done in a singleplayer experience. No crafting, just fun. The PC version of ZOMBIU is a fun, but flawed game. Melee combat is very dull with a total of three melee weapons to find in the game, and one move to execute. The atmosphere is amazingly done, and will give you a real feel of dread through the whole game. Death plays a key part in ZOMBI and you'll get attached to your character even though he has no real voice and backstory. ZOMBI is overall a real joy to play, the game is flawed, but knows how to make a great zombie survival without a dull online open world with a crafting mechanic.

Zombi is a survival horror game that puts the player in the shoes of a survivor during a cursed blight that is plaguing the streets of London. Apparently, a 16th century magician, John Dee, had predicted this “blight” but he was considered a heretic for believing such nonsense. Fast forward to present times, the world is in chaos and probably John Dee is rolling in his grave saying “I told you so.” Now, with no means of developing a cure, some people turn to the lost writings of John Dee as their only salvation. They believe that the only way to stop this disease is to locate the writings of John Dee and produce the “panacea” that is described in his manuscripts. Guess what? It’s our job as the main character to find these writings and at same time, ensure that we survive long enough to see the next day.
In terms of the port, it’s decent enough, with hardly any drops in framerate. The graphics options are bare which is disheartening but there’s nothing I can do about it.
In my 10+ hours worth of gameplay, I only crashed 3 times at a certain part, which I believe is a game breaking bug. I’ve read in the forums that some people are crashing at the intro scene and that is a rather unfortunate.
See here:

I have no complaints with the graphics because the game is quite pleasant to look at. I’m not really playing it for the graphics so I can’t complain. There is also that pesky Uplay DRM so if you don’t want to deal with Uplay, do not buy the game.
To tell you the truth, Zombi offers nothing new to the table, in terms of a survival horror zombie game. You kill zombies, loot, scour for supplies, and kill some more zombies. You know, the usually Friday night. The several locations we visit in Zombi tend to be small but there are hidden nooks and crannies to be explored and shortcuts to open (God, I love shortcuts). Our pad, a multipurpose scanner that can hack doors, check for hostiles and useful items, and reveal hidden messages, is our best friend and I found myself using it more when laziness kicked it (I don’t want to go to a locker, only to find that it’s empty. You crazy.)
Crafting isn’t available. However, there is a way to upgrade your weapons with parts found in the world. There are four types of upgrades: firing speed, capacity, spread and firepower. From what I can tell, once a certain upgrade has been installed in a weapon; a second upgrade of the same type cannot be placed in the weapon again. For example, let’s say you placed a firepower upgrade into a shotgun. You cannot modify it again to strengthen the shotgun’s firepower. So once a weapon has all the necessary upgrades it can hold, that’s it. Your brand new shiny weapon is fully upgraded. It’s simple and there is no way of upgrading a weapon further unless you find a stronger version of the weapon.
The weapon diversity is pretty good, ranging from your average pistol, to the more practical shotgun. Additionally, your skill in using a specific type of weapon increases the more you use it. This allows for faster reload, lower recoil, and better stability when aiming (from what I can tell).
My favorite so far is the crossbow. It’s silent and there is a 100% chance of recovering the bolt from the zombie, if you manage to hit the enemy, of course. To my surprise, the game doesn’t flood you with ammo or curatives as I thought it would. Granted, I am playing on Survival Mode (perma-death) so maybe that changes how much items spawn in the world. With me, I have to make each shot count, or else, it’ll be awhile till I find another ammo cache.
That’s where our melee weapons come in. We have a starter Cricket Bat that makes me appreciate the sport in ways I never thought I would. There are other melee weapons but why use them when you can Cricket…ya know? Common sense, people! Besides, there is no way of dropping or storing the starter weapons (I tried) so they waste two valuable slots in your already skimpy backpack space so might as well use them. Speaking of backpack space, they can be increase by finding upgrades for your backpack…yay! Gotta get all them pockets for your dru—food. I mean food.
There are different kinds of zombies friends we can meet in our arduous journey. There are spitting ones, exploding ones, always want to be the center of attention ones, and just plain ‘ole regular cute ones that enjoy a good buffet of humans. Their A.I. are nothing special and can be exploited by finding their “how much can I back up until the zombie turns away, forgetting they were ever pursuing a juicy human” limit. It’s a mouthful but I am working on an alternative title. Unless it’s a horde mode section, you can do this to almost all zombie mobs. I do find the brain eating fellows hilarious sometimes because they will do whatever it takes to get to you if you’re in their aggro range. You see one on the floor above? Don’t worry; they’ll drop down to you so you can beat them to death...again?
I do find the game easy at times, even in Survival Mode. Despite that, I did get cocky and ended up dying at the hands of the exploding monster because I had the audacity to whack it on the head with a bat. Such a diva. From that point, I was a bit cautious and I actually began taking Zombi seriously, which surprised me because I tend to fool around too much in games.
I really do enjoy it, especially survival mode. Normal mode is an alternative if you don’t fancy perma-death situations and if you die in normal mode, the birth of a new survivor occurs and you have some time to gather your belongings from your dead character. The tension does increase in Survival Mode because you don’t want your person to meet a terrible fate, right?
All in all, $20 is a fair price for this game. It’s fun and engaging enough to hold your attention. Buy it if you can.

The game's title doesn't lie: this is a story about a bird. It's also about a boy.
