But if you've played To The Moon and are interested in a short story with some simple interaction to supplement it, here's your game. You'll mostly perform some simple, guided tasks to move the story along, and there's not much element of choice or exploration.
A Bird Story's real strength is in its masterful storytelling-- without using any dialogue, it tells you a story from start to finish about a boy and an injured bird he finds.
It's not a very long story either, so you might want to spring the extra few bucks for the soundtrack, which is worth the price on its own.

I tried it out for a bit, tried to get a handle on the world and see why this game went from being an expensive purchase to free-to-play knowing that it was a hyped game.
I always wanted to play it, but Evolved was like $50-$60 which was insane knowing that the DLC's also costed up to like $100. So I never bought it.
I have to say the fun of it is being the beast and fighting or being the hunters and battling a monster controlled by a person.
The game feels massively sided to the hunters, you can kill the monster within the first 10 minutes of a match easily. Find it, shoot it a lot, and since it starts weak it's easy.
The maps are small, far too small to make it feel like you're hunting an amazing beast. Instead as the monster you are skirting the far outsides of the maps trying to get away from the hunters so you can get bigger and stronger before they find you. Which, I'll be honest here, it's extremely easy to find the monster.
This game needs to make tracking the monster harder, make it punishable to just burst at the monster. It should be a hunt, to gear up for the fight, and make it challenging to kill it.
The maps need to be larger, MUCH larger, so that the monster has a better chance at getting to the later stages so the hunters have something to fight.
It feels so... unintimidating to fight the monster. It feels less like a great hunt and more like a 4v1 in Halo matchmaking. Lots of noise and explosions, but it's still only one person you're fighting.
I would love to see a conflict of the hunters and the monster both struggling for control of their situation.
For instance:
If the monster can keep the hunters on their toes, ambushing, making it seem genuinely scary with something, anything.
The hunters trying to keep the monster in front of them, tracking it and laying traps, not just barreling full speed at the monster.
A creature this big shouldn't be so squishy. It's a massive alien lifeform, all of them are. Hunting them shouldn't be like slapping a deer. Sure the deer can fight back and they will, but in the end there are four of you, all with guns, and one deer.
If the devs wanted to find out how to make the game better, please make it more challenging. I don't care about having fancy outfits, characters, or skins. I care about how intense the game is.

I honestly had my doubts when it came to another RPG Maker game. I waited until it came packaged in a bundle sale, and I actually feel I made away like a thief for the price I paid.
I've been playing RPGs since the early-mid eras of the Final Fantasy (and other 8-16-bit console games), Wizardry, and Might and Magic games, as well as a fair share of "real" indie RPGs like the Avernum series, Planet Stronghold, Loren Amazon Princess, Deadly Sin 2, and even Science Girls! I'm getting a bit jaded on the whole grind-heavy RPG genre as a whole, but even so, I had no real qualms about this game.
You can honestly play the game how you want:
- No random encounters
- level-ups give you very few stats in comparison to equipment, i.e. you can skip as much as you can sneak past
- powerful equipment is found via exploration, crafting, or the optional dungeons and colosseum battles
- crafting is actually useful and you find all the materials you need during normal gameplay: no random drops or farming!
- many of my "expert" tier craft items were actually used instead of my "unique" endgame loot
- powerful augment items and accessories to further customize the roles of your equipment and characters
- a number of class changes that include skill and stat choices for all characters
- incentives for exploration: rare equipment, unlocking new areas, and experience bonuses
- surprisingly strategic combat skill decisions and equipment trade-off choices
The characters and story are somewhat typical JRPG fare, but they maintain enough character to be interesting enough in their own right and be fairly memorable, helped by the well-drawn and expressive character art sprites (as seen in the pics). There's also a fair bit of light humor, although it's usually not the blatant laugh-cue type of humor. Instead, it tends to be due to quirks between the characters' interactions; you can take it or leave it without offending you either way. An example of this might be meeting an oddball NPC and having two of your characters giving each other wide-eyed looks.
Production quality seemed pretty good overall, excepting the usual annoying RPG Maker limitations like game settings being tied to your save file instead of globally, so you have to switch to windowed mode every time, or the game's volume is always at full blast when you start the game -- use your Windows volume panel to adjust the game's volume individually instead. The music, sound, and special effects aren't going to win any awards, but they're all better than average.
The game is indeed a bit short: Played at a leisurely pace, 17 hours in Steam, 12 hours logged in saves, and that's with all the optional content. However, you never really feel like you're wasting your time. Even the larger areas manage to mitigate extreme tedium, being that most treasure and combat is optional.
I remember playing many crappy RPGs on my SNES as a kid. I could easily see this game being something I would've really enjoyed back then and reminisced on as an adult. I can't say this game will distract you from the flashier games available on Steam, but if you're for a good, low-key, SNES-style RPG that's not too time-demanding, Skyborn should be at the top of your list!

You get what you pay for, assuming you bought this on sale.
Con:
The mechanics are as simple as the graphics once you master the non-intuitive controls and menus.
The characters' voices get really annoying really quickly, since they never stop chirping their single line over and over.  And I would swear that intro sfx when you first start the game is a dev's idea of a jump-scare joke.
You spend more time micromanaging cleaning up poop and feeding your crew than the exciting parts of sailing and fighting.  Everything is more or less a passive experience.
Poop jokes get old when it's ubiquitous and poop never stops in this game.
There isn't enough variety in the encounters to make sailing not feel repetitive.  You meet different sprites and environments to interact with, but each interaction is more or less the same.
Pro:
Good music.  Not great music, but good music.
There's enough item, perk, and equipment variety to keep you interested.
Leveling and RPG elements for customization of pirates and your ship.
There's some suspense in making sure you have enough food and funds to keep your characters happy and alive.
You can play it windowed as you do something else, like listening to audiobooks or watching youtube videos.
________________________________________________________________________________
Conclusion:  For a couple bucks it's fine.  It's definitely no Terraria, but it's three steps up from playing solitaire or minesweeper.  You will playing on autopilot without paying too much attention to what's actually going on in the game for stretches, but there are moments when you succeed and you think to yourself, "Hey, that's pretty nice," and moments where you are in trouble and think, "Uh oh.  I better focus and pay attention."  And that's good enough.

A fun retro-style metroidvania game that I would recommend to any fan of the genre. The gameplay stresses exploration, getting lost, and fun combat gameplay. New areas are unlocked by tools found, with each tool providing unique and interesting functionalities. Graphics are done in a NES-style 8-bit feel with modern touches that really feels like an alien world. The soundtrack is superb with chiptune sounds and amazing sound effects. Even after completing the game, hours can be lost in searching for remaining items. Multiple playthroughs are encouraged with randomized areas and a speedrun mode that challenges players to play through the game in as short a time as possible. It's still astounding this was developed by a single person, considering the care and execution on all areas of the game.

A Bird Story is an hour long surreal story of a boy and an injured bird. The story plays out as expected and the phenomenal music is something to marvel. The gameplay is sparse and there isn't any chance or point (or as it seems) to pause or save the game's progress.
In comparison to the studio's other title To The Moon, this attempts to capture an essence of the emotional moments with some humour as To The Moon, but doesn't quite grasp it as well.
The surreal dreamscapes make it somewhat confusing, but interesting journey, making a child and their injured pet story stand out from other creative works in the same genre.
It's a nice little piece of work, but only for those who are strong fans of the people who made To The Moon.

God, where do I even start. Everything about this game is utterly fantastic. The gameplay, the graphics, the music (good lord the music). Axiom Verge is a love letter to Metroid in video game form. It is -unabashedly- Metroid. If you grew up on 2D platformers, this will be your jam. Even if you didn't, PLAY THIS GAME. It was made by a single dude!
It's a short but sweet experience. I'd say on average it'll last anywhere from 8 to 12 hours. I clocked in at 11 and a half hours as my clear time. There's a ton of collectables and hidden items scattered throughout the game, but most are pretty optional.
Speaking of collectables and hidden items, Axiom Verge has a lot of weapons. A LOT of weapons. I think there's 20 or so? A minor gripe I had was that despite the vast array of weaponry, only a handful are actually useful. It seems like the design mentality was akin to "sounds cool on paper", but in practice it ends up being pretty useless. Fortunately, the handful of weapons that are good are REALLY GOOD. And to be fair, some of the "useless" weapons are really useful against certain bosses.
Another gripe I had was regarding some of the controls. Two upgrades in particular, the Grapple and the various Dash upgrades you get have kinda... janky controls. They're pretty unwieldy. The grapple's just plain hard to use, and the dash, well... The dash activates by doubletapping a direction, but often times I'd find it would activate randomly on its own just from normal movement. I would much have prefered the dash being mapped to a button instead.
Overall, solid Metroid-y experience. I'd recommend it to anyone who's a fan of 2D platformers or Metroidvanias. GREAT GAME A+++++ ALL THE THUMBS UP.

ZOMBI is an excellent horror-survival game where you will roam through a masterfully-recreated London, guided by your mysterious helper, "The Prepper".  The story starts with the tale that England's capital has been struck down by a foretold (but ignored!) plague.  Your shelters are mapped out for you but you need to scavenge for edibles (to repair your health), ammo, wood for boarding up doors and just about any salvageable weapon.  As usual, there never, ever seems to be enough ammo, so get used to that cricket bat!  There is no manual save either; instead, you must find a shelter where you can sleep, at which point the game is saved and your health restored.  A word of warning: shelters are few and far between, so staying safe
matters in this game.
, and where the rough edges show particularly is in textures and any close-ups of just about anything.  Images don't look as sharp as those advertised on the store page thanks in part to an overly zealous chromatic aberration effect that muddies outlines somewhat.  Unfortunately, there is no way to alter any of the game's graphic settings beyond v-sync and resolution (not even a config file) so if you want to improve the game's looks, you're going to have to dig into your GPU drivers for some AA settings, and maybe blag SweetFX or whatever you do when you have a game that offers nothing more than V-Sync and Resolution.  However, even without extra settings, the graphics really do generate a dark and desolate atmosphere and play a huge part in the setting of this story.
It is not all that similar to
.  I mention this because some reviews and forum comments imply that it is.  It's quite linear, there is no parkour and you can rarely climb anything, but survival is MUCH more emphasised in this title and the atmosphere is much more oppressive.  This truly feels like a very different - though equally enjoyable - game.  Where
feels like an energised romp to save the world and defeat a power-hungry institution while everyone awaits rescue,
feels bleak and desolate, with no hope.  This is the first of many, many survivor games where I truly felt like I was merely a survivor clinging to life, and despite my unseen helper's presence, I felt very alone.
No, but there are a good range of locations you can revisit at any time to gather remaining consumables that you've pinned on your map for later use, and some areas are huge.  Some locations are frustratingly linear where you are forced by a tumble of boxes to walk a specific route (despite the boxes being low, or very few - something you could easily climb over in real life).  That makes the game feel a tad old-school.
The atmosphere can make it very tense, especially in dark areas, and there are occasional, rather too well done jump-scares that will catch you out if not expecting them!  As usual, there are no gore filters in zombie-world, so only buy if you find lopping off heads quite a casual pastime!
For the Easily Bewildered (of which I am one), it's not overly hard, but hard enough.  Meeting an individual zombie is easy, but being flanked by three or more becomes very difficult - harder than
so don't get flanked!  There are two modes you can play: the standard mode and a survival mode (permadeath).  The Easily Bewildered will need to join me in the first (standard) queue where you can elect to play as CHICKEN or STANDARD difficulty (Hint without spoilers: choose the one that clucks and lays eggs unless you're brilliant at games).
The game has a novel mode where you will continue to play until you die (at which point you have now become a zombie yourself (too bad), and as zombies aren't playable (see - told you it's not like Dying Light...) you respawn as an entirely new person back at the shelter without any of your much-loved kit and so your first task is to set off and find your zombified former person and wrestle it (you?) for your previous back-pack.  Be warned: if you die AGAIN on the way, you will lose access to the full back-pack because you will again respawn, and of course the back-pack you find will be empty because former-you never found the full back-pack!  The random respawn is a great twist to survival and really enjoyable.  Even if I was any good at games, I think I'd prefer this to the harder mode.
The harder 'survivor' mode for grown-up gamers is permadeath.  Yes, you only have one life and when you die, it's GAME OVER.  The emphasis here is on how far into the game you can get.  After a certain point in the story you are given a limited tool that will save you from a single zombie-bite, but it won't help you if you're mobbed.
No - it is the original game, along with some of the original incidental bugs.  The main change made is to overlay the map and back-pack inventory onto the screen (these used to be shown separately on the Wii U controller's digital pad).  Curiously, a couple of graphics effects (like dirty lens view) have been dropped from this version.  Otherwise, it is the exact same game with no extra frills - hence that cheap (for Ubisoft) price.
Well, there's everyone's favourite whipping-boy, UPlay, though of late the client is MUCH better than it ever used to be...  Secondly, it loves to crash, and given that your progress is only saved when you sleep in a shelter (and shelters are as rare as hens' teeth), inopportune crashing is frustrating and can lose a lot of progress, so make a habit of returning to your safe-house or shelter often.  There's that lack of graphic settings (a bit naughty of Ubisoft) so you have very little visual control over your game.  Finally, it does its absolute best to insist you have a gamepad connected, so get ready to disconnect everything that isn't a mouse or keyboard if you do want to play with mouse and keyboard.  Oh, and there's no multiplayer in this version.  Me being anti-social, I'm not at all bothered, but the removal of multiplayer has upset a few fans of the original game.
Ordinarily, the answer to this kind of question is nearly always 'PC', but in this instance that might not be so true.  If you own a Wii-U, then buying the game on that platform is recommended because your backpack is managed on the digital display of your controller, ramping up the scare factor because you
to look away from what might be behind you in order to change weapons.  Or, if you have a PS4, the game is arguably better there too because the mysterious 'helper' voice comes through your controller's speaker and feels for all the world like a portable walkie-talkie or ear-piece as it would be.  Graphically the game is no different on either of these platforms, but those little extras are neat touches on Wii-U and PS4.
ZOMBI is a fun (in that horrific-fun way) and atmospheric crawl around a gorgeously painted plague and smog-ridden London.  It's not a massively long game, but there is plenty of game provided.  Its 'mixed' rating on Steam is largely down to three problems: it hasn't been enhanced for PC at all, it uses UPlay (which has been improved massively in recent months so is not really an issue any longer) and many people have been blighted by frequent crashes or have not been able to get the game running at all.  As a result, PLEASE use Steam's 14-day 2 hour refund window to test at least the first 'proper' mission in the supermarket.  If you get through that and are then able to move on to the next part of the story, you should be absolutely fine.

tl;dr: Get it, it's great.
I read a fair number of visual novels, including fan translated ones and officially released ones. I read Little Busters! when the fan translation came out several years back and it's safe to say it's my favorite visual novel of all time. It isn't without its flaws; for one, there were a couple of character routes that were either a bit confusing or maybe not the greatest, but this is limited to those particular character routes. The common route, the main story, and the routes written by Yuuto Tonokawa and Jun Maeda were all extremely good and memorable. The main storyline especially is one of the best I've ever read in a visual novel, and the main cast especially is an absolute blast and very memorable. The heroines are a bit more of a mixed bag; some of them really stand out and had a strong presence, while others... not so much. But even the ones I'm not huge on are, at worst, just not very great. There's nothing there that's offensively bad, and far more often than not what is there is extremely good.
This release adds three character routes (Sasami, Kanata, and Saya) that were not present in the original fan translation. These routes are locked behind the main story as far as I can tell; you can't complete them until the main story is complete, and there is no option for returning players to specify that they have already completed the story. While this is kind of understandable, I think it would have been nice to include some way to unlock it for people who have already read the fan translation. As far as the quality of the routes, I can't comment since I haven't read them yet, but based on the writers responsible for each route, I expect two of them to be pretty high quality and the remaining one could go either way.
All of the other features you'd expect from a VN are, for the most part, present. There's a mouseover encyclopedia for Japanese terms that English readers may be unfamiliar with, which is a welcome and common-sense addition in my opinion. There is also the option to switch everything to Japanese text, which (although kind of strange in an English release) would be perfectly fine except that there's a mouse shortcut to toggle this that's relatively easy to trigger on accident (click LMB and RMB at the same time). Volume settings for BGM, character voices, individual character voices, and sound effects are all there, which is good because the defaults seemed really strange to me; sound effects and male characters were extremely quiet while the BGM and certain female characters were all very loud. Other than that, this release is supposedly also compatible with touchscreens. I can't comment on that, but it does look like the settings are there, so if you like to play on a tablet or something, it seems you can do that.
Overall, this is a great release. There are minor things here or there that stick out to me, but nothing really earth-shattering. If you have even the slightest interest in this kind of visual novel or if you're a fan of any of Key's other works, definitely pick this up right away. If you played the original fan translated version, I'd recommend grabbing it for the extra character routes; I believe there is an unlocked save file for you in the "guides" section on the Steam Community if you really don't want to do a full replay (I'm just going to do a full replay, though). Either way, this is a definite buy for me.
Edit:
When I wrote this review, the last time I had read Little Busters! had been in 2013 or so. Now that I'm almost finished with it again (I've completed all the main routes again as well as two of the added routes; I still haven't read Saya's), I want to say that I liked Chika Shirokiri's routes a lot better now than I did the first time I read them. It's also worth saying that the additional route that he (she?) wrote (which is great on its own and feels like a full, complete route) adds a sort of resolution that was kind of lacking in one of the original routes and made what I thought was already a good scenario even better.
As for the additional route written by Tonokawa, it was nice and very cute but rather short and lacking in the impact that his other routes had. It's not bad by any means, but it definitely feels more like a fandisc route. A little disappointing, but it was fun so I can't complain.
Saya's route was all right. A lot of fun but I personally wasn't huge on the way it played out.

Lost Planet 3 - The Adventures of a Forklift Driver in Space :)
The game is a third person shooter with a cover system, creepy aliens and a giant robot you can drive. Imagine "Gears of War" meets "Dead Space", with a little "Titanfall" thrown into the mix.
+ I have not played the previous games of the series, but this is a prequel, so that wasn't a problem.
+ The sci-fi story is good, definitely one of the selling points of the game.
+ The presentation is very cinematic. The characters are mostly interesting, the major roles are well acted, although some of the smaller roles are a bit cheesy.
+ The atmosphere is well done, the colony feels like an industrial outpost.
+ The game has some very nice country/southern rock music, you can listen to it in your cockpit while walking across the snowy planet. It's a nice touch, fits well with the whole frontier theme.
+ Having a giant robot with a claw and an industrial drill is FUN. Very satisfying to crush hard enemies into a pulp, that annoyed you while on foot :)
+ There are side-quests beside the main missions, so the game is not entirely linear.
~ The grappling hook is a nice idea, but its use is very limited, it can only be used in predefined places. Feels like a missed opportunity.
~ There is multiplayer, I suppose, but I have not tried it. Also I expect it is dead this late after the release.
The game has some faults too, that can be annoying:
- Aiming and shooting is awkward, feels every bit the console port it is. The crosshair seems to move with discrete increments instead of smoothly.
- There are a couple of long segments of the game without the possibility of upgrade.
- Remapping keys is buggy.
- There are 3 unnecessary interaction buttons.
- The AI of the human enemies is dumb, as a bag of rocks.
- Some checkpoints are horribly placed. You have to watch cut-scenes over and over if you die, and you cannot skip them.
- There are many QTEs, and some of them are as annoying, as you would expect :/ But not the worst, I have seen in games. The hardest are the QTE-based boss fights in your robot.
Despite the faults and problems, I recommend the game for the story, setting and the giant robot.

Don't buy. I've played through LP1 and LP2, and both of  those games are way more enjoyable than this mediocre title. It's like what happened to the Dead Space trilogy all over again.
The Pros:
- The main character; Design-wise he's pretty solid. Enjoyable too.
- Visuals: The visuals are good, although a frozen planet with one type of texture doesn't bode much of a challenge.
The Cons:
- Slow combat. As in all LP games you'll have to shoot their red glowing parts to do real damage, which was fun and challenging in the first two installments. In this one however, it's really annoying. Enemies have just one glowing red part that they always cover up in every animation state. Slows down combat immensly.
- Movement: It's sluggish. Controlling the character feels like he perpetually moving in slow motion, except for when he's rolling. So you're incentivized to use your dive roll as this is 200% faster than normal walking. (Zelda on the N64, anyone?)
- Gameplay: Horrendous , non-intuitive and just plain old boring. Following waypoints in your incredibly slow mech (no sprint option either) is what you'll be doing 80% of the game. It's not fun to walk somewhere, turn a generator on or turn a cog clockwise, and go back to base. Honestly, the first three hours of the game is only this.
- Story: It's very generic. You're trapped on an ice-planet and energy is running low. Feels a bit manufactured, especially compared to the first two LP titles.
Final verdict: Pretty meh, if you're in doubt of purchasing this game, don't do it. If you really want to experience it for yourself for some reason, pick it up on a sale when it's 9.99$ or watch some youtube videos.

Fort Defence is a simple tower defence game where you protect your fort against enemy ships by building towers on pre-defined spots. The battle arsenal contains few upgradable towers and some spells.
Sadly this game does not offer a story at all, like some other tower defence games manage to do, instead it just throws you into the level with some minor tutorial on how to place and upgrade towers aswell use spells. The gameplay overall is absolutely boring since each level is almost the same - enemy ships always follow pre-defined ways while you build towers on pre-defined spots.
If you played any TD before, you will most likely build on the right spots from the first try even on hard difficulty. The worst part about the challenge in this game is that you can simply grind yourself up by finishing easier level and getting "barrels" to upgrade your towers and spells. So basically you dont have to figure out how to pass a certain level if it becomes challenging, instead you farm the barrel to have maximazed towers and spells in just few hours and after that the game is a walk in the park even on hard difficulty.
There are in total four spells that you can use and 2 or them are damaging, while 2 are utility. The damaging spells are more for starter levels while enemies have low HP, but the utility are far more useful at higher levels.
The graphics in this game are simple and sadly look absolute lifeless. Its like chess pieces moving on a board - nor the enemies nor the environment have any special details or graphical immersion effects.
As stated before, the progress is simply based upon grind for barrels. If you cannot pass a level, grind barrels until you upgrade your towers and spells and try again. That makes even the hard levels be not hard anymore at all.
Both the sound and the music are good for first 5 minutes, after that you most likely will turn it off and listen to your own music. There are no immersion sounds at all, so you will build towers without any immersion to the game.
Fort Defence is a boring grindy tower defence game, without any real strength but quite some weaknesses. There are tons of tower defence games that offer you a story, better sounds and immersion, far better progress system than simply farming upgrade material and some building freedom.
I hope this review helps you making the decision if its worth buying this game. Rate and leave a comment if you enjoyed reading it.

Personally, and I mean personally, I really love this game. The visuals, designs, music, and especially the atmosphere is absolutely incredible and are definitely this game's strongest features. The gameplay and controls are simple and easy enough, however it can be a bit counterintuitive and don't be surprised if you find yourself completely lost on what to do next or where to go.
While i personally do enjoy the surrealist nature of the story and Fyn's unconventional characterization, this is very much objective and I can easily see why others would hate them. The narrative is disjointed and hard to understand, and as of right now, it's hard to tell where it's going or even if the writers know what they're doing. Fyn is unlikable, straight up, but while I feel like that's sort of the point, I don't blame others for disliking her for it. There's no consistent cast, it's really just Fyn drifting throughout the city and meeting random people who either help or hinder her strange quest.
Overall, if you're one who enjoys a really good aesthetic, music, and surrealistic stories, I recommend it--but just be aware that this is a very "you hate it or you love it" kind of game. Regardless, I very much love this game, flaws and all.

Putting aside the hatred for this game regarding initial advertising, I still found it very appealing. To this day, I enjoy a couple of hours of Brink every now and then. I only wish the multiplayer scene wasn't completely dead. This would attract more gamers, I'd imagine. The gameplay is standard FPS fare with a little parkour thrown into the mix. The basic plot is, well, very basic, but it's the audio logs you unlock through gameplay that is to me an allegory for human nature. Both the Security forces attempting to protect the Ark and the Resistance forces attempting to flee the Ark make so many errors and foolish moves. Through pride, anger and personal resentment, the two opposing factions tear each other apart when it was so easily avoided if either side had stymied their rage long enough to come to a reasonable solution. You are told how the Ark is falling apart because the resources that keep it functional are being used to manufacture ammunition to fight the Security forces, and how Ark Security is unwilling to venture outside of the Ark to find signs of civilisation due to an incident many years earlier which resulted in the deaths of an expeditionary team previously dispatched. All in all, the story is great. Neither side is good or bad. both are wrong and right in their own way and both really screw things up in their own way. As I said, an allegory for human nature. If you're interested in the single player campaign, I recommend it, but the multiplayer scene is long dead.

Most people tend to avoid games made by RPGMaker, and I can understand why. They are used to create games that are everything a good JRPG should never be. However, every now and then, a new game is made with this engine that just blows away the minds of the players. Skyborn is one of those games.
The storyline is perfect, and the timing of events really helps keep the player engaged.  The protagonist of the story investigates the more grey areas of life, and how "even the most broken of things can be made into something great". Throughout the whole game I was sucked into a world of humor, action, and beauty, which leads onto my next point: the graphics.
The majority of the graphics are custom, and the graphics that are not, are used perfectly. The tiling was very well done, and I only noticed a few problems here and there, but all and all, it was very well executed.
What makes many JRPGs boring is the repetitive and often hard battles. Skyborn does not follow the classic random battle system, but rather the player can see what enemies are on the map, and can avoid about 90% of them if they want (something I am guilty of, I must admit). Also, as the game progresses, the player can choose to upgrade the character's classes. This makes the battles very appealing and fun to engage in. There are 3 battle difficulty settings on this game, and the player can change the difficulty when ever he desires. I myself decided to play on Normal, and only switched to Easy for one boss midgame that was incredibly hard for me to defeat. The combat is turnbased, but with a large amount of strategy involved. I often found my characters taking on specific roles. For example, I had 3 support characters (1 heals, 1 buff, and 1 tank), and then I had 2 characters (female, typically :P ) that were the kickass dps of this game. I rather enjoyed this approach, and loved that I could not just barge in a battle, but rather had to think about every move I made.
The game has a pretty sweet crafting system that is indispensable at the beginning of the game, but useless at endgame. Ore would be mined, with which could be crafted into armour at an anvil, which can be found all over the world. Armour and weapons can also be "Augmented", which is the equivalent to enchanting/socekting an item. This allowed for an even more extended customizability, though I did find the lack of speed increase augmentations quite distressing (there are a few, but not many).
Though I tried hard to find fault with this game, it just isn't happening. If you are not into linear and short games, then this is not for you, however if you have 3-5 hours to spare, than buy this game right now, you will not regret it, I promise.

Do you like stories that manage to contain both a great deal of hillarious comedy and heartbreaking drama? How about a memorable cast of characters who are all well-developed and are just fun to spend time with? Perhaps some quirky minigames where "battles" are fought with whatever random objects happen to be at hand? Or perhaps a story revolving around themes such as friendship, growing up, and facing up to painful circumstances? If so, then Little Busters is the game you want to play.
Originally this game came out in 2007, had an "expanded" version released a year later, three seasons of an anime adaptation in 2012-2014, and likely more. But only now, 10 years after the original release, has this game finally recieved an official English release. To say that this was a highly anticipated release for me would be an understatement: Little Busters is one of my favorite VN's ever alongside the likes of Steins;Gate, Umineko, and its "elder sibling" Clannad that was made by the same developers back in 2004. Anyone who has already played Clannad on Steam, or is otherwise familiar with the works of Key/Visual Arts, has a pretty good idea of what to expect from this. And yet Little Busters, in my opinion, is an improvement upon its infamous predecessor.
A major reason why I think this is in no small part due to the cast. At the start, you are one of five childhood friends: Naoe Riki (you), Natsume Kyousuke, Inohara Masato, Miyazawa Kengo, and Natsume Rin. Now in high school and thinking about the unfortunate fact that adulthood will likely split them up, the Little Busters decide to have another fun adventure before that day arrives. As that adventure plays out, the group recieves new members and gets involved in all sorts of whacky shenanigans and hillarious conversations. Every major character (of which I count 13) is very well-developed and has a large amount of screentime. Characters that initially seem stereotypical or one-dimensional (such as the idiot friend Masato, the moe blob Kudryavka, and the hardass rules enforcer Kanata) end up revealing far more depth than first impressions would suggest, particularly when you get involved in their individual storylines. Lastly, one of the big plus points is that regardless of what story path you pursue, the other main cast members remain part of the plot, rather than just disappearing as they tended to do in Clannad and many other VN's.
The storyline for Little Busters is large, with no less than nine different character storylines to play through. There are a huge number of dialogue choices to make which can decide everything from what route you will pursue, what minor (potentially missable) scenes you will find, or what crazy battles you may end up getting involved with. It actually gets a little complex, as you will need to play the original six storylines (Komari, Rin 1, Kurugaya, Haruka, Kudryavka, and Mio) before being able to dig into the heavy drama and soul-crushing heartbreak that follows (Rin 2 and Refrain). Even after that is done, you still have even more to look for, with the unlocking of the three "extra" routes (Saya, Sasami, Kanata) as well as alternate endings for ones you have finished already. In other words... this game is massively packed with content, with something in the order of 100+ hours of gameplay to be had. There's probably plenty of stuff in this game I don't even know about. But despite its length, unlike many other VN's this is one I don't get bored playing. There's just too much fun (and drama) going on keeping me interested... and losing track of time in the process. This is the greatest visual novel ever written. A fine example of not dismissing a story solely based upon the medium with which that story is told. Life-changing, and much more than the lighthearted, playful romp all sorts of media outlets are claiming it to be now that the English version is out. Clannad may have the superior anime of the two, but Little Busters has the better novel, and overall the better story.
And yes, Little Busters will make you cry harder.
Seriously, this is a story that is brilliantly executed, with foreshadowing done so masterfully, you'll be both shocked at the plot twists, yet wondering how you didn't see them coming before then. Masquerading as a slice of life, this story lulls you into a false sense of security before hitting you where it hurts, over and over.
I'm one of many people that, if I could, would erase my memories of this game simply to play it all over again fresh. If I could make everyone in the world experience this beautiful story, I would.

Short review:
If you want to babysit some agents through linear, scripted cover based firefights to crawl your way through an ok story, which was developed as a misguided attempt to enlarge the XCom-franchise, this game might just be the thing for you. If any of this raised a warning sign for you, better keep away, there are a plenty better games you can spend your time and money on.
Thorough review:
The good parts:
The game is definitely not completely bad. The perk system is nice, you can work your way up to some nice combos to make a way out of a tough situation, or wreck your enemies, which can feel satisfying. The story seems kinda promising, though i can't say for sure, since it certainly wasn't enough to keep me hooked. And i think the visuals are quite good, in a way it manages to capture a "noirish-scifiy-actiony" feel, which can be an enticing mix. The sound is ok, nothing special.
The bad parts:
Overall, it's just not enough! The perk system is nice, this plus the squad & command system could make a fundament for a good strategy-shooter... but it just isn't. Since you can actively only control one squad member and the rest of the squad usually acts like the biggest morons you can imagine as "agents", it becomes incredibly difficult to just enjoy the action, while the command system becomes obligatory to keep your mates from killing themselves, i.e. you have to babysit them. All of this made the characters in this game, which are supposed to be more fleshed out a lot less interesting than the generic soldiers in "XCom:Enemy Unkown". And in a game from 2013, i definitely expect some better A.I., or a way to deal with what's there more effectively, but neither is given here.
Now add to this a very linear progression with scripted encounters and little varieties to approach them, but "use perks to set up enemies, shoot enemies", which became a boring task for me way too soon and what you get is a game with little things to play with and no motivation.
And though i didn't seem to encounter as many problems as some other people, the game lacks a lot of polish and can too easily bug out or crash on you.
Recommendation:
Well, if you really want to play it, for the niche it provides, or for the little addition it does to the XCom franchise, do as you please. If you want to play a good squad-based tactical game, grab something else, like XCom proper, Shadowrun, Fire Emblem, or Hard West. If you want to play a good squad-based shooter, you might want to check out the Rainbow-Six series (Ubisoft warning). If you want to play a pure shooter or strategy game, reorient yourself.
It's an OK game, but nothing to write home about.

This game is frustrating in the fact that yes, it's beautifully designed, the music is flawless, has so much atmosphere etc etc...however, it doesn't save it from the awful truth that the narrative is inconsistent and lackluster. To be completely honest there is not much of a story going on here at all that isn't defined in one complete sentence.
"Cyberpunk junkie has lost their memory and is trying to find her deeper meaning among gender/species bending characters in an anarchical hacker underworld " ... I wish there was more to it, however there is not.
Fyn's character design is straight up "Jane" from the tv show "Daria". Full of angst, cynicism, bad attitudes, and awkward humor. Her dialogue comes out of a whiney, teenage goth girl's diary, who just thinks they're so much better than you because they're so " A E S T H E T I C ".
The typos and grammatical errors are extrememly annoying simply for the fact that you can see all of the effort that went into creating such a visually beautiful game. Why not follow through to the very end and not allow your work to come across as though you've given up and that you don't care?
Designing another character after Hunter S. Thompson was an interesting touch given the main topic of the story, quoting a Cure song called " A Forest " ... I can't tell if the awkward placement of this was intentional or due to the lack of having any idea on how to progress the story further.
Gameplay drags out far too long, having to revisit places over and over again, one minute the character can run, the next she can't .... the puzzles are a mess to figure out .... most have nothing to do with the story at all, and I feel as though this occurs only for the need to make up for the fact that the story is quite hollow.
Even the characters in the story don't really know what's going on.
I truly wanted to like this game and gave another chance within hopes of the second episode carrying the story.
It just didn't happen.
I can see the dedication behind the art. It's just not enough in my opinion.

Portal is by far one if the best puzzle games of all time, no doubt about it. The puzzles may not be hard to figure out, but that's actually the charm of them. I usually never talk about colour pallets in games, but Portal's colour pallet is great. While the only colors used are orange, Grey and blue, they are very vibrant and never feel repetitive or boring to look at. The reflections of light off of the walls also give it a very nice tone.
The only flaw I can give this game is it's short length. I managed to complete it in about 2 hours. I wish it was longer, especially for it's price.
So overall, Portal is one of the best games I have ever played. And this is from a guy who doesn't like puzzle games! I would stony recommend this masterpiece to anyone with a little bit of money spare in their wallet.

Controls:

You also have 3 specialized interaction buttons. E gets you inside and out of stuff. T lets you stab the earth. You could also do sidemissions. of which there are...3. And they get you great stuff like Special ammo that actually does decent damage; useless upgrades for your reload speed and heal time and of course vital mech upgrades without which you'd never survive the QTE Kaiju combat since whatever you do, you'll take damage and have no clue how to QTE properly; of course they are also multi-staged and if you die somewhere down the line, you obviously start from the beginning.
Story is explained in clunky cutscenes with creepy emotionless/off beat lipflaps or prerendered cutscenes that make you expell your digestive system with the grace and skill they were paced both narratively and lengthwise.

Skyborn is a fun RPG, and deceptively simple!
I tried to go into a in-depth review of it, but it turned out way too long, so I'll just go into a Pros and Cons type of points, with the full analysis for myself. If you're interested in it, I'll send you the whole review, just!
-Great world! It starts out fairly average, but it later reveals itself. It has a few interesting concepts, worth looking into.
-Unique combat system. It's a mixture of the classic turn-based combat, with a few more modern Skills and Gameplay concepts, akin to MMOs, like a threat system, big focus on buffs and debuffs rather than pure firepower, and good interaction and role separation between classes.
-It looks pretty good.
-Music is simply fantastic! It really reminded my of Golden Sun. While it's not quite at that level, it's still very good, and it feels more modern sounding. I really liked it.
-Provides a good challenge on Hard Mode without feeling too frustrating (until the last 2 Bosses, which are impossible unless you do absolutely every objective before heading into the final section of the game. However, nothing previously indicates that to be the case, which one is likely to miss, not realizing it until it's too late to go back.)
-No random encounters! You can see those encounters on the screen, approaching at will.
-Retry feature to get right back into a battle when you're defeated.
-Good control scheme (I personally used a controller for a more laid back experience, and it worked fine).
-Lack of any resolution options, leaving you with a very badly scaled game in Fullscreen, or just a small window (the latter is recommended, Fullscreen looke hideous).
-Poor interface design, looking very average, and not very functional.
-The crafting system was awful to navigate, and didn't provide much benefit, as you could earn enough gold to render it useless, as everything would be for sale.
-The game loved to surprise you with Boss Fights, and having you walk for half an hour if you did something wrong regarding leveling, or equipment. Some Boss Fights also appeared out of nowhere, sometimes making it impossible to procceed without reverting a couple of Saves.
-Low amount of Save Slots (only 4).
-The last few maps seemed a bit too clustered and confusing.
-Lack of information. This game is not very informative regarding some of its details, leaving it all to trial and error. Sometimes, it can be very damaging to the player's experience. Every shop, forge (for crafting) is very far apart, leaving the player with empty hands for long periods of time.
In the end, it was my downfall, as I literally couldn't go back, but HAD to, to be able to finish the game. Again, it does NOT give the player enough information for the player to make some decisions safely, but it was a big sore spot for me.
Overall, Skyborn was an enjoyable experience. I liked a lot of it! But, looking back at it, it is also riddled with so, so many issues...!
Some of those are inherent to RPGMaker, but some of those were also huge design flaws, which is disappointing.
If you're looking for a JRPG with a more modern feel, give this one a try! I enjoyed most of it.
Not recommended at full price, though, 15$ seems way too high for this game. It feels small at times,and just doesn't seem worth that price point, with so many amazing games at 10$.

First off, ignore all the complaining about RPG maker.  If an RPG has a good plot in an interesting setting with unique characters and a good combat system, who cares how it was made?  Luckily, Skyborn has all this and more.  It starts off fairly easy but the combat system has enough depth to really give you a challenge after the first few areas.  I played on medium difficulty and I found the battles challenging and fun.  There are also plenty of optional battles in the late game that will challenge you, but they're not needed to beat the game. The story is the best part of Skyborn.  There's a unique setting combined with memorable characters.  The game is a nice length as well.  It's probably 11 to 15 hours total.  I did all 4 sidequests along with the arena and the Venom Depths which are optional, along with maybe 45 minutes of afking for dinner, beer, and bathroom breaks.
As far as the details of the game go, I enjoyed the level design.  Graphics are SNES level, but I'm playing for the plot and there were some moments where certain levels looked quite pleasing and so I'd say the graphics are fine for the genre.  The plot and setting were great.  This isn't a generic steampunk cliché universe.  There's no annoying puzzles and all but one time it was clear where to go next. The crafting and augmenting system is deep enough to cause you to put some real thought into what to upgrade and it's fairly open.  You can skip crafting if you like, but it's fun to forge very powerful weapons for your favorite character.  The music was ok, not fantastic.  Sound effects were solid.  In the first 2 to 3 hours of the game, the enemies can seem a little repetitive and it's a bit too easy (on medium) but that changes.  There's also no real "grinding" levels.  Enemies do not respawn so it's to your advantage to fight every enemy, but you don't just have to sit around leveling up.  Bosses are challenging and feel epic.  Overall, I'd give the game an 8/10 for being an enjoyable, well made RPG.  It's a bit expensive at the current 15$ price tag, but if you can pick up this game on a sale, it's worth it.

Ok, this will be a fairly long rant but here goes:
The servers-
I spent 30 minutes trying to connect to the servers (bear in mind Steam says you cannot have more than 2 hours in a game if you want a refund.) It's launch day, fair enough, but still. I joined the discord, apparently the devs said it would be fixed in 20 minutes (it wasn't) so I waited, when people asked when it would be ready, the devs went AFK, dodged questions and replied to other concerns, rather than the pressing matter, the awful connection. I decided to take this time to explore the gear and character customization options, there were what appears to be the bare bones of a skill tree and equipment selector. For example, there are 5 weapons available to the player from the get go, A 1 handed wooden club, a 1 handed axe, a 1 handed sword, a 2 handed polearm, and a bow and arrow. (You can apparently progress through this and unlock more types of these weapons, but I've yet to see what difference they will even make, considering the exact same animations and fighting style is used no matter what weapon you wield. The only difference I could see was range and slight damage modifiers. Some may argue that the club would clearly be better against armoured targets, sticking to the realism! But this brings me to my next point: The armour. There is 8 armour options available at the start. 3 types of helmets, a useless straw hat, and 2 almost identical mail coifs. 2 types of tunic, sleeved and unsleeved (No statistical difference what so ever), and 1 pair of pants. I didn't even check if the progression existed for these if I'm honest, as I'm sure it would make 0 difference in the long run.
The Game-
I finally managed to connect to a match. I soon learned, to my dismay, that every single player, was wearing the exact same white-ish gray tunic, and the only differences were that some wore the rounded coif, some wore the square, and some wore the straw hat. Other than that, and what weapon they used, everyone was identical. There is no way to change the colour of the tunics, and the only identifier between friend or foe is a miniscule white triangle above allies heads, which is easily lost amongst the sea of the white burlap excuses for apparel. In terms of combat, the system they designed seemed to improve upon the classic Warband system, in theory it was more advanced. But in reality, it's just the same old spamfest as usual. It was to be expected, but unless you're fighting a 1v1 duel against someone who is interested in a cinematic duel, all you'll see is people walking forward or backwards while spamming left slash or overhead. Archery is as to be expected from a game like this, just shoot at the swarm of serfs slashing at each other with what appears to be foam styled into the shape of medieval weaponry and hope that you get lucky. I've yet to mention that the game is sold as a "Persistent Medieval War" game. The main game mode, the only reason anyone bought this, is locked away, unfinished and unreleased to the public. And instead we were given this less than half-baked shocking PvP experience on stale maps with innane combat systems. "The Epic" as they call it, is supposed to be an enormous open map, in which players can build cities and settlements. God, where do I even start. Everything about this game is utterly fantastic. The gameplay, the graphics, the music (good lord the music). Axiom Verge is a love letter to Metroid in video game form. It is -unabashedly- Metroid. If you grew up on 2D platformers, this will be your jam. Even if you didn't, PLAY THIS GAME. It was made by a single dude!
It's a short but sweet experience. I'd say on average it'll last anywhere from 8 to 12 hours. I clocked in at 11 and a half hours as my clear time. There's a ton of collectables and hidden items scattered throughout the game, but most are pretty optional.
Speaking of collectables and hidden items, Axiom Verge has a lot of weapons. A LOT of weapons. I think there's 20 or so? A minor gripe I had was that despite the vast array of weaponry, only a handful are actually useful. It seems like the design mentality was akin to "sounds cool on paper", but in practice it ends up being pretty useless. Fortunately, the handful of weapons that are good are REALLY GOOD. And to be fair, some of the "useless" weapons are really useful against certain bosses.
Another gripe I had was regarding some of the controls. Two upgrades in particular, the Grapple and the various Dash upgrades you get have kinda... janky controls. They're pretty unwieldy. The grapple's just plain hard to use, and the dash, well... The dash activates by doubletapping a direction, but often times I'd find it would activate randomly on its own just from normal movement. I would much have prefered the dash being mapped to a button instead.
Overall, solid Metroid-y experience. I'd recommend it to anyone who's a fan of 2D platformers or Metroidvanias. GREAT GAME A+++++ ALL THE THUMBS UP.
10/10 Hard to believe that one man made it all. Excellent game for those who are looking for a old school challenge. Music is just brilliant and keeps the atmosphere.

Axiom Verge is Metroid at its core. The story is different, the weapons are different.
But you jump around, exploring areas with funny names on an alien planet, fighting hordes of enemies, and bosses that are waaaay bigger than  you.
For something made by one person, and their vision. It's pretty damn amazing.
Axiom Verge does, what Nintendon't (Or haven't done in a god damn while).
I'm not going to give a score, because I don't think games can be label good or bad with a single number.
I will say that this game IS amazing, and hits a lot of the right notes for me.
Given there are a few things I don't quite like/agree with design-wise. Though this should be taken as a way to make the game better.
Pros:
- Amazing visuals, things look pretty... well, there are some ugly things, but that's intentional!
- Interesting story (I wanted to know more and more about where I was and what was going on).
- Tight controls, walking and jumping around feels good and responsive.
- Rewards gaming instincts.
- JUSTIN-BAILEY
- Tutorials through experimentation/gameplay.
- Music is great and fits the setting. Elements of the HUD, and cutscenes are in time with the music. I love this stuff!
- I want more of it.
- Characters are well rounded, and have emotions. One of the "Good" characters even kills you at one point out of anger.
- Moral ambiguity, makes for interesting story, and thought provoking situations.
- Many hidden secrets, but much like Metroid, they can be in stupid places. Though I found 70% of items my first time.
- Lots of weapons, all act differently. I found a use for most of them at least once, but I stuck with the main weapon.
- Cool toys! You get a bloody corruptor, you can glitch out enemies and make them do weird stuff!
- Not too much backtracking, not until you're tricked out with all the fancy toys, making it easy to get around.
Cons:
- The Final Boss is a bit... Hard. Could just be me, but it's way too hectic. And was pretty much "Shoot the thing and win".
- I would have liked to see the final boss actually use some of the tools and tricks you picked up.
- The "Invalid" hit noise, that Metroid had too, is freaking loud, and can play over the top of itself!
- Some areas, mainly the first and second one, kind of blended together for me.
- I want more of it.
- Kinda open/underwhelming ending, this could be for a sequel though. Which I would be interested it.

11 hours, 34 deaths.  77% items 96% map
This is a good game.  This is an awesome game.  This is something that feels like it came straight out of the early nineties. Something that could almost have existed on the SNES with a bit more of the harsh pixels of the NES. A soundtrack that is electronic; Dark and brooding that still somehow seems like it could also be coming from one of those old consoles.
It plays and control in nearly the same way as Castlevania Symphony of the Night, and Super Metroid. Running around collecting items and equipment to run around again, getting farther, deeper, to collect more items and equipment.  The game can be grueling if you aren't an explorer.  Finding weapon damage power ups as well as the weapons themselves can be hard.  Some of them much more well hidden than others.  Maps, and the "cheat codes" are mandatory for some pickups.  Searching the web for secrets made me feel like I was back on dial up just hoping I could figure it out.
I recommend a controller.  I found it the easiest way to pull off some of the harder "jumping teleporting pet lobbing teleporting again and then again" jumps.  The game can be beaten in under four hours with a map and a plan, but it's much more fun to go it yourself. When you get stuck, get help with that part and then continue.  You can always come back when you miss something.
The only two things I might gripe about are the asking price and the myriad of weapons that are either useless or bothersome to use.   I would have been a bit more solid on the price if it were 15 or closer to that.  Many weapons are specialized.  None seem to be "super effective" against any one kind of enemy, nor are there really any types of enemy.  They all seem to just have a base health pool, and you deal damage until they are dead.  No shielding, no regenerating and no armor.  There is a hotswitch button to change weapons without opening the weapon wheel.  This is underused completely. I simply stuck to the most powerful gun in the game until I found a more powerful one.
If you're having trouble progressing, a power upgrade or two can let you breeze by.  I found particularly the last boss to suffer from this.  It seemed near impossible with my weak weapons.  Even the enemies leading up to the boss were giving me trouble.  I went back and collected a few upgrades and a weapon I missed.  Returned swiftly to the boss and there was no difficulty.  I simply destroyed him.  Unlike most of the bosses there was no pattern, nothing to learn.  I just shot the weak spot and I won in seconds.  Sadly a weak ending gameplay wise.
This is still an amazing game, beautiful to look at, slightly upsetting sometimes as well.  With it's near gore style in some sections, mechanical biological machine in others... the "friends" that you meet on the way are also terrifying monsters in their own right. Brothers in Arms and Mass Effect got together, had a baby, and then named it The Bureau: XCOM Declassified.
It's an unweildy name, but the genetic test is a match: The Bureau is a tactical squad-based sci-fi third person shooter. If that's not enough to get you excited, then, well...throw in some XCOM!
Which actually seems to be the source the problem. The initial reviews were overly harsh and critical, and the main source of angst I can find is whiny fanboys decrying the fact that this game isn't XCOM
for their tastes. Simply put: it's not a strategy game.
I think overall that they're mostly wrong and it's a great game, but its potential was even more than it turned out to be. And I think we can also blame part of that on the XCOM name. It limited them in terms of setting and enemies and weapons and story. A fresh IP would've eliminated the fanboy backlash
given them more flexibility to create something truly creative. But I get it. An unknown name is harder to market.
There's not much meta-management here, which is fine, but it's yet another point against using the XCOM name. Although I will say that getting to walk around a base and talk to people with a zoomed-in perspective after spending 200 hours or so removed from them in the other XCOM games was a fun and refreshing change.
The Bureau has the same problem Mass Effect and a lot of other games where you unlock abilities as you progress do: at some point you become totally overpowerd and the difficulty significantly ramps down as time goes on, even as tougher enemies in greater numbers are thrown at you.
The weapons were ok, but I felt myself coming back to the same few ones over and over again. I think the single biggest improvement to gameplay they could've made would've been to allow for gun customization. Let me add or remove a scope or a stock or a barrel and then change some properties based on that. My second choice would be simply adding higher levels and more abilities for my characters to acquire.
The story was good, but again, I felt it was hamstrung by having to follow all the typical XCOM tropes, which I've seen too many times at this point to be surprising.
The DLC was by far the worst part. Endless waves in a small arcade is not how I want to spend my time. Story DLC would've been a much better choice. But again, I get it. The devs are making the most of limited resources.
If you like third person shooters, sci-fi, and/or having to manage a squad and their abilities, then you should absolutely give The Bureau a try. Just don't expect a strategy game to be hiding inside it somewhere.

Overall, I'd totally recommend this game.

Recommended with reservations (after completing Episode 1).
Void and Meddler has a gorgeous aesthetic. The beautiful graphics and music combine to create a lovely cyberpunk city populated with the best kind of strange characters. Regular humans, humans with horns, cat people, bird people, and others all intermix beneath the neon lights. It's a unique and refreshing setting, and I find myself wanting to explore more of it. The game looks even better in play than in screenshots.
Void and Meddler grows on you. There are amusing and clever bits that you discover throughout. The first "quest" is to turn on some music to relax, and of course the protagonist's relaxing music is the most horrendous noise. There are different ways to finish each act, and the way you pick describes the character you're playing - a violent solution paints a violent character, while a clever solution a clever one.
The protagonist is unsympathetic, which makes for an unusual game. You can do something really awful in Episode 1, which I found horribly distasteful, but who could I blame? Sure, the devs coded it in, and the protagonist carried out the action, but I was in control - I was the one who chose to do something I knew was wrong, that I didn't have to do to advance the story, so who can I blame other than myself for the awful outcome? Where Spec Ops' nastiness was forced, here it was optional - I didn't have to turn off the game to make it stop, I merely had to find another way to advance.
The writing was a mixed bag. The descriptions of people and things were often lovely, but the sometimes long monologues upon visiting a location for the first time seemed unnecessary and out of place. It seemed that the writing was trying too hard at times, and worked better when it wasn't. Part of it is expectations - I expect a description when I examine an item, I don't expect a monologue when I arrive at a new place.
Other reviews mention the walking speed, but it seemed perfectly fine to me, and at times beautifully synchronized with the music. Episode 1 does lack quick transitions for double-clicking on an exit, but that is added in Episode 2.
Unfortunately, despite looking into the future for its setting, Void and Meddler brings with it frustrations from Point & Click Adventure past. There is little direction, though it's partially forgivable given that the protagonist is supposed to be aimlessly stumbling her way through the night. I was able to get through the normal ending of Episode 1 without a guide - relying on just stumbling around, clicking on everything, talking to everyone, picking up everything in sight. But the alternate and hard endings to Episode 1 require leaps of logic that seem impossible without a guide - having to examine or use the same item twice, trying to pick up things you'd never think to pick up, combining items without any reason or explanation for doing so. I'm not sure if Episode 2 improves on it yet.
So I recommend Void and Meddler, but with reservations. If you like cyberpunk and unique games, and don't mind having to blindly stumble around or use a guide to get through the illogical puzzles, you'll find a lovely neon city to explore and bizarre characters to encounter. The visuals and music are a potent and delightful combination, and the setting is refreshing and begging to be explored.
Also, note that you do not need to purchase the Deluxe edition if you don't care about the soundtrack. The Season Pass includes all the episodes, and is less than half the price of the Deluxe edition.

After reading through the reviews, it seems like a lot of other people feel the same way as me.  I really wanted to like this game. I am a huge fan of all think cyberpunk, synth/retro/vaporwave, and 80s dystopian - and I've been an adventure game player for many decades.  On paper, the formula for this game was perfect.  The atmosphere and aesthetics of the game are really well done, very beautiful -  and the music fits perfectly.  But for me, that's where the strengths of the game end.
I'm not going to go crazy bashing it, as I know how much time and effort it takes to make a game, but as constructive criticism for the developers, I would just make my own personal suggestions of working on coherent story (even given the literary style, there are still ways of connecting story elements better and not going overboard with cryptic dialog), better puzzles (more logical and with more depth), and some technical improvements (I only played story 1 so far, perhaps this is fixed later) - specifically, the ability to run and/or skip walking in large rooms.  There were a couple achievements I could have had that I just skipped as I didn't want to deal with walking across a long expanse for the 6th time.
So, for those on the fence on this one - I would go into it as an aesthetic experience and leave it at that.

Truthfully, I love this game, and I have a lot of thoughts on it, so I apologize in advance for how long this is. I would like to note that I’ve only played through the first episode and only gotten two out of the three possible endings, so my review is based on that.
First of all, the art style and the graphics are incredible. I love the streaks of water that drip down my screen, and with that in contrast to the bright neon lighting in the background, it was so easy for me to feel engaged from the moment I saw Fyn’s room. My interest only grew with each new area I explored, and I’m just truly enthralled by the look of this game. It is unlike anything else I’ve ever played before.
Along with the art style, the music also plays an important role in setting the scene. I saw another reviewer call the music “repetitive,” but I really don’t see that as a bad thing. The tunes are stuck in my head even after I leave the game, which sort of just makes me wanna jump back in and explore more, or maybe even just leave it open, listening to the music as I watch people rush by in the rain outside Fyn’s condo. The music only ever added to the overall scene and feeling of the game for me. I would say the music is definitely one of the strongest areas of this game. It really captures the overall mood and atmosphere of each scene, and made me feel somewhat of an attachment to each scene as well. The music makes the game what it is and really brings the whole artistic style together.
As far as story goes, I like the overall organization of it. The bits of foreshadowing that I caught on my second playthrough are an excellent touch, and it’s easy to see how one event leads to another after seeing the story unfold once. The writers definitely excelled in this area, and although some parts of the story do seem a bit random, I feel as though everything done to this game was intentional in some way. I trust the writers in that respect.
Honestly, I would have
to write for this game. To be able to explore this world and Fyn’s character would be a dream, and I feel as though toying with the dialogue and working to further capture Fyn’s character would be so fun. I think that more realistic dialogue would make this an even more special, relatable, and, ultimately, better game.
There are many areas of writing that strike me, such as the
, as well as Fyn’s description of the club. I also like this description of the game a lot: “In a city where genders and species melt into each other, maybe she’ll find the long lost touch of humanity missing from her life.” It really captures that diversity that is so prevalent in this game, as well as the overall theme of finding Fyn’s lost memories. The different animals, orientations, and genders really make this game unique, and I can easily say this is another favorite aspect of mine. (Especially as a queer individual, it’s nice to see this inclusion. Everyone is different in this game, but no one is treated badly because of it.) Along with this, I like the hints to the futuristic  technology (like robots, the road, “the system,” and “tangible memories”) in this game and would really love to explore that aspect more.
Overall, there are quite a few areas of writing that could have been improved and made to read more realistically, but there are also a ton of areas in the writing that really shine. Just a simple proofread with a good writer focused on improving the writing rather than changing it would be all it needs to be perfect.
As far as characters go, I like that Fyn's gender is more androgynous than anything, and that she’s (at least to me) shown to be, at the very least, queer. The side characters are written excellently, and their dialogue stays true to their personalities.
Speaking of, I actually do like Fyn's personality. It's not that she’s likable, it's that the writers have done such an excellent job of, not only creating this flawed, intriguing character, but to staying true to her abrasive personality. I only wish she had some kind of redeeming characteristic, though I imagine I’ll learn more about her in Episode 2. For now, it’s obvious that she’s not her full self right now, and I think that’s an extremely important aspect to consider about her character.
On that note, the only other thing I would really change would be adding more dialogue options with individuals. It would be nice to be able to flirt with others, be mean to them, or even just simply have more of an option in how we interact (not necessarily just with important characters, but with side characters as well). This game is reminiscent of a game I used to love (and can sadly no longer play), and I only wish it had more of that “dating sim” aspect in a way. I guess the game just puts me in very much a “party” world, allows Fyn to bring home people to “use,” but when I want her to flirt with someone, she’s completely and entirely against it. (I will say she at least has good taste, but this game just made me want more options and more immersion.) I guess, ultimately, I wish this had more of an RPG/dating sim factor, but I can see why that isn’t relevant to this type of game and story.
This game left me with a familiar feeling—A feeling of never wanting a game to end. A feeling of looking back on the moments I spent with a game, and feeling that strange, indescribable feeling that only playing a good game can bring about. Ultimately, I enjoyed this game immensely, and I very much look forward to where the story takes me next. I enjoyed writing this review, and I’m so excited to see what the creators pursue next!

I really, really wanted to like this game. On paper, it's basically my dream game. The graphics are gorgeous. The music is nice but very repetitive. The world building, what I saw of it, was great. I want to play a game in this world.
But not this one. I feel like this game should have been built on Ginsberg's Howl and Kerouac's On The Road and instead I got Camus' The Stranger. Everything feels disjointed and like nothing happens for a reason. I'm down with that, that's very mid-century existentialist. But it also feels very pointless and dead. Where Kerouac saw a world without purpose and decided to make his own purpose, Camus' protagonist Meursault, and Void and Meddler's protagonist, see a world without purpose and decide to be pointlessly cruel.
It's not fun, but I've played and enjoyed many artsy games that were not fun. This is both not fun, and bad philosophy. Enjoy the screenshots and play something else.

This is a game from publisher Creobit, who seem to specialize in casual games. This can be considered sort of a trilogy with their other tower defense games, Royal Defense and Day D: Tower Rush, in that if you've played one, it seems like you've played them all. I went with Fort Defense, since I liked its aesthetic the most. Instead of dealing with enemies traveling by ground or air, here every level is water-based, with enemies to match.
I wasn't expecting to enjoy Fort Defense very much, since reviews are pretty mixed, with some saying it doesn't work at all for them. It does for me, and after about an hour I've found it a decent game, so you long as you accept it doesn't really do anything that innovative. The ocean aesthetic is mostly window-dressing, as the levels are fairly standard (although quite pretty), and on them I've fought quick, fragile enemies, tougher slow ones, medic ships that heal others - standard stuff. Your towers are a bit more interesting, with your first pea-shooter having an upgraded form that stuns enemies, and the cannon becoming a machine gun. There's also factories you can build to harvest extra gold if you're willing to give up a few tower positions for them, although on Easy that doesn't seem wholly necessary; the game isn't a complete push-over on that difficulty, but so far it's been mostly clear sailing.
Fort Defense is a fairly obvious mobile port, and not an in-depth one. The buttons for your settings, including a pause and extra speed, are only clickable without any hotkeys assigned to them, and the game actually refused to go into windowed mode because my screen resolution was too small for it. I can see the framework for it in other places, like certain spaces in levels requiring you to pay barrels, your upgrade currency, before you can build on them. It doesn't ruin the game, but it is apparent.
There are only two campaigns in the game, the former in tropical seas, the latter arctic ones, and it seems like you could complete the game in only a few hours, so if you're looking for an 'in-between game' or a simple introduction to tower defenses you could do worse. However, this only applies to the base game; Fort Defense does have two DLC campaigns for half the cost of the main game, but both of them are apparently glitched(?) in different ways to make them impossible to beat. Oops.
