This game was pretty fun and is the first good RPG maker game I've played that wasn't done by Freebird.  Here are a few things that stuck out to me:
PROS:
-lots of polish. plenty of little animations and cinematics that make the game feel more immersive. The character thumbnails are drawn with multiple different facial expressions to be used when appropriate, etc.
-characters and writing are both very good. I really enjoyed the dialogue and the storytelling had me really interested in what was happening just minutes into the game. The story isn't groundbreakingly original persay, but I did really enjoy it, and the execution was very good. I felt genuinely interested and invested in what was going on in the Skyborn world all the way through the end.
-good combat mechanics - I really had to think about how I was going to equip my characters  and what actions to choose in a battle.
CONS
- bit pricy. I thought it was worth it personally, but it only took me 15 hours to beat, and a dollar per hour of gameplay seems a lot higher than most games on the market.
- very linear. no worldmap to move around on, and only a handful of towns. I usually enjoy games that are more on the linear side, so this will be a bigger con to some people than it is to me.
- you'll have to look up the stats online to figure out what they do, or you'll be somewhat blind in choosing how to augment your equipment. As another  reviewer is saying, it's not explained and it's not obvious. Even knowing a little bit, I never quite knew whether I was making the best choices with my equipment, and I made lots of costly mistakes that I couldn't undo without reverting to a save.
- enemies wander on the map instead of having random encounters. This would be fine, but when you kill them, they never come back, so if there's a way to grind in this game, I never figured out what it is, which is really frustrating since I couldn't figure out how I was supposed to beat the next guys at the colluseum. I just wasn't strong enough and had no idea how to get stronger. I suppose I could've looked online, but I really prefer to avoid walkthroughs if I can.
Overall, excellent game. Engaging story, lovable characters, fun combat, and just the sort of retro RPG experience I was looking for.

Where do I even start? This feels like a dream. Little Busters, officially released in English and accessible for everyone to enjoy on Steam. Acknowledged as one of the best visual novels of all time, and ten years later here it is. The three Ecstasy routes have been translated and made accessible for the first time, and just Little Busters as a whole is being made accessible to anyone. This game is the pinnacle of Maeda Jun's work no doubt. The pinnacle of Key, and the visual novel medium as a whole. Little Busters is an experience like no other, and now it has finally made it to today where there is an official English version based on the translation patch from years ago. No longer just a game that a very select few love and discuss the impacts of, but one that the rest of the world will be able to see, and hopefully discover for themselves too. No longer does the best visual novel of all time have to be obscure and hidden away, whilst I know that something like Key and Little Busters only attracts a select few for reasons such as being able to be immensely engaged in lengthy games that challenge philosophy and psychological viewpoints no matter your age or background, merely from a human standpoint. Something that only Maeda himself can and could master. I sincerely hope more people, people who maybe have never even played a visual novel, give it a chance and let themselves be immersed into one of the most life-changing experiences from a true masterpiece.
I cannot encourage you enough, no matter your opinion or where you stand on the idea of VNs or Japanese games and media. Try Little Busters. Little Busters changed my life, impacted the way I was wired and how I process my own thoughts. Not only me, the other fans will agree, Little Busters will have your sub-conscious processing all sorts of ideas without you even realising. For you to piece it all together at the end and conclude how you too view not just the ideas conveyed in the game, but how you even live as a human in this world. The characters, whilst fictional, are written in a way where their relationships and feelings are intertwined with each other and feels real. Especially the original five, the warmth of their closely-knit childhood friendship is written beautifully and will engage you through a surreal experience like no other. When things become serious and you slowly make realisations throughout the game, you will cry like you never have before.
Then there is the soundtrack. Maeda Jun, Orito Shinji, PMMK and more. True geniuses of composing. The soundtrack of Little Busters will blow you away, lift you up, hit you hard on the floor and make you bawl, and put you at peace. Even the menu music, "Born into This World" (Umareochiru Sekai), is incredibly beautiful. Every detail of the whole game is wonderful and intricately placed and built together to create the masterpiece that is Little Busters.
I cannot recommend Little Busters enough, no matter who you are, please try Little Busters!

Let me open this review by saying I'm extremely biased. Little Busters changed me, it set my life on a course I never would've expected and allowed me to meet so many fantastic people, it shaped who I am as a person, and became part of who I am. I'll always remember one day I was in Tokyo wearing my Little Busters jumper and a salaryman excitedly shook my hand and did the muscle dance with me. This is a work which affects people on a deep and personal level. This is not an objective review, it's just the musings of one of those people it impacted. I'm writing this review based on the old fan translation of the game.
Little Busters sets up with a very humble presentation. A bunch of childhood friends in high school do a bunch of wacky stuff together to pass their time, a clique full of such unique energy that the rest of the student body can't possibly ignore them, many drawn to them and wanting to join in. The game is full of silly minigames that will keep you coming back and complement the story nicely; I've spent many hours chilling out with the batting practice, it's the perfect stress relief. It's hilarious and heartwarming watching their circle grow and the scale of the shenanigans increase, it takes me back to an idyllic representation of youth, where I could just laugh with my friends every day without a care.
But please, don't mistake Little Busters for a comedy series. Little Busters is a story about youth, and the process of growing up, and it doesn't shy away from the harsh realities that come with that process. It's about finding one's own identity, clashing with the identites of others, and finding a way to live. Each character in the story feels very much a real person, and they all have their own crises to deal with in their process of growing up. The writing is beautiful, and you'll find yourself hitting the screenshot button every other minute. It's positive representation of mental health issues and it's atypically feminine male lead is particularly praiseworthy.
But that's not all, Little Busters is filled with intrigue thanks to an overarching mystery that gradually presents itself throughout the various character routes, culminating in the most incredible final route of any visual novel I've read. And then there's the EX routes which are available in English for the very first time!
If you open the game and you find the characters and dialogue very annoying, maybe Little Busters isn't for you. A concept with potential that died as a game with hubris and imbalance.
Turtle Rock released Evolved as a free to play game after a much anticipated debut that did everything wrong. It charged $60 for the base game which should have been a mere $40 due to its scope. Further it pushed a torrential amount of DLC adding over $100 in cost for the entirety of the offerings (this is on top of the $60 you paid for the game).
Now as a free to play price is off the table but the gameplay just isn't enticing enough to keep people engaged. The issue here is balance. Turtle Rock's former effort in Left 4 Dead did not have a progression & class system to worry about in it's well balanced a-symmetrical gameplay. With Evolved, Turtle Rock is either in over their heads or cannot resist the temptations of overpowering certain classes while handicapping others. The most obvious example of this is in the new medic paladin class that can practically go 1v1 with a Monster without the need of his team. Another example is the tracker class that sniffs out monsters routinely before they can reach level 2 making victory all but a certainty for the hunters. There are other examples like this that people have been vocal about on the Evolved forums but since Turtle Rock has now abandoned the game these imbalances will be cast as permanent.
Evolved isn't a terrible game - it just isn't worthy of much of your time.

I never expected there to be a complex and grisly plot in a "bird dating game".   You learn of hidden mysteries, spies, murders,  and the pasts of many of these characters interwoven cleverly in the "true ending" of the game.
The gameplay is fairly simple and if you are familiar with visual novels, it's quite standard. There's a fastfoward button which can be useful when unlocking various endings of a specific route, however when you are in the "true ending" route (you'll know it when you see it), I'd recommend to read everything carefully.
In conclusion, don't be fooled by the game's slapstick and happy appearance. It is an emotional rollercoaster with a dark mystery and rich plot which will leave your feathers ruffled.

This is my FAVORITE zombie survival game in recent years.  On the Wii U.......
In my mind, this title could have sold millions of Wii U consoles as it was available upon launch of the console and took beautiful advantage of the gamepad functionality.  I still play the game from time to time and have pumped in hundreds of hours of gameplay on that version.  Even beat survival mode twice, which is frustratingly difficult.
As for this PC version after my first quick playthrough:
The Good:
The HD and increased frame rate looks and plays great.  So thats a plus.
The game itself is a lot of fun for single-op, survival strategy.
Controls on an Xbox controller are intuitive enough that with a little practice its easy to pick up and go
The Bad:
Overall Wii U kinda sucks, BUT this game was practically designed FOR that gamepad.
Using the Prep pad was a unique immersive experience with this title that is missing in this incarnation
There is literally no new content to speak of, cept for 2 different melee weapons
No online connection for leaving behind messages, warnings, etc. (similar to Dark Souls but via graphiti)
No online survivors who were killed pop up in your game to be looted.... This was a serious boon sometimes
So in actuality, content has been removed from this version, which I hope will be fixed with an update
Overall Impression:
I will still recommend this game, as it's pretty damn awesome.  However, it IS NOT a new release, and is more or less un-altered from the Wii U version so there is no new content or "scarier than ever" elements.....
So it looks pretty cool, but is still a game that is ultimately several years old.
If you enjoy a single-player Zombie survival game that values patience and itelligence vs. run-and-gun.  This is a really cool experience.
If you haven't played the Wii U version, then you don't know what your missing, so this version is going to be pretty awesome to play.
If you did play or still play the Wii U version, a lot of the missing elements and game functionality being gone is going to be missed, or at least severely noticed.
I'm going to play this version enough to grab some achievements and enjoy it to the end without dying once, but I still have my copy in the Wii U to fall back on when I want the full-immersion experience

), which in turn is based on those old-fashioned electrified wire loop games that used to be popular at funfairs and in game shows. You know, those contraptions where you need to guide a metal loop along a serpentine length of wire without actually touching the loop to the wire.
In
, your hand-eye coordination and fine motor skills are tested by having you navigate the mouse pointer through a very short maze while avoiding touching the edges. On your way to the exit, you can pick up three stars, which serve as some sort of score reflecting how well you performed.
It isn't much of a game, though. Everything depends on your mouse pointer speed. These days, most gamers have a gaming mouse that allows the mouse pointer to move at great speeds. And other people will often just increase the mouse pointer speed through Windows' configuration options. Well, at high mouse pointer speed,
is near impossible to play.
So I lowered my mouse's DPI from 4000 to 400 and finished the game with little effort. If lowering your DPI and/or mouse pointer speed doesn't do the trick for you, you can temporarily enable mouse keys, meaning you can control the mouse pointer with the arrow keys of your keyboard. To enable mouse keys, press Left Alt + Left Shift + Num Lock on your keyboard at the same time. To disable mouse keys, repeat this process.
In the end,
seems to be a test of your ability to reduce the mouse pointer speed rather than a test of your dexterity. There are a few more things to note that didn't sit well with me:
has 5 Steam Trading Cards. You'll get 3 while running the game.
The Steam Achievements consist of two types: achievements granted for finishing each level with 1, 2 and 3 stars (so 24 total) and achievements for just starting each level up to five times (so 40 total). There are four more redundant achievements granted for finishing 2, 4, 6 and 8 levels, totalling 68 achievements.

Axiom Verge has a pretty great intro. It reminded me of the games from the time-period when I got into this hobby. It's got a great soundtrack, very Metroid-like graphics and encourages exploration, like this genre of game should. At first, it seemed like the sort of game that I was going to enjoy.
Unfortunately, around halfway through the game, it takes a turn for the worse and the whimsical exploration from the early game is replaced with spamming every metroidvania ability on every surface to make sure that you aren't missing a deviously hidden main path.
(If you're going to play it: Use the disruptor on the slightly pinker goo than everything else that 2 fishlobsters jump out of)
Another problem is the controls (I played using gamepad) become overburdened with half-baked exploration mechanics that never quite feel good enough to pull off what the game is trying to get you to do, instead just putting you in a nightmarish loop of repeating the difficult parts over and over until you get it right by virtue of chance... and then you get killed in the very next room and have to do it all again.
For now, I've decided to put the game down, at what I believe is the final boss, because it is more frustrating than fun. Will I come back to it? I don't know - probably not.

This title manages to overcome many of the issues that it could have faced and really raises the bar for what I'll be coming to expect from indie JRPGs and titles using the RPGMaker engine. Of the indie old-school RPGs I've played thusfar, it is the best title of that sub-category that is available on Steam right now and excels in every area, exceeding all my expectations. Though this is going to be quite a glowing review, I'll get into some of the downsides toward the end.
There are largely original assets in terms of graphics- an original, rarely-explored Steampunk setting to explore, well done full-screen character designs, and a bunch of animations and effects that add more immersion and personality to the cut-scenes. It all ends up comparing favorably to retail classics. This is one of those titles where you can just look at the screenshots to see if it will be pleasing aesthetically, the actual game does not deviate far from that though unfortunately many of the dungeon areas fall into the typical types of rainforests, caves, mines, etc. Battle graphics are quite simplistic. I greatly enjoy the character designs which seem like a curious blend of Eastern and Western ideas.
As for gameplay, there are enough nooks and crannies to the systems that it better resembles early PS1 RPGs like Grandia or Wild Arms rather than NES/SNES RPGs. The battle system is reminiscent of Grandia with multiple gauges and turn order being dictated by a character's speed stat and also by a weight stat, based on how many items they have equipped. There are some unusual ideas here, such as physical offensive characters having an "energy" gauge that fills up and makes more of their abilities accessible and a "threat" gauge that affects which character will face the brunt of attacks. Buffs, debuffs, and status effects are also available very early on and relevant quickly during battles. The most noteworthy thing about character management is about halfway through the game and again 3/4 of the way through, you receive special items that allow non-linear character classes. For example, a character can choose to learn high level healing OR offensive magic so your choices can accommodate your play style.
There is a weapons and armor crafting and customization system along with the option to use multiple weapon types such as guns, dual-wielding swords, etc. In addition to seeking out treasure from dungeons you also seek out resources to create much stronger versions of the weapons and gear you'd buy from the shops in town. There is a battle coliseum and super tough optional enemies that add a few hours of gameplay.
Dungeons are well-designed areas rife with very simple puzzles to work out. Towns are attractively intricate in design but have little to do beyond speaking to some NPCs, perhaps accepting a quest, and checking out the shops. This is perhaps an overly relaxed game in terms of complexity, but also a fast-paced one, which is a huge factor in its enjoyability. I would recommend choosing hard difficulty though my first playthrough (clocking in at almost 9 hours) was on medium.
The menus are polished and a handy quest log can keep track of where you're at and what you're to do next (this could have been useful for so many old-school RPGs..) lack of cursor memory is my only complaint with the menus.
Music is excellent, the original soundtrack sounds very reminiscent of earlier JRPGs but with enough technical merit to avoid sounding generic. The story is similarly exceptional- usually I expect these homages to old RPGs to come across more as fanfiction than an original story but Skyborn's writing may even exceed (or at least manage to bypass) limitations of both its peers and forebears. There are no issues with translation here, since the story is originally drawn up in English. Didn't catch any grammatical errors, it just seems also at a high standard of quality and the first hour alone is brimming with excitement. The characters are lively, amusing, and  mature in their actions. Those who dislike the slapstick that is common in more lighthearted RPGs will likely find this title appreciable.
The story takes place in an alternate, very steampunk-inspired universe where there are three races- humans, the winged Skyborn, and the unfortunate half-breeds that are at the bottom of the hierarchy and face violent discrimination from both groups. There is another race to speak of, but I'll get on with things. The heroine, Claret, works at a mechanic shop until she finds herself caught between an escalating conflict between humans and the very powerful Skyborn who are seeking to enslave and decimate the other races. She's a plucky but strong and capable heroine who isn't over-the-top; rather, she reacts very relateably to the unfolding story and does what she can to help. From there the conflict becomes more chaotic and both allies and enemies are not as they may seem. Some entertaining twists along the way.
Flashbacks with gameplay portions and specialized artwork to match add an extra bit of attention to detail in the story and help flesh out the characters. It's not the most original storyline in the world and I wish there were just a bit more character interactions since quite a likeable group is assembled, but it is one of the high points of Skyborn overall.
Now for some of the downsides- this game's standard price is $15 and is about 8 hours long. Almost $2 per hour. Give or take a few hours if you wish to thoroughly explore each of the minor quests and grind out levels for a tough optional boss. That is still a lot to ask for a short title, and especially for a short title with as many old-school sensibilities as this one has. Absolutely worth the time if it's on sale. Even though I loved it, I can really only recommend this title at its full price wholeheartedly to someone who is looking for an old-school indie JRPG that performs exceptionally in its class.

That's the game content itself, but now that I've played this version a bit I can talk about the port.
Honestly, I'm not a fan of this HD version. The game is better off being 4:3 instead of 16:9.
All the CGs are zoomed in on to get them widescreen, and in order to see the whole image you have to hide the text box and scroll back with the mouse wheel.
In addition to that, there's a bunch of options missing from the game menus and keyboard shortcuts that it doesn't tell you about. Things like 'A' for auto mode and 'Q' for going back to the last choice.
The manual tells you about the shortcuts, but you can't remap them in-game.
The original game engine used the same menus and layout as Clannad, which is also on Steam, and I think that version worked better.
This port caters too much to touch screens for my liking, and switching the aspect ratio was a mistake in my opinion.
Bad port aside, this is still my favorite visual novel, and if you're the type of person who can fall in love with fun and quirky characters and get immersed in a lengthy story that drags you through an emotional roller coaster, then this game is for you.

I wasn't expecting much when I started up Skyborn, but was pleasantly surprised almost immediately. It has a very well-developed and likable cast of characters. The combat and game mechanics are just deep enough to make you plan things out, but intuitive enough that you'll know what you're doing right away. I especially enjoyed the Augment system, which allows you to add various effects to your gear and dramatically improve their usefulness. The music is also very well done, enough that I would even be willing to pick up a soundtrack. The story isn't anything spectacular, but it's simple and engaging enough to keep you interested for the entire length of the game (which was about 11 hours, including all of the sidequests). The adjustable difficulty level is also extremely useful, because with a bit of planning and sidequesting, you can become pretty much unstoppable and render most end-game foes meaningless.
All in all, I give this an 8/10, and definitely recommend it for anyone looking for a good retro-style RPG.

Skyborn does a lot of things right and a lot of things wrong. In general I can tentatively recommend buying this game. Best to wait for a sale.
Having said that here is a rundown of things that the game does right, only to squander it.
-The game introduces early on an airship. This is great and makes for a nice start. Only it goes nowhere with this, you can only use it very late in game to travel to old areas and not many at that. Considering the short length of the game, I wonder why it was included at all.
-Tileset and general look of the game is very nice, if you like the RPGmaker. It feels all very cohesive and fitting. Sadly there is very little interaction with the environment. No flavor text when looking through bookshelfs or things like that.
-No random battles is a nice change of pace. In general the combat is well thought out and nuanced. Such a shame then that the game can't be arsed to tell you that. Nearly all mechanics go unexplained, the different dmg sources and how they are dependent on your stats goes unmentioned and the buff mechanic is a huge mess.
The only indicator what buffs/debuffs your characters have are small shifting Icons, which I still haven't completely learned by the end of the game. Though that is still a lot better than what you know about the enemy. You can't check whether your debuff is still active on him, only see once it's applied and it pops out briefly once it fades. If you haven't paid attention for a single turn, you might have missed that your debuffs are gone. Which can mean instant death against the tough optional bosses.
So why recommend it? The story is nice and manages to tell a tale driven by it's characters. Those same characters manage to feel real enough, though I guess that is a matter of taste. So again, a tentative recommendation.

It's a clunky piece of garbage.  I've seen better first year game dev student projects than this "finished" game.  I'll start with the worst of it.
1. A.I. is god awful.  See, all these game designers out there think they're going to be the next god's gift to squad based A.I. teammate shooters, and they all fail.  Some just fail more horribly than others.  The Bureau is one of those hideous fails.  The worst part?  You can't choose to go solo.  You're required to take two more gibbering monkeys on every mission that refuse to listen to anything you say.  Coupled with awful cutscene interruptions that place your team into the worst possible tactical positions before every major firefight and you'll find yourself save-scumming to reload every skirmish until you get a lucky break.  I could write an entire college dissertation on how terrrible the A.I. is.  Basically the entire game is a complete distraction from shooting aliens.  Instead you're trying to prevent your idiot teammates from being killed.  And guess what?  They can't hit anything.  If 100 aliens are killed in a skirmish your main player character has killed 90 of those aliens every single time.  You're literally anchored with two slobbering morons that can't kill more than 10 aliens between them.  I'm not even exaggerating.  The game shows you a statistics screen after every mission blatantly pointing out this fact.
2. The sound / voices could use a lot of work.  The guns all sound ok and feel like they have some power, but the way the voices and conversations were recorded leave much to be desired.  They all sound phony and fake.  You can tell they were recorded flatly in a studio.  The engine doesn't have dynamic volume related to the range of the player, so most every line of dialogue has a constant volume.  It's hard to explain with words, but it's there.  The conversations in the base with the crew are ok, but in the field every spoken phrase feels grossly out of place.  It doesn't help that your A.I. teammates are constantly screaming for healing every 20 seconds, either.
3. There is no base management.  You play as the main character, shuffled from action scenario to action scenario.  You don't struggle to collect and research anything.  You're not scrounging for parts.  The only things you're picking up are ammo packs lying on the ground for whatever random guns that are strewn about in a field mission.  All the tech is doled out systematically as you proceed through missions, the same as any generic run and gun 3rd person shooter, like the Uncharted series.  The fun of choosing where to focus your resources is completely gone, and the most customization the game seems to give you is choosing between a few rudimentary weapons and "backpacks" (aka buffs).  You can change the colors of your idiot squadmates' uniforms, but after that there's nothing else to do in regards to this.
4. There are no "tactics" to speak of.  When you finally get to the shooting bits these involve being surrounded by overpowered enemies with better buffs and guns than you in a rudimentary "speedball" paintball course full of fences, walls, and barriers for no reason other than the game engine is built around cover mechanics.  These firefights involve ordering your A.I. friends to hide behind half-cover walls hopefully avoiding being flanked by enemies, while trying to have the main player character run from ammo drop to ammo drop without being shot.  Yep, that's the difficulty.  You're always out of ammo and every stupid enemy is some kind of ridiculous bullet sponge.  While rising from cover to shoot an enemy you'll have five other ones minimum tearing you to pieces.  Instead of relying on your skills as a player that involve aim, the game pigeons holes you into utilizing the "magic" abilites your team gets for no good reason other than leveling up.  Which leads me to the next part...
5. Abilities.  If you've played Mass Effect you'll see the similarities here, at least, what The Bureau was going for.  As you and your squadmates level up they gain magic alien super powers.  Why?  The game doesn't say.  Each soldier has a magic arm bracelet Pip Boy strapped on, along with a Ghostbuster Proton Pack, to gain telekinetic, shielding, and healing type abilities, because = science.  The game glosses over anything tech related, boiling it down to the bare minimum.  They sucked the fun out of it all.  You don't feel like you earn anything or learn anything about the aliens.  All you need to do is have your guys survive long enough to level up and they gain their abilities right there in the field, while picking up ammunition dropped by dead enemies.  Your abilities come because the plot needs you to have them.  You don't actually have to work for them at all like in other XCOM games.  Uncharted type games do the same thing by refusing to give you a rocket launcher until later, when the plot requries it because a tougher bossfight is on the way.
The game has countless other problems, including shoddy writing basically ignoring any other XCOM game ever made, awful UI controls especially during the firefights, the uncanny valley of humanoid dolls flapping their mouths at each other during cutscenes, and most of all, no sense of dismay or urgency.  You're rushed around from plot device to plot device because the writers have no idea on how to get you there naturally.  Everything is an awful deus-ex-machina trying to avoid painting itself into the corner.  It's like the devs wrote the end of the game and made up the beginning as they went along.  Instead of having a fun 60s style wooden pastiche ala Fallout or All Humans Must Die, it falls flat, tripping over itself the entire way.  The whole game is one giant stumbling block and it never finds its footing.
After reading up on countless other XCOM "sequels" made over the last few decades, I can safely tell you that even on sale, getting the entire thing plus DLC for all of $6 is not even worth it.  If you avoid this game and pretend like it doesn't exist you won't be missing out on anything.  I've been an XCOM enthusiast since the original game and I've been putting off this game until recently.  I finally got it super cheap and went in expecting nothing due to all the other horrible reviews, but don't be fooled.
It could have been an amazing game, but it's just not, no matter how hard you want it to be.  This game is terrible, and trying to hold it steady at $20 here on Steam is the biggest joke of all.

I am very glad that this is not the direction XCOM took for the main games.  But as a side game?  It's not bad.  There are some problems with it, of course, and some shooter conventions that don't really work in XCOM's universe, like ammo and weapons all over the place.  (Particularly later on when you're grabbing enemy weapons to replenish ammo, enemy weapons that are supposed to be self-destructing becuase of lore.)  It is neat seeing more of the XCOM universe, even if this is non-canon.  You can also see the XCOM influences with the tactics and being able to command your team.
As a shooter, it's decent enough.  I know some people have complained about the teammate AI, but I didn't have an issue with them.  There are several unnecessary side missions, which is a dual-edged sword.  And the power ups you can get in the campaign can be very powerful, especially when used together.
All in all, yea.  I'd recommend this game.  On sale, and if you KNOW you're getting a third person shooter, and not a "real" XCOM game.

To paraphrase Denethor of Lord of the Rings, 'You think you are wise, Kan Gao. Yet for all your subtleties, you have not wisdom. Do you think the memories of 'To The Moon' have been wiped clean?'
Weighing in at a meager 90 minutes to complete, 'A Bird Story' clearly failed to shine brilliantly any where nearly as it's predecessor. In honesty, this game was in effect a ponderous, meanderingly minimal interactive 'adventure' that spectacularly failed to deliver.
Yes there was the broody music and the familiar gameplay but the overtly sentimental, forcefully connective tale of a boy who befriends a bird felt overplayed and, frankly, dull. This was not Kes. I felt no love for the daydreaming boy nor could I fathom the fraudulent emphasis of the boy befriending his wounded bird. This was hollow, in terms of gameplay, story and characterisation.
I sensed a genuine love from Gao about this tale, but his bludgeoningly stubborn execution, the narrow scope and, particularly, the awkwardness of shoving a falsified emotional attachments onto the gamer just made me reach for the brown paper bag.
I hope 'Finding Paradise' rekindles the oozingly flambuoyant 'To The Moon' and showcases the talents of Gao better than this ditty. Then I can consign 'A Bird Story' to the digital waste basket and turn a blind eye.

If anything, I wish the character's movement could have been faster; it was a little sluggish but the game tries to compensate by directly transitioning into the important locations so you don't have to constantly walk the same paths with no events occurring. A Bird Story makes some smart choices on how to set up the scenes to convey the story without having to use words.
The stylistic choice of portraying the characters was interesting:
. I'm not sure if this was to achieve a minimal style, but it did seem a little odd.
Art and music are top notch. There's one point where you get to see several overhead scenes, and it's just very pretty and breathtaking at some points.
. The music is playful, beautiful and soulful. It fits perfectly with the sound effects and colours.
If you take the game as an interactive silent film than a typical game, the experience is more enjoyable. If you just care about the gameplay, then this isn't really a game that will entertain you. For me, I don't mind games that can deliver on story and have minimal gameplay, so overall, I had a good experience. Not sure if I'd replay it again anytime soon, but  I'm glad to have purchased this game at the sale price, at least.

Man, oh man, I *DO* love me some Metroid. That said, Axiom Verge really fills that nostalgia void without being cliche, trite or otherwise deniable. It manages to keep its own style while still paying heaps of homage to the classics of my generation. HIGHLY. RECOMMENDED.

Axiom Verge = Metroid - brain-sucking aliens + more guns + existential crises
This is a hell of a game, with classic Metroid exploration and huge bosses. There's a ton of stuff hidden away in the nooks and crannies. The Address Disruptor (glitch gun) is a nice genre-savvy twist. Speaking of twists, there are a few nicely-executed ones in the story, so don't skip the cutscenes... at least until you beat the game once and shoot for a speed run.

This game is incredible.  From the mind of one man, who made all the art, music, story and gameplay, comes one of the best Metroid games I've ever played(my favorite game series, sans Other M).  Now, that's being a bit disingenuous, since Axiom Verge very much adds a lot to the Metroid formula, though makes no bones about where its inspirations initially come from.
Through abilities such as teleportation, the Address Disruptor(a gun that creates NES-era visual data corruption on objects and enemies, similar to if you put an NES cart in wrong), the drone, and other abilities, it expands on the standard 2D Metroid gameplay in a huge way.  The lack of a run button is kind of a bummer, but that's a minor quibble, and the only major gripe is that teleportation requires a double-tap in the direction you want to teleport, which means trying to do this on an analog stick is pretty much luck-based.  I wind up going sideways when I want to go up, up when I want to go sideways far too often, but there's other means of movement that I can resort to to avoid that.
The graphics are incredible.  Using a faux-8-bit style with setpieces and bosses that fill the screen(or beyond!), I would say it is a visual combination of Metroid and H.R. Geiger.  Every single tile and object is covered with minute details, from dents and rust on bosses and enemies, to throbbing veins in organic scenery.  The Rusalki are incredibly unnerving looking, as you'll see as you play the game.  The gross organic look of many objects and enemies mixed with the technological parts of others makes for horrible techno-organic nightmare machines.  Backgrounds and terrain are lovingly detailed, and the special effects are straight-up surprising.  While I've been following the game for a while and thus knew about things like the Address Disruptor's effects, or what a boss death looks like, these things will likely shock a new player with their "oh, right, this is a modern game!" effect.
The weaponry is plenty and varied.  Not all are useful, plenty are gimmicky, but most have their time to shine.  I wound up sticking with the starter weapon for long range, and the Kelver for close up for most of the game, switching to about a half dozen other weapons throughout the game for specific reasons.  At the end I still hadn't found a full half of the total weapon count, so I'm eager to get back in and track them down.
The music is outstanding.  The boss fight themes are all frantic and intense, and the general world exploration themes are fitting to their respective zones.  I am definitely going to buy the soundtrack once it goes on sale.
The story starts off as basically Half-Life 1.  Lab experiment goes wrong, you get teleported to hostile alien world full of horrible death creatures.  Trace is a pretty interesting character whose reactions to things are pretty justified.  The Rusalki, your "narrators", essentially, are alien AI and have different personalities themselves that evolve as the game progresses.  By the end, I was mostly satisfied with the story, and a few sections of the game blew me away(the Hallucination section, in particular, was one of my favorite parts of a game in years).  Athetos, Trace, the Rusalki, they COULD have had more fleshed out stories, but I think it was fine as it was.  There's more to the story in hidden notes and such, possibly a true ending as well?  Not entirely sure, still haven't collected everything as of this review.
Game time clocked in at around 12-13 hours total for a 70% playthrough for me.  I'm the sort to fumble around trying to find secrets though, so an 8-10 hour playthrough wouldn't surprise me, and there's a speedrun achievement for beating it in 4 hours, so there's that.  It's definitely a much longer Metroid game than most Metroids tend to be.
Overall I'd say this was a 10 out of 10.  The only complaint of mine, detailed earlier, is for a single movement ability that works most of the time.  I was constantly exploring new regions and surprised by the variety in terrain, the music is great, very fitting, and only gets better as the game goes on, the gameplay was fun and very varied while providing plenty of options for weaponry, the visuals are some of the best 8-bit style graphics ever made, and the story is perfectly serviceable.  A must-buy if you enjoy Metroid games, or platformers in general!

I really wanted to like this game. I think those are the most popular first words in any review ever; but for me, this was depressingly true. I am a science fiction writer with focus on alien races and combating gender stereotypes and roles, so this game immediately piqued my interest. I even waited until my younger sibling was available so we could play it together, as it looked promising.
The game itself looks beautiful. You may have heard in the reviews of the "rain sequence" -- and let me tell you, it's every bit as amazing as it's been chalked up to. The art is phenomenal -- the music is enchanting -- it all WORKS in the world. It shows future, but grit and sadness, and it's GOOD and it WORKS.
But here's where the cons come -- the biggest one being, sadly, the downfall of this game. Have you ever played Broken Age? Did Broken Age, ever, at any moment, annoy you, even slightly? If the answer is, "Nope, not for a second!" then you may like Void And Meddler. If the answer is anything more than "NEVER", you will not like Void And Meddler. Void And Meddler is Broken Age on acid. It is a point and click game, and the focus of the game is getting the main character's "memories" back by clicking on items and adding them to your inventory. That's fine and all, but unlike Broken Age, where there was a singular "interact" button, this game has four. FOUR interact buttons. Your buttons are, as close as I can guess from my gameplay, "look", "grab", "use", and "speak about". Sometimes you specifically need to grab something to add it to your inventory. Sometimes you need to look at it first. Sometimes you need to use it and speak about it BEFORE you can grab it. This means that EVERY. SINGLE. ITEM. in this ENTIRE game needs to be interacted with FOUR times MINIMUM before your character decides they'll like to pick it up -- and sometimes, you can't interact with some items in the way you need to until AFTER a certain thing has happened, meaning you need to revisit certain items. I spent over an hour JUST doing "look", "grab", "use", and "speak about" on all the items I'd see. Items also aren't clearly outlined from the background, so you end up combing through an area and missing the one thing you needed simply because it was dark and hidden.
The next issue is that this is one of those games that advance the longer you play it. You have to go through to all the areas, open up new dialogue options with new characters, grab new things, then come back AROUND and get more little pieces of story. A game that does this right either keeps you in so much suspense you have to finish the game, or gives you an interesting draw. Unfortunately, Void And Meddler has absolutely nothing to draw you in but the art. Sadly, a game is not a comic book -- it cannot ride on art alone.
My final gripe with this game is the main character. I hate her. (And I'm also disappointed that, as far as I could tell, she appeared to be gender-specific and slightly stereotypical when this game promised the death of genders.) Now, don't get me wrong; I love mean, harsh, dark characters. I write them. My icon is Midna, for God's sake.
I know that kind of hinges on who she is as a person, but characters, especially in games like this, need CLEAR motiviations and CLEAR personality traits to make them more believable and understandable -- subtleties can come in later. I understand that she's forgotten herself, but for Christ's sake. She flipflops on opinions, first acting as if she couldn't care less about herself and the world around her, then pretending it all really matters and she needs the help of a character around her. It may have been what the writers were going for in this game, but it doesn't work. It's one thing to have a character that doesn't remember who they are and does things, not knowing why, for enjoyment or sentimentality that they recognize but do not fully understand yet, and it's another thing to have a character just do things with no clear motivation at all. You cannot have a unclear story, motivation, AND character.
You MUST give clarity in one area of a story in order to draw the audience in. This was just a failure in story telling.
The game, however, is beautiful. The fourth wall breaking is hilarious. This could have had so much potential. Unfortunately, the crux for me was the four interaction system. After an hour of it, I couldn't take it anymore and uninstalled the game -- and it's RARE that I uninstall a game after only a few hours play.

Pros:
+ Great Modding community; Allowing you to actually be historically accurate and add a swastikas in the game, Highly recommend Kasierriech mod and Millennial Dawn mod
+ Fun alternate history paths; How would the war change if France went Communist and joined the USSR's "defensive" faction instead of Great Britains? Make Turkey into a golbal superpower by seizing European colonies in Africa. What if the Republicans won the Spanish Civil War? The possibilites are endless.
+ Easy to learn mechanics; The vibrant HOI4 (Hearts of Iron IV) Youtube community helped me understand the core mechanics and what exactly to do within a day or two, unlike Victoria 2 wich required a college degree to understand.
+ Fun with friends; One time, I played as Hungary and reformed a Fascist Austria-Hungary while my two other friends went Fascist France and Nazi Germany. We accedentially started a war with the USSR and had over 1000 divisions at our doorstep. That War created so many memes and memories that we still talk about today.
Cons:
- Stupid AI; Allies will fail to organize and actually assit you in the war effor, most of the time you won't see your troops fighting along side an ally unless the two allied countries are very close together (Looking at you Great Britain).

One instance I had Germany declare war on me even though I was in the Axis, breaking the game. Allow me to note that this is a very minor complant, as most of my playthroughs have been clean of bugs
- Bad DLC policy; Paradox is known world wide for it's ♥♥♥♥♥♥ DLC prices; DLC are extremely overpriced but add a fun aspect to the game that adds more hours to the experience
Bottom line is Hearts of Iron IV is a game I will countine to play and will anticipate it's coming DLCs and updates. For those that enjoy a good Grand Strategy Game, love the history of this bloody era, and have the patience to understand its mechanics, then I HIGHLY recommend this game for you.

The game definitely lives up to its reputation of being reminiscent of old-school entries in the Final Fantasy and Mana series of games, but visual effects and in game interfaces do also have a modern aesthetic.  You may not want to pay full price considering the short length and lack of replay value, but this is definitely a good choice for any real fan of the genre, and a fantastic snag if found on sale!

When the touchy subject of RPG Maker commercial games comes up, I am not one to judge or deny the legitimacy of RPG Maker games as a commercial product. I have seen some fantastic games made on the engine like To The Moon, and I have seen absolute garbage like the Laxius Force and Millenium Quest series being put up for sale. My interest for this title was raised when the discussion on RPG Maker commercial games mentioned Deadly Sin and its sequel as an example of good RPG Maker games, and one of the studio's earlier titles was this.
This game is a short story set in a steampunk fantasy world where the plot involves Claret Spencer, a mechanic who is about to get entangled in a pivotal racist conspiracy involving the Skyborn, a race of magic users with Dragon-wings, Humans, the ancient and near-extinct Fey, and Half-Breeds, the result of a Skyborn and a Human mating. The story is really focused in scope, goes through predictable motions and doesn't do enough world-building to be compelling. However, what it does have as far as story goes is quite competently written, and the characters in the story are fairly consistent in their actions.
The gameplay has a few unique twists to the bog-standard turn-based RPG and equipment system in that armor doesn't  directly come into play for damage-reduction, but instead, they increase various stats depending on type. In a way, the type of armor used determines the type of build for each character. The combat system is a standard Conditional Turn Based system but with a twist to keep things interesting, and encourages players to use more support skills, and it's the Threat system. Characters with the most threat will be targeted for single-target attacks, dealing damage and killing enemies will increase the threat of that character for the duration of the battle. This system allows for the utility of skills that can transfer threat from one character to another, or to gather an enormous amount of threat for one's self. This combination of systems allows for a lot of min maxing to be employed, which is pretty refreshing for an RPG Maker game. There is also an augment and forging system that allows players to further customise their gear, which is good.
What is not so good, however, is the unintuitive way of how the stats are used and how they are never explained ingame. See, the Strength stat determines the damage dealt by regular weapon attacks regardless of type, Intelligence determines the effectiveness of special skills, and Agility merely determines the Speed, Critical and Evade chance. While this would make sense normally, there is also the idea that there are 3 different types of damage ; Physical, Magic and Tech and one would easily be forgiven for thinking that Strength, Intelligence and Agility would determine the effectiveness of Physical, Magical and Tech attacks respectively. This leaves for some results that just plain doesn't make sense, like Corwin's (The designated mage/healer.) magical blast weapon damage that is determined by his strength instead of Intelligence. The other issue with the combat and gameplay is that on Normal, it is either too easy, or you get wiped out real quickly, with no battles that provide an evenly-matched struggle, and the being wiped-out part only ever happens if you don't do the side-quests before the point of no return. Once you did all the side-quests before the endgame, then the endgame becomes ridiculously easy again,
Another bugbear of the gameplay of this game is that very few of the objects in the game can be interacted with with any measure, which brings us back to the point of the game being very focused and limited in scope to the point of its own detriment. It would have been nice if there are more props that give you flavour text, added an effect to your party, or can be interacted with to produce a sound effect. (Piano jingle, anyone?) As an RPG afficionado, I can tell you that most RPGs offer an immense amount of non-plot-relevant interactivity, which goes a long way with the immersion.
Another issue is that there aren't enough variety in the enemy mobs to keep things interesting. All the enemy mobs have a role that is theoretically mirrored by one of the characters', and very few of the skills that enemies have are unique to the enemies, as a result, most enemies are very predictable, and thus very easy to deal with, even enemies with the ability to OHKO half your party. That said, the abilities that you do gain throughout the game are very useful and are a nice change from the generic damage ones that plagues most RPG Maker games. I also do like the design of the dungeons themselves which strayed a lot from the conventional square-like design that even commercial RPGs from the 90's suffer from, this results in a lot of the dungeons and natural cave systems looking very very organic, which is a great plus for this game.
The strongest point of this game though, is the music. The soundtrack is very well-mastered with a lot of nice orchestral stings and swelling chords befitting of a fantasy RPG. It is no Falcom Sound Team JDK, but as far as indie RPG Maker projects go, the fact that the soundtrack isn't a set of crappy generic MIDIs alone is something I can appreciate a lot.
So the final verdict is, do I recommend this game? And the answer is unfortunately, nope. Don't get me wrong, I did enjoy this game, and as far as RPG Maker games go, this is one of the better ones. However, with how limited and focused the scope of the game is, there is not enough world-building and lore to keep the player invested in the story and its characters, and the paltry offering with regards to interactivity and side-quests certainly didn't help it. Ultimately, the biggest drawback of this game is that it is not ambitious enough for the premise it presents, and maybe if the combat system is given more depth, if there are more character and story arcs, and if there is a less-linear progression through the story, then it might be worth the $15 asking price. As it stands, I cannot really recommend this game, outside of at least a 50% off sale, unless you really like RPG Maker games.

After playing Lost Planet 1 and 2 on Xbox 360 back in the day, I was shocked to see that Lost Planet 3 is waaaay different from its predecessor. The game definitely flows better in my humble opinion than the prequels, but sadly I'm way too occupied with other video games to complete this one... For what it's worth, it's a pretty good title, and highly underrated. I don't think I've even scratched a good chunk of the story - mostly been doing side quests. The story is kinda predictable if you've seen it all before; however it is very well told, especially with the voice acting. I'm not too fund of the anime-like voice acting in Lost Planet 1 & 2, and this one seems very western.
Since I never actually got around to beating the game (possibly a thing to do in the future), I'm not sure about how fast paced the game is later on, but from what I've done, and with the equipment and upgrades I've acquired the game is kinda slow... It's definitely a huge world, but for what the prequels had back in the day was that going through levels didn't feel too much like a chore. This game wants you to go to places, activate stuff, do some fetch quests, and yada yada... As for the previous games it was get through the level - I prefer that in games like these.
I would say Lost Planet 3's single player is very comparable to Red Faction: Guriella and Armageddon, but in the lore of Lost Planet. Some of the creatures even have the same weaknesses, but I also found that those creatures were easier to defeat in the previous titles - again, slow paced.
I unforunately never got to play the multiplayer since the online is practically dead, but from what I've seen on YouTube it looked kinda fun. No way revolutionary I'll tell ya that much, but fun nontheless.
If you find this game on a sale, I'd say jump on it! If you have 'nothing' to play, I'd say give this a shot. The mechanic's are fluid, the story telling is great, but the multiplayer is dead.

Lost Planet 3 is somewhat within the same vein as Dead Space, if Dead Space were more focused on Aliens and not on Space Zombies or what have you. Jim Peyton sets out to E.D.N. III to find his own fortune as a freelance contractor taking a contract from NEVEC to supply for his Wife and Child back on Earth. Using your rig, your own wits, and the weapons you carry about with you, you are tasked to survive on the inhospitable planet of E.D.N. III.
Lost Planet 3 has quite a lot of issues, however the majority of them are easily fixed, such as the keyboard control issues from being poorly ported. With solid music, enjoyable gameplay (if you like the Lost Planet series) and an interesting atmosphere, let's get into the pros and cons of this, shall we?
Pros:
- Solid gunplay, being akin to that of the first Lost Planets with the run and gun style, as well as dodging to mitigate any damage.
- Extremely varied arsenal, with a multitude of interesting weapons to choose from. From the Assault Rifle to a rapid firing Nailgun, there's quite a lot of variety to go along with.
- Well designed mecha, being based around being a utility platform instead of an actual unit to fight in, whilst also being an intimidating powerhouse.
- Excellent music choices whilst exploring, allowing you to set the music to specific soundtracks whilst in the rig.
- Decent storyline with a relatable protagonist in Jim Peyton. Sending messages back and forth to his wife about their son, his job, and answering her pleas of safety and reassurance whilst working in hazardous areas.
- The ability to converse with NPC's as well as find audio logs and text logs for worldbuilding experiences.
- Non-linear exploration.
- Interesting RPG elements.
- Ammo conservation being a key point within this game, juggling between your primary and secondary weapons, as well as your infinite ammunition pistol to handle small grunts within the game to conserve ammunition.
- SOME Decent boss fights, being akin to that of the original Lost Planets. SHOOT THE GLOWING ORANGE SPOT.
- A plethora of interesting Akrid to fight, some of which being familiar faces from the original games.
Cons:
- Horrible controls for keyboard and mouse that don't work correctly off the bat, however can be fixed in a matter of a minute. Regardless of whether this can be fixed, it is still inexcusable.
- No truly random or hazardous storms upon EDN III, allowing for you to get out of your mech and traipse around in the blurry and white overworld.
- Some boss fights are extremely time consuming, and seem as though they were implemented to lengthen the players playtime with the game. Whilst none of the bosses are BAD, some of them just aren't exceptionally well done.
- Extremely underplayed cover system, which almost does not belong within the game and relies heavily on a specific enemy to actually have any real utility.
- Extremely stoic protagonist outside of cutscenes and videos to his wife. Essentially wandering the wastes and surviving death defying stunts with the expression of ":|" the entire time.
- 30FPS low-res cutscenes unless you have the hi-res cutscene DLC, making it abundantly apparent that this was a rushed port of the game.
Overall: 7/10. If you're coming to Lost Planet 3 expecting the same gameplay and style as the original Lost Planets, you're going to have a bad time. Come to this game expecting a somewhat darker atmosphere, non-linear exploration, and overall satisfying gunplay/weaponry. This game has a LOT which it could've improved upon, even though most of the flaws can be easily rectified, they are flaws present within the game which makes them inexcusable. Lost Planet 3 would have done better as its own stand alone title, instead of carrying the expectations of the Lost Planet series upon its shoulders.
Worth $25? Hellllllll no. Whilst the game is enjoyable, and I found it charming, it is awash with flaws and so on. Wait for it to go on sale and then purchase it.

That was an incredible ride, and the more I think about it, the more I'm amazed by the initial camoflauge done to the plot and game's contents. The plot gets deep and dark, and if you haven't started crying, you imagine that it's good, but not that heartbreaking. But then things come crashing down...and you realize that it wasn't just a dating sim with pigeons.
No...it was a dating sim about BIRDS. All KINDS of birds--in fact, ALL DIFFERENT KINDS OF BIRDS!
10/10 would tear up again (because of the sheer diversity in avian culture).

I can't believe the day has come when I can unironically recommend a video game about dating pigeons, but to be fair I did also unironically recommend Euro Truck Simulator 2.
Hatoful Boyfriend (if you're wondering, "hatoful" could be read as "heartful" or "hurtful"; and also triples as a pun to the Japanese kanji for pigeon) shows that no matter how silly the premise, you can still make a great story out of it. What originally started out as a visual novel about dating pigeons, eventually becomes a visual novel about dating pigeons with deep and complex personalities.
The game (or should I say the visual novel) itself is nothing complex, the closest thing to gameplay here is making a decision. Though your decision will ultimately decide who you choose to get close with and how the game ends.
Speaking of the story, it is quite entertaining. The writing is fantastic, and all of the characters have their own lovable quirks, in fact the route you take can vastly affect the mood of the story. After going on a certain route, you can do the hidden route which unless you've gotten all the ending (which includes both the normal and true ending for every character) you won't see the epilogue. Getting all of the ending means you have to read through a lot of the things you've read before, there is a fast forward button; but sometimes new dialogues could appear in a scene that you expected to play as usual.
Overall Hatoful Boyfriend is an entertaining visual novel about dating pigeons...

Mediocrity, thy name is VITATIO 2.
You know those game/contraption thingies where there's a length of curved wire attached to a base, and a rod that you have to navigate around the curves from one end of the contorted wire to the other, and if you touch it with the rod then it sounds a buzzer? Well, this is essentially the video game of that, but with pick-ups and achievements.
Starting at one point on a 2D, maze-like track, you must use your cursor to guide a shape through the course without touching the walls. Collect three stars along harder, out of the way routes if you like, or just go straight for the slightly less troublesome exit, if you prefer. That's the game in its totality... and by "totality", I mean eight short stages.
There is some skill involved in having a steady hand and staying straight and true, but one big gripe I have with the game (aside from getting an irreversible black screen whenever I tried to expand the windowed mode to full) is it felt as though the collision detection was a bit dodgy. Maybe it was just me and my twitchy trotters, but I could damn near swear the game said I failed while I was actually dead centre of the track. I wondered if the mouse sensitivity would apply to the in-game sensitivity too, and sure enough, it did. And even with it cranked all the way down and me having to practically fling my mouse across the desk to get the cursor to move a single pixel, I was still failing on occasions when it seemed I completely in the clear.
This isn't a bad game really, it's just thoroughly middling. The graphics and presentation are minimal at best, the audio underwhelming (and maybe even feels a little out of place in a way), and the gameplay seems like a test of patience more than anything else. If this were the free Flash game that it seems like it should be, then it would be a neat little distraction, but as a product for you to spend your money on, much like the walls within the game, I'd probably give this one a miss.

I want to be able to recommend this title...I just can't.
I love the XCOM series but Bureau feels so off and disjointed.
The premise is interesting but it begs the question of why its never mentioned in any other title in the series or why humanity hasn't -radically- changed with the introduction of alien technology that is clearly lightyears ahead of what we had in the 1960's.
XCOM has always had a kind of magical approach to technology in that we can adapt and utilize alien technology, of which we know nothing, to our own ends after a few hours of poking at it and that can be overlooked in a near-future type scenario with XCOM or a future scenario like XCOM 2 but when you're dealing with a time period where computers had less actual computational power than a 1998 dumb phone, it seems really off.
Most of that can be overlooked but the gameplay really can't. It's a lot of slow jogging around punctuated by very clearly outlined combat areas. Combat itself fluctuates between overwhelmingly hectic and sheer boredom. The weapon variety is incredibly sad and there’s nothing to really tell you what weapon is more useful against what targets. You’d think the laser weapons would be inherently better but they’re actually not. The weapons also feel like toys, with none of them giving you a solid report to create the feeling of an actual weapon.
You can’t carry much ammunition (why this is never gets explained) so you will -always- run out during a fight. This might be ok if you weren’t having to semi-pause the game every few seconds and tell your squad mates what to do. As it is, it’s usually a mad scramble for ammunition. You are invariably the most valuable member of the team but your attention is mainly devoted to babysitting your cohorts so they don’t die.
Combat just feels awkward and sticky but they tried to fix it by adding some grease but they just dolloped the grease on a few spots so they’re now overly slick without the rest of the problem being handled.
Your character must have excellent cardiovascular health because you spend a lot of goddamn time jogging around. Getting from place to place is annoyingly slow, especially in the base where you will often be asked to run and talk to so-and-so or push that button or pickup this thing. There’s bits of paper scattered around to read to get more backstory and audio logs (because reasons) but if you want to read the papers you have to stop whatever you’re doing and the audio logs are centered on the actual tape itself so if you walk away you stop hearing them which means you have to stand there and wait for them to finish if you want to listen.
There’s no sense of pacing or flow in the game. Maps are clearly broken up into combat zones, each easily identifiable at a glance, and “point of no return” transitions are as smooth as a gravel driveway, consisting of some chest high wall or embankment you have to jump down. Moves that enemies will make are clear once you’ve observed them for a bit and even when being flanked or shot, enemies tend to not want to respond. The only reason a sniper rifle doesn’t dominate the game is the low supply of ammunition because even if they’re behind cover, aliens almost always have their head sticking out.
A lot of this sounds like nitpicks and it probably is but all together it just feels slow and unpleasant.
Customization is nil. You can create the same carbon copy of you to follow you on missions and pick their class which gives you a couple skills to choose from. You get “backpacks” (and no, what they are or what they do is never actually explained) which give you some kind of bonus however the bonus is never quantified so when you get two packs that do roughly the same thing you then get to guess which one does it better. Weapons can’t be customized, nor can skills to any meaningful degree.
You have missions but there are precious few to actually do and the ones you do actually go on feel so bland and same-y that they’re actively boring.
Technically the game is competent but there are still issues with the camera being very comfortable pointed in a certain direction and really resisting being moved. Characters often start lines of dialogue assuming you have a certain piece of information when you don’t so you’re left wondering what they’re talking about until you accidentally bump into someone who fills you in.
The combat AI isn’t atrocious but it definitely feels like herding bricks. Getting stuck in a corner or vaulting forward when you meant to go sideways is a frequent occurrence. They were clearly shooting for a Mass Effect vibe here but managed to get none of the fluidity and speed that made Mass Effect combat so fun.
Overall there’s no one thing that sinks the game but the overall experience of so many “meh” elements comes together to create a lukewarm experience at best. It’s like a bowl of pasta with too little sauce; it isn’t actively unpleasant but it’s not enjoyable, you can get through it but after a while it just starts feeling like work and what held your interest after the first couple of bites now just feels bland and uninteresting.

This game would be a very average FPS, but manages to pull off a few good tricks to lift itself above mediocrity.
Most of these tricks owe to a nod to Dark Souls. Levels are nicely interlinked, if linear, but more importantly, the death system helps you get a sense of affinity for your character, and makes you want to survive and plan rather than quickload. Death results in you spawning as another randomly generated survivor, with a need to hunt down your previously zombified self if you want to reclaim your backpack. The game puts some effort into giving each new survivor a unique character, from their own outfit and gender down to an ID card with their age, occupation, and stat tracking of how long they've survived and their individual score. As a result, you tend to get the same involvement as with a squad member in X-COM - after you've struggled through a few hours as the same character, you really want to see how long you can last.
It's important the game generates tension this way, since combat itself is fairly simplistic and where the similarities with Dark Souls end. For a large part of the game the default cricket bat will serve you well, to the extent that guns are largely unneccessary. This has a knock-on effect of you saving ammo to the point it's scarcity isn't an issue in the later stages of the game, which is a shame. This isn't a hard game, but the desire to stay alive rather than save-zerg helps maintain suspense, and it is certainly possible to meet a swift end if you make a mistake.
Visually, the game has some interesting locations, and whilst it's not going to be picking up any awards for next-gen graphics or push a high-end PC to its limits, it looks suitably atmospheric. I've seen some reports of crashing, but on my vanilla rig (i7/9700) I've yet to experience one. The audio gets the job done, with the usual zombie moans alerting the player and some good player voice acting reflecting their terror after caving in a zombie's head.
In terms of the negatives, a uPlay account being needed is an obvious one, but not too much of a pain to set up if you don't have one already. The plot is rather scattered and implausible, with your character unswervingly doing what they're told even if it flies in the face of common sense or survival instinct, and not helped by the questions raised by the player character changing but the NPCs treating them as the same person. Given the alternative of a single character with a quicksave/load function, though, it's a worthwhile tradeoff. Multiplayer was dropped for the port, but it wasn't that great in the first place, and there are many better multiplayer zombie games out there.
This is basically a solid 20 hours or so of atmospheric, single-player FPS gaming. Not a AAA title, but a worthwhile experience at the price tag.

I love zombie games...of all sorts.  Left4Dead, Dying Light, State of Decay, Dead State, Dead Rising, etc, etc.  So when I heard ZombiU (a game I had never played) was coming out on other consoles after being a WiiU exclusive, I was excited, and bought it on day one. During game play, glitches abound.  Hits often don't register, prompts to execute zombies while on the floor are ignored, and things like that.
Then the game crashed right at a cutscene on the top of the London tower.  Disgusted, I decided to take a break from it. Let's be honest, Zombi is just a quick cash grab from Ubisoft to make some dosh this summer, so you should not expect an amazing port. So what did they do? They took a WiiU exclusive game and ported it to others platforms. Basically, you are playing a zombie game where death is permanent. You die, you loose all the stuff your character was holding and you start from scratch with another character. It's a cool concept, it reminds me of Diablo II where if you died, you were starting from scratch and you had to get your stuff back.
The gameplay consists of looting areas, fighting the zeds with your melee weapons or fire weapons, and of course, do the quests your being told to do. Talking about weapons, there is a nice variety of weapons like MP5,UMP, AK, silenced pisol, pistol, shotgun, M1014, crossbow etc... . To help you in your looting you have a scanner that tells you the locations of loot in your area, reveals code for numpads, reveals if an infected has some loot on it. That feature on WiiU was done with the gamepad, but here it's everything on one screen, just like all the gamepad feature in fact. Since we have no wiiu gamepad, all the stuff is done via one screen, same goes for the map that is on the bottom right corner. So when it comes to immersion and all, you could say that the WiiU is superior in that point. The main issue about the gameplay is that we have WAY TOO MUCH ressources. Seriously, you have a really big arsenal of ammunition.  There are so much ammunitions to find, that I found myself just not caring in some areas at some point because I knew in the safehouse I had enough to keep feeding my trigger friendly fingers.
The story is pretty much meh. Another zombie infection where you'll try to find a cure or a vaccine and get the hell ouf of there with the same old clichés that you've seen a hundred times either in moves or in other games. I guess the cool thing in the story is that you get to see a zombie eating a child. The main story is kinda short as well. I've completed the game in 9 hours and I could have beaten it faster if I didn't have so much trouble to find the 7 Dee's letters. Talking about those letters, they are just there to do some padding and try to increase the length of the game artificially. At least, if you are a good explorer, you can get some of them in advance on your first run and won't have to do too much back tracking.
The port in itself isn't very exceptionnal. You got FOV settings, resolutions, vsync and that is it. At least, the frame rate is completely uncapped. Overall, the game is running fine, but there are some areas where the frame rate will just drop from 125fps to 45fps in just a matter of second. I didn't experienced frame drops too much but it was happening often in the roof of the London Tower and the turret areas near Buckingam. The game isn't looking very good and it has some physics issues with the zombies.
Overall, this game is okay, I had fun playing it and I'll probably go back to it at some point.
