A brief interactive story (about one hour from title to credits) created by Kan Gao, and the spiritual successor to To The Moon. It's kind of odd that the same person made both games, since To The Moon is a throughly amazing experience, while A Bird Story...isn't.
A Bird Story is told without text or dialogue of any kind, purely through actions and expressions. It follows an elementary school-age boy, whose parent[s]/guardian[s] are frequently out of the house (presumably at work). He gets picked on at school and doesn't have many friends, so he's a lonely kid, until he saves an injured bird from a badger, at which point the boy and the bird become inseparable. After this, a large part of the game focuses on their friendship: he tries to teach the bird how to fetch paper airplanes, he brings it in to show and tell, they eat ice cream, etc.
My problems with A Bird Story are not the story or subject matter, nor is it the wordless style of storytelling (a concept that I actually quite like). The problems are twofold: the first is that it makes me feel unintelligent. That's not to say that I feel like the smartest person in the room 99% of the time - it's that I feel like I should understand some deeper meaning or symbolism behind some of the moments in the game, and the fact that I don't makes me feel embarassed.
Why did the kid jump off his balcony and use an umbrella to slow his descent, as opposed to just taking the elevator? How did the kid know that the blue bird is the brown bird's mate? Why are they on a giant paper airplane going from floating island to floating island? Are they looking for the blue bird? Are they looking for the brown bird's friends or family? When the veterinarian and the teacher have the kid cornered on the cliff. why and how did he escape on the giant paper airplane? Why is he face to face with a faceless clone of himself, and why is that clone sealing all of the doors in the hallway? Does the kid have some sort of deep, dark secret? (spoiler alert: no)
The entire story is also told in a dream-like way, with areas flowing into one another - bedroom doors open to forests, said forests lead directly to classrooms, living rooms appear in the middle of playgrounds, etc. I guess this helps give the game a sense of child-like whimsy, which is cute, but it clashes with some moments that are clearly meant to be serious (see: the teacher and vet on the cliff). The overall confusion as to what's going on severely hampers the game's emotional impact; it's difficult to be invested in what happens to the boy, the bird, and their friendship when you're still trying to work out whether the story as a whole is supposed to be a dream or in the kid's imagination.
The second problem is that there's virtually no interaction. A Bird Story very clearly wants to play itself, with you, the "player", along for the ride, instead of being an active participant. What little interaction there is is so brief and trivial you're left wondering why there's even any interaction to begin with. A big chunk of the interactions are simply pressing two arrow keys simultaneously. There's exactly one scene of stealth where you have to sneak past the guard in the boy's apartment complex (which doesn't allow pets) without the guard spotting the bird.  The most engaging sequence of events goes like this: enter apartment. Enter bedroom. Unpack bookbag. Go to kitchen. Get bread for bird. Go to balcony. Tear up bread for bird. Go inside and to bathroom. Pick up bowl. Fill bowl with water. Bring filled bowl outside to bird. Watch five minutes of the boy and bird being friends, which ends with the boy putting the bird in his backpack and jumping off the balcony with his umbrella. Press left or right to steer the umbrella during descent for two seconds (that's not a lorem ipsum, it really does last about two seconds) before landing on the ground.
The best way for a game to get the player engrossed in the story is to help them feel like they are contributing - like they are an active participant. Say what you will about Gone Home, but it did a good job of helping you play detective - you, as Katie, were the one going through the house, piecing together the mystery of what happened to your sister and her relationship. To The Moon was also light on interaction, but it had enough - even though Watts and Rosalene were the main characters, you were the one guiding them through the memories, and the (incredibly well-written) banter between the two made them feel like you knew them, like they were real people, people with whom you enjoyed spending time.
A Bird Story has none of this. Whereas I, a fairly stoic man in his mid-20's, can't keep from tearing up everytime he hears "Everything's Alright," my reaction when the credits started rolling on A Bird Story was basically, "oh. Neat. I guess that was cute. I'm sure glad I got it in a bundle, though." I wasn't expecting something as good or as impactful as To The Moon, but I obviously would have preferred something better than what I got.

Summary:  A polished, thoroughly inspired metroidvania experience which delivers to on all fronts.  If you're into this genre or have a craving for a game filled with exploration, powerups, and rewarding backtracking, then look no further.
Pros:
-- Do you know what metroidvania is?  This is a near-perfectly executed game if you're into the genre.
-- Challenging gameplay (you must set it to hard for the true experience!!!)
-- Fantastic weaponry, powerups, and upgrades do what you hope they would:  expand your abilities and open up new areas for exploration.
--  I especially liked that your upgrades didn't suffer from the "grapple hook" phenomenon where the only thing you can do with your tools is use them on tiles specifically marked (like the grapple hook tiles from the Metroid games).  The game probably won't stump you completely with the platforming puzzles, but it won't make it stupidly obvious with grapple hook/power bomb tiles.
-- Great, difficult level design will have you praying for save points.  Really satisfies your urge to explore and backtrack.  There are scripted sequences, and often times when you're going through a new level that you'll have sections between save points you'll have to retry many times until you figure out how to tackle the enemies.
-- Disturbing bio-mechanical themes (think Geiger without all the sex).
Cons:
-- The color palette was often abrasive and muddled to me.  There were times when I couldn't distinguish background from foreground/boundary tiles.  This isn't a deal-breaker, but I would love to see someone mod this particular aspect of the game.  The concept of the art is great, just not the color...in my humble opinion :)

Was expecting something that looked like NES Metroid; not something that played like it. Controls are unresponsive and awkward and there's no dual-stick option, which is ridiculously anachronistic for any side-scrolling shooter released in 2015.
Only two bosses in and I'm also thoroughly unimpressed with the boss design. The first boss is just a generic bullet-hell spammer, while the second boss might as well be from a rhythm game. Both follow the formula of getting gradually faster as you tediously chip away at their health 0.5% at a time. The second boss also appeared to be glitched, as ducking under the high bullets only worked about half the time. This meant jumping over the high bullets, which the timing doesn't seem to realistically allow once the boss is at its fastest.
Coupled with the damage knockback and maybe only 200ms of immunity after taking damage, there's no recovering after you inevitably get hit. Outside of that boss battle, the knockback also has a tendency to send you through doors and, upon reentering the room you were just kicked out of, the enemy who knocked you back is often sitting on the door and instantly depletes your remaining health.
Art is fantastic, soundtrack is pretty decent (although the bass mix is ridiculous, turn down your sub before playing unless you enjoy head-throbbing migraines), and the concept is solid. I just wish its dev had put as much thought in to the game's controls and boss design as he did towards original weapons and powerups. Instead of an homage to the best bits of the NES, this game is currently a slavish recreation of everything that sucked about that era of gaming.

Dishonored is a stealth-action game with a dash of magic. You play as Corvo Attano, the royal guard which sets out on a revenge-seeking quest after the queen was assasinated, in order to avenge her and save her daughter from her kidnappers. Are you tired of games directing your path and blocking you off from exploring the world? Well, Dishonored is the perfect game for you. It's open world, and it encourages you to take different paths other than the main road, but you can if you wish. The game also lets the player decide if they want to play stealthily or paint Dunwall in red with the blood of royals and guards. A great strength of this game is that Corvo is not pre-ordained to be a mass murderer. The entire game can be completed without killing a single person, so guards can be avoided or knocked unconscious, and non-lethal options can be found for assassination targets if the player wishes to opt for that instead.
Dishonored has nine missions, and they are all very distinct. You’ll attend a society gala in disguise, scale a bridge, escape from prison, wander through flooded slums and stalk across rooftops. You'll take part in a duel, carry an unconscious man through a gauntlet of enemies and decide whether or not to become a torturer. Each mission is designed as a sandbox, allowing players to utilise whatever approach they want. The beauty of Dishonored is that taking your time and exploring the game rewards the player instead of giving you a time limit. You can collect runes and bone charms, which help you upgrade your gear, making you an almost over-powered badass. A minor complaint regarding that, though, is that in some situations, your enemies, no matter how many, stand no chance against you. If you're like me and reach the point where nothing can be upgraded anymore and you're full on everything, you're invincible, which can cause some players to get bored. I myself don't, but I can see that some people get bored when they're practically gods.
There are also different endings, which are tailored by how you play the game, so if you kill everyone and show no mercy, the NPCs will treat you poorly and you will have a killer reputation, resulting in the bad ending. On the other hand if taking revenge isn't about killing everything in your path, you can get the good ending, which makes Dishonored an interesting game worth replaying. A complaint would be that the endings are unsatisfying. The game just ends. You do get an ending scene, but after all the hard work to gain all the runes and bone charms, the way the game ends doesn't do it for many players including myself. Aside from that, the gameplay itself was a unique experience which should be tried out by as many people as possible, which is why I give Dishonored a 9/10.

TL;DR : This game is aesthetically pleasing, some puzzles/situations with more than one way to solve (though some are harder to solve than others), will make you pratically work for the  solutions, and has some nice music references (there's a robot named Goo that spouts some Sonic Youth lyrics). If you are a fan of, let's say, Gerard Way's style of story telling, you'll like this.
Now, for a bit more in depth of a review, lemme just list the cons right of the bat. You have to comb pratically every inch of every screen (area) to find interactables. Solutions to puzzles will not always be obvious; you'll probably spend a lot of your time trying to figure out what item combines with which. It took me a good amount of times to figure out what the hell I need to do just to progress or even to get certain achievements. This is the first episode of this series (at least only the first episode at the time) and it definitely feels like the pilot episode of a show, except you can interact with it. I don't know particularily if there are any decent walkthroughs for this game rn, but when I intially picked this up, I had no help at all. I had to stumble my way through the game. Another issue some people may have is with the main character, Fyn. They're extremely apathetic. Like, to the point of commiting several crimes and having no regrets and no emotional reaction to the outcomes as long as it means they get what they need out of the situation. In that regards, you can sort of say that it is a commentary on how apathetic the player is towards the consequences in-game to a decision they may make in a game. They could care less as long as it progresses the story or game. (There are sort of two acts in the first episode that I have a bit of a bone to pick with. Once you complete the first act, you wake up in the second act and lose just about all your items from the first act, which I find quite frustrating.)
However, this game is ♥♥♥♥ing beautiful, even for a pixel game. The effects are great and it feels very immersive. The setting is clearly dystopian, yet the neon-glowing cyberpunk feel of the enviroment kinda breaks through the grime of the dystopia to give this bright visual that makes it look beautiful. Main character wise, this game perfectly captures what it's like to be a dissociative (20-something?), night owl, punk in a big city. I have problems with dissociation and live in a big city and feel/go through a lot of things that Fyn does. (Albeit, a bit more sympathetic) You lose touch with your surroundings, time becomes meaningless, and it often feels like you are living a devoid existence. With Fyn, you can tell that they are experiencing all of this and more. They wake up from this surreal dream and feel like they finally have a purpose and set out to finally prove this, by any means necessary. Gameplay wise, you have a number of paths you can take, and even on the first episode, you have completely different experiences per playthrough. For example, I did one playthrough and completed the first episode; next playthrough, I found an area I didn't even know existed and that area even had different outcomes.
Overall, this game does have it's flaws, but it makes up for it with abstract story telling and beautiful visuals.

Very fun retro RPG! It's a classic story of rebellion set in a steampunk world.
Pros:
* No random battles to annoy you - instead, it uses a Lufia mechanic, where the monsters move around the map, and the battles only trigger if you run into them.
* The battle mechanic itself is interesting too: there's a concept of "Threat", and the party member with the highest amount of Threat will be targeted for all enemy attacks, which makes it easy to designate a "tank" for receiving the brunt of the damage (all but AoE). It gets tricky, though, when your DPS characters start dealing out considerable amounts of damage, and thus, increasing their own Threat. It often begs the decision whether your DPS character should kill an enemy and receive the bulk of the Threat (and the full force of the next enemy attack), or do something else and let that enemy live to attack one more time, but give your tank an opportunity to rebuild their Threat.
* The game rewards exploration by way of "exploration points" - free XP just for exploring the map.
* There are plenty of secret treasures to be found in the game! Completing the few hidden (and not so hidden) optional highly-challenging bosses and dungeons will result in great rewards.
Cons:
* Doesn't support the Steam overlay (Shift+Tab).
Overall, with full completion, this game took me about 12 hours to beat. I thoroughly enjoyed it and highly recommend it.

Great story so far, and the game feels fairly polished. I'm enjoying it a lot; I'm a fan of the snes jrpg genre and strongly story-driven games. This game makes excellent use of in-game storytelling and ambient story through characters in towns etc. Characters are convincing and dialog is well-written and tailored to each character. There is a quest log (somewhere) but you won't need it because your goals are integrated into the story like they should be.
There are a few RPG-maker glitches which detract from the game a bit: fixed screen resolution, lack of freedom to walk up and down stairs and climb ladders, not many walk-behinds around buildings and fences, some mistached graphics (e.g. the graphic style of explosions doesn't match the rest of the game) but nothing terrible.
I also feel that some of the maps are a bit too linear (in terms of choices) and could do with some more player-driven exploration and discovery rather than boxing the player in. That said, map layout is good and does show you areas you cannot reach yet, and bring you back around through places you've been before, which is great. They are also well finished, rather than chopped off randomly at screen edges like a lot of poor quality games.
I haven't seen many other modern jrpgs around that are actually good enough to pay for, so if you're a fan of the genre, this one is worth checking out.

For a casual RPG player like myself, Skyborn was a wonderful little game with a poignant story, fun gameplay, and quick pace.  There was never a need for tedious grinding--in fact, you could avoid most battles if you wanted to, but I don't know how that would affect your leveling.  Shops were placed conveniently between stretches of dungeon to buy (or make) better weapons and armor.  You could also buy supplies, although the plentiful item chests usually provided enough for me.  Some areas (Nordenwald Forest *cough*) were rather lengthy with extended puzzles involving painful walking from one end of the map to the other.  Aside from the particularly grueling dungeon and the utter lack of promised side quests, Skyborn proved to be a short but delightful game.  I'll certainly be replaying it in the future to try different class combinations and fighting styles.

I was originally gifted this game in jest, and one day decided to further the joke by making this a 'perfect game' on my account. What's ironic is that without gunning for all the achievements on this, I would never have played Hatoful Boyfriend past the first one or two endings. Why? Well, the surface dating sim is fun enough - but unless you're using a guide or are very skilful with your save points, it can get tedious working through each bird's story branch as you're left sitting through a lot of repetitive text again and again.
Now don't get me wrong - some of the storylines are truly adorable
, a handful aren't afraid pull hard on your heartstrings
, while others are legitimately insane and make me worry for the developers
. But after a while, the number of new choices you make in comparison to the amount of old text you have to skip through skews unfavourably, and has probably stopped thousands of people from perservering with getting all the endings. It's just a bird dating gimmick, so why play any more - right? But it's a real shame, as by dropping out early they miss the
end to the game... which is where the real meat of Hatoful Boyfriend lies.
What was once a bizarre, fluffy visual novel turns into... well. I don't want to give too much of the game away, but what I
say is this; the final ending for Hatoful Boyfriend masterfully elevates a goofy gimmick into one of the most breath-taking segments of in-game storytelling I have ever come across. What the developers have managed to do with a few still shots and some bird photographs is spectacular, and I will never be able to sing enough praise for the range and depth of emotion this final chapter hauled me through. I also love how skilfully all the other endings feed into the story being told, and after completing it you'll completely understand the developer's decision to make it inaccessible until you've seen everything else first.
Hatoful Boyfriend is simultaneously as much of a car crash as it is a masterpiece, and if you are a fan of gaming classics then I cannot recommend this little gem of a title enough. There's a long, hilarious, bizarre and eventually boring lead-up to the real meat of the game, but if you can stay patient and let yourself warm up to the crazy cast of characters the game has to offer, your efforts will be rewarded with a level of storytelling that puts many bigger titles to shame. If you were actually after a dating sim then don't expect anything too romantic or racey - the storylines are fluffy at best and heartbreaking at worst. 'Dating sim' might be the cutesy pink wrapping paper, but it's the emotional journey you are taken on which lies at the heart of this wonderously endearing game.

Vitatio 2 is basically a digitised version of the classic electric loop steady hand (buzz wire) skill tester.  The aim is to pilot the pointer through a maze with the mouse, avoiding the maze boundaries.  There are only eight small mazes, which seems like a pretty half-hearted effort at game creation.  This is highlighted by the torrent of achievements - one for each of the first five attempts at each maze.  An attempt ends as soon as the pointer touches a boundary, so you could quite easily accumulate 5 achievements within 10 seconds of loading the game.  Completing a maze nets you another 3 achievements if you piloted the cursor to all three goal locations en route to the ultimate destination, and this scenario is repeated for each maze, with bonus achievements after every second new maze completed, for a total of 68 of the least satisfying achievements available.  The store description actually says there are 85 achievements to unlock, so the mind boggles to think of the 17 that have been culled.
On a personal note, I would like to punch Level 5 in the face.  Although a more difficult maze was a welcome change, the collision detection will have you questioning your eyesight and the consistency of the game mechanics, and never before has your gaming success been so contingent on your hardware and workstation setup.  I spent about 45 minutes on it before changing my mouse and completing it on my first attempt.
This wasn’t my cup of tea and even if it is yours, it’s probably far too small a cup.

Being a metroidvania fan, I've been hyped about Axiom Verge for months. I couldn't wait for it to drop on Steam. So, I never thought I'd be writing a negative review for it.
I did have fun with the game, but that's where the praise begins and ends. Of course, the soundtrack and art style are very cool and attractive, but the game proper underwhelms.
The game length is quite short (8 hours with ~85% completion), and the early parts are fun, but you quickly become too powerful for any of the game's enemies to be a threat to you, even on Hard mode. Basically, that means Axiom Verge quickly becomes focused on the exploration aspect.
While exploring is half the fun of any metroidvania, the game gets into a slump where you're just dashing around the map like a mad man toward any undiscovered map tile, ignoring enemies and trying to find the next powerup (which you only need to get to the next powerup, anyway). The enemies might as well not even be in the game; you hardly deal with them past the first couple hours of the game.
The real problem with this game is the controls. Bosses get damn near impossible at the end of the game; one tiny tap on the control sticks will switch out your weapon, or enter the radial weapon select menu, or send you double-tap dashing in a random direction. The final boss fight was a nightmare akin to a Mario Party minigame, where I was spinning my D-Pad around and mashing buttons like crazy, just praying to get through it. The final upgrade you get is practically impossible to control, since it seems to have a mind of its own in terms of controller deadspace and which directions it "thinks" you wanted to double-tap.
The bottom line is that the game suffers from simplistic level and enemy design. If enemies were designed to be tough at first but then much easier to beat with each successive upgrade, there would be a sense of difficulty progression, but the game feels like a flatline item-hunt after the first couple hours. Also, the story is mostly incomprehensible, although to be fair, I haven't read all the collectible note logs. It's possible that the story does get fleshed out and has a great ending, but I personally wasn't gripped by anything the story had to offer.
That being said, I still think any self-respecting metroidvania fan ought to give Axiom Verge a go. I'd just wait for the game to go on sale.

Looks like Metroid, plays like Metroid. Follows the formula; Start exploring, see something you can't interact with, find the item to interact with it and get through, repeat.
Platforming/Movement: MegaMan-like, no momentum and instant acceleration. Works well enough when the platforming isn't where the challenge is, it's the shooting. Only problem I ran into was the dash ability you eventually unlock, which is a little too sensitive. Works by double-tapping a direction, and from fidgeting on platforms, I would constantly dash myself off of them.
Combat: Easily the game's biggest strength, there are a ton of different weapons to find, and all of them are optional (apart from the first), I think. I found a use for just about every weapon at some point, which is a nice surprise given the lack of ammo/damage types that are usually present to force weapon variety. Somewhat challenging boss fights, though it helps if you have the "correct" weapon for the fight.
Story/Exploration: Story was weird enough to keep me guessing at where it was going, but interesting enough to keep me invested in what was going on. Granted, if it takes too long to progress and get to the next story beat, you might not care about the plot anymore. Nearing the end, I took about an hour and a half of backtracking to find the one room I needed, which was starting to get to me. The map would feel familiar to anyone that's played Super Metroid, with the different zones having their own look, but fitting together nicely. Trying to find secret passageways is nicely rewarded, decent total number of collectables in the world, that have immediate benefits.
Overall, I enjoyed it, recommended if you enjoy metroidvania platformers.

Why a regular gamer should play this game. The answer is: for experiencing the history.
In HOI4 you are going to choose a country and lead your country to the end of the WW2. You can do whatever you want to your country such as join Allies as German Reich.
In my last save, I played as Poland and did survive the WW2 in a different way. Heres the story:
1. Gave up part of the border in order to prevent Axis attack poland in the early game.
2. Facing Soviet Union while Japan was taking control of mainland China.
3. With Japan(Axis)'s support (but I was not in any fraction), Successfuly took down USSR and also saved Finland from Soivet's hand.
4. Moved my divisions to west frontline for next combat in 1942, yet the Allies hadnt attacked German but West of euorpe was occupied by Reich.
5. Join Allies in 1942, started WW2.
6. Reich was soon to be captured in 1944, but rest of the Axis members were still fighting.
7. Divisions continued to the south, free/gained control of France, Italy, and Spain in 1946.
8. Ottamen empire joined Axis and started attacking the new russia at the beginning of 1947.
9. Divisions arrived at North of mainland China, started attacking Japan and its puppet states with support of UK, USA, CA, and other euorpe countries and their puppets.
10. After gaining control of mainland China in 1947, Allies started attacking remaining Axis troops in Africa, South East Asia and Japan.
11. Without Atomic bombs, USA occupied Japan in 1948. WW2 ended.
12. Poland released its puppet states and remained the same. German started a new government, and also rest of the Axis members. USA and UK occupied most of the Asia.
13. My divisions were been to Soviet Union's land, Europe, North of Africa, and Asia.

An endlessly charming and simple Japanese-style RPG that brings to mind Square's SNES efforts, as well as lesser-known Genesis and Turbografx adventures (Lunar and Cosmic Fantasy come immediately to mind).  Easy to grasp mechanics and an interesting story punctuated with excellent writing and the first truly likeable cast I've come across in quite some time.  It speaks volumes that I enjoyed this humble little title more than recent multi-million efforts from big name developers.  It's quite succinct at only 7-10 hours long, but there's also little pointless backtracking and padding to slog through.
Absolutely recommended to gamers that look back fondly on the golden age of console RPGs.
Note: Disregard people dismissing Skyborn because of the engine it was built with.  RPG Maker is fully capable of producing unique and captivating games in the right hands, as evidenced by Yume Nikki, To the Moon and the subject of this review.

A Bird Story is the greatest silent film of this decade. For this reason, Dove Tales is wonderful to watch on a sad day! A perfect pick-me-up. The Bird Store is inspired by birds, for birds. Pure authenticity, so much research went into making sure this Story was actually very Bird. My recommendation is that anyone who is a bird or is thinking about becoming one someday should really look into this title. DuckTales gets an [8 / 10].

Wistful and sweet. Highly recommended.

I have a lot of mixed opinions on this game. On the one hand the story is interesting and provides a neat setup to the rest of the XCOM reboot games, and the 60s aesthetic does make for interesting setpieces and enviroments.
But this game also came across as a very watered down Mass Effect with some very light RPG elements and squad management. The game started out strong for me in the begining, but as it went on just started to feel like a more like a chore. With very little variety in terms of enemies, and with most missions basically boiling down "Shoot some aliens and press a button to shoot more guys" it just got very stale fast. By the end of the game, the story missions became more frustrating than challenging.
To add to it, the UI was tactical mode was very annoying to deal with. Often felt unresponsive and clunky, which in a tense firefight just made for a frustrating experience.
Frustrating would be a pretty okay word for this game. This game probably could have been a lot better had it not just defaulted to being another run of the mill cover based shooter that plagued the early 2010's. Personally, I would have loved if this game had a lot more emphasis on being a secret agent investigating alien ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t and having to maintain coverups from the public instead of having to deal with samey combat scenarios all the time.
For the price now, I'd say it's worth it but in all honestly I can't really reccomend this game to anyone.

Even though this game got a pretty rough treatment from the gaming press, I was always curious about it because the art direction and setting looked interesting. So I picked it up for a few bucks during a Steam sale and gave it a shot.
I'm not going to pretend that it's some sort of hidden gem or flawed classic, because it's not,  but it's also not anywhere near as bad as some people might have you believe. It may fail at being an XCOM game, but it's got heart. The setting and characters are interesting, the gameplay is decent enough and the game totally nails the 50-60s creepy scifi vibe it was going for.
But there are some serious problems, too. The core of the gameplay is basically console style chest-high wall shooting, so it's a bit of a shame when you enter a new area and already know there will be a fight because the area is littered with said chest-high walls. Breaks the creepy vibe, for real. What's worse, your teammates have a tendency to run into dangerous situations, and it's almost impossible to micromanage them all the time. The narrative, while interesting and entertaining for the most part, also kind of falls apart towards the end of the game.
But overall, I enjoyed the game well enough. If you loved TV series like Dark Skies and aren't too bothered with clunky combat mechanics (they're probably not even that bad, or I wouldn't have finished the game) then this game will resonate with you, I think. It's just a shame they 'had' to use the XCOM brand for it. Instead of hating it for being a failed attempt at an XCOM reboot/prequel, people might have welcomed it for its fairly unique style and setting if it tried to be its own game. But alas...

I will recommend this game, but cautiously to a few.
Pixel piracy offers a 2D RPG platform game with minimal controls. Pirates in essence manage themselves while you the player, tell them where to go, organize them in groups, and ensure they have enough food to eat.
The mouse allows you to control your pirates. Jumping ship to ship or to land is as easy as clicking over the location (or at). Some ships cannot be boarded right away, but are in range of cannons. Cannons fire while the ships approach one another. Boarding another ship can take some time as the ships have to come into proximity with one another. The ships don't physically move, but the timer countdown at the bottom does (
). There are different types of cannons, and not everyone can use a cannon. Different pirates can acquire different abilities once given a skill book. Some can navigate faster, some can heal others, some can repair the ship, and some can specialize in combat. Pirates can be put into groups by the player to make selecting easier. For example, some pirates will have the ability to fire cannons, therefor putting these pirates into the "cannon" group can keep them on your ship while telling trainees, ship crew or other groups to go board and attack. There are specific attributes that can be upgraded with each pirate. Strength, vitality and dexterity are a few attributes to consider. I've mostly focused keeping them all nicely rounded, but it does help to have a few guys with good aim on the cannons, or wielding a gun. Passive items such as cooking knives can be given to pirates, as well as a secondary side arm meant for ranged attacks. Ranged attacks can be in the form of tomahawks, to flintlock pistols. When boarding or attacking another pirate's ship, once all the opposing pirates are deceased, the player may choose to capture the ship or sink it once all crew members are safely aboard your ship. Sinking a ship will give you some material and gold.
Ships can be modified to ones will, given the right materials. When docking on islands, the ships food supply can be restocked, cannons can be added, and even ship materials can be added to expand the boat. Building the boat in the editor doesn't require a lot of skill and is straight forward. Islands boast different shops. Some will have taverns (to hire pirates), some will have goods and item stores, some will have weapon stores, and some will have ship stores. Within these stores small little gimmicks appear as the player should read the fine prints of each item carefully. Pirates need certain items like fruit to prevent scurvy (you'll notice randomly some pirates will simply lose HP). Some pirates that you hire are not up to par, and at the ship store, spare swords can be bought for them to practice with. They need to be installed on a ship manually for it to come into effect.
The visuals are appropriate for the game, and have some small effects that really require a double take. Animations are smooth and kept simple. Sounds are varying as all pirates will have something different to say, but have no problem repeating themselves! The most notable sound in game is the splashing, it's refreshing!
I like the game, but once you get to a certain point you'll have enough of it. You'll feel like you've done what you can and the only difference is the level of your opponents. This is why I'm carefully recommending it. For a game that is ON SALE and worth a couple of bucks, it's not bad for a few hours of entertainment. If you really want replayability from this game, you'll probably lean to one side of the fence. There is the exception for those who like endless adventure and like competing for a top score.

Difficulty is very front-loaded on each level - if you manage to get through the first two waves with a decent insfrastructure (ie. protected key points, 2-4 money generating towers), then the remaining waves are way too easy. The entire game is very easy - until you start the second campaign, which is more challenging even with all the upgrades in place. So it's fine, eventually.
My only serious gripe is unit diversity - cannon towers and money towers are way more efficient than anything else.
Even so, I can recommend this game.

It seems Arkane Studios has been around forever, and if you look for it, you'll find info about Arkane being involved in a lot of interesting games....wich...never came to be sadly. Such as the cancelled half life sequel (if you care about half life) and also LMNO and undisclosed game project with steven spielberg attached to it (if you ever though spielberg can manage to make a game, wich i really don't) Sadly, gaming studios (the good ones) that try to collaborate with a well known filmmaker or other "big name" enterprise ends with and identity crisis or just plain disaster. One of those two seemed to be the case for Arkane Studios, wich had a good start with Arx Fatalis and Dark Messiah and then ended up jumping places several times... but they persevered, they endured, and finally they've got they're golden oportunity in the form of Dishonored. A game created by Arkane, with the support of Bethesda, wich seems to not have bothered too much Arkane or anyone this time as they were able to finally do their thing.
In Dishonored you play Corvo Attano, royal protector to the empress and her daughter wich it all kind of goes to a rough start when , just beginning, the empress is killed and her daughter is kidnapped, you are framed for murder (of course!), but you didn't do it, so you start your quest to avenge the empress and find her killer and the missing daughter...
The story is simple, but the game world is very well though out. The city of Dunwall is not just the main decor for the political drama that goes on. It is in fact, it feels like, one of the main characters,   the depiction of what could be a city, partially covered with water, ravaged by a a rat plague,  just told through skteches and illustrations and what not. The game doesn't go for photorealistic graphics, but instead with a graphic novel style, dark and crumbling, but full of life and it works very well, because it has character and style through out the whole game.
The gameplay itself it's, really, the star here. You start with practically nothing, and already you have to find out ways to stealth (or kill) your way through. The gameplay is pretty much open to a lot of ways to do things, but at the same time is very well though out. Meaning, everything you do or you try to do, could really work (and often it does).
I've seen some playthroughs of this game and they look nothing like the way i've played it, to the point i though i was playing a different version, but no, it is the same game, after trying different things myself i can be sure of it.
On one hand you have your weapons, you have a sword, pistol, normal and explosive bullets, then the crossbow, sleeping darts, then the normal ones. And bombs, also sticky boms,  You can use all that, or a combination, or nothing, and stealth your way through, knocking out guards.
But then you have the outsider powers, you have blink, the ability to transport from one place to another. Also you can sense through walls enemy presence, and in a more advance state you can sense machines and mechanisms.
Then you have the ability to slow time...for a short amount of time (no pun intended!) and also the ability to posses animals and people! speaking of animals, one ability lets you summon an army of rats to eat your enemys :D
Of course, you have to learn this abilities, they don't come for granted, you have to get them  through the game.
It is very interesting the many ways in wich your gameplay style evolves, you can combine all these things. You can for example slow time and get behind a guard and posses him to go some other place or just knock him down right there. Or for example, you can posess a rat and go through a small tunnel.... you can also slow time and fire 3 arrows to three guards at the same time and watch later as they all die..
But its not only for different ways to incapacitate people that you have all this. At the beginning of each level you have to think about what you re  going to do, and make a strategy (especially if you care about going stealth)
Once you learn a level its amazing the things you can do, and in how many different ways.
Also It is so much fun to have played this game and then compare certain levels decisions with other players, not only because they play diferent, but because often they will do unexpected things that you wouldn't think about doing and thats part of the fun of this game. You play it your way and it feels even more unique because of that.
That said, the story in it was , rather straigh to the point and simple wich it is not bad, it serves its purpose right but  it dragged a little in a certain part of the game.
The voice acting was very well done, with an all around very good cast  and it really  added more personality to the game  The music itself its well done and works very well when it is used..
It is always a pleasure to find out about a nice game even many years after its release, and Dishonored has stood the test of time, in a wich a good game will always be a good one indeed.

Solid, enjoyable, well put-together game.
The game's difficulty on Normal is a bit too easy, although Hard mode presents a decent challenge, especially earlier on in the game (before you get access to the really OP debuffs).
Despite the RPG Maker feel that a lot of people seem to detest, Skyborn's a very polished package.  I noticed a couple small bugs and a couple typos, but that was it on the negatives.
I was able to play this with a controller, which was very appreciated.  I used a 3rd party knockoff Xbox360 controller, which didn't require any additional setup upon booting the game.  However, I was able to hit F1 in-game and remap the buttons to something more sensible, the defaults didn't make sense on my particular controller.
Dialogue was well-written, enjoyable, and fairly humorous.  Plot, while a bit short, was interesting and flowed well.  Combat system had a nice brisk pace, with good yet swift animations for attacks.
The leveling and itemization was a stand-out success, in my mind: armor is equippable by all characters, but if you weigh a character down beyond their carrying capacity, their speed drops off.  There are a few ways of increasing that capacity later in the game.  But that broad eligibility allows a much wider amount of equipment options for each character, as you can trade off weight between different slots to equip items you REALLY want.  The augment system is simple yet robust, offering another layer of customizibility to your characters.  Furthermore, there are two "class up"s during the game, where you can upgrade each character to a new job class.  The game does a great job of explaining the options prior to selection, so you don't need to consult a third party resource for information.
It took me about 15 hours to complete the game, playing in hard mode and completing all optional content&bosses.  I'm a bit of a slow player, though, so most folks will probably take about 7-12 depending on difficulty and completeness.
I don't think I'd pay the full $15 for this one due to its length, but at sale prices it's a great purchase.
Enjoy!

Played through this in about six hours; in one sitting.  Why in one sitting, you ask?  Because I couldn't tear myself away!  The story here does a rather good job of telling itself during that six hours(which could be four or less if you're in a hurry).  It's a fairly nuanced tale with all the proper tragic hero tropes, plot twists and surprise endings, but it doesn't do a lot of padding to get there.
If you're looking for any kind of gameplay balance, do speed runs.  Otherwise this game is incredibly easy even on its hardest settings, although there is one battle you will never win ;).
All in all, for $7.49 (at half price) I felt like I got my money's worth and then some.  This is a rather well-polished RPGmaker gem that will leave you wanting more from this developer in the future!

I couldn't remove a selection and I couldn't make an intermediate selection so I went with yes.  I enjoyed playing the game for the most part.  The story may use a tried and true plot device, but it does contain a few twists that I, at least, didn't see coming.  The world is fairly small, but most of the areas are very diversified so it doesn't feel that way.  Also the smithing is a nice touch, though I would have liked to make higher quality armor as well.
My problem with the game was the combat balance.  For one I almost immediately turned the game up to hard.  This is something I almost never do as I generally like to keep combat just difficult enough that I keep interested without becoming a hassle.  On Normal there was absolutely no challenge.  For most random encounters that didn't change much on Hard.  Boss battles, came in two varities: 'What just wiped me in 2 seconds' or 'what did I just roll over.'  There are certain skills in the game (For you and your enemies) that are just ridiculously strong.  But if you don't use them, then battles just drag on because at least with how I was building characters (trying to emphasize +Str as much as I could!) only 1-2 of my characters ever did appreciable amounts of damage.  Also the character classes are very specialized. Only certain people dealt damage, and at times it really felt the only reason "threat" existed was to give the tank something to do on his turn.
Overall Story is a +, game balance is a -.  Take your pick on which is more important to you.

Happily Skyborn is pure gold and while the actual tile sets are mostly of the stock type that come with the set, the character portraits are amazingly detailed and expresive and the author is himself a professional musician so the soundtrack is incredible. Set in a steampunk world where the humans are oppressed by a group of winged beings known as the Skyborn, the reluctant heroine Claret is drawn into a rebellion, first merely to save her brother but then out of altruism as she sees just how badly the Skyborn treat the lower classes. It has a great cast of likeable characters and while, as with many RPG's the combat can be a bit grindy, it has enough clever mechanics to keep you going til the end. 20 hours game for $14.99 is pretty good value. It seems to me that this game was primarily made by an artist: The art is beautiful, but the programming / systems involved are not particularly complex. Fortunately, there was a lot of hard work put into them, and despite being a simplistic affair, the combat is balanced and even strategically challenging on harder difficulties. One particular (optional) fight, which I later discovered defaulted to the hard difficulty, was amoung the most challenging RPG fights I have ever done, and yet, it was not arbitrary... it just required a lot of strategy... though by the time I finished it, I was pretty much untouchable.
In the meantime, if you don't care too much about the battles, you can drop the difficulty to easy and enjoy roughly ten hours of a well told story. It's not quite Bioshock, but many a sucessful AAA title has gone to field with worse, and it's engaging enough that I played through it in one go, without feeling any desire to stop midway through. Nor did I feel the need for a walkthrough or to look up advice on the game, which was fortunate, since there is rather little.

I really love this game.  It's simple.  It's old-school.  It's turn based.  While these are amazing things in and of themselves, they combine to make a very lovely, relaxing game here.
The story doesn't blow you away, sure.  It is fun and enjoyable though.  Satisfies nostalgic feelings for RPG's from my childhood.
Characters are fun and relatable.  Battle is a cake walk until you select "Hard".  Then you're actually in for a bit of a fun challenge.  This is one of the few games I actually can find excitement to play lately.  There's just something satisfying about it.  I purposefully engage every enemy (enemy sprites move around the map and you can avoid them if you desire to do so), and don't find it to feel tired and repetitive thus far.
Weapons and armor are augmentable and there is actually some thought required to be optimal, which is a nice change.
That having been said, I would not pay $15 for this game.  At all.  I find the sale price to be perfectly reasonable however.  I even feel that it's a worthwhile purchase in that price range and would buy it again in a heart beat.
There's a certain zen-like simplicity to this game, its combat and music, that just make it very relaxing and surprisingly addictive.
Stop thinking about it and buy it already!
To the Devs, thank you so much for this! I really hope you have more things in the works!

However, if you enjoy writing that is off the beaten track that needs a little patience and a certain sense of humor, then go ahead and spend the 5 bucks to have a dry life and explore the interesting, atmospheric world that has been created.
I genuinely enjoyed the experience of this game because of its atmosphere and the dark humor behind the writing that tends towards exstitential and perhaps a bit pretentious. It has a certain poetry to it that I enjoyed, however I understand how others may not enjoy it. The gameplay is pretty straightforward, point and click with a few different actions, and there are different routes to play the game that are worth exploring.
I hope that they do decide to continue this game, as I would be very interested in a second episode. This game does not finish in a way that it could stand on its own and I'm eager to see how the story progresses.

Mechanically, the game is unremarkable, a fairly linear point and click adventure. The puzzles are simple, though sometimes nonsensical. Aesthetically, there is a lot to praise - a strong visual style with rich use of light and shadow, a simple yet flavourful soundtrack, crisp details - the cyberpunk setting really comes together. Unfortunately, the powerful setting and solid mechanics are in the service of a game which is not enjoyable.
Fyn, the protagonist, lacks both empathy and any measure of self-awareness, which renders play somewhat unpleasant. The dialog is disjointed, repetitive, and at times painfully derivative, unintentionally reflecting the shallowness of the protagonist in musical references and nihilistic cliches. The plot itself, already hampered by Fyn and the dialog, is uneven and underdeveloped. Void & Meddler touches upon well-established cyberpunk tropes and themes, but in an exploitative manner, without any discussion or - in some cases - reason.
It is hard to pan a game at all, let alone one which clearly has so much earnest effort behind it, but I would counsel most to avoid Void & Meddler. You
like it if you are a fan of cyberpunk and neo-noir from a stylistic perspective, particularly if the sociopathy of the protagonist is no barrier.

A very fascinating punk rock/dystopian/cyberpunk/no wave adventure. The game reminds me of Akira mixed with a Death Grips record. It runs well. . . mostly. It does however have good dialouge tree puzzles at times. Other times it feels linear even though the game actually is open ended to an extent. The game is similar to say. . . a piece of art work. It is beautiful to look at, it is creative, and you can tell it took a long time to make. But what can you actually DO with it? Where is it going to go with its direction? It might not go anywhere, and what message is it trying to portay anyways?
Length wise the game is a ♥♥♥♥ing joke. It's insultingly short. But I honestly think that is the point. It is an experience, not really a game. It's like if Blade Runner took a bunch of coke, LSD, and meth and went on a killing spree. Blade Runner (for me) is much more of an experience than a movie. It's thought provoking. The main character reminds me of Soko or Patti Smith or something. She is sexually questionable and rebellious. I like her, she is pretty memorable. The whole atomosphere is very depressing and delerious similar to Hotline Miami or say I Have No Mouth And I Must Scream, it's a deep game. It almost seems to question the whole idea of human anatomy or sexual preference in literally all aspects of the design and gameplay.
Overall it is a good game for me due to my taste. I like it alot actually, however the length is pretty hilarious, and the frame drop in the one area is unacceptable for how well all of the other areas hold up. I would give it an 8/10 or a 7/10. It is no masterpiece but rather a beautifully degenerating experience. At least it isn't a walking simulator.

This game takes you back to the age of Metroid and Castlevania. There are so many secrets and fun areas its hard to stop playing. This game a a big challenge as well but it doesn't feel like it's unfair. If you want a challenging game with lots to discover, Axiom Verge should be your next pick.

Axiom Verge manages to encapsulate the feeling of the Metroid series but plays it safe by pretty much copying Metroid and not building on top of the proven formula. However it turned out surprisingly good for a one-man project. Not bad at all, Mr. Happ.
Axiom Verge's story is alright but nothing that will stick with you. It does start out promising but as I've uncovered more of the story, either via "cutscenes" or hidden collectable letters (an idea I always welcome), the less I cared for it. It's really hard to win me over with a story so take this information with a grain of salt.
Graphically it looks very reminiscent to Metroid and the games' overworld provides some beautiful sceneries, tho I think that fore- and background visuals often look very inconsistent. Nevertheless they get the job done and I really love the overall asthetic, right down to the garbled mess of glitchy sprites. The music is for the most part well done and greatly add to the isolating atmosphere of the game, but the instrumentation in some of the tracks can get very annoying.
There are over 20 different modules for your "Axiom Disruptor" to find, and while I haven't unlocked all of these modules yet, I've found myself only using 2 of them in my entire playthrough as both were efficient enough to destroy whatever came in front of me. Along your way through the game you will also pick up items that allow you to literally glitch through obstacles, dash or let you cling on ceilings and swing across pits "Bionic Commando-style". Player control is well done with the exception of performing dashes which require you to double-press your analog stick or digital pad to the intended direction. It often happened that I dashed without actually wanting to do that maneuver. Not only that but the analog stick control in the main menu is overly sensitive. I've played Axiom Verge with a XBOX360 controller and I'd like to hear feedback regarding this issue from other players.
Thomas Happ did a really good job with the design of the overworld. I haven't found myself stuck at any point during my playthrough despite the lack of information given to the player (as it should be). Even backtracking to locations you've already been at before doesn't feel like a chore. Secrets are very well hidden and will require some extensive searching. I'd argue that the level design is Axiom Verges' strongpoint.
And despite all the good things I have to say about this game, it somewhat lacks its own identity. It lends itself way too much to Metroid and plays it safe. And the somewhat lackluster story doesn't help to emigrate that feeling.
Also I don't think that the game provides enough content for the 20€ Steam is asking for it. I think that 15€ at max are a good investment.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Axiom Verge schafft es, das Metroid-Feeling im Spiel aufkeimen zu lassen, geht aber auf Nummer sicher und kopiert Metroid lediglich, anstatt auf dem altbewährten Konzept der bekannten Reihe aufzubauen. Dennoch ist es eine respektable Leistung für ein Ein-Mann-Entwicklerteam, gute Arbeit Mr. Happ.
Die Geschichte von Axiom Verge geht in Ordnung aber es ist keine, die den meisten Spielern lange im Gedächtnis bleiben wird. Am Anfang beginnt sie vielversprechend doch je mehr von der Geschichte aufgedeckt wurde, entweder durch Cutscenes oder versteckten Notizblättern, desto weniger interessierte sie mich. Ich bin nur sehr schwer mit einer guten Videospielgeschichte zu überzeugen, daher solltet ihr meine Meinung zur Geschichte nicht zu wörtlich nehmen.
Die deutsche Übersetzung ist tolerabel, einige Rechtschreibfehler gilt es zu verkraften.
Grafisch lehnt sich Axiom Verge an Metroid an und die Overworld bietet hier und da auch einige schöne Kulissen an, auch wenn es öfters vorkommt, dass Vor- und Hintergrundgrafiken oftmals sehr inkonsistent zueinander wirken. Die Ästhetik des Spiel gefällt mir sehr gut, bishin zu den grotesken Glitchgrafiken. Die Musik ist größtenteils sehr gut und verleiht der Overworld auch eine unglaublich gute Atmosphäre der Isolation. Nur wurde die Instrumentation für einige Musikstücke ünglücklich getroffen, was beim längeren Verbleib in einer bestimmten Sektion auf die Nerven gehen kann.
20 verschiedene Waffenmodule gilt es für deinen "Axiom Disruptor" zu finden. Allerdings habe ich während meines Playthroughs nur von zwei von diesen Gebrauch gemacht, da beide sich gut komplementiert haben und der Rest nicht wirklich hilfreich erschien. Außer Waffen findet man in Axiom Verge noch weitere Items, die einem ermöglichen, sich durch Wände zu glitchen, einen Dashmove auszuführen oder sich an Decken anzuhängen und über Abgründe zu schwingen, wie in "Bionic Commando". Die Steuerung wurde im Großen und Ganzen gut umgesetzt. Allerdings hatte ich das Problem, dass die Spielfigur öfters den Dashmove eingesetzt hat ohne dass ich dies auch wollte (Doppel-Tippen des Analgsticks oder Digitalpads in eine bestimme Richtung). Außerdem ist die Steuerung im Menü mittels Analogsticks viel zu empfindlich. Ich habe Axiom Verge mit einem XBOX360 Controller gespielt und würde gerne wissen, ob auch andere User die selben Probleme hatten)
Thomas Happ hat hervorragende Arbeit bei der Gestaltung der Overworld geleistet. Nicht einmal während meines gesamten Playthroughs bin ich irgendwo hängen geblieben, trotz spärlicher Informationen, die dem Spieler vorgesetzt werden (wie es auch sein sollte). Selbst das Backtracking in Areale, die man schon besucht hat, belastet nicht. Secrets sind sehr gut versteckt worden und es bedarf ein waches Auge um sie alle zu finden. Meiner Meinung nach ist das Leveldesign die größte Stärke von Axiom Verge.
Und trotz all den guten Dingen, die ich über das Spiel zu sagen habe, fehlt diesem eine eigene identität. Es lehnt sich einfach zu sehr an Metroid an und geht auf Nummer sicher. Und auch die schwache Geschichte des Spiels trägt nicht dazu bei, es vom Muster zu differenzieren.
Und ich denke nicht, dass das Spiel genug Content abliefert, um die 20€ rechtfertigen zu können, die Steam für das Spiel verlangt. 15€ wären noch in Grenzen.

I've been a fan of Isuna Hasekawa for a while now. Ever since I watched the anime Spice and Wolf. To say this review could be a little biased would be an understatement, but at the same time I think if I hadn't read or watched Spice and wolf, this game would still at least be a 9/10
The entire series as a whole has been a rollercoaster, with it's most impressive bit being the character development. In this final episode the characters own arcs and convictions really shine, and the result of their development blossoms in ways that really moved me to tears.
The story itself, the narrative contents and the themes shine. Although it can be a little bit of a grind to work through all the economics, it certainly provded a lot of insight into investment as a whole. To note, the themes of investment are based upon the author's own experience and knowledge in the field so it certainly has credibility if you are looking for that kind of realism. The bredth of the writers knowledge in market crisis is quite educational. Although there is some critiscism that economics hasn't progressed all that far compared to the norm of the present day. But hey, I don't know much about economics so I couldn't really tell.
The art is a huge goodie. Though it's lacking on content, the CG's accompanied with scenes can be very powerfull and provide the mood very well. It certainly was much like watching a drama, except I was projecting my hallucinations onto a 2D still.
The music is some funky sheeeeeet! I can't describe it much more than that. It's wonderfully made, with one or two exceptions, the majority of tracks will make you forget they are even on repeat.
I bought the entire set of games individually for £30 pounds. I've gotten at least thirty hours out of them all accumilated, and I'm a very fast reader. I would say after it all, yes it was worth it for me. It may be for you, but always be on the look out for deals. I'd suggest buying the first one at full price if you aren't confident, rather than jumping into the full bundle discount. From there if you like it, buy the bundle which will give you a good discount on the sequels, and then enjoy.

I write this review after beating the game.
I played through this one on its "Veteran" difficulty, the third most difficult out of four. It took approximately sixteen hours to play through this, with a few challenges along the way but nothing that was too tough for the experienced strategist/xcom series veteran. Most importantly, it was fun. Not amazing, best game ever, but fun.
The story is decent. It isn't ecpecially original, but rather is a strong rendering of a traditional sci-fi theme complete with a self loathing drunken field agent, a shady but good hearted agency director, the veteran turned scientist, and a grizzled old veteran that happens to be the Directors friend. There's even a former Nazi scientist! It is well executed for what it is, and was enjoyable.
The game play is striaght forward, though it has a few flaws. The controls are acceptable, if a little less than precise. Playing as a third person shooter, utilizing cover is a must. This is done well enough, though from time to time trying to move in cover can be frustrating. The most frustrating part is keeping your squadmates where you put them. Issue orders, they obey, then from time to time wander off on their own. Other than the AI being a turd, the game plays quite well.
Your mission choices are kind of funny. You send off spare agents on side missions, each of them gaining a level and you getting a reward when its complete. You spend your time on the maps (which are rather simple and impossible to get lost on) fighting enemies and looking for new back packs, since the back packs are the only "gear" you can change other than weapons. You scavange weapons and ammo in battle, which is fine. There is a lack of "urgency" though, because you can complete ALL lesser missions before moving to the next big one, regardless of what the story says. "omg earth is dead in a few hours, maybe a day" "its cool. just let me wrap up these side quests first..."
The xcom story is fun for what it is, and provides a kind of prologue to the XCOM: Enemy Unknown reboot of the series, which was nice and has me wanting to go back and replay those games.
Over all, this game was worth the time and money, though it didn't seem to have much replay appeal, at least not fresh off beating it. Maybe someday. I believe most of the negative reviews come from the following: XCOM veterans who are frustrated that the game is third person live action not turn based, and less complete than other xcom titles, Mass Effect players that are annoyed the game is far simpler than ME and not as well executed, or players who purchased the game expecting something more than it is.
With that said, so long as you know what you are getting, you will enjoy this game. It is a reasonably fun, decently length strategy/shooter. It is not genre altering, it is not the best of the best, but it is a solid 7/10 and one that I will recommend.

A small and fun tower defence game. Though it's not adding anything new to the genre and is kind of generic, it's still fun enough and worth playing if you are into tower defence games. You get to play through 40 levels of naval battles. Build giant crossbows, cannons, and other mounted guns to take down pirate ships that are coming at your base kamikaze style.
The variety in enemy ships is quite big and each one has its own distinct weaknesses which you have to exploit via certain towers. The towers mostly come in 4 basic types, which in turn can be upgraded into other types. You have crossbows which are fast but weak. Cannons which are slower but strong. Artillery which are very slow but can hit groups. And finally the support buildings that generate you money on a regular basis, which I think is a pretty cool idea in a game like this.
The levels are divided into 2 acts: Caribbean Sea (first 20 levels) and Arctic Ocean (last 20). When you beat each level, you get a rating out of 3 stars. Not letting any enemy attack your base grants you 3 stars. If, however, some did manage to damage it, you get only 1 or 2 stars. Unfortunately the stars do not mean anything in this game. In other tower defence games the stars act as upgrade points of some kind, hence incentivizing the player to replay missions and do better. But this game doesn't do that and collecting stars is only there for boasting.
The upgrades are instead handled via collecting barrels, which randomly drop from destroyed enemies. There are tonnes of upgrades for each tower and magic spell, and you're unlikely to upgrade everything by playing through the game once. This means you might occasionally have to grind for barrels by replaying earlier levels, which is a bit of a bad design in my opinion (when in doubt, keep replaying level 20 of Caribbean Sea; it gives A LOT of barrels usually). What's worse about this design, some of the tower spots on each map are locked and require you to spend several of your barrels before you can build anything on those spots. Those are usually good, strategic spots, so you have to either waste some of your precious barrels on one map, or compromise on your setup.
Visuals are very beautiful and shiny. Sound effects are nice, and the music is all right, although you pretty much have the same short track playing in every level, so a bit more musical variety would've been nice.
Overall this is a fun TD game. There are better TD games out there, but if you're looking for a new one that you haven't played yet, then this one is well worth a try, since it's very affordable and will entertain you for several hours.

The fact that the game uses a standard currency (gold) and a premium currency (barrels, though the recycled copy from their previous game still calls it crystals), that the premium currency is usable to make just about anything easier, and the low drop rate of the premium currency (requiring tedious grinding) all suggest to me that Fort Defense (or the predecessor game that they reskinned for Fort Defense) was originally designed to be a P2W mobile game, and selling it instead as a conventional game was a change of plans made late in the development process.

The Good:

The Bad:
Short:  I did unessisary grinding, exploration and all the side quests and still finished at under  hours on my first playthrough.
Almost 0 replay value: not even a + game option to let you play through again with all your stuff intact.  If you want to play through again you gotta lose all you've don so far and start fresh.  This is made worse by the shortness of the game itself.
Crafting:  Normally a plus in this game it's a minus because it is pointless.  9 times out of 10 you are better off selling off the crafting materials and buying the gear that you need in the next town since it is the same stuff you would have crafted anyway and the money you get will go further than if you had made the gear instead of buying it.
Side Quests:  I found around 3 of them and I feel confident that I explored enough to say that is close to if not all there are.  If your going to have side quests have a bunch otherwise just skip them. The Ugly:

this game is an emotional trap. you buy it because the idea of a dating simulator with pigeons is 'LOL SO RANDOM!!11 XD' and full of 'teh lulz', but then you accidentally end up playing a parody game that turns out to be
the writing is thoughtful and well-balanced, containing humor of the rare 'actually funny' type, which will result in feelings of warm attachment to the characters... before TWISTING THE KNIFE OF FEELINGS DEEPLY as a tragedy of Shakespearean proportions overwhelms the plotline arc and cast.
the writing
has a highly surprising amount of depth, as the characters (including your own) must make some morally ambiguous choices, and even the most immoral characters have a few redeeming, wholly human features to their personalities which make them relatable and strangely likable.
there are 16 different endings to the story that are achieved based on the choices you make, with one 'true ending' and 15 'alternate endings'; notably, the alternate endings to this story are cleverly interwoven into the 'true' ending plotline, as with each new ending you discover, you are given new revelations that consistently give you deeper insight into the events that unfold prior to the finale of the 'true' plotline. this means that there is an actual reader's value that goes beyond shallow 'what if' ideas to following every path to its ending, which is fairly uncommon in the genre of multiple-choice story games.
the art is also clean, colorful and high quality, and the music sets the tone nicely. honestly the only thing i could wish for is that it was fully voiced (it isn't).
recommended for people who actually enjoy good stories in visual novels, as opposed to the endless list of VNs with vapid, soulless storylines that rely on a cast of waifus and husbandos to appeal to buyers... although, you have been warned- after playing this game, the odds that you will have horrifyingly/ heartbreakingly fallen in love with your first ever 'pigeon husbando' are high...

Суть такая. Город, который нужно защитить от Дракулы. Дракула насылает на город нежить. Нужно защитить последнюю базу сопротивления от нежити и по возможности убить Дракулу. Вот-с.
На карте города разбросаны дома. В некоторых прячутся выжившие, их можно завербовать в качестве охотников на вампиров. В некоторых расположены оружейные магазинчики. Не стрелять же бойцам из ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥енького пистолета всю жизнь, правда? Есть аптеки, которые ускоряют выздоровление героев, есть пивнушки, куда бегут отдыхать уставшие бойцы, есть магазины и кладбища, дающие бонусные деньги и экспу для персонажей.
Здания открываются по очереди. Кликнули на одно - бонус. На второе кликнули - бонус. На третье - ой, на нас напааалии.
И вот здесь включается боевка. Клеточки, как в PvZ, по ним шагают зомби-скелеты, как в PvZ, на их пути расставляем бойцов из заначки. В зависимости от того, какое оружие парни выловили в оружейных магазинах (чистый рандом, повлиять никак нелья), у них изменяется площадь атаки. В отличие от PvZ, сколько у нас бойцов есть, столько мы выставить и сможем. Они еще могут сместиться на пару клеток, если пунктов выносливости хватает, но не более того.
Очевидный вопрос: а может ли случиться так, что нападающих будет больше, чем защитников? Ну, мало ли, может убьют кого, что тогда делать?
А вот и главная проблема. Да, количество зомбаков МОЖЕТ быть больше, чем герои смогут сдержать. Игроку может просто не повезти на выживших, может Дракула со своими войсками объявится на втором ходе, а может у солдат закончится выносливость (примерно три пункта на брата, один тратится за высадку во время боя и еще по одному за каждое перемещение), и тогда они пойдут бухать всей толпой. Кто останется драться? Может вообще никого не остаться. Зомби будут маршировать свободно.
Дойдут до конца поля - снимут у базы немного здоровья. Здоровье дойдет до нуля - ну, вы понимаете.
Теоретически таких неприятных ситуаций можно избежать. Допустим, повезет найти кучу народа, и кучу пивнушек для них, чтобы они отдыхали быстрее, а еще отспавнится куча старых фортификаций, которые можно разобрать на кирпичи для базы. А может и не повезти, тут чистый рандом. Каждый - абсолютно каждый - ход может закончиться дракой. Количество нападающих предугадать тоже непросто. Более того, время от времени вылезает сам Дракула. Он быстро движется, телепортируется с клетки на клетку и в драке 1 на 1 может закошмарить любого охотника. Если пройдет, то врежет по штаб-квартире в три раза больнее, чем любой монстр.
Чтобы игра не казалась такой уж несправедливой, в игре есть четыре пауэрапа, которые можно активровать на вырученные за победы (если таковые будут) деньги: можно дать солдатам двойную экспу после боя, вылечить всех, добавить огневой мощи или убрать всех врагов (кроме Дракулы) с поля. Или - все золотишко сохраняется после поражения - можно в стартовом меню купить парочку бустов: стартовать с дополнительными наемниками, с дополнительной экспой, с дополнительным оружием, с дополнительными хелсами у базы. Но все это дроч, дроч, дроч и череда бессмесленных поражений.
Да, и про "ролевую систему". Пушек всего пять: пистолет (слабый, медленный, но далеко стреляет), пулемет (мощнее пистолета, но стреляет на одну клетку короче), снайперка (бьет всю линию, но у стрелка слепая зона в две клетки), дробовик (стреляет буквой "T") и меч (очень крутой, но только по одной клетке). Левелап только повышает статы, судя по всему.
Итого: вместо того, чтобы покупать Hunters of the Dead, можно играть в кости с самим собой. Тот же эффект, только дешевле. Или просто подрочить. Еще веселее, и вообще бесплатно.

- Enemies deployed with seemingly random lane coverage at times. Not feasible to cover all lanes effectively at times.
- Game relies too much on luck . Lack of houses for additional hunters usually spells an early death.
- Random enemy encounters. It is a complete crap shoot to decide if you will be attacked when hunters need training or rest. Sometimes you will just need to watch your base get destroyed.
- Game seems to be based on grinding upgrades until you can get powerful enough to actually finish it. Early runs seem futile and like a waste of time.

A Bird Story is considerably shorter than the first game, To The Moon (just under 1 and a half hours vs. about 4), yet it still packs the same storytelling punch that I loved about the latter. The feels are strong with this one...

Just a disclaimer for everyone: this is legitimately A STORY and not so much of a game. Having said that...this story has gotten a really bad wrap because it hasn't lived up "To the Moon," it's predecessor that has won so many hearts over. Everyone is entitled to how they feel about the stories/games from Freebird, but as A STORY, this game is exactly what it was intended to be, a story. Nothing more and nothing less than this. Having said that, let's get the game part out of the way first for you gamers out there.
As a game, it's extremely limited of gameplay. The story needs to unfold in the way that it needs to, so this creates a linear play style, where exploring isn't really an option either. As for when you are in control, the story does take over a lot, but it does let you know when to take control again with the control notification coming up. If you're looking for a GAME, I don't think this will satisfy you. It's best to spare yourself the disappointment of really getting to play something and will definitely lessen some of the ridiculous reviews of people saying that this is a terrible game. Such reviews (like i said, everyone is entitled to feel how they feel) are unfair to this art medium. It's like being upset that an apple doesn't look or feel like an orange. They shouldn't be compared, much like this story should not be reviewed as a game, but as a story. To reiterate, if you're looking to game, look elsewhere.
As a story, it's actually pretty charming, though VERY short. This story can be fully experienced in about an hour. For all that, it's whimsical and full of imagination. You play as a child and the perspective is definitely child-like. As you progress, you get more insight into how this boy views the world, some of his troubles, and how something as simple as a bird can change all of this. There is an evolving friendship between the boy and the bird and you get to be a part of the process. The interesting thing about this story is that there are no words being spoken and no dialogue. Every emotion and action is expressed through body language and noise cues. Though this may seem a bit strange, it actually adds to the feeling of the game. Some of the other reviews will disagree, but you'll have to judge for yourself, as there seems to be a love or hate going on here. I think if you're looking to experience a fun, short story, this story is right for you.

The story is nice and sweet and very well done, and in my opinion the pixel graphics add to the experience. Were A Bird Story done in FMV with photorealistic graphics it would be less than what it is now. That said, I found the speed of movement and flow to be frustratingly slow, with the all-too-present fade outs and fade ins taking far too long.
I would really like to recommend A Bird Story, but for the price asked, I just can't bring myself to do so. Pick it up in a bundle, definitely, but don't expect an immersive gaming experience.
